*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Scroll One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of the Great Ci’en Monastery.
I bow my head to the perfectly luminous original nature, quiescent, To the assembly of the True Dharma with its sovereign expedient means;
Gathering and synthesizing the subtle without omission, May the nectar-like rain of flowers descend upon me and arise [within me].
The light of his writings and the sword of wisdom are ever held aloft to illuminate; the ocean of meaning and the boat of compassion transport beings without end.
Unrivaled, transcending the mundane, his virtue is renowned; those who hear or see his Way never grow weary of it.
This wondrous jewel of a bright pearl is easily understood by those who delight in liberation; having abandoned me, he personally received the teachings from the Great Compassionate Honored One.
The subtle words have all ceased and are utterly without support;
following what was heard in the past, I now record the true, pure, and ultimate principles of the various assemblies, which serve as the basis for the simultaneous benefit of oneself and others.

The commentary states: To begin the treatise, I shall briefly explain it through six sections: first, the causes for the arising of the teaching; second, the purpose for which the treatise was composed;
third, the elucidation of its essential nature (*svabhāva*); fourth, the manifestation of its fundamental tenets; fifth, the explanation of the title; and sixth, the interpretation of the main text.

The meaning and principles of this treatise are profound and extensive; even a mere presentation of its own school’s doctrine is difficult to grasp, let alone if one were to include [the views of] heterodox systems.

The Master’s minor treatises exhaustively investigate every detail to reach their source; however, they do not merely result in voluminous scrolls that needlessly trouble scholars and further increase their exhaustion.

Now, having extracted the beauty and propagated the essentials from the *Pañcavastu-vibhāṣā-śāstra*—its ten topical outlines—I have compiled this record to recount what I have heard, so as to preserve the precious great meaning and set aside my own humble minor views.
I urge the wise, including those from Shi and Ji, not to remain ignorant of this. The detailed analysis of the schools is recorded in a separate chapter.
Regarding the cause for the arising of the teaching, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been ignorant of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and have held perverse attachments, thereby creating two kinds of karma and undergoing the fruits of the three sufferings. The Tathāgata, according to their capacities..."
By teaching the true nature (*dharmatā*), one causes [beings] to know that all phenomena are thus: they are neither empty nor are they existent.

Having understood that all phenomena are neither existent nor empty, one becomes free from ignorance, doubt, and perverse attachments. According to the distinctions of their spiritual lineages (*gotra*), they give rise to the Middle Way;
they eternally extinguish all hindrances and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there are demonic activities (*mārakarma*).

When the disputes and sectarian attachments arose and proliferated, giving rise to many views of existence, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna collected the Mahāyāna teachings on the emptiness that dispels signs and composed the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and other works to thoroughly elucidate the True Doctrine and eliminate those attachments to existence.

Subsequently, the holy Āryadeva and other great masters composed the *Śataśāstra* and other treatises to propagate and clarify the Great Meaning; however, because of this, sentient beings again gave rise to [the view of] emptiness.
Seeing that the Bodhisattva Asaṅga had ascended to the first bhūmi and realized the Samādhi of Dharma-Light (*dharmāloka*), thereby attaining great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*),
he requested the Great Compassionate Honored One to expound the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, to reveal the Middle Way, to shatter attachments to emptiness and existence,
to exhaust all principles, to fathom all phenomena, to elucidate all meanings, to explain all texts, to dismantle all dogmatic attachments, and to dispel all doubts.

There are no practices that are not cultivated and no fruits that are not realized; yet, there are bodhisattvas who, fearing the vast ocean of textual expositions, have not yet aroused the wisdom of hearing and reflection, and thus prematurely give rise to cowardice and retreat.

The Great Sage Asaṅga, endowed with extensive wisdom and compassion, compiled the essential tenets of the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-sūtra* and condensed all the dharma-gates of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. He has now composed this treatise to expound upon the original text.
This wondrous meaning was received from the former teachings by the Master Bodhisattva Siṃhabhadra, who further provided this subsequent commentary.

Prajñākaragupta, having mastered its beginning and end, synthesized these two texts so that those who fear the ocean of words might first rely on this concise instruction for easy retention, and ultimately endure extensive study to comprehend the great meaning, realize the fruit of Bodhi, and bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings; it is also intended for this purpose.
Those of the two vehicles each rely upon their own vehicle to realize the fruits of self-benefit.
Regarding the purpose for which this treatise is composed, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are briefly two conditions: first, to cause the True Dharma to abide long in the world;
and second, to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings. Furthermore, for two additional reasons, it is taught so that [the Dharma] which has already vanished may [be restored].

Because it is reopened and revealed so that what had not yet vanished may flourish once more, sentient beings with the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) each rely upon their own vehicle to swiftly emerge from birth and death;
those without the lineage rely upon the vehicles of humans and devas to sever the evil destinies.

Furthermore, for two reasons, there are those who, regarding the teachings on emptiness and the sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), adhere to them literally, repudiating all that was spoken [in the definitive teachings].

There are those who, out of hatred and opposition, revile the teachings on existence in order to lead others to realize that all phenomena possess characteristics; they understand the profound meaning of the sūtras by abandoning the view of non-existence.
Furthermore, there are those who, regarding the sūtras of interpretable meaning concerning existence, adhere to them literally and cling to the existence of all things;

yet, toward the teachings on emptiness, they feel aversion, fear, and revilement. This is in order to lead others to realize that all phenomena are without characteristics and to understand the profound meaning of the sūtras.
Because the mental faculty (*manas*) possesses views, the other seven [faculties] do not; furthermore, as explained extensively therein, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"For the benefit of oneself and others, and so that the Dharma may endure for a long time. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "For the long endurance of the Dharma and to deliver all sentient beings.

Both are identical in this regard. The first explanation is thus established. Furthermore, the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states: "Now I shall expound the Vinaya rules so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time."

It is solely for the sake of the endurance of the Dharma and not for the sake of sentient beings. The preface states: "The *Vyākhyāyukti* [or *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*] proclaims the holy teachings out of compassion;
its phrasing is concise, its meaning is comprehensive, and it is easy to understand. It is said to be "only for the sake of sentient beings and not for the sake of the True Dharma.

The six reasons for composing the treatise in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* clarify that the cause for its composition is precisely this: the long-term endurance of the Dharma. This commentary on the preface is the explanation of Sthiramati.

It is said that this is intended so that students may be free from all fears; it is for the sake of sentient beings and not for the sake of the True Dharma, so that sentient beings who believe in and study the Dharma may cause it to abide long.
Although various different intentions for its composition have been stated, when one investigates the principles and extends the analysis, they are all subsumed within the first two.
Regarding the elucidation of the essential nature [of the teaching], there are briefly two types:

first, according to the school of Bhāviveka following Nāgārjuna, it is said that within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), all phenomena are signless and empty; thus, the teaching has nothing to be taught and its essence is not an essence.

Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), however, it may be said that words, phrases, chapters, treatises, and sounds constitute the essence of the teaching. In Sanskrit, this is called *pada*.
Translated as "traces," these correspond to the phrases of antiquity, which are of two kinds: first, phrases that fully encompass the Dharma;
second, phrases that completely manifest the meaning. For example, the statement: "Neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, neither one nor different, neither permanent nor annihilated.
Although the meaning of each individual phrase here is not exhaustive, it is still called a "phrase."
Because it fulfills the Dharma, it is the name designated by the Yogācāra school.

Since the Yogācāra does not permit a term that lacks the differentiation of expression to be called a "phrase" (*pada*), it is in Sanskrit *vākya*, which here means "speech. This refers to the "phrases" spoken within the Middle Way.
Because its meaning is complete and perfect, it is in Sanskrit *pariccheda*, which here means "chapter" (*pāda*). A chapter is...
The chapters and sections clarify the various meanings within the Middle Way. "Lun" (論), in Sanskrit called *śāstra*, is translated here as "treatise";
this name is established for the entire work as a whole. These four [types of expression]—the sounds that serve as the means of communication—constitute the essence of the teaching (*śāsana*).
This follows what is stated in the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*; furthermore, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there is a further basis for the essence of the sūtras.

Second, there are two aspects: the phrasing (*vyañjana*) and the meaning (*artha*). The phrasing is the basis (*āśraya*), while the meaning is that which depends upon it (*āśrita*), because the meaning is manifested through the phrasing that expresses it.
Briefly stated, there are two explanations. First, the master Nāgārjuna, Asaṅga, and others state:
"In this context, it is the manifestation of a collection of direct and indirect expressions as they appear upon the consciousness of the listener, occurring in accordance with the eight stages."
Regarding the essential nature of this meaning: it takes the sounds and so forth transformed by the consciousness of the listener as the substance of the teaching.

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "By the power of the Buddha’s compassion and the conditions of his original vows, for those who are capable of hearing, mental images of words and meanings arise within their own mental consciousness, appearing as if they were spoken by the Tathāgata.
Through the Buddha’s original vows acting as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the listeners..."

Consciousness possesses the appearance of words and meanings; although these appearances of words and meanings arise through the power of one’s own proximate reliance on roots of virtue, they are designated as "the Buddha's teaching" based on their primary object (the Buddha), for the Buddha is in reality without speech.
Therefore, Wu-xing said: "Because this arises through his sovereign influence (*adhipatya*), it is spoken of in this way.
It is, for example, like how through the sovereign influence of the gods and others, one may obtain treatises, mantras, and so forth within a dream.
If one were apart from consciousness, how could the Buddha have taught this? Regarding its fundamental conditions, the Buddha did not speak of dharmas;

there is only untainted (*anāsrava*) great meditative concentration, wisdom, and compassion. If it relies upon what is heard, it is the manifestation of one’s own consciousness as tainted mind appearing as if it were the essence of untainted sounds and so forth;
when untainted mind manifests, it takes the names and so forth that are truly untainted as its essence. This...

Thus, although the Tathāgata in truth did not preach any dharma, it is said in various places: "Since I attained enlightenment, I have not spoken a single word," and you yourself have not heard [any such thing].

Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states that the three realms are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Therefore, one knows that the substance of the teaching is merely what is transformed by the mind, having both text and meaning as its substance;
this is in perfect accord with the sūtras and does not contradict the principle of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Question: If one takes the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching...

This may be so; however, if one asks how an understanding can arise as a collection upon consciousness when the teaching heard has already passed and the future does not yet exist—since neither is substantially real and there is no dharma that remains once it has arisen—the answer is:

As Vasubandhu explains, it occurs "in accordance with [the stages] falling within the eight moments," even unto its manifestation as its essential nature. This means that during these eight moments, one hears.
Regarding the manifestation of the appearance of "direct" and "not-direct" upon consciousness, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there are briefly five types of mind:
first, the sudden (*ābhoga*); second, the seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*); third, the determining (*niścaya*); fourth, the defiled or pure (*kliṣṭa-avyākṛta*); and fifth, the resultant flow (*naiṣyandika*).

These are analyzed in detail within the chapter on the five minds, as taught in the holy scriptures. When the word "all" (*sarva*) is uttered in the phrase "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" (*sarvasaṃskārā anityāḥ*), it is the [first] sudden mind.
Once the mind has arisen, it necessarily gives rise to seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*). Although the initial arising may last for many moments, its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is singular;
thus, it is collectively termed "seeking" because it has not yet reached a definitive cognition regarding the objects it targets. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Furthermore, once the five consciousnesses have arisen for a single moment, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) must necessarily arise immediately thereafter. It further explains that during this period of activity, [the seeds] are perfumed by what precedes.

Regarding the arising of the three minds through the cultivation of the understanding of continuity, they manifest as follows: the sudden (ābhoga), the seeking (paryeṣaka), and the subsequent determination (niścaya).

Because the mind of determination knows all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) in their entirety, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that immediately following the state of seeking, if there is no distraction, the mind of determination arises;
however, if there is distraction at the time of its arising, it is indeterminate. Although its own nature is known, it is not yet fully understood.

In order to facilitate understanding, it is further stated that at this time, there are three preceding moments of mind regarding the syllable "non-existence" (無), yet only two actually exist upon that syllable—namely, the sudden encounter (*ābhoga*) and the seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*). This is because there is no object of non-existence to be determined as absent.

Thus, following the moment of determination, one again gives rise to seeking; however, the treatise definitively states that the sudden encounter and the seeking definitely do not exist [in this context].
Since it is admitted that distraction occurs after the search for meaning has arisen, it is further stated that at all times the five types of mind are simultaneously present;

this meaning is easily understood. By the power of preceding syllables, which successively perfuse one another, subsequent syllables arise, and only at the final moment can the meaning be comprehended.
Thus, only through minds that are either defiled or pure can [cognition] proceed; therefore, although past and future [dharmas] do not exist [in a substantial sense], the teaching [remains valid].

The substance [of the consciousness] is also established as such; if we consider the "new and new" (kṣaṇika-kṣaṇika) explanations together with the four terms beginning with "sudden" (*ābhoga*), there are invariably two minds present above each.
That is to say, the "sudden" (*ābhoga*) and "seeking" (*paryeṣaka*) minds are followed by twelve minds gathered simultaneously at the very end:
the first and third [moments] each have two, the second has three, and the fourth has five, thus totaling twelve. Since this occurs at the initial syllable...
There is an initial mind of sudden engagement (*saterika-citta*); subsequently, there are minds of investigation and determination; and finally, there are minds of outflow, whether defiled or pure.
Only when these five minds are complete is it termed a "conjunction" (*samnipāta*). Herein, we have distinguished these five minds based on the fulfillment of the meaning of a phrase;
it is not the case that all teachings are invariably fixed in this manner. This is merely a statement of names, as in the Buddha’s own words: "One."

Regarding the five mental states arising within a word: as it is said that within the two characters "Devadatta" (天授) five mental states arise, and as it is said that within the three characters "Maitreya Buddha" (慈氏佛) five also arise;
so it continues until the completion of the sequence, where the five mental states are fully present according to the number of characters involved.
This should be understood accordingly. If this is so, then the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that the first three mental states are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and the latter...

Regarding the question of whether the second and third natures (*dvitīya-tṛtīya-svabhāva*) take the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) as their essence of teaching (*śāsana-śarīra*): one interpretation holds that all five minds (*pañca-citta*) can pervade all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), and that the designation of them as indeterminate is based on the majority of cases;
furthermore, because the object (*viṣaya*) is predominant, they are considered indeterminate, and thus all constitute the essence of teaching.

Another interpretation maintains that it is only upon reaching a defiled or pure mind (*kliṣṭa-kuśala-citta*) that the essence of teaching is finally established, for only then does the understanding become complete and perfect; therefore, the first three [minds] do not [constitute the essence].

Some say that because a small portion [of speech] arises from a great deal, it is also subsumed under "teaching" (*śāsana*), since the majority of it is wholesome. Thus, the first interpretation is superior. [Objection: Since its sounds, names, and phrases are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), how can they constitute "teaching"? [Response: This is based on the designation of names and so forth as heard by the ear; thus, they are said to be exclusively indeterminate. However, if they are heard by the mind, they also pertain to the nature of the wholesome. Therefore, they serve as the substance of teaching. Hence, according to the *Vijñaptimātratā* [school]: [The verse: "The sound is the teaching; the name and phrase are not. The commentary says: "The sound of speech is the teaching, because it is the cause for understanding the meaning. The name and phrase are not the teaching, because they are merely the basis for designating the sound. Regarding this, the Vaibhāṣikas hold that the sound itself is the teaching. The Sautrāntikas hold that the name and phrase are the teaching, while the sound is merely the medium for manifesting them. Regarding the teaching that their essential nature (*tattva*) constitutes two [categories], Dharmapāla, Jinaputra, Prabhāmitra, and others state that, in general, there are four levels for establishing the essence (*svabhāva*) of a treatise:
first, the essence of subsuming characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) into their nature (*dharmatā*), which is that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are the stainless suchness of their nature (*prakṛti-tathatā*).
As the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra says: "All sentient beings are suchness; all phenomena are also suchness. This includes both the conditioned and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
There exists a distinct entity that is the characteristic of suchness (*tathatā*); it is like the ocean water which, when struck by the wind and other forces, gives rise to waves.
How could the substance of these waves be different from the water? All phenomena arise as their own substance and characteristics through the convergence of the four conditions;
yet, because they do not depart from suchness and all possess the nature of tainted seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), they are termed "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).
In this manner, these two categories subsume the remainder; since all phenomena (*dharma*) are identical in essence to consciousness (*vijñāna*), they are all "mere consciousness" (*vijñaptimātra*).

Therefore, mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth do not exist apart from the mind (*citta*) and its associates. As the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras state, the triple world is but a single mind. Regarding the three categories [of the three natures], conventional designations (*prajñapti*) follow the substance of their reality:
that is, all conventional phenomena take as their essence whichever real phenomenon (*dravyadharma*) they depend upon, just as the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) do.

The states (*avasthā*) of matter and mind take the states of their respective bases as their essence. This treatise explains below, within the section on non-associated [conditioned phenomena], that these are established by way of designation (*prajñapti*).
Regarding their four natures and functions, their essences are discussed separately; matter and mind—whether provisional or substantial—are each categorized in their own distinct places.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts provide numerous such explanations. Here, I shall cite a few passages for proof, as discussed in detail in a separate chapter.

Regarding the explanation of these four [types of] "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*) as encompassing the meaning of all phenomena (*dharma-artha*), they are explained according to their respective applications for all phenomena.

Dharmapāla and others explain the essence of the various teachings as follows: it is the arising of the forms of words and meanings upon the consciousness of the Tathāgata—due to the power of the original vows and conditions of those who are to hear them—which constitutes the essence of the actual signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*). The intention of this master is that the original vows of sentient beings [are the cause].
"I wish to hear the Buddha’s teaching on how the appearances of words and meanings arise within the consciousness of a Tathāgata.
When the listeners heard the Buddha’s teaching, their own consciousnesses likewise produced similar appearances of words and meanings. As the *Parable of the Leaves* Sūtra says:

"The Buddha took some leaves from a tree and asked Ānanda, 'How do these leaves compare to all the leaves in that forest? He further told Nandika (Qingxi): 'What I have not yet taught is [far more vast than what I have taught]...'"

There are as many as twenty such [arguments for] the twenty-fold *vijñaptimātra*. Vasubandhu further states: "Through the successive power of mutual dominance (*adhipatipratyaya*), two consciousnesses become determinate;

that is, because the distinctions in the consciousness-streams of one cause the production of distinct consciousnesses in other streams, they act as successive and reciprocal dominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Therefore, although the Blessed One truly taught the Dharma, he did not say [it was taught]."
This is a teaching of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*): because it is taught that within the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*) there is no such thing as speech;

and because within the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*), there is only conventional, apparent speech and no speech that possesses ultimate reality. Since the characteristics of words and meanings within the listener’s consciousness are established by principle, there is no doubt regarding them.
Therefore, the essence of all teachings takes as its substance the words and meanings spoken by the World-Honored One, which are fundamentally untainted (*anāsrava*).

If one takes as the essential nature [of names] only the sounds that express them, the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* states that both speaker and listener reach completion through two things: first, sound; second, well-formed syllables.

Furthermore, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other texts state that in the ninth stage (*navamī bhūmi*), one abandons two kinds of ignorance: first, regarding the immeasurable teachings spoken; second, regarding the immeasurable... [omitted].

Regarding the statement that mastery over names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-dhāraṇī-vaśitā*) constitutes the perfection of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), the phrase "immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables" refers to the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).
This treatise and others state that "sounds produced by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-maya-śabda*) refer to the sounds spoken by the noble ones (*ārya*).

The statement that this constitutes the perfection of *vijñapti-mātra* is because there is a distinction between the objects of the two analytical knowledges—of phenomena (*dharma*) and of expression (*nirukti*)—wherein the former takes phenomena as its object.

The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that names (*nāman*) and so forth depend upon sound; it says that you [the opponent] hold these to be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), whereas my Dharma is determinate (*vyākṛta*).
Therefore, the substance of the teaching is solely sound, while the substance of names and so forth is solely untainted (*anāsrava*) and solely wholesome (*kuśala*).

This is taught in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and other texts according to the perspective of the "conforming gate" (*anuvartana-mukha*) and for the sake of those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka-yāna* and *pratyekabuddha-yāna*), who maintain that fifteen of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are exclusively tainted and that names and phrases are merely conventional designations.
The phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*) are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Now, according to the Mahāyāna, if it is the sound, name, phrase, and phoneme of the dharmas taught by the Tathāgata’s post-attainment wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), they are truly wholesome and untainted (*anāsrava*), as stated in the various scriptures cited previously.

However, if it is the sound, name, phrase, and phoneme of the dharmas taught by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages or those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), they are exclusively tainted (*sāsrava*) and of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*). As for those who hear them...
The textual meanings transformed by consciousness may pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Among those who can hear the Dharma, all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage possess only contaminated [consciousness] during their subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
However, for all those of the two vehicles prior to the seventh stage, as well as for those from the eighth stage onward, it exists upon their uncontaminated subsequently attained wisdom.
The sounds, names, phrases, and syllables that are manifested are all exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); they are designated as "teaching" (*śāsana*) according to their respective functions.

Since they are equally objects of veneration, just as the essence of the Three Jewels is taken as the substance of the teaching, the sounds and so forth that constitute the teaching-body are likewise taken as the substance.

These appear upon the consciousness of the speaker; this does not contradict the principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). If they are manifested as teaching by the consciousness of a listener, then the teaching exists in accordance with that [consciousness].
The three natures (*trisvabhāva*) constitute its essence; likewise, that which is named "equality" (*samatā*) constitutes its essence, as both are capable of conveying meaning.

Based on the four ways of establishing the essence previously explained, the essence of the teaching (*deśanā*) now presented should also have four aspects. According to the first [aspect], which subsumes characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) back into their nature (*dharmatā*), the teaching is *tathatā* (suchness).
As the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The emanated and transformational Buddhas are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma. It is said: [they are merely manifestations].
The Dharma is non-dual, free from grasping, beyond verbal expression, and devoid of conceptual characteristics. Vimalakīrti said: "The nature of words and letters is detached;
there are no words or letters—this is liberation. The characteristic of liberation is precisely all dharmas. Furthermore, it is said that all dharmas are likewise suchness (*tathatā*).
Thus we know that the nature of the teaching's essence is itself suchness. According to the second [category] mentioned previously, all other [dharmas] are subsumed within consciousness.

If one takes the consciousness of the fundamental speaker of the Dharma as the essence, or if one takes the consciousness of the derivative listener of the Dharma as the essence, then—as Vasubandhu said—through the power of mutual predominance, these two consciousnesses constitute the definitive basis.
As for the third [category], it subsumes the provisional according to the real; thus, the essence of all internal teachings is solely sound, by means of names and phrases.

The linguistic units (vyañjana) are conventionally existent; they are described as such because they follow after the real. Therefore, the subsequent treatise explains that sound (*śabda*) is what is established as the derivative [teaching], rather than naming the "name" (*nāman*) and so forth as the derivative.
This is based on the previous fourth characteristic, which discusses them separately according to their functions.

Taking the sounds, names, phrases, and linguistic units that appear upon the consciousness of the speaker as the essence of the teaching is a conventional designation. This is because the conventional and the real differ in their meaning and function.

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "First, sound; second, excellent syllables. Herein, these four essences are distinguished according to their functional meanings, yet they do not contradict the principles of the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) regarding the ultimate and conventional truths.
Although it is taught that there is a single essence, this does not conflict with the meaning [of multiple essences], for all phenomena each possess these four essences.
Thus, while the teachings on the essence of the Dharma present many approaches, they have not yet explained the teaching of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Regarding how their nature is explained: they are gathered upon consciousness, causing those who hear the Dharma to gather and give rise to understanding.

The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that there are syllables (*vyañjana*) that are not names (*nāman*), meaning a single syllable may constitute a name; and there are names that are not phrases (*pada*), meaning a single syllable may constitute a phrase.

A phrase must necessarily have a name, and a name must necessarily have syllables; however, syllables do not necessarily have names, and names do not necessarily have phrases. This is the great [distinction].
Because it is taught as being equal by way of conforming to the meaning of the sounds, it is said to be "equal" and not the sense of the Hīnayāna.
Now, according to this explanation, within the consciousness of both the speaker and the listener, all [syllables] gather and appear together.

For example, when one says, "Commit no evil," at the moment the syllable "e" (諸) is spoken, the other syllables such as "va" (惡) and so forth are all yet to come; there is only that single syllable and its basis.
When syllables are combined to form a name, it appears upon the mind; this is called the "explanation of the meaning based on a single syllable.
Subsequently, it is called the "explanation of the meaning based on the formation [of the name]. Furthermore, when speaking of "evil," all other constituent syllables remain in the future.

Although the preceding syllables have entered the past, by the power of prior perfuming and the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*), one still speaks of "evil" within this present moment of thought.
When the syllable is manifested upon the mind, there are two instances of the single-syllable *akṣara-kāya*;
that which is formed by these two single-syllables is called one *nāma-kāya*.
That which is formed by two syllables is further said to consist of three single-syllables and two *akṣara-kāyas*, namely: first, "all evils" (*sarvapāpa*); second... [text fragment].
That is to say, when two [phonemes] are combined, it is called a *pada-kāya* (phrase-body); the same should be understood by analogy for those below.

Because they cannot be separated and must be joined, there are no cases where multiple [phonemes] are combined. A name-body (*nāma-kāya*) consists of one single phoneme; a phrase-body (*pada-kāya*) consists of three or more phonemes;
and a group-name-body (*nāmakāya-samukti*) consists of two or more names formed from single phonemes.
A name-body (*nāmakāya*) formed by two syllables is one; a name-body formed by three syllables is another.
Furthermore, it is said that at times there are four single-syllable bodies, two multi-syllabic three-syllable bodies, and one multi-syllabic four-syllable body;
these are the names formed by four single syllables.
Three single-syllable [phonemes] constitute one *nāmakāya* (name-group); two single-syllable [phonemes] constitute one *padakāya* (phrase-group);
one single-syllable [phoneme] constitutes one *vyañjanakāya* (syllable-group); three single-syllable [phonemes] constitute many *vyañjanakāyas*.
Three double-syllable [phonemes] constitute two *nāmakāyas*; two double-syllable [phonemes] constitute one *nāmakāya*; one double-syllable [phoneme] constitutes many [names].
A "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) is formed by two syllables; that which is formed by three syllables is one name-body;
that which is formed by four syllables is another name-body.

Furthermore, at the time of its formation, there are five instances of single-syllable name-bodies, three instances of three-syllable name-bodies, two instances of four-syllable name-bodies, and one instance of a multi-syllable name-body consisting of five syllables.
Up to this point, the *vyañjana-kāya* (phoneme-body), the *vyañjana* (phoneme) itself, and the multiple *vyañjana-kāyas* are combined in total.

There are fifteen instances: four instances of names (*nāma*) formed by a single phoneme, three instances of name-bodies (*nāma-kāya*) formed by a single phoneme, and four instances of multiple-name-bodies (*aneka-nāma-kāya*) formed by two phonemes.
A single *kāya* (body) consisting of one *akṣara* (syllable) is called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*); a single [name-body] consisting of many [syllables] is called a "multi-name-body" (*bahunāmakāya*).

Four [names] consisting of two syllables each are called a "word-body" (*padakāya*); three [words] consisting of two syllables each are called a "multi-word-body" (*bahupadakāya*); two [words] consisting of two syllables each are called a "phrase-body" (*vyañjanakāya*);

three [phrases] consisting of two syllables each are called a "multi-phrase-body" (*bahuvyañjanakāya*); a single [phrase] consisting of two syllables is called a "sentence-body" (*vākyakāya*); four [sentences] consisting of two syllables each are called a "multi-sentence-body" (*bahuvākyakāya*); three [sentences] consisting of three syllables each [are likewise].
Regarding the designations formed by two or three syllables, there is one designation called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) consisting of three syllables;

regarding the designations formed by multiple [syllables], there are two [instances] of name-bodies consisting of four syllables; regarding the designations formed by four syllables, there is one designation called a "name-body" consisting of five syllables.
Up to this point, these are collectively termed "names," "name-bodies," and "multiple name-bodies."

There are thirty-five *saṃyoga* (conjunctions), for the meaning of each phrase is complete; in Sanskrit this is called *anustubh*, which consists of eight syllables per line, being neither too long nor too short because it is perfect.
Within this, one must take those that are joined without interval (*nirantara*) to form what is called a "name" (*nāman*) and so forth;
they cannot be combined by skipping over intervening syllables. Those syllables that are separated do not constitute a name or the like.
Since they would otherwise be useless, this basis [of designation] functions through a successive process of increase.

Now, taking a single sentence as an example, when the matter is finalized, the collection of syllables (*vyañjana*), phrases (*pada*), names (*nāman*), and sounds (*ghoṣa*) together still amounts to fifty aggregations.

If one were to calculate the aggregations of syllables, phrases, names, and so forth for a single verse, a section, a fascicle, or an entire treatise, the principle is that they are indeed infinite. This is according to the Sarvāstivādins and others.

When syllables such as "a" (the letter for evil) and so forth are uttered, because all preceding syllables have already ceased and no longer exist as a collection, they arise sequentially rather than simultaneously;
and because there is no perfuming (*vāsanā*), it is impossible for a previously uttered syllable to appear later upon the subsequent mind.
Thus, the determination of the meaning of that teaching is not established. Nor is it [established] by the power of the final syllable resulting from the force of the preceding syllables.

Furthermore, since the final syllable and so forth can produce the manifest name, yet the past has no substance and there is no perfuming (*vāsanā*), by what power could the final syllable produce the name and so forth?
Therefore, at this time, both the speaker of the Dharma and the listener of the Dharma are still within the causal stage;
having already perfumed the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) with the initial syllables and so forth, they subsequently connect with and depend upon the final [syllables].
When the consciousnesses of the characters from the first "者" (zhě) arise, up until the final character "作" (zuò), they all first gather together due to prior perfuming (*vāsanā*).

Subsequently, these gathered [impressions] manifest upon the later consciousnesses; because they perfectly express the distinctions of meaning, this is called "preaching the Dharma" and is termed "hearing the teaching.
Even if it is the Buddha’s own preaching, although there is no [external] perfuming, it occurs solely through the power of the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*).
Because they arise through aggregation, although past and future do not exist, the teaching of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is established;

both speaker and listener take the collection of sounds and characters manifesting upon the mind as the essence of the teaching. Thus, these four kinds of essences, according to their respective applications, are each distinguished within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the five dharmas (*pañcadharma*).
Although there are three categories of teachings in the Mahāyāna, because the nature of their essential substance is easily understood, [they are subsumed here].
Furthermore, because it would also overextend to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), we do not adopt that [definition] here. To briefly state the essential nature of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*):

the essence of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) is simply the total absence of the intrinsic nature and characteristics of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*). As for the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), each has two types:

first, the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Since all uncontaminated phenomena are termed "perfected," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "If one speaks of... [and so forth].
The fourfold purity is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Second, regarding the gate of the permanent and the impermanent: that which is eternally abiding is called the perfected nature, which is subsumed solely under True Suchness (*tathatā*), for the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that among the five dharmas, only True Suchness is the perfected nature; thus, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are the dependent nature.

Because arising occurs in dependence upon other conditions, the aforementioned teaching-body (deśanā-dharma) subsumes its characteristics within its nature as solely the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);
the remaining three natures may be categorized across all three natures, as uncontaminated conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*) pertain to two of them.

Regarding the elucidation of the fundamental tenets, there are briefly two explanations. First, according to Bhāviveka, who follows the intent of Nāgārjuna and the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras*, all phenomena are empty.

Although all phenomena are inexpressible because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and thus cannot be said to be either empty or existent, nevertheless, the two categories of conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are distinguished according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Because that which has a distinct essence depends [on causes and conditions], and because its nature and characteristics are empty according to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it is said in verse:
"The true nature of conditioned phenomena is empty, For they arise dependently like illusions; The unconditioned has no reality, Not arising, it is like a flower in the sky.

This term "true nature" refers to the ultimate truth itself; because all phenomena are empty according to the ultimate truth, in that school's system, conventional phenomena are all [of the nature of] that [emptiness].

Because it is not empty, Nāgārjuna and others state that things exist conventionally (*saṃvṛti*). When the sūtras speak of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) and the "three natures" (*trisvabhāva*), these are all based on the conventional and not the ultimate (*paramārtha*) perspective.
Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), consciousness is supreme; therefore, they say "consciousness-only," not that objects do not exist.

This is like saying "the king arrives," which does not mean there are no ministers or attendants. The intended meaning of this master’s school is that both the ultimate and the conventional are empty.
It is like having a cataract in the eye and seeing floating flowers in the sky; if the cataract is removed, the floating flowers vanish.
Although the ultimate truth is empty, the conventional truth exists as a matter of course. While this is indeed the tenet of the Mahāyāna school, it is not the intended meaning here.

As for the intent of the tenets taught by Maitreya and others—such as Vasubandhu—in support of the Great Compassionate One based on the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other sutras: they explain all phenomena by relying upon the two truths, the ultimate and the conventional.

Regarding the principle of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which is both empty and non-empty, because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is empty while conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena exist,
the treatise states that conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are called "existence," and the notions of "self" (*ātman*) and "mine" (*ātmīya*) are called "non-existence.

Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), although the essence of all phenomena may be either existent or non-existent, because it transcends verbal expression, it is neither empty nor existent.

Because its essence is empty, it is called "ineffable," and the statement that it is "consciousness-only" is made in reliance upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), for therein the mind and its expressions are transcended;
thus it is neither empty nor existent. Furthermore, he cites a verse spoken by Maitreya: "The false discrimination exists;

within this, both [subject and object] are entirely absent. Herein there is only emptiness, and that [emptiness] is also present in that [discrimination]. Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are neither [existent nor non-existent]."
Because emptiness is not non-emptiness, and because both existence and non-existence exist, this accords with the Middle Way.

Herein it should be explained that although the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is inexpressible when based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are nevertheless described through conventional designations as being empty or existent;
yet this is not the ultimate truth itself, which is solely True Suchness (*tathatā*), as is taught in the *Catuḥsatya-śāstra*. For this reason, only...

By establishing the principle of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the emptiness of the objects of self and phenomena, and the meaning of the Middle Way—which is neither empty nor non-empty—is realized through the consciousnesses of the ultimate and conventional truths.
This is because the meaning of the Middle Way, which asserts that all phenomena are neither empty nor non-empty, is taken as the primary tenet.
This teaching of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in its ten sections is the common goal of our school; if one considers it from the perspective of our own sect...

That which is esteemed and honored as the fundamental tenet (*mūla*) is the subject matter of the three categories (*triskandha*), which this treatise elucidates at its outset; therefore, these three categories constitute the tenet of this treatise.
Furthermore, when explaining the tenet by means of two divisions: first, the *Vastusamgrahaṇī* (Compendium of Bases) clarifies the essence (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena;

second, the *Viniscaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (Compendium of Ascertainment) clarifies the meaning (*artha*) of all phenomena. This latter division is precisely the differentiation of the characteristics and natures (*lakṣaṇa-svabhāva*) of the aforementioned bases.

Since the two subsequent sections have already completed the comprehensive coverage of all phenomena (*dharma*) and explained every meaning without exception, the entire body of the work—both its subject matter and its meaning—is taken as the primary thesis. Regarding the title:
at the beginning of the treatise, it is titled *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā-vastu* (The Basic Subject Matter of the Mahāyāna Abhidharma Compendium).
The first chapter, "The Three Dharmas within the Divisions," consists of two parts: first, an extensive and detailed exposition, and second, a concise synthesis.

Regarding the extensive and detailed exposition, the *Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra* explains the Mahāyāna through six meanings: (1) it is superior to the Two Vehicles; (2) the Buddha is the greatest; (3) this vehicle can reach [the goal];
(4) it is that which the Buddhas ride; (5) it can extinguish great suffering; and (6) it brings about matters of great benefit.
1. It is that which is ridden by the five Great Beings, such as Avalokiteśvara; 2. It is that which can exhaust the limits and depths of all phenomena;
3. "Great" (mahā) means vast and expansive; 4. "Vehicle" (yāna) refers to the meaning of conveying and transporting—namely, the principles of teaching, realization, practice, and fruition;
5. Regarding the seven meanings [of "great"], the eleventh section below states: first, the greatness of the object, which consists of immeasurable teachings.

1. Greatness of objective realm (*viṣaya-mahattva*): because it takes all phenomena as its object; 2. Greatness of practice (*caryā-mahattva*): because it accomplishes the two benefits for oneself and others; 3. Greatness of wisdom (*jñāna-mahattva*): because it thoroughly realizes the two kinds of emptiness;

4. Greatness of diligence (*vīrya-mahattva*): because it cultivates difficult practices throughout three great *kalpas*; 5. Greatness of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya-mahattva*): because it does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; 6. Greatness of realization (*prāpti-mahattva*):
because it realizes the one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*); 7. Greatness of activity (*karma-mahattva*): [it is] inexhaustible...

The Mahāyāna as the vehicle for those who teach the Great Vehicle—that is, the texts and meanings of the Tripitaka of the Mahāyāna—is so called because it is vast in its expression and meaning, and because it possesses a great ford that conveys [beings] across. Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* speaks of the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-sūtra* and so forth, either because they are mutually understood or because they serve as a mark (*cihna*). This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative determinative compound) based on this principle. As for the Mahāyāna as the principle: [The text continues:

...because it is the object of the mind of the Tathāgata, which is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). It is the Mahāyāna because it is the vehicle that carries one to the state of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Furthermore, it is the Mahāyāna because it is the great vehicle that carries the bodhisattvas, who possess the vast resolve (*mahāśaya*), toward the attainment of the two kinds of benefit (*dvividha-artha*). This is an *upapada-samāsa* (dependent compound) based on the fact that it is the vehicle for the great ones. As the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states:

"The Mahāyāna is the teaching that is vast in its basis, its mental engagement, its practice, and its attainment. This is an *upapada-samāsa* based on the fact that it is the vehicle of the great ones. Finally, as for the Mahāyāna as the fruit: it is the Mahāyāna because it is the vehicle that carries one to the state of the Buddha, the ultimate fruit of the path. This is an *upapada-samāsa* based on the fact that it is the vehicle for the attainment of the great fruit. Thus, the three types of Mahāyāna—vehicle, principle, and fruit—are established.
That is to say, True Suchness (tathatā) is the basis for all virtues and is able to sustain all phenomena; it is supreme and universally designated as "Great" (mahā).

Because one can travel by means of this true principle through practices such as the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), it is called the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). Thus, Asvabhāva stated that it is called the Great Vehicle because it is a vehicle of the "great nature.
This is an explanatory compound (*bahuvrīhi*). One who "practices the Great Vehicle" refers to those who transport themselves by means of the six perfections and so forth.

It is called "Great" (*mahā*) because its name and its essence-and-function (*tattva-vṛtti*) are vast and expansive. Thus, Wu-xing said: "Because it is both a vehicle (*yāna*) and great (*mahā*), it is called the Mahāyāna.
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative compound). The "Resultant Mahāyāna" refers to the *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* possessed by the Buddha;
it is called "great" because its essence and function are supreme and all-pervading. It is called a "vehicle" because it carries both oneself and others. [This is from] the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The Sūtra says: "Within the single Buddha-vehicle, one distinguishes and speaks of three," and it further says: "Because of speaking of the Buddha's wisdom, the Buddhas appear in the world;
this alone is the true reality, while the other two are not. This is the abiding nature of phenomena and the fixed position of dharmas; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.
Having realized this at the site of enlightenment, the Guide speaks through skillful means. This passage explains the Buddha’s bodhi.

The designation "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle) applied to the fruit of *nirvāṇa* is also a *karmadhāraya* compound; thus, all aspects of teaching (*śāsana*), reasoning (*yukti*), practice (*caryā*), and fruit (*phala*) are collectively called Mahāyāna.
The Buddha himself rides this vehicle to reach the ultimate goal, and he constantly rides it to deliver sentient beings according to their respective capacities;

therefore, it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*) and "great" (*mahā*). Question: Since conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) involve movement, they may be called a "vehicle," but [how can unconditioned phenomena be so called]?
For one who is immovable, there should be no vehicle; this citation of scripture merely indicates the general direction, and all other passages should be interpreted accordingly.
Regarding the *Abhidharma*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* may be called "the treatise on the Abhidharma" (*Abhidharma-kośa*), for it says that this [treatise] is able to lead toward [the Abhidharma].

Alternatively, it is that which can analytically contemplate whether a phenomenon (dharma) is a conventional phenomenon (saṃvṛti-dharma) encompassing the four noble truths, or an ultimate phenomenon (paramārtha-dharma) which is exclusively nirvāṇa.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 12, states that the twenty-fourth great master further says:
"Furthermore, because it can analytically distinguish all phenomena through immeasurable gates, it is called Abhidharma. It is also named... [text truncated]
It is called *dharma* because it distinguishes phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). Furthermore, it is called *Abhidharma* because it can subdue all the heterodox arguments of other schools;
since even the great masters of those [other schools] and their misguided followers and rival sects are unable to oppose it, it is also called the "Subduing Dharma" (*abhibhava-dharma*).
As the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The various sūtras are called *dharma*, and this [treatise]..."
It is called "Abhidharma" because it penetrates those [dharmas]. The Dharmaguptaka school says that this dharma is preeminent (*abhyudgata*), hence it is named Abhidharma.
The Mahīśāsaka school calls it "Illuminating Dharma" (*dharma-prabhāsa*). The Dārṣṭāntika masters call it "Successive Dharma," because it is the most supreme among nirvāṇas.
The Śabdika masters say: *abhi* has the meaning of "removal" (*apoha*), and *dharma* has the meaning of "discernment" (*viniścaya*); this dharma...

Because it is able to eliminate the fetters (*saṃyojana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and to discern the essential nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena (*dharma*), it is called Abhidharma.
The Mahāsāṃghika school names it *Mahādharma* (Great Dharma) or *Uttaradharma* (Superior Dharma). [The work] was completed by Kātyāyanīputra and offered to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"Because it is a superior dharma, it is therefore called *Uttaradharma*. According to the commentary on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, Vasubandhu explains that *Dharma* is named "Dharma" because it is the teaching.

The term *abhidharma* has four meanings: first, "counteracting" (*pratipakṣa*); second, "numbering" (*saṃkhyā*); third, "overpowering" (*abhibhava*); and fourth, "thoroughly understanding" (*parijñā*).

Regarding the meaning of "counteracting," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Because it can counteract [the afflictions] and lead toward [nirvāṇa], or because it can counter-observe [the truths], it is called *abhidharma*; because it maintains its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is called *dharma*. If one speaks of the ultimate *dharma*, it refers exclusively to nirvāṇa;
if one speaks of the *dharmas* of phenomenal characteristics, they encompass all four noble truths. This is the initial [explanation of] *dharma*.
This fruit, which follows [the path], consists of the pure wisdom that accords with the principles of reality, all forms of wisdom, and the teachings that lead toward Nirvāṇa;

because it confronts and contemplates the principles of the Truths (*satya*), it is called *Abhidharma*. Although both meanings—confrontation (*abhi*) and phenomena (*dharma*)—apply equally to teaching, principle, practice, and fruit, here in the *Abhidharmakośa*, "confrontation" refers to the teaching and practice, while "phenomena" refers to the principle and the fruit. Since the text is thus incomplete, the meaning is also... [incomplete].
Regarding the meaning of why all [treatises] are known as *Abhidharma-piṭaka*, the first volume of the *Vibhāṣā* contains explicit textual evidence;
however, as this is not our own primary school (*mūla-nikāya*), it is omitted here. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Vasubandhu states:

"This dharma is directed toward non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*) because it can explain the various truths, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), and other sublime practices. Now, based on this...
The essence of the Abhidharma is not merely wisdom (*prajñā*), because it encompasses both doctrine and reasoning, as well as practice and its fruit;

thus, it differs from what is taught in the *Abhidharmakośa*. According to this interpretation, the essence of the Dharma is the teaching itself, for it is the teaching that articulates sublime conduct which leads toward the fruit.
Furthermore, since this Dharma can explain the various truths (*satya*), it may also be said that the teaching is contrasted with the principle (*tattva*). Moreover, this [teaching] can...
When one speaks of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) and so forth, it can also be said that the teaching is contrasted with practice;

that is, the teaching (the doctrine) is contrasted with the fruit of rational practice, and thus the meaning of "Abhidharma" (*abhidharma*) as a sequential correspondence is established even with an interval.

Furthermore, when it is said that the truths (*satya*) lead toward nirvāṇa, this means that the rational dharma is contrasted with the fruit; the intent here takes only the realized truth (*tattva*) as the referent.

That which can lead toward *nirvāṇa* is not the teaching that expresses it; furthermore, since it is said that "sublime conduct" (*sucarita*) can lead toward *nirvāṇa*, the term "concordant" (*pratisaṃyukta*) here refers to the relationship between the method of practice and its fruit.
In all the aforementioned cases, these are *karmadhāraya* compounds.

Since the essence of the principles, teachings, and practices of the Dharma is itself concordant [with the goal], although the text does not explicitly state it, by analogy with the meaning, one should understand that the principles and teachings are concordant with the practices, and thus are called "Abhidharma" (*abhidharma*). For now, this is based on the teaching.
The sequence of principle, practice, and fruit explains the names through their mutual determination based on cultivation, causes, and the attainment of results.

However, by inferring the meaning and correlating the teaching with the principle, three explanations should be established: first, the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) explanation, because it is the correlation of the dharma of principle; second, the *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) explanation, because it takes the dharma of principle as its correlate;
and third, the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) explanation, because the teaching of the dharma is itself the correlate. In Vasubandhu’s commentary, he explains that the dharma is exclusively...

Because they exist within the teaching, they all constitute the activity [of the path]. Regarding the sequence of following and reversing the order, and the meaning of transcending the forward order, the ancient explanations are as follows:

first, the self-nature, which is untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*); second, the retinue, which is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); third, the skillful means, such as hearing and reflection; fourth, the letters, which are the various teachings;

and fifth, the objective sphere, which refers to the principles of the truths (*satya*). The first three constitute the practice, while the letters constitute the teaching; these are the spheres of the former.
The *dhātu* (realm) is the principle (*tattva*); it comprises only the three [roots] and does not include the fruit.

Consequently, while the five names mentioned previously were broad in their application but narrow in their essence, the four names now explained are narrow in their application but broad in their essence. Furthermore, because the ancient texts state that "acquisition" (*prāpti*), "opposition" (*virodha*), and so forth are not part of our school’s doctrine of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), they are all omitted here.
As for the term "enumeration of dharmas" (*dharmasaṃkhyāna*), it refers to the repeated proclamation and instruction regarding each individual dharma.

The commentary states that because the words themselves possess characteristics such as identity and so forth, if one follows this meaning, taking "reason" (*yukti*) as the *dharma* (the thing) and "teaching" (*śāsana*) as the *saṃkhyā* (the number), then the "number of the dharma of reason" is called the "dharma of number" (*saṃkhyā-dharma*), which is an *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Although the text does not explicitly state it, the teaching itself is the number; thus, it is also a *karmadhāraya* compound, and its name and meaning should likewise be explained.
As for the term "subduing the dharma" (*vibhava-dharma*), it is because this fulfills the locus of the treatise (*śāstra-sthāna*).

Because it is able to equally overcome and subdue the heterodox and divergent arguments of others, I shall now explain this meaning: the essence of "subduing" (*vibhava*) consists of the principles (*yukti*) and the teachings (*āgama*).

The methods that express these principles and teachings and distinguish them as the means of subduing are called "the methods of subduing" (*vibhava-dharma*), which is analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Alternatively, the teachings themselves are the subduing;

because these various teachings, through their treatment of the points of debate and so forth, are able to overcome and subdue others, they are analyzed according to the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound, and the term applies to both [principles and teachings].

Because this is able to explain and clarify the meaning of the sūtras, the meaning of the sūtras is called "Dharma" (teaching). Since this [treatise] is able to penetrate that [meaning], it is termed "penetrating Dharma" (*dharmābhisamaya*).
Because it is the penetration of Dharma, it is analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* compound. Based on this, it is not only the meaning of the sūtras that it penetrates;
it is also able to penetrate other teachings, practices, and fruits. Furthermore, since other sources speak of the two dharmas of practice and fruit, this principle is able to penetrate them as well.

It is called "penetrating the Dharma" (*abhidharma*), as it penetrates the meaning of the teachings through reasoning; the principle applies similarly [to other terms], all being explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.

Now, following the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, I shall briefly enumerate four names. If one were to rely on various texts, there would be forty-one explanations, but fearing that the text might become too cumbersome, I shall stop here with this brevity.
Although there are various explanations for the name of the *Abhidharma*, one should observe how Vasubandhu established these names.
The Dharma is merely the teaching; although all four [aggregates] are indeed so, the essence of the Dharma corresponds to the number [of categories], as it subdues and penetrates.
Thus, it is the same here: because the fundamental Buddhist scriptures are called *Abhidharma*, they reside primarily in the teaching and not in the other three [aggregates].
Because it encompasses the meaning, the Sanskrit term is retained; one must not simply take "Dharma that is opposed" (*pratidharma*) as its name. Wuxing’s commentary states:
Because it is the cause for the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), or because they are mutually understood together, the *Abhidharma* serves as a general designation.

Thus, even untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) and so forth are called "Dharma" (the Abhidharma). Based on this, when one asks about the relationship between "dharma" and "that which possesses dharma" (*dharmī*), these two meanings correspond equally.
Why, then, is it named only "Dharma" (Abhidharma) and never called "Dharma-possessor" (*dharmī*)? This meaning is not the same [as the previous one].
In the *Pramāṇavārttika*, that which can maintain its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is designated as "dharma" (*dharma*);

whether it possesses a substantial entity or lacks one, whether it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and all distinctions of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) receive the name "dharma.

That which gives rise to understanding in beings through its normative function (*viniyoga*) is called a "dharmin" (*dharmin*). Since the meaning of "dharma" applies universally to these designations, it is termed *Abhidharma*.
The Dharma-arthādhikaraṇa (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya) does not establish [the term] as a counter-correlative; this is based on the previous interpretation. Furthermore, regarding this "Dharma":

it refers to rules and rituals that definitively distinguish the correct from the erroneous, and its essence is solely the Noble Teaching (*ārya-śāsana*). Because this teaching can counteract [ignorance] through principles and so forth, and because it definitively establishes [truth], it is called *abhidharma* (counter-dharma).
Since the meanings of phenomena (*dharma*) that deviate from such definitive establishment do not stand in opposition [to it], for this reason, all sūtras and śāstras...
The title at the beginning designates it as the *Abhidharma* (the "Dharma of Non-opposition"), not as the "Dharma that opposes existence.
Regarding the term *Saṃgrahaṇī* ("Compendium"), Asaṅga’s commentary states there are three meanings: first, equality; second, pervasiveness; and third, correctness.
Siṃhabuddhi states that because it was compiled by great Bodhisattvas who have realized the direct intuition (*abhisamaya*) of truth, it is called "equal" (*sama*).
There are two meanings to this "compilation" (*samuccaya*): first, they acted together; second, they practiced together.
This means that although the meaning contained in this treatise is individually attributed to Asaṅga as its author, it was compiled by Bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

It demonstrates not only that [Asaṅga] compiled it based on his own realization, but also that they practiced together to show that he was free from error; thus, the term "compilation" is used to indicate such collective agreement.

The title *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Compendium of Abhidharma) is explained by the Master Siṃhabuddhi as being so called because it universally encompasses all the analytical sections (*viniścaya-sthāna*) found within the *Mahāyānābhidharmasūtra*.
This name carries three meanings: first, it briefly summarizes the extensive; second, it collects the dispersed into a compendium;
and third, it relies solely upon that [sūtra]. This means that although the text of this treatise itself is not extensive, it encompasses all the principles and meanings of that sūtra.

This treatise exhaustively elucidates and clarifies its reliance upon those sūtras; furthermore, it demonstrates that the text and meaning of those sūtras were previously scattered and extensive, whereas here they are comprehensively integrated through both detailed and concise explanations.
Vasubandhu further stated that without citing the names of the sūtras, one would not understand that this treatise is the authoritative instruction of the Sage.
Regarding the term "comprehensive collection" (*saṃgraha*), Siṃhabuddhi remarked that it is so called because it is free from error.
Because it involves the skillful means of compilation up until the realization of the bodhi of all Buddhas, it is called the "Right Compilation" (*saṃgīti*). This has two meanings:

first, being oneself free from error; second, causing others to achieve [the goal]. That is to say, regarding this fundamental treatise, those who compiled it sought only bodhi and did not hope for anything else;
furthermore, by compiling it through unerring skillful means, they enabled those who practice and study to ultimately [attain it].

Because it attains awakening (*bodhi*), its etymological interpretation is thus established. Regarding the true collection of names, Saṃghabhadra’s own commentary explains that "collection" (*saṃgraha*) is a composite term.
There are three types of such composites: first, the composite of the expression of the teaching; second, the composite of the text and meaning; and third, the composite of intermingling.

If the composite refers to the expression of phenomena, it is called *sūtra*; if it expresses the composite of conduct, it is the *vinaya*; and if it expresses the composite of principles, it is the *abhidharma*.
The Abhidharma now designates this as the *Saṃyukta* (Miscellaneous) because it consists solely of reasoning and nothing else. Regarding the Three Piṭakas:

the Sūtra seeks sequential order, the Vinaya seeks causes and conditions, and the Śāstra seeks essential natures and characteristics. Because the text and meaning here are intermingled, it is given the name *Saṃyukta*.

Since the original commentaries circulated separately, their essential natures and characteristics were difficult to discern; and because the text and meaning were quite extensive, they were difficult to master and retain. Therefore, they have been synthesized and integrated so that...
Because it is easy to enter [the meaning], this treatise designates the title at its outset with the term "Miscellaneous" (*saṃkīrṇa*).
While the latter single section is explained by the Master himself, the principle regarding the first two "miscellanies" is certainly as follows.

Although there are many commentators on the Bodhisattva-bhūmi, the most detailed and essential compilation is that of Buddhasiṃha (known as *Jue-shizi*, "Lion of Awakening") and the most excellent son [Sthiramati] and others; they explain the title of the treatise as follows: [The text continues with their interpretation of the title.]
It is called a *śāstra* (treatise) because it resolves and determines the nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena through questions and answers.

This intention explains that by provisionally establishing the roles of interlocutor and respondent to investigate the profound nature and characteristics of all phenomena, proclaiming the essential tenets, and establishing the name "treatise.

Furthermore, the term *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* (Commentary on the Treasury) is used because it instructs and exhorts students; that is, it teaches and admonishes them regarding the meanings of the Dharma.
Regarding the title of the treatise: first, it is based on the name of the teaching (*dharma*), and subsequently, it is based on the designation of the person (*pudgala*).

Having provided a detailed and extensive explanation, how is it summarized? The term "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle) applies to all three piṭakas, while the term "Abhidharma" (Ultimate Doctrine) permeates both vehicles.
Therefore, Vasubandhu stated that in order to distinguish it from the Śrāvaka Abhidharma, he again specified "Mahāyāna. Furthermore, he said:
To distinguish it from the other piṭakas of the Mahāyāna, he further states "Abhidharma"; this is a *karmadhāraya* compound because the Abhidharma itself is the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Vasubandhu says that the term "Mahāyāna" is used to manifest the general name, while "Abhidharma" is cited to manifest the specific name;
thus, "Mahāyāna" is the general [designation], whereas "Abhidharma" is exclusively this specific one.

The term "Mahāyāna-abhidharma" is an *upapada* compound (*tatpuruṣa*). Regarding the subsequent explanation of "based on the treatise" (*śāstram āśritya*), it refers to the fact that this Mahāyāna [Abhidharma] and so forth are the "collected" (*saṃgīta*) from the original Buddha-sūtras;
thus, those sūtras are the "object of collection" (*saṃgīta*) and this treatise is the "agent of collection" (*saṃgītr*).
To call it the "collection of the Mahāyāna-abhidharma" constitutes an *adhikaraṇa-sarva-dharmaka* (possessive) compound, meaning "that which possesses the collection. If one speaks of the treatise...
This is the compendium of the Mahāyāna Abhidharma; thus, its name is formed by the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound "that which is the compendium" (*tasya saṃgrahaḥ*).
This is explained according to the *Saṃgraha-sūtra*, as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that this treatise was taught in order to enable the realization of the *yogācārya-bhūmi*;
therefore, it is named accordingly, just as the *Abhidharma-śāstra* is named. Thus, one should know that this treatise is also called the Mahāyāna Abhidharma.

Because it is the *dharma*, it is without intrinsic nature; because it is the cause for discerning phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), or because it is commonly understood [as such], this is based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises.

Regarding its meaning: if one says that the expressed referent (*abhidheya*) is called the "Mahāyāna Abhidharma," then the teaching (*deśanā*) is named "Abhidharma" and the referent is named "Collection" (*piṭaka*);
alternatively, if one says that the teaching is named "Mahāyāna Abhidharma" and the referent is named "Collection," both cases follow the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
Furthermore, since the *Abhidharma* that possesses its own activity is itself the "Collection" (*Saṃgraha*), "Collection" is the name of the master Vasubandhu’s original treatise.
If "Collection" refers to the principle (*nyāya*), it is called the *Saṃgrahanirukti*, which is an *upapadatatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound;

if "Collection" refers to the teaching (*śāsana*), it is called the *Saṃgraha*, which is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. This is the name of the original treatise, to which Sthiramati has added a title by synthesizing these meanings.
Because it is a compendium, we know that the explanation of its name as "a compendium" (*samuccaya*) is merely a general designation that applies to both principle and teaching.

As for the title *Mahāyānābhidharma*, it is a designation based on the person who upholds it, employing both the *upapada* (dependent) and *karmadhāraya* (appositional) interpretations, as explained above. Why is this treatise not only named a "compendium" but also designated as the *Mahāyānābhidharma*?

It is because [the author] desires to cause all sentient beings to realize that [Abhidharma], for it is the cause for the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). Furthermore, it is for this reason that it is so described.
Because of the meaning of that sūtra, if one were to omit the name of the sūtra, one would not understand that this treatise is the holy teaching (*āgama*).

Alternatively, because this [treatise] arises based upon that [sūtra], it is designated as such—just as flowers are named after their source, whether they grow in water or on land. This serves as a proof for the title.

Furthermore, regarding the reasons for the names and meanings of "the true direct realization" (*bhūtābhisamaya*) and "the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the ten stages," these shall be analyzed in detail later in the main body of the text (*śarīra*).

Regarding the interpretation of the main text: in general, when categorizing the structure of a text, names are established according to the force of the composition and its underlying meaning; it is not that the meaning differs while the name remains as it was previously established.

This consists of three parts: first, the section on the integrated preface; second, the section on the combined exposition of the main text; and third, the section on explaining the titles to clarify the intent.
Because it does not err in its integration, because it comprehensively encompasses [the subject matter], and because it realizes perfect awakening, herein, first...

The first part was composed solely by Sthiramati; as for the other two parts—the root text and the commentary—both the various teachings and the fundamental school definitely possess both the beginning and the end, though some have them while others lack them.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* lacks the end, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* lacks the beginning, and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* lacks both;

yet the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* possesses both. One should examine in detail the author’s underlying intention regarding these differences. Within the first part, it is further divided into... [text continues].
Regarding the first part, there are three verses that praise and pay homage to the Honored One and provide a general introduction;
regarding the latter part, there are two sections that clarify the preceding homage and praise and explain the introductory verses. First, within the three verses, there are two parts:

(1) the first two and a half verses praise and pay homage to the Honored One, and the final half-verse provides a general introduction. Within the initial section clarifying the praise and homage, there is further [subdivision].
In the first two verses of the initial section, there is praise and homage to the Three Jewels; in the subsequent half-verse, there is a dedication and praise to the two teachers.
