Within the text of the praise and homage to the Three Jewels, there are further two parts: the first, one and a half verses, separately praises six aspects;
the latter, a half-verse, offers general homage to the Three Jewels. Within this separate praise, one verse separately praises the three bodies, while the final two lines provide a general summary.
In this hymn of praise, which enumerates the various virtues in correspondence [with the three bodies], the first line clarifies the *dharmakāya*; the next two lines manifest the *saṃbhogakāya*;
and the final line explains the *nirmāṇakāya*. Furthermore, the first line reveals the virtue of primordial existence, which is manifested through realization;
the next two lines reveal the virtue born of cultivation, which arises through the practice of training; and the final line reveals the virtue of functional utility.

The fulfillment of the fruit brings about transformation: furthermore, the first phrase reveals the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*), the next two phrases manifest the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), and the final phrase clarifies the virtue of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*).
Moreover, the first phrase explains the permanence of the original nature; the next two phrases reveal the permanence of non-interruption;
and the final phrase clarifies the permanence of continuity. Furthermore, the first phrase takes refuge in *nirvāṇa*, and the next two phrases take refuge in *bodhi*.
The final phrase, "returning to the three wheels, the ultimate principle of true purity across all assemblies," reveals that the qualities of the Dharmakāya are primordially present;
it shows that the nature of the perfection of abandonment is eternally in a state of nirvāṇa, and that the true nature expressed by all such terms possesses six meanings.
While previous interpretations restricted these terms solely to the first phrase, a detailed examination shows this is not the case; they apply throughout the subsequent sections as well.
The general meaning of these words is to demonstrate that there is no factionalism; rather, because they possess those virtues, I now take refuge in them all.

Although these words apply generally to other Buddhas as well, it is specifically the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body) that can realize the principle, for it is through this body that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is realized and verified; thus, it is called "conforming to the truth" (*yoga*).

The term "non-delusive" (*aviparyāsa*) excludes the two types of reality [the imagined and the dependent]; "self" (*ātman*) and "purity" (*śubha*) exclude defiled phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), as they signify being stainless (*vimala*).

Because hindrances are exhausted and the Path is perfected, it is called "ultimate. It is distinguished from the conditioned reality of pure mundane existence, which refers to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as manifested by the two kinds of emptiness;
this reveals its own intrinsic nature. Alternatively, the false principles falsely grasped by non-Buddhists are not true, and the principles realized by the Two Vehicles are defiled rather than pure.

Although Bodhisattvas realize the pure principle of true emptiness, because their abandonment [of afflictions] and their realization [of the path] are both incomplete, it is not yet termed "ultimate."

This name is established because only the Buddha alone is fully perfected. If one explains it according to the lower interpretation as the *dharmakāya* of principle (*tattva*), then by citing all the capacities for realization, one reveals *tathatā*.
Furthermore, the explanations herein state that the various assemblies possess wisdom that is truly pure; thus, in principle, these are all called the *dharmakāya*.
Other teachings also speak of the *jñāna-dharmakāya* (wisdom-body of phenomena), and therefore, in the following passage, it is provisionally stated that it is "without arising or ceasing. Third.

In the section on the body, the two phrases "extensively differentiating the ocean of noble conduct, ascending to the further shore, and attaining mastery over all phenomena" reveal the qualities of wisdom and virtue cultivated through enjoyment, which are uninterrupted and eternal. Awakening illuminates the Dharma; having already crossed over, it is called "transcending.

Penetrating the truth is termed "noble" (*ārya*); the cultivation of practice is termed "conduct" (*caryā*); its vastness and depth are termed the "ocean" (*sāgara*); and these wondrous practices are [the subject].
The ocean is used as a metaphor for the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) because its boundless, shallow wisdom is difficult to fathom yet gives rise to the jewels of the noble ones;

the ocean-like conduct of the noble ones constitutes this shore, while bodhi is the further shore. Compassion and wisdom are like a boat, and the Buddha’s ascent to bodhi is called "ascending to the further shore.
That which can transcend is the fruit, and that which is transcended is the cause; this is raised from the perspective of the ocean-like cause of noble conduct throughout great eons.

Those who have ascended to the other shore obtain the boundless fruit; yet those who have not yet resolved upon the true mind take birth-and-death as this shore, giving rise to waves of affliction, abandoning the ship of *prajñā*, and turning their backs on the other shore of perfect quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*). Now, clarifying the departure [from this state], one takes compassion and wisdom as the vessel.
The "ocean" refers to the noble practices (*āryacaryā*), and the "other shore" is that which arises from the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
Because the habitual tendencies of all obscurations have been exhausted and one has personally attained mastery, it is called "realizing all phenomena.
This means that regarding all objects, one understands them without obstruction and is not constrained by external things; hence, it is called "mastery.

Furthermore, "all" refers to all meritorious qualities, which are realized through cultivation within the ocean of noble practices of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), thereby transcending and severing all obscurations and habitual tendencies.
Having ascended to the other shore and realized awakening, one attains great mastery over the qualities of merit;

because one understands the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*) and is able to fully accomplish all boundless merits, or because "mastery" refers to the ten masteries which are manifested as being fully realized, it is therefore called "all.
This is the Dharma, meaning that it arises from those noble practices (*āryacaryā*).
Because he has ascended to the other shore from within the ocean [of existence], he is able to realize the tenfold mastery over all dharmas of merit;

thus, he enjoys the Buddha’s infinite qualities. Alternatively, the phrase "the inconceivable one who realizes the tenfold mastery within all objects and skillfully guides through transformation" reveals the utility of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
The virtue of grace and the continuity of that virtue constantly transform sentient beings through the three wheels; this virtuous activity of the Sage is termed "skillful means" (*upāya-kauśalya*).

It is called "expedient function" (*prajñapti*) because it conceals the ultimate truth while manifesting the conventional in accordance with the capacities of beings. To encourage those of initial capacity, it is called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*);

to cause those who have long practiced to grow and be established, it is called "sage-activity" (*ārya-karma*). Only through vast and profound realization and convergence can one reach it; the path of discursive thought ceases and names and words are exhausted.

The Path is severed; it is not the domain of other forms of knowledge and is termed "inconceivable. Furthermore, another explanation is as follows: "Expedient" (*upāya*) refers to manifesting supernatural powers in response to sentient beings;

"Transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) refers to reading their minds and preaching the sublime Dharma; "Guidance" (*vinaya*) refers to instructing them to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*); and "Reception" (*saṃgraha*) refers to leading them [to liberation].

These three are all subtle and skillful, collectively designated by the term "excellent," and are all inconceivable, transcending the reach of all verbal expression. This interpretation accords with the subsequent detailed exposition in the introduction.

The text further states: "Transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) refers to crushing the heterodox and entering the orthodox, encouraging those of the Small Vehicle toward the Great, and guiding—that is, leading—ordinary beings so that all may enter the state of a Sage;
it is a provisional name established according to the capacity of the recipient.

The phrase "praising and recounting the immeasurable, rare, and supreme merits of the three bodies' essence and function" is a eulogy corresponding to these virtues, such that their number cannot be known through calculation.

Investigating this, one finds it unfathomable; it exhausts the limits of emptiness and establishes names of the immeasurable that have never existed in the world, being called rare and marvelous, surpassing all else, and further receiving superior titles.
"Merit" (*guṇa*) refers to practice (*caryā*), action (*karma*), and virtue (*guṇa*). Virtue arises from this;
only through the diligent accumulation of practice and action can one attain these immeasurable, rare, and supreme virtues.

This passage permeates the three bodies (*trikāya*) because its textual meaning is comprehensive; it is stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* that the association with qualities (*guṇa*) extends to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

and since the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts state that all three bodies possess boundless virtues and the marks of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) are most prominent, this section specifically discusses them.

Furthermore, that which ordinary beings cannot fathom is called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*); that which the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not know is called "rare" (*āścarya*); and as for Bodhisattvas...
It is called "supreme" because it is fully realized; furthermore, this term should be applied accordingly to distinguish it from those three [bodies].

This statement belongs specifically to the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), as it is taught below that it is produced by boundless practices and is said in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* to be the retinue of wisdom.

Although both the *dharmakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya* possess a multitude of virtues, their characteristics and functions differ; [the former] is exclusively the enjoyment [body]. Furthermore, it is taught that the *dharmakāya* and...

Because it is endowed with the qualities that realize the path, it possesses the unconditioned qualities of the *dharmatā*; this phrase also encompasses the profound meaning of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Regarding the phrase "the basis for the benefit of both self and others": this praises and describes the specific benefits of the three bodies;
as will be explained below, the *saṃbhogakāya* is the basis for self-benefit, the *nirmāṇakāya* is the basis for benefiting others, and the *dharmakāya* is the basis for both types of benefit.

Regarding "cessation" (*śamatha*), the meaning of the three Buddha-bodies is discussed differently in other treatises; these shall be reconciled below. At the beginning of this treatise, all teachings are identical in their opening homage.

Why, then, are the six meanings first manifested at the outset? Because the present work synthesizes various doctrines to reveal the body and activity of its own master, which are supreme and transcend those of all other sages;
therefore, one first praises his virtues before proffering respectful salutation. This concludes the specific [explanation].
Following the praise of the three bodies and the six meanings, there is a half-verse that generally pays homage to the three bodies and takes refuge in the Three Jewels;
whereas the preceding section praised the six meanings specifically, the following section pays homage to the Three Jewels in general.
"Homage to the Great Awakened Honored One, the Peerless Sublime Dharma, and the Assembly of Noble Ones.
The commentary states: The first two characters represent the "characteristics of the one who takes refuge," while the remaining characters represent the "essence of that which is taken as refuge.

Although the *Abhidharmakośa* speaks of "bowing the head and touching the feet," this describes only the physical act (*kāyakarman*) of reverence; it does not fully encompass the aspect of profound veneration. Thus, "reverence" (*jing*) refers to the internal state of sincere respect, while "homage" (*li*) refers to the external formal rite.
Truly giving rise to sincere devotion, one adopts a formal posture to offer praise and extends the way of reverent respect, marking it with the name of "homage" (*namas*).

What is the nature of this? It is precisely the three wholesome courses of action (*trividha-karma-patha*). As Vasubandhu said: "Therefore, with utmost sincerity, I repeatedly cultivate through body, speech, and mind the unerring act of taking refuge and offering homage.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* also states: "I now, with utmost sincerity, first offer praise and homage," as found in other [texts].

The body and speech of a Buddha are not merely contaminated (*sāsrava*); rather, prostration extends to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Alternatively, even within the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages, body and speech arise.
Since the essence of bodily and vocal karma is capable of generating volition (*cetanā*), it may extend to the uncontaminated mind.

As for the uncontaminated manifest (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest (*avijñapti*), these cannot be produced by those of the Two Vehicles; therefore, they are indicated as extending to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated.

Regarding what was previously stated by the Virtuous One as "thus and thus," why is it so? The Honored One of Great Enlightenment and other such beings are called "Great" because their realization is supreme;

they are called "Enlightened" (Jue) because they alone are victorious; they are named "Honored" (Zun) because, although they have perfected myriad virtues, wisdom is the foremost of the Way. They are called only "Great Enlightened Ones" (Dajue).

As for the previous [state of] the Dharma-body and Transformation-body, these are the essence and function of principle; the present title "Great Enlightened One" does not apply to those [distinctions of] nature and characteristics.

By virtue of the principle of the single essence (*ekakāya*), they are neither identical nor separate; thus, they are all designated as "Awakened" (*buddha*). Because their excellence is beyond comparison, they are called "Incomparable" (*asama*).

Being truly good and providing a standard for emulation, they are further termed "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*). Paying homage to those who flow forth from such [qualities]—in this context, the manifestation of the aforementioned six meanings constitutes the "Incomparable Dharma.
Those who taste its flavor and partake of its harmony are called the "Noble Assembly" (*āryasaṃgha*); this refers to those possessing such virtuous qualities.
The phrase "not one" refers to all those who pay homage; this also applies to the assembly of noble ones (*ārya*).

The *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states that the Tathāgata is itself the triple refuge. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* also explains that the Triple Gem is eternal because it is identical to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Within the Dharmakāya, the Triple Gem of identical essence is established by way of six meanings; this is the Buddha-gem, which consists of these six meanings.
This refers to the Dharma Jewel: its skillful means (*upāya*), its doctrinal principles (*naya*), its practice as cause, and its realization as fruit.

Since it was previously stated that the "One Vehicle Sangha" transcends [the ordinary] causes, there is an interpretation that the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) is included within the count of the Sangha; for this reason, the subsequent passage further states:

"It should be known that this also praises the merits of the Dharma and the Sangha, because from this Buddha-Dharma one trains and gives birth [to realization]; having first praised [them], one then takes refuge."
The knowledge [of the Three Jewels] applies to what follows below; by citing the superior to reveal the inferior, it is certain that there is a Saṃgha.

Furthermore, such statements do not apply to what follows below because they refer to the same essence despite distinct characteristics, as both the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles all return to and pay homage [to the Jewels].

If one relies on the text below, it clarifies the distinct characteristics of the Three Jewels, for the characteristics of each Jewel are explained separately; therefore, this verse generally pays homage while the subsequent text specifically elucidates the principle.
There is no contradiction; it should be understood accordingly that this [initial salutation] applies only to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṃgha, as there is no need for such [repetition].
Nevertheless, since it is stated below that the first two verses reveal the six meanings of the Buddha, it is clear that the Three Jewels are subsumed within these six meanings.
Why, then, does the treatise begin by paying homage only to the Three Jewels? It is because of five reasons.
First, because the Three Jewels are the most auspicious, I state them at the beginning of my sutra to distinguish it from the heterodox schools;
furthermore, to differ from worldly conventions, I employ the *āyuṣmat* [honorific] and the *siddham* [mangala] at the outset.

Second, as they are true fields of merit capable of receiving the world’s most exquisite offerings, I first praise and pay homage to them now that this is an offering of the Dharma. They possess great power, adorned with merit and wisdom.
His majestic supernormal powers are peerless; may he secretly bestow his aid and protection. First, one pays homage to that which is the ultimate refuge. Second, one brings forth four aspirations:

to open up right mindfulness, to manifest true virtues, and to cause those who hear the Dharma to give rise to a heart of profound reverence. Fifth, [the teaching] is supremely excellent, for there are four conditions:
first, because his nature is well-disciplined and virtuous; second, because of his skillful means; third, because he possesses great compassion; and fourth—
Because one rejoices at the time of making the offering of the Dharma (*dharmapūjā*), it is said that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and others cannot be taken as objects of refuge.
Thus, at the beginning of this treatise, one pays homage solely to the Triple Gem (*triratna*) to clarify the meaning of taking refuge and paying respect.

This is as explained in the sixty-fourth and seventy-fourth fascicles of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the sixth and thirteenth fascicles of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, and the specific chapters on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, which treat the Triple Gem.

Regarding the meaning of the essence, it shall be understood below. The two preceding verses have praised and paid homage to the Three Jewels; the latter half of the verse now pays homage to and extols the two masters.
"I pay homage to the master who expounded this treatise, who personally received the holy intent and made the distinctions."
The commentary states: The first two characters [“I prostrate”] refer to the two masters; the remaining characters below praise the two masters.

Alternatively, one may explain that this section contains only salutations and no formal praise, as the mention of “opening and expounding” (*kai-en*) serves to identify the individuals involved. Thus, the term “reverential salutation” (*namas*) applies universally to both sections:

the Bodhisattva Asaṅga is called the master of the root treatise for opening and collecting its textual passages, while he is called the expounder for unfolding their meanings; therefore, he is the primary guide.
To "expound" (*ākhyāna*) means to explain for the first time; to "elaborate" (*vibhājana*) refers to further explanation after long practice, or to speak now what was never spoken before.
Alternatively, to "expound" means to speak extensively what has already been spoken previously, while to "elucidate" (*uttānī-karaṇa*) refers to collecting the teachings and explaining them oneself.

This constitutes the interpretation of the sūtras, which is further termed "elaboration. "In person" (*sākṣāt*) means entering the inner chamber [of the teacher]; "receiving" (*anuśrava*) means accepting instruction, or alternatively, internalizing the teaching.
"Saint" refers to Asaṅga; "purport" refers to the essential tenets. To investigate through wisdom and understanding is termed "discrimination.
Whether one discriminates while abiding in non-attachment or discriminates by inheriting the Saint's purport, it is through such understanding that virtue is perfected.

This work is titled [The Commentary] because the master Buddhasimha—a disciple of Asaṅga who received benefit from his staff-case and was thoroughly proficient in the essential meanings—excellently explained the original text.
As for the distinction: because the teachers and disciples possess the Path, I pay homage to them all. Now, why must these two teachers be paid separate homage?

Because the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains the dharma of reverence, one pays homage to the Fundamental Teacher (*mūlācārya*) in the sense of reverence; and because one honors those who have expounded [the teachings], one pays homage to the Expounding Teacher (*vyākhyānācārya*).

In the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, there is also a separate homage; the first two and a half verses praise and pay homage to those worthy of veneration, while the subsequent half [verse] [pays homage to the Expounding Teacher].
The verse summarizes and integrates [the preceding discussion].
It states that through the realization of the sūtras and their commentaries, one gives rise to right diligence, which constitutes this integration.
The commentary says: the first phrase clarifies the cause for the compilation, while the second phrase explicitly explains the integration itself. As for "by" (*yao*), it serves as...
"Awakening" (*vibhaṅga*) means "explanation. A *sūtra* (契經) refers precisely to the collection of discourses by the Original Teacher;
because it skillfully compiles the original discourses and accords with their meaning, it is called a *sūtra*. It is not that the *śāstra* (本論) itself is named a *sūtra*.

[The term *sūtra* here] refers to that which can accord with the *sūtras*, rather than a *sūtra* that accords with the principle. Furthermore, since it is not permitted for disciples to compose *sūtras*, "explanation" (*vibhaṅga*) refers to—

"Explanation of the Text" (*Jiewen*) refers to the commentary on the meaning; it either translates these explanations or provides an interpretation where the literal text lacks explicit meaning. This was composed by Master Jue-si (Buddhasimha).

The use of the term "and" (*yi*) indicates that there were differences between the original commentary and this one, which have not yet been synthesized. Each version has been placed separately to show their divergences.

Herein, "herein" (*yuan*) means "at," and "arising" (*fa*) means "to originate. "Non-erroneous" is called "correct" (*zheng*); "courageous exertion" is termed "diligence" (*qin*); and "now" (*nai*) signifies "thereupon."
Yi-shi and Yi-can harmonized the meanings, while Yi-zong compiled them. In my own writing, I have now composed this commentary on the original text for the sake of leisurely study;
yet, as others may wish for a further explanation of the treatise’s original commentary, I have thus undertaken this with unerring diligence, merging the two texts into a single work.
Now, within this verse (up to the words) "I reverently prostrate," the commentary states:
The three preceding verses were a praise and prostration to the Honored One, serving as an introductory preface. From the following two sections onward, the previous homage and eulogy are clarified.
Regarding the explanation of the verse’s stated cause, there are two parts; the first passage generally clarifies what was previously honored and praised.

In the latter section, there is a separate explanation of the causes indicated in the verse. This section consists of two parts: first, a general explanation of the characteristics of "reverence," and second, a specific manifestation of the objects of refuge and praise.
Thus, regarding the initial text of this verse: the phrase "in this verse" serves as an opening to introduce, distinguish, maintain, and specify;
it refers to the fact that, with an undistorted mind, one seeks *bodhi*, and therefore offers exaltation and praise for the six [perfections].

The supreme qualities of the Three Jewels of Meaning are also praised with an undistorted mind; to respectfully offer salutation is to proclaim them face-to-face, while to extol them from behind is called "praise.
To call them "foremost" or "supreme" is to express their excellence; "reverence" refers to being devoutly respectful, and "to offer" means to present it.
To bow the head down to touch the feet is what is meant by "prostrating"—this is the expression of praise within the verse that speaks with an undistorted mind.

The body performs homage by being complete in the three wheels; or rather, this passage speaks only of verbal praise and physical homage because these two are not perverted, and thus can be clearly manifested as being without error.

As for mental action, it is also included in "taking refuge," yet since there can also be perverted praise and perverted taking of refuge within it, [the text] specifies that [verbal and physical acts] are without error.
"Making offerings to the Triple Gem" (up to) "according to what is appropriate.
The commentary states: Below, there is a specific explanation of that to which one takes refuge. Within this, there are two parts: first, the specific explanation;

second, the explanation based on these [verses]. Regarding the first part: because it involves the offering of the True Dharma, one first employs the offering of practice to honor those who are revered.

To whom does "that to which one returns" refer? It refers to the Three Jewels and the two teachers; according to their power and virtue, they are able to provide protective mindfulness, and thus whatever is praised and venerated, all of that is praised and venerated.

The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used because it is a term of praise. Alternatively, since the virtues were already praised in the preceding verse regarding the Three Jewels, one also pays homage to those two teachers;
however, in this case, there is only homage and no further praise of their virtues, as their qualities have already been partially established.
The general term "fulfillment" (*pūrṇa*) encompasses both the collective and the individual, according to what is appropriate.
Why is this so? The commentary states:

below, the cause for this is explained, beginning with a formal inquiry (*praśna*) followed by an explanation (*vyākhyāna*). This is the wording of the inquiry; first, the explanation of "according to what is appropriate" is provided.
Since this inquiry possesses such power and virtue that it is praised and venerated accordingly, what is the reason for this alone and not others?

Later, in the explanation, one should interpret this inquiry as appropriate: what is the reason that among the Three Jewels, one both praises and venerates them, whereas regarding the two teachers, one only venerates them without praise?
Or, taking the inquiry collectively, it concerns the reason for venerating the Three Jewels and so forth.
"What does 'for what reason' (yat kasmāt) mean? It does not refer to a separate inquiry into the meaning as it applies in each case;
rather, it refers to that upon which this treatise relies and from which it arises.
The commentary states: "From here below is the explanation; first briefly, then extensively. This is the brief text. Regarding the initial inquiry, it is a praise.
The *Treatise on Paying Homage to the Three Jewels* (*Lǐ sānbǎo lùn*) relies upon [the preceding work]; it praises and pays homage to the two masters who were able to originate this treatise.

For this reason, the praise and homage are limited to these alone and no others. Regarding the subsequent inquiry: although the *Treatise on the Three Jewels* relies upon the praise and likewise pays homage to the two masters who originated it, it offers only homage without praise.
Alternatively, this may be explained as a general explanation of the reasons for the objects of refuge and homage, rather than a separate explanation according to each specific case.
*Arthaviniścaya* (The Ascertainment of Meaning). From "The Buddha, the Bhagavat" up to "the basis of equality.

The commentary states: Below, the two meanings of "basis" (*āśraya*) and "arising" (*utpatti*) from the preceding section are explained in detail; first, the meaning of *buddha* as "the Awakened One" is explained.
As is commonly explained, the Bhagavat is so called because he is able to destroy the four māras and possesses six qualities.
The "māras" refer to the afflictions (*kleśa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), death (*maraṇa*), and the celestial being (*devaputra*). The "six qualities" are: first, sovereignty; second, brilliance;
third, majesty; fourth, renown; fifth, auspiciousness; and sixth, nobility. These are explained in detail in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*. Why, then, is there a pair here?
The two designations are not one, yet neither is it otherwise; this reveals the awakening to all phenomena. By citing the name "Buddha," its virtues are manifested as a basis for reliance.
Both names—“Bhagavat” and “Buddha”—are supreme and not otherwise. This is because none of the twelve divisions of the teaching, such as the *sūtras*, exist apart from the World-Honored One.
Thus, the Buddha and the teaching serve as a common basis of reliance, or alternatively:

Only after the Buddha has realized the Great Samādhi, the Fundamental Wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), the Subsequent Wisdom (*prṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*), and Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is he able to give rise to the teaching of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Since all phenomena are the equal basis for the Buddha, and the Dharma is the Teacher of the Buddha, how can it now be said that the Buddha is the basis for the Dharma?
"Self-awakened without a teacher" (up to) "because of the basis upon which one relies.
The commentary states: This explains the reason for relying [on this]. One realizes it through self-awakening in one's final body;

thus it is called "without a teacher," which distinguishes it from others who awaken to the path through reliance on another. As for the true nature, it is because one realizes it through reasoning that the teaching is subsequently expounded.
Since those teachings are revealed and explained by the Buddha alone, it is said that the Buddha and the Dharma are the two supports;
this is not based on the relationship of teacher and disciple, but rather on the basis of their explicit explanation.

Furthermore, since the discussion of these teachings and principles constitutes the Teacher, and because the Sūtras and other scriptures are established through these principles—and since the principles are the fruit while the means of realization are the practice—all treatises rely upon them. Therefore, it is said that both the Buddha and the Dharma are the supports.
As the basis for the treatise:
immediately following this [passage], up to "studying in accordance with the Dharma," the commentary states:
"To clarify the sequential dependence, having realized the Dharma through the Buddha's testimony, he then skillfully expounded it for his disciples; this is called 'instruction'."
Because the noble disciples— who follow and train in the Dharma as taught by the Uninterrupted Noble Ones— compile and disseminate it,
and because the treatises can only arise through this successive transmission, the Jewel of the Sangha is said to be the basis of the treatises.
"Dharma is the reliance" means that it flows from the *dharmadhātu*.
The commentary states: This explains the reason why the Jewel of the Saṃgha relies upon the Dharma; it means that the teaching flows forth sequentially and equally from that pure *dharmadhātu*.
By relying on this teaching to practice, one subsequently achieves the realization of the fruit; or, [it arises] by way of the *dharmadhātu*.

Because the outflow of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is superior in both its origin and its culmination, the noble disciples (*ārya-śrāvaka*) all declare that one should rely upon the Dharma first, as appropriate.
According to the former interpretation, the Three Jewels (*triratna*) serve as the basis for this treatise; therefore, it is only they who are praised and venerated, and not other categories.
According to the latter interpretation, because the Three Jewels are the refuge, possessing both power and virtue, they are both venerated and praised. Or...

The above provides a general explanation that the Three Jewels as objects of reliance are all worthy of praise and veneration. The Buddha possesses the four conditions, such as being well-disciplined by nature, as previously explained;
because he has taught the Dharma and his noble disciples, they too are worthy of taking refuge. The above generally clarifies the meaning of the basis upon which this treatise relies.
Hereafter, the composition of the treatise and the commentary on the sūtras by the two masters will be introduced.
Regarding the two masters who commented on the Sūtras: [the text] says they composed their treatises in accordance [with the teachings].
The commentary states: "The True Dharma spoken by the World-Honored One is vast; it is not something that can be heard and studied in its entirety by other noble ones alone.
These two masters also understood a portion of it. The term "also" (亦) refers to the remaining noble ones and others; "契" (qì) signifies realization or verification.
One part [of this] reveals that the dharmas of the higher stages remain as yet un-realized and un-attained;

or, because one has merely understood this explained sūtra, and through the fulfillment of hearing, reflection, and cultivation regarding what has been attained and understood, this treatise was composed based upon those three types of wisdom according to what was heard and so forth. This is the intended meaning.
Since this is explained in accordance with the *Vyākhyāyukti*, one knows that this treatise certainly accords with correct reasoning.

According to the first interpretation, as the case may be, since this treatise arose only through the two masters, it specifically praises and pays homage to them, while not praising or paying homage to others.

According to the latter interpretation, the two masters merely understood how to originate the teaching of this treatise; they were not the supreme basis [of its authority]. Thus, one pays homage to them but offers no praise.

Alternatively, this is a general statement praising those two masters because they composed this treatise based on their unerring understanding of one portion of the Tathāgata’s teaching concerning the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*);
it is not a separate explanation of the specific meanings as they apply.

Although there are three interpretations, the first and last accord with the text regarding the meaning of the gateway of the three wisdoms, as explained in detail in another chapter. This [treatise]...

The general text above provides a manifest praise of what precedes it without specifically identifying the reasons for its composition; the following sections provide a detailed explanation of the causes indicated in the verses,
from the first two verses up to the meaning of their distinctions.
The commentary states: Within this section there are two parts. First, the individual explanation of the six meanings of the Three Jewels (*triratna*);

second, the specific explanation of the reasons for the composition of the introduction. The first part has two sub-sections. First, a general reference to the six meanings of the Buddha from the preceding verses, as they are explained sequentially according to the difficulties encountered.
Second, the individual enumeration and textual exegesis following the headings. This is the first [sub-section]: the individual and general praise.

The ritual [of homage] consists of two verses; since both are indicated here, it is said that the first four lines constitute one verse. This is certain because, in the subsequent detailed explanation, the homage is praised through six distinct meanings in total—there are no more than six—and this reveals their specific distinctions. To explain them individually: "text" (vyañjana) refers to the words, while "meaning" (artha) refers to the content; "name" (nāman) and "entity" (vastu) refer to the difference between the designation and the substance. Regarding the term "Tathāgata," etc.: * **Tathāgata**: Because he has come from suchness (*tathatā*) and gone to suchness, or because he has come from suchness and does not depart from suchness, he is called a Tathāgata. * **Arhat**: Because he has destroyed all defilements (*kleśa*), he is called an Arhat. * **Samyaksaṃbuddha**: Because he has perfectly awakened to all phenomena, he is called a Samyaksaṃbuddha. * **Bhagavat**: Because he possesses the six types of excellence, he is called a Bhagavat. * **Śāstṛ**: Because he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, he is called a Śāstṛ (Teacher). * **Devamanuṣyāṇām**: Because he is the most honored among gods and humans, he is called Devamanuṣyāṇām. * **Mahāśramaṇa**: Because he is the greatest among those who have renounced worldly life, he is called a Mahāśramaṇa. * **Buddha**: Because he has awakened to all phenomena, he is called a Buddha. * **Bhagavān**: Because he possesses the six types of excellence, he is called a Bhagavān.
