Citing six meanings to honor the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, it is said that because his speech is free from falsehood, he is called the Tathāgata;
because his words accord with reality, he has attained Buddhahood and is thus the Tathāgata. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Just as the past Buddhas taught the sūtras and other discourses, [the Dharma] proceeds from the pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eleven kinds of emptiness, and so forth, until it reaches nirvāṇa."
The name "Tathāgata" is explained here as follows: it means that, like all Buddhas, he has preached the sublime Dharma;
because he has come from the cultivation of the myriad practices to reach Nirvāṇa, his words are not false—this is the meaning of Tathāgata.

Furthermore, because he has constantly practiced truthful speech without falsehood and reached the stage of Buddhahood, he is called Tathāgata. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "He should have already destroyed the thieves."
He should not undergo rebirth and should receive offerings; therefore he is called "one who should enter parinirvāṇa.

He is also said to be "one who should destroy the world," "one who should abandon afflictions," and "one who should receive various offerings from devas and humans. These [qualities] apply generally to all three vehicles, yet one should explain that the Buddha’s "shoulds" must be distinct:
he should destroy the two obstacles, he should be free from the two types of death, and he should receive the wealth of the world.

The *Ratnārcana-yogācāra-śāstra* states: "That which has been received, that which should be attained, that which should serve as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), and that which should be offered—therefore it is called 'worthy' (*arhat*).
The first [of these] corresponds to the first two yogas; the latter two correspond to the final yoga.

Furthermore, regarding the word "offering" (*pūjā*), there is no further meaning [beyond this]. The *Yoga* [Śāstra] also says: "In accordance with ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), one awakens to all..."
Because he has realized the Dharma, he is called the "Perfectly Awakened One" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). This explanation takes the realization of ultimate truth as the name for *nirvāṇa*.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that "perfect" means non-erroneous, and "thorough knowledge" means being fully penetrating regarding the four inversions.

This sūtra also says that one obtains the name "thorough knowledge" by contemplating the principle of the Truths. "According to reality" (*yathārtha*) means that, regarding all external objects and the heterodox views of outsiders...
Knowing now and knowing by name refers to the two vehicles' partial realization; realizing now and realizing the two selves refers to equality, meaning sameness.
Bodhisattvas whose knowledge is not yet full are likewise not called "equal-knowers. This present [term] generally distinguishes and upholds the name "Perfectly Equal Awakened One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
The remaining seven names are as described in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicles 38 and 83, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 17.

Furthermore, since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, and the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*—the eighteenth [treatise]—extensively explain that the Buddha possesses the ten titles (*daśa-nāmadheya*), why are only three mentioned here?
This is because these three manifest the perfection of the merit of wisdom and the repayment of gratitude.

While they are explained separately through different enumerations, the general name "Tathāgata" encompasses the remaining nine titles; thus, it represents the shared virtues, whereas "Samyaksaṃbuddha" (the Perfectly Awakened One) represents the unique virtue. This...

Because the general and specific, common and uncommon virtues are all-encompassing, nothing else [can be so]; for this reason, these various sūtras speak only of the six meanings of the supreme virtues such as *tathāgata* and so forth:
the name "Buddha" refers to the primary essence (*svabhāva*); the characteristics of cultivation and realization refer to the cause (*hetu*);

the characteristic of having already realized fulfillment refers to the fruit (*phala*); the characteristic of initiating activity refers to the function (*karman*); and that which is conjoined with these merits is called the endowment (*yoga*).
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises all distinguish between the various names for the essence and function of the nature of correspondence (*yoga-lakṣaṇa*).
This is because all assemblies of true purity take this as their essential nature.

The commentary states: Below, the individual items are distributed and explained according to the text. This section has two parts: first, the six meanings are cited and explained by distributing them according to the text;
second, from "It should be known" onwards, the distinct aspects of the Dharma and Sangha are cited and explained, which also generally apply to the praise of taking refuge.

In the first part, there are six sections, as there are six meanings to be explained; thus, within each textual unit, there are two sub-sections: first, citing the verse text, and second, [explaining it] by means of the six...
The meaning belongs to the subsequent section, which provides a general explanation of the meaning of the verse.

Herein, from "the various assemblies" up to "the meaning of self-nature," this constitutes the first citation of the verse through six meanings, namely, "all Buddhas" and so forth, which provide a general explanation of the meaning of the verse;

all subsequent sections should be understood accordingly, as they are not explained again. "All kinds" (*sarvākāra*) refers to the various categories and distinctions of all that is contaminated (*sāsrava*), or alternatively, it refers to...
The seeds of all two-fold hindrances are transformed; this basis of tainted *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness) is replaced by the basis of non-*dausthulya* *tathatā* (suchness).

This treatise explains below that there are three types of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): first, the mind; second, the path; and third, the transformation of the basis of the coarse and heavy mind.

Regarding the transformation of the basis of the mind of *dharmatā*: because the mind of *dharmatā* is eternally free from adventitious defilements, it is called "transformation"; it is the transformation of *dausthulya*.

"Reliance" refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), from which all internal afflictive latent tendencies (*kleśānuśaya*) are forever and completely separated; because the cause has been extinguished, the fruit likewise ceases to exist.

Furthermore, the text itself later explains the term "self-nature body" (*svābhāvikakāya*): it takes the *tathatā* (suchness) as its basis for transformation (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) and constitutes the Dharma-body.

Thus, what is here called "all aspects" (*sarvākāra*) refers to the fact that through the transformation of all contaminated (*sāsrava*) states, these coarse and heavy obstructions (*dauṣṭhulya*) are eliminated.

The attained basis of mind is the common essence of all Buddhas; it is termed "self-nature" (*svabhāva*) because it is the meaning of being the self, and it is also called the "Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*) because it is the support for all virtues.
Thus, the Buddha's Dharma-body has this attained transformation-basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) as its nature.
Furthermore, "all modes" (*sarvākāra*) refers to the various categories of conditioned phenomena that serve as the supported [virtues]; they are called "all modes" because their types are manifold.
This *tathatā* (suchness), which is the basis for this transformation and the essence of its intrinsic nature, is difficult to understand in terms of its own nature;

therefore, by presenting that which depends upon it (*āśrita*), the basis (*āśraya*) is made easy to comprehend. Furthermore, the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is explained as the sense of "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*);

the various assemblies and meanings are explained as the sense of "purity" (*viśuddhi*); and all transformations are explained as the sense of "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*). Thus, *tathatā* manifests the meaning of the "essence" (*svabhāva*).

The meaning of the nature (*dhātu*) and the principle (*artha*) shall be explained individually as appropriate; the meaning of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) will be explained extensively later.
[This refers to the passage] from "surpassing the ocean of noble practices" up to "because it is produced by causes."
The commentary states: There are two kinds of bodhi: first, wisdom (jñāna); second, abandonment (prahāṇa). This wisdom-bodhi arises from causes;

therefore, "all modes" (sarvākāra) refers to the noble practices of the ten stages, the One Vehicle, and the Three Vehicles. Within the One Vehicle alone, the varieties are numerous, and for this reason it is called an "ocean.
This follows the Sanskrit original; thus, according to these words, one should say "arising from... [omitted].
The "aeons" (*kalpa*) of all types of noble conduct throughout the ten stages, such as the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā*), refer to temporal divisions.
If based on a *mahākalpa*, the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) lasts for three incalculable aeons (*asaṃkhyeya*).

Only after passing through immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* great aeons—where "immeasurable" (*aprameya*) means "incalculable" (*asaṃkhya*), and "incalculable" means "the incalculable of the incalculable"—is that [stage] finally completed.
The *asaṃkhyeya* must necessarily be fulfilled through the causes of cultivation over three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;
that is to say, the Buddha’s *bodhi* arises only when the causes for all aspects of noble practice (*sarvākāra-ārya-caryā*) cultivated throughout incalculable eons have reached perfection.
This demonstrates that because the time is long and the practices cultivated are vast, it is only when the fruit of perfected cultivation is complete that it arises.
If one does not cultivate [the path] perfectly, the fruit will certainly not arise; because it reveals that from which the fruit proceeds, it is termed "cause" (*hetu*).

Furthermore, the Buddha’s *bodhi* has the meaning of "reaching the other shore. When one reaches all modes of knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) over countless eons, the ocean of noble conduct (*ārya-caryā-samudra*) is revealed through its long duration and extensive manifestation, thereby clarifying the profound cause from which it arises.
The term "reaching" (*prati*) also carries the sense of "transcending and ascending," and it should be understood as applying specifically according to the context.
Regarding the previous verse, the phrase "in every way" (*sarvākāra*) means that there is no stage among the various stages traversed that is not passed through.

The mention of the "ten stages" (*daśabhūmi*) specifically reveals the preeminent positions, while "every way" applies universally to all immeasurable and incalculable eons (*kalpa*). The meaning of the "ocean of noble conduct and understanding" is as follows:
there are three incalculable eons, not merely immeasurable ones; thus, even the *mahākalpa* (great eon) can be understood in the same manner.
The meaning of the names of the ten stages will be explained by the text itself below.
"Attaining all [perfections]" clarifies the meaning of the fruit (*phala*).
The commentary states: This cites the verse text and assigns it to six distinct meanings; because it brings benefit to the cause (*hetu*), it is called the "fruit."
This refers to the permanent abandonment [of the afflictions] up to their residual impressions (*vāsanā*).

The commentary states: To provide a general explanation of the meaning of the verse, prior to explaining the "attainment" (*prāpti*), it first clarifies the cause, namely that one realizes nirvana only by abandoning the obstructions.
Therefore, the obstructions are called *kleśāvaraṇa* (afflictive obstructions), which shroud the objects of knowledge and prevent wisdom from arising.

What is called the "obstruction to the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—whose essence consists of seeds, manifest states, and latencies—is precisely the causal obstruction, because it is the state of unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*) possessed by all [afflictions].
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 50, states that the Buddha, by abandoning this, is said to have abandoned "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*);

the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that abandoning this is called "abandonment in the three dwellings" (*tri-vihāra-prahāṇa*), distinguishing it from the two vehicles (*śrāvaka-yāna* and *pratyekabuddha-yāna*). Therefore, it is specifically designated as "habituation" (*vāsanā*) to establish its uniqueness.

The essential meaning of the two obstacles within consciousness has already been analyzed in detail, as explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and in the separate chapter of the ninth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
This is because one attains the mastery over the transformation [of the basis] that reaches the infinite.
The commentary states: This is the formal explanation of the verses regarding the meaning of "attainment" and so forth.

"Threefold Enlightenment" (*tri-sambodhi*) refers to the essence of what is realized, which is boundless, marvelous, and unsurpassed. These three terms are all words of praise. "Boundless" means vast and manifold;
"marvelous" means difficult to encounter; "unsurpassed" means most excellent. "Threefold Enlightenment" means the meaning of perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). By means of abandonment...
Having eliminated the habitual tendencies of the obstacles, one realizes the fruit of supreme awakening, which is vast, manifold, difficult to encounter, and most excellent.

This meaning reveals that one attains mastery over all dharmas of merit, or alternatively, that by completely severing the habitual tendencies of the obstacles, one realizes the rare and unsurpassed bodhi;
therein, the latter two of the four wisdoms regarding all objects constitute the ten masteries.

Arising therein manifests mastery over the object; as explained in the verse, although the qualities are immeasurable, only *bodhi* (awakening) is mentioned because wisdom is primary and awakening is supreme.
The distinctions in the meaning of the added or omitted characters may be understood by applying them according to the structure of the verse, and thus they are not assigned individually here.
"Skillful means of transformation and guidance... [up to] the meaning of manifesting activity.
The commentary states: These are called "activities" because they consist of six meanings belonging to the transformative functions of all Buddhas.
That is to say, from transcending what is not [the path]... up to the skillful means of subduing.
The commentary states: This explains the meaning of the inconceivable skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). With the exception of the Buddha, all others are termed "not omniscient" (*asarvajña*).
When the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) initiate these three wheels and so forth, they are known by them as their own objects.

However, the Buddha’s three wheels and transformative functions are vast and profound; they are not known by those [followers], and thus they are not their objects. This is because they are not [omniscient].

The objective realm is called "inconceivable" because it is not within the scope of others' knowledge or verbal discourse; thus, the *Daśacakra Sūtra* states that the Buddha’s three supreme wheels are unique to him and not shared by anyone else.
Because the Buddha can manifest the three wheels and other such skillful means in accordance with sentient beings, his mastery is described as "inconceivable.

These supernormal powers and transformations—namely, the transformation of the physical environment (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), the reading of minds (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*), and [the demonstration of the Dharma] (*anuśāsanī-prātihārya*)—are what are referred to here as "supernatural transformations."

"Discourse" refers to the miracle of discourse (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*); "instruction" refers to the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsana-prātihārya*). Regarding the statement that these three miracles are the three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*)—namely, the supernormal knowledge of the power of transformation (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*), the supernormal knowledge of the discernment of others' minds (*cetaḥ-paryāya-jñāna*), and the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna*)—one should distinguish how they correspond among the six supernormal knowledges. Briefly, they are analyzed through four gates: 1. Distinction by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). 2. Distinction by way of their basis (*āśraya*). 3. Distinction by way of their object (*ālambana*). 4. Distinction by way of their function (*karman*). First, the distinction by way of their intrinsic nature: the miracle of transformation has as its intrinsic nature the supernormal knowledge of the power of transformation; the miracle of discourse has as its intrinsic nature the supernormal knowledge of the discernment of others' minds; and the miracle of instruction has as its intrinsic nature the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows. This is because the miracle of transformation consists of the various modes of movement and transformation; the miracle of discourse consists of the teaching of the Dharma through words and phrases; and the miracle of instruction consists of the teaching of the Dharma through the various methods of training. Furthermore, the miracle of transformation is included within the supernormal knowledge of the power of transformation; the miracle of discourse is included within the supernormal knowledge of the discernment of others' minds; and the miracle of instruction is included within the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows. This is because the miracle of transformation is the manifestation of various forms of movement and transformation; the miracle of discourse is the teaching of the Dharma through words and phrases based on knowing the mental states of others;

and the miracle of instruction is the teaching of the Dharma through the various methods of training based on knowing the exhaustion of the outflows in oneself and others. Thus, it is established that these three miracles are subsumed within the three supernormal knowledges. Second, the distinction by way of their basis: all three miracles have the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their basis. Third, the distinction by way of their object: the miracle of transformation takes as its object the various phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). The miracle of discourse takes as its object the mental states of others. The miracle of instruction takes as its object the phenomena of the three realms (*traidhātuka*). Fourth, the distinction by way of their function: the miracle of transformation functions to cause sentient beings to generate faith and respect. The miracle of discourse functions to cause sentient beings to enter the path and attain realization. The miracle of instruction functions to cause sentient beings to sever afflictions and attain liberation. Thus, the three miracles are briefly analyzed through these four gates. First.
I. Establishing the Substance; II. Explaining the Names; III. Abolishing and Establishing; IV. Discerning the Characteristics.

Regarding the first, "the emergence of the rite," according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 69), among the first five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), those arising in ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*) do so because the power of their contaminated paths (*sāsrava-mārga*) is weak.
Those arising in those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are all produced by the powerful force of uncontaminated paths (*anāsrava-mārga*). Therefore, in this context, only the Tathāgata is mentioned.

That which arises is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-abhijñā*) is, as that treatise states, of the nature of the two knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and is exclusively untainted.
This statement refers specifically to [the knowledge] that takes the exhaustion of outflows as its object;

however, it may also be said to apply generally, because the mind-reading knowledge (*paracittajñāna*) and others achieved by the body through the exhaustion of outflows are also entirely untainted. Thus, the first five supernormal powers are the characteristics of the exhaustion of outflows.
Because they continue to be accomplished, they are all termed "untainted" (*anāsrava*); it is not that the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) does not accomplish the untainted.

By this, it is revealed that the three wheels herein are exclusively untainted, yet all three are worldly (*laukika*), because the wheel of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) instructs others.

Therefore, these three exist solely within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) based upon the levels of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Having wisdom as its nature, it is further said that because all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth, can serve as a basis for inducing it,
even though the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) also possess the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), Bodhisattvas and others may, by means of those [formless] minds,
comprehend all phenomena and likewise rely upon them to transform various objects and so forth, just as they do when abiding in the presence of a Buddha.

Because it is narrow, it is not called "universal" (*sāmānya*); whereas the mind of the form realm is broad—excluding the *anāgamya* stage—and possesses various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) because concentration and wisdom are balanced.
Since the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that these three wheels are universal, they are identical to the universal [minds] and do not exist in other stages.

Regarding the second explanation of the name: because this wisdom is endowed with majestic power (*prabhāva*), being the fruit produced by cultivation, its activity is difficult to fathom; thus it is so named.

That which is subject to transformation and instability by means of the *śakti* (potency) is called "change" (*vikāra*). Here, "change" refers to the object, while "potency" refers to the wisdom (*jñāna*).

The potency of change is the "transformer" (*vikartṛ*), and the transformation of the potency is the "transformed" (*vikārya*). Both are explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* compound where the first member is predominant (*upapada-śeṣa*). Alternatively, "potency itself is the change," wherein the change belongs to the transformer; this is explained according to the *karmadhāraya* compound.
In this context, only the first and third explanations are adopted. As for "wheel" (*cakra*), it means to crush and subdue.
Because it subdues the wrong views and other afflictions of others through its meaning, the "supernormal power" (*ṛddhi*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound [meaning "the wheel that is the power"].

"Mind" (*citta*) refers to the various distinctions within the minds of others; "recollection" (*vidyā*) means discernment (*vijñāna*). Discerning those minds is called "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*).
Although one can also recollect the mental factors (*caitasika*) of others, because the mind is primary, only "knowledge of others' minds" is mentioned. As for the mind...

Because it is a "recording" (*vijñapti*), it is also an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound); because the mind that records is itself the wheel, it is also a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).

"Instruction" (*anuśāsana*) means teaching so that the good may arise; "admonition" (*avavāda*) means exhorting so that evil may be extinguished. Instruction is itself admonition, and admonition is itself the wheel—all are *karmadhāraya* compounds.
Third, regarding the establishment and exclusion [of these categories]: the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi* states that by manifesting supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), one causes others to...

Having already generated a mind of respect, they listen attentively; through the power of prophetic declaration (*vyākaraṇa*), he discerns the distinctions in their mental conduct and characteristics and teaches them the sublime Dharma;
through the power of instruction (*avavāda*), he provides correct guidance according to their faculties, conduct, and stage of realization;

or, for those who have not yet resolved their minds toward enlightenment, he manifests miraculous transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) and, regarding those who do not practice correctly, he makes a prophetic declaration concerning their mental state.

There has not yet been any realization attained to serve as an instruction; furthermore, because body, mind, and speech transform through these three types of karma in their respective order, these three wheels are neither increased nor diminished.

Regarding the fourth point, the characteristics of the analytical exposition, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that there are briefly two kinds of characteristics for the first supernormal power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*):
first, the power of transformation (*pariṇāmana*), and second, the power of emanation (*nirmāṇa*). These can further transform other things, and they possess intrinsic nature.

To cause one thing to become another thing is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). To transform according to one's will into something that has never existed before is called "emanation" (*nirmāṇa*).

As for transformation, it refers to the eighteen transformations: (1) shaking, (2) blazing, (3) spreading, (4) manifestation, (5) transmutation, (6) coming and going, (7) contraction, (8) expansion, (9) entering all forms into one’s body, and (10) [becoming] identical...
13. Manifesting the eleven types of beings while concealing the twelfth; 14. Attaining mastery over what is to be done; 15. Restraining the supernatural powers of others;
16. Being able to bestow eloquence; 17. Being able to bestow recollection; 18.
Being able to bestow peace and happiness; 19. Emitting great radiance. Regarding those who perform emanations (*nirmāṇa*), there are three kinds: namely, emanating as a body, or...

Transforming into objects, speech, or bodies: transforming one's own or another's body so that it resembles the body of another, whether as a single form or in multiple forms—such categories as these include transforming into objects by manifesting what resemble mani-jewels, food, drink, utensils, and the like;
and transforming into speech by producing sublime or coarse sounds associated with oneself or others.

There are five distinctions in the mental characteristics of all sequential declarations (*anupada-vyākaraṇa*): first, the declaration of a mind that is both possessed of fetters (*paryavasthāna*) and possessed of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and a mind free from both fetters and latent tendencies;

second, the declaration of a mind that is defiled and characterized by wrong aspiration, and a mind that is undefiled and characterized by right aspiration; third, the declaration of minds pertaining to the five destinies (*gati*) of the desire, form, and formless realms;
fourth, the declaration of one [object] by means of one [mind], and the declaration of many [objects] by means of one [mind]; fifth, the [declaration of] all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...

Regarding the characteristics of the instructions for establishing all sentient beings—according to their respective faculties (indriya), whether superior or inferior, their various inclinations (adhimukti), and their various elements and behaviors (dhātu-carita)—within the bodhisattva practices, the Blessed One has taught five methods:

namely, prohibition, permission, admonition, censure, and consolation; or else, within this same context, the five methods such as demonstration and guidance. These constitute the meaning of the three wheels.

This is explained in detail in the fourth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the sixth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*, and the twenty-fifth and twenty-seventh chapters of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
"Showing and guiding" (*saṃdarśana*) refers to what was taught in the older translations as "showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening" (*saṃdarśana-samādāpana-samuttejana-saṃpraharṣaṇa*).
Alternatively, it is said that there are five phrases: causing one to leave desire, showing, instructing, encouraging, and gladdening; these manifest the [teachings].
The twelfth discourse explains the censure of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) in order to bring about detachment from craving; this is called "manifesting.

It manifests four kinds of true principles (*tattva-yukti*), which is called "manifestation. It causes those who have already attained faith and understanding (*adhimukti*) to correctly practice and receive [the teachings], which is called "instruction" (*anuśāsana*).

If they should become discouraged or regress, it rouses and impels them to advance, which is called "encouragement" (*samādāpana*). This is their practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*).

Praising [others] to make them joyful is called "rejoicing" (*ānanda*). That treatise further states that there are those who cause one to become free from desire (*vairāgya*) without demonstrating it;

those who cause one to feel aversion toward evil without teaching how to perform good; those who merely demonstrate [something] without causing one to become free from desire; and those who show forth virtues to encourage cultivation without obstructing their faults—all such combinations of categories can be understood.
Causing those who have not yet studied to study is called "instruction" (*avavāda*); causing those who have not yet progressed to progress is called "guidance" (*anuśāsana*).
The five types—encouraging, praising, exhorting, and rejoicing—are explained in detail as they appear there; all five are characteristics of instruction (*avavāda*).
Here, only the four gateways for cultivating the wholesome are mentioned, while the "causing one to leave desire" is not discussed.
Alternatively, this may refer only to the two types of guidance (*nidarśana*); all other three, as well as the ten activities in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, and so forth, are likewise included.
This refers to the manifestation of immeasurable means of discipline through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), as explained in the third and eighth [sections].

There are five kinds of immeasurables: first, the immeasurability of the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*), which refers to categories such as those with one leg and so forth, or the sixty-four types including those in the hells;
second, the immeasurability of the world (*loka-dhātu*), which refers to the realms of the ten directions; third, the immeasurability of the dharma-realm (*dharma-dhātu*), which refers to...
The immeasurable realm of those to be disciplined (*vineya-dhātu*) through the four categories of wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth— namely, the three vehicles and the five types of natures—

is distinguished from the aforementioned realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*), which includes both those with and without the nature [for liberation], because this realm consists exclusively of those with such a nature. Second,

the immeasurable realm of the skillful means for disciplining (*vinaya-upāya-dhātu*) refers to manifesting either supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) or prophetic declarations (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*) according to what is appropriate.
The Bodhisattva’s skillful means in manifesting instructions for the discipline of all beings is rooted in compassion and wisdom;
for the sake of sentient beings, they must rely upon places of residence to undergo transformation, as these beings achieve both defilement and purity through various dharmas.
Therefore, observing which types of beings are capable of reaching nirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva finally employs skillful expedients, whereby the five immeasurables do not diminish.
These categories of meaning are not expanded here, as they are explained at length in other chapters and in that treatise. "Taming" (*damana*) means harmonizing and guiding;
"subduing" (*vinaya*) means restraining and gathering. "Skillful means" (*upāya*) carries the sense of being adept.

Thus, by means of these three types of miraculous transformations—harmonizing, controlling, subduing, and gathering—one is called "skillful in means" (*kauśalya*), which refers to the method of taming among the immeasurables.
Thus, the realms are immeasurable. The "three wheels" (trimaṇḍala) are demonstrated as the manifestation of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya);

this refers to the essence of such categories, whether they have measure or not, and the various skillful means for taming beings, including those that do not involve taming, which are specifically assigned to the three wheels.
"Because those who can be guided can be transformed into purity. The commentary states:
This explains the meaning of "transforming through guidance. "Those who can be transformed" refers to sentient beings who are not devoid of the potential for Buddhahood (*gotra*).

Among the five immeasurables, this refers to the immeasurable of the realm of those to be disciplined (*vineya-dhātu*), because that very mind-realm of both the discipliner and the disciplined is [the basis].

Regarding the "Dharmatā-tathatā-dhātu" (the realm of the true suchness of the nature of phenomena): it is called "nature" (*dhātu*) because it is the nature of the mind's own essence; alternatively, it is called a "realm" (*dhātu*) because it is the self-substance of the dependent mind.

By means of such immeasurable skillful means of subduing as the three wheels and so forth, one guides those sentient beings who are capable of being transformed, causing their true mind-realm to be free from the defilement of adventitious obstructions. Thus, by severing the dependent mind, they attain purity.
Because it is associated with the Dharma-jewel, which is immeasurable and rare. The commentary states:

"Transcending conceptual investigation" does not refer to the four types of conceptual investigation (*catasraḥ paryeṣaṇāḥ*), for these four exist only prior to the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Since the causes cultivated in that stage are not merely what is transcended, that which is transcended here refers to transcending them as appropriate; however, it is not an object of those [four] cognitions.
All of these are the measure of this transcendent meaning; because their practice is boundless and exceeds all calculation, they transcend these two [categories], and thus are called "boundless.
Because the causal practices are not singular, they are termed "various. Because [practices] such as giving away one's head and eyes are not easily performed, they are called "difficult.

Because these practices involve oppression, they are called "austere practices" (*duṣkaracaryā*). This reveals that the causes are immeasurable and rare, and thus [the fruit] produced is [immeasurable].

The fruit is furthermore immeasurably rare; that is to say, because of these boundless superior practices, there arise the power of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth, which are likewise boundless.
It is said that [the Buddha] is "endowed with" such treasures of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*).

As for the term "endowment," it means that the general conventional person (*pudgala*) is associated with specific real qualities, or it carries the sense of accomplishment—that is, the general [state] accomplishes the specific qualities.
Therefore, since the fruit may accord with the nature of the primary cause, there is a sense of mutual conformity between them that exists at all times;
herein, however, only the correspondence of enjoyment is discussed, as has already been explained previously by the statement "because it is produced.

Alternatively, this passage mentions the "produced" because the *dharmakāya* is able to give rise to transformative activity (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), such that all three are fully present; while the text here mentions only the *saṃbhogakāya*, two types are provisionally cited within this context.

The boundless, inexhaustible, and ultimate limits of emptiness are omitted here for brevity; the ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and so forth will be explained in the lower text of the fourteenth fascicle.
[This is] because it is the basis for benefiting both oneself and others.
The commentary states: Within this, there are two parts; the first is a general attribution, and the following is a detailed explanation. This is the initial passage.
The subsequent correlation can be understood [by the reader]. Regarding the "basis" (upadhi), it extends to "without distinction."

The commentary states that the detailed explanation of the text below consists of three parts: first, the explanation of the basis (*āśraya*); second, the explanation of the three benefits; and third, the conclusion regarding their distinctions.

This explanation of the basis follows the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, which states that because the meaning of "basis" (*āśraya*), "body" (*kāya*), and "collection" (*caya*) are identical, they are collectively termed "body" (*kāya*).
Thus, the term "basis" and the term "body" are not distinct.
"Benefiting both self and others" (up to "speaking according to what is superior").
The commentary states: This explains the three benefits; first, the general meaning of the explanation is given, followed by the specific explanation.

Regarding this general meaning, the three benefits that are taught are spoken of in terms of their predominance; it is not that they are fixed as such in principle. This shall be understood further below.
This refers to the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) [up to] the noble wealth of the Dharma.
The commentary states: regarding the detailed explanation below based on the superior causes, there are two types. The self-enjoyment body dwells in its own Dharma assembly;
that which dwells in other assemblies is the other-enjoyment body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), both of which are able to experience the most supreme and foremost [Dharma].
Because it is the vast and profound noble wealth of the Dharma, it is comprised solely within self-benefit;
the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other treatises state that there are seven types of noble wealth—namely, faith, ethical discipline, shame, dread of blame, learning, renunciation, and wisdom.

That [text] speaks of seven kinds based on their predominant functions, whereas here, we speak of them as "noble wealth" because they are the requisites for the noble ones' merit, and because they give rise to joy when gathered in a great assembly. This is based on [the perspective of]...

In reality, this body also truly benefits others, and its increase in the experience of bliss differs from the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), which frequently manifest through supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) for the sake of others.
According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it encompasses both types of benefit.

Therefore, this treatise speaks of it in terms of its predominant quality, stating that because the experience of the bliss of the Dharma increases, it is called "enjoyment" (*saṃbhoga*). Furthermore, it is said to be in the midst of a great assembly, referring to itself.
Because it is the assembly of the vast *dharmatā*, it pertains solely to the body for one's own benefit.
As for the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), it is [so called] because it performs what ought to be done.

The commentary states: "Like" (*yathā*) has the sense of "for example"; "craftsman" refers to those skilled in arts, namely the practitioners of illusion; "Buddha’s transformation body" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya*.
"Benefiting beings according to their forms, that which was non-existent suddenly appears; this illusory artifice is no different from an illusory phenomenon.

Since [the transformation body] arises from the wisdom of skillful means (*kauśalyajñāna*), the analogy of that [illusion] is cited to reveal the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Furthermore, because the craft of skillful action can manifest various conditions and images, the transformation body is likewise like this;
thus it is raised as an analogy. Regarding the phrase 'equal to that illusory artifice,' the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* explains that the word 'equal' refers to..."
Among the three types of bodies, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)— which, like a master artisan,
manifests within all worlds simultaneously and in uninterrupted succession, appearing and disappearing, being born again and establishing emanations without ever resting—
is so called because it takes forms solely for the benefit of others, manifesting according to their inclinations. This is named the transformation body.
Regarding the *svābhāvika-kāya* (Self-nature Body) [up to] the *sādhāraṇa-dharmakāya* (Shared Dharma Body):
The commentary states that the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* explains that because it ascends to the ultimate limit and never regresses, it is called "Sugata" (*śubha-gata*).

The first part of the term means "excellent" (*śubha*), and the latter means "gone" (*gata*). It is called "gone" because one has already arrived; thus, there is no regression. Alternatively, "ascended" (*udgata*) refers to...

Furthermore, because he has passed away (*gata*), the *Vijñaptimātra* and other treatises state that while the various bodies of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) and transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) are each produced by distinct causes and possess distinct,

substantially existent natures with differences, they are said to be "without difference" in terms of their non-dual grasping, their similar benefit and happiness, and the equality of their intentions and activities.
Because the *svabhāva-kāya* alone is shared by all Buddhas, it is called the "Well-Gone" (*sugata*).
The *dharmakāya* is shared by all because its essence is the most extremely subtle [state]. The commentary states:
Because it obstructs only the fruit of Buddhahood, the seeds and habitual tendencies that are extremely subtle are not of a single kind; rather, they constitute all obstacles.
That dharmakāya is attained by transforming and abandoning the basis of all seeds, latencies, and heavy obstructions (*dausthulya*) of the two hindrances;

because it has as its essence the suchness (*tathatā*) obtained through that transformation which is free from heavy obstructions, the true reality attained in the other ten stages is not called the dharmakāya,
for the seeds and latencies of all hindrances have not yet been exhausted.
"Regarding the benefit of self and others... until the attainment of the remaining bodies.

The commentary states: "The characteristics of the two benefits are difficult to know within one's own essence; they are illustrated by the fact that through the attainment of these two remaining bodies, the distinctions between the two benefits are revealed, and both benefits are shown to be universal.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that this *svabhāva-kāya* (self-nature body) is quiescent and blissful."
Because it takes self-benefit as its predominant condition while universally benefiting sentient beings, it belongs to the benefit of others;

furthermore, because it serves as the basis for both types of bodies that benefit both self and others, it is subsumed within both benefits. This is explained again by way of manifesting its function, and moreover, because here the teaching is stated according to what is preeminent.
These three Buddha-bodies constitute the meaning of their differentiation. The commentary states:
In the third section of the sub-text, the differentiation of the three bodies is briefly analyzed through three gates:

first, the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*); second, the explanation of their names; and third, their establishment and rejection. Regarding the determination of their essential nature: first, the *svābhāvika-kāya* (Self-nature Body) consists of all Tathāgatas...

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* explains that the essence [of the svabhāvakāya] consists of the support for the enjoyment and transformation bodies within the true, pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and is endowed with infinite, true, and eternal merits;
it is described as "eternal, unchanging, and consisting solely of consciousness" (*vijñaptimātra*).
It is the actual nature of all phenomena, or the common self-substance of all Buddhas, and is called the "svabhāvakāya" because it is the basis upon which great meritorious qualities depend.
It is also called the *Dharmakāya*. The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that when it is not separated from the storehouse of afflictions (*kleśakośa*), it is called the *Tathāgatagarbha*;

when it is separated from the afflictions, it is called the *Dharmakāya*. Although some also claim that the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) constitutes its essence, this is not the correct interpretation and is therefore not recorded here.
Next, the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) has two categories: first, the self-enjoyment [body], which is cultivated over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

The body of ultimate purity and permanence, which arises from the boundless, true merits produced by the accumulation of provisions, has as its essential nature all the real virtues of the four wisdoms;
because it experiences the bliss of the Dharma for itself, it is called the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Although some claim that the middle two wisdoms constitute the substance of this body, this is not the correct interpretation. Therefore...

It is not said that the second, the *parasaṃbhoga-kāya* (body for the enjoyment of others), has as its essential nature the manifestation of a body shown by [the Buddha] to great bodhisattvas in a purely pure land through the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), so that others may enjoy the bliss of the Dharma; this is also called the *saṃbhoga-kāya*.
According to the correct principle, it is taught that the mental states of the four wisdoms manifest as the Buddha-body for great bodhisattvas, which is explained as the *parasaṃbhoga-kāya*.

Because the wisdom that observes the manifestation of mastery in severing doubts is the basis for equality; because the essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*) is the object of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*);

and because the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) manifests great supernormal powers—since the objects and functions of these four Buddha-wisdoms are all-pervasive—the wisdom of equality possesses the strongest power of activity in manifesting this body, thereby striking forth the mirror-like wisdom to manifest the body.
Because they are equal, the treatise speaks of their principle as being fixed; yet this is not so, for this body would otherwise lack a fundamental essence.

To resolve doubts, preach the Dharma, manifest supernatural powers, and initiate transformations, the subsequent *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) takes as its substance the various forms manifested according to what is appropriate for all sentient beings who have not yet reached the [bodhisattva] stages, within both pure and impure lands, by means of the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom that accomplishes activities).
By nature, it manifests various kinds of transformative activities for the benefit of sentient beings; therefore, it is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Body).

In principle, this body has as its essence the transformed objects manifested by the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*). However, because these characteristics are coarse and accord with the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks), the treatise speaks of it specifically.

It does not explicitly indicate that the *vipākaja-kāya* (Retribution Body) and the *nirmāṇakāya* are manifestations of the [other] wisdoms; yet, this interpretation is logically certain and thus superior.

Alternatively, because this body and the bodies for the enjoyment of others each manifest a single wisdom sufficient to benefit sentient beings, without requiring anything else, the treatise does not speak of two [bodies].
Regarding the explanation of the names: the term "Dharmakāya" (Dharma-body) is explained solely as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound, meaning "the body of the Dharma.

Alternatively, the *svābhāvikakāya* (Essential Body) may be explained as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) compound, meaning "the essential nature itself is the body," or as a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compound.
Because the *svābhāvikakāya* (nature body) is the body itself, its *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body) is explained by the *karmadhāraya* compound.
As for the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), it is also of two kinds: first, that which consists of the emanator—namely, the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom) and so forth;

this is called the "emanation body" by the *tatpuruṣa* compound [meaning "the body of the emanator"]. Second, that which consists of the emanated object itself; this is the *karmadhāraya* compound [meaning "the emanation that is the body"]. Three.

Regarding the distinctions between the abandoned and the established, the realized and the realizer, the ultimate and the conventional, principle and phenomenon, the primordially existent and that which is produced through cultivation, and the differences in nature and characteristics, the first two bodies (the *svābhāvika-kāya* and *sambhoga-kāya*) are established.

Furthermore, based on the distinctions of self-benefit and benefit for others, their essential natures and functions, the transformed and the transformed-into, the increase of wisdom and compassion, and the differences between the Great and Small Vehicles, the *nirmāṇa-kāya* is separately established. These two pairs of doctrinal gateways each possess immeasurable [subdivisions] that cannot be fully enumerated.
Although it is said that there is only one [Buddha-body], because its meanings are manifold and its categories are limited to these alone, it cannot be said to be many.

Furthermore, because its nature (*svabhāva*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and functions (*karman*) correspond to the world’s body—which possesses substance (*tattva*), form (*ākṛti*), and capability (*samarthya*)—the three bodies (*trikāya*) are established; they are neither more nor less than this.

Other thematic gateways are explained in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Tri-kāya-śāstra*, and other treatises such as the *Prakaraṇa*, the upper section cites the six meanings and provides a detailed commentary on the text;
the lower section explains the Dharma and the Saṅgha, which also universally extends to the praise of taking refuge.
One should know that herein the merits of the Dharma and the Saṅgha are also praised.
The commentary states: "The former is general and the latter is specific. This general section belongs to the textual passage;

the intended meaning here is that, within the preceding praise of the Buddha by means of six aspects, there is a pervasive praise of both the Dharma and the Saṅgha. Since the first three Jewels were already universally encompassed in the praise, they are subsequently included within the act of taking refuge and paying homage.
Therefore, the general refuge is taken in the Dharma and the Saṃgha; this term also encompasses praise. For this reason, one subsequently takes refuge in all three Jewels.
As for the Jewel of the Dharma, it is because [all things] are subsumed within it.
The commentary states: This reveals that the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the Dharma-jewel which is praised is the principle (*dharma*).

Because it is the cause for practice and the fruit of realization, its meaning as a name, activity, and so forth is consistent with the teachings; the distinctions among them can be understood from what precedes.

Therefore, it says "and so forth" (*ādi*), as these meanings are subsumed within the Dharma-jewel. By means of these six meanings, they also universally praise the Dharma, for apart from this, there is no other Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
The Sangha Jewel is so called because it arises from training in accordance with this [Dharma].

The commentary states: within the exposition of the characteristics of the Sangha Jewel as that which is praised, it is precisely because it is the cause for the ocean of noble practices to be transcended that the Buddha’s entry into the Sangha is not mentioned as being subsumed therein;
furthermore, the preceding chapter spoke of the teaching of the Buddha Bhagavat.
Because the basis [of the Sangha] relies upon the study of the Dharma, it is said that the Sangha arises through cultivation based on this Dharma.
Since the Dharma to be studied has already been praised, the Sangha who studies it has also been praised; apart from this, there is no other Sangha of the One Vehicle.

Although the aforementioned True Principle is identical to the Sangha of the same essence (*samatā-kāya*), for fear that the praise might not be exhaustive, the Sangha of distinct essence (*prthak-kāya*) is mentioned—or rather, to manifest the Oneness [of the Sangha].

The Vehicle of the Multitude (*yāna*) is distinct from the Buddha’s essence because it consists of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); the Vehicle of the Single Path (*ekayāna*) is distinct from the Buddha’s essence because it consists of the Saṃgha.

Since this praise refers to the Saṃgha who follows and trains [in that path], it is not directed toward ordinary beings; as it speaks of "sages" (*ārya*), it is a general praise of the Triple Gem of the Single Vehicle.

Because this constitutes a general homage, within the act of taking refuge, one simultaneously takes refuge in both the general and the specific. By this, it is revealed that the object of homage and the object of praise encompass both the common and the particular.

The characteristics [of the One Vehicle] do not pervade the two vehicles; furthermore, the preceding praise of the One Vehicle’s principle and wisdom may be so designated because they are not found in other vehicles.
The subsequent homage and prostration constitute a general salutation to the Three Vehicles, for those with power and those with impartial minds are all worthy of refuge.
