[The text] from "Answer" up to "my own essential nature" (*svātmabhāva*) is explained as follows:

the entirety above constitutes the questions and answers of the root treatise, wherein the two characters "to manifest" (*pradarśana*) serve as a thread that贯通 (penetrates) through the following four bodies.

"Endowment" refers to the self as form (*rūpa*), because it is produced as a basis; "experience" refers to the self as feeling (*vedanā*), because it is the recipient of sensation; "expression" refers to the self as perception (*saṃjñā*), because it grasps mental images;

"activity" refers to the self as formations (*saṃskāra*), because it performs volitional actions; and "the essence of the self" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*), because it is capable of discerning objects.
Thus, "object" (*artha*) signifies the meaning of the essential nature.
Regarding these five [categories], up to "the matter of the mark of self," the commentary states:
In the following text there are two parts. First, the Master explains the underlying reason for the preceding meaning:
because it belongs to the self, it is called "that which belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*); because it is the very essence of the self, it is called "the mark of self" (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "the body as a basis" (*kāyāśraya*), it is subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

The commentary states that there are three parts to the subsequent detailed explanation of this meaning: first, the explanation of the aggregate of form; second, the indication of the [remaining] three aggregates;

and third, the explanation of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). Within this explanation of the aggregate of form, that which is the basis for my own existence—the physical sense organs—is called the "body."
The form aggregate (*rūpaskandha*), which is the object of the body, is called one's "possessions" (*upakaraṇa*). How can the consciousness aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*) be considered the basis?
There are two kinds of bases for the name-body (*nāmakāya*): first, that which performs activity (*kāraka*), and second, the place of residence (*sthāna*).
Consciousness is said to be the basis for the activity of the self, while the sense faculties (*indriya*) are said to be the place where the self resides.

Because these two bases are distinct, they do not contradict one another. Alternatively, it may be explained that because the sense faculties (*indriya*) possess the sense of being an accumulation, they are called "body" (*kāya*);
and because the objects are what are utilized by the sense faculties, they are called "possessions" (*upadhi*).

While this interpretation may be acceptable in meaning, according to this [analysis], the body and possessions are not "mine," because the sense faculties can utilize the objects but the self cannot; thus, the objects are received by the faculties and not by the self.
Furthermore, it is proclaimed as "mine," and it is said that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is entirely that which is experienced.

This is because the five types of material sense-faculties (*indriya*) are experienced by way of being grasped and supported, and the various material objects (*viṣaya*) are experienced by way of being the objective referents (*ālambana*).
Therefore, as previously stated, this is correct.
The aggregates such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth will be explained under the section on their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states: "This refers to the fourth gate of characteristics concerning the three aggregates; it shall be analyzed in detail there.
As for the meaning of the object of the characteristic of self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa-vastu-artha*), it is that upon which those [aggregates] depend."

The commentary states that the explanation of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has three parts: first, a general explanation; second, an inquiry into the cause; and third, the manifestation of the intended meaning.

This general explanation states: the aggregate of consciousness is the "body" (*ātman*)—the basis—for those other four aggregates, and it is the "function" of the "mine" (*mama-ātman*) consisting of the other three aggregates.
Thus, consciousness is described as the basis, and consciousness is described as the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the self.
Why is this so? It is stated:
This inquiry [seeks to determine] whether the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) constitutes the essence of the self (*ātman*).
Worldly sentient beings, from this point up to [the verse], conceive of a self and cling to what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).
The commentary states: Because most people in the world conceive of consciousness as the "self" that performs cognition and possesses objects of knowledge,
and because they conceive of the other four aggregates as "belonging to the self" (ātmīya) since they serve as the basis for consciousness— just like a house or other such things—
they conceive of a self within these aggregates in twenty ways, sixty-five ways, and so forth, pervading all five aggregates.
Regarding the question, "Do you now merely say that consciousness is the self?"—this statement primarily refers to the view that consciousness is the self.
However, among the twenty types of views and so forth, these are either specific reckonings regarding each individual aggregate (*skandha*) rather than reckonings regarding the other aggregates;

therefore, they are not mentioned here. This does not mean that there is no reckoning of a self within the other aggregates at all. The intent here is to state generally that the world mostly reckons consciousness as the self.
The aggregates constitute the self; form constitutes my body; I am the possessor who experiences objects; I am the one who initiates speech;

I am the one who performs all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). Since feeling, perception, and formations are all functions of the self, and the self is their master, [the opponent] now maintains this attachment.
To refute it, it is said that there are five aggregates: the body is the basis for consciousness, or its substance is an accumulation, and it possesses the sense faculties.
Objects are not my body; feeling is that which experiences and receives; perception is that which gives rise to speech; volition is that which constructs phenomena;
and consciousness is that which cognizes and discerns. Since none of these constitute my essence, for this reason the five aggregates are neither diminished nor increased.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, chapter five, states: "Because these five types encompass all matters of saṃsāric flux, they are neither diminished nor increased."
The expanded text is identical in meaning to this.
Question: For what reason is it said that the *dhātu* (elements) have the nature of being objects of experience (*upabhoga*)?

The commentary states: This is the second section clarifying the *dhātus* within the "Gate of Abolition and Establishment" (*pratyākhyāna-vyavasthāpana-mukha*). Below this original treatise, the Master [Yaśomitra] provides his explanation and so forth.
The term "these" refers to the six consciousnesses because they can maintain their own substance; thus, the meaning of this passage should be read as follows:
by means of the body and its faculties, the past and present six modes of activity (ṣaḍāyatana) are maintained, while those same six modes of activity maintain experience (upabhoga).
"The body" refers to the six objects, beginning with form (*rūpa*).

The commentary states that the explanation of the text has two parts: first, revealing the nature of that which sustains; second, explaining the meaning of that which sustains. There are two types of nature:

first, the bodily faculties (*kāyendriya*) possess the capacity to sustain the six modes of activity; second, the six modes of activity themselves possess the capacity to sustain themselves. This is what is meant by the statement.
The body (*kāya*) has the sense of being the basis for consciousness, not the sense of being an accumulation.

Since the mind (*manas*) is not a material obstruction that can be accumulated, it is said here that "possessing" means either providing the conditions for the arising of consciousness or providing the necessary equipment; this is because the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) also possesses derivative matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
"Past and present six modes of activity (up to) what are called the six consciousnesses.

Commentary: This reveals that the dharmas supported by the body and its faculties constitute their essential nature, and it reveals the meaning of the six consciousnesses as being able to maintain their own nature through the sense of shifting and flowing.
Since consciousness perishes moment by moment and its activity rapidly fades away, it is analogous to how consciousness, in other instances, is frequently interrupted.

Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the name "independent activity" (*svatantra-vṛtti*) and "activity with aspects and objects" (*sākāra-sālambana-vṛtti*), this passage intends to clarify that the body and its equipment (*kāya-pariṣkāra*) are the supported phenomena (*dharmin*) which are maintained by the supporting factors (*dharmas*).
These are the six activities of the past and present; for it is by means of those supporting factors that they are brought to experience.
Moreover, it clarifies that the essence of the six consciousnesses possesses the capacity to maintain their functions, or that the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) maintains them.

Because the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part) and so forth can maintain their own essence and experience objects, the third fascicle [of the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*] and the fifth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* both state that one portion of all [dharmas] is future. Why, then, is the future not mentioned here among the eighteen *dhātu*s?

The nature of these realms actually extends to the future; however, because their essence and function have not yet arisen, their capacity to maintain [their own nature] is obscured. Furthermore, as for the future...

The meaning of consciousness having no "function of maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*) is not explained here in brief; rather, it is because the past and present, whose essence and function have already arisen, clearly manifest the meaning of being able to maintain.
Furthermore, since the arising of consciousness's function can be said to be capable of maintaining, the treatise speaks of it specifically in this way.

However, when it is said that the future also possesses "elements" (*dhātu*), this is because each maintains its own essence; thus, there is no contradiction in not speaking of the "function of maintaining" in that context.
"Because that which can maintain [the faculties] takes the objects of perception as its basis.
The commentary states: The following explains the function of "maintaining. This interpretation holds that the sense organs (indriya) and their objects (viṣaya) maintain the six consciousnesses;
since they serve as the support (āśraya) and the equipment (sambhāra), this constitutes the meaning of "maintaining."
"Because the six consciousnesses of the past and present do not abandon their own characteristics.

The commentary states: This explains that the six consciousnesses are not merely supported [by the body]; they themselves can also support [the body], because they do not abandon their own characteristics and are capable of initiating activity.
This clarifies that the term "capable of supporting" mentioned above in the *Mūla-śāstra* regarding the six modes of conduct does not refer solely to the physical faculties.
The six consciousnesses are able to maintain [the body], and their own essence is likewise able to maintain it; this term "able to maintain" (能持) applies both to the higher and lower levels.

Furthermore, it reveals that the phrase "possessing the aggregates" (*skandha-saṃgraha*) mentioned below in the root treatise implies that not only are the aggregates themselves able to maintain the past and present six modes of activity, but it also reveals that the essence of the six consciousnesses—which are the objects maintained—is itself that which maintains them. Therefore, it should be understood as follows.
The fact that one world-system supports another does not mean they are different world-systems; this is called "support" (*dhṛti*) because it relies on causal support, not because it supports itself.

Otherwise, consciousness would lack the capacity for support, which would contradict the meaning of the "elements" (*dhātu*). Alternatively, [the term] may rely on the sense of "that which can support" rather than the sense of "intrinsic nature as support," and thus there is no contradiction.
Now, by means of this principle, the interpretation of the establishment and abolition of the elements (*dhātu*) should accord with the original explanation and harmonize the two schools.
It should be understood that they are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because [they possess the capacity for] such [functions].
The commentary states: Although the meanings of "element" are manifold, here it is explained as "the cause capable of sustaining the fruit.

This is because it universally establishes the objective spheres of the practice of the three vehicles; since the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are mutually related in their capacity to sustain one another, neither fewer nor more than eighteen can be stated. Therefore, only eighteen are taught.

The *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Based on this teaching, one is able to enter into the selflessness of the *pudgala*, but it does not say that one enters into the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
therefore, it speaks only of eighteen [bases]. If they were maintained solely by themselves, why would there be only eighteen?
Each possesses three aspects; thus, there are two meanings: first, maintaining itself; second, maintaining others."
Question: For what reason [is it] "the gate of growth"? Commentary:

This is the third section, the Gate of Abolition and Establishment, which clarifies the *āyatana* (bases) from the main text of the treatise. "Arising" (*jāti*) refers to initial growth; "growth" (*vṛddhi*) refers to long-standing growth;

"gate" (*mukha*) refers to the source from which things emerge. It is the gateway through which the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) of past and present existences arise.

Because the characteristics and functions of future consciousness are manifest, it is established as a "base" (*āyatana*). However, according to the actual reality of the Mahāyāna, cause and effect belong to the same time-period, and the body possesses the capacity for the simultaneous arising of consciousness in every moment;
since this meaning is hidden [in the present context], it is not mentioned here. Because the future fruit is manifest, it is said that [consciousness] arises therein.
This is not the same as the Sautrāntika school’s assertion that cause and effect occur at different times; such is not the case for the base of mind (*manāyatana*).
It certainly cannot be established, because it is not admitted that [the basis] of the past and present could arise in the future;

furthermore, the principle that "a portion of all things is called the future" is also untenable, because it is not admitted that the future possesses a body and sense-faculties as the meaning of being a "basis" (*āyatana*).
Therefore, this passage merely indicates that the past and present body and faculties serve as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the arising of future consciousness.

This explanation does not exhaust the full meaning of the principle. Furthermore, this interpretation clarifies that the future body, which possesses the capacity to produce future consciousness, is designated as a "base" (*āyatana*) because it constitutes a simultaneous cause and effect;
it does not refer to the past or present, which can produce the future, for that would contradict our own school’s tenet that the characteristic of arising belongs only to the present.

Although the status of being a "base" is established for the past and present as well, the term "arising" (*jāti*) applies exclusively to the future, as it refers specifically to that which is about to come into existence.

Therefore, it is not the case that the past and present lack any essence whatsoever. This interpretation of the treatise is excellent for the present age, as it does not contradict our fundamental tenets.

That which sustains the function of producing consciousness is established by the name "dhātu" (element). In the future, because it sustains [consciousness] in a latent state, it is not called a "dhātu"; rather, it is called an "āyatana" (base) because it is the source from which [consciousness] arises.

It is necessary to establish this because the future is defined by the potential for what is to arise, while the past and present are defined by what has already arisen; thus, while the meaning of the future is implicit, the meaning of the past and present is explicit.
It is not said that the dhātus and āyatanas of the past and present are real entities that also pervade the three periods of time;

for the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 3, section 9 on the "Explanation of Consciousness," as well as sections 55, 56, and 69, and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, fascicle 5, all state that the dhātus and āyatanas pervade the three periods of time.
This is the original text of the treatise cited above, while the following is the commentary by the Master.
This means that just as it was for the past and present [up to the point mentioned], so it is here.

The commentary states: "The meaning is 'object' (*viṣaya*). To explain: because they serve as the basis by which the body and its faculties can produce future consciousnesses and experience objects, they are established with the name 'base' (*āyatana*).
This refers back to the manner in which the six consciousnesses of the past and present experience [objects] as the eyes and other sense-bases."

The meaning of "constituting its realm" (*dhātu*) is now established; it is precisely by means of the future consciousness and its objects of experience that the sense bases (*āyatana*) serve as the gateway for growth, thereby manifesting the meaning of "base.

Thus, it is said: "and so too [the others]. That which is supported refers back to the aforementioned constituting of the realm, while from "the future" onwards, the meaning of the base is properly established.
Regarding the statement "only" (*mātra*) up to "the consciousness of the aspect of enjoyment," the commentary states:

This explains the word "only" in the response of the root treatise as having the sense of exclusion and retention (*pariccheda*). It means that the definition of a "sphere" (*āyatana*) is established based solely on the faculties and objects, and not based on the six consciousnesses.
As for the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*), it is defined as "holding" (*dhṛti*); since all functions of holding are called "elements," they are so named because they give rise to [phenomena].

The locus (*āyatana*) is established by way of its function of producing [consciousness]; it should be understood as having a self-nature that maintains itself, not merely maintaining its own function.

For this reason, the six [bases] also receive the name "elements" (*dhātu*). Since the locus is that which produces, and the self-nature does not produce, the eye-consciousness and so forth are not established as loci.

Furthermore, the body and its faculties are separately designated as "gates" for the production of consciousness; although the substance of consciousness and its function of production are one, they are distinguished as gates based on their different meanings.

The inferior interpretation states that [the six consciousnesses] are not established as bases (*āyatana*) because they arise simultaneously with their objects; since they are capable of producing consciousness, they should be called bases, and thus are termed "causes" (*hetu*).

Because they reside in a different time period, they are called "mind" (*manas*) and are not termed "consciousness. Since they obtain their bases, they are also called "bases"; for this reason, the six consciousnesses are not established as bases.
The faculties and objects are capable of producing consciousness and reside in the same time period, so they are called bases; consciousness is capable of producing [subsequent moments].
Regarding the point that mental factors (caitta) simultaneously obtain their bases (āyatana), this meaning should be carefully examined and deliberated:

although there is no sequential order in the future world, that which can produce consciousness is itself designated as a "base"; therefore, the mind-base (manāyatana) is also established in the future world.
Question: What is meant by "appropriating aggregates" (*upādāna-skandha*)? [The text continues] up to: "is called appropriating aggregates. Commentary:
This sequence is the third explanation of the verse’s term "appropriating" (*upādāna*). It is a section of questions and answers concerning specific names.

While the three categories of phenomena (*triskandha*) generally include both the untainted (*anāsrava*) and other types, the Noble Ones speak of them as "appropriating aggregates," "elements" (*dhātu*), and "bases" (*āyatana*) only when they are defiled (*sāsrava*) and not pure; therefore, this is explained.

The alternative names and the force of the phrasing have two parts: first, the analysis of the aggregates of grasping (*upādāna-skandha*); second, the analysis of the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*). Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the analysis of the cause of the name;
second, the analysis of the essence of grasping; third, the analysis of the characteristics of grasping. This is the first [section].

"Combination" (*saṃnipāta*) has the meaning of harmony, the meaning of conformity, the meaning of non-separation, and the meaning of mutual supportive power. Because the aggregates and grasping are mutually harmonious and conforming...
Because they are inseparable and cause further growth, they are established as "appropriation" (*upādāna*). They arise from appropriation, like fire from grass or chaff;

they can produce appropriation, like a tree that bears flowers and fruit; they are bound to appropriation, like a subject to a sovereign. These three [explanations] are all *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds.

In this treatise, however, it is stated that when desire and greed (*kāmarāga*) have not yet manifested their own essence, they are called "appropriation"; thus, they are simply the aggregates (*skandha*).
The term "clinging" (upādāna) arises from the act of grasping; it does not denote other meanings. However, logically there is no contradiction, as it is explained according to its predominant sense.

Furthermore, while the aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandha) are necessarily aggregates (skandha), there are aggregates that are not aggregates of clinging, because the untainted (anāsrava) aggregates do not conjoin with clinging.
"Grasping" (upādāna) refers to all forms of desire and lust (*kāmarāga*).

The commentary states: this reveals the nature of grasping as being characterized by craving (*tṛṣṇā*) associated with desire, which—within the aggregates (*skandha*)—either initiates karma or moistens rebirth, whether as an object of focus or arising simultaneously, mutually increasing [the afflictions]. This is according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 65.
Furthermore, since it is taught that craving alone is designated as "clinging" (*upādāna*), the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states that the increase of craving is called clinging.

Although various treatises explain that the four types of clinging (*catvāry upādānāni*) encompass all afflictions (*kleśa*), within the context of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), during the stage of pervasive increase and moistening that leads to rebirth, greed (*rāga*) is preeminent;
therefore, it alone is termed "clinging. This is not like the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), where [all] six [types of craving] are considered to encompass all afflictions.
The *Paryāya-paṭala* explains that there are one matter, two stages, three times, four realms, five searches, and six kinds;

this is discussed further in the sixth fascicle of that treatise. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that if that which grasps, that which is grasped, and that for the sake of which there is grasping are all termed "grasping" (*upādāna*).
Why? Because of not abandoning sensual desire (up to the point of not abandoning it).
The commentary states: This explains its characteristic as taught in the sūtra, which says that craving is of four kinds:
craving for the present body, craving for a future body, craving for renewed existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*), and craving accompanied by joy for present objects.

Because one gives rise to various forms of longing and craving toward future objects, this term "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) refers collectively to its ability to draw forth and prevent the relinquishing of the aggregates (*skandha*) across both time periods.

Although craving can also arise with respect to past objects, this statement specifically describes the "longing and defilement" directed toward the future; thus, the name "grasping" (*upādāna*) must be established [to distinguish it].

Alternatively, based on its function as the condition for moistening rebirth within one's own internal continuum, the past aspect is omitted from mention because it is obscure; this will be explained further below.
Because it speaks of self-love (*ātmasneha*), the longing for the future up to sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) is called grasping (*upādāna*). [The commentary] states:
"The preceding passage explaining how sensual desire arises in the two time periods is easy to understand. Thus, based on the root treatise...
The following explains the text:
"Desire" (chanda) has the characteristic of seeking, while "greed" (rāga) has the characteristic of attachment.
The commentary states: "By distinguishing desire and greed as belonging to the characteristics of seeking and attachment respectively, their established meanings are each distinct."
"By means of desire and aspiration... [it] causes [them] to arise and manifest.

The commentary states: If there were no desire as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), the fruits of past karmas would not be moistened, and thus the future aggregates (*skandha*) would not arise;
because those [aggregates] arise preceded by that [desire], it is said that this desire has the characteristic of aspiration, even though various [objects] exist.
Because the essence of delighting in and craving one's own objects is that of a master, it is simply called "desire" (*chanda*) as a longing;
although it is not itself an affliction (*kleśa*), it increases greed and is thus designated by the name "desire," just as in the case of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Through the defilement of greed and attachment, it causes one not to relinquish [the object].

The commentary states: Although there is also craving that accompanies joy (*nandī*), this [craving] is specifically described as the defiled attachment to one's own internal self-substance (*ātma-bhāva*).
Because it clings to the aggregates (*skandhas*) so that they remain constantly present, these two are called "grasping" (*upādāna*).

The commentary states: The specific characteristic of *upādāna* (clinging) is the crooked binding of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). This statement that there are "two" is made because they are distinguished by way of their worldly basis and their objective mode of activity (*ākāra*).
Alternatively, this "desire" refers specifically to the mental factor (*caitasika*) of desire among the object-specific factors;

since it is taught that there are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as perverse desire, this meaning takes both the fundamental affliction of greed (*lobha*) and the secondary affliction of perverse desire as its two constituent phenomena.
Because they are grasped, these two are always present together; though they are distinct, when the aggregates (*skandha*) are enumerated, there are ten types.
Although no single location explains all ten, a comprehensive study of the various treatises logically establishes that there is one untainted (*anāsrava*) wholesome aggregate (*kuśala-skandha*).

Some say it consists only of the matter produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is a small portion of the aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*), because it lacks the five sense faculties (*indriya*); this is the correct position.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "One abandons impermanent form and attains permanent form," and so forth. The *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra* states:

"The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "The thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics have as their substance the bases of the four faculties and the faculty of the tongue.
The *Buddhabhūmi Sūtra* states that there exists... [the faculty of the eye].

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, in its tenth chapter on the *Vijñaptimātratā* of the Great Enlightenment Ground (*mahābodhibhūmi*), states: "The fivefold dharmas subsume [the qualities of] the Buddha-ground;

they are comprised within the aggregates, bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*). Such textual evidence is manifold and cannot be cited exhaustively here; all subsequent passages should be understood accordingly.

Thus, these five aggregates all pertain to untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena. With the exception of the third [aggregate], the others all fully possess both [types of phenomena]. Furthermore, two additional [bases] are included.
In the fourth section of the *Kushalaskandha*, it is stated that one portion of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is wholesome (*kuśala*).

Furthermore, regarding "wholesome through application" (*prayoga-kuśala*), the *Śrāvakabhūmi-viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, fascicle 54, states that it refers to relying upon a virtuous person (*satpuruṣa*), hearing the true Dharma, and practicing the cultivation of pure dharmas according to the Dharma.

It further notes that the physical form resulting from the power of meditative concentration (*vairya-samādhi-rūpa*) also includes that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*). These points constitute the general explanation.

The nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of the forms such as visible matter (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are the objects of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) produced by the wisdom arising from hearing and so forth;

these are included in the two bases of form and sound (*rūpa-śabda-āyatana*) and the five types of matter within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), because they are actually present in the five [senses].

Furthermore, the treatise below states that the "virtue acquired at birth" (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) refers to the previously mentioned "virtue initiated by effort" (*prāyogika-kuśala*) and so forth, namely, the bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) and the like.
Due to prior habitual practice, one experiences this retribution; as explained at length, it arises spontaneously in conjunction with faith and other [wholesome factors].

Therefore, this intention refers to the wholesome mind acquired through past habit (*upapattilābhika-citta*) as its cause, which gives rise to bodily and vocal actions and the third and fourth bases among the *dharmāyatana*.
These are of the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). This [category] encompasses the five aggregates; the four unwholesome aggregates are discussed below.
The fourth [point] states that a portion of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is unwholesome (*akuśala*).

Therefore, it should be understood that they are subsumed under the aggregate of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), including the five aggregates, bodily and vocal karma, and so forth, according to their respective meanings.

Regarding the fifth point, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* explains that the delusion regarding karmic destinies (*gati-moha*) is abandoned in the second stage (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts state that a bodhisattva’s clinging to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) is of an obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature.

Because they are initiated by body and speech, those factors such as the concealing (nivṛta) [states] of Brahmā, flattery and deception, and the "horse-hand" gesture (*aśvavāla*)—these types of things included in the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), excluding the third [of the five], constitute the general nature of form (*rūpa*). Thus, they pertain to all five aggregates.
Regarding the aforementioned statement that "if a factor in the desire realm is obscuring-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), it lacks superior efficacy in initiating various karmas," this is based on...

Since afflictions (*kleśa*) are not cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they are not mutually exclusive. Furthermore, regarding the obscured (*nivṛta*) states of the desire realm, this refers mostly to the outflows (*sāsrava*) of the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*);
since these no longer function [in the higher realms], what contradiction is there? Deceit (*māyā*) and guile (*śāṭhya*) initiate karma in the first dhyāna.

Regarding the six types of resultant (*vipākaja*) aggregates, the fourth section below states that "innate neutral" (*upapattilābhikāvyākṛta*) refers to the outflows of wholesome (*kuśala*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*) resultant states.
A portion of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), namely nine bases (*āyatana*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*).
Regarding the calculation of vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*), there are two theories; therefore, it is included within the five aggregates and the aggregate of deportment (*airyāpathika-skandha*).

This treatise states later that "deportment produced by a mind that is neither defiled nor pure is indeterminate in nature. This intent reveals that [vocal intimation] is produced by a mind of deportment.
Furthermore, because that which takes form, odor, taste, and tangibility as its objects constitutes the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), it pervades all five aggregates.

This implies that [the aggregate of form] does not include sound and so forth, because these do not belong to the *airyāpathika* (postures) category. Regarding the eight *śailpasthānika* (crafts) aggregates, the subsequent text states:
"Those crafts produced by minds that are neither defiled nor pure are of an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature. This clarifies that [the crafts] are produced by those specific mental factors and—
Because they take form, sound, odor, taste, and touch as their objective conditions (*ālambana*), the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) pervades all five aggregates;

however, since the paths of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) pertain to all three moral natures (*tridharmatā*), this treatise speaks here of them as being neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, the treatise states below that the various minds of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) and their associated and co-existent factors are called "neutral transformations" (*nirmāṇāvyākṛta*).
If it arises for the sake of play, it is subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); if it is for the sake of benefit and happiness, one should know that it is wholesome (*kuśala*).
Regarding the third [topic], the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there are two kinds of transformation (*nirmāṇa*): first, the wholesome; second, the indeterminate.

In the fifty-fourth [fascicle], it says that the form which is the object of meditative concentration (*samādhi-gocara-rūpa*) also extends to the out-flowing (*sāsrava*). In the fifty-third [fascicle], it says that if one relies on superior concentration, one attains mastery over all forms.

Because they must be manifested through the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), the *Abhidharmakośa* (in its ninety-eighth verse) states that the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) cannot transform four things:
namely, the sense faculties (*indriya*), the mind (*citta*), and so forth. Consequently, these [powers] consist only of a single portion within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

Since they have the nature of form (*rūpa-skandha*), they pertain to all five aggregates (*skandha*). If they are wholesome (*kuśala*), they are subsumed under the first two doors [of the faculties of faith, etc., and the faculty of mind]. Although this is the case according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*,...

It is taught that the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) also possesses various minds of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*). These pertain to all three moral natures (*trividha-śīla*); they are transformation-minds acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*), and not the fruits of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*). Therefore, they are not included in this present category.

Regarding those of indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), they are subsumed under the category of "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*). The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, fascicle 66, states that there are five types of indeterminate [minds]: the first four are as previously described, and the fifth— [The text continues: ...is the mind of transformation acquired at birth. This is because it is not a fruit of supernormal power.

Furthermore, regarding the tenfold indeterminate aggregates (*skandha*), the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states that there are five types of indeterminate [states], the first four of which are as previously mentioned, while the fifth...

It is taught that they are "neutral by nature" (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*). This refers to those material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) that are nurtured (*aupacayika*), as well as external material bases (*rūpāyatana*) not subsumed under [the categories of] maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth;

all these are neutral by nature. Excluding the wholesome (*kuśala*) and defiled (*kliṣṭa*) material bases and the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*), the *Yogācārabhūmi*, third section, states that there are four types of neutral [phenomena];
this fifth type does not exist. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts explain the dharma [in this way].

Because they cannot be defiled by grasping (*upādāna*), [the form aggregate] is subsumed under that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*). This manifest color-aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*) is comprised within the five types of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);

it is not the fifth [aggregate]. It is not merely because there is no textual statement that it is included in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); rather, it is accepted that it possesses an intrinsic nature, just as the wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth also possess an intrinsic nature.
Regarding the associated (*samprayukta*) and the originating (*samutthāna*) [factors], if one follows this principle, then the deportment (*airyāpathika*) is produced through conditions.

The mind termed "demeanor" (*airyāpathika*) and likewise that of "crafts" (*śailpasthānika*), as well as the distracted indeterminate mind (*vikṣipta-avyākṛta-citta*)—excluding these, all are comprised within what is born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
This is because they arise at all times from the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*); it is not the case that they are produced solely by karma.
According to the Sarvāstivādins, the ripening mind is narrow while the demeanor mind is broad; however, in the Mahāyāna, the ripening mind is broad while the demeanor mind is narrow.
Therefore, the claim that the tenth aggregate consists solely of matter and nothing else is untenable. Why?

Because it is not the case that the aggregate of matter is exclusively non-retribution (*avipāka*), nor is it the case that the four aggregates subsumed under the fifth [aggregate] are not so. If the other four aggregates were called "not of the nature of matter" simply because they arise constantly from the retribution-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), then the same should apply here.
Furthermore, if one maintains that these are produced as retribution based on the teaching of the Dharma, [the same logic would follow].
Therefore, the four aggregates would lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), since the treatises state that there are four indeterminate categories;

furthermore, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) would not be subsumed under the fifth category. Moreover, regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi* that external sense-fields (*bāhyāyatana*) such as forms are not subsumed under "maturation" (*vipāka*) and so forth, what would be the purpose of the terms "intrinsic indeterminacy" (*svabhāvāvyākṛta*) and the rest? Only maturation is truly [indeterminate] in the primary sense.

The nourished (*aupacayika*) and the outflowing (*naiṣyandika*) are both of the nature of self-characteristic (*svabhāva*); the four aggregates that are not maturation (*vipāka*) are also of the nature of self-characteristic.
How could those terms be established in vain without a basis? Furthermore, there are briefly two senses in which something is "born of maturation":

first, as the fruit of karma; second, as arising from birth. However, when only the four [aggregates] are mentioned, it is because the category of "arising from birth" is broad and inclusive, whereas for matter (*rūpa*), this is not the case.
The dharmas are also included within those born of maturation (*vipākaja*). If one speaks of "five," this is from the perspective of the results of karma;

that which is not a result of karma is the fifth [category]. Thus, the four aggregates are also "neutral by nature" (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*). The treatise states that the attachment to dharmas is born of maturation; this is said in the sense of being produced from it.

Form and so forth are "neutral by nature" in the sense of being the basis [of that attachment], while karma is neutral by nature in the sense of being the result of karma. This is because of this [distinction].
The principle that all treatises are mutually non-contradictory applies equally here;

however, when the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that [certain forms] are "not maturation" (*avipāka*) and so forth, it excludes the three types of form—those of deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and transformation (*nairmāṇika*)—because these are of a different nature. Internal form (*ādhyātmika-rūpa*) is not like this, and thus cannot be used as a valid objection.

Furthermore, there is no scriptural passage in any teaching stating that the various neutral (*avyākṛta*) states possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in the same way that wholesome and unwholesome states do.
Because these four categories are distinct, the four [types of avyākṛta] are wholesome according to the latter sense;

since there is no possibility of speaking of them exclusively [as such], all five aggregates may be established as having an intrinsic nature that is neutral (avyākṛta). This is because, by way of ten aspects, they all pertain to the five aggregates.

According to the former sense, fourteen [of the eighteen dhātus] belong to the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), while nine [of the remaining] belong only to the other aggregates. As for their connection to the realms (dhātu-pratisaṃyukta) and at which stage they are abandoned, and so forth—all [these points] apply.
As stated below, because the nature of the present "appropriation-aggregates" (upādāna-skandha) is with-outflows (sāsrava), they exclude the first [aggregate] and comprise the remaining nine types.
Question: Why [is it said that] "it should be explained according to the aggregates"?
The commentary states: This master of the root treatise explains the reason why the two categories of *dhātu* (elements) and *āyatana* (bases) are termed "with-grasping" (*sopādāna*).
It should be understood that from the elements to the bases, these are called "factors with grasping.

The commentary states: This master of the explanatory treatise interprets this according to the same meaning as before; because they are all associated with grasping, although the untainted (*anāsrava*) factors...
It is not that we are taking a composite phenomenon as the subject of our discourse, nor is there any contradiction.
Question: What is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)? [The text continues] up to:

"What is the characteristic of form? The commentary states: From here below is the fourth section, the "Gate of the Essential Characteristics through Question and Answer," which explains the verse regarding the phrase "what is the characteristic" within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).
The separate texts consist of three aggregates and five types of passages; furthermore, within these five, there are initial generalities followed by particulars.

Here, the general definition first establishes the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of form through two meanings—transformation and manifestation—and subsequently explains it in accordance with that establishment.
This has two types (up to) "manifested in the two directions. The commentary states:

this extensively explains the previously indicated meaning of "transformation-manifestation" (*nirmāṇa*). "Contact with transformation and decay" (*vipariṇāma*) explains the previous meaning of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*);

"manifested in the two directions" explains the previous meaning of "manifestation" (*prabhāva*). Regarding "contact with transformation and decay," the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other texts state that there are ten material phenomena (*rūpadharma*).
Regarding the term "having resistance" (*sapratigha*): although the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are by nature resistant, they cannot be destroyed by physical contact;
rather, because their bases are subject to destruction by contact, they are designated as "changing through contact.

As for the form (*rūpa*) belonging to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*), although it is resistant due to its karma and meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—and despite the presence of various faculties and objects—it is not included in this specific category of yoga.
It is taught that [this form] is not subject to contact or destruction; this should be understood later when discussing the forms within the *dharmāyatana*.

Regarding the objects of meditative concentration (*samādhi-viṣaya*), the Yogācāras teach that they are truly substantial forms (*dravya-rūpa*) that are "invisible and non-obstructive" (*anidarśana-apratigha*). These arise only when induced by the power of meditative concentration, and their essence is distinct from the objects of other sense faculties;

thus they are called "invisible and non-obstructive. Nevertheless, because they are induced by another [the mind], they also possess visibility and obstructiveness according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

It is said that others are able to see [the subtle] through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); this is not so, for otherwise sentient beings would lack any sensory enjoyment.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that because the touch of hands, feet, and so forth cannot damage them, they are without transformation; this is likewise the case for the "extremely subtle" (*paramāṇu*) and the "extremely remote" (*dūra*).

These are conventional designations (*prajñapti*); the "extremely subtle" refers to matter derived from sensation (*vedanā-samudgata-rūpa*), which is conventionally established as non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), arising from conceptual construction (*parikalpita*).

That which is mentally constructed is neither resistant nor subject to tactile destruction; yet, because it follows its basis and its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is conventionally designated as "form" (*rūpa*).
Accordingly, it may also be said to possess tactile destruction as appropriate.

However, according to the actual reality, this applies only to the ten material bases (*rūpāyatana*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which are termed "tactile destruction. As for the form of the two upper realms and...
Regarding the fact that the matter of the *dharmāyatana* (the sphere of mental objects) is not explicitly taught in this context as being spatially manifest, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"If all matter were established according to its respective locations, and if its distinctions of location could be articulated, this would constitute the first common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
This context, however, refers to the five sense faculties and the five sense objects throughout the three realms."

Within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), whether provisional or substantial, that which is produced by determinate cognition, the basis for conceptual construction, and the delineations arising from it—

analyzed down to the ultimate atoms of the sense bases and their objects, including the "extremely subtle" (*sūkṣma*) and the "distant" (*dūre*), as well as all color-forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), directions, locations,
and distinct names that can be described or manifested— all are subsumed under this category. This includes only that which is induced by sensation (*vedanā*) and is entirely devoid of color-form.

Because it can be manifested by relying on the prevention of form (*rūpa*), it is likewise subsumed under this category. Although the principle is thus established, there is indeed authoritative evidence:
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the "form of majestic power" (*prabhāva-samādhi-rūpa*) exists; once it has arisen, its location can be perceived, as the subsequent passage explains:

"in such and such a way," referring to the skeleton-chain (*asthi-śaṅkalikā*) and so forth. Therefore, whether the form of the meditative object is provisional or real, it is all included within this category.

Furthermore, that which is gathered consists of various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), such as the perception of signs (*nimittasaṃjñā*); thus, it is also subsumed under this category of pervasive imagination (*parikalpita*).

Whether it be extremely condensed or extremely remote, whether it be an object of meditative concentration (*samādhigocara*) or a conceptual construction, it is "matter derived from feeling" (*vedanā-niṣyanda-rūpa*). It follows its basis and can be demonstrated;
for yoga already states that all matter is called "demonstrable" (*nidarśana*) by virtue of its common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

One should know that this gate subsumes all form (*rūpa*); however, because the characteristics of transformation and decay predominate when contact occurs through the conditions of the sense faculties and objects of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), a separate first gate is established.
In reality, this first gate does not subsume all form;

for there are ten types of resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*), such as those described in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Chapter 5) and others, as well as the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all form as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

Regarding the sixty-five [categories] and so forth, within the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there are three common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Apart from these two, a further "purified" and "object of purified observation" are established.
However, this [classification] does not exhaust all phenomena subsumed under the five faculties and their objects, nor is it a universal gateway (*sarvatraga-mukha*).
It is merely a demonstration of one gateway that is broad and pervasive; because its specific meaning is superior, other gateways are further established, but it is not [the case that]...

Each individual gate exhaustively encompasses all phenomena. Furthermore, that second [gate], which demonstrates the gate of the relative correspondence between faculties and objects and the gate where only objects exist without faculties, clearly reveals these characteristics.
Having already explained that one [of these] exhaustively encompasses all phenomena, there is no need to state the others.

"Contact and transformation" (referring to the point where it "immediately transforms")—the commentary states that the preceding section has individually assigned the two characteristics of transformation and manifestation, yet their specific distinctions have not yet been explained; hereafter, the differences between these two characteristics will be analyzed individually.
Regarding this explanation of the characteristic of transformation, the root treatise states: "That is to say, by means of hands, feet, clods of earth, stones, swords, or staves..."
When encountering cold, heat, hunger, thirst, or being touched by mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, and scorpions, the [body] immediately undergoes transformation and decay.

To these, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* further adds wind and sun, making sixteen conditions in total. Therefore, the lower treatise states: "up to the point where mosquitoes and snakes act as causes of destruction, yet they are not yet exhausted.
The *Vyākhyā* (Explanatory Commentary) omits this, hence it says "up to" (*yāvat*). As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "Just as..."
This is a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) that is not omnipresent (*asarvatraga*), with the exception of the gods of the desire realm.

It pervades all other beings of the desire realm who possess form, such as those with hands and feet, and is subject to transformation by the six types of tangible objects. It is also subject to transformation by the ten types of tangibles, such as cold and heat.
Although their food and drink arise according to their desires, even when hunger and thirst occur, they do not cause them harm; this refers to the various forms of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, there is no destruction by contact with hands, feet, or other such things; nor is there any destruction by other forms of contact.
Moreover, because it possesses majestic power and consists of the form of the meditative sphere (*samādhi-gocara-rūpa*), even contact with hands, feet, and so forth cannot destroy it.
Thus, this first characteristic is absent in the higher realms as appropriate; it exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Regarding what is manifested as spatial location (up to) various configurations," the commentary states:
This explanation of spatial location consists of two parts. The first is the general section regarding spatial locations that can be indicated;
the remainder constitutes the specific sections. There are three types within the specific sections: first, "in this way and that way"; second, "thus and so"; and third, "seeking."
The contemplation and conceptualization of whether [a state] is determinate or indeterminate merely reveals that there are distinctions among these three stages; it is not a separate category.
Regarding the passage from the main text of the treatise on form, the commentator explains below:
"Place" refers to the location present before one.

The commentary states: To explain the preceding general gate, all forms currently present—whether belonging to the three realms or nine stages, whether contaminated or uncontaminated, whether in meditative concentration or in a distracted state, whether faculties, objects, or conventional or substantial—all such manifold forms are termed "forms with spatial location" (*dig-deśa-rūpa*).
Whatever possesses the characteristic of form is subsumed under this gate, as has already been explained above.
"Thus and thus... (up to) similar images. The commentary states:

This separate section clarifies that within the previously mentioned general category of matter (*rūpa*), there are two divisions: first, that which is associated with a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*); second, that which is not associated with a concentrated mind (*asamāhita-citta*).

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises state that the matter of the objects of concentration (*samādhi-viṣaya-rūpa*) is invisible (*anidarśana*), non-obstructive (*apratigha*), and does not occupy a spatial location (*adeśastha*). Now...

This demonstrates that although the imagined skeletons and so forth within the meditative object are images of the same class as the substantial objects of knowledge, they nonetheless possess spatial location because their color-forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) are manifest.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Once they have arisen, their location can be found;
since this is the case for imagined form (*prajñapti-rūpa*), it is likewise for substantial form (*dravya-rūpa*)."
"Such and such forms" refers to the distinctions between shape (*saṃsthāna*) and color (*varṇa*). [Commentary:

The preceding section clarified that the various forms within the meditative object are of a conventional nature, having the five sense-objects as their essence. The following section clarifies all the various forms existing in the state of distraction;

this is divided into two parts: first, obstructive form (*sapratigha-rūpa*), and second, form belonging to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*). Since their categories and types differ, [the distinction is made].

Therefore, it is divided into two types. Here, among all *sapratigha-rūpa* (resistant forms), only shape (*saṃsthāna*) and color (*varṇa*) are mentioned because their essential characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) are manifest and visible to the eye;
thus, the others are omitted for brevity. However, in reality, this category subsumes all resistant forms.
Otherwise, what would be the specific reason for establishing a separate category for them? All other [categories] possess this same principle.
Beneath "manifest form" (rūpa), there should be the word "and so forth" (ādi), though it is omitted because the text is abbreviated; its meaning must certainly be present.
"Various mental constructions" (vicitra-vikalpa) refers to conceptualizing according to the characteristics [of objects].

The commentary states: The preceding section clarified the existence of these [objects]; this section clarifies that the categories of the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) are exclusively threefold: first, the extremely concise; second, the extremely... [text fragment ends].

The extremely concise and extremely remote objects of concentration that arise from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) are included in the aforementioned [section on] "such and such doors" as the objects of the concentrated mind;
those objects of the distracted mind are subsumed under this present section.

Whether it be the mind alone or the distracted mental consciousness, whatever mental factors transform them into sense organs, objects, water-moons, mirror-images, and so forth—all these are termed "arisen from pervasive conceptualization," just like [the case of] visible form (*rūpa*).

Because it arises through the perception of signs, it is subsumed under this category. Since the form that is the object of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) belongs to this initial category, so too does the form induced by feeling;
however, formless form lacks these characteristics and is not subsumed under this category.

Alternatively, if one provisionally designates it as "form" based on its function of protection, then it is subsumed under the aforementioned categories according to the fundamental meditative mind or the non-meditative mind.

Because it belongs to the third stage, it is not cited and explained here; although the textual structure of this section is easy to understand, if one exhausts the underlying principles to their source, the meaning must necessarily be as follows.
If one were to grasp the intent of the former masters and apply it to the texts of various treatises, yet investigate them differently from this, I fear there would be errors and discrepancies.
Question: What is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*)? [From "up to" ... "All fruits obtain maturation (*vipāka*).

The commentary states: This second explanation of the characteristic of feeling takes the experience of the self-body and objects summoned by both wholesome and unwholesome karma—namely, all various fruits of maturation as appropriate—to be the characteristic of feeling. The reason this text is not clear is as follows:
Why is this? It is because [the sūtra] speaks of tainted feeling (*sāsrava-vedanā*) and not untainted feeling; it speaks only of the four feelings and not the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*);
it speaks only of resultant feeling (*phala-vedanā*) and not causal feeling; and it speaks only of ripened feeling (*vipāka-vedanā*) and not non-ripened feeling.
The above is the original treatise, while the following is the commentary by the Master.
"If one performs pure karma (up to) not desiring its maturation (*vipāka*). Commentary:

This explains the preceding [passage on] the reception of the characteristics of the fruit. Since "reception" (*vedanā*) is broad in scope while the "characteristics" are narrow, these three are explained collectively.
Herein, the reception of the pleasant maturation of pure karma refers specifically to the fruit obtained from *vipāka-karma* (maturation-producing karma). (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Chapter 9)
To speak of meritorious karma refers to wholesome karma that brings about maturation in the happy realms (*sugati*) and is conducive to experience within the five destinies;
this clarifies that pure karma brings about results throughout all five destinies up to the third dhyāna. Specifically, it brings about the fruit of pleasure:

through the five consciousnesses in the desire realm, through three consciousnesses in the first dhyāna, and through the mental consciousness in the third dhyāna. Within the desire realm, [this applies to] the pleasure experienced therein.

Regarding the statement that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) associated with the joy-fruit (*prīti-phala*) of the two lower dhyānas pertains to all five destinies (*gati*), there is an explanation in the *Yogācārabhūmi* that this is based on the six destinies, excluding the hell realm (*naraka-gati*), and refers specifically to those who are "non-devas" (*a-deva*). This is because there is no fruit of joy within the hells.

Others say that these five [destinies] are themselves the hell realm, for the *Yogācārabhūmi* does not state that there are non-devas distinct from the other destinies; thus, they exist within the hells.

Regarding the fifth [point], it is further stated that sentient beings in the hells possess a subtle form of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), namely a subtle wind that enables them to endure for a long time. As for the five destinies (*gati*), this also includes the hells.

Vasubandhu, however, speaks only of those with "outflowing" (*niṣyanda*) pleasure because pleasurable *vipāka* is so slight that it is not mentioned. Although there are these two interpretations, the former explanation is superior.

Since it is nowhere stated that there is a pleasant fruit for such [actions], impure karma produces the bitter fruits of the five destinies only within the five consciousnesses and not within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because [the latter] possesses the two natures of sorrow (*daurmanasya*). Furthermore, it does not exist in the higher realms.
Why is this? The commentary states:
Below, the text addresses the objection regarding the explanation of the "minority" [of those who experience equanimity]. It asks:
Since the ripening of wholesome karma is characterized by the tranquility of equanimity (*upekṣā*), how can unwholesome karma also ripen as equanimity? What is the reason for its ripening as such?
"From pure and impure karma... up to being associated with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
The commentary states: Although the fruit of the sensation of equanimity extends throughout the six consciousnesses, here, based on the general fruit, only the eighth [consciousness] is mentioned;
this meaning shall be understood from what follows below. In response, it is said: "Since you admit that wholesome karma can induce the sensation of equanimity, this case should likewise be so."

Because the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) does not conflict with the categories of suffering or pleasure, just as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas can be produced by both wholesome and unwholesome [actions], how is it that this consciousness arises only in conjunction with equanimity?
This is as explained in the third fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
"Only this neutral feeling (upekṣā-vedanā) [is] conventionally designated as maturation (vipāka).
The commentary states: This excludes the positions of other schools which hold that suffering and pleasure are also substantially real maturations.

It clarifies that only this neutral feeling is both universal and substantially real maturation, whereas the two feelings of suffering and pleasure are not; those feelings summoned by karma arise from maturation.

The "distinct maturation" (*vipāka-viśeṣa*) of birth is conventional and not the ultimate substance of total maturation (*vipāka*). "Distinct" (*viśeṣa*) refers to the difference between cause and effect, as their natures are distinct.

"Maturation" (*vipāka*) refers to the arising of the substance through transformation as a retribution for the cause. When one speaks of the "maturation of the distinct," the "distinct" belongs to the cause;

if "the distinct" were itself the "maturation," then the "distinct" would belong to the fruit. This can be understood respectively according to the *adhikaraṇa-sādhana* (locative sense) and *karmasādhana* (objective sense). It cannot be otherwise.
It is said that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) ripen through transformation, for all conditioned phenomena are subject to transformation.

However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 63, states that this neutral sensation (*upekṣāvedanā*) is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*); fascicle 57 states that all twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) possess seeds of maturation;
and herein it further states that suffering and pleasure are not real. Based on these [points], [the following is argued].

The text now provides an interpretation according to its meaning: If a phenomenon is a maturation (*vipāka*), arises from a maturation, and is uninterrupted and pervasive, it receives the name "maturation" (*vipāka*);
because it also arises from its own kind, it is likewise called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*). Therefore, this [neutral feeling] receives both names.
If a phenomenon is a maturation, arises from a maturation, but is intermittent and non-pervasive, it is called "born of maturation" but not "maturation."

Therefore, while painful and pleasant feelings are subsumed under the category of maturation-born (*vipākaja*), the text here distinguishes them from the general by relying on the conventional designation of "maturation.

As explained at length in the commentary on the second fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there is an interpretation which states that this neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*) as a fruit extends to all seven consciousnesses—
excluding only the manas— whereas that which co-exists with the eighth consciousness is produced by both types of karma and pertains to the two destinies within the three realms of existence.

That which is produced by karma belongs to one realm (*dhātu*) and three destinies (*gati*). It is summoned by evil karma; as for the remaining [mental states] associated with the six consciousnesses, they are produced solely by wholesome karma.

There is no textual statement that these also pertain to the results of evil karma; therefore, it is logical that those associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) pertain to all three realms.

As for the five consciousnesses, three of them pertain to one or two stages (*bhūmi*) as appropriate. They exist only within four destinies and not within the hells, for those [consciousnesses] do not exist there.
Because the fruit of wholesome karma is not subject to adventitious sensation, other sources state that from the fourth dhyāna upward there is only equanimity (*upekṣā*).

However, the claim that there are only the two sensations of joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) as the pure karmic fruits below that level is based on the majority of mental continuities (*saṃtati*) and is not an exhaustive presentation of the principle.
According to one interpretation, the distinct retribution (*vipāka*) of wholesome karma as the sensation of equanimity exists only from the fourth dhyāna upward.
Regarding the remaining lower stages, as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 9) and other texts,

"karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" refers to karma that can induce the maturation (*vipāka*) of the *ālaya-vijñāna* in all stages, as well as the "immovable karma" (*āniñjya-karma*) from the fourth dhyāna upward.
Since it is not stated that there is karma conducive to equanimity (*upekṣā*) in the lower stages, one knows that there is no distinct retribution in those lower stages.
If even the fruit of wholesome karma is abandoned, how much more so the fruit of unwholesome karma? Now, in evaluating this point, it is generally difficult to understand.

If you admit that the eighth [consciousness] is associated with both [types of feeling] and can induce the six consciousnesses simultaneously, why do you not admit the same for the former [the sixth consciousness]?

The former masters, however, maintain that the distinct retributions of the three realms and four destinies consist solely of the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), which is the fruit of wholesome karma alone; they further maintain that the five upper stages possess wholesome karma that induces such [retribution].

Why is it not accepted that the fruit of abandonment (*prahāṇa-phala*) resulting from distinct karma exists in the lower stages? Regarding this, the latter master does not accept its existence in the lower stages.

If the former master asserts that the feeling of abandonment resulting from distinct karma is so because of its tranquility (*śāntatva*), then the karma that abandons [the defilements] associated with the eighth [liberation] should be exclusively pure (*śubha*).
If the latter master asserts that the coarse wholesome karma of the lower stages cannot induce that [feeling], [then the argument holds].
Regarding the eighth [point], the simultaneous abandonment of both the distinct retribution (*vipāka*) and the fruit of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*):

it should not be that lower realms fail to attract wholesome karma, for such karma is coarse. Therefore, one must state that the distinct retribution of the sensation of equanimity is produced by all three types of karma and is present throughout the three realms and five destinies.
As for those who claim it is produced by wholesome karma, this does not contradict reason within the hells, as has already been explained previously. Furthermore, why is this so?
Regarding the reason why the two names "suffering" and "pleasure" are designated as *vipāka* (maturation), various treatises state that they are produced from maturation (*vipākaja*).
In response, the treatise states: "The *ālayavijñāna* is actual maturation; others are called 'maturation' by way of metaphorical designation. Thus, there is no contradiction.
Alternatively, this may be a general inquiry concerning the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
Question: What are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)?

[The text continues] up to: "the characteristic of perception. The commentary states: This is a general indication of the nature and marks of perception. "Constructing" (*vikalpa*) refers to mental construction and delineation;

it exists only within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. "Apprehending" (*upalabdhi*) refers to discernment and understanding; it pervades all eight consciousnesses and also extends to the signless (*animitta*).
"Because of this perception (saṃjñā), [it leads] up to the arising of various verbal expressions.

The commentary states: This expands upon the preceding point regarding the construction of cognition (*vijñapti*). It means that one first constructs the images, categories, and essential natures of all phenomena—such as what is seen and heard—by means of perception;
subsequently, based on these [mental] visions and so forth, various verbal expressions arise. This clarifies that perception is the cause of verbal expression.

"Conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) is a synonym for "discrimination" (*parikalpa*); it refers to the mind that takes the signless (*animitta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object, rather than the mind of universal imagination (*parikalpa*).
It is not otherwise, for [otherwise] it would be too restrictive. The above is the original treatise; the following is the Master’s commentary.
Regarding the meaning of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing (up to) "this is the meaning of knowing":
the commentary states that first, the four meanings of seeing, hearing, and so forth—which are what is followed—are the objects (*viṣaya*).

Because verbal expression arises in accordance with those four objects, and because that which is experienced is taken as the "seen" and so on, it is said that "that which is experienced by the eye" is the meaning of seeing.
