Regarding the "essence" (*tattva*), both the second *yoga-sthāna* and the fifty-sixth [chapter] of this treatise state as follows:

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), seeing and so forth are neither faculties nor consciousness, because they arise from a collection of conditions, because they are momentary, and because they lack functional activity.

Because they exist through a combination [of factors], they are conventionally designated by the name "seeing" and so forth. According to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), seeing and so forth are indeed faculties.
Because that consciousness and its associates possess five characteristics—as explained in detail later—the second fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Seeing" refers to the visual faculty directly perceiving external forms; "hearing" refers to the arising of verbal expression from what has been heard from others;
"awareness" refers to that which is neither seen nor heard, but is merely one's own reflection, weighing, and investigation; and "knowing" refers to what is internally experienced.

That which is realized, touched, and attained—these ninety-three are said to be comprised of two kinds of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): seeing (*darśana*) and knowing (*jñāna*). Inferential cognition (*anumāna*) is [the third];

"hearing" refers to that which arises from sacred scripture (*āptavacana*). According to this, the eye-faculty is called "seeing," while the mind, ear, and the conditions for the arising of teaching are called "hearing.
This is because they arise from the three types of linguistic expression—name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and phoneme (*vyañjana*)—which are all pervasive. Thus says Dignāga.

That which is authoritative verbal testimony (*āptavacana*) is subsumed under inference (*anumāna*), because hearing is the cause for the mental consciousness; it is called "hearing" because the ear hears the sound.

Since the ear cannot actually apprehend names and so forth, and since [verbal testimony] is not [itself] inference, even when it apprehends what is not authoritative verbal testimony, it is still included within this "hearing.
This treatise mostly relies on such authoritative verbal testimony; thus, "cognition" (*buddhi*) refers precisely to that which does not rely on seeing and the like.
Regarding the claim that the yoga of the solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the seventh consciousness is described as being only inferential (*anumāna*):
this is stated with respect to the mental consciousness, for the *manas* is also capable of giving rise to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Furthermore, when there is no smelling, no touching, and no cognitive realization, but rather the arising of reflection, deliberation, and investigation, this is also subsumed under "cognition" (*buddhi*). In the treatises, however, only [the former] is mentioned.

Because it has been seen and heard that the superior [cognition] is mentioned, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises subsequent to the five sensory consciousnesses—which is an inference (*anumāna*) or non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*)—is also subsumed under this "awakening" (*buddhi*).
However, only the "independent" (*mukhya*) [mental consciousness] is mentioned here to manifest its predominant function;

otherwise, the mental consciousness associated with the eighth mental state (*citta-kalāpa*) that accompanies the five [sensory consciousnesses], as well as all others, would be omitted. As for the "knower," it refers precisely to the mental consciousnesses concomitant with the five [senses] of ear, nose, tongue, and body.

Because the *Samāhitacitta-yoga* (Concentration of the Settled Mind) specifically explains what is internally experienced and realized, and because it further states that this knowledge is subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it reveals that "seeing" (*darśana*) and "knowing" (*jñāna*) are subsumed solely under direct perception.

It also reveals that "hearing" (*śruta*) and "inferential awareness" (*mata*) both pertain to inference (*anumāna*) and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), and that while "seeing" and "knowing" may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), "hearing" and "inferential awareness" are exclusively contaminated; all uncontaminated minds take [the uncontaminated] as their object.
It is because [the teaching] is intended for those who have been born [into this state] to know what is subsumed; it is not because it is an inference (*anumāna*).

Alternatively, it is said that these four do not exhaustively encompass all consciousnesses, because there are objects of hearing that are neither taught nor inferential and are thus not included. Furthermore, the mental faculty (*manas*) constructs through conceptualization and is therefore subsumed under non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*);

thus, it is not included within [the category of] awakened awareness (*buddhi*). Or, the four [consciousnesses] are discussed solely with reference to the six consciousnesses, as the seventh consciousness cannot function with such clarity.

Because verbal expression arises from the comprehension of objects, and because the *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Teachings), fascicle 18, states that within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) all four types of verbal expression are present, while in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) there is no inferential deliberation due to the absence of vitarka, and in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) they are entirely absent;

thus one might conclude that these four do not exhaustively encompass this meaning. However, this is not so, for both noble (*ārya*) and non-noble speech universally depend upon these four, and it is based on these seven [factors] that [verbal expression] arises.

It is said that because they are not included within the [sensory] bases (*āyatana*), the verbal expressions arising after the defiled mind of the mental consciousness in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are likewise not included within the bases;
however, while the minds of that realm mostly give rise to verbal expression without conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is not that they entirely lack the cognition of verbal expression.
When it is said that there are no four types of verbal expression in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), does this imply that cognition is also non-existent in that realm?
Is it that the cognitions of the heterodox and their false views are also non-existent?

Because this realm of form possesses the four [immeasurables] and the formless realms possess cognition while lacking verbal expression, we know that what was previously stated is correct. Regarding the establishment and exclusion of these two:

according to reason, only two should be established—namely, knowledge (*jñāna*) and cognition (*vijñāna*). All direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is subsumed within both knowledge and cognition. All [objects] are known by them.

Inference (*anumāna*) and non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*) are both subsumed under awareness (*buddhi*); alternatively, one should establish three [categories]: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference, and non-valid cognition, because they are distinct.

Now, for the sake of establishing four [categories], the function of the eye—which clearly knows distant objects—is extracted from within [awareness] and established independently as "vision" (*darśana*).

The function of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—which encompasses hearing, feeling, and knowing—is broad; its states (*avasthā*) are divided into three: external conditions (the teacher's instruction) and internal investigation through one's own reasoning.
Because it takes realized objects as its domain, the manas-consciousness possesses only two categories: defiled and pure;

because it constructs and realizes two types of objects, the five other consciousnesses do not have such distinct or superior functions. The internal deliberation and so forth are collectively termed "cognition.

Furthermore, when first encountering an object, the eye is able to see it first, and having heard the verbal descriptions of it, the mind subsequently constructs an image, after which the other sense faculties perceive the remainder.
Since the sequence of the spheres (*viṣaya*) is thus, their functions may be superior or inferior, whether combined or separated; therefore, they neither increase nor decrease.
Other categories of meaning are explained in a separate chapter.
"Various verbal expressions" refers to the articulation and discernment of meanings.
The commentary states: This explanation follows the preceding discourse on verbal expression—namely, that words which define and distinguish are such as "this matter is thus" or "it is not otherwise.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its third [section], states that there are eight kinds of noble and non-noble speech, each having four types.

Therefore, these "noble" words correspond to the actual state of affairs; because they accord with reality, they are called "noble," meaning they are spoken based upon reality regarding all phenomena.

There are four types of non-meaningful speech regarding the attainment of the fruit: the noble and the non-noble; the opposite of these constitutes the four types of noble speech. Regarding "seeing" and so forth:
to say one sees when one does not actually see, and to say one does not see when one does actually see—these four constitute the non-noble. Regarding "seeing" and so forth:

to say one does not see when one actually sees, and to say one sees when one does not actually see—these four constitute the noble. These eight categories, each having two aspects, form sixteen types.
When the conceptualizations and verbal expressions are combined, they further constitute sixteen; when these are joined with the aforementioned discourse, there are thirty-two.
Therefore, the treatise states "all. *Commentary on the Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, Fascicle One.
*Commentary on the Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya*, Fascicle Two, composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of the Great Ci’en Monastery. Question:
What are the characteristics of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*)? [It continues] up to: because it drives and employs the mind.

The commentary states: That which flows and migrates is called *saṃskāra* (formative forces). This term applies extensively to many factors, namely all non-associated [conditioned phenomena] as well as associated phenomena.

However, this treatise explains that "constructing" (*abhisamskāra*) refers exclusively to associated phenomena; regarding associated phenomena, it speaks of only volition (*cetanā*), because volition is the primary factor that drives the mind toward the wholesome and so forth.
Since volition is the sovereign, it alone receives the name *saṃskāra*. [The following is] the main text of the treatise above, and below is the explanation by the Master.

Furthermore, regarding the passage from "various" up to "because of driving and employing the mind," the commentary states:

The Original Teacher (the Buddha) spoke only of employing the wholesome mind and so forth; here, however, we clarify the driving and employing of suffering and other [unwholesome] minds according to their respective stages.
The state of sensation (*vedanā*). Question:
What are the characteristics of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)? [From "various objects" to...

The commentary states: This refers only to the objects understood within the scope of this treatise; it merely manifests the six objects and so forth, while other factors such as the sense faculties (*indriya*) are not included.
Having already distinguished the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) regarding all objective spheres, what are the characteristics of the elements (*dhātu*)?
Question: What are the characteristics of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), up to [the question] "What are the characteristics of the eye-element"?

The commentary states: Within the analysis of essential characteristics, the characteristics of the aggregates have already been analyzed; next, the characteristics of the elements are analyzed. In this passage, there are three parts: first...

Having distinguished the faculties (*indriya*), one next distinguishes their objects (*viṣaya*); having distinguished the objects, one returns to distinguish the faculties. Within the distinction of the faculties, first the eye is distinguished, and subsequently the others are illustrated by analogy.

Regarding this section on the eye in the root text, the later commentators explain that "that which has been seen" and "that which is being seen" refer to the manifest functioning (*pravṛtti*) to illustrate the characteristic of the eye.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter nine, states that "the eye has already seen, will see, and is currently seeing," which actually applies to all three time periods. The former [interpretation] refers to the past.
The section on "Abolishing and Establishing" relies solely on two lifetimes to clarify the meaning of the *dhātu* (element/realm); therefore, it is omitted [here].

As for the phrase "one should see that the seeds, etc., are included," this refers to seeds to clarify the nature of the *dhātu*. Both seeds and active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) are the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), because they are neither identical to nor separate from one another;
thus, they are subsumed within the eye-element. Otherwise, the term "eye" would not carry the sense of "seeing. The following cases should be understood accordingly. Some say: [text missing].
Some maintain that only the seeds are the eye, not the manifest; others maintain that only the manifest is the eye, not the seeds.
There are also those who assert both, as well as the non-Buddhists and followers of the Hīnayāna, who claim that the essential natures of the five faculties are each distinct.

Regarding the seeds giving rise to the manifest, they are sometimes in the same world-period and sometimes in different world-periods, as explained in the fourth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the first fascicle of its commentary, and further in the fourth sub-commentary.
Commentary:
From "the eye has previously seen forms" up to [the end of the passage], this is to reveal the nature of the *dhātu*.

The Subcommentator explains that the meaning of the two preceding "sustaining" (*dhṛti*) functions involves the possession of sustaining activity; thus, within the present life, they sustain one another as characteristics.
As previously stated, because clear observation and focus are established under the name "seeing," they are able to sustain consciousness and thereby manifest the nature of the sense-field (*dhātu*);
furthermore, these seeds [reach] the present eye-faculty.
The commentary states: Regarding the explanation of the "seed-element" (*bīja-dhātu*), this refers to the seed that is the cause for the arising of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-dhātu*).
Some say it is exclusively innate (*upapatti-lābhika*); some say it is exclusively newly perfumed (*navābhyāsa-ākṣipta*); and others say it consists of both the innate and the newly perfumed.

Because the conditions have not yet converged, while in the state of being unmoistened, both types accumulate as causes capable of projecting the future eye-faculty; or, once the conditions have converged... [in the moistened state].

In the stage already moistened, both [the past and present] are established as causes for growth; they cause the seeds of the present eye-faculty to arise and bring about dharmas, thereby manifesting the nature of the *dhātu*.
It is only the two time periods that are mentioned, because the substance produced in the past no longer exists and is therefore omitted.
The present eye can sustain the arising of consciousness; by means of this function, it manifests the nature of the *dhātu*, whereas the future is not mentioned.
Since that which has not yet arisen has never been used, it is also omitted from discussion.

As for the eye that is currently functioning, because it has already passed through the present, its seeds—the past eye—are also established as being the seeds of the present eye. Both the seed-eye and the manifest eye pertain to all three time periods;

they are each described according to a specific sense, resulting in different temporal designations. This is consistent with their respective principles and involves no contradiction. Furthermore, when speaking of the "seed" in terms of its essence, it possesses the capacity to produce [the manifest].

Regarding the two periods [of past and future], the present is established as the basis; thus, the increase of faults through the apprehension of objects does not contradict the doctrines of "original existence" (*pūrvabhāva*) and so forth, nor the doctrine of "perfuming" (*vāsanā*), as explained in the second and third chapters of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Because these two [types of seeds] are the causes for the arising of the eye.

The commentary states: This explains the reason why the seeds that are drawn forth and those that produce are called "elements" (*dhātu*). Since the nominal seeds are the direct conditions that can differentiate the causes and conditions for the arising of dharmas, they are termed "elements.
However, according to the actual meaning, the seed itself is not the eye; it is only the element that manifests as such.
Because these two types cannot see, the others are all to be understood accordingly.
This is the same as the characteristics of the visual faculty (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to [the mental faculty].
The commentary states: "The Master of this treatise, by referring to this, indicates that the other elements are to be understood in the same way."
Question: What are the characteristics of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)? [The text continues] up to: "These are the characteristics of the form realm. The commentary states:
This separate section is explained as in the case of the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*). Regarding the observation of objects, it is said that there are five conditions:

taking past objects, taking present objects, and simultaneously grasping objects. Since the preceding reliance on the two time periods is used to define the eye-faculty, within the context of the form realm—
Based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts, it is taught that each of the eighteen *dhātus* and so forth possesses its own seeds;

the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises state that internal and external phenomena take internal seeds as their cause. Furthermore, the proponents of seeds (*bījaka*) maintain that the characteristics of form and the other [objects] should likewise be explained as seeds.

Moreover, in order to clarify the distinction between the internal and external realms and to demonstrate that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), they designate the sense organs (*indriya*) by the name "seeds" based on the meaning of "that from which something arises. As for the objects (*viṣaya*), they are designated as such because they are the causes of the arising of consciousness.
It is not a faculty-seed, nor does it belong to the form realm; for this reason, the root treatise omits it and does not explain it.

The preceding portion is the original text of the treatise, while the following portion is the commentary by the Master. This is because the visual faculty arises here in relation to external objects.
The commentary states: Having refuted the previous objection, it is now shown that since seeds are non-material (*arūpa*), they do not possess the characteristics of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Rather, it is demonstrated that the sense organs (*indriya*) must exist because they exercise a dominant influence (*adhipati-pratyaya*) over the experience of objects; only through this dominant force do external objects arise. Thus, it is shown that they possess superior efficacy.

When considering the object of perception (*ālambana*), one speaks of functional objects where the material forms (*rūpa*) serve as mutual causes for one another. However, while the sense organs (*indriya*) continue in a stream, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is subject to interruption; therefore, the object serves as the basis for the organ.
It is explained that the object arises by means of the sense faculty (*indriya*), not by means of consciousness (*vijñāna*); it is because the sense faculty arises toward the object.
This applies likewise from the characteristics of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) onwards.
The commentary states: the original text of the treatise should be recited according to the preceding [explanation].
Question: From the "eye-consciousness element" up to "this is the characteristic of the eye-consciousness element.

Commentary: That which relies on the eye is the supporting faculty (*āśraya-indriya*); that which takes form as its object is the perceived realm (*ālambana-viṣaya*). The discernment that resembles the apprehension of form is called consciousness;

its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is the very nature of consciousness. As the second [chapter] of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Consciousness has discernment as its mode of activity"; therefore, it is described by its mode of activity.
The differences are as explained in the second fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Its fifth [fascicle] states:

"In this context, for the time being, we speak of the uncommon support (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*) during the stage when the basis has not yet been transformed (*aparivṛtta-āśraya*), which is clearly perceived by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). It continues:

"Since the types of these faculties and objects are numerous, and the activities of the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and so forth are each distinct, the root verse says: 'Five, four, six; two, seven, eight, one.'"

Regarding the simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*) and the leading causes (*āksepaka-hetu*), each increases by two objects of cognition (*ālambana*). As the verse says: "Due to seeing, they follow their respective [conditions]:

five, three, six, two, six, one, and one; they are not fixed. The distinctions regarding the sovereign and so forth are fully analyzed in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-pañjikā* (Essential Summary of the Establishment of Consciousness-only).
As for what is called "resembling form" (*rūpa-nirbhāsa*), it refers to the reflected form within the visual consciousness.

That which is "essentially form" (*rūpa-svabhāva*) or "resembling form" (*rūpābhāsa*) indicates that it is the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) at the stage of the causal basis for the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), and not the manifestation of actual form.
According to the true meaning, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is not form; it manifests as if it were the form of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Because it arises resembling that [imagined form] through deluded cognition, it is said to be "resembling form. The *Saṃgrahaṇī* and other texts state that while the substance of external objects such as form is actually not form, they appear as if they were form.
It should be understood that these seeds and so forth manifest as previously explained.
This applies likewise from the *cakṣurvijñānadhātu* up to [the final element].
The commentary states: The above consists solely of the root treatise; there is no explanatory commentary on the text.
Question: What are the characteristics of the bases (*āyatana*)? [The text continues] up to "according to what is appropriate.
The commentary states: Since the internal and external bases are similar in their characteristics, they are explained by analogy with the elements (*dhātu*); however, there are slight differences.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "according to what is appropriate," the original treatise is cited above, while the explanation by the commentator is provided below.
This means that the eye shall see forms (*rūpa*), and so on, up to [the mind], which should be explained according to their respective meanings. The commentary states:

The internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) pertain to both [past and future], whereas the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*) do not constitute the "seed" (*bīja*); they belong only to the future. This is because the realms (*dhātu*) pertain to the past and present as well, yet they share some commonality with the [internal] bases while differing slightly from them;

therefore, they are not mentioned here according to their specific application. As for the seventh and eighth consciousnesses being separately established as realms and bases: [The seventh and eighth consciousnesses are established as separate realms and bases because they serve as the support for the six consciousnesses, possess a distinct nature, and have different objects of perception. (To be continued...)
Because there are no distinct faculties or objects to be contrasted with it, it is nonetheless subsumed within the mental element (*manodhātu*).
How is it established [as being] derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*)?
The commentary states: This is the fifth section, the door of questions and answers concerning the distinctions that can be established according to the verse. The main text contains...

Second, first distinguishing the three categories (skandha, dhātu, āyatana) and subsequently responding to questions regarding the *dhātus*. Within the section on the three categories, the text is further divided into two parts:

first, the explanation of the main body of the treatise; second, the explanation by the commentators of supplementary meanings. In the explanation of the main treatise, there are again two parts: first, the individual analysis of the three categories;

second, the general explanation of their inclusion of all phenomena (*dharma*). Alternatively, following the general division of the main treatise into three, the first part establishes them individually.

The third section clarifies the mutual inclusion of the three dharmas. Following this, there is a question-and-answer session explaining the *dhātus*. The Master’s commentary distinguishes the meaning of the secondary vehicles.
This initial section is divided into three parts; the aggregates (*skandhas*) are further divided into five. Within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the text is again divided into two:

first, a general question-and-answer that reveals the essence of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*); second, a detailed explanation following the specific categories, beginning with "the four great [elements]," etc. The first of these [sub-sections] is further divided into two. First:

In the subsequent commentary on this passage, the Master explains that "all matter whatsoever" in the root text refers to the aggregate of matter (*rūpaskandha*) in its totality, while "the various kinds of derived matter" specifically indicates the distinct categories of visible form (*varṇa*).
Thus, the root text provides the general inclusion, and the subsequent commentary provides the specific clarification.
Regarding "that which is produced" (upādāya-rūpa) up to "is called 'produced'":

the commentary states that although the Great Elements (*mahābhūta*) and the nature of the derived [elements] are explained extensively in the root treatise, the meaning of "derived" (*upādāya*) should now be explained separately.
Herein, first, the five causes are collectively termed "derived"; below, the five specific types of the meaning of "derived" will be individually revealed.
Regarding the "causes of arising" (upapattihetu), [it is said that] matter does not arise [without them].
The commentary states: Although all derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) arises from its own seeds, it cannot necessarily arise if it is separated from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

If this were so, then since the Pratimokṣa, Dhyāna, and Path restraints are separated from the primary elements, they should not be able to arise. This [restraint], however, follows wherever one goes.
The name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that is prevented also follows those two in being conventionally designated as "great elements" (*mahābhūta*) and "derived matter" (*upādāyarūpa*).

There are two senses in which they are not separate: first, they necessarily occupy the same location; second, they must depend upon one another. The *prātimokṣa* vows and so forth necessarily depend on the great elements for their arising; thus, while they do not necessarily occupy the same location, they are still called "not separate.
This applies equally to the separation of substance from sound and light. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that these are the fruits of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
If form relies solely on superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and not on the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), how do you explain that? He himself explains it, saying:

"However, because it arises from a samādhi that manifests an image (*pratibimba*) of that same kind based upon those [elements], it is said to be 'derived from them' (*tadupādāya*); it does not mean it is produced by relying upon them.

This will be explained further below. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Moreover, within various meditative concentrations, one first transforms the primary elements and subsequently creates [the derived matter]."
The transformation of matter arises; some say this cause is not universal, because it would lack a supporting cause— such as the light of a wheel—
and because a supporting cause depends upon a distinct location.
The commentary states: Since all derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) arises based upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it lacks a separate locus of existence apart from them.
This being so, how does one reconcile this with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 54), which states that light, fragrance, and so forth are not found apart from their primary elements?

Here, we rely on the principle that the basis (*āśraya*) is identical to the substance (*dravya*) itself to explain the cause of dependence; for light and other such phenomena that are separated from their substance, there is no basis or cause.

Because they are [distinct] meanings, there is no contradiction; or it is said that those rays also consist of the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*), since wherever light exists, the great primary elements exist there.
This explanation is incorrect, because sound and fragrance are separated from their substance—what great primary elements could they be derived from? Therefore, the previous explanation is correct.
Regarding the establishment of the reason (up to the point): "because it changes accordingly.

The commentary states: Since the primary creator (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*bhautika*) must necessarily share the same security and peril, when the great elements undergo transformation, the derived matter changes accordingly.

As for the distinct non-informative (*avijñapti*) [matter] that arises subsequently, how does the informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) continue once it has changed? Some say it is due to its basis (*āśraya*).

If there were still something that remained unchanged according to the true meaning [of reality], then this would follow wherever one wanders; however, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are to be restrained are not thus.
Furthermore, since the precepts associated with the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samādhi*) and the Path lack a physical basis, these causes [for restraint] should not exist.

If that were so, then since that which is to be restrained has long since been severed and extinguished, and there is no longer anything capable of being produced by the elements, there should be no establishment of causes at all. It is not possible to prevent what others call "names" (*nāma*).

Regarding the claim that matter (*rūpa*) is produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of another for the sake of one's own non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), this is merely a designation based on the sense of "distant counteraction" (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratipakṣa*), because it belongs to the category of what has previously existed.
This is likewise true for the non-informative matter of the two higher meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

The argument that it is produced by the four great elements of another in order to prevent others is incorrect; for since it is not one's own transgression, prevention would be impossible, and thus it should not be so.
The antidote to this meaning is that the designation "derived" (*nirmita*) refers to a remote antidote (*viprakṛṣṭapratipakṣa*) to the nature of being produced (*kṛtatva*); thus, there is no fault.

Since non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), such as the precepts, lacks the sense of having a cause for its establishment, whereas substantial matter (*dravyasat-rūpa*) possesses the sense of having a cause for its establishment, if one were to take the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which the body depends as the "derived," then noble ones (*ārya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) would lack non-informative matter; they would consequently not be Mahāyāna practitioners, and it would also contradict what is explicitly taught.
The various types of restraint (saṃvara) are established as having the nature of matter (rūpa-dharmatā) because they depend on matter that does not manifest;
they are produced by those primary elements (mahābhūta),
and they function as supporting causes (dhāraṇa-hetu) because they prevent [the restraint] from being interrupted.

The commentary states: Derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) arises in succession by virtue of being sustained by the primary elements (mahābhūta). If this were not so, derived matter would necessarily be subject to interruption.

Since this is the case, the third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that it is called "sustaining" (*upastambha*) because it does not perish as long as it is equal in measure to the primary elements.
[Objection: We clearly observe that sounds and lights differ in their magnitude; how can it be said that they do not perish as long as they are equal in measure? [Response: This is based on...

This is stated because, while the causes for maintaining [the aggregates] are explained in their entirety, they are spoken of here based on only a partial aspect; or, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (54),
it merely mentions that the "great" [aggregates] maintain an equal measure without being destroyed, without stating that the "great" and the "derived" [elements] are equal in measure—
this refers to the sense of similarity between the preceding and following passages.
Regarding "nourishing causes" (upastambha-hetu), [it means] "because they cause growth.
The commentary states: Because the derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) grows or increases due to the nourishment of great relatives, it is called a "growth cause" (*vṛddhi-hetu*), or a "cause of growth.
If this is so, how is it that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts speak of food, sleep, celibacy (*brahmacarya*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth [as growth causes]?
Because they are able to nourish, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as the cause for the growth and nourishment of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, while [the derived matter] serves as the condition;

since each is established according to its own specific meaning, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, because those conditions first nourish the great elements, causing the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) to increase, there is no fault.
Alternatively, they collectively nourish both the great elements and the derived matter, as well as the mind, mental factors (*citta-caitta*), and so forth.
All phenomena arise from this; only derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) can nourish its specific causes because, being dull by nature, it is not like the mind and so forth.
Thus, it relies on the two types of nourishment, whereas the mind and so forth do not. In the third [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, a question is raised:
"Since all phenomena arise from their own seeds, why is it said that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) can produce derived matter, and so on up to the fifth [point], which can cause it to grow?"

When asked whether they are nourished, he himself replied: "Because all seeds are attached to the internal mind, the seeds of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that have not yet arisen cannot produce the seeds of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
It requires that the seeds of derived matter first arise for derived matter itself to be produced;
since it takes these as its precursor, it is said that [the mind] can produce them. This is also stated similarly in the *Ṣaṭṣaṣṭitantra*.

This continues up to the fifth [point]: because one avoids the five types of uneven nourishment—food, drink, sleep, celibacy, and meditative concentration—by means of these causes, the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced thereby increases and expands further; this is called the cause of nourishment (*puṣṭihetu*), and thus it does not contradict reason.
Furthermore, in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (54), there is another question: "Do all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise from their own seeds?"... [as above] ...just as... [as above].

Why is it said that the primary elements (mahābhūta) produce derived matter (upādāya-rūpa)? It is because [derived matter] undergoes transformation in accordance with their transformation, and because it is established and sustained by them.
This is explained at length in that same fascicle and in the fifth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, which states:
"Based upon the primary elements, other derived forms are subsumed into a single location; this is called 'produced by the great [elements]. This meaning is thus revealed."

That which exists through mutual dependence is the meaning of "derived" (*nirmita*), not the definition of its essential nature (*svabhāva*). When manifest activities are compared with one another, they function as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Thus, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) are explained through five gates: first, distinguishing their illumination; second, explaining their names; third, distinguishing the great elements and derived matter based on causes and conditions;
fourth, distinguishing the derivation by comparing the great elements and derived matter with one another; and fifth, a detailed analysis through questions and answers.

First, regarding their essential nature: these four are subsumed under the two natures of *paratantra* (dependent) and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected). They are comprised of two things: characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*).

They generally possess the natures of being untainted (*anāsrava*), wholesome (*kuśala*), or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). As for derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*), that which is substantial is exclusively indeterminate, while that which is conceptual (*prajñapti*) pertains to all three natures.
The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are exclusively substantial, whereas derived matter pertains to both the substantial and the conceptual.

Second, regarding the explanation of the names: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle three, states that these are called "great elements" (*mahābhūta*) because their nature is great and because they serve as the seeds from which [derived matter] arises.
"Great" has four meanings: first, being the basis; second, having an extensive substance; third, having a large physical form;
and fourth, performing great functions. "Seed" means cause; these four act as causes for the arising [of derived matter].
"Because they consist of various colors, these four are [called] 'great' (mahābhūta) in terms of number. Although space is great, it cannot serve as a cause;
others can serve as causes because their essential characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are great. Since this 'greatness' is also a genus (jāti), they are called 'great elements' (mahābhūta).

This is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning 'that which is a genus,' or 'that which is a class,' because there are four distinct classes. As for 'derived matter' (upādāyarūpa): that which is derived is matter; thus, it is a *karmadhāraya*."
The name "great derived matter" (*mahābhūta-nirmita-rūpa*) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound; its specific meaning is easily understood.
Third, regarding the analysis of the great elements and derived matter by way of causes and conditions: first, the creation by causes is analyzed, followed by the creation by conditions.

There are two types of creation by causes: first, the ten causes; second, the six causes. Regarding creation by the ten causes, there are eight causes in total when considering the great elements in relation to derived matter.

1. The projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*); 2. The producing cause (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*); among the indeterminate causes (*avyākṛta-hetu*), [there are those] that have not been moistened and those that have already been moistened, as in the case of external grains such as rice and barley in relation to their sprouts;
3. The sustaining cause (*parigraha-hetu*), because it is sustained by the locus of human effort (*puruṣakāra-adhiṣṭhāna*); 4. The drawing-forth cause (*āvāhaka-hetu*); 5.

The cause of specific differentiation (*pratiniyama-hetu*), because it draws forth the arising of similar types and [determines] their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); 6. The cooperating cause (*sahakāri-hetu*); 7. [The homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)].

The non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*) subsumes the aforementioned causes because it consists of these two; thus, the eight contradictory causes (*virodha-hetu*) are mutually capable of counteracting one another as causes.

"Great" does not refer to verbal expression, for there is no "conformity-to-expression cause" (*anuvāda-hetu*). Regarding the aspect of dependence (*apekṣā-lakṣaṇa*), there is the "dependence cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*);
since there is a specific meaning [for this], it is established as ninefold, excluding only the conformity-to-expression cause, as this one also extends to dependence. Thus it is composed.
Form is also the cause of the great elements in eight ways: first, as the cause of designation, because sounds and verbal expressions define and distinguish the great elements;

second, as the cause of projection; third, as the cause of origination; fourth, as the cause of defilement and purification—referring to the non-restraint, restraint, and the morality concomitant with meditative concentration, which serve these two [unmoistened and moistened] states;

fifth, as the cause of support; sixth, as the cause of sustenance; seventh, as the cause of transformation; and eighth, as the cause of maintenance. Fourth, it is the cause of appropriation, being the locus upon which functional activity depends.

1. Because of being appropriated (*upātta*), there are five; 2. because of being determinate (*niyata*), there are [five]; 3. because they are determinately distinct in their ability to project their own specific maturation (*vipāka*); 4. the cooperating cause (*sahakāri-hetu*); 5. the non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*); 6.
the contradictory cause (*virodha-hetu*)—excluding the projecting [cause], because it can project its own kind, its similar grade, or its superior grade as the cause for that [result];

7. the cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*), which is as previously explained; and 8. the cause of apprehension (*parigraha-hetu*), in the sense that existence does not arise without it, serving as the ninth.
Regarding the "waiting cause" (*pratīkṣā-hetu*), some say there are ten; adding the meaning of the "inducing cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*) as previously explained, there are six causes.

As for their manifestation, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (18th fascicle) states that all [of these] are sovereign conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*). This fourth [section] explains that the single efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is differentiated into six.
If one distinguishes the six causes according to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* [provide the following].

The statement that seeds, in relation to manifest phenomena, do not have the nature of being derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) is now explained by way of their predominating condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

Regarding the six causes that constitute "derivation," when the great elements relate to derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), they possess only three causes: first, the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), because they provide power by way of non-obstruction;
second, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), because they cause it to increase. The following discussion relies solely on seeds as being this cause.
The meaning of "a small portion" is irrational; it refers only to these three types of co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
This treatise explains below that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) must arise simultaneously, and thus they function as co-existent causes.

It is not because they attain the same single fruit, nor because they are mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), nor because they are wholesome or unwholesome karma, nor because they are of the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*); therefore, they lack [the other] three causes. Derived matter is likewise [a co-existent cause] in relation to the primary elements.
There are three causes: first, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), because this cause is broad; second, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), because they are not separated from one another;

and third, the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), because both the vows of restraint and non-restraint, as well as the morality associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*), are capable of producing great results.

There is nothing else that can be known. This teaching refers to the same world-system (*loka-dhātu*) and not to a different world-system; for while there is a basis for the creation [of form], it does not exist apart from the world-system. Thus, it concerns contaminated form (*sāsrava-rūpa*).

Sound is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) in nature; however, in the state of being untainted (*anāsrava*), it is wholesome (*kuśala*) because it arises together with the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Therefore, it should be understood exactly as stated here. Thus, one should say that the fault lies in the past cause and the future cause, but not in the present. This is because the present serves only as a cause for the present, not as a cause for the future;
nor is the future a cause for the future, since the past and future do not exist [as substantial entities] at that time, and [the present] is also not [a cause] in that sense.

Because the posterior limit serves as the cause for the anterior limit, thereby inverting the order of cause and effect, one distinguishes between "causally constructed" (*hetukṛta*) and "conditionally constructed" (*pratyayakṛta*). How so?

Regarding the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), when they are viewed in relation to one another, there is only the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), because they are not like the mind and its mental factors; furthermore, there are no other two conditions [the object-condition and the immediate condition], because their essence is not being distinguished.
As for the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*), it consists of the five causes such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth; since these are the dominant condition, this [latter] is the causal condition.

Regarding the establishment [of causes], it is explained based on general characteristics by considering the presence or absence of outflows (*anāsrava*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the three realms (*tridhātu*), as they are mutually related;
whether comparing the great with the great, or the created with the created, the number of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) is as explained in the separate chapter.

Regarding the four ways in which the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) are distinguished from one another: first, they are distinguished by way of their different categories;

second, they are distinguished by way of their identity or difference. Regarding the distinction by way of different categories, the third chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 54) states that there are three types of "different categories":
first, the category of maturation (*vipākaja*), which has two kinds: first, that produced by karma... [text continues].

That which first arises consists of the two types of continuity of total maturation (*vipāka*); that which transforms at a later time consists of the two types of specific maturation and the two types of nourishment (*aupacayika*).
These, in turn, are twofold: first, those whose location is broad and pervasive, being nourished by food, sleep, celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*);
second, those whose characteristics increase and flourish, also due to food, because it is their support, and through the cultivation of superior activity.

Because they are mental and because they have been thoroughly matured over a long period, they are said to be "nourished" (*paripuṣṭa*). There are four types of such similar outflows (*nisyanda*): first, the outflow of maturation (*vipāka-nisyanda*);
second, the outflow of nourishment (*puṣṭi-nisyanda*), which refers to the two aforementioned categories as both being outflows; third, the outflow of transformation (*vikāra-nisyanda*);

and fourth, the outflow of original nature (*prakṛti-nisyanda*). Those not included within the two types of maturation and nourishment are all subsumed under the latter [the outflow of original nature].

Because there are two [types of matter], the five sense-faculties (*indriya*) possess only *vipāka* (maturation) and *aupacayika* (accumulative/nourishing); apart from these two, there is no separate *naiṣyandika* (outflowing).
This is stated based on the distinction between the three categories of substantial entities; however, non-faculty matter possesses all three categories.
Alternatively, this does not mention the sound element (*śabdadhātu*), because sound is excluded from being maturation, as it consists only of the accumulative and the outflowing. Apart from these...

The various forms that constitute the sense faculties (*indriya-rūpa*) also lack maturation (*vipāka*). Among the aforementioned forms, those belonging to the three categories possess two types of maturation, two types of nourishment (*aupacayika*), and four types of outflow (*naiṣyandika*);
those not belonging to the three categories—the five internal sense-faculty forms—possess two types of maturation and two types of nourishment.
As for the forms included in the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), there are subsequent nourishments; as for the pervasive forms, there are subsequent [outflows].

Regarding the three types of outflows (*āsrava*) that lack an initial maturation (*vipāka*): although the various minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) possess all three categories, the long-cultivated matter (*aupacayika-rūpa*) lacks an initial [maturation].
Within the aggregates (*skandha*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), those cultivated by edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), sleep, and the holy life (*brahmacarya*) are excluded;

thus, the long-cultivated matter of the three realms is entirely comprised of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Among the internal and external aggregates, there are accordingly three, two, or one category of great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Regarding the statement that derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) arises in dependence on the primary elements (mahābhūta) as appropriate:
all such derived matter exists in dependence upon all the primary elements, because this is the sense of "derivation" (upādāya), not because it establishes their essential identity.

Furthermore, when it is said that derived matter arises in dependence on the location of the primary elements, one should understand that each [element] acts as a basis for derivation, and that within this aggregate, the derived matter produced by those primary elements is obtainable.

Since those dharmas exist within this very context, all derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) that arises from the same assemblage of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and exists in mutual dependence may be called "derived" and can mutually bear the sense of being "derived.
This is not a fixed, exclusive relationship; the principle differs from that of the Hīnayāna, which does not provide such a distinct explanation.
Regarding the analysis of "derivation" in relation to the great elements themselves: it refers to the derived matter and the [great] elements.
That which is not separated from its primary elements (*mahābhūta*) in terms of location is called "produced from the substance itself" (*dravya-nirvṛtta*).

If derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) were to have a physical separation from the locus of the primary elements, it would be called "produced apart from the substance. Regarding the sixty-four [types of] light, fragrance, and so forth that are said to be produced apart from their wheels [or bases], they are all unobtainable as being separate from the substance;
rather, light, fragrance, sound, and the like arise precisely from the four great elements at the place of their emission.

Regarding the nature of matter (*rūpa*) established based on the vows of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states that it is established based on non-manifest phenomena (*anabhisamudācāra-dharma*),
as all [restraints] are composed of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) derived from those which prevent the unvirtuous conduct (*asaṃvara-śīla*) of the desire realm.

Regarding the nature of matter established based on the manifestation of unvirtuous conduct, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states that it is established based on manifest phenomena (*samudācāra-dharma*), as it consists of the great elements derived from the actualized branches of unvirtuous body and speech.

That which is produced from a distinct substance is called "produced apart from its substance" (*viprayukta-kṛta*); all others are called "produced not apart from their substance" (*aprayukta-kṛta*). The extremely concise (*paramāṇu*) and the extremely remote (*dūre*) follow the magnitude of their original substance;
they may be termed "identical to the substance" (*tad-rūpa*) or "produced apart from the substance. The same applies to that which arises from conceptual construction (*parikalpita*).

Furthermore, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) and the unmanifest of the Buddha’s body—by what primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are these produced? One should consider this in relation to the precepts of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna-śīla*) and the path (*mārga-śīla*), as well as those of the lower realms.
This should be analyzed.

Regarding the analysis through five questions and answers: a question is asked concerning how many entities can be found within the various material aggregates (*rūpa-kalāpa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The third [section] of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that there may be an aggregate in which only one great element (*mahābhūta*) is present, such as a stone, a mani-jewel, a river, or a pond.
There may be fireflies, flames, lamps, or candles; there may be dust or wind; or there may be only two great elements (*mahābhūta*), such as a hot *maṇi* gem, snow, or a moist tree;
or there may be only three great elements, such as a moist and warm tree, or a tree swaying in moisture;

or all four [great elements] together; or there may be only visible form (*rūpa*), such as light separated from a wheel; or there may be only sound, such as sound separated from its substance; or there may be only odor, as in the case of a solitary [fragrance].

In the case of the "incense offering" and so forth, if there is taste and touch, there must be touch, taste, fragrance, and color; or there may be only four [objects] when the external vessel-world excludes sound;
or there may be only five when the external vessel-world possesses sound and so forth; or there may be the body-faculty together with the four beginning with color;
or there may be only six according to the presence of the eye-faculty and so forth along with the five beginning with the body-faculty; or there are seven when sound is added, as described above.

In the formation of the body, the primary elements (mahābhūta) increase to six; with the addition of the eye and so forth, they become seven; adding water, fire, and wind, they become eight, nine, or ten;
and by adding sound, they become eleven. Depending on what is appropriate—such as the wheels or light—the four primary elements increase to form various numbers, such as sixty-four.
It should be understood that within this aggregate, the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) produced from the primary elements can be apprehended.

If the primary elements (mahābhūta) and the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) were entirely devoid of their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa), one should know that such a place would lack those phenomena.
All the extensive questions and answers regarding this are as explained there. Herein, it is stated that these characteristics may either exist or not exist;

if categorized according to the inclusion of the realms (dhātusaṃgraha), they all exist accordingly, as explained extensively in the third fascicle of that treatise. [The sixty-sixth discourse] speaks of desire (kāma).

The realms (*dhātu*) include the stages (*bhūmi*) as well as form, odor, and taste; the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) possesses only form; and that which is bound to the form realm excludes odor and taste.
Furthermore, there is form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) according to what is appropriate. Some say it can be perceived there, but fearing excessive prolixity, I shall stop this discussion.
Now, regarding the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm that arise within a body belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): do those great elements [produce] the form of the lower realm?

Question: Do they abide in the same location or different locations? Answer: They abide in the same location, like water and sand. This is because within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), there are two types of seeds:

those that produce exclusively [one type of great element] and those that produce mixedly. Since the former induces the arising of a specific great element while the latter brings about its cessation through mixture, they do not abide in different places.
One interpretation holds that this is a method for conforming to the principle; it demonstrates that they abide in the same location, just as the great elements of different classes [can coexist].
Since the two types of matter are fundamentally not mutually obstructive, why would they need to occupy separate locations? Therefore, in response to the question regarding the "Gate of Conformity":

If the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) are both resistant (*sapratigha*) yet occupy the same location without obstruction, why is it not said that they possess the nature of being non-resistant (*apratighatva*)? Answer:

Because they arise in mutual conformity and do not obstruct one another; furthermore, the sense faculties (*indriya*) produced by the predominant influence of this type of karma pervade those [elements].

Because they are experienced together, just as in the case of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and others, although they possess the quality of resistance (*sapratighatva*), they do not obstruct one another;

this [case] should be understood in the same way. Question: How do the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) abide? Do they exist one above the other, or internally and externally, or are they intermingled?
Answer: It is said that they exist simultaneously and are mutually inseparable, due to their common nature (*jāti*).
Because it is produced from causes, it is augmented by a single "flavor-mass" (*rasa-piṇḍa*) that mutually interpenetrates and pervades all locations;

it is not like a heap of flour, rice, or mani-jewels. Furthermore, this [pervasion] has three aspects: (1) being in the same location, (2) mutual commingling, and (3) being combined without separation.
These will be analyzed in detail in the Chapter on Correspondence (*Saṃprayoga-varga*). For now, we shall rely on the third [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi* to explain all forms (*rūpa*).
There are two types of non-separation regarding location: first, non-separation by being in the same place; second, non-separation by intermingling.

Regarding non-separation by being in the same place: for example, when one *aṇu* of the sense organ and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)—along with their corresponding derivative matter (*upādāyarūpa*) *aṇus*—interpenetrate one another to form a single location without any distinct spatial divisions.
Within one *aṇu* of form, there are eight *aṇus*; adding sound makes nine, and adding the body makes ten;
according to the other sense organs, it becomes eleven. Alternatively, when the eye, the body, the earth, and the objects of form, odor, taste, and touch are present, there are seven *aṇus*.
One cause and one fruit coexist in a single location, mutually interpenetrating, unlike the Sarvāstivāda school’s view that atoms (*paramāṇu*) are discrete and distinct from one another.
The formation of an *aṇu* (atom) is also not as the Sautrāntikas maintain. Now, in the Mahāyāna, there are originally no infinitesimal particles (*paramāṇu*).
When matter reaches its smallest limit, it becomes an *aṇu*; at that point, depending on the circumstances, many [atoms] may occupy the same location.
This is because the sense faculties can universally apprehend them, and because the mind cognizes objects; thus, the mind arises from those objects.
Therefore, although they are identical in name and share the same location without being separated, their coexistence and non-separation means that the aforementioned *aṇu* (atoms) of form,
which share the same location without being separated, involve a mutual interpenetration between the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*bhautika*).

Although they abide in the same location within a single place, they do not enter into one another to merge into a single entity, because the sense faculties and their respective objects remain distinct from one another.
However, it cannot be said that they are "conjoined and inseparable" simply because they can be analyzed like a heap of sesame seeds or beans;
rather, when primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the same kind reside in the same location relative to one another, this is called "residing in the same location and being inseparable.
Furthermore, when primary elements of different kinds reside in the same single location relative to one another, this is also called "conjoined and inseparable."
It is distinct from the atoms of other schools, which—whether of the same or different classes—are separate and do not occupy the same location. One might ask:
since *vipāka* (maturation) is sometimes increased and expanded, why is *vipāka* not identical to *aupacayika* (accumulated growth)? The answer is:
because that *aupacayika* is able to encompass and sustain the continuity of *vipāka*, appearing as its increase and so forth, just as an external rampart provides defense and support.
Regarding the internal city, it is not the case that those [elements] are identical to it.

To the question of whether one great element produces one derived form or many, or whether many great elements produce many derived forms or one, the answer is: they exist in mutual dependence, and the designation "producing" is established on this basis.
Whether one produces one or many, there is no logical impediment. As stated in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, the primary elements must first arise before [the derived forms].
Based on their location, derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) arises without departing from that place; it is called "derived" because it is produced there.
Just as the light of the solar disc produces much from little, and sounds such as those of a drum produce little from much, all such categories should be understood accordingly.
Since there are no atoms (*paramāṇu*), it is possible for all [matter] to be obtained.
Regarding the "four great elements" (up to) "the nature of lightness and motion":

the commentary states that the preceding section, consisting of general questions and answers, reveals the essence of the primary and derived elements; the following section provides a detailed and specific explanation. This text has two parts:

first, the analysis of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and second, the explanation of the derived matter (*bhautika*). This explanation concerns the true great elements and the conventional four great elements; the latter will not be discussed here in brief.

The remaining text is easy to understand, so it is not all explained here. How is it that the three elements of earth, water, and fire each manifest their own essential nature, while the wind element manifests its nature by means of lightness?

This is because the Sūtra states that lightness is a derived tangible object (*upādāya-spraṣṭavya*). Furthermore, the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* states that the nature of movement is similar to lightness and other such qualities;
thus, "lightness and so forth" are cited to manifest the essential nature of wind. This is because the essential nature of wind is difficult to know.
Because these [qualities] such as motion are light, they are described as "light-motion" (*laghu-samudīraṇa*); the word "etc. (*ādi*) is omitted for brevity.
Regarding "derived matter" (*bhautika-rūpa*), [the text continues] up to "matter that is subsumed.
The commentary states: below, the derived matter is analyzed first in general and then in detail; this is the general statement.
The eye faculty (up to) has pure matter as its essence. The commentary states:
there are three ways of explaining the derived [matter] in detail: first, the five faculties; second, the five objects; and third, the matter of the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

In explaining the meaning of the five faculties, each has three aspects: (1) being derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), which cites the cause to reveal the effect; (2) being apprehended by consciousness...
"Dependent upon" (*āśrita*) refers to citing the effect to manifest the cause; "pure matter" (*rūpa-prasāda*) reveals the essential nature of the sense-faculties (*indriya*).

Furthermore, the term "greatly produced" (*mahābhūta-nirmita*) distinguishes [the faculties] from the tenets of the Vaiśeṣikas, who hold that the five great elements themselves are the faculties. The term "pure matter" distinguishes [them] from the Mahāsāṃghikas, who maintain that the five faculties have the physical mass (*piṇḍa-rūpa*) as their nature.

By stating that they are the supports of visual consciousness, the meaning of being a faculty is established; they are not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), but are inferred by citing their effects.
By way of this explanation, the second interpretation of the names of the five faculties is clearly shown to be superior. Herein, the eyes and ears are comprised of both the fleshly and the divine;
the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body are not divine but only fleshly; those resulting from cultivation are called "divine," while those of other births are called "fleshly.

The fleshly [faculties] are comprised of both the maturation (*vipāka*) and the nourishment (*aupacayika*); the eyes of the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are only fleshly, neither divine nor resulting from cultivation.

Because it is a result, some heterodox masters claim that the Sarvāstivādins assert that when one in a lower realm generates the supernormal power of a celestial body, other faculties are also present because ten matters are established.

This is also incorrect; for if other faculties were present in the desire realm, they would necessarily establish those ten matters, yet it is not said that the generation of the divine eye establishes the material faculties of the body. Furthermore, this contradicts the *Jñānaprasthāna* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

Fearing that the text would become overly verbose, I shall briefly conclude this inquiry. Regarding the statement that the "great elements" (mahābhūta) and their "derivatives" (upādāyarūpa) are not seeds, and that only the present [dharmas] are so designated—how then can the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) also be considered a seed?

Answer: That which serves as a supporting cause is termed a "realm" (*dhātu*); thus, even a seed receives the name "realm. That which exercises predominance is termed a "faculty" (*indriya*). Seeds are not included within the category of faculties. Question:

It is the manifest state (*pravṛtti*) that gives rise to consciousness and thereby acquires the name of a "faculty"; however, since seeds increase consciousness, they too should [be called faculties].

Furthermore, regarding the inclusion [of seeds] within the faculties (*indriya*), as the treatise states: "The seed of consciousness arises from the seed of the faculties, and only then does it manifest. Answer:

The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the present acquisition of the name "faculty," yet because the seeds are not composed of the primary elements, they are not included among the faculties. Question:

Since the present eye arises based upon the primary elements, and that eye is also called a "faculty," how can the primary elements—which serve as the basis for the seeds of the eye—not be included among the faculties?

Answer: This is based on the principle that manifest characteristics (*nimitta*) are seeds but are not the fundamental substratum (*āśraya*); it follows the textual tradition where even seeds are subsumed under the "root" (*mūla*).
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states that the five faculties, such as the eye, encompass both the manifest and the seed.

As extensively analyzed in the *Weishi shu* (Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), all the preceding passages are merely the root text of the treatise; it is only when explaining external objects below that there are explanatory glosses.
"Visible form" (rūpa) [extends] to "the single manifestation of emptiness.

The commentary states: the following explains the five sense objects (*viṣaya*). Herein, first the characteristics of visible form are analyzed; subsequently, the causes for its establishment are discussed.

Within the analysis of the characteristics of visible form, the phrase "produced from the great elements" (*mahābhūta*) cites the cause to manifest the effect. The phrase "the domain of the eye faculty" (*cakṣur-indriya-gocara*) cites that which is not yet mastered.
The objects apprehended by the individual sense faculties refer to the distinctions among manifest colors, such as blue, yellow, and so forth;

the subsequent sections should be understood accordingly, without further separate categorization. In the third chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the five sense objects (*viṣaya*) are explained with variations in their expansion and contraction.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that within a collection of matter (*rūpa-skandha*), when one perceives a large portion of a single surface, the cognition of "long" arises; when one perceives a small portion of a single surface, [the cognition of "short" arises].

When one perceives a short form, the cognition "square" arises; when one perceives all four sides as equal, the cognition "square" arises; when one perceives all sides as full, the cognition "round" arises; when one perceives the center as protruding, the cognition "high" arises;
when one perceives the center as indented or concave, the cognition "low" arises; when one perceives the surface as level and even, the cognition "even" arises;
when one perceives the surface as uneven, the cognition "uneven" arises. The radiance of the sun is called "light," while other radiances are called "flame."
Brightness and shadow are the opposites of these; bending and stretching, and so forth, are manifest colors (*vijñapti-rūpa*) because they reveal one's internal mind to others.
Regarding the aforementioned explanation of long, short, high, and low colors: both horizontal and vertical perspectives are established.

Alternatively, long and short are established through mutual comparison from a horizontal perspective, while the two colors of high and low are established as distinctions through mutual dependence from a vertical perspective. Other colors are easily understood.
Therefore, the first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* does not provide a separate explanation; it extensively clarifies that the "manifest" (*varṇa*) is distinct [from the "shape"].
This further consists of three types, up to "contrary to both. The commentary states:

this refers only to the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*) within the aforementioned common characteristic yoga; it is explained from the perspective of what is clearly evident, and is not [the case for shape].

To exhaustively clarify the principles, or to distinguish based on sentiment, or to explain based on the objective realm, [the author] comments on the original text of the treatise above, while the commentator explains it below.
This [section on] blue and so forth (up to) each and every one...

The commentary states: "Because the characteristics of the preceding [categories] regarding their establishment or exclusion are distinguished collectively by means of the six causes" refers to the fact that the fundamental substance and manifest characteristics of the first four colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—are established.
"Because they are established" refers to the subsequent ten [characteristics], such as long and so forth;
these include length, shortness, squareness, roundness, coarseness, subtlety, height, and lowness, whether regular or irregular. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there are only these [ten].

Furthermore, the differentiation of the accumulation of matter (*rūpa*) is necessarily established through mutual dependence, and because of its capacity for benefit or harm. This refers to the next eight types of matter:
light, shadow, brightness, darkness, cloud, smoke, dust, and mist; these eight act as a basis for benefit or harm according to their respective functions.

As for being the "basis for what is produced," this refers to the next type, distant matter (*dūra-rūpa*), which can serve as a basis for all other forms of matter; or alternatively, it means that this [matter] itself...
Because it serves as the support for sentient beings, this form is also called "form adjacent to space" (*āgāsasāmanta-rūpa*). Regarding its being the "characteristic of manifestation":

it refers to the fact that it follows after manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) and possesses the characteristics of performing actions such as bending and extending; or, it refers to the fact that it can manifest the characteristics of the mind.
Regarding its being "for the sake of adornment": it means that the single manifest color of space adorns the world of space, and thus it has no distinct parts.
A "segment" (vyañjana) may consist of only manifestation (varṇa) without shape (saṃsthāna), termed "one," such as blue and so forth; thus it is called "manifestation.
Because it pervades space, it is called "space-one-manifestation. One should understand that these are assigned respectively as appropriate.
Furthermore, because they are established based on the six causes, the twenty-five types of form are neither more nor less, and are fixed at exactly that number.

However, [the masters] such as Kātyāyanīputra do not state that [the cause] is established through specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), because while the specific characteristics are numerous and thus explain their differences, the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) are few and therefore remain implicit and are not discussed.
This applies down to the specific characteristic of taste; since it is either non-existent or extremely minimal, one should not demand equal scrutiny regarding the establishment of the cause.
"Remote color" (or "distant color") refers to that which can be apprehended within a specific location.
The commentary states: This explains the preceding difficulty; it means that apart from other obstructive contacts, all places possessing form can be apprehended within their respective locations.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that dark color and bright color are designated as the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) because they refer to voids and apertures.

That which is a continuity of darkness refers to the intermediate space between worlds; that which is a continuity of light refers to the realm of radiant light (*ābhāsvara*). Other instances are termed "interruption.
This demonstrates that [space] is not a material form, as it can only exist by being free from obstruction.
Regarding the single manifest color of space, it refers to manifest colors such as blue and so forth.

The commentary states: Since blue and other [colors] appear as empty, they constitute manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*). This color will be briefly analyzed through four gates: first, the difference in their enumeration;
second, the distinction between shape and manifest color; third, the difference between the conventional and the real; and fourth, their presence or absence across the three realms.
First, regarding the difference in the enumeration [of matter]: this treatise states that there are twenty-five kinds, as listed in the text itself.
The *Pañcaskandhaka* (Treatise on the Five Aggregates) states that "matter" refers to visible form (*varṇa*), shape (*saṃsthāna*), and informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*).

The first fascicle of both the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-bhāṣya* likewise state that there are three types: visible form, shape, and informative matter. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* also states that there are twenty-four or twenty-five [kinds].

Among these, only the *dūrasaṃjñaka* (distant) visible form is excluded; the *Prakaraṇābhidharma* later states there are twenty-four, while the twenty-fifth [category] excludes both the *dūrasaṃjñaka* and the *pratibhāsa* (manifested), adding the *pratibimba* (reflected image) visible form.
The *Pañcaskandhaprakaraṇa* and other texts initially state there are three types. The nature of the visible forms apprehended by visual consciousness is only one;

it is distinguished solely by differences in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), manifestation (*abhivyakti*), accumulation (*saṃcaya*), and functional activity (*karmaprayoga*). Thus, the inclusion of all phenomena is exhaustive.
