In terms of general categories, there are three; in terms of ultimate reality, one should establish only these three types. Alternatively, one may generally establish two, as "informative form" (*vijñapti*) is itself shape (*saṃsthāna*);
all other forms are merely distinctions between these two. The later *Yogācārabhūmi* states that there are twenty-four types, excluding "pervasive color" (*prabhāvarṇa*).
Its third section says: "Dark color and bright color are called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*). This space element is divided into two: first...
Regarding the distinction between *vibhūta* (the remote) and *avabhāsa* (the manifest): because the manifest is subsumed within the remote, it is omitted here.

However, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (*Xianyang*) later states there are twenty-four types, excluding both the remote and the manifest while adding "images" (*pratibimba*). As for the reason why the remote is not mentioned [in some contexts], it is as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

Alternatively, that *Xianyang* treatise also speaks of "remote color" (*vibhūta-rūpa*), and since the four types of manifest color are followed by the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is not the case that they are excluded.
The statement [that it is non-informative] would thus become useless, because colors such as light and shadow are listed by [the Vaibhāṣikas] themselves;

therefore, in this context, there is an interpretation that "image" (*pratibimba*) refers to the shadow of the karma of volition (*cetanā-karman*) set in motion by volition. Otherwise, it would contradict the separate listing of the first three types of informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*), since an image is not itself informative matter.
There is another interpretation that "image" is simply the color of the distant object (*dūra-rūpa*), namely the manifest colors of light and darkness.
The claim that "because it is a reflection, manifest color (*vijñapti-rūpa*) is simply a differentiation of shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), and thus this is not mentioned" is incorrect.
For if that were so, the first three categories of total matter (*samasta-rūpa*) would not be distinct from shape-color, since those reflections are not manifest color.

Furthermore, no other passage is seen that mentions manifest color instead of "distinctive color" (*prāsādika-rūpa*). Therefore, this [definition] may be treated as identical to what is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi*. Or...
The claim that this treatise contains twenty-five [categories] is also incorrect. For the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, chapter eighteen, states that seven things lack substantial reality:
first, informative intimation (*vijñapti*); second, shape (*saṃsthāna*); third, reflections (*pratibimba*), and so forth.

Since it mentions reflections as distinct from informative intimation-form (*rūpa-vijñapti*), one knows that a reflection is not identical to informative intimation-form. Thus, this objection is invalid; among the seven, the reflection is simply water.

Phenomena such as the moon in the sky or reflections in a mirror are subsumed under the "matter derived from the pervasive conceptualization of the sphere of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana-vikalpa-ja-rūpa*), and are not the same as the matter that constitutes the "reflected image" within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). Why is this so?

Because the first three chapters of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* state that there is "informative matter" (*vijñapti-rūpa*); thus we know that the separate explanation of the reflected image refers precisely to informative matter.
Otherwise, for what reason would it separately explain manifest color and shape (*varṇa-saṃsthāna*) without explaining informative matter? (The latter part of that volume.)

Regarding the colors of the locus where the Dharma is taught, there are twelve, namely the seven beginning with "reflected images" (*pratibimba*). Among these, the reflected image in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is certainly not the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*);
it is the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Furthermore, regarding the "reflected images" of the sense-sphere of form, there is another explanation:

they are objects perceived by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), unlike those transformed by the five [sensory] and eighth [storehouse] consciousnesses, because they possess actual efficacy. Therefore, this [reflected image] is also not [of the nature of the sense-sphere of form].

However, it might be argued that this reflection is included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) because it is the object of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), being the image of another eighth object;

yet this reasoning is also incorrect. For if that were so, all five objects would have to be said to possess images, and among the seven categories of provisional entities, the objects of the five consciousnesses would also have to be considered provisional.
Therefore, one should know that the first explanation is the correct one; this treatise explains [the matter] exhaustively.
For these twenty-five reasons, the various treatises do not contradict one another.
Regarding the distinction between manifest color (*varṇa*) and shape (*saṃsthāna*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there are thirteen types of manifest color:
blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, light, brightness, darkness, cloud, smoke, dust, mist, and the color of space; while there are ten types of shape: long, short, square, round, and so forth.
Regarding "color-form" (*rūpa*), it refers to coarse and subtle, high and low, upright and inverted, as well as the manifest actions of taking up, discarding, bending, extending, and so forth.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* explains that these include primary colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white; secondary colors such as long, short, square, round, and even light, dark, space, and the single color of clarity.
As for reflected images, these are also termed "form. Some commentaries explain that the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* mentions only four primary colors and two [secondary ones].
The ten types of material form, such as smoke, clouds, and so forth, are also subsumed under shape (*saṃsthāna*);

this differs from the *Yogācārabhūmi*, which—relying on the gate of distinguishing manifest characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)—states that there are thirteen types of manifest color (*varṇa*) and ten types of shape-color.

The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), relying on the gate of provisional and real characteristics (*prajñapti-satya* and *dravya-satya*), states that four types of color are manifest and the remainder are shape-colors. Furthermore, its eighteenth fascicle explains that seven types of color are provisional, while one is informative action (*vijñapti*).

The two genders, the three reflected images, the four echoes, the five tangibles produced by transformation, the seven types of restraint, and the seven types of non-restraint are not explained separately as [distinct] colors.

This is because smoke and other such things are considered "manifest color" (*varṇa*) only in a conventional sense; thus, it is known that the color of smoke and the like is subsumed under "shape" (*saṃsthāna*).
Some maintain that this is not the case, arguing that while that treatise speaks of "wholly conventional" phenomena, there are also real entities within the category of manifest color.

Therefore, they are omitted and not mentioned; since the initial statement regarding blue and other colors already includes the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one knows that manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*) is not limited to only four types.
Furthermore, while length and so forth are collectively termed "form" (*rūpa*), smoke and the like are not all included within "shape-color" (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*);
thus, one knows that shape-color does not encompass smoke and the like, because the nine categories such as smoke and clouds lack the nature of shape.

At the outset, based solely on the distinction between the conventional and the substantial, two categories are established: the four—blue, yellow, and so forth—are called "manifest color" (*varṇa*) because they are substantial;

all other colors are merely conventional. Since neither manifest color nor shape is specifically distinguished [in those cases], they are collectively termed simply "color. By including the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is shown that the nine types such as smoke are also manifest color;
by stating that "the rest are collectively termed color," it is shown that the four—blue and so forth—are exclusively substantially existent.

Regarding the mutual reflection of the two theories of shadow, the explanation of shadow as manifesting reality does not contradict [the other]; among the twenty-five [categories], fourteen are color-manifestations (*varṇa*).

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, thirteen are added by including "distant color" (*prāsādika-varṇa*). Ten of these are shape-colors (*saṃsthāna-varṇa*), or eleven types, because informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) is also a differentiation of shape.

Regarding the difference between the three types of conventional existence and substantial existence: blue, yellow, red, and white—these four are substantially existent; all others are conventionally manifest.

The second chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (*Xianyang lun*) states that length, shortness, coarseness, fineness, squareness, roundness, height, lowness, as well as regularity and irregularity, light, shadow, brightness, and darkness—categories such as these are subsumed under conventional form (*rūpa*).
That treatise further states that seven matters lack substantial reality, namely: [the first five sense objects], informative intimation (*vijñapti*), and...

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its first section on "Form and so forth" (*rūpādi-yoga*), explains that among manifest colors (*varṇa-rūpa*), light, shadow, and so forth, as well as informative form (*vijñapti-rūpa*), are all distinctions of matter (*rūpa-viśeṣa*).

Furthermore, the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states that formal shapes (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) such as long and so forth are all conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*), because they are accumulative in nature and because they are relative in nature.
Moreover, the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states that all informative form is conventionally existent; therefore, it is excluded [from the category of ultimate matter].
4. To show that all others are not real, because other forms are merely established in dependence upon these four. 5.
Some say that among the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the first nine and a portion of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) exist as substantial entities (*dravyasat*). 6.

Others say that all forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles that are considered real are stated according to their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); this is not the door of ultimate reality. This [analysis] is also based on the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding the preeminent objects.

That which is accomplished as non-manifest possesses form; this refers to bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*). That which is non-manifest and possesses manifestation refers to the wheel-light (*cakraprabhā*) and so forth.
That which is both manifest and possessed of form refers to other aggregates of matter (*rūpaskandha*). According to the principle of superior differentiation, there should be no contradiction.

Regarding the presence or absence of [shadow] within the three realms: since light is the radiance of the sun, and in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) there is definitively no shadow—because shadow arises from light—it is also not present there.
Furthermore, because it is perpetually luminous, there is no color of darkness; even the internal organs are perpetually luminous.
Since the three causes of obscuration—dust, mist, and smoke—are absent where there is no obscuration, the manifest color (*vijñapti-rūpa*) of dust, mist, and smoke is likewise non-existent.
It exists only in the Desire Realm and the First Dhyāna; the remainder, as appropriate, pervades five stages.

This is produced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) based on causes such as maturation (*vipāka*-karma) and so forth, and it exists throughout the three realms according to whether it is present or absent and its degree of extent. It is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

The manifestation [of forms] is explained through the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), both collectively and individually. The experience [of sensations] is explained through the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*).
Question: Among the aggregates (*skandha*), both the general and the specific are called "feeling" (*vedanā*). Within feeling, there are no distinct categories; only the general is named "feeling.

Within form (*rūpa*), there are distinct categories, and both the general and the specific are named "form. Question: Within consciousness (*vijñāna*), there are also distinct categories; should these also be given distinct names? Answer:

The three—mind (*citta*), mentation (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—are themselves the distinct names for consciousness. Question: Within consciousness, there are general and specific [categories]; should the specific consciousnesses be given distinct names?
Question: Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is designated by incorporating the name of another [factor], whereas form (*rūpa*) has distinct names that incorporate the name of itself.

Answer: The mind has a basis and is designated as "consciousness" according to its faculty; form has no basis and is not designated according to another. Question: The six consciousnesses have a basis and are designated as "faculties" (*indriya*) according to their support;

the mind and faculties have a basis and are designated as "mind" (*citta*) according to their support. Question: Regarding the six feelings (*vedanā*), what are the six? Answer: The six feelings are the six... [text ends].
Regarding the feelings of the body and the feelings of the mind among the faculties (*indriya*), they are named according to their basis (*āśraya*). Question:

Since there are many types of consciousness regarding form—both general and specific—and since mental formations (*saṃskāra*) regarding phenomena (*dharma*) are also numerous, both general and specific, why are they not named according to their basis? Answer:

Because the specific analysis of the "limb of formations" (*saṃskāra-aṅga*) discusses the consciousness that possesses form, it should likewise be named according to its basis. The six groups of volition (*ṣaṭ-cetanā-kāya*) are named according to their basis.
It is through reflection that one attains [understanding].
Regarding the statement "sound... is not included among the words of the Sage," the commentary states:
"In this fundamental treatise, the eleven categories of sound are divided into four types; the three meanings, such as 'agreeable' and so forth, [are explained therein]."
As previously stated, based on the three factors beginning with sensation (*vedanā*), and by way of their causal basis, sensation is distinguished as being of two types:

first, *vijñapti-vedanā* (cognitive sensation), which pertains exclusively to body-consciousness because it cognizes pleasure and pain; second, *anubhava-vedanā* (experiential sensation), which consists of the experiencing of all minds and mental factors as the body.

Since all sense organs (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) likewise depend upon the body organ, they are all termed "possessing cognitive sensation" (*sāvijñaptika-vedanā*) according to their support (*āśraya*). If one relies upon...

This produced sound, together with the four great elements and the body-faculty, is called "appropriated sound" (upātta-śabda); because it arises from these [elements], it is "caused by appropriation.
Since its substance is not itself appropriated, it cannot be cognized; as the treatise itself states below that one portion of the four external [elements] is appropriated.
If one relies on the latter [definition] where "appropriation" means being received as the body, then it is not only because of the [term] "great" (mahābhūta) that something is called appropriated.

The sound produced by what is appropriated is also included within "appropriated" (upātta); this is explained in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* as stating that one portion of the five external objects is appropriated.

Thus, according to the second fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (*Cheng weishi lun*) and its commentary, the three [categories] beginning with "worldly consensus" (*lokaprasiddha*) are established based on persons, while the two beginning with "sacred word" (*āptavāda*) are explained based on conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and language (*vāk*). This shall be understood in detail below.
Thus, from the eleventh [point] up to the "distinction of words. The commentary states:

"The Master of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) explains below that the preceding refutations and establishments are based on four kinds of reasons; furthermore, he follows these difficulties to explain them.

This refers to the characteristics of refutation and establishment themselves, as will be explained in the text below. It does not refer to the establishment of sounds or their increase and decrease."
The three types, beginning with the "agreeable," arise from the excellence or inferiority of the object and from the presence of favorable or unfavorable conditions;
thus they either cause harm or benefit. The "agreeable" causes benefit, the "disagreeable" causes harm, and the "neutral" pertains to both.

Alternatively, they are so called because there is a distinction between the causes—namely, the three [types of] feeling—and because of the great differentiation among their causes, such that sound becomes differentiated. Or, it is because of the distinction of the causes themselves.

Regarding the statement that there are distinctions among sounds such as "with reception" (*sopādāna*) and so forth: although the terms "worldly" (*laukika*), "established" (*pratiṣṭhita*), and so on are identical, they differ based on the person who establishes them, or because the persons themselves differ.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because of the distinction in speech," the two types of noble speech (*ārya-vāk*) are distinguished by whether the speaker's intention (*citta*) is compliant or contrary.
Because these five causes establish them, there are eleven types of sound.
Neither increasing nor decreasing.
"Characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the object apprehended by the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*).

[The commentary] states: Below, following the objection, the initial explanation of the five causes is given, followed by a specific explanation of sound. Prior to this, the cause of the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa-hetu*) was addressed.

Regarding the statement that the four [objects], such as blue and so forth, are now the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of sound and are thus apprehended by the auditory faculty, and that this is distinct from visible form (*rūpa*): what is the reason for this?

While the distinct characteristics and essential natures (*svabhāva*) of visible form and taste are easy to discern, the distinct characteristics of the three—sound, odor, and tangibility—are difficult to grasp.

Alternatively, since both visible form and taste possess both hidden and manifest aspects, and it is the manifest aspect that is designated as their characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the other three are likewise similar in this regard, being categorized under the same class of "characteristics."
Since "root-grasping" and "grasping by the root" are themselves the three roots, they serve as the causes for establishing distinctions; thus, the differences are explained.
As for the explanation of these distinctions, it proceeds according to what is appropriate.

The commentary states: Regarding the distinctions mentioned within the third [reason], those pertaining to "establishment in the world" (*loka-siddha*) and so forth are assigned to other reasons based on the different categories of persons.

Here, only the middle meaning is cited to illustrate the three points of the beginning and the end; since these have already been reversed, they should be assigned to the preceding reasons as appropriate.
How has this been separately explained?

Regarding "sounds derived from the primary elements" (upādāya-mahābhūta), such as the sounds of hands, drums, and so forth—the commentary states that these three categories, "agreeable" and so on, are the same as those for the sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) regarding what is "exquisite" or "unexquisite," and thus they are not explained here in detail.

Among these, vocal sounds (*vāg-śabda*) are said to be "sentient-being-included" (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*); however, the sounds of forests, trees, or the principles of the Dharma are not derived from the primary elements. This [explanation] merely illustrates a small portion.
This is also not contradictory, because within the term "arising from the great elements" (*mahābhūta*), it is accepted that many [great elements] produce a single derived form (*upādāyarūpa*).

Thus, sounds such as those of strings arise based on two great elements, just like blended perfumes and the like. Furthermore, the fact that these sounds of forests and so forth can produce names and so on is all as explained in the second fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
"Established by common consensus" (upapatti-sādhana), up to "as taught by the non-Buddhists.
The commentary states: That which is commonly accepted by both those who speak of truths and those who speak of non-truths in worldly discourse is therefore called "established by common consensus.

"Established" (*siddha*) has the sense of "fulfillment" (*paripūrṇa*); it refers to the fulfillment of the knowledge of truth that is universally accepted by all noble ones (*ārya*). Because it arises from causes and is established through speech, it is termed "established by common consensus" (*upapatti-sādhana*).

Citing the attachment of non-Buddhists who hold that the mind is called the cause of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), they state that its verbal expression is the arising of pervasive conceptualization.
In this context, based on the conventional and ultimate truths, there are three divisions of attachment. An ancient objection states:

"If pervasive conceptualization is subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) among the spheres of form (*rūpāyatana*), then the sound arising from pervasive conceptualization should not belong to the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*. They answer this themselves: "The sound of the teaching carries the essence [of the object]."

If it is asserted that sound arises as the substance of informative intimation (*vijñapti*) and is subsumed under the sphere of sound (*śabda-āyatana*), yet it is not the essence of instruction and does not manifest a substantial object, then the arising of material phenomena would be subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharma-āyatana*).
Furthermore, since things such as a second moon are not seen by the eye, this explanation is difficult to understand; one should follow the literal sense of the text.

If sound possesses the substance of informative intimation and is subsumed under the sphere of sound, then why are fragrance and so forth not admitted as informative intimation? If they were, they too would have to be subsumed under the sphere of mental objects. If both are subsumed under the sphere of mental objects, then what [is the distinction]?
If it were the case that only *nāmarūpa* [is so designated] and not otherwise, why would *rūpa* alone be thus?

Regarding the inclusion of *rūpa* within the *dharmāyatana*, while it is true that *rūpa* therein is restricted solely to the *rūpāyatana*, this should not be considered different from the case of sound being subsumed under a separate base. If one considers *rūpa* within the *dharmāyatana* to encompass both faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*), how could it be permissible for sound and visible form to be collected in separate bases?

It is in order to manifest that the adherence to dharmas arises through verbal expression (*śabda-abhidhāna*) that only the *śabdāyatana* is said to be the locus where the adherence to dharmas is conceptualized (*parikalpita*).

The arising of form that expresses conceptualization (*parikalpa*) is subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*); furthermore, the sound that manifests the distinct conceptualization of sounds is subsumed under the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*).
When there is no searching for form, the conceptualization of various phenomena arises as form and is included within the sphere of phenomena;

moreover, the form that is the object of conceptualization is subsumed under the sphere of phenomena, while the sound that arises due to the conceptualization of sound is subsumed under the sphere of sound. Furthermore, [the same applies to]...
The sound apprehended by a clear mental consciousness arising simultaneously with the auditory faculty is subsumed under the "pervasively imagined" (*parikalpita*) sound;

likewise, the sound apprehended by an unclear mental consciousness arising independently is also included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). Although such [imagined] form exists, because it lacks the nature of being a teaching (*deśanā*), a separate "pervasively imagined" sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is not established.
"Statements of the Noble and the Non-Noble" (up to) "the eight types of discourse.

The commentary states: herein, that which is spoken by the Noble Ones is not false; because it accords with reality, it is called "Noble. It does not refer to those who have realized the fruits [of the path].
In Sanskrit, this is *āptāgama*, which is translated here as "authoritative teaching" (*zhìjiàoliàng*) or "authoritative statement of the Noble Ones" (*shèngyánliàng*). This is precisely...
Words that are trustworthy and accord with reality are called "expressions arising from what has been seen, heard, and so forth. The opposite of these are the non-noble expressions.

These eight expressions either consist of two each—noble and non-noble—based on seeing and the other [faculties], or they consist of eight each based on seeing and the other four [faculties], as has already been analyzed.
This sound shall now be briefly explained by way of four gates; first, the manifestation of their number.

I. Differences in Number: The *Pañcaskandhaka* speaks only of the three causes, such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth; the first chapter of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states that sound has nine types, including the agreeable and so forth; the *Yogācārabhūmi* mentions striking hands, plucking strings, worldly livelihood, proclaiming the Dharma, and echoes. II. Differences in Abolition and Establishment: [The treatises differ on] what is established and what is abolished. III. Discernment of the Conventional and the Real: [The treatises differ on] the conventional and the real nature of the elements. IV. Presence or Absence of the Elements: [The treatises differ on] whether certain elements exist or not. [The above constitutes] the first section: Manifesting the Differences in Number. The *Pañcaskandhaka* says: "Only the three causes, such as feeling, etc. The first chapter of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* says:
"Sound has nine [types]: the agreeable and so forth; striking hands; plucking strings; worldly livelihood; proclaiming the Dharma; and echoes. The *Yogācārabhūmi* [also treats these].

The first explanation states that there are three categories: the first consists of eighteen types, such as conch-shells, drums, and so forth; the second category consists of three types, such as those arising from sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth;
the third category also consists of three types, such as agreeable (*manojña*) objects and so forth. This treatise mentions eleven [types].

Furthermore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Xianyang lun*) does not differ from this regarding the three types beginning with the agreeable. The three kinds—striking with the hand, an echo in a valley, and plucking strings—are, respectively, these very [categories].

These—namely, sensation (*vedanā*) and the other two—are the three types of conventional dharmas for sustaining life, which correspond respectively to the worldly, the established, and the noble/non-noble;
they are further distinguished by the meanings of being agreeable and so forth, based on the distinction between truth and untruth.

Although these were briefly mentioned without detailed exposition in the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, the nine previously mentioned categories do not exhaustively encompass them, because the term "appropriation" (*upādāna*) is used as a cause.
It is not merely striking with the hand, nor even up to the ninth [type] arising from conceptual construction; it is not merely for the sake of sustaining life.

For this reason, that treatise mentions them only in brief. In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, three categories are taught, each having three types of "agreeable causes" (*iṣṭa-hetu*) and "feelings" (*vedanā*), as their respective names indicate.
Regarding the first category, eighteen [factors] are explained based on the distinctions of the objective bases (*vastu*), rather than being categorized by way of a general class.
The analysis of sound is already fully subsumed within the latter two categories;

therefore, the five factors such as "worldly convention" (*loka-saṃvṛti*) and so forth—which differ in their expansion or contraction according to their respective applications—are not mutually contradictory. Second, regarding the differences in their establishment or exclusion:
based on the distinction of causes, since the three [factors] beginning with feeling (*vedanā*) fully encompass sound, the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* speaks only of these three. However—
Based on the distinctions between inferior and superior objects and conditions, and because these six— namely, the three categories of "agreeable" and so forth established upon causes,
feelings, and so on— comprehensively encompass all phenomena, the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other treatises speak only of these six. Now, in this treatise, based solely upon causes, feelings,

and a small portion of the three categories such as "agreeable," the three perceptions and expressions— "worldly convention" (*loka-saṃvṛti*) and so forth— are established according to the distinctions among persons.

Because they differ and because the terms "noble" and "non-noble" are established, some treatises mention [the categories] while others do not; now, examining the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*), it should state either only three or only six.
However, based on the preceding meaning, the latter five are further divided, such that the groups of three, six, eleven, and so forth, are all equally equal.
Third, regarding the distinction between the provisional and the real: each of the three—agreeable (*manojña*) and so forth—is [further divided].
Because there is a partial [aspect] and because one does not accept even a partial [aspect] as being real, while the remainder are all real;
thus the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, chapter eighteen, states that echo-sound (*pratiśrutkā-śabda*) is conventional (*prajñapti*), but does not say that other sounds are so.

Some say that among the six [realities], the latter five are all conventional because they are designated (*prajñapta*) based upon the former six. Regarding this very point, if an objection were raised: "Is it agreeable?"...

Since the three [categories] such as "equality" are also designated based upon causes such as sensation (*vedanā*), they too should not be real. Furthermore, since the substance of shape (*saṃsthāna*) depends on manifestation (*varṇa*) and accumulation (*saṃcaya*), its essence might not be ultimate.

As for the five [categories] beginning with "worldly convention" (*loka-saṃketa*), how could these latter five be merely nominal and not real, given that they do not depend on the six preceding categories for their designation as distinct states?
This objection is unreasonable; for even if the first six were reduced to the limit of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*)...
Because their subtle self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not lost, they are real and not provisional. As for the latter five [objects], they must depend upon the former six;

through the reliance on designations (*nāman*) and so forth that involve sequential continuity and differentiation, they are established as conventional designations (*prajñapti*). This principle is like the case of shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), which is not real but merely provisional, because its characteristics are lost at the moment of an ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).

According to one interpretation, all [the objects] may be understood as either provisional or real as appropriate, because they are designated based on the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).
Since manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*) and sound are conventional (*prajñapti*), they are not [ultimately] received;

since echoes are conventional, they arise from sounds and so forth, and because their logic is not real, all else is likewise categorized as both conventional and real. This is because the logic of that which arises from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) is not real.
Although this principle exists, no authentic textual evidence has been seen. How could even a single moment of the Buddha’s voice preach the Dharma? How could it be [the work of] a sage?
Regarding the statement that what is produced by causes (*nisyanda*) is invariably not real, and that one should adopt or reject between two alternatives according to the circumstances:
the presence or absence of the four elements is not a noble teaching. Sound exists only in the two lower stages because it is present where there is deception and guile;

thus, we have not seen it stated that those [higher stages] possess sound and so forth. Furthermore, the characteristics such as "having a cause" and "being simultaneous" are also difficult to discern if one relies on this [position].
Regarding the meaning: only that which has a cause is accepted, while that which is causeless or involves both [cause and non-cause] is not accepted by the Noble Ones.

As for the remaining sounds that may exist, although they pertain to all five stages (*bhūmi*), those that constitute the nature of karma belong only to the Desire Realm and the First Dhyāna. This explains that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) produced by karma, which serve as the cause of sound, pertain to both the Desire and Form Realms.

If it is sound included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) transformed through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth, its realm and stage depend upon the specific state of that transformation.
Regarding the question of whether sound is substantial or nominal according to its various applications, one should consider it as follows:

it is substantial, because even a single moment of sound functions as a signifier. If that is so, why is it said that body and speech are nominal? It is because they are merely the substrata upon which the signifying sound depends.
"Regarding fragrance (up to) 'transformed fragrance' (*vikṛtagandha*)," the commentary states:

"The Master of this Treatise here enumerates the causes of fragrance and the perceivers [of fragrance], listing their distinctions. Below, the Exegetical Master explains the first three based on the distinction between the sentient being and the object;
as for those established based on the object, 'good fragrance' (*sugandha*) refers to fragrance such as that of aloeswood (*agaru*) and musk (*mṛgamada*')."
"Equal bad odors" refers to things such as garlic and leeks, which are foul-smelling; "equally both [neither good nor bad]" refers to things such as clods of earth or stones.
When distinguished according to human sentiment, each of these three preceding categories contains three further types. Why is it that garlic and the like are called fragrant rather than foul?

This is because what is commonly referred to in the world as fragrance is also called foul. To say that the fragrance of orchids is "foul" is truly different from worldly convention; even that which is foul may be called fragrant.
Therefore, one should not find fault [with this].
One should know that this fragrance [extends] to its various distinctions.
The commentary states: "This establishes the characteristics of the six preceding fragrances by means of three causes" refers to what was previously apprehended by the olfactory faculty.

Regarding the explanation of benefit and harm within sound: this refers to the three [qualities] beginning with "pleasant. If explained in terms of the object, "pleasant" is beneficial, "unpleasant" is harmful, and "neutral" is neither.
If explained in terms of the subjective feeling, both fragrant and foul odors possess the sense of being either beneficial or harmful. Regarding the distinctions:
these three, beginning with "innate," are simply distinctions among the aforementioned three types of fragrance; therefore, these six odors do not... [redundant].
It increases but does not decrease.
Regarding "arising simultaneously with fragrance" (up to): this refers to ripe fruits and the like.

The commentary states: following the previous difficulty, it is explained that as soon as [the fruit] arises, there are the three [qualities]—good, bad, and so forth—which arise together with the production; therefore, they are called "arising simultaneously."
Innate fragrances such as *candana* (sandalwood) and so forth refer to things that possess their meaning through their actual substance;

these are what were traditionally called "sandalwood scents," such as *vāśī* grass and others—there are many such types. As for "transformed fragrances," this refers to ripe fruits and the like, where the fragrance increases precisely at the time they ripen and undergo transformation.
This fragrance shall be briefly explained by way of three categories: first, the difference between increase and decrease; second... [text continues].

Regarding the question and answer concerning the establishment and abolition of the three [categories] based on the distinction between the provisional and the real: first, the difference in increase and decrease.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Five Aggregates section) states that there are only three, namely the pleasant, the unpleasant, and so forth. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Exposition of Manifestation) states that there are briefly two types;

the three—pleasant, unpleasant, and so forth—and the three—co-arising, and so forth. These six kinds are the same as this [text]. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* does not state that the three—co-arising, and so forth—are identical to the pleasant, unpleasant, and so forth.
Because they are equivalent, the first three [categories] encompass them all, so the latter two are not mentioned. As for the difference between the provisional and the real: these six are all real;

there is no textual passage stating that fragrance also extends to the provisional. Since form is constituted by the accumulation of manifest colors, both form and its manifestation are termed "provisional.

If fragrance were accumulated to constitute a "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), then this conjunction ought not to be real. The same logic applies to the objection raised previously regarding the word "simultaneous" (*saha*). This is the characteristic.

When one form is depended upon, that form is lost; thus, both the form and its manifestation become merely conventional (*prajñapti*). When depending on other fragrances, they still exist in a state of combination (*saṃyoga*); therefore, they truly constitute an accumulation.

By taking the short to be long, the original shortness and length are lost; thus, shortness is not real. If one analyzes those [fragrances] produced together, it should be established that the two fragrances in combination are merely conventional.
Regarding this objection, one should apply effort [to provide a response]. Third, as for the questions and answers concerning refutation and establishment: the question is as follows.

Since the three categories beginning with the unwholesome (*akuśala*) already encompass all phenomena, why is it necessary to further establish the three categories beginning with the co-nascent (*sahaja*)? Answer:

They are established because their objective entities (*vastu*) and types (*jāti*) differ. The first three are established based on the distinction in the timing of their functional activity (*kāritra*).

Furthermore, the latter three are established based on whether one considers the object from the perspective of the mind, or speaks of the object while setting aside the mind. Through these analytical perspectives, they are distinguished into six.
Regarding "types" and "tastes" (up to) "if they change":

the commentary states that the distinctions among the six tastes—bitter, sour, and so forth—and the six [qualities] such as being agreeable to the mind are their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). This is to be understood accordingly.
It should be understood that what precedes is the main text of the treatise, while what follows is the Master’s commentary.
The establishment of this "flavor" (rasa) should be explained according to the discussion on "odor" (gandha).

The commentary states: The principles for the inclusion or exclusion of the three causes are based on the analogy of odor; odor is analogous to sound because their characteristics are identical, and thus the sense organ perceives this [flavor].
Furthermore, by analogy with the preceding [argument], suffering and so forth would likewise lack the characteristics of having causes.

Since it has been established that the six objects—such as bitter and sour tastes—which are apprehended by the tongue-faculty, are established as being without causes, one should know that this intention is based on the three [qualities] being identical to fragrance.

If they were established separately, they would differ from the preceding [category of] fragrance; therefore, they are the very roots of the six tastes, such as bitter and sour, just like the four [objects] beginning with fragrance.
The remaining two causes should be understood according to the previous explanation regarding odor; they cannot be assigned separately, as their meaning is identical to that of odor.

Furthermore, this was already briefly demonstrated within the section on the sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). Thus, the twelve tastes neither increase nor decrease. This taste will be analyzed briefly by way of three sections: first, establishment and exclusion (*pratiṣedha*);
second, the conventional and the real (*prajñapti-vastu*); third, questions and answers. Regarding the first, establishment and exclusion, it is stated in the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*:
The *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* contains these latter six [factors] but lacks these former six;

the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* contains these former six, as well as "agreeable" (*manojña*) and so forth, because the general includes the particular, and thus the five aggregates do not mention these latter six types.
Since the particular includes the general, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* does not mention them.

Regarding the first six types, the general and specific meanings are fully established by the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which does not mention the three categories such as "innate" (*sahaja*) because these are already subsumed within the general categories such as "agreeable" (*manojña*).

Therefore, when these arise in relation to objective entities (*vastu*), it is most free from contradiction to establish the general and specific categories—such as "innate"—distinctly outside of "agreeable" and so forth, thereby completing the system.
Consequently, there are differences in the inclusion or exclusion [of categories] in various treatises, which are merely two kinds of conventional designations (*prajñapti*).

Regarding the argument that because there is no textual statement [of them] as being conventional (*prajñapti*), they must all be substantially existent (*dravyasat*): this is difficult to reconcile with the principle of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) and so forth; thus, it should be explained like the case of fragrance.

Just as fragrance and flavor exist as two distinct types through conjunction, so too the latter five [objects] are also conventional and not substantial, because they are established in dependence upon others and because their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are lost when they are analyzed.
Third, regarding the question and answer: why is it that sound and fragrance exist only in a collective sense and not [individually]?
Regarding the contact of a single part of a distinct object, there is only the distinct [contact] and not a collective one; this applies to both color-form (*rūpa*) and taste (*rasa*).

To illustrate the principle of collective and distinct contact, the correspondence between color-form and taste—which includes the collective—is established; subsequent cases are omitted as they follow the same pattern as the former.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that while pleasant and unpleasant contacts are both present, the three types—sound, odor, and the third [taste]—are such that the collective is itself the distinct. Since the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inherently diverse, one should not demand uniformity across all cases.
For what reason do odors and tastes possess these three types—such as co-arising (*sahaja*) and so forth—whereas among visible forms, sounds, and tangibles these three types are absent?
Furthermore, while the characteristics of these three—visible form, odor, and taste—are explained in detail, the characteristics of sound and tangibles are mostly omitted and not explained.

Moreover, it is logical that in the three stages [of digestion], the characteristics of odor and taste increase, and thus they are described as "conjoined" (*saṃyukta*) and so forth, whereas in those stages the characteristics of visible form, sound, and tangibles are obscured and therefore omitted from the explanation.
Since they all truly exist, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "Whether co-nascent (*sahaja*), whether combined (*saṃyukta*), or whether transformed (*vikṛta*), there is contact (*sparśa*).

Furthermore, shapes such as length are caused by [the conjunction of] atoms; sounds such as 'conjoined' are caused by striking. There are sounds that arise from striking but lack co-nascence and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "in the state of purity, 'roughness' is established as a designation for what is weighable":

this means that lightness and heaviness are explained such that the state of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) being solid and firm is established as heaviness, while the state of not being solid and firm is established as lightness. In the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), that which cannot be weighed is called light, whereas that which can be weighed is called heavy.
Since both of these [lightness and heaviness] are weighable, they are therefore designated [as such]. Even when compared to a heavy object, that which is weighable remains light.
"Because it is not known what kind of tangibility it is" refers to softness (*mṛdutva*);

that treatise establishes softness as a state of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) among the [six] tangibles, whereas this treatise clarifies its name and position. "Because of grasping at the basis" refers to laxity and tension;
since those [elements] lack these two, they are mixed. "Because of cold and stickiness" will be explained in the text below; that treatise is the same as this one.

"Because of the inequality of the elements (*dhātu*)" means: hunger, thirst, weakness, fainting, itching, disease, old age, death, and fatigue. "Elements" refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
It is taught that hunger and thirst are established due to the inequality of the deficiency in their support (*upastambha*);
fainting is established due to the inequality of impure food and drink; and itching is established due to the inequality of the presence of defects in the blood.
Illness is established due to the inequality of transformation and confusion; old age is established due to the inequality of the transformation of time;
death is established due to the inequality of the transformation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); fatigue is established due to the inequality of the exhaustion from coming and going.
As for "the equilibrium of the elements" (*dhātu-sāmya*), it refers to strength, rest, and vigor; that [equilibrium] is said to be due to the absence of [disequilibrium].

The power (*bala*) is established because of the equilibrium of the constituent elements (*dhātu*); the rest (*praśrabdhi*) is established because of the removal of fatigue through the equilibrium of the elements;

and the vigor (*vīrya*) is established because it removes the impurities of illness and eliminates exhaustion. This [text] calls the strong "power" and the weak "inferior," while that treatise calls them "strong power" and "weak power.

It is taught that the elements (dhātu) are equal because they serve as the superior sustenance [for contact]; it is not taught that they are "satiated" by the unwholesome. This is because those [elements] rely upon the great elements (mahābhūta), which exist in six distinct states:
namely, the pure state and the impure state; the solid state and the non-solid state; the tense state and the relaxed state;
the combined state; the unequal state; and the equal state. Accordingly, the aforementioned contact is established as neither increasing nor decreasing.
When analyzed, they become eight, or eight, or six, because their characteristics are equally equal and because they belong to the same collective grasping;
since those [distinctions] do not exist, they are equal.

"Because the elements are in equilibrium, the power of exertion is courageous.
The commentary states: This reveals one cause; that is, the "resting" (*śvasa*) of the aforementioned three contacts. "Not being in equilibrium" (*viṣama*) reveals the remaining nine.

"The brave are fearless. The commentary states: The meaning of "brave" (*vīra*) is difficult to understand; therefore, it is explained further. To be uplifted and vigorous is called "brave. Because one is brave, one is fearless (*abhaya*).

Fearlessness is precisely the absence of timidity or dread in the mind. Since that [fearlessness] can produce contact (*sparśa*), the cause is used to manifest the result; thus, it is termed "fearless."
Alternatively, that which is fearless is the very substance of contact.

The yoga of inequality, which causes hunger and other states, is simply described as the equality of the elements (*dhātu*).
