Regarding "form arising from conceptual construction" (*parikalpita-rūpa*): it also admits of two interpretations. Regarding "form produced by mastery" (*vaibhutvika-rūpa*):
it definitely refers to that which is unobstructed and is thus called the "fruit of mastery. Form that arises from that [mastery] is called "that which is produced by it";
this "produced" is itself form, hence it is called "produced form. Form that is produced by mastery is called "form produced by mastery."
The two explanations are as before.

Regarding the fourth point, the distinction between the provisional and the real: the sixth fascicle [of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] states that atoms have no substantial entity (*avastuka*), being revealed through the analytical discernment of wisdom;

the fifth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that one establishes the atom by analyzing gross matter with wisdom down to its most subtle limit, rather than because it possesses an intrinsic existence.

Because it is their very nature, it is said that atoms (paramāṇu) are without arising or ceasing. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle three, states: "Within a mass of form, there has never been an atom;
when [form] arises from seeds, it arises solely as a collection, nor is coarse form composed of an accumulation of atoms.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also says: "The atom is a provisional designation established at the limit of form. These and other [texts], such as the fifty-fourth [fascicle], all teach this.
For this same reason, both the first and second types of matter are all conventionally established (prajñapti-siddha).

The term "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) refers to the conventional designation of non-informative action (avijñapti), which is established based on the limits of volition (cetanā) and aspiration (praṇidhāna) regarding good and evil. It is also said that the non-informative restraints (saṃvara-avijñapti) of good and evil are conventionally established based on the state in which the two seeds have not yet been destroyed.
Since there are many such proofs, it is known that what is "conducted by undertaking" (samādāna-ākṣipta) is also [conventionally established].
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, chapter eighteen, states that seven things lack substantial reality because they are three types of images and four types of echoes;

therefore, even the form of the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) is conventionally existent. Chapter fifty-four states that among the forms included within the *dharmāyatana* (sphere of mental objects), some are substantially existent and some are conventionally existent.
If there is a majestic power such that it is an object of meditative concentration, like a transformation (*nirmāṇa*), then its fruit, its object, and its [basis]—[are substantially existent].
The objective forms corresponding to consciousness and so forth are substantially existent;

this is because the teaching of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) states that the *ālayavijñāna* transforms into the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the manifest forms included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Therefore, the essence of "form resulting from meditative concentration" (*samādhiphalarūpa*) is substantially existent.

Regarding this, there is an interpretation that among the five kinds of form, the first four are nominally existent while only the fifth is substantially existent, as stated in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.

In the exposition of the seven provisional phenomena (*prajñapti*), only the provisional nature of restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is mentioned, while the meditative fruits (*samāpatti-phala*) are not said to be provisionally existent.

Furthermore, in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is stated that among the matter of the sphere of dharma (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), the matter of majestic power and meditative matter (*vaśitā-samādhi-rūpa*) are substantially existent (*dravyasat*), whereas both restraint and non-restraint are provisionally existent.
It is also not stated that the matter within the objective field of this meditative state is provisionally existent.

There is an interpretation that the fifth [category] also includes the provisional existence of the Bodhisattvas, the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), and so forth, as well as the colors of liberation (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
These are all conceptualized forms (*parikalpita-rūpa*) which lack any actual utility. If they were not included here, under what category would such colors be subsumed?

Since they are objects of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are not included among the five sensory domains (*pañca-viṣaya*). Furthermore, their nature is not that of atoms (*paramāṇu*), nor are they non-informative matter (*avijñapti*); for those liberations and so forth are not [states of] meditative concentration [in the sense of being physical].
Furthermore, this imagined nature (*parikalpita*) does not belong to the first four types of form; if it were not the fifth, it would have no category to which it belongs.

Thus, these five types of form would fail to encompass all phenomena. Nor can it be said that imagined form is subsumed under "reflected images" (*pratibimba*), for are not all meditative minds characterized by mental construction?
And do not minds such as the untainted (*anāsrava*) lack such conceptualization? [The answer is: The Buddha’s wisdom is fully endowed [with such qualities].

Because it can manifest various images, this treatise also states that the forms within the range of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*) are called "forms produced by concentration" (*samādhi-ja-rūpa*).
However, because those transformed by noble beings (*ārya*) are all truly accomplished and extremely sublime, the *Yogācārabhūmi* speaks of only them as being produced by concentration;
since those [images] arising from conceptualization (*parikalpa*) are not sublime, they are omitted and not mentioned.
The transformations produced by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are visible only to others and cannot be utilized; how, then, are they not provisional?

The first chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that the matter induced by meditative concentration arises from three grades of mind: the nature of the objective image (*pratibimba*) and the nature of the accomplished matter (*niṣpanna-rūpa*) produced by it.
The former is provisional matter, while the latter is substantial matter. Furthermore, the first chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* [states...]

Among the eighteen categories of form (*rūpa*), the provisional nature of color is explained through the provisional nature of reflected images (*pratibimba*). Furthermore, among the twelve types of form included in the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), the first is the reflected image.

If this provisional reflected image were not the result of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*), that treatise would not have stated that there is no other form in the sphere of mental objects besides the result of meditative concentration (*avijñapti-samādhi-phala*).
Since it must be accounted for within the category of form, we know that the result of meditative concentration exists.
The provisional existence [of objects] as being posterior to their reality is considered superior because it accords well with the meaning of the scriptural teachings.

Fifth, regarding the manifestation of the presence or absence of substantiality: the seventh fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that there are two kinds of objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*):

first, the immediate (*sākṣāt*), and second, the mediate (*pāramparya*). That which is not separate from the substance of the perceiving consciousness is that which is internally relied upon and reflected upon by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and so forth.

One should know that when these [objects] serve as the substantial basis (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the arising of internal objects of cognition despite being separated from the essence of the cognizing subject, they are to be known as the remote objective condition (*parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya*).

Although these five kinds of form are mostly nominal (*prajñapti-sat*), the characteristics of the direct objective conditions for the cognizing mind are invariably present; therefore, he further explains the direct [condition].
Regarding the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the subjective cognizer (*ālambaka*), both are devoid of the nature of being able to arise from an internal object of cognition;

this is because they are dependent on others (*paratantra*) and originate from causes. As for those non-substantial forms (*rūpa*), they are produced from the seeds of the cognizer and so forth, and thus lack the function of formless [entities].
Consequently, either there is no distinct seed, or they arise from the same seed as the essential reality (*svabhāva*). However, they possess no practical efficacy. If...
That which is substantially existent possesses the function of form; thus, it arises from a distinct seed and does not arise from the same seed as its corresponding cognitive faculty (*ālambaka*).

As explained in the *Commentary on the Essential Points* (*Śūtra-vṛtti*), one should interpret these five [objects] according to their distinct seeds: either they appear as form, or they possess the function of form.

Because these two types serve as the direct objects of perception (*pratyakṣa-ālambana*), all five are termed "form-bases" (*rūpāyatana*). According to the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, [the remaining objects] are considered remote objects (*parokṣa-ālambana*).

Regarding the statement that all minds arising through objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) are necessarily determined to possess the Buddha-ground and so forth, it is because non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), when taking true suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, also transforms it into an image (*pratibimba*).

Since all minds that arise must necessarily have an underlying essence (*svabhāva*), based on this principle, four out of the five types of form (*rūpa*) among the five categories must necessarily have an underlying essence.
First, regarding extremely subtle form (*paramāṇu-rūpa*), it exists within the ten types of material phenomena in the desire and form realms.

Regarding the bases (*āyatana*), they take the substantial form that is the fruit of the meditative attainments of the form and formless realms as their essential nature; this is because it is taught that there are fifteen atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Next, regarding the "distinctive form" (*prāsādika-rūpa*), it takes the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) of the desire and form realms as its essential nature, since there is no separate location for the formless realm.
Thus, all that is described here takes as its essential nature that which is produced by the analysis of those coarse forms.
That which is not of such a nature is not said to be the substantial basis (*bimba*) of what is induced by feeling, because it is neither a transformation of the mind nor a reflected image;
therefore, it is not called the "substantial basis" arising from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

This is because the ten material bases (*rūpāyatana*) of the desire and form realms, as well as the matter produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the two higher realms, can all serve as substantial bases upon which reflected images are projected.

The matter produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) takes as its essential nature the matter of the sense faculties and their objects belonging to the desire and form realms; this is explained in fifty-four ways.

Furthermore, it is said that the matter which is the fruit of superior concentration arises from a samādhi that is an image (*pratibimba*) of that same category based on those [real] objects, and because it is said to be "greatly derived" (*mahābhūtika*), it takes the matter of both realms as its essential nature—whether that prior matter has a real object or lacks a fundamental objective referent.

Since it is accepted that consciousness and its activity share a commonality regarding their seeing and their images, and because they take the named teachings (*nāma-dharma*) as their essential substance (*bimba*), we know that the objects of cognition (*ālambana*) must necessarily possess both an image and a substance.
By these four types of matter, the essential substance is established, thereby fulfilling the teaching of *Vijñaptimātratā* (Cognition-Only).

This is because a remote object-condition (*parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya*) may exist, and even in the absence of an external basis upon which it relies, [cognition] can still arise; this applies to the eighth and sixth consciousnesses.

The objective essence (*vastu*) upon which various mental states depend may either exist or not exist; thus, the presence or absence of the distant object-condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*) is indeterminate.

If one relies on this principle, then regarding the objects of conceptualization—namely, the extremely subtle, the extremely remote, pervasive [space], and matter arising from imagination—the causes for analyzing these various forms consist of names, teachings, and objective essences as previously described.
Furthermore, based on one’s own discursive investigation, one imagines the self and phenomena to be like empty flowers, rabbit horns, or the past.
In future kalpas, when they reach their end, these [forms] are always subtle and do not depend on the instruction of others; they all lack a substantial basis (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, regarding the matter of the fruits of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), there are those that transform, those that manifest, those that arise dependent on others, and those produced by the power of concentration. If it is a transformation dependent on others, it must have a substantial basis.

However, as for manifestations produced by the power of concentration and those occurring in the state of mastery (*vaśitā*), they do not require others to arise. Therefore, whether this substantial basis exists or not [is irrelevant].

Although it is said that the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is common to both the vision (*darśana*) and its image (*pratibimba*), who would grant that it pervades all minds?

For if correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, it must take it as a single [object], just as an activity takes a single [object]. If the cognition that takes suchness as its object also possesses an image, who could illuminate that [image]?

Furthermore, if one knows that true suchness exists, then the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*) should likewise have no distinction. Moreover, even though Bodhisattvas enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), [they do not lose their continuity].

Yet they still manifest majestic deportment while wandering through various pure lands. This occurs because the mental intention (*āśaya*) prior to meditative concentration strikes the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), causing the various modes of deportment to appear.
Although the mind has subsequently ceased, the deportment does not perish, for it is maintained by the eighth consciousness as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Upon what objective essence (*bhāva-svabhāva*) does the deportment in this state depend? It is not otherwise; for when Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward enter [meditative absorption]...
In the state of meditative absorption (*nirodha-samāpatti*), there would be no prior mental consciousness to trigger the arising of deportment (*airyāpathika*);

thus, the manifestation of deportment would be impossible. Furthermore, it would not be the case that one enters absorption moment by moment while simultaneously manifesting various forms of deportment; such a view would contradict the various sūtras everywhere.

Moreover, when the Brahma King and others transform their original physical forms to listen to the Dharma before the Buddha or engage in conversation, the preceding transforming mind must be the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

When that which has already ceased is not necessarily present before consciousness at the time of its cognition, the transformed appearance (*nirmāṇa-rūpa*) is exclusively an object of the eighth [consciousness].

What dharma serves as its substantial basis (*svabhāva*)? Since the objects of the eighth consciousness are also necessarily results of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*), the existence or non-existence of the substantial basis relied upon by these results of concentration is therefore indeterminate.
Thus, the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) accords with the profound school and is consistent with the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.

The modes of activity follow the nature of the objects as taught in the present teachings; they do not follow the mind. "Solitary images" (pratibimba) arise solely from the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*); "images with substance" (*sanimitta*) pertain to both the mental aspect (*savitarka*) and the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*), following their respective seeds and so forth as appropriate.
As for "extremely condensed matter" (*paramāṇu-rūpa*), it refers to matter that is free from other obstructive contacts.
The commentary states: The following is the master’s separate explanation of the first five [categories]. In the Indic language, *paramāṇu* is rendered as *parama-aṇu*;
here, *parama* means "ultimate" and *aṇu* means "minute. Among material forms (*rūpa*), that which is the smallest is designated by the name "ultimate atom" (*paramāṇu*).

Seven *paramāṇus* constitute one *aṇu*; thus, from seven ultimate atoms, one minute particle (*anu*) is formed. This is the meaning of the old terminology. Regarding the phonetics: [the term is *paramāṇu*].
Because it is a conventional designation, it is called *aṇu* (atom) or *paramāṇu* (extreme atom); this "extreme" signifies the limit.

As stated in verse 54, the extreme atom (*paramāṇu*) is established by analyzing all material forms with discriminative wisdom until reaching their ultimate limit; it does not exist as a substantial entity.
Therefore, the extreme atom is neither produced nor destroyed, nor is it a collection of atoms that constitutes matter. This is also stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Although these atoms possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*), they cannot be further divided; if one were to divide them further, they would appear as mere space and would no longer be called "form" (*rūpa*).
Therefore, it is said that the atom is the limit of form (*rūpaparyanta*). Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its third [section], states:
"Aggregates of form have spatial dimensions, and atoms are likewise. Aggregates of form have parts, but atoms do not; the atom is precisely..."

Because these are divisible, there are no further atoms (*paramāṇu*); thus, the textual meaning of the fifth, sixteenth, and eighteenth fascicles of the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (Exposition of the Teachings) is identical, and it is unnecessary to cite them here.
Since they are divided according to spatial directions (*dig-bhāga*), those atoms would themselves lack parts.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation as stated in the *Weishi shu* (Commentary on the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi) regarding "extremely remote form" (*atyanta-dūra-rūpa*).
That which is this very [atom] devoid of other obstructive contacts is precisely the aforementioned "extreme atom" (*paramāṇu*).
This extreme atom, when devoid of other obstructive contacts, is called "extreme distant color" (*parama-pratighāta-varṇa*);

this same extreme atom, when not devoid of other obstructive contacts, is called "extreme condensed [color]" (*parama-saṃkṣipta*). Alternatively, "this very" refers to this extreme distant color being devoid of other obstructive contacts.

Because it is the ultimate subtle particle (*paramāṇu*) of distant color, it is called "ultimate-distant color" (*dūratama-varṇa*). Since that distant color is manifested by being free from obstruction, any obstructive tangible object is termed "the other.
These two [categories] are briefly explained through three gateways: first, determining the conditions for the eye;
second, resolving contradictions and difficulties; and third, the excellence of liberation. Regarding the first, determining the conditions for the eye: first, the physical eye, karma, and so forth.

Because they are produced [from causes], these two—the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and the cultivated eye (*bhāvanāmayacakṣus*)—arise through the application of skillful means; thus, both of these belong to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as the faculty of the eye.

Third is the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*); fourth is the Dharma eye (*dharmacakṣus*). These two are both untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*). Fifth is the Buddha eye (*buddhacakṣus*), which consists of the preceding four.
This will be analyzed in detail in the chapter on the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) below. As stated in [text] 54, the fleshly eye and the divine eye are excluded.
The other eyes take all atoms as their objective range;

however, that divine eye perceives only the external, upper, lower, front, and rear sides within a mass of form—whether light or dark—and can by no means apprehend the location of individual atoms, because the substance of an atom is established only through analytical discernment by wisdom.
If this is so even for the divine eye, how much more so for others?

Regarding the contradiction between the two explanations of the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that Bodhisattvas can know how many atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute the palaces of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
It says: "Briefly stated, there are fifteen kinds of atoms," and such scriptural teachings are found in many places.
If atoms did not exist, how could these passages be reconciled? Although they lack ultimate reality (*tattva*), [they are taught for the sake of conventional understanding].
The nature of the atom (*paramāṇu*) is as it is analyzed by wisdom; its measure is likewise established because one knows that atom to be of the same measure as that which was analyzed.
(54) It is said that coarse matter is not formed by the aggregation of atoms; thus, the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) is established.

However, when consciousness undergoes transformation, it manifests instantaneously as a single appearance according to the magnitude [of the object], whether large or small, rather than transforming separately into a multitude of atoms.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also states that when various aggregated forms first arise, they arise as a whole, and when they finally perish, they do not reach the level of atoms;
they are extinguished in the interim just like drops of water.

The meaning of this statement is to demonstrate that when water in a heated cauldron is boiled away gradually until it vanishes, it does not reach the edges [of the vessel] before being completely exhausted; thus, it proves that matter is destroyed instantaneously.

Having read the preceding text at length and further analyzed these various forms (*rūpa*), one finds that they perish instantaneously without reaching the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*) before being utterly extinguished.

This is not like drops of water which gradually reach their limit; while the various forms finally come to an end, they do not even reach such a limit, let alone a truly existent atom that can be perceived.
Therefore, one knows only that [form] is what is dissected by wisdom; furthermore, it possesses both essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*kāritra*).
If the absolute minimum is what is called an *aṇu* (atom), and this is designated as the "extreme subtle" (*paramāṇu*), what fault would there be?
To state the benefits of the threefold explanation: since there is no such thing as an atom, what benefit would there be in stating it? The fifty-fourth [verse] states that there are five benefits:
by means of the method of analyzing a composite mass of form (*saṃghātarūpa*) and establishing it, one is able to purify the objective sphere (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, by practicing this vast purification, one can gradually sever the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), eliminate all forms of pride, subdue the entanglements of the afflictions (*kleśaparyavasthāna*), and swiftly dispel all signs (*nimitta*).

The intent here is to explain that in cultivating the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), one must first analyze all form (*rūpa*) down to its ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*);
only after severing the afflictions in this manner does one subsequently enter into emptiness. It is for this reason that there is such great benefit.

Therefore, it is said that atoms can analyze that mind; as for who gives rise to it, which truth it is subsumed under, whether it is untainted (*anāsrava*), and so forth—all these should be considered according to other chapters.
"Matter derived from feeling" refers to unmanifest matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
The commentary states: All monastic precepts must be received from a teacher, because the teacher discriminates between those who are capable and those who are incapable.

For the two groups of lay followers and the bodhisattva precepts, as well as for non-virtuous non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), one may receive them from both oneself and others; these do not require such discrimination because their benefit or harm is broad in scope. The aforementioned cases are all termed "receiving" (*samādāna*).
The non-informative matter of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the path (*mārga*) is acquired without depending on another; these are all [of this latter type].
Because it can manifest one’s good and evil deeds to others, it is collectively termed "non-informative" (*avijñapti*).

Its essential nature and categories are designated as "induced by undertaking" (*samādānāhṛta*) based on their mutual conformity. The meanings of these various categories will be explained below in the eighth chapter and in the separate section.
"Form arising from pervasive conceptualization" refers to reflected-form (*pratibimba-rūpa*).

The commentary states: In the state of distraction, when the contaminated mental consciousness (*sāsrava-manovijñāna*) arises independently, it transforms into form-sense-bases (*rūpīndriya*) and objects; these have no actual utility whatsoever.
Because they must rely upon a primary object (*bimba*) to arise, they are called "reflected-form. This form is briefly explained by way of two gates: first, the analysis of the conceptualizing mind.

Second, regarding the distinction between those with and without outflows (*anāsrava*), concerning the mind that performs discernment and calculation (*vikalpa-vijñāna*): in the causal stage, the five sense-faculties have two objects of perception—first, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and second, the foundational consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

Regarding the five objective spheres such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, there are three [consciousnesses] that perceive them: first, the five sensory consciousnesses; second, the mental consciousness; and third, the foundational consciousness.

Regarding the various forms that are the fruits of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), there are two [consciousnesses] that perceive them: first, the mental consciousness, and second, the foundational consciousness. As for the mental consciousness...
There are three categories of objects of focus (*ālambana*): first, the category of objects of meditative cultivation that are the fruits of concentration;

second, the category of clearly manifest objects of the distracted mental consciousness that arise together with the five sensory consciousnesses; and third, the category of unclearly apprehended objects constructed by the solitary, distracted mind.

Among these, all forms (*rūpa*) may be objects of the five sensory consciousnesses, objects of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), or objects of the mental consciousness at its initial stage.
The objects of the first two categories are each subsumed under their own respective realms as appropriate.

As for the third category—the objects of the mental consciousness—with the exception of the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), they are all subsumed under the matter produced by this pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). This cognizing mind pertains to both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Although the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that the stages of the form realm lack "discursive speech" (*anuvyavahāra*), the "scattered and solitary mental engagement" (*vyagrā-kevala-manasikāra*) encompasses both.

If the nature of the mind transforms to take various forms as its objects, how could it be said that they do not exist? It has already been explained previously that this would imply consciousness arises without a cause.

The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Exposition of Ascertainment), Chapter 18, states that the mind bound to the desire realm can take as its objects the three realms as well as objects not bound [to any realm];
the minds of the two upper realms likewise each can take these four kinds of objects. Furthermore, the sixty-fifth [chapter] states: "If an Arhat does not..."
The wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) also takes all phenomena of the lower stages as its object.

Based on such proofs, although the mind of the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) can take the lower stages as its object, it cannot give rise to this pervasive conceptualized conventional form (*prajñaptirūpa*).

Therefore, that which can take this as an object is restricted to those bound to the two realms (the desire and form realms), the two types of existence, and the untainted (*anāsrava*); there is also the view that it certainly includes the tainted (*sāsrava*), and some maintain that even the conventional forms of the marks of the untainted are included.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* and other such treatises included herein state that the form resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) is exclusively substantially existent (*dravya-sat*).

Therefore, it cannot be said that the form resulting from concentration subsumes uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) nominal form (*prajñapti-rūpa*). If this were not the case, it would either not be included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) or these five types of form would fail to exhaustively encompass all phenomena.

Furthermore, because such conceptual construction (*parikalpa*) arises predominantly from the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), it is designated as "conceptualization" (*parikalpa*) and is not [the result of] meditative concentration.
Only this interpretation is correct: this matter is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), because it is taught that what can give rise to the mind is called "universal imagination" (*parikalpa*);

furthermore, uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) provisional matter is subsumed under the fifth category, as has already been extensively established within the preceding discussion of the provisional and the real.
Between these two views, the latter is superior.
Regarding "matter produced by mastery" (upapatti-vaśitā-rūpa) up to "matter that is the object of activity":
the commentary states that "liberation" refers to the four liberations (*vimokṣa*), namely the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*); "meditative concentration" refers to the four dhyānas.
It is stated in the *Ṣaṭpañcāśatka* that this matter which is the fruit of these concentrations belongs to those fundamental concentrations (*maula-dhyāna*) that possess majestic power (*prabhāva*).

The object of focus is not that of other concentrations; it is said that the fifty-fourth [type of] meditative fruit-form is exclusively mundane, outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*), and produced by the activity of tainted conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Because this concentration serves as its cause, it can only be manifested by those possessing great majestic power through the eight fundamental dhyānas, and not by the eight preliminary stages (*anāgamya*). (53)

The statement that "form arises from karma" refers to form [produced by karma], whereas it is not the case that "formless [states] arise from karma. This is because the superior meditative absorptions (dhyāna) do not exercise mastery over all forms;
rather, it is through the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of those specific absorptions that they are brought into manifestation. Furthermore, it is said:

"The gods of the Form and Formless Realms transform their bodies into ten billion forms and together stand upon the tip of a single hair. From this, it is proven that the meditative absorptions of the eight higher stages are all capable [of such transformations].
Regarding "manifestation" or "liberation": because the first seven liberations can manifest form (*rūpa*), their meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are as previously described.

There are two interpretations regarding the nature of the fruit of this concentration: some explain it as being both nominal and substantial form; others maintain that the liberations are equivalent to the four *dhyānas*, asserting that one must first be free from the obstacles to the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-āvaraṇa*) before these forms can arise.
Here, based on their vast majesty and power, we briefly omit the formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*), for such form does not exist there.
Briefly, this is analyzed through three sections: first, the arising of ordinary beings and noble ones; second, the extent of the objects; third, the production from the great elements.
Regarding the first, the arising of ordinary beings and noble ones: there is an interpretation that this form arises from both ordinary beings and noble ones.
The fifty-four words concerning "the subtle nature of mastery over mind" refer to the various forms of the two realms—the realm of form and the formless realm—as stated in the sūtras.

Because the gods of Equal Mind (Samatā-citta) once cultivated and polished their minds while among humans, they abide within a space the size of a single hair-tip through the power of such cultivation, remaining there in mutual succession without obstructing one another.

Furthermore, the Āgamas state that the tears of the formless gods (ārūpya-devas) fell like rain as they stood by the Buddha’s side; such scriptural evidence exists in various places, as seen in those texts.

Since it has already been stated that the gods of the two upper realms manifest their bodies here, and it is further said that this form also includes the contaminated (*sāsrava*), as the cited scriptural authority is as previously mentioned, we know that both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*) are capable of manifesting it.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* mentions only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas because it speaks according to those of great majesty and superior power;
how could it be that the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) and others are likewise unable to transform [matter] from the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?

Because the gods permitted the raining of tears, the *Yogācārabhūmi* further states that although it is not an object traversed by supramundane meditative concentration (*lokottara-samādhi*), there is one who can manifest it through the sovereign power (*adhipati-bala*) of that concentration.
This indicates that noble ones (*ārya*) possess both mundane and supramundane knowledge; it does not exclude ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), as they are incapable [of such manifestation].
Because it manifests, this form-samādhi arises; there is a sense in which it is common to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).

Regarding the meaning that this form is not produced by ordinary beings, the *Śāsanodbhāvana* (XVIII) states that among the twelve types of forms at the place of teaching, it is said that these are transformations produced only by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Although it is not within the range of supramundane concentration, it occurs through the dominant power (*adhipatibala*) of that concentration."
Therefore, since even a single capacity to manifest [this] cannot be produced by any of the noble ones (*ārya*), how much less so by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)?

(65) It is said that only a mind of extreme purity and great majestic power (*mahānubhāva*), attained through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), can serve as the condition for the arising of this matter of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-rūpa*).

Furthermore, how could it be that such a state is the object of perception for an ordinary being who lacks a mind of great majestic power or one established in meditative concentration? How could they possibly belong to the class of ordinary beings?
It is said that one who has attained majestic power and supreme meditative concentration can manifest various forms; furthermore, it is stated that this matter is inconceivable.
If it were produced by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it would be categorized as something conceivable. Therefore, it is produced solely by noble ones (*ārya*) and not by ordinary beings.

However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on Yoga Practice), fascicle 33, states: "The matters manifested through the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of noble ones correspond to everything according to their resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)."
All of these can be accomplished in accordance with reality without alteration, being capable and functional; such is not possible through the supernormal powers of non-Aryas.
Because they are like magical illusions—merely visible but unfit for actual use—the former interpretation is correct.

Regarding the second point, the extent of the objects [of mastery]: the *Pañcāśatikā* (Treatise in Fifty Verses) states that one attains mastery over all forms through the form produced as the fruit of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, the fourth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Exposition of the Noble Teachings), in its section on the first *abhibhvāyatana* (sphere of mastery), says:
"Whether superior or inferior" refers to forms comprised of the pure and impure colors, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. Based on such scriptural authorities, [the objects are established].
Because it is established by valid cognition, one knows that these forms—whether provisional or substantial, contaminated or uncontaminated—all possess the five objects.
The *Ninety-eight [Treatise]* states that transformations cannot perform four functions, namely: karma, its fruit, mind and mental factors, and the sense faculties;

therefore, all others can be transformed. The *Fifty-four [Treatise]* states that one should know that the forms which are the fruits of superior meditative concentration possess only [the aforementioned characteristics].

Regarding the statement that "the characteristics of visible form and so forth are absent in those [realms] because they lack the causes for the production of odors and so forth, and are useless," the intended meaning is this:

because the causal preparation (*prayoga*) prior to the meditative absorption of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is necessarily inferior, they are unable to transform and produce the forms of odor, fragrance, and so forth.

Even if they were to transform them, these would have no practical utility. Furthermore, the power of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) meditative absorptions of noble ones (*ārya*) is not weak or inferior.
Only [the mind] can transform and produce the three objects of form, sound, and touch; because there is no prior preparatory cause for odor and taste, it cannot transform and produce them.
Even if it were to transform them, it would be useless. Furthermore, non-outflow (anāsrava) minds cannot transform and produce them, nor can those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
Moreover, as for bodhisattvas, when taking the desire realm as their objective essence (ālambana), they possess all five sensory objects.

That which has the form (*rūpa*) of the upper realms as its essential substance lacks both odor and fragrance; this is because in the two higher fruit-stages there is no seed, and because there are no two kinds of causes upon which to rely.

Furthermore, when transforming the objects of the desire realm, all five types [of sensory objects] are present, whereas when transforming the objects of the form realm, only three are present according to their presence or absence.

Even if one relies on a transformation of those [upper realms], it lacks practical utility because the essential substance does not exist. This is the case whether it is meditative concentration (*samādhi*)...

The colors of the fruits do not change; regarding their fragrances, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the olfactory faculty of a bodhisattva perceives the scents of the palaces in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says that by upholding this sūtra, one can perceive through fragrance all beings—from the Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna heavens up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)—as they are first born or pass away, knowing fully the nature of their karmic maturation (*vipāka*) in those realms. If there were no fragrance, it would not be a determinate state.

If this is the case, what kind of fragrance is it? It is not merely a transformed fragrance (vikṛta-gandha), for its flavor does not transform; thus we know it is certainly a fruit [of meditative concentration] that pervades both fragrance and flavor.
The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states: "This is the realm of wisdom, known by the olfactory faculty. Therefore, one cannot say that the mutual functioning of the faculties is impossible.

Furthermore, the sixty-fifth [treatise] explains that while the form of meditative power (*vaibhutvika-rūpa*) is not included among those ten material bases (*daśa rūpīṇy āyatanāni*), it is nonetheless established as a distinct category.

Although they manifest as having a nature similar to their respective self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) through association, the five faculties such as the eye lack the functional capacity of a faculty;

thus, the two factors of odor and taste likewise lack such function. While the three factors of form, sound, and tangibility possess actual utility, the faculties serve as the supports for consciousness.
Since the transformed faculties do not serve as supports for consciousness, they may lack actual utility; however, this is not the case for odor and the others.
How could it be that there are no odors, tastes, visible forms, or tangibles? Since their categories are identical, they are like the sense-faculties;

however, they are merely comprised within the five [objects] such as visible form, as has already been extensively established by the aforementioned principles. Therefore, the matter produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) certainly possesses all five objects, for the food of the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa possesses all five objects.
Regarding that which is derived from the three great elements (*mahābhūta*), fifty-four [treatises] state it is the "form resulting from superior meditative concentration" (*samāpatti-phala-rūpa*).

If one relies on the meditative concentration bound to a particular realm, then it is derived from the great elements belonging to that very realm. Furthermore, it is stated that this form does not rely on the great elements;

rather, because it arises from a *samādhi* that manifests an image (*pratibimba*) of that category, it is also said to be derived from those great elements, though not in the sense of relying upon them.

Because it arises from that, it is called "derived. (66 words) Question: World-Honored One, you have taught that there is non-obstructive form (*arūpa*) derived from the view of existence and non-existence;
by what kind of primary elements (*mahābhūta*) should it be said to be derived? Answer:

If, through concentrated thought, an image of the various phenomena possessing form in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) arises, it should be said to be derived from the primary elements of the desire realm. If one contemplates the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)...

The same applies to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). In the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (XVIII), among the twelve characteristics of the matter of the locus of dharma-exposition, it is stated that the fifth [characteristic] does not arise from real primary elements.

Although there are various differing interpretations regarding these five texts, upon careful examination of the meaning of "derivation" (*upādāya*), it cannot exceed two types, because the primary elements that serve as its direct or indirect objects of perception (*ālambana*) are of only two categories: first, the sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*).

The primary great elements (*mahābhūta*) produced by karma and so forth are the objects of both the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), as well as the mind—the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Second, the great elements that are the fruits of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*) are exclusively the objects of the mind in concentration and the eighth consciousness, or they may be the objects of the body-consciousness.

The former [karmic elements] include those that are matured (*vipāka*), nurtured (*aupacayika*), and outflowing (*naiṣyandika*); the latter [meditative elements] are not matured. The former exists only in the desire and form realms.

Regarding the elements (*dhātu*) to which they are bound, or whether they are universally unbound: the latter [category] includes those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and the unbound.
Among these five, the initial passage relies on the latter [view]. The great elements (*mahābhūta*) follow their respective objects of cognition (*ālambana*) in being bound to a specific location;

therefore, this term "bound" (*baddha*) carries the sense of being subsumed or belonging to, rather than the sense of being fettered. Otherwise, the untainted (*anāsrava*) would not be composed of the great elements, as they would not follow their respective objects.
Because they are produced from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) within the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the meaning of the preceding second passage is also the same as this:

by means of the superior concentration, the primary elements first undergo transformation, and subsequently derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) arises. This means that [the derived matter] is produced from the primary elements of the specific level (*bhūmi*) of the concentration that acts as the causal condition;

it is described according to the preceding cause of the concentration and its meaning that those primary elements arise first, though in reality they arise simultaneously. Thus, this [explanation] is comprehensive.

It is also accepted that the objects of these two consciousnesses arise because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and other resultant objects of meditative concentration arise first through the power of concentration, and only later are the derived elements (*bhautika*) produced;

or because this passage states that based on the primary great elements (*mahābhūta*), the derived elements of the sense-field of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) are first struck up by concentration and only later produced.
Although the previous third passage relies on the primary great elements for its production, even though concentration transforms them, the great elements remain the direct [cause].

Because the mind that initially transforms the object upon arising must depend upon the sense bases of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*) and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) to arise, it is said that the primary great elements (*mahābhūta*) produce the determined great elements;

however, the inferior [elements] are not said to be the basis for their arising. Yet, it is not the case that the primary great elements can directly produce them, for that which can directly produce them are the determined great elements.
Thus, the meaning of the fourth section of the preceding text is also the same as this: it follows whatever one contemplates as the basis.

Because they are the "great producers" (*mahābhūta*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (or *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*) explains that they are not truly derived from the sense-base of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*). It states that they are produced directly by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) themselves, and thus are not "derived" (*bhautika*) in the strict sense.

Furthermore, it is not the case that they do not exist within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If the initial primary elements are accessible as objects to the three types of consciousness, then all primary elements are capable of producing subsequent "form resulting from concentration" (*samādhija-rūpa*).

Because these subsequent forms exist in mutual dependence, they possess the status of being "produced" (*bhautika*) in a derivative sense; however, this is a remote production rather than a direct production. If...

Furthermore, the great elements that serve as the common objects of the three consciousnesses are capable of acting as the basis for the production of derived matter; thus, they constitute direct production rather than indirect production.

If one relies on the first type of production, it is possible for lower-level great elements to produce higher-level derived matter, for out-flowing (sāsrava) elements to produce non-out-flowing (anāsrava) matter, or for elements of one’s own realm to produce matter of another realm.
If one relies on the latter type of production, however, [derived matter] is produced only by its own [great elements].
That which is produced by the earth element is not produced by other elements; it is produced by the impure (sāsrava) only to produce the impure, and by the pure (anāsrava) only to produce the pure.
It is produced by its own level (svabhūmi) only to produce its own level, all being produced solely by their own kind and never by another.
Therefore, even if various levels manifest different modes of production, when examined according to principle and scripture, they do not exceed these two [categories]. This is one interpretation.

In general, these [attainments] should be established as being threefold, for there are cases where the attainment of the fruit is accomplished without depending on the primary substance (*upādāna-rūpa*).

As stated in the initial passage regarding those "created by the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the specific dhyāna to which they are bound," this refers to that which is created by the great elements of the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
For example, when one enters a particular meditative absorption based on a certain locus, one does not rely on a primary substance; rather, the previously determined mind remains unchanging.

Since the derived matter produced by those [great elements] must necessarily be produced by great elements belonging either to the bed, seat, or other objects upon which it rests, or to the body that serves as its support,
a third locus of dependence should be established. Although there is no preparatory effort (*prayoga*) involved,

it is nonetheless subsumed under the principle that it is included within the first of the two great elements among the great elements of the tangible base (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), namely, the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).

Regarding the methods of cultivation as explained in the sixty-second fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, such as how one first initiates the practice by taking the signs of other realms as objects,
these matters are discussed in detail in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-ṭīkā* and in its separate chapters.
Commentary on the Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā, Volume Two;
Commentary on the Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā, Volume Three.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of the Great Ci’en Monastery.
How is the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) established—[extending] up to feelings produced by mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja-vedanā*)?
The commentary states: In the fifth section of the ninefold establishment of the aggregates, following the initial establishment of form (*rūpa*), the establishment of feeling begins.
First, the five bases are presented; then, seven categories of feeling are enumerated. Subsequently, responding to objections, this is explained through four reasons. This is the first base.
In the third [chapter] on Consciousness-Only, "feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to the experience of receiving; its intrinsic nature is solely the reception of an object.
It is not an intrinsic feeling such as that described at length elsewhere. When its own substance is categorized in total according to its various bases, it is divided into six kinds.
Regarding the term "unreasonable determination," "body" (*kāya*) refers to the accumulation of its own substance, which is thus called a "body. If one follows its respective basis, then...
The contradiction is resolved by explaining that those [mental factors] are designated as "mental feeling" (*citta-vedanā*) because they do not rely on the five [physical sense bases].

Alternatively, the basis (*āśraya*) is collectively termed "body" (*kāya*), just as it is said that the three bodies (*tri-kāya*) subsume the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Since both the primary and secondary [feelings] rely upon this same basis, the statement that they are "bodily feelings" (*kāya-vedanā*) is made according to their classification;
thus, the meanings of being the basis for body and mind are identical and are not mutually contradictory. As for the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these feelings, there are three...

Because they are harmonious, how is it that here only contact (*sparśa*) is said to give rise [to feeling]? According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, because contact is proximate and predominant in producing feeling, only contact is said to produce it.
Furthermore, the fifth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and the fifty-third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* state that all feelings arise from sixteen types of contact:
the sixfold contact of the eye and other [senses], the contact of resistance (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*), and the contact of designation (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*).

The three types of craving—namely, for pleasure and so forth—as well as aversion, clarity, ignorance, and that which is neither clarity nor ignorance, are established by way of the faculties and their objects.

The first six [types of contact] and "contact with resistance" (*pratigha-sparśa*) are established because they differentiate the objects; "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-sparśa*) is established because it apprehends the object through verbal expression.

The three types corresponding to pleasure and so forth are established by way of the agreeable and so forth; the remaining five are established by way of defilement and purification. Because these contacts are distinct, the arising of feeling (*vedanā*) is likewise distinct.
Because they are distinct, and because the proximate and superior [condition] is predominant, it is said that [feeling] arises from contact alone.
Whether it be pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—the commentary states that this refers to the second stage;
based on the classification of their modes of activity (*ākāra*), these are divided into three, though the sense of "experiencing" (*anubhava*) applies to all of them.
Regarding the three [feelings] that subsume the five faculties, their scope of meaning is restricted to being distinct from joy (*prīti*) and sorrow (*daurmanasya*).

Why are the names of the three feelings designated as suffering (*duḥkha*) and pleasure (*sukha*), rather than using those terms "sorrow" and "joy"? This is because suffering, when contrasted with pleasure, applies to all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*);

however, it is not logically possible for sorrow to be contrasted with joy in the same way. Some explain that both pleasure and suffering apply to all six consciousnesses, whereas suffering and sorrow belong only to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It is not otherwise. Furthermore, because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of suffering and pleasure are clear and sharp, whereas those of grief and joy are not, one should not raise the objection:
"Why are suffering and pleasure each divided into two types, while the mental and physical sensations of equanimity (*upekṣā*) are definitely established as one?

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle five, states that the two sensations of suffering and pleasure are each divided into two because the modes of activity regarding the gratification of body and mind differ respectively.
Therefore, because there is non-discrimination and discrimination, and because there is a distinction between the heavy and the light, that which is neutral is neither "satisfying" nor "pleasing.
Because its characteristics are not distinct, it is non-discriminative, and it functions with equanimity.

For what reason is this feeling called suffering, pleasure, or neutrality? When one experiences the characteristics of a favorable object, such that the body and mind are satisfied and pleased, it is designated as a pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
The experience of an object that is disagreeable, which oppresses both body and mind, is called the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhā vedanā*).
The experience of an object that is neutral, which neither oppresses nor delights either body or mind, is called the feeling of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*).

These three are all common to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), because feelings of suffering can also arise from the uncontaminated. Alternatively, each may be divided into three types, such as those abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth, up to those of the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Because painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*) is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*), and because all three [types of persons]—the learner (*śaikṣa*) and so forth—are connected with it as appropriate, since painful feeling accords with the state of being a learner and so on;

or alternatively, they may be divided collectively into four, such as wholesome (*kuśala*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*), or each may be divided into four. In the realm of pure suffering (*ekānta-duḥkha-sthāna*), there is the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*);

the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) possesses only two natures, for it is never indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If one speaks of five feelings, they are associated with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).

That which is constant satisfaction is called "pleasure" (*sukha*). That which is associated with the mental consciousness (*manas*) in the Desire Realm and the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the first two *dhyānas* is called "joy" (*prīti*).
In the fundamental states (*maula*) of those two, it is called both "joy" and "pleasure. In the preparatory stage and the fundamental state of the third *dhyāna*, it is always called "pleasure.

That which is associated with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) and is characterized by oppression is always called "suffering" (*duḥkha*). Regarding that which is associated with the mental consciousness, one interpretation holds that it is exclusively "grief" (*daurmanasya*), because it oppresses the mind.

There is an interpretation that [feeling] applies to both humans and devas; it is called "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*) among animals and hungry ghosts, while it is called "suffering" (*duḥkha*) because there are mixed feelings and pure feelings, and because there are light and heavy degrees.
In the hells, it is called only "suffering" because there are pure feelings that are especially heavy and lack discrimination.
The detailed scriptural and logical proofs cited in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* regarding whether these exist within consciousness shall be discussed later. If...

In the state of Buddhahood, there is only pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), because the Buddhas have already severed all matters of sorrow and suffering. The remaining points of interpretation are as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Weishi shu).
Furthermore, there is bodily sensation that is pleasant (*sukha-kāyikī vedanā*) up to mental sensation that is not pleasant (*asātā-caitasikī vedanā*).

The commentary states: Because the third stage [the stage of non-conceptualization] generally manifests the basis for the distinct modes of activity, there are three types of each regarding body and mind.

This equanimity (*upekṣā*) is subsumed under mental feeling (*citta-vedanā*). As for the other three [feelings], they depend on the five sense organs; their feelings follow the specific nature of each organ.

For what reason, then, are they collectively designated by the name "bodily feeling" (*kāya-vedanā*)? It is because the substance of these five organs is entirely of the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*). If that is so, [what of] the eye...
Likewise, the consciousnesses arising from the individual bodies should all be designated as "bodily" (*kāyika*), yet their specific characteristics differ.

If they were not designated as "bodily" due to these differences in characteristic, then they would not be "bodily sensations" (*kāyikavedanā*) even when arising according to distinct [sensory] bases. Since the four [consciousnesses] of the eye and so forth are not separate from the body, they are collectively termed "bodily sensations" based on their support;
the mental faculty (*manas*) is also like this, for it too is not separate from the body and should thus be termed "bodily."

It is not said that mental feeling is inseparable from the body, as the desire-realm, form-realm, eyes, and so forth are certainly not so; however, the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) of the formless realm functions apart from the body.
How then can bodily feeling be established? Since their essential natures (*svabhāva*) differ, they are divided into two types.

The body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) serves as the basis for a collection of many factors, and thus it alone receives the designation "body" (*kāya*); the other faculties, such as the eye, do not, because they are merely the bases upon which [the collection] depends.
This refers to the "body of names" (*nāmakāya*), as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 53.
Furthermore, there are "receptions of the flavor of pleasure" (*sāsvāda-vedanā*) up to "receptions devoid of flavor" (*nirāsvāda-vedanā*).

The commentary states: these correspond to the fourth position, consisting of the fourth and fifth categories, which are the objective spheres (*ālambana*) for the phenomena of defilement and purification based upon the body.

Although they are of the same category, they are established as distinct through different modes of activity. Inferior understanding is "without flavor" (*arasa*) because it is untainted (*anāsrava*); suffering is "only tainted" (*sāsrava*). Why is the untainted called "without flavor"?
Because it is induced by [the state of] being without flavor; since sorrow induces the untainted, it is termed "without-flavor-feeling. This is not because it is an object of experience (*gocara*).

However, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Xianyang lun*) sometimes establishes one type of feeling, because all are of the nature of suffering; or it establishes two types of feeling: those of body and mind.
They are established as three feelings due to their distinction; or four feelings due to the distinction between those bound by attachment (*saṃyojana*) and those not so bound;
or five feelings due to the distinction between pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*prīti*), and so forth; or six feelings due to the distinction of their bases (*āśraya*);

or eighteen due to the distinction of the three types of mental applications (*manopavicāra*)—joy, sorrow, and equanimity. Of these, the former [set] corresponds to the sixth [category] of the latter.
The second [category] is that which was previously the third; the third is that which was previously the second.

This is because they differ according to their respective bases (*āśraya*) and modes of activity (*ākāra*); thus, body and mind each have three. Since these are based on both the union and separation of the six consciousnesses, they are equally balanced.

Furthermore, because the modes of activity of joy, sorrow, and equanimity are broad and distinct in relation to the six consciousnesses as their objective conditions (*ālambana*), they are established separately as "near-approaches" (*upavicāra*) in substance.
Since these are included within the three types of feeling (*vedanā*), they are not mentioned here separately.
Furthermore, there is the feeling based on attachment (*gardhāśrita-vedanā*) up to the feeling based on renunciation (*naiṣkramyāśrita-vedanā*).

The commentary states: this refers to the fifth stage, and the sixth and seventh categories, which take external objects as their conditions and consist of the aspects of defiled and pure mental activity.

These are established as distinct categories based on similar types but different modes of activity; they are named according to the three feelings, specifically pleasure (*sukha*) and pain (*duḥkha*).
Following this principle of their mode of activity, there are thirty-six "teacher-words" (*śāstravākya*), for the meaning of feeling (*vedanā*) applies universally.

This pleasure is based on attachment (*gardha*), which constitutes six instances of attachment-based pleasure; this pain is based on attachment, which constitutes six instances of attachment-based pain; and this [neutral feeling] is based on attachment, which constitutes six instances of attachment-based grief (*daurmanasya*).
Equanimity based on attachment consists of six types of equanimity based on attachment; equanimity based on renunciation of that pleasure consists of six types of joy based on renunciation;
equanimity based on renunciation of this suffering consists of six types of equanimity based on renunciation.

Herein, all are based on the three sets of six [types of] renunciation, which involve the vomiting, harming, and abandoning of the three sets of six attachments, and through the joy based on renunciation, one eliminates the joy of attachment.
Because the Great Teacher spoke thirty-six phrases concerning the basis of sorrow, renunciation, equanimity, and the abandonment of the joy of renunciation, these are used as names.
Based on the three periods of time, this constitutes one hundred and eight feelings, as explained in detail in the fifth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.

However, the Master of the Root Treatise, wishing to distinguish between that which has flavor and that which is flavorless, and between attachment and renunciation, [classifies them] internally and externally.

The objects differ, and the modes of defiled and pure conduct vary; or [they differ] according to the three feelings, as the names suggest. Regarding the "modes of activity" (*ākāra*), the following explains them based on the five desires, distinguishing between attachment and detachment;
this should be understood according to the meaning, as these are the words of the Master. Alternatively, adding this explanation does not contradict the meaning:

internal craving has a mode of activity whose nature and category are subtle, so it is described as being "associated with feeling" (*sāsvāda*) and so forth; external craving, however, has a different mode of activity.
The characteristics, natures, and categories are further elucidated by explaining that "feeling" (vedanā) is designated as the "basis" (āśraya) because it arises from craving (tṛṣṇā), and so forth.
Furthermore, there is a distinction between the two: internal craving arises on account of feeling, while external feeling arises on account of craving.
"Experiencing through body" (referring to) feelings associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Commentary: Above, five categories were raised and seven classes of feeling were enumerated; below, the difficulties are addressed and explained, establishing the text by means of four causes.

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the explanation that addresses the difficulties, and second, the establishment by means of the causes. This explains the meaning of the third section previously mentioned.
The meaning of the term "body" (*kāya*) for the five consciousnesses is as explained previously. Here, the word "mind" (*citta*) subsumes the other three consciousnesses;

now, based on the fact that the three types of feeling share a single basis in the mind, only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is mentioned, while the other two are not. Otherwise, this section would fail to encompass all phenomena exhaustively.
"Feeling with attachment" (*sāsvāda-vedanā*) [up to] "incompatible feeling.

The commentary states: "Attachment" (*āsvāda*) has the meaning of clinging; it is self-love (*ātma-sneha*). Feeling that is associated with that [self-love] is called "feeling with attachment," which pertains to all three realms and exclusively takes as its object the love for one's own body.
"Without attachment" (*nirāsvāda*) is the opposite of this; it takes favorable objects as its condition.
If suffering arises from oppression, how can there be a sensation of enjoyment (sāsvāda-vedanā) that is devoid of suffering?
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 58, part 2, states that these two are incompatible; thus, as explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, they are contradictory:
defilement and oppression are opposed to suffering, while joy and sorrow are mutually exclusive, and craving and aversion arise together. This difficulty also applies here.

One should reflect upon the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explication), which states that "savoring feeling" (*sāsvāda-vedanā*) refers to feelings bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which take as their objects both one's own body and the five sensory desires, and are associated with craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

It further states that "non-savoring feeling" (*nirāsvāda-vedanā*) consists of feelings bound to the two higher realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*) and those that are unbound (*anāsrava*), being the opposite of savoring feeling.
By this analogy, it should be understood that savoring feeling encompasses both the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*).
The wholesome alone also extends to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding "reception based on indulgence" (*gardhāśrita-vedanā*) up to "incompatible reception" (*asamprayukta-vedanā*):
the commentary states that reception associated with craving for the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) is called "indulgent"; renunciation (*naiṣkramya*) is explained as the opposite of this.

The *Yanglun* (Exposition on Arising) states that attachment is the same in this regard. The wholesome feeling induced by those who have left the household life is called "feeling of renunciation" (*naiṣkramya-vedanā*), because they feel aversion toward the five desires. That "feeling of savoring" (*āsvādana-vedanā*) generally takes as its object both internal and external things within the desire realm; it is associated with craving for both, and is further characterized by attachment to the five desires through their general and specific aspects. One should know that "renunciation" is the opposite of this "savoring. Regarding the latter: The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* says: "The feeling of savoring is associated with craving. It is the feeling of one who, while experiencing a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. Furthermore, the *Śāriputrābhidharma* says: "What is the feeling of savoring? It is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* says: "There are three types of feelings: pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. The feeling of savoring is the pleasant feeling that arises when one experiences a pleasant feeling and gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arises when one experiences a painful feeling and gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arises when one experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling and gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The *Abhidharmadīpa* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The *Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The *Abhidharmakośa-vyākhyā-sphuṭārthā* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā-ṭippaṇī* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā-ṭippaṇī-ṭippaṇī* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, gives rise to neither craving nor aversion. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā-ṭippaṇī-ṭippaṇī-ṭippaṇī-ṭippaṇī* says: "The feeling of savoring is the feeling of one who, having attained a pleasant feeling, gives rise to craving. The feeling of renunciation is the feeling of one who, having attained a painful feeling, gives rise to aversion. The feeling of equanimity is the feeling of one who, having attained a neither-pain

The treatise states that where there is an object (*viṣaya*), the realm (*dhātu*) may be broad while the object is narrow; where there is no object, the realm is broad while the object is narrow. This treatise [proceeds] by reversing this.
