Regarding their breadth and narrowness, each is established according to a single perspective and thus does not contradict one another; these shall be explained again below in the sixth fascicle.
The above is the original text of the treatise; the following is the commentary of the Master.
"Thus established... up to... because of purification. The commentary states:

"Below, the four causes establish that the preceding five stages serve as the basis for feeling without increase or decrease" means that the six groups of feeling are distinguished according to their six respective bases. "Because of its own nature" refers to pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth.

Third, because the self-substance is specifically revealed according to the three stages, that which is the basis for the accumulation [of suffering] refers to the defiled and purified sensations (*vedanā*) of body and mind;
this establishes the mental sensation (*citta-vedanā*) among the other two stages.
The commentary states: Because these two causes are difficult to understand, the term "aggregation" (*samudaya*) is explained again. "Aggregation" is a collective term;

it refers to the gathering of individual phenomena into a single name. Thus, the five classes of material sense-faculties are collectively termed the "body," and the three classes of mental faculties are collectively termed the "mind.
That which arises from these two is called "mental-physical sensation" (*kāyikī vedanā*).
"Due to affliction (*saṃkleśa*)... up to 'without flavor' (*arasa*) and so forth.
The commentary states: "Having flavor and being addicted to it are both termed affliction; being without flavor and renouncing it are both termed purification.
Since each encompasses two aspects, the word 'and so forth' (*ādi*) is used for both."
"This craving is dissociated [from it]... up to... it is conducive to disjunction. The commentary states:
This explains the two items previously cited—being "without flavor" (*asvāda*) and "renunciation" (*niḥsaraṇa*). As for "dissociation" (*visaṃyoga*), there is no need for further explanation;
it is simply the essence of the aforementioned "absence of flavor" (*asvāda-vedanā*). Because it is free from the two bonds, it is not craved by the body and is conducive to disjunction.

This refers to the fact that renunciation (*naiṣkramya*) is wholesome for householders and conducive to liberation; therefore, one should consider whether these [states] possess "taste" (*āsvāda*) and so forth, as well as their definitions and existence or non-existence.
Fearing prolixity, this discussion is here suspended.

Later passages and the sixty-fifth [verse] both state that "taste" and "relishing" (*gardha*) are two types that pervade all afflictions (*kleśa*). Why, then, is it said here that their essence consists solely of craving (*tṛṣṇā*)? Craving...
The Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) increases and accumulates the capacity to produce moistening rebirth and serves as the cause for feeling;

furthermore, because the two types of craving—those arising from maturation and those arising from objects—are produced by feeling, it is only craving that is taught as the essence of these two. What fault is there in designating this general term separately?
How is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) established? [It ranges] from perception born of eye-contact up to perception born of mind-contact.

The commentary states: First, three positions are designated and seven types of characteristics are listed; subsequently, the master provides a sequential explanation. Thus, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* says:
"There are three kinds of characteristics: first, difference in basis; second, difference in attention (manasikāra); and third, difference in object (ālambana)."

Now, in this first stage, the self-nature [of consciousness] is collectively subsumed and divided into six types according to its six bases; thus, it is called "representation-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*).

It is taught that its nature is the grasping of images. Regarding the statement that contact (*sparśa*) arises, it is because contact—produced by the differentiation of the three-fold conjunction—is the most preeminent among all mental factors (*caitta*).
As stated in the *Udayavyaya-sūtra*, the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations all have contact as their condition, as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
This contradicts the detailed exposition.
Due to these characteristics, [the practitioner] either perceives signs or realizes signlessness.
The commentary states: In this second stage, because it differs from the previously mentioned mental application of perception (*saṃjñā-manasikāra*), it is divided into two types.
"Or one attains the small, the great, up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The commentary states: "This refers to the third stage; as for the others, they are divided into four kinds because their objective spheres (*ālambana*) differ.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Xianyang lun), fascicle 2, states: "Regarding 'nothingness,' it is the investigation of the objective sphere above the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*)."
At that time, there is not even the slightest attainment; apart from non-existence, there is no distinct objective realm.
This very state is called "non-existence" because there is not even the slightest thing to be found, and since one can realize this, it is named the Sphere of Nothingness (Ākiṃcanyāyatana).
"Those with perceptions of signs" (up to) "the perceptions previously eliminated.
The commentary states: In the lower text, the Master of the Original Treatise provides successive explanations following the text; therein are two parts:

first, the Master of the Original Treatise explains by pursuing the preceding objections, and second, the Master of the Commentary further provides distinct explanations. This explanation concerns the second differentiation of attention (*manasikāra*).

Excluding those minds of the desire realm belonging to infants and the like, excluding all untainted minds in the higher realms that take *nirvāṇa* as their object, and excluding all perceptions other than the non-perception (*asaṃjñin*), the remaining perceptions that take conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as their objects and give rise to signs are called "perceptions with signs" (*sanimitta-saṃjñā*).

The three types of perceptions excluded previously are called "signless perceptions" (*animitta-saṃjñā*); they are also termed "clearly discerning" (*paricchedaka*) when they possess signs, and the opposite of this is termed "signless."
Characteristics.
Regarding the minor characteristics (up to the perception of the sphere of nothingness):
the commentary states that this explains the distinctions in the spheres of the third stage, as well as the bodies and environments (*bhājana-loka*) of the two realms of desire and form.

Having accomplished the mental aspects of the infinitudes of space, consciousness, and nothingness by taking broad objects as their objects and fully comprehending those various perceptions, these are called the "mental aspects of the immeasurables.

Taking all objects as their objects, because there is not even the slightest thing remaining, it is called the "sphere of nothingness"; taking those various perceptions as its object, it is called the "perception of the sphere of nothingness.
[The above is from the original treatise; the following is the commentary by the Master.]
Regarding the phrase "those who speak unskillfully" (up to) "therefore it is called the perception of signlessness":
the commentary states that it is not merely the failure to understand this that is termed "form" (*rūpa*). The term "form" is employed to include other objects as well;
it is not the case that the perception of signlessness cannot be understood. Thus, it is called the perception of signlessness.
Regarding the definition of the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) as "the perception of the signless" (*animittasaṃjñā*):
[The commentary] states that "signs" (*nimitta*) refer to characteristic marks. These are of ten kinds: the five sense objects, male, female, arising, and the characteristics of change and cessation;
alternatively, they are said to be thirteen. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, chapter thirty-one, states that nirvāṇa is free from these ten or thirteen signs.

Suffering, pleasure, equanimity, and nirvāṇa do not possess these characteristics; it is because one establishes the name "signless" (animitta) by taking them as objects that the perception directed toward them is called the "signless perception" (animittasaṃjñā).
It is not because those characteristics lack an objective domain that they are signless.
The characteristic of the meditative absorption of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is what is termed the "signless perception."

The commentary states: "Summit" (*bhavāgra*) carries the meaning of "extreme. Because it is the extreme limit of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), it is called the "Peak of Existence" (*bhavāgra*).

Since the perception (*saṃjñā*) there is indistinct and cannot delineate the characteristics of various objects, even that distracted mind lacks the perception of signs (*nimitta-saṃjñā*). This is stated here from the perspective of meditative concentration;

it does not mean that there is nothing else. One must possess both clarity and discernment (*vikalpa*) to be designated as the realm with signs (*sanimitta-dhātu*) or the realm without signs (*animitta-dhātu*).

Although meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is clear and distinct, it does not involve conceptual differentiation; although the meditative absorption of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) involves conceptual differentiation, it is not clear.
Infants possess neither of these, and thus both are termed "signless" (*animitta*). Conversely, that which possesses these is termed "with signs.

If one follows this principle, even the perception (*saṃjñā*) of the untainted (*anāsrava*) conditioned phenomena would be signless; therefore, the treatise relies on the fundamental [state] and does not mention other minds. If one follows...
Nirvāṇa receives the name "signless" because it is not subsumed under the signs that necessarily exist in conditioned phenomena;
this is because, according to the fifty-three [categories], all contaminated minds are signless.
"Small" refers to [the range] from small to great and immeasurable.

The commentary states: Above, the three signless perceptions (*animitta-saṃjñā*) were explained as aspects of mental attention (*manasikāra*); below, the distinctions between the three signs (*nimitta*) as objects (*ālambana*) were explained.

Now, the Master explains "small" and "great" based on the superiority or inferiority of the stages (*bhūmi*). He explains the preceding "immeasurables" (*apramāṇa*) by means of their boundless practice;

however, he does not explain them here because the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is easily understood. Nevertheless, these fifty-three types of small, great, and immeasurable [perceptions] possess signs (*sanimitta*).

The various perceptions of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) at the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) are called "non-perception" (asaṃjñā), because they do not involve unwholesome speech and because their objects possess characteristics.
Alternatively, they may be divided into six categories by excluding the basis (āśraya). Or, they may be categorized generally into two types:
mundane (laukika) and supramundane (lokottara). Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* explains the small, great, and immeasurable [perceptions] through thirty-seven repetitions.
He explains at length that the three causes [of perception] have already been revealed; since these various perceptions are easy to understand, he does not state the establishment of their causes.
How is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) established? [It extends] from volition (*cetanā*) born of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja*).

The commentary states: Regarding the fourth section below, which establishes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), there are two main parts. First, a general summary indicating the essence of the aggregate of formations;

second, a detailed explanation of the phenomena previously indicated. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, the indication of the subject of the aggregate and the phenomena subsumed within it;
second, the master of the treatise’s re-explanation of the preceding meaning. Within the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the indication of the aggregate.
The Master [Vasubandhu] subsequently clarifies the remaining dharmas: these six groups of volition (*ṣaṭ-cetanā-kāya*) are the primary subject of the aggregates (*skandha*).
It is due to this volition that [the various states] reach their distinct phases. The commentary states:

among the many factors of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), volition alone is singled out because it is the most preeminent, being capable of causing the mind and its concomitants to perform [their functions].

Furthermore, because they are virtuous and so forth, and because it is by means of this [volition] that the various states are differentiated and the non-associated formations are established, volition alone is taught as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). This explains why volition is uniquely designated as an "aggregate."
Furthermore, this very volition (cetanā), [extending up to] the aforementioned, is collectively termed the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).

The commentary states: This demonstrates that other dharmas are also the aggregate of formations; among all mental factors (caitta), with the exception of sensation (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā), all remaining mental factors as well as those non-associated with mind (cittaviprayukta) are of the nature of the aggregate of formations.
The exclusion of sensation and perception is for the purpose of distinguishing them from the aggregates of sensation and perception.

Because it is designated by another name as a "skandha," non-Buddhists reckon this to be the cause of birth and death; they cultivate meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and the formless realms (*ārūpya*), and because these two are most excellent, they are established separately as two skandhas.
Therefore, they are not subsumed under *saṃskāra*. In reality, however, it is volition (*cetanā*) and action (*kriyā*) that bring about the wholesome or the defiled.

The fifth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇābhidharma-śāstra* states that there are three distinctions regarding *saṃskāra*: first, the distinction of superiority, meaning that volition is capable of accomplishing both the defiled and the pure.

Therefore, regarding what was previously explained as "volition" (*cetanā*) in accordance with the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*), there are two bases for its differentiation: namely, the six groups of volition (*ṣaṭ-cetanā-kāya*) and the three designations (*prajñapti*).
These [three] are the distinctions between the states of defilement and purity. Based on this text, the preceding section is divided into three parts.
As for the "six groups of volition," this refers to the differentiation by basis; as for "performing wholesome [actions] and so forth," this refers to the differentiation by excellence.
The remaining members of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) are designated separately and categorized into two groups, which accords somewhat with this text;

they are explained as "wholesome" and so forth because they account for the preceding causes. As stated in the *Pañcāśatikā-śāstra*: "By way of their objects," referring to the six groups of volition (*ṣaṭ-cetanā-kāya*).

This clarifies that the meaning is based on the faculties' ability to apprehend objects, rather than being named after the six objects themselves. In the main body of the treatise, the Master designates these as "formations."
Regarding the statement that the master of the aggregates (*skandha-svāmī*) is included within the aggregates, the commentator (*śāstrakāra*) re-explains the preceding meaning.
Although the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) has been excluded [from the category of "formations"], [the text continues] up to: "Therefore, it is specifically mentioned.

The commentary states: The commentator, intending to explain that volition (*cetanā*) alone is designated as "formations" (*saṃskāra*), first cites what has already been established in order to manifest its exclusive significance.

Although the following [sections] have already been established by the preceding [analysis], the subsequent reflection is intended to clarify why the term "aggregate" (skandha) is used exclusively here;
it is because this volition guides all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), and as the primary factor of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha), it is therefore mentioned specifically.
To clarify this meaning, [the text] states, "performing wholesome dharmas," and so forth.
The commentary says: This citation of the preceding root text—"performing wholesome [dharmas]" and so on—serves to establish the aforementioned meaning of being designated as "conduct" (*caryā*);

alternatively, it uses the root text to establish the meaning of one's own statement that "volition is the precursor"; or it uses the meaning of one's own statement that "volition is the precursor" to establish the point.
Regarding the commentary on the root text concerning the performance of wholesome actions and so forth, the initial interpretation is correct.
"Wholesome" refers [to states] up to the minor afflictions. The commentary states:
this explains the nature of the performance of wholesome and defiled actions and so forth. "Wholesome" refers to faith and the others; these eleven will be explained later as the "mixed" factors.

The various types of afflictions, such as the eleven beginning with attachment (*rāga*) or the ten beginning with anger (*krodha*), are differentiated based on their specific bases (*pratyaya*) and general bases;
furthermore, they differ in terms of being nominal (*prajñapti*) or substantial (*dravya*).

Alternatively, the ten beginning with anger are termed "partial" (*pradeśa*), while the ten beginning with lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) are termed "states" (*avasthā*). Or, the term "partial" refers to the specific divisions of the afflictions themselves. Below [is the detailed explanation].

To explain the above: because the various secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) share a partial identity and similar categories with [the universal mental factors], even though volition (*cetanā*) also functions as a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*), this discussion concerns their essential natures;

thus, it speaks only of the wholesome and the defiled. Furthermore, since volition can also produce the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature and possesses no distinct category [of its own] apart from these, the treatise does not mention it.
Regarding the distinctions of states (from "the distinctions of states" up to "factors dissociated from mind"):

The commentary states that because there are various mental factors—such as wholesome and defiled states—arising from volition (*cetanā*), the factors dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are provisionally established based upon them.

Although these factors are dissociated from mind, they nonetheless depend upon both mind and matter (*nāma-rūpa*); however, since we are currently discussing the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), we do not mention their dependence [on other bases].
Furthermore, others state that the "non-associated basis" refers to that which is produced by volition (*cetanā*), and not exclusively to mental factors (*caitta*);
therefore, there is no fault in this treatise either.
Question: What are [the states] up to and including remorse (*kaukṛtya*), vitarka, and vicāra?

The commentary states: The above provides a general summary of the essence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Below follows a detailed explanation of the phenomena previously indicated. This main section has two parts:
first, the analysis of the formations associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta-saṃskāra*); second, the analysis of the formations dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).

The beginning and middle sections consist of two parts: first, the listing of the individual names of the fifty-three mental factors (*caitta*); second, the explanation of these fifty-three mental phenomena.

Among these mental factors, there are actually fifty-five; however, since the two factors of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) have already been discussed within their respective aggregates, and the primary factor of volition (*cetanā*) has already been mentioned as the head of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), these three factors are not included in the list of names, even though they were indicated as belonging to the aggregate of formations.

The aggregates (*skandha*) have already been explained, but the nature and function of what is called "mental factors" (*caitta*) have not yet been elucidated. To clarify their nature and function, there are fifty-three distinct explanations.
Why are these termed "mental factors"? The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "They always arise based on the mind (*citta*), they are associated with the mind, and they are bound to the mind;
therefore, they are called 'mental factors' (*caitta*). This is like establishing 'mine' (*mama-ka*) for things that belong to the self."

The mind (*citta*) is so named because it apprehends only the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of its objects; the mental factors (*caitta*), however, also apprehend their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

They assist in accomplishing the work of the mind, and thus the mental factors are termed "acquired by the mind" (*cittānuvartin*). This is like a master painter and his apprentice: the master provides the outline, while the apprentice fills in the colors.

The remaining points regarding these categories will be understood as they arise below. Within the enumeration of names, there are two meanings: first, the Master of the Treatise himself establishes and enumerates the mental factors.
The Master of the Commentary (*Vyākhyā*) below provides a specific allocation across six stages.
Regarding [the passage] from "Thus, volition and so forth" up to "indeterminate," the commentary states:
"This listing of the names of the stages is followed by their individual assignment and analysis; what was previously explained as 'fifty-five' makes this explicit."

They are similar in kind. Although the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that there is no difference in the names or meanings of the mental factors (*caitta*), there are six categories of types because they are invariably found within all states of mind.
"Universal" (*sarvatraga*) means "pervasive. It signifies the sense of arising;

because they arise pervasively throughout the mind, they are given the name "universal. Being both universal and arising, they are called "universals. [This refers to their] objects of perception (*ālambana*).
Because their objects and spheres differ in many ways, they are established as distinct mental factors with the name "distinct-sphere" (*viśeṣa-bhūmika*).

Because they can arise only within wholesome minds, they are termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*) as they accord with benefit. This [term] is not a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive compound), as there is no separation or combination [of meanings].

Because it lacks discernment (*pravicaya*), its nature is subsumed under the root afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*). Since the nature of affliction is itself distressing, it is called "affliction" (*kleśa*); it is exclusively afflictive.
Because they are of the nature of an outflow (*niṣyanda*) from the various states of affliction (*kleśa*), they are called "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*).

Since they are indeterminate with respect to being wholesome, defiled, or otherwise, and since—unlike contact (*sparśa*) and so forth—they do not necessarily pervade the mind, and unlike desire (*chanda*) and so forth—they do not necessarily pervade all stages [of consciousness], they are designated as "indeterminate.
Like non-attachment (*alobha*) and the others, this term is not included within the six types of *vyākhyāna* (explanatory compounds); here, it is simply a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*).
There are three types of explanation: *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound), and *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound).

However, in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, these six are combined into five because both the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are equally defiled. Furthermore, the distinctions between the five categories are established by means of the "fourfold universality" (*sarvatraga*):

namely, universality of nature (*svabhāva*), universality of stage (*bhūmi*), universality of time (*kāla*), and universality of every moment (*kṣaṇa*). Regarding the meaning of "stage," there are two interpretations; one holds that it refers to the nine stages (*navabhūmi*).

The second [category] refers to the five mental factors—such as *vitarka* (applied thought) and so forth—which exist in the third stage (*bhūmi*). Among these, the universal factors (*sarvatraga*) possess all four types of universality;
the object-specific factors (*viniyata*) possess only the first two types; the wholesome factors (*kuśala*) possess only one type; the defiled factors (*kliṣṭa*) are entirely absent from all stages;
and the indeterminate factors (*aniyata*) possess only one type. Because these five categories differ in their nature and scope, each receives its own specific name without redundancy.
The meaning of "not diminishing" is still somewhat redundant; the explanation of names and meanings as taught in the *Vijñaptimātra* is most excellent.
This should be understood according to their respective order.

[The commentary] states: these are specifically assigned to the exhortation to know. Although the first five universal phrases are listed in two lines, they pertain to both the categories of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.

To speak of them separately: there are five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), eleven object-specific factors (*viśeṣabhūmika*), ten wholesome factors (*kuśala*), twenty afflictions (*kleśa*), four secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*).

Regarding the establishment or rejection [of these categories] and the expansion or reduction of the six classes, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Chapter 5) extensively cites scriptural authority and reasoning as explained therein.
These various mental factors are as described in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter [18].
The first, third, eighth, fifty-fifth, fifty-eighth, and fifty-ninth [fascicles] of the *Xiǎnyáng shèngjiào lùn* (Exposition of the Sacred Teachings),

as well as the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* (Treatise on the Five Aggregates) and others, explain each [of these] in accordance with the commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Having listed the names above, they will now be explained individually below.
Furthermore, this [section] up to "should be analyzed in detail" is explained as follows:
there are three distinct expositions. First, the Master of the Commentary explains the sequence of the subsequent discourse.

Second, the Master of the Original Text provides a specific explanation of the essence and function. Third, he explains the common activity of both wholesome and defiled states. This initial passage concerns the characteristics, which constitute the essence.
This reveals the essence and function of the mental factors (*caitta*). It reveals the functions of the mind.
Regarding "volition" (*cetanā*) [up to] "its function is to employ the mind":

the commentary states that in the subsequent detailed explanation, there are six categories according to their respective positions; since three of the first position have already been explained, [the remaining] two are now discussed.
Regarding all mental factors (*caitta*) explained below, first their essential nature (*svabhāva*) and function (*karman*) are clarified;

this treatise’s main text reiterates that nature and function, and this commentary further explains them so as not to trouble the student with further references—this the scholar should know. Above, the main treatise [presented] the lower explanation of the treatise's own words;

for the subsequent mental factors, one should understand them all according to this principle. Previously, the Master of the *Abhidharmakośa* stated that "activity" (*kāritra*) constitutes a mental factor; now, this treatise...
The separate explanation mentions only the formation of the mind because they manifest one another, or because the mind is preeminent;
thus, it specifically refers here to volition (*cetanā*) as the mental concomitant karma, providing a proximate etymological definition as that which is capable of producing the mind.
Regarding the phrase "mental construction" (*citta-abhisaṃskāra*) [up to] "this distinguishes its activity," the commentary states:

The Master [Vasubandhu], fearing that [the reader] might again be unfamiliar with the distinction between essence and activity, has separately cited and assigned [this term] as an illustration for other mental factors (*caitta*).
"Because of the mind that initiates [action] regarding what is to be done. [The commentary] states:
This means that the mind which apprehends the characteristics of the correct causes and so forth of an object, drives its own mind to perform wholesome actions and the like.

Now, considering the intent of the treatise, it cites the "dharma to be performed" (the effect) to reveal the essence of the "performer" (the cause); thus, it speaks of the "mind of action" by citing the state of that which is to be performed.
Because it manifests the performance of an action, it is said that the mind is directed toward those [objects] such as the wholesome;
otherwise, there would be no distinction between the essence and the action.
Furthermore, since it is manifested by its activity, attention (*manasikāra*) has the function of holding the mind.
The commentary states: "Initiation" (*pravartana*) has the meaning of "arousing. This means that this arousal should cause the seeds of the mind to arise and lead them toward their objects;
therefore, it is called "initiation. It is not merely an arousal of the mind. As for the term "generating the mind" (*cittotpāda*), since the mind is primary, it is used in this sense.
Regarding the "raising of the seed," this refers to the arising of activity within the causal state, similar to the "future activity" (*anāgata-vṛtti*) asserted by the Sarvāstivādins.
The term "arousing" (*utthāpana*) refers to the capacity to alert and explain the manifestation [of mental states];
it is called "attention to the attainment of the object" (*ālambana-pratilambha-manasikāra*).

The commentary states: This explains that the operation of the aforementioned "action-attention" (*karma-manasikāra*) applies to both the distracted and concentrated states; however, it is specifically said that the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for concentration [is what is intended here].
The statement that "retaining the mind" (*cittadhāraṇa*) clarifies its function by manifesting its activity;
because it repeatedly draws the mind toward this object, the term *vijñapti* (representation) refers solely to the activity of drawing the mind, which constitutes its universal function.
Contact has the function of serving as the basis for sensation (*vedanā*).

The commentary states: when the faculty (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) mutually accord with one another, this is called the "conjunction of the three" (*trikasamnipāta*). Contact depends upon that conjunction;
therefore, the Sūtra says that contact is the conjunction of the three. Now, the Master of this treatise does not say it depends on that conjunction, but rather says it arises based upon it.
Therefore, it is said that "contact" (*sparśa*) depends upon the conjunction of the three. Even if these three have not yet conjoined, they merely abide in their own nature;

however, in the subsequent state of their conjunction, each possesses a functional capacity (*vṛtti*) conducive to the arising of mental factors (*caitta*) that differs from their former state, and thus they are all termed "altered.

Among these three transformations, the faculty (*indriya*) alone is predominant because its basis (*āśraya*) is continuous and proximate; therefore, it is not only the [other] three that are capable [of such transformation].
The mental factors (*caitta*) that arise from the contact of the mind are all likewise able to produce [their own effects];

however, because contact based on the harmony of the [three] is preeminent, although contact experiences what resembles the threefold transformation, it is said to "discriminate" the transformation of the faculty because it most closely resembles the power of the mental factor arising from the faculty.
This "discrimination" has the sense of experiencing what resembles [the cause], just as a son who resembles his father is said to be "a portion" (*bhāga*) of him.
Feeling is distinguished [from contact] because it arises from that [contact] and not from another; it is said to depend on its immediate proximity because it is predominant, as previously explained.
This treatise has not yet stated the distinct mode of activity of contact; rather, the very nature of contact is that which causes mental factors to simultaneously touch a single object.
Regarding its function toward objects, the masters distinguish it as "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*), while the Sūtra itself speaks of it as "discrimination" (*pratisaṃvedana*).
For now, following the sūtras, there is no separate activity;
that is to say, when consciousness arises (up to) the arising of contact through discrimination.

[Commentary: Before consciousness has arisen, the sense organ abides in its own nature; when consciousness reaches the stage of arising, the characteristic of the sense organ differs from its former state and becomes capable [of functioning].

There are mental factors (*caitta*) that arise in accordance with the power of the sense faculties (*indriya*) as causes, and because they accord with their results, they are called "conformable to arising.

Following these faculties, there arise sensations (*vedanā*) and modes of activity (*ākāra*) that possess the capacity to experience and resemble those [objects]. Through the power of contact (*sparśa*), which arises from the discernment of these, and because the faculties possess the capacity to produce them, the state of sensation is distinct.
Due to the immediate production of sensation by contact, the Sūtra states that consciousness (*vijñāna*), contact, sensation, and so forth, are all causes.
The second, third, and fourth [mental factors] arise through combination, as explained at length in the third fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Regarding the similarities and differences among various passages, I shall refrain from citing them here as they involve complex arguments and contradictions; these have already been explained in detail in that commentary (*ṭīkā*). Since [these factors] pervade all minds, there is no distinct category for them;
the preceding section explains the "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*) factors, while the following section explains the "object-specific" (*viṣayapratiniyata*) factors.
Desire (*chanda*) has "aspiration" as its essential nature.
[The commentary] states: "That which is desired to be experienced" clarifies that desire has an object (*ālambana*). "Desired" refers to an object that is pleasing;
because one aspires to see, hear, or otherwise engage with such a pleasing thing, [desire arises]. [This applies] to objects that are loathsome as well as to neutral objects.
In one sense, "absence of desire" (*anicchā*) means that there is no longing for what is pleasing and no expectation; nor does it mean the arising of desire.

According to another interpretation, "the object of delight" (*iṣṭa*) refers to the sought-after object, because one has expectations regarding things to be delighted in or loathed, such as seeking union or separation.

According to yet another interpretation, "the object of delight" refers to the object of contemplation, because those who wish to investigate all phenomena have expectations. Conversely, this is also "absence of desire."
The three [points] are explained at length in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. Below, those mental factors that are identical [to others] are not described, while those that differ are set forth;

there is no need for further reference to the treatise, as scholars should already know them. Regarding the term "each respective" (*tatra tatra*), it refers to the four distinct objects such as what is seen and heard.
As stated in the fifty-fifth [verse]: "That which, toward each respective object, pursues and delights in it is called desire (*chanda*); therefore, it is an inducer."
This refers to the activity performed for the purpose of desiring to see and so forth regarding an object;

that is to say, the activities such as seeing. The meaning of this statement is to clarify that the activity induced by the desire to see and so forth regarding various respective objects—this very aspiration is the essential nature of *chanda* (desire).
Its function is to serve as the basis for right effort (*samyak-pradhāna*).
The commentary states: This explains that wholesome karma gives rise to right effort, because it induces various [wholesome factors] until all activities are accomplished.

The commentary states: Because one desires to initiate all functions, such as seeing and so forth, with respect to various objects, it is said that "the performance of various inducements" [is involved];
this aspiration is the essential nature of desire (*chanda*).
"Adhimokṣa (resolute conviction) has the function of directing [the mind].
The commentary states: "The phrase 'determining an object' indicates that this [adhimokṣa] does not arise with respect to indeterminate objects and the like."
"According to what has been determined, up to the point of definitive resolution and resolute conviction.
Commentary: This explains the preceding "seal of essence. "Seal" means that this matter must be so; "holding" means definitive resolution without hesitation.
"By virtue of resolute conviction (adhimukti)... it cannot be diverted.

[The commentary] states: This explains that the preceding karma—whether by means of scripture, reasoning, or realization—is thoroughly determined and confirmed regarding the object of apprehension through the power of the correct or the erroneous;
because of this, it cannot be diverted by other conditions, and thus it pertains to an object that is not subject to doubt.
Adhimokṣa (resolute conviction) is entirely absent where there is no decisive resolve, nor is there adhimokṣa in such cases.
Smṛti (mindfulness) has the function of non-distraction.

[The commentary states: "That which is familiarized" refers to this throughout its categories; otherwise, the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) would not be objects of mindfulness.
Because one who hears that name and is able to recollect it has also practiced such matters, this is categorized as "initial" [recollection].

Since there is a recollection of what was never previously attained—that is, the true [state]—it exists by virtue of being of the same class as what was previously named. All such cases should be understood in this way:
namely, the repeated recollection and maintenance of objects previously experienced so as not to forget them, which is capable of inducing meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Therefore, because this reveals the basis for the three trainings—the tracks of the Dharma—it is able to produce meditative concentration;
even regarding objects of a type never before experienced, or those previously experienced that cannot be clearly remembered, no recollection arises.
Regarding the practice of cultivation (*abhyāsa*), it means causing the mind not to be distracted.

[The commentary] states: Even if mindfulness arises by taking the future as its object, it takes as its object either the substance or the category of what was previously experienced—such as mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) and so forth.
As for mindfulness that is not distracted while taking the three periods of time as its object, this is certainly explained in reference to wholesome karma (*kuśala-karman*).
"Samādhi" (up to) "is its function. Commentary:
*Samādhi* is translated here as "equipoise" (*samāhita*). It refers to holding the mind in equilibrium so that it reaches the object. *Samāpatti* is translated as "attainment" (*samyak-āpatti*).
This is because it is reached through the state of meditative equipoise induced by the preceding preparatory mind; it is the "reaching" (*āpatti*) of the state of equipoise.

Because in the state of meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*) one is tranquil, free from sinking (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*), that which precedes it consists solely of mind and may be either distracted (*vikṣipta*) or concentrated (*samāhita*);
whereas that which follows exists only in concentration and may be either with or without mind. From this, a fourfold classification (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established:

there is meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that is not meditative equipoise, namely exclusive focus on a single object within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); there is meditative equipoise that is not meditative absorption, namely the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

The two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) possess both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). There are four types each of dhyāna and formless attainment (*ārūpya*), which are meditative concentrations but not meditative absorptions.
Non-concentration refers to the lack of focused attention in the desire realm; *samāhita* is translated as "equipoise" (*samāpatti*).

It is "equipoise" because it is drawn forth by that which is equalized, and because through meditative stability (*samādhi*), one is free from sinking and agitation. These exist only in the realms of form and formlessness.
Regarding the mental application (*manaskāra*) that corresponds to the first two gates, one should analyze it according to what is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter thirteen.

As for the object of observation (*ālambana*), in reality it is exclusively the domain of wisdom (*prajñā*). Alternatively, because hearing and so forth share the same objective sphere, they are termed "objects.
Furthermore, since concentration (*samādhi*) does not cause the mind to arise by itself alone—because the mind is the primary agent—it is simply described as being "wisdom" and "mind."
It is taught based on karma, the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*), and the three trainings (*śikṣā*).
Regarding "causing the mind to be one-pointed" (up to) "knowing things as they truly are":

the commentary states that this refers to focusing the mind through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) so that it does not scatter, while observing within the objective field of qualities, faults, and that which is neither.
Thereupon, the wisdom of decisive discernment arises, and the mind becomes focused; the term "intentionally" indicates the desired state of abiding, which is then able to abide accordingly.

It does not refer to a single object alone. When the treatise speaks of a "single object," it means each individual object, not that the preceding and succeeding objects are collectively one single object.

Otherwise, since the Path of Vision (darśanamārga) involves observing the various Truths with distinct preceding and succeeding objects, there would be no meditative concentration (samādhi). If this were not so...
When one is focused, concentration does not arise.
Regarding the statement that "wisdom has the function of severing doubt":
this means that when one observes qualities, faults, or that which is neither within an object, one attains certainty through the investigation and inquiry of wisdom. Thus, [it severs doubt].
In a mind that is ignorant regarding the object of observation, wisdom does not arise because there is no discernment.
As for "severing doubt," it refers to attaining certainty.

[The commentary] states: Although doubt is accompanied by a wavering wisdom, this [term] refers to the decisive resolution that definitively severs doubt; it is not [merely] the presence of hesitation.

This is the activity that universally manifests wisdom. These five [factors] are briefly analyzed through four gates: (1) their simultaneous and individual arising; (2) which consciousnesses they accompany; (3) their association with the three types of feeling; and (4) their nature, realm, and so forth. Regarding (1) simultaneous and individual arising:

one interpretation holds that these five definitely support one another, such that when any one arises, the other four must necessarily arise as well. Another interpretation holds that this is not necessarily the case. [The text continues: "There are four [possibilities]. Regarding the first gate, there are two interpretations.

One view maintains that these five are invariably mutually supportive, such that whenever one arises, the remaining four must necessarily arise. Another view maintains that they are not necessarily so. There are four [cases]. (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly after "four," indicating the analysis of the first gate is incomplete.)
Because the latter two do not exist among all [beings], and because the four objects arise, they are not necessarily simultaneous.

Since the four objects arise separately, one should explain that there are five [types of] arising according to the objects: (1) two [arise] according to the objects, totaling twelve phrases; (2) three [arise] according to the objects, totaling thirteen phrases;
(3) four [arise] combined according to the objects, totaling five phrases; (4) five [arise] according to the objects, totaling four phrases; and (5) only one phrase in total.

There are thirty-one propositions regarding their separate combination. As for which consciousnesses possess them: in the state of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), all eight consciousnesses are universally present.
In the causal state (*hetu-avasthā*), the eighth consciousness possesses five, while the others do not. Regarding the manas-consciousness: according to one interpretation, it lacks them all;

according to another, it possesses three—defilement, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—as these are admitted to coexist with it. According to yet another interpretation, these five are all associated with its defiled portion (*kliṣṭa-bhāga*). Thus, there are ten [propositions].
Because the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) universally defile the mind, according to the true meaning, with the exception of wisdom (*prajñā*), these four do not coexist [with one another].
While mindfulness (*smṛti*) and the others that belong to the category of delusion (*moha*) may coexist with them, those belonging to the category of defilement cannot.

According to one interpretation, all five of these are absent in the five sensory consciousnesses; according to another interpretation, these five may exist in the five sensory consciousnesses, but they are definitely present in the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Regarding the possibility of these five being associated with all three feelings (*vedanā*): one interpretation holds that among the five mental factors, joy (*prīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) may co-occur, while the remaining four—excluding suffering (*duḥkha*)—may do so;
another interpretation holds that these five may co-occur with all five feelings, as this does not contradict either scripture or reason. Regarding their nature, realm, and so forth:

they all pertain to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), they all pertain to the three realms (*traidhātuka*) as well as that which is not included within a realm (*anāpta*), and they all pertain to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

The three faculties beginning with *śraddhā* (faith) all pertain to what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and what is not to be abandoned (*aheya*). One should reflect upon and apply these principles accordingly across such categories.

As extensively cited in the fourth and fifth fascicles of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, both reasoning and scripture cannot be quoted here in full for fear of prolixity. [This concludes] the five specific object-conditions (*viṣaya-niyata*) above;
next are the eleven wholesome (*kuśala*) mental factors below.
Faith has the function of serving as a basis. The commentary states:
regarding the essence and qualities [of an object], the conviction toward the object of cognition is called "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*), which is the cause of faith;
the aspiration for it is called "desire" (*chanda*), which is the fruit of faith. As for "purity," because the essence of faith can purify the mind, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains it thus.

Faith is further divided into three types. First is faith in real existence (*astitva-śraddhā*), which refers to the profound conviction and acceptance regarding the actual reality and principles of all phenomena.

This treatise explains that "acceptance" means the endurance of the existence of an essence; when one accepts and endures all phenomena, whether they are truths or non-truths, this is called faith in the existence of an essence.
The intent of this statement is to clarify that even if one were to believe in emptiness and non-existence, faith would still arise; it is not [the case that faith only arises toward existence].

Only when there is an object of perception does faith arise. Because the cause of faith—namely, receptivity (*kṣānti*)—is used to manifest the essential nature of faith, it is called "receptivity-approval" (*kṣānti-abhyupagama*).
Regarding the two types of faith that possess virtue: this refers to having deep faith and delight in the true and pure virtues of the Three Jewels.
Thus, this treatise states that there is purity through virtue. Whether it be a virtuous quality or a non-virtuous one, if it causes the mind to become pure, faith arises.
Only when there is virtue does faith arise; otherwise, if one were to believe in non-Buddhist paths that lack virtue, faith would not arise.
Because the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* speaks of this as being "profoundly faithful and joyful," it also cites the fruit of desire to reveal the intrinsic nature of faith.
Now, since the essence of faith arises toward the object of virtue, the statement that it is "pure" is not contradictory. Regarding the capacity of the three types of faith, it is said that:

Because all wholesome qualities possess the power of deep conviction, they can be attained and accomplished; since one gives rise to hope for them, this treatise states that there is the capacity for hope.
Whether there is the capacity [to attain] or the lack of capacity, hope arises through cultivation and abandonment, and thus faith is produced.

It is not necessary that there be actual capacity for faith to arise; otherwise, the faith that all evils are dharmas that can be abandoned would not arise. This is what is meant by "raising up faith."
Because it reveals the nature of faith as its fruit, it is called "aspiration.
It is said that this nature is pure and capable of purifying the mind and its concomitants, like a water-clearing jewel that clarifies turbid water.

Furthermore, while its own characteristic is defiled by lack of faith and thus turbid, it can also turbid other minds and mental factors, like an extremely filthy object that soils itself and others. Faith is the direct opposite of this.
Therefore, purity is its characteristic. Herein, three particularly excellent objects are cited to illustrate the focal object (*ālambana*) of faith;

although faith is indeed produced toward that which is truly peerless, this explanation serves as the cause for entering the Dharma and initiating [the path]. Its function is to serve as a basis for aspiration.
According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, its aspect (*ākāra*) to be eliminated is lack of faith, and its function is to cultivate delight in the wholesome.
This refers to the practice of faith characterized by aspiration toward that which truly exists [up to] the three aspects of the three objects.
The commentary states: This is specifically attributed to the first three objects;

while the three aspects possess substantiality and are described as being broad and pervasive—such that one may give rise to patience, possess virtue, and be worthy of honor—it is said that through aspiration one may attain purity and capability. Thus, it is called "aspiration," though in principle, all three objects are involved.
It can be further explained that because the characteristics and functions of the other [faculties] are subtle and inferior, they are described here according to their predominant function;

otherwise, since their objects and modes of activity are identical, they would not be universal. However, this purity is the very essence of faith (*śraddhā*); it is spoken of specifically as arising toward virtues, yet in reality it extends to all three objects, for it is only when one possesses virtue that faith and joy arise.
This means: "I have the power to attain and to accomplish.
[The commentary] states: This reveals that regarding sentient beings, there arises the hope and faith that the unconditioned can be attained and the conditioned can be accomplished;
for the two categories of the path—the moment of its attainment and its growth—are distinct.
"Shame (*hrī*) has [the function] of being a restraint as its activity.

The commentary states: "Regarding 'various transgressions' as the object, 'self-shame' as the condition, and furthermore, because the essence of shame shares a common characteristic, it is established according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* that 'revering the noble and the good' is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of shame;
with respect to the objects of faults and evils, self-shame constitutes the condition."
That which gives rise to reverence and respect is the essence of *hrī* (self-respect), for it brings about the cessation of unwholesome conduct; this is the general function of *hrī*.
As for its specific function, it directly opposes *āhrīkya* (lack of self-respect).
Regarding *apatrāpya* (dread of blame), its functions are explained in the same manner as those of *hrī*.
The commentary states: Regarding the objects and conditions, the meaning of their common characteristics is identical to that of *hrī* (shame).

According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the nature of *apatrāpya* (modesty) is the feeling of loathing, contempt, violence, opposition, and resistance toward unwholesome phenomena; thus, it is the essence of *apatrāpya*. Its general and specific functions should be understood as corresponding to those of *hrī*.

Although the essences of both *hrī* and *apatrāpya* are here described as "shame" (*lajjā*), this is a figurative designation of their distinct essences based on their shared characteristic. This is because the two types of shame do not arise simultaneously.

Therefore, *hrī* (moral shame) is called "internal" because it pertains to oneself and the internal factors (*dharma*). It is called "self-king" (*ātmarāja*) in the Buddhist teachings, while worldly discourse refers to it as "other.
Alternatively, honoring what is wholesome is called "self" because it benefits oneself, and rejecting what is evil is called "other" because it harms oneself.
As previously stated, the objects of these two—manifesting their respective specific and general characteristics—are all as explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
"Non-attachment" (up to) "is its function. The commentary states:

"Existence" (*bhava*) refers to the three existences, which are the fruits of the three realms; "possessions" (*pariṣkāra*) refers to the requisites, which are the causes and conditions for the three existences.

That which gives rise to the three existences is all termed "possessions of existence. Defiled conditions as well as untainted (*anāsrava*) things are included within this truth as "possessions of existence."
"Non-attachment" refers to the nature of non-greed; this term applies generally to the non-arising of unwholesome courses of action. "Arising" means to initiate.
It specifically excludes attachment.
"Non-hatred" [extends] to its function as an action.

The commentary states: Regarding "the suffering of sentient beings," this refers to the *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* (suffering of conditioned existence) or the *duḥkha-duḥkhatā* (suffering of pain) within the three realms.

By mentioning only "sentient beings," it highlights the primary object of hatred; for even the Noble Path and its Cessation can provoke hatred due to being viewed with aversion. If this were not the case, the absence of hatred (*avyāpāda*) would conversely result in having too narrow an object.

As for "instruments of suffering," these refer to the causes and conditions of the three types of suffering, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and so forth, because there is no absence of hatred toward them, and because they apply both generally and specifically.

All karmas are to be understood according to what was previously explained. Regarding the statement that "non-greed and non-hatred exist," etc., this is established in dependence upon greed and so forth; it does not mean they must take those as their objects.

If it were otherwise, these two would not be universal to all wholesome states, just as the case of shame (*hrī*) and dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*) is established by observing the wholesome and the unwholesome. If it were not so, these two would likewise fail to be universal to all wholesome states.
"Non-delusion" (amoha) [extends] to its function.

The commentary states: According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, its nature is clear understanding regarding both principles (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*). Some maintain that its nature consists of the retribution of merit and so forth;
however, the essence of non-delusion is precisely the nature of discernment (*viniścaya*). Therefore, the treatise uses the term "by means of" (*yuan*) to manifest the four stages as causes.
Since all forms of decisive discernment (*niścaya*) have this as their essence, the four stages are not merely wisdom (*prajñā*); therefore, it is said "by means of.

According to another interpretation, non-delusion (*amoha*) has a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). By citing its results—such as [right] action and cause—its nature as non-delusion is revealed;

thus the treatise says "by means of non-delusion. If it arises, it is necessarily accompanied by the four types of wisdom; from the inferior grade, the superior arises, and from the superior, the inferior again arises.

Therefore, by citing cause and effect, the nature of non-delusion is revealed; the general and specific [aspects] and their respective antidotes are also to be understood according to what was previously stated.
As for the first three [faculties], only the general antidotes were cited because they are easily understood and thus do not require further explanation.
The commentary states: This master of the treatise explains that he does not provide a redundant explanation of the four causes, such as shame (*hrī*) and so forth.
Regarding "knowledge derived from maturation, teaching, and realization," one should understand them respectively.

The commentary states: The four kinds of wisdom are correlated with the previously mentioned wholesome dharmas—those acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*)—which have past habituation as their cause; [these arise] as soon as...
That which arises at birth and constitutes one’s own essence is called "retribution" (*vipāka*), or it is so named because it arises together with retribution;

this is based on its support. Wisdom acquired through hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) arises solely by taking the teaching as its object; thus, it is named after its object, "the teaching. Wisdom acquired through reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is able to give rise to cultivation; thus, it is named after its result, "realization.

Because the wisdom acquired through cultivation directly perceives and realizes the Dharma through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the wisdom produced by cultivation is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) in terms of its essential nature.

For the sake of the names, it is said that, in sequence, there are seventy-seven [stages] as explained. The wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) relies upon the words, yet has not yet grasped the intended meaning;
it has not yet attained the realization of the meaning that leads to liberation.

The wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) relies both upon the words and upon the intended meaning, yet has still not attained the realization of the meaning that leads to liberation. Now, the wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) relies upon...
Regarding the words, one does not rely on the words themselves but is able to correctly understand the underlying intent;

having thus been able to receive and comprehend the meaning that constitutes liberation, this demonstrates that the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) mostly takes the teachings as its object and only rarely takes the meaning as its object, whereas the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) takes both the teachings and the principles as its objects, and the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) mostly takes the meaning as its object and only rarely takes the words as its object.
This refers to the lack of skillful intent in merely reciting and studying the scriptures.

What is the difference between the wholesome [wisdom] acquired through birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*) and the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*)? Since their clarity and obscurity differ, their objects (*ālambana*) also differ.

Wisdom derived from hearing takes either the text or its meaning as its object, whereas that acquired through birth takes the text entirely and does not understand the meaning at all. This is stated in the *Madhyānta-vibhāga*.
That is to say: by copying, making offerings, giving to others, listening to, opening [the text] for, reading, receiving, upholding,
correctly expounding, reciting, and reflecting upon and practicing it— those who practice these ten dharmas obtain an immeasurable mass of merit because it is supreme and inexhaustible,
due to its unceasing gathering of others.

Maitreyanātha explains that the first eight [factors] constitute the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), the ninth constitutes the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), and the tenth constitutes the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

If one were to argue that reciting scriptures and so forth consists only of innate virtue (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*), then such acts could not produce immeasurable merit; therefore, these eight factors do not consist of innate virtue alone.
Since the essential natures of hearing, reflection, and cultivation are all fundamentally wisdom, the term "wisdom" refers to the essence of the knowledge produced by these three causes.

Because they are types of wisdom (*prajñā*), this treatise explains that they consist of the wisdoms derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī*) and so forth; these are explained either as *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) or *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compounds, and one must not simply refer to them merely as the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā-prajñā*).

Among these, the wisdoms of hearing and reflection exist only in the distracted state and are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), whereas the wisdom of cultivation exists both in meditative concentration and is also accessible to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

As the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states that a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage is capable of contemplation (*cintā*), Vasubandhu’s commentary clarifies that this refers to the wisdom of hearing and reflection.

The "wise" refers to the single category of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*); it is explained as distinct [from the others], for the *Śāstra* states that in the desire realm there is only wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī*) and reflection (*cintāmayī*), while in the form realm there is no wisdom derived from reflection, and above that (in the formless realm) there is only cultivated wisdom.
Furthermore, the "contemplative realization" (*manasikāra-abhisamaya*) and so forth are all exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).

If one were to allow that wisdom derived from hearing and reflection could also be uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), then such wisdom would have to exist in the higher stages; moreover, it would contradict the *Śāstra* to claim that these exist only in the distracted state (*vikṣipta*).
It is said that the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*) truly penetrate the untainted (*anāsrava*). However, this is stated based on the tainted (*sāsrava*) perspective;
it is said that the higher stages lack the tainted because the higher stages are coarse, whereas the untainted is subtle. Why would the higher stages not possess [the untainted]?

Because the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses (*ghrāṇa-vijñāna* and *jihvā-vijñāna*) are tainted, while in the higher stages there is no untainted [consciousness], and because the innate wholesome dharmas (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala-dharma*) arise only in the same place as the body.
The arising and manifestation [of wisdom] through hearing and cultivation are not fixed, as will be explained later.
"Definitive discernment" (*viniścaya*) refers to wisdom conjoined with vigor and diligence.

The commentary states: this is an explanation of the general name for wisdom; "vigor and diligence" refers specifically to *vīrya* (diligence). Because wisdom is conjoined with that [vigor], it is called "definitive."
Discernment (*pravicaya*) is not a definitive determination (*niścaya*) regarding the category of indolence and hesitation;
therefore, this explanation that wisdom (*mati*) is associated with non-delusion (*amoha*) is incorrect, for otherwise, wisdom would not function within a defiled mind.
Diligence (*vīrya*) has as its activity... [to reach]... its function.

The commentary states: "Mental fortitude" (*cittaudārya*) is its essence, because it causes the mind to give rise to courage and vigor. It is the differentiation of the five types of diligence, such as armor-like diligence (*saṃnāha-vīrya*), and so forth.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states that its nature is mental courage and vigor, or that it is established through the five differentiations beginning with armor-like diligence.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun) says that its nature is courage and vigor regarding the tasks of cultivation and abandonment within the categories of the wholesome and the unwholesome; that [wholesome]...

The "object of application" (*pragraha*) refers to the domain of diligence regarding the category of unwholesome states. This statement that "mental vigor" (*citta-pragraha*) is the fruit of diligence is based on their respective individual meanings;

thus, there is no contradiction in principle. "Vigor" (*vīrya*) signifies superior progress, thereby distinguishing it from all defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), for defiled phenomena involve regression from the wholesome and cannot be called "vigor.

"Martiality" (*parākrama*) signifies purity and intensity, thereby distinguishing it from the pure-neutral (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*), which lacks such intensity. Furthermore, because it endures weariness and fatigue, it manifests as "purity" (*viśuddhi*).
Progress consists exclusively of what is subsumed under the nature of virtue; this is explained in the eighty-ninth [section] of the *Viniscayasamgrahanī*.
First, the initial arousal of intense aspiration is called "donning the armor" (*sannāha*), because it is like first putting on armor before seeing an enemy.

Next, the arising of firm and courageous skillful means is called "application" (*prayoga*), because one exerts the mind with determination and acts with courageous resolve. Finally, for the sake of attaining realization...
Being free from self-contempt and devoid of timidity is called "absence of inferiority" (*anavalīnatva*);

because one is neither inferior nor timid, one subsequently becomes capable of enduring sufferings such as cold and heat. Furthermore, not becoming weary or satisfied with inferior or mediocre virtues, but instead joyfully seeking subsequent superior qualities and so forth, is called "absence of regression" (*asaṃlīnatva*);
this is because one does not feel insufficient upon obtaining only a small amount, nor is one defeated or diminished. Thereafter...

When one gradually enters the contemplation of the truths and advances toward the subsequent superior path, it is called "insatiable" (*atṛpta*). Although the merit has already been accomplished, one further prays for the great fruit;

because one does not consider even what has been attained as sufficient to satisfy the mind, this is explained based on its cause. If based on the fruit of Buddhahood, it is because one delights in benefiting others;

if based on the fruit-stage of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is because they aspire to the great fruit. Generally, it refers to the fulfillment of wholesome karma; specifically, it excludes indolence.
This refers to what is said in the Sūtra [up to] "not abandoning the noble yoke.
The commentary states: The masters who treat the distinctions of diligence establish these names because they fear the meaning might lack a basis;

therefore, they cite the Sūtra as proof. Because one first dons the armor, there is vigor; because one avoids the enemy and exerts effort, there is diligence; and because one is able to enter the mind without cowardice or inferiority, there is application.

Possessing courage, he first receives wounds from spears yet does not retreat; firm and fierce, he advances further. Having scattered the fruits [of lower realms], he has no more need to seek them, but pursues the supreme path.
From moment to moment he increases his cultivation, never abandoning the "yoke" (*yuga*) of virtue. "Yoke" refers to the yoke of a chariot; because the ox is yoked, it moves forward without stopping.
Being footless yet diligent and courageous, he likewise does not abandon the yoke of virtue. This constitutes the five [factors] of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

"Distinction" refers to the distinction between the three grades of the stage of self-perfection (*svabhāga*) and the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*) at the initial generation of the mind; or the distinction between the four types of cultivation at the initial generation of the mind;

or the distinction between the five paths, such as the path of equipment (*sambhāra-mārga*); or the distinction between the two vehicles’ stage of fulfillment and the Great Bodhi, or the result of the Buddhas which is perfect, eternal, blissful, and beneficial;
or the distinction between the two types of preparatory application (*prayoga*) and the four paths. These are included within the category of those lacking the nature [for enlightenment] (*agotra*).
Five [terms] are grouped into three, because the latter three are combined into one.
Following this sequence, [the text] proceeds through the various phrases. The commentary states:
the five phrases of the sūtra are assigned to the five names of the treatise; "the courageous one who dons the armor" refers to the first five [qualities], beginning with "donning the armor."

Because the mind itself is courageous, the phrase "courageousness of single-minded resolve" (ekacittavīrya) permeates the preceding five types, ranging from the courage of donning armor (saṃnāhavīrya) to the courage of being tireless (aparikhinnamānasavīrya).
Having explained their essential nature above, the function shall now be explained below.
Regarding "fulfilling the category of virtue" (up to) "thoroughly cultivated":

the commentary states that even in states such as the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), there are two types—the fulfillment of diligence (*vīrya*) and the fulfillment of virtue (*kuśala*). This refers to the stage of progressive cultivation (*abhyāsa-avasthā*).

When speaking of entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), other mundane states of detachment from desire (*laukika-vairāgya*) are omitted; it is only the attainment of the fundamental concentrations (*mauladhyāna*) through the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*) that is fully described.

When the category of wholesome qualities is fulfilled and one further severs pervasive hindrances and so forth, one is able to attain the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the like; the subsequent cultivation and purification of these is called the "accomplishment of the wholesome category.
The supramundane state of freedom from desire follows this same principle.
"Peace" (śānti) refers to [the state] up to its function as an activity (*karman*).
The commentary states: "Coarseness and heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) refers to the defiled, rigid, and unstable factors that obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

"Harmony" (*praśrabdhi*) is the fruit of peace; it causes the body and mind to become harmonious, supple, and refreshed. This explanation applies generally to the activity according to what is appropriate in each case.
Regarding the specific function of counteracting torpor and its removal:
it removes all [hindrances] up to the point where the basis (āśraya) functions. The commentary states:
by the power of pliancy (praśrabdhi), the obstructive factors of meditative concentration are removed, and a superior basis arises in which body and mind are harmoniously refined and supple.
"Non-negligence (apramāda) has [the cultivation of wholesome states] as its function.

The commentary states: Because the four factors such as right effort (*samyak-pradhāna*)—which are the basis for non-negligence—are superior in their capacity to exert energy for the cultivation and abandonment [of the unwholesome], they manifest the function of cultivating the wholesome and preventing the unwholesome.
This explains its general activity; specifically, it excludes negligence.
This refers to the essence of right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*) up to heedfulness (*apramāda*).
The commentary states: Because the four dharmas beginning with right effort serve as the prerequisite, one is able to cultivate the wholesome and guard against all outflows (*āsrava*);
since there is a distinct general capacity [arising from these], this [heedfulness] is established as a conventional designation.
Regarding "defiled phenomena" (*sāsrava-dharma*) [up to] "objects":

the commentary states that among the various defiled phenomena within the previously explained essence, those that function as the most excellent locus for the untainted (*anāsrava*) are explained here.

As for the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it says that while these generally prevent all evil outflows (*āsrava*), they specifically refer to the locus of the outflows of the afflictions (*kleśa-āsrava*). "Locus of the outflows" means the place where the outflows reside.

Regarding the sense faculties (*indriya*), outflows (*āsrava*), and objects (*viṣaya*): the phenomena that serve as the objects of the outflows—whether they be the faculties, the objects, or the various afflictions (*kleśa*)—are all termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) because they mutually increase one another.
This is as explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* regarding the meaning of being "with outflows" as a cause.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) has [the faculty of] equanimity as its essence.

The commentary states: In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is said that because it is distinct from the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), it is called "equanimity of formation" (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*).

The four factors, such as right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), have this as their basis, as previously explained. Regarding the "abiding" (*sthiti*) of defilement: the basis upon which the factors to be abandoned by equanimity rely is called "abiding."
Formerly relying on affliction (*saṃkleśa*), one now abandons its opposite; through equanimity (*upekṣā*), one brings the mind to a state of balance.
Its function is to cause the mind to abide in equanimity by means of relinquishment, thereby not allowing for the basis of affliction.
The commentary states: "To contain" means to receive. Because one first eliminates defilements through heedfulness (*apramāda*), one does not admit them during the state of equanimity (*upekṣā*);
this non-admission constitutes the basis for its function. According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, its activity consists of counteracting restlessness (*auddhatya*) and abiding in tranquility.
Through heedfulness, within the same moment, one first eliminates defilements, and subsequently, equanimity causes [the mind] to remain [in that state].
The mind abides in tranquility; alternatively, because the mental aspects of preceding and succeeding moments each increase, defilement is excluded and cannot arise.
Or rather, this is said because equanimity (*upekṣā*) and the abandonment of defilement each possess their own specific capacity.
Regarding the section on the distinctions of equanimity (*upekṣā*) up to "the equality of mind":

the commentary states that the subsequent explanation has three parts: first, a general explanation of the three stages of the aforementioned equanimity; second, an inquiry into the reason for this; and third, a detailed explanation of each. This is the first part.
It clarifies the characteristic of the practice of equanimity based on a continuous stream of consciousness (*saṃtāna-citta*), rather than within a single momentary thought (*ekakṣaṇa*).
"Wholesome relinquishment does not arise. Why is this so?
The commentary states: This is an inquiry into the reason why relinquishment is distinguished across the three preceding stages.
"By means of equanimity and the mind [reaching] the state of mental equilibrium.
Commentary: This explains in detail the departure from sinking and so forth; it interprets the aforementioned contradiction with the defiled states to be countered.
Because one is free from sinking and excitement through equanimity, one first realizes the state of mental equilibrium, as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
