"The increase of the first [grasping at views] refers to the aspect of viewing [something] as supreme and so forth; the 'purity' [of the second] refers to the aspect of viewing [it] as a cause of purity.
However, according to the previous explanation of the two entities and their functions, it is simply the estimation of [something] as supreme."

The view of holding to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is not here described as a cause for purification; previously, it was merely designated by the name "precept-and-vow adherence" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) because it was considered a cause for purification.
Now, it is no longer said that its essence is the most excellent. Each must possess two aspects to constitute the two types of adherence.
Alternatively, this is a reflection that distinguishes it from the preceding text; regarding this very view, the commentators explain it as being based upon the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
The explanation of the view of superimposition is concluded.
"For the most part, it is the view of negation.
The commentary states: In this treatise, the Master [Vasubandhu], in the second section, clarifies that false views are for the most part views of negation (*apavāda*).
"Regarding 'one part' and 'many parts' (up to) 'because of diminution':

the Commentary states that the Master’s explanation of these terms 'one part' and 'many parts' is as follows: the false view of superimposition (*samāropa*) consists of reckoning that Brahmā is eternal and so forth;
the false view of denial (*apavāda*) consists of repudiating the Four Noble Truths. Now, this explanation of false views differs from that of the Hīnayāna."

Since all diminution of false conceptualization is subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), it is not necessarily the case that all [instances of] diminution are [wrong view], as some may also involve augmentation (*samāropa*);
nevertheless, the fifty-eight [types of diminution] are described only as diminution, as has already been reconciled above.
Question: [Up to] "or all. Commentary:
This constitutes the second set of questions and answers concerning mutual inclusion. First, the original master of the treatise provides two sets of questions and answers;
subsequently, the commentator explains the meaning of those answers. This is the first set of questions and answers. "One who views the prior limit" refers to the past.
Because the entirety of the present depends in part upon the future and because it is the cause of the future, [the former] is called the "prior limit" (*pūrvānta*).

Because the entirety of the future depends in part upon the past and because it is the effect of the past, [the latter] is called the "subsequent limit" (*aparānta*). To give rise to views based on these two is termed the "view of the two limits.

This refers to the "views regarding the primary eon and primary views" (*pūrvakalpa-pūrvadṛṣṭi*) and the "views regarding the final eon and final views" (*paścimakalpa-paścimadṛṣṭi*) found in the tenth chapter of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the "Brahmajāla Sūtra" (*Brahmajāla-sūtra*).

Although the names differ while the essence remains without distinction, [this point] is explained extensively in the eighth, fifty-eighth, and eighty-seventh [chapters] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*;
the sixth [chapter] of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*; the tenth [sūtra] of the *Dīrgha Āgama*;
the sixty-second [chapter] of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*; and the one hundred ninety-ninth and two-hundredth [sections] of the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-vibhāṣā*.

However, since the *Dīrgha Āgama* and other such texts differ from the Mahāyāna in their doctrinal perspectives and cannot be relied upon as authoritative here, we shall follow what is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other works as correct.
In fascicle 58 and fascicle 87, it is stated that regarding the past (*pūrvānta*), there are five positions:

first, the four types of proponents of eternalism; second, the four types of proponents of partial eternalism; third, the two types of proponents of causal theories; and fourth, the four types of proponents of finitude.
In the *Samayabhedoparacanacakra*, following the four types of evasive speech regarding immortality (*amarāvikkhepa*), there are five categories for the future limit (*aparānta*):

first, sixteen proponents of the existence of perception (*saññivāda*); second, eight proponents of non-perception (*asaññivāda*); third, eight proponents of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññināsaññivāda*); fourth, seven proponents of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*);

and fifth, five proponents of nirvana in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda*). Thus, there are eighteen views regarding the past limit (*pūrvānta*), while for the future limit, they total [thirty-seven].

Question: Among the forty-four types of views, how many are subsumed within the five views? Answer: By way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are subsumed under two views, namely the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) and false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).
As for their attendants (*parivāra*), they are subsumed within all five views.

Although the *Pañcavastuka* states that they are subsumed under three views, that text itself explains that when [the view of extremes] is opened up into the eternalist and nihilist positions, it is collectively a single view of extremes. What, then, is their intrinsic nature?

Regarding the two views subsumed within the ten stages: the view of eternalism (śāśvata-dṛṣṭi) subsumes five, namely the four [theories of] universal eternalism, the four [theories of] partial eternalism, and the sixteen [theories of] existence with characteristics;

the view of non-perception (asaṃjñika) comprises eight; and the eight [theories of] "neither" comprise eight. The view of annihilationism (uccheda-dṛṣṭi) subsumes one, namely the seven [theories of] annihilationism.
Thus, the view of extremes (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi) subsumes six positions in total, comprising forty-seven views. The false view (mithyā-dṛṣṭi) subsumes four.

Regarding the categories: there are fifteen types of views, namely the two [views] regarding causelessness, the four [views] regarding finitude, the four [views] of the "immortal crooks," and the five [views] regarding nirvāṇa.
Thus, these two extreme views are subsumed under two categories. As for the four proponents of universal permanence:
first, because they are able to recollect one, two, three, or even up to eighty eons of dissolution and formation, they consequently cling to the notion that both the self and the world are eternal.

1. Because they are constantly hidden or manifest; 2. because they can remember one, two, or three lives, up to hundreds or thousands of births, they then cling to the view that both the self and the world are eternal;

3. because they see with the divine eye how the aggregates of sentient beings continue at the time of death, they then cling to the view that both the self and the world are eternal; 4. because their investigation and reflection are not in accordance with reality.
The view that both the self and the world are eternal arises from four factors: eons (*kalpa*), birth and death (*saṃsāra*), vitarka, and vicāra.

This view is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Since there is a view of permanence on the path of seeing, and because it takes phenomena of the three realms as its object—since all such phenomena are [erroneously perceived as] eternal—it takes the three realms collectively as its object;
nevertheless, it should be understood according to its specific application as pertaining to each of the three realms.

Regarding those who hold the doctrine that one part of the four [aggregates] is eternal: first, there are those who, having passed away from the Brahmā realm and been reborn in this world, attain the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives and form this attachment:
"We are all emanations created by Brahmā; Brahmā is eternal, while we are impermanent.
Second, there are those who hear that Brahmā holds such views as "the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are eternal, while the mind is impermanent," or the reverse.

This refers to those who share the same view as that "endurance" (kṣānti) [of the eternalists], or those dwelling in the Brahma-world, or even those who have heard such principles through successive transmission, thinking, "I take the Brahmā King as my standard" and thus believe his words.

Therefore, among those in the world for whom one portion is eternal, they first pass away from the Heaven of Forgetfulness through Play (*krīḍā-pramoṣaka-deva*) and are reborn here; having attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), they give rise to this attachment regarding that realm.
The gods who do not sport and so forth dwell there eternally, whereas we are impermanent. From the four states of existence, due to mental agitation, they pass away from that heaven;
this is as previously described. These two classes of gods reside in the four abodes of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as will be explained later.
These four arise from grasping at the Great Brahmā, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), or the mind, and from the four matters of sporting, forgetfulness, and anger. This—

The eight views arise based on the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), because they conceive of Brahmā as "another self" (*parātman*). Thus, the view that conceives of [Brahmā] as being partially eternal is subsumed under the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*);
otherwise, it would not be subsumed under the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

However, since it is accepted that one may take the phenomena (*dharmas*) of other stages as one's own self or another's self, there is no logical contradiction in its causing [the notion of] permanence and so forth, even if it were directed toward oneself.
Since the self is also included within the body, that which is eternal in one part is the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*); as for that which is impermanent, what kind of view is it?

Although this is not [the view of] annihilationism, because it is a stubborn adherence, it is also defiled (*kliṣṭa*). It is not subsumed under the five views; rather, it is simply defiled wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, it is explained as being subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). This differs from the "unexpounded points" (*avyākṛtavastu*), which are subsumed under the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
As for his statement that "impermanence" means "annihilation," the former interpretation is superior; it is not said that a single portion [of this view] extends to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the sixteen aspects of the "existent" (*sat-lakṣaṇa*): the first four views are established based on three [other] views: (1) the soul is identical to the body; (2) the soul is different from the body;
(3) this [soul] is the self, all-pervading, non-dual, undifferentiated, and without deficiency. This is based on the second...

The first [view] establishes the first self as "possessing form" (rūpin) and "possessing perception after death" (saṃjñin); because it takes the self to be form, it is called "possessing form," and because it grasps the characteristics of phenomena, it is called "possessing perception.

This applies to the entirety of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), a portion of the form realm (rūpadhātu)—excluding the heaven of non-perception (asaṃjñisattva)—and those who assert that the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) possesses form;
this [view] also exists in those [three] aforementioned formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti). This is "possessing perception."
Therefore, it does not exist in the latter [station]; because it relies on the second view, the second self is established.

This is because one clings to the formless aggregates as being the self and so forth, maintaining that there is perception after death in the formless realm. Its explanation of the name and other details should be understood as before.
This exists from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness, excluding the heaven of non-perception; it is established based on the third view.

Third: "I am both with form and without form; after death, I possess perception," and so forth, extensively explained as being entirely within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and so forth. Fourth: "I am neither with form nor without form;
after death, I possess perception. This negates the third [view] and has no separate basis in terms of views. Thus, these four types are either based on...

Vitarka and vicāra may arise based on either the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) or the [lower] dhyānas; furthermore, the next four views include: (1) the view that "I am finite," which, after death, holds that there is a perception [of such a self].

This includes the case where one grasps form (*rūpa*) as the nature of the self and considers it to have limits—such as being within the body or having a specific size—and so forth, as explained at length.
It also includes the case where one grasps non-form (*arūpa*) as the self and likewise considers it to have limits, whether in terms of its basis (*āśraya*) or its object (*ālambana*).

Therefore, within the entirety of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), a portion of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), as previously described, there are two types of grasping at a self as infinite:
either after death one possesses perception, or one grasps form as the self as being omnipresent.
That which is not known by this [grasping] is all asserted to exist; it is not that what is seen can know the infinite three-thousandfold world system and so forth.

Because of its limited extent, the following cases are explained by analogy: one who knows but does not know the ultimate limit is said to have "the boundless," which does not mean knowing what is distant.

The rest is as previously stated. Third, those who grasp at a self as both finite and infinite, and who hold that after death there is perception, maintain that the self expands or contracts according to the body;
thus its measure is indeterminate, for the body is immeasurable, and so is the self.

There are also other meanings such as "immeasurable" and so forth, which should be understood by analogy with the above. The four attachments—that the self is neither finite nor infinite—exclude the third [view].
These four arise based on vitarka and vicāra within the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). Next, the four [views] arise based on differences in characteristics:
(1) the self has a single perception; (2) the self has manifold perceptions; (3) the self has limited perceptions; and (4) the self has immeasurable perceptions.
Next are the four views based on feeling: (1) "I am purely happy and shall have perception after death"; (2) "I am purely suffering and shall have perception after death";
(3) "I am both suffering and happy and shall have perception after death"; (4) "I am neither suffering nor happy and shall have perception after death.
One [view] pertains to those in the three lower formless realms, while those with various perceptions pertain to the [higher] formless realms.
In the desire realm and the form realm—excluding the Heaven of Non-conception—those with "limited perception" (parītta-saṃjñin) grasp limited forms as "I," as "mine," and as "I am united with that";

this is called limited perception. In the desire realm and the form realm—excluding the Heaven of Non-conception—and as previously stated for the formless realm, those with "immeasurable perception" (apramāṇa-saṃjñin) grasp immeasurable forms as "I," as "mine," and so forth, as previously described.

It is taught at length, as in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts, that these four types of attainment involving vitarka and vicāra can all arise for one who possesses exclusively pleasure and perception—
this applies to the first three dhyānas, and so forth— and for one who possesses exclusively suffering and perception,
which occurs in the intermediate state of hell; and for one who possesses both suffering and pleasure and perception, which occurs among animals.
In the realm of ghosts (*preta*), among humans, and among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those who possess perception (*saṃjñin*) experience neither suffering nor pleasure.

From the fourth dhyāna upward, within the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) where vitarka and vicāra have ceased, it is possible for the eight views regarding non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) to arise. Regarding these eight views, there are four concerning form (*rūpa*) and four concerning the finite (*antavān*).
As for the four concerning form: first, one holds that "I possess form" and that after death there is no perception, grasping form as the self (*ātman*).
1. Having attained the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and seeing others attain that concentration and be reborn there, one forms such a conception:
"I am formless; after death, I shall be without perception," and clings to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as the self. This is explained at length, up to: 2.
Clinging to the self as being both with form and without form, and after death being without perception, one clings to both the physical form and the life-faculty as the self. And so forth.
Among these two, one gives rise to the notion of a self (*ātman*), and so forth, as explained at length regarding the four types of grasping.

[The view that] the self is neither material nor immaterial and that there is no perception after death excludes the third [view]. There is no separate entity [therein], and both *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) can arise.

Regarding the four [views] such as "having limits" (*antavān*) and so forth: first, one grasps that the self has limits and that there is no perception after death, taking form (*rūpa*) as [the basis].
1. Grasping at the self as being limited and small, such as attaining the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and so forth, as explained at length; 2.

Grasping at the self as being infinite, grasping that after death there is no perception, grasping form as the self, and grasping it as pervasive throughout all places, and so forth, as explained at length; 3.
Grasping at the self as both limited and infinite, grasping that after death there is no perception, grasping form as the self, and grasping it as either contracted or...

Expanding upon this, it is explained at length that among the four types of grasping, one does not hold the self to be either finite or infinite, nor does one hold that there is no perception after death—this refutes the third [view].
Regarding the attainment of meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*), both vitarka and vicāra are capable of arising.

As for the eight [types of views], they consist of the four regarding form (*rūpin*) and so forth, and the four regarding being finite and so forth. One grasps that the self possesses form and that, after death, there is neither perception nor non-perception.
Regarding form as the self, some sentient beings enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; because their perception is not clear, they form such an attachment:
"It is merely through vitarka and vicāra, and not through the attainment of meditative concentration," and so forth, as explained at length.

Regarding the two attachments to the self as being formless after death, as previously stated, they attach to the formless aggregates as the self and so forth, entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception with unclear perception.

Because [this] is understood, it is stated as follows: "up to and including the detailed explanation that even in the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), vitarka and vicāra may arise; there are three types of grasping:
the grasping that 'I have both form and no form,' the grasping after death as before, and the grasping that 'form and no-form are the self.
When sentient beings perceive with unclear ideation, they form such a grasping; this applies only to those possessing vitarka and vicāra," and so forth, up to the detailed explanation.
The four views that the self is neither material nor immaterial after death are refuted as before.
Regarding the third set, the four views concerning having limits and so forth: first, the view that the self has limits after death;
up to the fourth, the view that the self is neither limited nor limitless after death. As with the case of being neither percipient nor non-percipient...
All of these grasp at the formless as "self" and have attained the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; thus, such grasping is possible.
First, because that absorption is actually of short duration, they grasp the self as having limits by taking each individual aggregate as their object.
Second, because that absorption lasts for a long period of time, they grasp it by taking the four aggregates collectively as their object.
Regarding the grasping at a self as infinite, there are three reasons: because its duration is fixed as either short or long; because one takes each individual aggregate (*skandha*) to be the self;
or because one takes the aggregates collectively to be the self. Thus, the third position is established. The fourth [position] is the negation of the third, as it is taught.

The aforementioned eternalist views comprise seven types of annihilationist theories (*ucchedavāda*): first, the view that the self possesses form and is composed of the gross four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

The view that there is absolute annihilation after death—that the body ceases to exist after death—is held because one perceives that whether it be one's own self or the self of another, both are composed of coarse primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives, and thus perish utterly after death. This present body is seen to arise from a previous birth, and likewise, another body is seen to arise later;
both cases are to be understood according to this principle. Furthermore, for these two types of selves, there is annihilation after death for the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
1. The self that ceases upon death in the heavens of the form realm; 2. the self that ceases upon death in the sphere of infinite space; 3.
the self that ceases upon death in the sphere of infinite consciousness; 4. the self that ceases upon death in the sphere of nothingness; 5.
the self that ceases upon death in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Among these, the latter four constitute attachments.

Because each respective stage (*bhūmi*) constitutes the pinnacle of birth and death, there is perception (*saṃjñā*); everything below that is designated as the "subsequent limit" (*aparānta*) because it is based on what follows after death.
Question: For what reason are the distinct stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) not mentioned, while the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is said to have two and the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) four?
Answer: To speak according to the actual reality, each individual stage and location has its own discourse on cessation; however, that...

This [view] reckons that the formless and formless realms are difficult to achieve through the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of meditative concentration; yet if that concentration were to arise, it would necessarily be a preparatory application.

Since no further dharmas of a higher stage are perceived, one separately reckons the cessation of the formal realm (*rūpadhātu*) to be easy to initiate through preparatory application and perceivable.
However, the dharmas of subsequent stages cannot be separately reckoned as cessation; this is merely based on...
In summary, these are explained as the basis for annihilationism; in reality, however, each stage [of existence] possesses it.

Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because there are distinctions between the human and celestial destinies (*gati*), they are discussed separately. In truth, at every location, annihilationism arises individually.

Altogether, these are subsumed under the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Among them, there are forty-seven views subsumed under the view of wrongness (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and fifteen views regarding the two types of causelessness.

First, one who has passed away from the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) and is reborn here attains the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), yet is unable to remember all the stages prior to the mind that emerged [from non-conception].
Consequently, they cling to the notion that "I did not previously exist," and thus conclude that all phenomena arise as if I likewise arose having been entirely non-existent in the past;
they further cling to the view that the self and the world arise without cause. Second.
Due to vitarka and vicāra, they do not remember their previous lives and thus give rise to the attachment that [existence] arises without cause, and so forth, as explained at length.
These two views arise from two factors: false vitarka and vicāra pertaining to the Heaven of Non-perception (asaṃjñisattva). Question:
Why is it said here that there are only these two types of "no-cause" [views], when there are also those who do not know [the realms] from the Desire Realm up to the Fourth Dhyāna?

If one were to argue that the preceding many bodies must be reckoned as causeless, the answer is that, according to reality, there is indeed a ground-to-ground ignorance regarding the origin from which causes arise.

Those who cling to the notion of causelessness merely rely on their *pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna* (knowledge of recollecting former abodes) regarding those who have passed away from the *asaṃjñi-sattva* realm; thus, they speak only of one instance.

Furthermore, if one traces back a single lifetime to the point before the mind emerges from the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi*), that subtle stage is difficult to perceive; therefore, they reckon it to be non-existent.
Because the causes from other stages that arose previously are coarse and easy to perceive, one does not conceive of them as being without cause. Regarding the four views of having limits:
first, by means of the divine eye, one sees downward only as far as the Avīci Hell and upward only as far as the Heaven of the First Dhyāna;
perceiving that the self completely pervades all within this range, one then forms the thought: "Beyond this there must be a self, for my self ought to be [present there]."
Because one sees [the world], one knows it has limits. Based on those two meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), one produces the pure divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and sees horizontally without limit;

because one clings to a self as all-pervading, one clings to it as being limitless. Thirdly, by means of the divine eye and the supernormal power of moving through space (*ṛddhividhi*), one sees below and above—just as when one moves the body horizontally from near to far, no boundary is reached—and thus one gives rise to the perception of limits regarding the vertical directions.
The fourth, "the perception of the infinite arising from the side," excludes the third [view]: that the self and the world cannot be definitively described as either finite or infinite.

Nevertheless, it is definitively established that they exist, and so forth, as explained at length. Although these four perceptions take the present as their object and depend upon the future, they are called "perceptions of the prior limit" (*pūrvānta*) because they are all capable of recollecting the kalpas of formation and destruction; thus, they are designated as the four [perceptions] of the prior limit.

Regarding "death through evasive equivocation": one who does not die is called a "god" (*deva*), and because the long-lived gods are eternal, non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) cling to them as being permanent and immortal.

Because he answered regarding the immortality of the gods without confusion when questioned, he was later reborn in that heaven; now, to disparage that [attainment] is called "evasive equivocation. [He says:
"In a single thought-moment, I do not know whether it is wholesome or unwholesome," and so forth; when there are further questions, he cannot provide a definitive answer.
He replied: "If I were to give a definitive answer, it would constitute a false awakening; fearing false speech, I said that I should not explain all the secret meanings of the heavens.
Furthermore, I thought twice: 'I do not know [the distinction between] wholesome and unwholesome, etc. When someone asks me a question, I cannot give a definitive answer.
If I were to give a definitive answer, it would constitute a wrong view; fearing wrong views, I acted in this way."
Regarding the three recollections mentioned previously, if I were not truthful when answering their questions, they might cross-examine me and I would be unable to know the answer;
through such ignorance, I would face the fear of being unable to be reborn in the heavens, as explained at length previously regarding the four recollections.
Furthermore, because my nature is dull and inferior, I am incapable of composing evasive or confused speech, yet there are those who question me.
Regarding the question "Is there a future life?", one should pose it back to them: "What do you assert?

Whether they say "it exists," "it does not exist," "both," or "neither," because they are terrified of and deluded by these four positions, this [speculation] regarding the future is also termed the "prior limit" (*pūrvānta*).

Furthermore, the four [types of views] that operate in the present all take as their object the teachings previously heard; thus, they are all subsumed under the "prior limit. These four [views] rely on the fear of falsehood.
Regarding those of wrong view, ignorance, and dullness who falsely claim to have attained *pañca-dṛṣṭa-dharma-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa in the present life), there are five [types]:
first, seeing that one currently experiences the fivefold sensual pleasures of humans and devas, they claim to have attained nirvāṇa;

second, being weary of the five desires, they dwell in the first dhyāna and take this to be nirvāṇa, perceiving it as pleasure arising within their own bodies; third, seeing others currently dwelling in meditative concentration... [and so forth].
The following points should be understood accordingly: 1. Because of aversion to vitarka and vicāra, one currently dwells in the second dhyāna, taking it to be nirvāṇa. 2.
Because of aversion to vitarka, vicāra, and prīti, one currently dwells in the third dhyāna, taking it to be nirvāṇa. 3.

Because of aversion to all desires up to and including inhalation and exhalation, one currently dwells in the fourth dhyāna, taking it to be nirvāṇa. These are called "waiting for the past" because they depend upon what has already occurred.

Regarding the future limit (*aparānta*): because this [view] holds that since there is pleasure in the present, there will likewise be pleasure in the future, it subsumes the present pleasure within the future limit;
by taking the future pleasure as primary, it is collectively termed "pertaining to the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma*).

However, one does not conceive of *nirvāṇa* in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) because the joy and satisfaction there are so subtle that they do not equal those of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); therefore, this [discussion] for now relies on the full scope of the [form] stages.
According to the actual method of practice, among the formless realms and the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are those who each conceive of their respective states as *nirvāṇa*.
While the former [view] distinguishes between the cessation of humans and devas, this present *nirvāṇa* establishes humans and devas together.

Because that [former view] arises based on a self (*ātman*) and subsequently conceives of cessation, it is included here as a collective conception of *nirvāṇa*; thus, they are combined. All of these do not rely directly [on the truth].

Because they arise from the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and are subsumed under false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), these various views concerning the past (*pūrvānta*) and the future (*aparānta*) are, by their essential nature (*svabhāva*), subsumed under two views.
However, if one considers them in terms of their associated factors (*parivāra*), they are subsumed under the five views;

for it is stated in the *Aṣṭasaptati* that the sixty-two types of evil speculative views (*dṛṣṭigata*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) arise with the view of a real body as their root. Thus, [they are rooted in] *satkāya*.

Because it is included among the retinue [of views] by virtue of being based on the *jātaka* [birth stories], the *Pañcāśatka* states fifty-eight [types]. Regarding "view-grasping" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*):

among the sixty-two types of speculative views (*dṛṣṭigata*), each is individually reckoned as supreme, as foremost, and so forth, up to the point that one thinks it can lead to liberation and deliverance;
this is called view-grasping. Thus, we know that view-grasping is also included within the retinue, because it arises by taking those [views] as its object. Furthermore...

Regarding "clinging to precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): it refers to whatever precepts or prohibitions one undertakes that accord with *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*, as well as the attendants of *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* and the teachings associated with them;
to falsely conceive of these as superior, up to the point of being able to attain liberation and deliverance—this is called clinging to precepts.
Thus, one should know that clinging to precepts is also included among the attendants, because it arises from a causal transformation. For this reason, the treatise answers [the objection] with "or."

Second, regarding the fifty-eight views mentioned in the *Śāstra* as being either two or all [sixty-two], these are all conceptually arisen (*vikalpita*) and are abandoned solely by the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*).

Now, following the sequence of the text, I shall first list their names. Their delusion regarding the truths and their bases arises according to whether they are associated with meditative concentration (*samāhita*) or distraction (*asamāhita*), and their objects belong to either one’s own realm or another realm, as previously explained.
However, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the twenty-fold view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) pertains to the body.
The sixty-two [views] based on the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and their temporal distinctions are not elucidated here;
therefore, they are not described now. *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Three.
*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Four, composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of Daci’en Monastery.
Question: Regarding the indeterminate matters (*avyākṛta-vastu*) [up to] "or all."

The commentary states: In the second question-and-answer section of the treatise, fourteen "unanswerable matters" (*avyākṛta*) are discussed, and sixty-four reasons are given for why they cannot be answered.
First, because [the object] does not exist; that is to say, there may be a question such as: "Is the self different from or non-different from the aggregates?
Second, because it would lead to what is meaningless; as stated in the *Śāṇavāsika-śākhā-śāstra-sūtra* (the Sūtra on the Simile of the Śāṇa Leaf): "I... [and so forth].
The Dharma that has been taught is such that any untaught portion of it cannot lead to meaningful benefit; furthermore, it is profound in three ways.
For instance, if one were to ask, "Do I exist? this should not be answered, lest they grasp at a self as being either identical to or distinct from the aggregates.
Likewise, if one asks, "Does the self not exist? this also should not be answered, lest they cause harm to the conventional designation of a person (*pudgala*).

The reduction of attachments regarding whether the Tathāgata exists or does not exist after death and so forth all arise from the fact that these four points are profoundly deep and undeclared by nature.
When asked, "Is True Suchness (tathatā) truly different or not different from all phenomena? this is an undeclared matter;
because the nature of phenomena is such that it cannot be definitively fixed, to all such questions one should respond by saying only: "It is simply..."
The Buddha stated that there are four reasons why these [fourteen] indeterminate matters are not to be declared:
because they involve proclaiming what is false, because they are irrational, because they lead to what is meaningless, and because they are the basis for contentious debate.

Since these fourteen types of indeterminate matters do not exist within the first four [of the four unanswerable questions], they are not to be declared. Furthermore, among the latter four [reasons], the first two are not applicable.
Furthermore, it is stated in various places that there are four ways of answering questions:

(1) answering categorically (*ekāṃśa-vyākaraṇa*), (2) answering by analysis (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*), (3) answering with a counter-question (*paripṛcchā-vyākaraṇa*), and (4) answering by setting aside (*sthāpanīya-vyākaraṇa*). How is the fourteenth [point] included within this "answering by setting aside"?
Why is it further called "unanswerable" (*avyākṛta*)? It is simply said that the Buddha declared this to be unanswerable; it does not mean that he failed to provide an answer.
That which is called "inexplicable" (avyākṛta) refers to those matters that should be set aside;

this is known as the "setting aside" (sthāpanīya) method of answering, as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (35), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (39), and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (19). Regarding the fourteen inexplicable points (*caturdaśāvyākṛtavastūni*), they are:
1. whether both the self and the world are eternal; 2. whether they are impermanent; 3. whether they are both eternal and [impermanent]; and so forth.
1. Impermanence; 2. Neither permanence nor impermanence; 3. The self and the world are finite;
4. Infinite; 5. Both finite and infinite; 6. Neither finite nor infinite; 7. The Tathāgata exists after death; 8. Does not exist; 9.
Both exists and does not exist; 10. Neither exists nor does not exist.
Thirteenth, that which has the self as its life-principle is identical with the body; fourteenth, that which has the self as its life-principle is distinct from the body.

Among these, "eternal" and so forth constitute the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), while "impermanent" and so forth constitute the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Because one calculates that the self will be reborn, or because one calculates that it will not exist hereafter, all four—beginning with "having limits" (*antavān*)—are false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Since they do not calculate [the self] as being either eternal or annihilated, the views such as "there is [a self] after death" are views of eternalism, whereas "it does not exist" is not.
The view that the body and the self (*ātman*) are distinct is the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); the view that the body and the self are one is the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).
The view of nihilism regarding the self is the view that "the self and the body are distinct," because [it holds] that although the body dies, the self does not perish;

the view of eternalism is the opposite of this. Within this context, the view of eternalism encompasses three views in their entirety and a portion of four views, while the view of nihilism likewise [encompasses a portion of four].

It encompasses three views in their entirety and a portion of four views; thus, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) subsumes ten views in total, while false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) encompass four views in their entirety.
The view of self and what belongs to self (*ātmātmīyadṛṣṭi*) subsumes [the remaining] views. Now, my intention in asking is this:

since the view of self arises subsequent to the question of whether the self is eternal or annihilated after death, it constitutes a view of extremes; I am not merely asking about the existence or non-existence of the self after death, but rather [the nature of that self].

Because they are views, the answer is that their intrinsic nature is subsumed under two views: because they arise based on the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because they grasp at a self as supreme, and because they conform to the grasping for precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
For this reason, the remaining three views are all subsumed as their attendants.
If they mutually support one another, all five views are attendants.
"Second, because of the retinue (*parivāra*). The commentary states:

This master of the treatise provides a general explanation of the preceding answer as previously stated: that which is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and includes itself is called "inclusion by essential nature" (*svabhāva-saṃgraha*);
that which mutually supports and gives rise [to others] is called "inclusion by retinue" (*parivāra-saṃgraha*). Otherwise, there would be only three types of inclusion for the retinue.
Question: Regarding the Bhagavat’s [statement] up to "denouncing the conception of a self" (*ātma-grāha*).
The commentary states: This third section explains the scriptural passage denouncing the self.

Although the Buddha denounces the self across all the various sūtras, what is specifically questioned here is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Abhidharma-sūtra; that is, it refers to the characteristic as a formal mark, for a formal mark is not the characteristic of a self.
Regarding the phrase "named 'defamation by characteristics,'" the five types of characteristics refer to the five mentioned previously, such as "difference" and so forth.

Although these five types of characteristics are briefly stated in the sūtras, their underlying causes have not been extensively explained; therefore, by means of this inquiry, the intent of the sūtra is sought to be revealed.
Answer: Because of [the resulting] faults. The commentary states:
There are two parts to the answer; first, a general summary that enumerates the names of the five faults, and second, a detailed specific explanation that establishes the five characteristics.
For now, we provide the general answer: for one who clings to a self through observation, there are five logical faults, by which the world is largely [afflicted].

Because the five aspects of disparaging what has been accepted (*parigraha*) signify the sense of "stubborn attachment" (*abhiniveśa*) or the sense of "appropriating" (*parigraha*), they refer to the faults of [clinging to] distinct characteristics up to liberation. Commentary:

This enumeration of the five names appears in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stages of Yoga Practice), fascicle 6 and fascicle 64, as well as in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Exposition of the Noble Words), chapter 10, as the five types of grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).

There are four [positions]: first, that it is identical to the aggregates (*skandha*); second, that it is distinct from the aggregates yet abides within them; third, that it is distinct from the aggregates and abides in phenomena separate from the aggregates;

fourth, that it is distinct from the aggregates, does not abide within the aggregates, and does not abide in what is distinct from the aggregates, yet there are no aggregates, as all phenomena of the aggregates are entirely non-corresponding.
These refute the first three [positions]; thus, those first three positions are lost.

This refutes the fourth thesis; namely, that the latter two faults will follow. This should be understood as occurring below. The main text of the treatise follows, and below that is the Master’s commentary.
[It addresses] the fault of the characteristic of difference, because it differs from the characteristic of the self (*ātman*).
The commentary states: All those [proponents] who maintain a self (ātman) assert that it is eternal, unitary, and substantially existent.

However, because the substance of the aggregates (skandhas) is neither eternal nor unitary, nor is it distinct [from them], the self as identical to the aggregates must differ from the characteristics of a self. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* establishes this through inference (*anumāna*), stating:

"Your self as identical to the aggregates must not be eternal or unitary, because you admit it is identical to the aggregates, just like the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the internal [aggregates]...
Form (*rūpa*) is certainly not a real self because it possesses resistance (*sapratigha*), just like external forms;

mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are also not a real self because they do not continue uninterruptedly and depend upon various conditions, just like sound, lightning, light, and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*);

other forms that are not faculties are also not a real self because they lack the nature of cognition (*buddhi*), just like space (*ākāśa*) and so forth. This section summarizes the meaning of the text.

However, since it is merely stated that form and so forth are not the essence of the self and are different from the characteristics of the self, without separately explaining the reason for this difference, they should be refuted by the same general and specific arguments as before.
As for the fault of impermanence: [it follows that] the self would have to be impermanent.
The commentary states: In this regard, the *Yogācārabhūmi* sets forth two challenges: if [the self] were to abide by means of the aggregates (*skandha*), it would be identical to impermanence;

yet, an impermanent entity distinct from the aggregates cannot be found. Furthermore, if the essence of the self were eternal while merely residing within the aggregates, then all transformations—such as the transition between various realms of existence (*gati*) and future changes, as well as the shifts in suffering and pleasure—would be impossible in the present.
Therefore, in this case, there is only the initial objection regarding impermanence; within that, there is only the fault of losing the basis.
Since the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which serve as the basis, are by nature impermanent, the self (*ātman*) must also be so. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
The self you postulate must be impermanent, because it is admitted to depend upon the aggregates, just like a jar or a bowl.
Why is this so? It is said: This meaning is difficult to explain in detail; thus, it is addressed through further inquiry and re-explanation.
For there can be no supported [subject] in the absence of a support.

The commentary states: It is not the case that while the substance of the aggregates (*skandha*) which serve as the basis is impermanent, the self (*ātman*) which depends upon them possesses the characteristic of permanence;

nor is it the case that although the substance of what is "mine" (*ātmīya*) as my basis has already ceased—as in the case of a corpse or a state of unconsciousness—the self that depends upon it remains eternally existent.

If this were so, the self would not be residing in the aggregates. Since it would be constantly dependent [upon them], its arising and ceasing would be identical [to those of the aggregates]. Therefore, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
At the stage of final death and cessation, the self should likewise follow impermanence because its basis, the aggregates, have perished— just like a broken jar or pot—
and because it lacks sovereignty, being unable to function with independent mastery.

The commentary states: One who clings to a self as distinct from the aggregates and residing within them—since such a self would have no connection or involvement with the aggregates and so forth—would consequently lack mastery over the aggregates.
Therefore, one should not regard the self as having form and other qualities.

Furthermore, you should not regard the self as possessing non-mastery over the aggregates, because it does not reside in them, just like space and other such things; nor should one regard the self [as being identical to the aggregates].
Because form and so forth lack self-mastery, they are like the son of a barren woman; as the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"If even a characteristic apart from the aggregates cannot be found, how much less can it be that which I dwell in?

It is like saying, "I truly know that the son of a barren woman has a garland of empty flowers bound upon his head"; since the head itself does not exist, the garland likewise has no basis for support.
Since [the aggregates] do not exist, the self-substance also does not exist;
for there would be the fault of being bodiless, and thus it should be without a body.
The commentary states: Regarding that fourth position, which conceives the self as distinct from the aggregates—neither abiding within the aggregates nor existing outside of them—since...
In that case, you would possess no bodily form (*vigraha*), because you are devoid of bodily form by virtue of being separated from the aggregates (*skandha*).

Consequently, the nature of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), such as good and evil, as well as the enjoyment of objects, would all be non-existent. Although there is a longing for the aggregates, since this [bodily] characteristic is absent, the same applies to the four aggregates beginning with the body.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: "Your 'self' (*ātman*) must be devoid of bodily form, as it is separated from the aggregates."
Because [the self] is admitted to be separate from the aggregates, it would be like a rabbit’s horn and so forth; therefore, the treatise refutes this, stating:
"The self does not exist as something distinct and in a different location apart from form and the other aggregates. Why is this? Because it cannot be apprehended.
The commentary states: Even the body, which you grasp as the self, cannot be found; yet to conceive of a self apart from the body is logically untenable.
Since there is no body, what is this "self"? Your "self" must not be a self, because it lacks the characteristics of a body, just like space and so forth.
"Because [the self] would not need to exert effort [to attain liberation], it would follow that it is already liberated.
The commentary states: The preceding fourth clause directly refutes the self; if this clause were absent, it would result in the fallacy of establishing the existence of a self.

Even if such a false conceptualization and attachment existed—claiming that the characteristic of a self exists apart from the aggregates—the principle would still not hold, for a self devoid of aggregates cannot exist.
Liberation would be achieved without the need for diligent effort.
Why is this? (Up to: "Liberation occurs spontaneously. The commentary states:
"I was not liberated because I was originally bound by the body; since I no longer have the bondage of a body, liberation occurs spontaneously."

Because liberation does not depend on strenuous effort to seek it, as one is already released from bondage; and because the self (*ātman*) is not associated with the aggregates (*skandha*), the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
"You have not yet abandoned bondage, yet the self must also be established as liberated, because it lacks bodily bondage, just like one who is already liberated.
Although this [text] enumerates four types of grasping (*grāha*) regarding the self and its yoga, even when formulated as five inquiries, it still states that there is nothing other than these.

Regarding these views, they merely refute the non-Buddhists and do not negate the Hīnayāna; as stated in the second chapter of the *Śata-śāstra* and the first chapter on Consciousness-Only, there are three types of such views:
first, those within the four [types] concerning the aggregates themselves; second, those apart from the aggregates, which comprise the latter three types of views;

and third, those that are neither identical to nor separate from the aggregates—whether their essence is not the aggregates or whether they abide within the aggregates—which are also included in the first category.
The schools of the Vātsīputrīyas and others do not include [the self] within the four [categories]; they assert a self that is identical with the aggregates (*skandha*).

Regarding this self that abides in the aggregates, the "Lord of Beasts" (Śiva) and the shameless ones (Cārvākas) maintain that it abides in phenomena both distinct from and simultaneous with the aggregates.

The Sāṃkhyas and others assert [a self] as described in detail in works such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, where their tenets are extensively refuted. Many ancient masters have stated that these include the Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Nirgrantha, and Jaina schools.

I have already refuted this in the *Catuḥśataka-śāstra-vibhāṣā* and other works; furthermore, as there is no authoritative statement [to the contrary], it cannot be cited as a valid account. For now, I shall follow our own school’s tenets.
Question: Among the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), up to how many are views of "mine" (*mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*)?
The commentary states: This fourth section concerns the distinction between "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to self" (*ātmīya*). Within it, there are two parts:

first, a general inquiry and response regarding the number of instances of "self" and "what belongs to self"; second, a specific inquiry and response regarding the number of instances of "what belongs to self. Consequently, the general inquiry asks: "In each and every aggregate (*skandha*), one calculates four [factors]:
(1) this is the self; (2) I possess [it]; (3) it belongs to me; and (4) the self exists within it. Thus is the general [inquiry].
These constitute twenty propositions regarding how many [of these aggregates] are viewed as "I" and how many are viewed as "mine.

In this current treatise, the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are each analyzed into four propositions; likewise, the same applies to the four propositions for the other three aggregates.
For what reason do they become twenty propositions? Because they arise from the non-discrimination of the basis upon which discrimination operates toward the aggregates, they constitute twenty.

"Discrimination" refers to the activity of interpreting meanings; "activity" refers to the two types of modes of activity, namely "self" and "mine. "Object-condition" refers to the two types of modes of activity as object-conditions;

since both types of modes of activity take the aggregates (*skandhas*) as their objects—specifically, that which is "mine" is the view of "mine"—this now explains how the two types of modes of activity, the views of "self" and "mine," each and every one of them, take the various aggregates as their objects through repeated engagement.
I do not provide a separate explanation for this "view of what belongs to me" (*mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*), because all views of what belongs to me arise subsequent to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*);
since the view of self is the root, it does not arise after the view of what belongs to me.
For example, when one conceives of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as "I," "mine," or "I am within it"—these three [conceptions] regarding what belongs to me—[do not arise independently].
Regarding the statement that from which aggregates the view of self arises, it is said in general that [the self] is identical with one aggregate;
since there are five aggregates and four [types of views] for each, they constitute twenty.
Answer: ...is what is seen as "mine."

The commentary states: The Master of the Treatise briefly answers [the objection] regarding the frequent occurrence of "I" and "mine. Below, the commentator clarifies the distinction between these two, stating:
"To reckon form as 'I'... [up to] ...to view it as 'mine'."

The commentary states: Regarding these four propositions for each of the five aggregates, the first proposition in every case is the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), while the remaining three propositions are all views of what belongs to the self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).

Since the grasping at a self is singular, there is no need to pose a question regarding it; however, because views of what belongs to the self are manifold, one should inquire about their explanation.
"For what reason are there fifteen [instances] of 'this is mine' that I perceive?

The commentary states: This is the second question in the root treatise: "For what reason, when the number of 'mine' is one and each aggregate (*skandha*) is also one, are there fifteen instances of the perception 'this is mine'?"
"Because it corresponds to a self" (up to) "because it is not separate from what belongs to a self.
The commentary states: The Master briefly answers that the essence of the self is one and permanent, while each aggregate (*skandha*) is singular and possesses many types of attributes;

thus, fifteen [conceptions] are established. Since each individual aggregate has three [aspects], these are collectively explained as the sentient beings' conceptions of a self regarding the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
There are five views of self, yet it is not the case that a single sentient being conceives of five selves or five things belonging to a self;
for otherwise, a single sentient being could be established as many.
As for the "belonging to a self" associated with these [views], it is because [the sūtra] states that they exist.
The commentary states: The following is the Master’s explanation of the characteristic of "mine" (*ātmīya*).

Regarding the phrase "I have aggregates" (*ātmanaḥ santi skandhāḥ*) within the initial response, it refers to a state of non-opposition and conformity; because the self and the aggregates are not opposed but are mutually conforming, those aggregates are said to be "mine.
The statement "I have form" (*rūpavān asmi*) up to "I have consciousness" (*vijñānavān asmi*) clarifies that "I" possesses the aggregates.
Pervading the five aggregates, they give rise to the five propositions; because the self is associated with them, it is said that "they exist [in the self].
This is established through the meaning of association, just as necklaces and the like do not contradict the self.
"Following and revolving as 'mine' (yāvad mama-īyam)" means: because it is mine. The commentary states:
this refers to the phrase "the aggregates belong to me" within the first answer. "Following" (anuvartana) means conforming; "revolving" (vartana) means moving.

Because the aggregates follow me in matters such as abandoning or employing them, they are called "following and revolving. Because they are like servants and so forth, they are said to "belong to me."
The phrase "form belongs to us" (*rūpam asmākam*) clarifies that by taking the aggregates as its universal object, it establishes five propositions.
The phrase "if it [the mind] proceeds by means of these" correctly explains the meaning of the mind's conformity to and belonging to the self. To establish this through an analogy, it says:
"Just as when a servant is released from the sovereign power of a lord, he is then employed by another; thus, in the world, it is said that he has been 'abandoned' by the former."
The servant is the subject of the master; therefore, because the objects formerly employed by him were "mine," the aggregates are likewise so now.

Because [the self] abandons them, all activities cease; because [the self] employs them, all activities are performed. Since they follow the movement of the self and are subsumed within it, they constitute "that which belongs to me" (ātmīya).
"Those who do not depart from what belongs to the self" (up to) "because they follow [it].
The commentary states: This refers to the phrase "the self is within the aggregates" in the first response. "Not departing" means being constantly present;

because it permanently dwells within the aggregates, it is called "not departing. The phrase "the self is in form, etc. demonstrates that the self is omnipresent throughout the aggregates, thus forming five [positions].
Regarding the phrase "they conceive of the referents of those [aggregates] as real self and so forth," this correctly explains the meaning of "not being separate from the self" within them.
Because the self constantly and pervasively accompanies and never abandons the substance of the aggregates, it is called "mine" (*ātmīya*), just like a cave or a dwelling.
This "mine" is subsumed under the aforementioned three phrases, which correspond respectively to "my ornament," "my servant," and "my vessel."

Because one does not separately distinguish the bases from which the notion of "mine" arises, twenty [positions] are established; furthermore, by distinguishing those bases of the notion of "mine," sixty-five propositions are formed.
That is to say: reckoning form as the self, the self as possessing feeling, feeling as belonging to the self, and the self as being within feeling—and so on, up to:
the self as possessing consciousness, consciousness as belonging to the self, and the self as being within consciousness. Thus, the aggregate of form is...
Because one regards the four aggregates as "I" and the form aggregate as "mine," there are twelve views of "mine" for each aggregate, plus five views of "I," making fifteen per aggregate.

Thus, across the five aggregates, this results in sixty-five views of "I. Regarding the sixty-five views of "mine," if one calculates the views of "I" with respect to the aggregates, there are twenty such views;
adding these to the sixty-five views of "mine" regarding the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), [the total is eighty-five].

The [afflictions] that arise from conditions involving conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*)—both those arising from non-conceptualization and those arising from conceptualization—are categorized by the number of their constituent phrases.

Based on this, one should further understand that the number of entities for the views of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) follows the same principle.

Regarding the twenty phrases and so forth, it is explained that all eighty-eight [afflictions] arise from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpita-utpanna*) and are abandoned solely through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). This is because they are constructed from [conceptual] formations.
Because the conception of a living being is not spontaneous, it consists solely of the imputation [of a self] within the aggregates; there is no imputation of a self apart from the aggregates.
Among these conceptions of a self or what belongs to a self, there are fifteen in total, as there is no imputation of the aggregates themselves as the self.
Question: "Is it definitive or not? The commentary states:
This is the fifth [section], clarifying the difficulty of grasping at persons and phenomena based on the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

It is not only this view, but other false views and so forth can also give rise to such grasping; however, because this [view] is fixed, real, and superior, it is specifically mentioned. This is raised as a question.

The same applies to the remaining examples. There are two kinds of objects (*vastu*): first, conditioned and contaminated things; when these serve as the objective condition (*ālambana*), the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) arises.

Second, the essential nature of things (*vastutva*) which includes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this reveals that the view arises through delusion regarding both principle and phenomena. Question:

Regarding the objective conditions of the preceding things, is the perceiving view direct (*pratyakṣa*) or indirect (*parokṣa*) with respect to its object? Answer: It is direct with respect to the latter.
Is the nature of the entity common to both proximate and remote objects, and is it characterized by being fully cognized or not?
Answer: [It extends] up to "the false arising of the cognition of a snake.

The commentary states: Based on the initial question and answer, the entity is indeed the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); because the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) arises by taking the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*) as its object.

Regarding this object as a direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*), the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) does not comprehend it, just as one falsely gives rise to the cognition of a snake upon a rope.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains that the rope is a metaphor for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the snake is a metaphor for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and the cognition is a metaphor for the view of self.

Because the view of self fails to comprehend the dependent nature due to false perception, the subsequent question and answer clarify that the "object" (*vastu*) applies universally, including the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus it is.

Because the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) arises through confusion regarding both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), it fails to comprehend both types of objects—those that are immediate and those that are remote.
This is like the false perception of a snake arising upon a rope;

it is not merely a failure to understand the conventional nature of the rope, but a failure to understand the four real elements as well. Thus, the view of self arises. (From the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*)
In the commentary below the text, Master Shi explains that regarding phenomena, one does not fall into the false view of a self. The sub-commentary states:

Before Master Shi explains the metaphors of the "indefinitive meaning" (neyārtha), he first reverses them to demonstrate that if one has definitive understanding of the object, [the metaphors do not apply].

If one relies on the first fact, the true nature (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) is the very essence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); it is called "true nature" in contrast to that which is grasped [as real].
If one relies on the latter fact, the true nature is the pervasive existence and non-existence as the objective sphere (*ālambana*).
If one can definitively realize the true nature regarding these two objects of perception, then false views of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) should likewise not arise; this is according to reality.

Regarding the knowledge [of the rope], the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the cognition which perceives a snake in a rope is abandoned when the rope is clearly understood; this is because there is no evidence for seeing that [snake].

When one perceives its constituent parts, it is known that the cognition of the snake was erroneous. Within this, there is a further meaning: based on the cognition of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the cognition of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is discarded;

based on the cognition of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the cognition of the dependent nature is discarded. These two cognitions that are discarded are the two natures, which are precisely what is signified by their respective names.
Since awakening requires the vision of *tathatā* (suchness) in order to bring practice to completion, there is a sense in which both types of awakening are objects of grasping.

The awakening that dispels the awakening [itself] as an object of grasping is like the teaching on "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), which dispels the awakening to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). This is because the grasped and the grasper within the consciousness that is clung to are dispelled sequentially;
otherwise, the dependent nature would be identical to the grasped nature, and its essence would likewise be non-existent, as the manner of their dispelling and severance would be the same.
The category of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) would likewise fail to be established.
This is like a person [who, upon seeing a rope] gives rise to the misconception that it is a snake.
[The commentary states: "The preceding dharma and its analogy are established; the text is easy to understand. Regarding the latter three natures (*trisvabhāva*), they shall be further analyzed."
"Anger" (up to its function). The commentary states:

Regarding the six categories of mental factors (*caitta*), this explains the fifth [category]. Within this, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the ten types of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that are partial;
second, the explanation of the ten types of secondary afflictions that are universal. The former consists solely of provisional designations established based on distinct states (*avasthā*).
The latter [category] also applies to the meaning of actual moments (*kṣaṇa*) when explaining the statement "established as consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

First, the ten [mental factors] such as anger (*krodha*) are merely distinctions of the states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*); the ten [factors] such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) are merely of the nature of outflows (*niṣyanda*) from the afflictions;
therefore, they are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Because this treatise states that they are "parts of a part," they constitute a distinction. In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, both...
Regarding the names: "one part" refers to those that do not possess this one part nor the differentiation of parts, or alternatively, they are divided into three categories.

First, the ten afflictions such as anger (*krodha*) arise individually, and are thus called "minor secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*). Second, the two beginning with lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) pervade all unwholesome states and are thus called "intermediate secondary afflictions.

Third, the eight beginning with restlessness (*auddhatya*) pervade all defiled minds and are thus called "major secondary afflictions" (*mahābhūmika-upakleśa*). The first explanation concerns both their essential nature (*svabhāva*) and their activity (*karman*), as discussed in the treatises.

The subsequent re-explanation of the text following the main body clarifies that the phrase "the Master’s commentary on 'reliance' and 'manifestation,' etc. reveals the objective referent (*ālambana*);
"a portion of hatred" reveals the basis upon which it relies; "having mental anger as its intrinsic nature" reveals its own specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*).

All subsequent points should be understood accordingly without further separate attribution. It is essential that the temporal period and the manifest object be present, and that they be non-beneficial.

The mind perceiving [an object] with anger constitutes *pratigha* (hostility). According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, *pratigha* can also take a momentary past [object] as its cognitive support (*ālambana*).

Therefore, it is designated by way of its temporal aspect as that which directly obstructs the absence of hostility (*apratigha*) when present before one. This point is not explicitly stated here, but all subsequent cases should be understood accordingly.

Specifically, one who harbors hostility frequently initiates the two types of unwholesome karma of body and speech; because it often manifests as bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), it is described as "wielding weapons."

Because it relies upon the arousal of indignation and the wielding of weapons, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (89) states that that which causes the facial expression to become contorted and fierce is called *pratigha* (anger).
It should be understood that *pratigha* and the others [the secondary afflictions] have no distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

The commentary states: This master of the treatise wishes to clarify that the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are for the most part nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*), or exist in dependence upon the characteristics of others;

therefore, he now speaks of them collectively as "nominally established" (*prajñaptitaḥ*). In reality, however, among these there are distinct entities with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which shall be understood below.

Alternatively, the master of the treatise interprets the phrase "a portion of hatred" (*dveṣāmśika*) in the root treatise to clarify that the ten [afflictions] such as anger (*krodha*) are definitely nominal.

Some intentionally make this statement, claiming that all twenty [categories] are not merely conventional existents (*prajñaptisat*); otherwise, it would contradict the explanations in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts.
"Resentment" (*upanāha*) has [the following] as its function.
The commentary states: "Holding a grudge without relinquishing" means taking as an object past evil deeds.
"From this point onward" means following after anger (*krodha*).

The commentary further explains that within the definition of its essential nature, because one does not relinquish evil with anger as the precursor, this [resentment] is established based on its specific state (*avasthā*).
Anger (*krodha*) is slightly distinct [from resentment].
Regarding "the inability to endure" up to "demonstrating acts of benefit," the commentary states that in the section on the function of karma,
one who harbors a grudge is unable to maintain forbearance toward the object previously felt as anger.
Inability to endure the harm inflicted by others—eighty-nine [factors] are mentioned here—and harboring resentment within is what is termed *upanāha* (enmity);
the rest have been explained at length, so I shall not cite them further.
*Pradāśa* (malice) has [the function of] acting as its own activity.

The commentary states: Because this mode of activity (*ākāra*) of concealment (*mrakṣa*) constantly covers over various transgressions, it is called "concealment" (*māyā*). Its nature is to hide committed offenses out of fear of losing profit or reputation.

What is now termed "being raised by others" (*parodghāṭita*) refers to practicing such hiding only when one is challenged; this is because the specific characteristic (*svabhāva*) is revealed at the time the activity increases.
For one who has committed an offense, the object being concealed is manifested; when another person brings forth the name of the offense, it is called "being raised by others."
At that time, this which manifests as the temporal state of concealment is the aspect (*ākāra*).
It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that [the mind] remains concealed until it dwells in peace.
The commentary states: This explains that for one who conceals a previously committed offense, whether proximate or remote, it is the natural law that they experience remorse.
Regarding the view that it is unwholesome (*avyavasthita*) and has a specific meaning: this concealment (*mrakṣa*) is exclusively a part of delusion (*moha*), because this treatise states so;

furthermore, one conceals one’s own transgressions only when one does not fear future suffering. Regarding the view that its nature consists of a portion of both greed (*lobha*) and delusion: fearing the loss of reputation and profit, one conceals one’s own transgressions.
However, the treatise, based on what is coarse and manifest, states that it is only a part of delusion—just as it is said that restlessness (*auddhatya*) is a part of greed.
"Affliction" (vyāpāda) has [the aforementioned] as its essence.

The commentary states: This refers to the mind becoming perverse and recalcitrant when one pursues past evils with resentment and anger at the forefront, encountering adverse conditions in the present;
its function is to produce haughty, violent, and coarse speech, and so forth.
The commentary states: Because one harbors resentment, one frequently generates evil karma and cannot abide in peace; because one stings and bites others, the harm inflicted is deep.
Thus, three types of karma are explained.
As for "arrogant and coarse speech," it pierces the innermost depths of people's hearts.

The commentary states: This explains that because one’s initial actions are lofty yet coarse, violent, evil, vulgar, and foul-mouthed, manifesting such ferocity and obstinacy, they deeply afflict the inner heart;
thus, envy constitutes their karma.

The commentary states: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains that those who sacrifice themselves to the pursuit of fame and profit harbor envy toward the success of others. Now it is said that such minds arise in many people;

however, this text speaks specifically of those who are addicted to gain. Once they harbor such jealousy, upon hearing of or seeing the success of others, they feel deep distress and cannot remain at peace.
Regarding "the stingy person" (up to) "acts as its function":

the commentary states that the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains this as being addicted to wealth and the Dharma such that one is unable to give them away; however, based on the coarse characteristics [of the subject], the addiction to the Dharma is not mentioned here.
Regarding "not abandoning" (up to the point of) "also constantly accumulating":
the commentary states that those who are stingy have minds that are largely base, mean-spirited, and miserly;
they hoard and accumulate things that are not even fit for use, let alone those that are serviceable.
"Deceit (leading to) its function.
The commentary states: This refers to one who is deceitful, harboring ulterior motives and manifesting fraudulent, unreal matters.
Because greed is primary, it serves as the basis for wrong livelihood; because delusion is primary, one fraudulently manifests what is unreal. [This is] stated in the fifty-fifth [treatise].
This is merely a manifestation of delusion that appears unreal; because it arises solely from an increase in delusion, it is explained as being "consciousness-only.

Thus, even though it bears the name of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it functions as deceptive pretension. Attachment to fame is common to both the foolish and the wise, and for brevity’s sake, attachment to improper livelihood is not mentioned here.

There are five types [of such deception]: first, manifesting wonders; second, proclaiming one's own virtues; third, divining good or bad fortune; fourth, raising one's voice to display authority; and fifth...
Exaggerating one's offerings to move the hearts of others is called "wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*) because it arises from greed.
Deceit (*śāṭhya*) has [the aforementioned] as its function.

The commentary states: although the fifty-fifth [mental factor] is said to be a portion of delusion (*moha*) alone because the characteristics of delusion predominate there, in reality, it also depends upon greed.
The designation "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) should be explained according to what precedes it.
[The text continues: "Deviously employing expedient means (upāya) to avoid other matters.
The commentary states: This explains that the aforementioned entity deviously employs expedient means, feigning reverence and respect, hoping that others will love him, while concealing...
