Because *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) is excluded, *vitarka* and *vicāra* both accompany [the primary afflictions] as they are universally present in all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of the seven root afflictions:

*kaukṛtya* (remorse) accompanies only *moha* (delusion), because greed and the others are subtle; the remaining thirty [secondary afflictions] accompany it, as there is no contradiction. Regarding the association with secondary afflictions:

*kaukṛtya* accompanies the latter ten [of the twenty secondary afflictions], while the others each act as the primary factor; the remaining three [root afflictions] may accompany twenty [secondary afflictions], as they are compatible.

Therefore, regarding the three natures of the ninth consciousness (the *vitarka* and *vicāra* of the third stage): they all pertain to the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), because remorse (*kaukṛtya*) also arises within neutral (*avyākṛta*) karma.

Regarding those subsumed under the twelve wholesome factors: one interpretation holds that remorse and sleep (*middha*) are exclusively innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*), because their mental characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are coarse and vulgar, and [in the case of sleep] dull and inferior.

*Vitarka* and *vicāra* pertain to both [innate and applied wholesome states]. Another interpretation holds that remorse and sleep are also applied wholesome states (*prāyogika-kuśala*), occurring during the stages of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*).
Because there are remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*), these are said to be correctly eleven. As for the two that are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):
sleep, vitarka, and vicāra are all comprised within both the defiled and the pure types of indeterminate; remorse (*kaukṛtya*), however, is not defiled, because it is coarse and intense.

There are four types of indeterminate: first, those born of maturation (*vipākaja*); second, the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*); third, the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*); and fourth, those resulting from application (*prāyogika*). Remorse is only of the middle [type].

The two *middhas* (sleep) exclude the fourth [dhyāna], and *vitarka* and *vicāra* (applied and sustained thought) exclude the first; this is explained based on the difference between karma and its resultant maturation (*vipāka*).

Those belonging to the category of adherence to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) and so forth are also of the first type, as they possess all four [mental factors] according to their respective conditions. The twelve [factors] bound to the three realms: *kaukṛtya* (regret) and *middha* (sleep) exist only in the desire realm;
*vitarka* and *vicāra* also extend to the first *dhyāna*, because in the remaining realms and stages, all phenomena are sublime and tranquil. Thus there are ten.

Regarding the third point, the mutual arising of the upper and lower [mental states]: remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) arise in the upper realms, but they certainly do not arise in the lower; whereas applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) arise in both the upper and lower.

This is said based on the majority of cases and is not an exhaustive explanation of the principle, because in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) which includes remorse.

Consequently, when one is born in the upper realms, there may be the arising of remorse directed toward the lower; however, according to the former interpretation, in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), neither [remorse nor the other states] can possibly arise.

Therefore, regarding the fourteen [mental factors] that take both lower and upper levels as objects: the vitarka and vicāra of a lower level can take both lower and upper levels as objects; regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) cannot take an upper level as an object.

There is a view that these two can also take an upper level as an object: regret, because it cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and sleep, because it has previously experienced [objects in a dream]. The latter explanation is considered correct.

Fifteen [factors], such as those belonging to the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*), are subsumed as follows: regret is not [present] in the stage of one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*); the others are common to all.
Because the three types [of mental factors] accord with those [states], sixteen [factors] such as those abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) are [discussed].

Regarding regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*), they are exclusively abandoned by both vision and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-prahātavya*), because they arise through the power of vision. If they have already been abandoned, they are termed "not to be abandoned" (*aprahātavya*); thus, the sleep of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is included among those not to be abandoned.
Both vitarka and vicāra are abandoned by both vision and cultivation. According to one interpretation, vitarka and vicāra are exclusively impure (*sāsrava*).

There is no [state] that is not to be abandoned, because it is the cause and fruit of that [state]. According to one interpretation, vitarka and vicāra are also untainted (*anāsrava*), because the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Second Chapter) states that right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is untainted, and further states that right thought causes seeking and so forth;

and because the first chapter of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states that right thought is the cause of verbal expression. This is because, at the stage prior to final realization, regarding the medicine and the disease...
Those who have not yet attained universal knowledge must rely on vitarka and vicāra when preaching the Dharma to others; this is unlike the effortless (anābhoga) teaching of the Buddha-stage.

Therefore, these two types [of mental application] pertain to both the causal stage and the untainted (anāsrava) stage. This reconciles apparent contradictions as explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
These four indeterminate factors are as described in the first, fifth, twelfth, and fiftieth fascicles of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
5, 56, 57, 58, 73, 89; *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 1, *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* 1, *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra* 20;
this treatise [the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*], this section [of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*], and the second [chapter] and fifteenth [chapter];

the *Skandha-prakaraṇa*, the seventh [chapter] on *Vijñaptimātratā*; these should be explained extensively as appropriate regarding their conditions, the characteristics of the truths, and existence or non-existence.

Regarding the presence or absence of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) objects, the term "objects of activity" (*vastv-ālambana*) should be understood accordingly in cases such as those involving maturation (*vipāka*);
however, fearing prolixity, I shall cease here for now.
Furthermore, [this extends] up to being the cause of karma.

The commentary states: Within the major section explaining the individual mental factors (*caitasika*), there are three parts; this is the third. It explains the common functions of wholesome and defiled phenomena:

wholesome phenomena have the function of being powerful and superior, and the function of severing hindrances and defilements; defiled phenomena have the function of deluding objects and obstructing the wholesome.
This is the original text of this treatise; the following is the explanation by the Master [Xuanzang].
"Such as faith, shame, and so forth (up to) lack of shame and so forth.
The commentary states: This explains the function of wholesome dharmas in severing hindrances. Faith severs non-faith, and so on, up to non-harming which can sever harming;
each of these eleven wholesome dharmas has its own specific object to be severed. This is based on their respective antidotes, as previously explained.
"Because [they] cause afflictions such as greed to not arise.

The commentary states: In explaining the functions of the root afflictions within the obstruction of defilement, from greed which obstructs non-greed up to wrong view which can obstruct right view, each has its own specific object of obstruction as previously explained; they obstruct wholesome dharmas so that they do not arise.
It should be understood that [the afflictions] from anger (*krodha*) up to [wrong view] are likewise.

The commentary states: this explains the karmic functions of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that act as obstacles. Anger obstructs non-anger, and so forth, until wrong wisdom (*duṣprajñā*) obstructs right wisdom (*samyakprajñā*), as previously explained.
The *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (4th fascicle) states: "The essence of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is non-hatred (*adveṣa*); the essence of compassion (*karuṇā*) is..."

The three—*vyāpāda* (ill-will), *arati* (discontent), and *īrṣyā* (envy)—are all part of non-hatred (*adveṣa*) and have equanimity (*upekṣā*) as their essence, since they consist of portions of both non-attachment (*alobha*) and non-hatred.
Now, the commentators of the *Śāstra*, because the specific obstructed phenomena are obscured and difficult to discern, explain that which is generally obstructed as being the specific obstruction;
thus, they maintain that dharmas such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and equanimity are obstructed by anger (*krodha*) and the like, so as to produce aversion [toward those afflictions].
Otherwise, it would contradict the explanations in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other texts.
Although the six categories of mental factors (*caitta*) explained above have each been individually analyzed, they have not yet been collected together in one place;

thus, having briefly summarized what has been clarified and what remains unexplained, I shall now provide a comprehensive exposition, first distinguishing them through five general headings: (1) differences in increase and decrease, and (2) the plurality of their essential natures (*svabhāva*).

There are three points of deficiency: the absence of the four realms (*dhātu*) and the four stages (*bhūmi*) at the stage of arising; the lack of [the discussion on] shortness and length; and the non-distinction between the five [mental factors] and the mind.

Regarding the first point, the differences in increase and decrease are explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 55), the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (fascicle 1), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (fascicle 5), and so forth.

The *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-dharma-prakāśamukha-śāstra* both state that there are fifty-one [mental factors], namely: the five universal (*sarvatraga*) factors and the five object-specific (*viniyata*) factors.
Regarding the objects (*ālambana*), there are eleven; the wholesome factors (*kuśala*) are six; the afflictions (*kleśa*) are twenty; the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are four;

and the indeterminate factors (*aniyata*) are as stated in the first *Yogācārabhūmi*, totaling fifty-three. Among those previously mentioned, two secondary afflictions are added—namely, wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*) and wrong resolve (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*)—so that according to this treatise, they are said to be fifty-five.
Regarding the fundamental afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*), four types are added, all of which are the same as the initial explanation.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Sixty-two [Fascicles]) states that there are eighteen secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), namely: guile (*śāṭhya*), deceit (*māyā*), arrogance (*mada*), hypocrisy (*kuhanā*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*),

lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), lack of concentration (*asamprajanya*), faulty wisdom (*duṣprajña*), pride (*māna*), laxity (*pramāda*), frivolous distraction (*vihimśā*), impulsiveness (*auddhatya*),

lack of application (*anārambha*), lack of detachment (*asaṃlekha*), lack of respect for the training rules (*aśikṣākāmatā*), disregard for the status of a śramaṇa (*aśramaṇakāraka*), and seeking only a livelihood (*jīvikāmātra*).
Regarding the eight [reasons] for seeking renunciation as a bodhisattva, they are the same as previously explained; ten more are added, bringing the total to sixty-three.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (89) states that there are seventy types of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), namely:
greed, anger, delusion, resentment, malice, concealment, vexation, envy, stinginess, deception, guile, lack of shame, lack of remorse, pride, arrogance, and negligence.

Heedlessness, arrogance, and the outburst of resentment; hypocrisy and the manifestation of deceptive signs; seeking profit through profit; lack of respect; evil speech, evil friends, and evil desires;
great desire, longing desire, and lack of forbearance; indulgence and pervasive indulgence;
greed for what is not the Dharma; attachment to evil greed; the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); the view of permanence, the view of nihilism; and lust, anger, and torpor.
Sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt, drowsiness, lack of joy, yawning, immoderation in eating, lack of attention, irrationality,
inferiority of mind, stubbornness, disparagement, lack of straightforwardness, lack of harmony and gentleness, lack of compliance with one's peers,
sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, thoughts of harm, thoughts of kin, thoughts of country, thoughts of immortality, and thoughts of contempt.

The twenty-nine secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), such as contempt (*māna*), investigation (*vitarka*), household-status-investigation (*kula-vitarka*), sorrow (*śoka*), lamentation (*parideva*), anxiety (*daurmanasya*), and suffering (*duḥkha*), are as previously described.
To these are added forty-one further dharmas, making a total of sixty-three; with the original [thirty-seven] factors, they sum to one hundred and four.
Although seventy-three secondary afflictions are mentioned in the *Dharmaskandhapāda* and the *Kṣudrakavastu*, they are omitted here because they do not belong to the Mahāyāna system.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises do not enumerate fifty-one [mental factors]; rather, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that a bodhisattva on the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) accomplishes ten "hundreds of dharmas.
These hundred dharma-gates are as follows: consciousness consists of eight; mental factors (*caitasika*) consist of fifty-one; matter (*rūpa*) consists of eleven;
non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) consist of twenty-four; and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) consist of six. Although these include mental factors and so forth...
Furthermore, there are many who, based on the realization of the first bhūmi, speak of fifty-one yogas; some speak of fifty-three.

They state that the four unconditioned states exclude the perception of immovability (*āniñjya-saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*), because their objects of affliction are distinct and their spheres of obstruction are profound.

Thus, it is said that [the secondary afflictions] such as forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*) are subsumed under the ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). According to this yoga system, these ten secondary afflictions are pervasive.

Among the hundred mental factors within the two natures of coarse and subtle, and the defiled mind, those that are universal (*sarvatraga*) and so forth—being factors that pervade all three moral natures—each have their own distinct status.
Therefore, they are not described as being subsumed under the three categories of forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), wrong wisdom (*dauṣprajña*), and distraction (*vikṣepa*).

Rather, these three are explained as secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and not as part of the five object-specific (*viṣayaviśeṣa*) factors; furthermore, even if these three were part of the object-specific factors, they would constitute defiled mindfulness (*kliṣṭā smṛtiḥ*).

That which obstructs the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*), and right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) is the obstruction to the category of defiled concentration.

That which obstructs the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) is the obstruction to the category of unwholesome wisdom.

That which obstructs the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), and the correct view of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasamyagdṛṣṭi*) constitutes the obstruction to the profound locus [of the path]. For this reason, desire and resolve are specifically mentioned; since they are not otherwise [obstructive], they are not mentioned.
Furthermore, regarding the fifty-five [factors] mentioned in the *Abhidharma*, those that lack improper desire (*mithyā-chanda*) have meanings identical to what was previously explained.
Among the fundamental afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*), the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of wrong views (*dṛṣṭi*) are each increased in intensity and their capacity for harm is profound;

therefore, to inspire revulsion, they are separately opened up into five. However, since the hundred dharmas and so forth involve deep investigation, the portions of afflicted wisdom (*kliṣṭa-prajñā*) are combined into one.

Although their classifications differ, they do not contradict one another. Regarding the addition of ten types of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) within the sixty-two [afflictions], that same text states:
"One should know that through the predominant power of lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) and laziness (*kausīdya*), four types of secondary delusions are initiated:
slackness, vulgarity, forward-striving, and the abandonment of the yoke of seclusion; furthermore, due to forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*)."
One should know that by the predominant power of confusion and impaired wisdom, three secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are initiated:
disrespect for the training rules, disregard for the status of a *śramaṇa*, and seeking only a livelihood rather than renouncing the world for the sake of awakening.

Based on this, it should be understood that [the former] is not distinct from distraction (*vikṣepa*), and that deceit (*kuhanā*) is not distinct from the pair of guile (*māyā*) and flattery (*śāṭhya*); thus there are six.
Regarding the twelve types of increase, there are ten kinds which constitute seven of the twenty [secondary afflictions].

Regarding the forty-one kinds of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that increase among the eighty-nine [mental states], five are secondary afflictions by way of their state (*avasthā*), and thirty-six are their outflows (*niṣyanda*).
As for the five that are secondary afflictions by way of their state, they refer to the two—flattery (*śāṭhya*) and deceit (*māyā*)—which are states of the insincere and crooked.
The two states of being dazed and yawning belong to the category of the sinking of sleep; the single state of lack of attention belongs to the category of heedlessness;
the thirty-two types belong to the category of the root afflictions;
and according to their respective correspondences, the eighteen types that are outflows of the secondary afflictions belong to the category of greed—namely, seeking profit through profit.
Evil desire, great desire, longing desire, relishing, pervasive relishing, unlawful greed, attachment, evil craving, lack of contentment with food, lack of moderation,
and improper sensual thoughts— namely, thoughts of kin, thoughts of country, thoughts of immortality, and thoughts of family power—
these seven are the states of anger, consisting of: outbursts of rage, harsh speech, intolerance, provocation, and disparagement.
The five types of vitarka—namely, ill-will (*vyāpāda*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), pride (*māna*), arrogance (*atimāna*), and mental inferiority (*ūnamāna*)—are states of pride (*māna*).

The one type of vitarka—namely, lack of respect (*anādara*)—is a state of both greed (*rāga*) and delusion (*moha*). The one type of vitarka—namely, contempt (*paribhava*)—is a state of greed, hatred, and delusion.
The four types of vitarka—namely, sorrow (*śoka*), lamentation (*parideva*), distress (*upāyāsa*), and affliction (*daurmanasya*)—are states of feeling (*vedanā*), as appropriate to each case.
Because all secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are outflows (*niṣyanda*) of these [root afflictions], for this reason they are *vijñapti-mātra*.

Furthermore, although the wholesome can be contrasted with the various secondary afflictions, and although they are spoken of under various names despite having distinct meanings, their essence (*svabhāva*) is not different;
therefore, they are not established separately. Why, then, are only eighteen secondary afflictions mentioned among the sixty-two, and why are no others mentioned? It is because...
The treatise itself states that because there are three bases for transgressions, there are only this many [categories]: first, the four types arise from a single residential community;

second, the [types] beginning with shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) arise from the two bases of moral discipline; third, the remaining types arise from the bases of mind and wisdom;
furthermore, lack of faith and laziness arise based on both [bases]; forgetfulness and distraction arise based on mental transgression; and corrupted wisdom arises based on [the basis of] wisdom.

The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as pride, negligence, and so forth, which arise from wisdom (*prajñā*), are produced by five [causes] as explained previously in the section on the "Outflows" (*niṣyanda*).
They pertain to both the mind (*citta*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Regarding their arising from the two transgressions, the *Ninety-eight* [Treatise] mentions only seventy;
the remaining fifty-eight secondary afflictions are not mentioned there because, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are said to function in dependence upon twelve bases (*āyatana*).
This refers to the fact that from attachment to the locus of unwholesome conduct, giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion, up to the twelfth locus where a multitude of sufferings accumulate,
giving rise to sorrow, lamentation, distress, and pain— as explained at length therein— there are exactly seventy [mental factors], neither fewer nor more.
Although there are this many mental factors (*caitta*), according to this treatise, the fifty-one realized in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) are taken as the definitive standard.
Although fifty-five types are taught, there is no contradiction because these entities are not merely conceptual imputations (*samāropa*).
Regarding the number of these two types of entities, one interpretation holds that among the fifty-five mental factors (*caitta*), twenty-seven are real:

namely, twenty-one—consisting of five each for the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) categories—and six from the wholesome (*kuśala*) category, excluding heedfulness (*apramāda*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Furthermore, excluding the five root afflictions of non-harming and the five evil views, there are four secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), namely:
lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), and laziness (*kausīdya*). The remaining twenty-eight are all nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*).

According to another interpretation, thirty-two factors within this category have a real ontological substance (*dravyasat*), as the three—restlessness (*auddhatya*), torpor (*styāna*), and distraction (*vikṣepa*)—are added among the secondary afflictions.
The various types of indeterminate [states], regret, and sleep—these twenty-three—are all conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*).

Those said to be substantially existent (*dravyasat*) arise from their own distinct seeds; they function independently of others, possess distinct modes of activity (*ākāra*) as appropriate, and actually evolve simultaneously with consciousness.
Those said to be conventionally existent are either individually or collectively bestowed by others, as the case may be, and are abandoned by the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
If there were no distinct seeds arising apart from others that have practical utility, and no distinct real characteristics of yoga, then according to one explanation,
from wrong desire and conviction up to the self-proclaimed sufferer— all such [categories] are provisionally established either according to their respective applications,
or according to the states of the preceding and succeeding moments of truly existent entities, or as having the meaning of a single moment.
Regarding the presence or absence [of mental factors] during their arising, we shall now briefly provide six examples based on the fifty-five mental factors (*caitasika*) in this treatise:

First, there are those that arise with five factors; these must necessarily be accompanied by five, namely the five universal (*sarvatraga*) factors. Second, there are those that arise with nine factors;

these must necessarily be accompanied by six, namely the five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) factors and four of the indeterminate (*aniyata*) factors; whenever one of these arises, it is necessarily accompanied by them.
1. Because they are omnipresent (*sarvatraga*), when these omnipresent factors arise, they necessarily accompany all minds; below, it should be stated that there are three [types].
There are nine factors whose arising is necessarily accompanied by fourteen: namely, ignorance (*avidyā*) and the eight great secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), such as torpor (*styāna*), etc.;
since these nine necessarily coexist, [they require fourteen]. 2. There are twenty-one factors whose arising is necessarily accompanied by fifteen: namely...

The ten wholesome factors (*daśa-kuśala-dharma*), excluding *praśrabdhi* (serenity), greed (*lobha*), pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*), guile (*śāṭhya*), deceit (*māyā*), and arrogance (*mada*), necessarily arise together with ten [factors] when they originate.

When any one of the defiled factors such as greed arises, there must necessarily be ignorance (*avidyā*) and the eight great secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Thus, these five [categories] have three types of arising;
when any one of them arises, there must necessarily be sixteen concomitants, namely: *praśrabdhi*, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), and *praśrabdhi*.

When [a root] arises, it is necessarily accompanied by eleven wholesome factors; these two—lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*)—are necessarily concomitant, as are the eight great secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Thus, there are six [factors]. When [a root] arises, it is necessarily accompanied by seventeen factors;

that is to say, when any one of anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), vexation (*pradāsa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), or harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) arises, it is necessarily accompanied by ignorance (*avidyā*), lack of shame, lack of dread, and the eight great secondary afflictions.

Since the delusions (*kleśa*) are pervasive across all [five] categories, this is established according to the correct meaning based on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Regarding what is determined to be concomitant and what is not:
all wholesome dharmas are definitely not concomitant with the thirty defiled dharmas; greed is definitely not concomitant with hatred or doubt;

hatred is definitely not concomitant with views, attachment to precepts and rituals, concealment, deception, or flattery; pride is definitely not concomitant with doubt; and doubt is definitely not [concomitant with any of these].
The five views do not coexist with one another; they definitely do not coexist with the first ten [mental factors] such as anger (*krodha*), nor do they coexist with doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Anger, resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāśa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) definitely do not coexist with greed (*lobha*) or hatred (*dveṣa*). Arrogance (*māna*) definitely does not coexist with greed or hatred.

Discursive thought (*vitarka*) definitely does not coexist with sustained thought (*vicāra*). Regret (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) definitely do not coexist with tranquility (*praśrabdhi*). [In the case of] regret, hatred is excluded.

Delusion (*moha*) and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) definitely do not coexist with the seven root afflictions such as pride (*māna*) and so forth; although the treatises state that there are nine [mental factors], they are not definitive.

Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) definitely does not coexist with anger (*krodha*) and the others, nor with the ten [minor afflictions]; this is based on what is taught in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* regarding those that are definitively non-associated.
As for those excluded here, they may potentially be associated if one relies on the fifty-first and fifty-third [mental states].
Regarding what has been taught, one must certainly state the verses: "Five dharmas arise together with five; nine dharmas necessarily arise with four; fourteen [arise] with twenty-one;
fifteen [arise] with three; sixteen [arise] with eight; seventeen always arise together with the mind-associates (*citta-samprayukta*);
the wise should study this."

Regarding the four realms (*dhātu*) and the short and long [lists] of stages (*bhūmi*): "realms" refers to the three realms, and "stages" refers to the ten stages. As for the short and long lists within the three realms:
among the fifty-five mental factors (*caitta*), the desire realm possesses fifty-four, excluding *praśrabdhi* (pliancy);

according to one interpretation, it possesses all fifty-five, with the former being considered correct. The form realm (*rūpadhātu*) possesses forty-three, and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) possesses thirty-nine.

Twelve factors are bound exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), namely: the seven [secondary afflictions] beginning with anger (*krodha*) and resentment (*upānāha*), as well as shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), and torpor (*middha*). Eighteen factors are bound to two realms, namely:
the nine root [afflictions], or pride (*māna*), and the eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Three factors are bound to two realms or are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*), namely: vitarka and vicāra.

The twenty factors of *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) are bound to the three realms as well as unbound; that is, all universal (*sarvatraga*), object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*), and wholesome (*kuśala*) factors, with the exception of *praśrabdhi* itself.

Authentic textual evidence for this is found throughout the sūtras and śāstras, so there is no need to cite them at length. As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and other such scriptures, there are ten stages:
first, the stage of pure observation (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*); second, the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*); third, the eighth [stage] (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*).
The first is the Stage of Seeing; the second, the Stage of Thinness; the third, the Stage of Freedom from Desire; the fourth, the Stage of Completion; the fifth, the Stage of the Pratyekabuddha;
the sixth, the Stage of the Bodhisattva; and the seventh, the Stage of the Tathāgata.

This exposition of the ten stages common to the three vehicles encompasses all dharmas exhaustively, as it includes those of gradual and sudden awakening, as well as those of fixed and unfixed lineage; thus, it is not restricted to the Single Vehicle alone.

The practice of the ten stages pertains only to the noble ones and not to ordinary beings, because it is neither cause nor fruit. Regarding the first two stages, there are briefly two interpretations:

one holds that the stage of pure observation (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*) exists only within the stage of liberation (*vimukti-bhāga*) of the śrāvakas and within the first three of the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*);

furthermore, the lineage (*gotra*) exists only at the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*). Another interpretation holds that the stage of pure observation exists only within the stage of liberation.

Because those in the stage of "liberation" (vimokṣabhāgīya) and so forth have not yet practiced the contemplation of the truths (*satya*) and their lineage (*gotra*) is not yet fixed, they merely purify the mind by contemplating the body, sensations, and so on—this being called "pure contemplation" (*śuddhaka-vipaśyanā*).
Therefore, the lineage is present throughout the four stages of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the others;

it is only upon reaching this [stage] that the lineage becomes fixed and can no longer be diverted. Thus, the eighth stage refers to one who is "stream-enterer-bound" (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*), meaning one who abides therein.
Regarding the fifteen moments of mind prior to the path of seeing that are dedicated toward the fruit:

because one counts backward from the Arhat, those who possess the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) refer to those in the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), as they are fully endowed with the sixteen moments of the path of seeing. The "thin stage" (*tanu-bhūmi*) refers to the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*);

this is because they have already become "one who has doubled their detachment" (*dvitīya-vītarāga*) within the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm by abandoning six grades. Thus, they are detached.
The Stage of Desire refers to the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), because one has definitively and completely abandoned the afflictions of the desire realm.

The Stage of Completion refers to the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), because birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.

The Stage of Solitary Realizers (*pratyekabuddha*) refers to all solitary realizers, whether they are of the rhinoceros-like type or those who travel in a group. The Stage of Bodhisattvas refers to the twelve abodes (*dvādaśavihāra*). The Stage of the Tathāgata [is as follows].
This means that within the stage of pure observation (*śuddhadarśana-bhūmi*) at the level of Buddhahood, there are fifty-five [factors];

in the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*) and the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), as well as the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*) and the stage of refinement (*tanu-bhūmi*), there are only fifty-one factors, excluding false view, doubt, adherence to views, and adherence to precepts and rituals.

Regarding the statement in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* that "in the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-avasthā*), the dual grasping of conceptualization has already been suppressed," this refers to the stage of detachment from desire (*vairāgya-bhūmi*).

There are only forty factors, excluding those previously mentioned and further excluding eleven: anger, resentment, concealment, vexation, envy, harmfulness, stinginess, lack of shame, lack of dread, and remorse.

In the stage of one who has already finished his task (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*) and in the stage of the Pratyekabuddha, only twenty-four factors are accomplished, excluding those previously mentioned and further excluding eight:
greed, pride, doubt, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), as well as flattery, deceit, and arrogance.

Among the secondary afflictions previously eliminated, those that are afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and those that are cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are all present across the eight stages;

thus, these scriptures state that there are fifty-five factors therein. Regarding the twelve *vihāras* (abodes) in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the first is the abode of the lineage (*gotra-vihāra*), which refers to abiding in the innate lineage of a bodhisattva.
The second is the abode of conduct through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*), starting from the beginning...
From the initial generation of the mind up to the first bhūmi, each of the subsequent ten dwellings (*vihāra*) constitutes one bhūmi:
(1) the Dwelling of Extreme Joy, also called the Dwelling of Purified Superior Intention; (2) the Dwelling of Superior Ethics; (3) the Dwelling of Superior Mind;

(4) the Dwelling of Superior Wisdom Corresponding to the Factors of Enlightenment; (5) the Dwelling of Superior Wisdom Corresponding to the Truths; (6) the Dwelling of the Flow of Dependent Origination.

The dwelling of superior wisdom associated with tranquility (śamatha-vipaśyanā-yukta-adhiprajñā-vihāra), the ninth dwelling of signlessness with effort (animitta-sābhoga-vihāra), the tenth dwelling of signlessness without effort (animitta-anābhoga-vihāra), the eleventh dwelling of unhindered analytical knowledge (pratisaṃvid-vihāra), and the twelfth dwelling of the supreme perfection of a bodhisattva (parama-pariniṣpanna-bodhisattva-vihāra).
In these, the first two dwellings each possess fifty-five [qualities]. This explains the sudden awakening; as for the gradual discourse, it follows whichever [stage] applies.

The number of factors possessed at each stage is as explained in the *Buzhu jing* (Sūtra on the Original Abiding). Although the tenth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the section on the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmika*), states:
"Having eliminated all afflictions so that they are forever exhausted without remainder, this is the unimpeded contemplation of tranquil extinction," which refers to the Buddha’s True Dharma;
the *Pratītyasamutpāda Sūtra* states that ignorance has four types: first, common; second, uncommon; third, entanglement (*paryavasthāna*); and fourth... [text fragment].
I say that all the karmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) regarding external phenomena (*bāhyadharma*), which are accompanied by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), have these four as their conditions.

Regarding internal phenomena (*ādhyātmikadharma*), I say that for those ordinary beings who are heedless (*pramatta*), all their karmas have the three types of ignorance (*avidyā*) as their conditions;

however, for those who are not heedless (*apramatta*), I do not say that their karmas constitute "formations conditioned by ignorance" (*avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*). They are established as such [only] in the case of the former.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states: "In the stage of the equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), although one has deep faith and understanding in the meaning of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), one has not yet realized the emptiness of the grasper and the grasped (*grāhya-grāhaka*).

Because one dwells frequently in external orientations (*bahirmukha*) to realize the bodhisattva practices, one still lacks the power to suppress and eliminate the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) induced by these two graspings, such that those two graspings do not arise as manifest."
Furthermore, in the stage of application (*prayoga*), one is able to suppress and eliminate all conceptualized forms of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) entirely;
it is not said that all afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Rather, this should be understood in accordance with the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, which states that within the ten stages, the four types of ignorance (*avidyā*)—which are not shared [with ordinary beings] due to association with false teachers and friends—and their associated categories, are suppressed.
Because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse, they arise from one's own conceptualization and initiate the karma of conceptualization;

these four types of ignorance and so forth can only be suppressed and exhausted upon reaching the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). Otherwise, it would contradict the teachings of the *Vijñaptimātratā* and other treatises.

Furthermore, it is not the case that all ignorance is entirely non-arising for all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the Buddhist tradition (*abhyantaradharma*). Therefore, one should understand that [the cessation of ignorance] must be analyzed as previously explained.
In the third through the ninth abodes, all [stages] possess the fifty-one [factors], excluding doubt, false views, adherence to views, and adherence to precepts and rituals—these being absent here.
All [factors] therein pertain to both the afflictive and cognitive obstructions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa* and *jñeya-āvaraṇa*).

Although it is said that there remain other afflictions, they can indeed be eliminated by the power of intentional effort; thus, it is not the case that they cannot be removed. Furthermore, although it is said that the view of a self-entity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is abandoned in the fourth stage, [it is actually abandoned earlier].
This explains only a small portion and not all without remainder; among the three types [of consciousness], there are thirty-five factors.

Excluding those previously mentioned, and further excluding anger (*krodha*), the two extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)—namely shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), and sleep (*middha*)—as well as greed (*lobha*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*moha*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and the eight great secondary afflictions that accompany the seventh consciousness, which is the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Because this exists, it is said that vitarka and vicāra are pervasive throughout the untainted (anāsrava).

If one were to say that vitarka and vicāra exist only in the tainted (sāsrava), then within those three stages of abiding, there would be only thirty-three factors, and within the stage of Buddhahood, there would be only twenty-one factors, as stated above.
All these [factors] are said to be manifest (samudācāra) and capable of arising; they do not refer to seeds (bīja). If one speaks of seeds...
Because the meaning of "subsidiary" (*paryāya*) is not fixed, the sense of "not arising" has already been explained individually within each of the preceding six positions;
therefore, here we need only discuss whether they are complete or incomplete.

Regarding whether the five [mental factors] are identical to or different from the mind, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), chapter seven, poses the question and answer itself: "Do the various mental factors..."
If there were a distinct intrinsic nature (svabhāva) separate from the essence of mind, it would contradict the five teachings;
if it were merely a differentiation of the states of mind, it would contradict three teachings.
According to conventional truth (saṃvṛti), one should say that there is a distinct intrinsic nature separate from mind; however, because mind is preeminent, it is said to be "only" [mind].

There is no fault whatsoever regarding consciousness and the other [factors]. If one relies on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), mental factors (*caitta*) are neither identical to nor separate from the mind (*citta*).

Now, based on the first [type of] ultimate truth: because of the distinction between king and minister; because of the distinction in their modes of activity (*ākāra*); because of the difference in their existence or non-existence; because they cannot be definitively identified as the same;

because they are difficult to discern due to their illusory nature; and because they can all be considered identical according to the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Therefore, there is no contradiction.
It is not definitively separate because it distinguishes the second ultimate reality; it is not definitively identical because there is no duality in principle;
it is not definitively separate again because, within the third ultimate reality, there is a difference in the expression of the causal nature, whereas there is no difference in its own nature;
and it is not definitively separate because the fourth ultimate reality is the internally realized object of knowledge of the mind.
It is said that the mental factors (*caitta*) and the mind (*citta*) are simultaneously quiescent, being neither identical nor distinct.
Furthermore, [the function of the hindrances] is to obstruct their own respective antidotes.
*Commentary*: This concludes the third section within the explanation of mental factors, which clarifies the common characteristics and functions of wholesome and defiled mental factors.

Within this, there are two parts: the first is the main body of the treatise, and the second is the Master’s commentary. Because the power of wholesome dharmas is strong, they are called "the severance" (*prahāṇa*) of the nature of unwholesome dharmas that are to be countered;
because the nature of those unwholesome dharmas is inferior, they are called "obstructions" (*āvaraṇa*) to the counteragents.

Furthermore, wholesome dharmas are termed "delightful" (*abhirati*) in accordance with their capacity for severance, while unwholesome dharmas are termed "repugnant" (*arati*) in accordance with their obstruction of the Path. Question: Since wholesome dharmas oppose unwholesome ones, does one immediately speak of "severing the seeds of evil" upon their opposition?

It should be said that evil contradicts the good and thus severs the seeds of goodness; however, the good is able to realize the principle, is superior, and is beneficial, so it is called the severing of the seeds of evil.
Evil dharmas do not realize the principle and are harmful, yet they cannot sever the seeds of goodness.
"Just as faith, shame, and so forth [function] up to [the point of] preventing [defilements] from arising.
The commentary states: This explains a specific meaning. Although previously [these factors] were mentioned collectively without specific indication, here they are specifically pointed out.

Each of the wholesome and defiled factors has its own distinct antidote for its respective obstacle; thus, the phenomena of obstacles and their antidotes are explained according to their individual names.
One should know that the antidotes for anger and the other [afflictions] are likewise.
The commentary states: Among the wholesome factors, the abandonment of their respective opposites has been generally presented. Within the defiled factors, two roots have already been explained;

now, regarding the secondary obstacles (*upakleśa*), they are each said to obstruct their own corresponding wholesome factor according to their specific names. It is now stated that anger and the others are able to obstruct loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, the second chapter on "Manifesting the Obstacles," it is stated that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is non-harming, compassion (*karuṇā*) is non-anger, and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is non-envy.
Regarding the specific obstacles, harming is identified as the immediate affliction that obstructs loving-kindness; anger is said to be its obstacle because it is a derivative of hatred (*dveṣa*).

These [definitions] based on general obstacles and so forth are not mutually contradictory. As for these [afflictions], they are subsumed within their own essential natures according to their names, as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The Sixth Fascicle.
*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Four.
*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Five.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of Daci’en Monastery.
What are called the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*)?
[The author] states: This is the second major section, providing a detailed explanation of the "formations" (*saṃskāra*) indicated above; previously, the first part distinguished the mind.

Having already explained the *citta-saṃprayukta-saṃskāras* (mental formations associated with consciousness) below, the *citta-viprayukta-saṃskāras* (formations dissociated from consciousness) will now be analyzed. According to the main text of the treatise, these are divided into two parts:
first, the presentation of their distinct names; second, the detailed explanation following those names. If one were to categorize and explain the text of the treatise, there are three sections:

the first two are as previously described, and the third provides a general analysis of the bases upon which they are established. Within the section presenting the distinct names, there is first a question and then an answer; this is the first [of those].

Furthermore, in the general summary of the preceding fascicle, it was stated: "Moreover, this very volition (cetanā), excluding feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā), together with the remaining mental factors (caitta) and the formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra), is collectively termed the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
For this reason, the following question is raised: "Dissociated" (viprayukta) means "not similar.
It does not share a similar ontological nature with matter (rūpa) or mind (citta) and so forth; that is to say, it is not something that possesses an object of cognition (sālambana).
Because their nature possesses transformation and resistance (*sapratigha*), they are called "dissociated" (*viprayukta*). Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 53, asks:
"For what reason are they called dissociated? This is a conceptual designation applied to various phenomena for the purpose of verbal expression;

it is neither of the two types that possess form (*rūpin*) and so forth, nor is it either of the two types that are visible (*sanidarśana*) and so forth. It is merely a name for consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
Because they are associated with mental factors (*citta-samprayukta*), the term "non-associated" (*viprayukta*) excludes other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

Now, they are specifically termed "factors dissociated from mind" (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) because the mind is the primary factor. Just as in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, "conditioned" (*saṃskāra*) refers to that which undergoes flux (*pravṛtti*), thereby excluding unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*);
this reveals that only acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth are non-associated formations.
This refers to "attainment" (*prāpti*), "conjunction" (*sāmagrī*), and so forth.
[The commentary] states: "Listing the names of the twenty-three dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), the word 'etcetera' (*ādi*) includes 'non-conjunction' (*asāmagrī*).

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* both state there are twenty-four; the intention here is to accord with those [texts], which is why the word 'etcetera' is used. However, it is not... [the case].
Regarding the separate enumeration of "non-concordance" (*apratisaṃyukta*), the Master [Vasubandhu] reveals that its essence is precisely "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*).

Since non-acquisition is not established separately from acquisition, non-concordance is not mentioned separately from concordance. Furthermore, he reveals that the term "non-concordant" is not exhaustive even when referring to the "dissociated" (*viprayukta*);
for instance, "noble nature" (*āryatva*) and "slowness" (*dhandhatva*) are both dissociated, yet they are not explicitly mentioned as such.
Therefore, the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*) indicates that there are many more [categories]. The *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (*Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*) states:
"Furthermore, it should be known that there are other such various types of distinctions. The above is the original text of the treatise; the following is the commentary by the Master.
"Thus (up to) because of the ground.

The commentary states: "The Master of the Treatise establishes this by means of five gates to show that the distinctions of 'attainment' (*prāpti*) and so forth necessarily have mind, mental factors, matter, and both manifest and latent seeds as their supporting bases (*āśraya*), for they are established based on substantial reality (*dravyasat*)."
"By way of its own nature" means that its essence (svabhāva) extends across three categories. "By way of being conventionally established" clarifies that its essence is not substantial.

"By way of mental attention" (manasikāra) reveals that it is induced by proximate preparatory application (prayoga). "By way of revealing the basis" indicates that although the basis consists of multiple stages, it receives the name "stage" based on a single stage.
Regarding the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), [it is said that] for the others, only the first three [factors] exist.

The commentary states: This generally clarifies the extent of the factors possessed by acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth. The attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) fully possess the five gates;

both are established based on the seeds of wholesome minds capable of revulsion, and their substance pervades the three grades [of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral], while their designation as "states" is a conventional fiction applied to a position where no mental state exists.

Because it is induced by mental orientations such as the "mind of aversion" (*nirvedacitta*) and relies upon the fourth dhyāna and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) possesses only the remaining four gates, excluding mental orientation;

it relies solely on the cessation of seeds within neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds and mental factors, and is established as a fruit common to all three categories [wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral] as a mere conventional designation (*prajñapti*). It exists in the fourth dhyāna without depending on preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
The mental application (*manasikāra*) induces the spontaneous mind (*svarasa-citta*) and so forth to extinguish the seeds;

based on this, the remaining twenty-one [mental applications] are established as possessing only the first three [characteristics], because they are not induced by immediate preparatory effort (*anantara-prayoga*) and do not belong to a single stage (*bhūmi*) alone—this will be understood in detail below.
"Attainment" (up to "obtaining maturation").

The commentary states: what follows is the detailed explanation, which consists of eighteen sections; four characteristics constitute one section, and name, phrase, and syllable constitute another section.
Thus, the first part clarifies the attainment of the main text of the treatise, while the subsequent part provides the master’s interpretation.
[This section] excellently clarifies the basis (*āśraya*).

The commentary states: Within the explanation, there are three parts: first, an exposition of the root text which possesses the first three meanings; second, an application by analogy to the remaining [meanings];

and third, this present clarification of the basis for the first meaning. There are three bases: first, the basis of that which is attained (*prāpti*), namely, conditioned attainment (*saṃskṛtā prāpti*) together with the dharmas to be attained.

1. Because they increase or decrease in accordance with their mutual connection and association, both types of paths—namely, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and the various non-analytical acquisitions (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—are associated with and connected to the path that arises simultaneously with them. 2.
Because they function according to the three grades [of defilements] through their association and connection with the nature of the path that arises at the same time as the six practices. 3.

"In accordance with the basis" means that, excluding the analytical [cessation], the non-analytical acquisitions of the six practices are either ultimately due to the absence of conditions or temporarily absent.

Regarding their arising, they have no distinct mutual connection; they follow their respective bases, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and the conditions for the absence of dharmas. Thus, among these three types of acquisition (*prāpti*), the first applies to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*);

the second is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*); and the last should be analyzed accordingly. As for "following the fundamental consciousness," it refers only to the wholesome and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

As for "following the conditions for the absence," it may apply to all three natures. Now, this treatise speaks of them collectively at the outset to clarify their basis, as explained in the commentary.
[Commentary on] the middle section.
Regarding "whether increasing or decreasing" (up to) "inferior-grade faith and so forth":

the commentary states that this explains the second meaning. In reality, all three natures possess both increase and decrease; however, by mentioning "faith and so forth," [the text] provides an illustration.

Because they are difficult to obtain, because they briefly indicate the Dharma, because difficulties may arise, or because they equally apply to the other two natures, these dharmas merely mention increase and decrease without speaking of the middle;

this can be understood by analogy. Alternatively, because they are not fixed, they are not explained separately, being subsumed under the two [categories] as in the case of the "power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties" among the ten powers, where fifty-two [factors] are said to increase.
That which is called "attainment" (*prāpti*) by virtue of its intensification is explained in terms of its function, because it can only be attained when one reaches a state of intensification.
Therefore, the statement that "attainment is the grasping of the conditions for arising" is explained in terms of its essence; thus, there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, both the categories of increase and decrease are established as "attainment" in a state of intensification; if there is no intensification, it is not so established.
Because they are attained.
[The phrase] "provisionally established" (upacāra) indicates that which is provisionally established.

The commentary states: this explains the third meaning; the *Abhidharmasamudaya-śāstra*, chapter eighteen, states that all non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are [provisionally established].
Provisional existence has six aspects: first, discourse associated with belonging to a master;
it is only through its association with a master that its characteristic is understood—for instance, "whose acquisition is this? referring to the acquisition of form, and so forth at length.

Because such words are employed, these dissociated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) are provisionally established. Furthermore, they are refuted as being substantially existent by two reasons, which will be explained below.
Because they are [merely] distinguished, they do not exist substantially.
One should know that this applies to the establishment of the others as well. The commentary states:

In the second example, the remaining [categories] possess the meaning of the five gates; the two meditative absorptions (samāpatti) possess the five [factors]; the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva) possesses four; and the rest [possess] the remaining [factors].

Since the first three [categories] alone are all explained according to this principle, it is said that they correspond accordingly. The commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa* explains "attainment" (*prāpti*) through three gates:
first, the basis; second, the essence; and third, the conventional and the real. Now, I shall further briefly analyze it by means of five gates: first, distinguishing between internal and external;
second, what is subsumed under the two times; third, manifesting the great and the small; fourth, previously attained and not yet attained; and fifth, the section of questions and answers.
The distinctions are as explained in the chapter [on the attainments].
Regarding the "attainment of non-conception" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), up to the point where it is "provisionally established as the attainment of non-conception," the commentary states:
"Within this, there are two [types]; according to the main text of this treatise, the later commentators explain that there are four."

"Having abandoned desire for the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven] but not yet having abandoned desire for what is above" indicates the stage (*bhūmi*). "The perception of departure" and so forth indicate the mental application (*manasikāra*).
"In the cessation of non-constant mind and mental factors" indicates the basis (*āśraya*). "Designated as 'non-conception' (*asaṃjñin')" indicates the conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
"The entity (*vastu*) is common to the three categories" because it is induced by that [designation]; it is omitted here because it is self-evident.
"Having already abandoned desire for the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven] up to having abandoned the craving of the higher realms.
The commentary states: The third heaven of the third dhyāna is named Śubhakṛtsna. "Higher desire" refers to craving;

because it is the most predominant among all afflictions, it is specifically mentioned. This means one has completely abandoned the craving of the third dhyāna, yet has not yet abandoned the craving of the higher realms.
The fact that various non-Buddhists are able to give rise to this meditative absorption also demonstrates that this absorption is bound to the fourth dhyāna.

This is stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, which explains that because the coarse movement of perception (*saṃjñā*) below is difficult to sever, and because there is no place for the retribution of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) above it.
The perception of renunciation (niḥsaraṇa-saṃjñā) serves as the preliminary application (*pūrvaprayoga*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 12, asks: "By what means does one enter these meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)? It answers:

"One contemplates [the lower realms] as a disease, an abscess, and an arrow; having entered the fourth dhyāna, one cultivates the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the perception of aversion toward them."
One dwells in aversion toward the arising of various perceptions and considers only non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) to be peaceful and sublime.

Taking the perception of non-perception as true liberation, one first applies the mental attention of the perception of renunciation and, through the remote preparatory application, enters this meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) by means of the sixfold method.
Because perceptions within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) serve as causes and conditions, one attains liberation [from them].

Perception (*saṃjñā*) serves as the preliminary means (*pūrvaprayoga*), yet it is not the case that the other [mental factors] do not cease; this is the teaching of the establishment of *vijñaptimātratā*. Because perception ceases first, the name "non-perception" (*asaṃjñika*) is established.
That which does not function constantly is subsumed under the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
The commentary states: Regarding the term "establishing consciousness-only," those [six consciousnesses] are called "non-constant" because they are interrupted;

the six consciousnesses—namely, the five universal, the specific-object, and the eleven wholesome factors—are distant from the five [sense objects], while the manas is near. Thus, they are termed "non-constant.
Since these alone are the coarse objects of observation that are to be loathed within the outflows, one extinguishes only these.
"Extinction" (referring to the distinctions of the states of its basis).
The commentary states: This explains the phrase "the extinction of non-permanent mental states and so forth," which correctly reveals the essential nature of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Because the mind of the fourth dhyāna—attained through the preceding preparatory means—is characterized by revulsion toward the mind and its associates, it induces the extinction of all non-permanent minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) accordingly.
The power [of the mind] ceases for a brief moment; because of this cessation, the body that serves as its basis becomes distinct from its previous state of possessing mind.
This is called the "unconscious" (asaṃjñika), which is tranquil and subtle. Within this unconscious state, one maintains the mind and abides.
Thus, by gradually departing from all objects of perception, the mind becomes utterly stilled. This cessation is itself meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which sustains the state of the body.

Entering that concentration through various names constitutes the teaching of Vijñaptimātratā (Cognition-Only); because it brings the body to a state of peace and harmony, it is also called "concentration" (*samādhi*).
Because it is able to extinguish [defilements], it is called "extinction" (*nirodha*).

The commentary states: This reveals that because it is distinct from the mind and so forth, it is able to extinguish them; therefore, these words are spoken. It is called the teaching of Vijñaptimātratā because it establishes this.

When practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because one feels aversion toward coarse and agitated mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), one generates a superior aspirational vow to restrain them, causing the mind and mental factors to gradually become subtle and increasingly refined.
At the stage of the extremely subtle mind, this perfumes the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) to form seeds of an extremely predominant state of aversion toward the mind and its factors.
Because these seeds of the mind and its factors are thus suppressed and subdued, the coarse and agitated mind and its factors temporarily do not arise.
Because the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*) is provisionally established based on this [attainment], it is provisionally termed "extinction" (*nirodha*).

Since the mind and mental factors are designated as the objects to be extinguished, the provisional and the real differ, and thus the extinguisher and the extinguished are distinct. Therefore, this attainment is taken as the essence of the extinguisher.
The treatise already provides a fivefold analysis: first, according to the stage (*bhūmi*); second, according to the aspect (*ākāra*); third... [and so forth].
Regarding the four entities of the cessation-aggregate and the five categories of the provisional and the real, they are now further explained by means of ten gates:

(1) explanation of names; (2) differences in cultivation; (3) inclusion within the [three] natures; (4) accordance with feeling; (5) inclusion within karma; (6) place of arising; (7) person who arises; (8) previously attained or not yet attained;
(9) inclusion within the two types of attainment; and (10) resolution of doubts and difficulties, as explained in the respective chapters.
Regarding the "attainment of cessation" (*nirodhasamāpatti*) [up to] "establishing the attainment of cessation":
the commentary states that in the third section below, which explains the attainment of cessation, there are two parts. In the first of these, the main text of this treatise contains four sections.
The first involves the mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward the perception of temporary rest in a stage higher than the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

First, it is shown that *manasikāra* (attention) serves as the basis for the provisional designation of the "cessation attainment" (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in relation to those [mental factors] that do not function constantly;

this demonstrates that the cessation attainment is a mere designation lacking intrinsic nature. Since it is admitted to be cultivated by all three classes [of practitioners], it constitutes the three types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

[This point] is omitted here and should be consulted in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and other treatises. Regarding the difficulty of establishing the "extinction of one portion of the constantly functioning [mind]," An-hui [Sthiramati] asserts that there is no such thing among the three vehicles.
Question: Since from the eighth bhūmi onwards there is no [defiled] seventh consciousness, why is it said that one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti)?

[The answer is: This refers to the fact that this specific portion did not previously exist. Question: According to the Dharmapāla school, since there is still grasping at persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*) as well as pure wisdom (*viśuddha-jñāna*), why is it said that one enters the meditative absorption of cessation?
[The answer is: This refers to the exclusion of the Buddha; for all others, the [defiled] portion exists only half the time.
The statement that "one part is non-existent" because the defilements have been rendered non-existent refers to those who have already abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness;
this clarifies that such attainment belongs to the two vehicles and not to Bodhisattvas, for Bodhisattvas attain meditative concentration without abandoning desire.
"Non-percipient fruition" (up to "non-percipient fruition"). The commentary states:
Within the fourth section, there is only the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*). Among these, the phrase "those among the non-percipient beings in the heavens" clarifies the level (*bhūmi*);
the phrase "the cessation of the mind and mental factors that do not constantly function" clarifies the provisional designation of the basis (*āśraya*).

Regarding the "maturation of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*): this indicates that because the three grades of causes—established as mere designations and lacking intrinsic nature—are present, the results are likewise of three grades, as explained in the seventh chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and in other treatises.
Regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)... [up to] "conventionally established as lifespan.
The commentary states: This fifth section consists of two parts; within the first part, there are three sub-sections.
The first clarifies the basis within the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*); herein, "homogeneous class" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) manifesting and maintaining [existence].

Regarding the seeds of the same category (*nikāya-sabhāga*), based on these seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), there is established the "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*) as a provisional designation for the power that maintains matter and mind and causes them to perish.

Alternatively, although the "same category" (*sabhāga*) applies generally to the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements across the various destinies and births, it refers here specifically to the eighth consciousness;
this [life-faculty] is established as a provisional designation based on its seeds, and it functions solely by way of projecting [the continuity of existence].
Furthermore, this *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is not merely spoken of as the basis for the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Because it is said that the dharmas sustained by the life-faculty are maintained by it, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "The life-faculty is a provisional designation for the fixed duration of the abiding of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as projected by prior karma;
therefore, it is called *sabhāgatā*. This [definition] is maintained by the life-faculty, which differs from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Regarding the statement "depending on that [life-force], etc.," the subsequent treatise says: "It causes the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) to abide constantly;

it reveals that the duration determined by the maturation of prior karma exists as the limit of the individual's own nature according to that karma; therefore, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is provisionally established. This indicates that it is a provisional establishment.
Regarding "the homogeneous class" (*nikāya-sabhāga*) [up to] "the continuity of the aggregates":
the commentary states that there are two parts to the Master’s explanation—first, an explanation based on the text, and second, an explanation of its essential nature. This is the first.

However, while the general homogeneous class is cited as the basis for establishing the specific life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the retributive fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is not cited as its homogeneous class.
Because the particular is not separate from the universal, its meaning is likewise not excluded; thus, both of the preceding two interpretations should be cited.
One should also cite the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* passages concerning "all" and "homogeneity. Regarding "stability and determination," [this refers to] the differentiation of functional capacities.

The commentary states: This explanation of the yoga of self-nature is taught in fifty-two [sections]; the determination or non-determination of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth should be cited according to that [text].
Other classifications by way of different gates are as set forth in a separate chapter.
Regarding "the homogeneous class" (*nikāya-sabhāga*) [up to] "provisionally establishing the homogeneous class":
the commentary states that this sixth section has two parts; within the first part there are three [sub-sections].

Thus, "such and such sentient beings" indicates the basis [of the designation], as it is established solely in dependence upon internal bases (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*), and therefore does not apply to non-sentient things.

The term "in various types" (*nānāprakāra*) indicates that the self-nature is manifested as similar; that is, whatever the category of self-nature may be, it is established as "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) because it is similar.

The phrase "manifesting its own nature" (*svabhāva-prakāśana*) further clarifies that this is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*). Furthermore, the expression "such and such sentient beings" (*evamrūpāḥ sattvāḥ*) indicates the meaning of a "multitude," as there is not just one.

The phrase "in various types" (*nānāprakāra*) indicates the meaning of "classification" (*bheda*); for "classification" means the division of categories. Thus, [the term *sabhāgatā*] signifies both the sense of similarity and the sense of classification.
The similarity of essence reveals the meaning of "sameness"; that is, the similarity among many distinct categories is termed *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity).
It refers to the nature of being a single category among various types of categories.
The commentary states: This master’s explanation is that "various types" (*nānā-jātīya*) refers to the general essence (*sāmānya-svabhāva*), while "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) refers to the particular.
Although there are many distinct categories within the general, the term "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) is established upon the similarity of one specific type among them.
One should verify this against the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 52, and other chapters.
"Regarding 'those who are born' (up to) 'provisionally established as birth.

The commentary states: In the seventh section there are two parts; first, the individual explanation of the four characteristics, and second, the general summary beginning with 'The Master of the Treatise should know that herein...
Furthermore, regarding the main text itself, within the individual explanation of the four types of birth, there are two [parts]."
In the initial treatise and the subsequent commentary, the Master [Vasubandhu] employs a question-and-answer format to address the great distinction between external formation and disintegration;

thus, he distinguishes the four characteristics based on a single lifetime (*kalpa*), yet they are not non-existent at the momentary level (*kṣaṇika*). Furthermore, this is presented as a formal treatise for clarity, following the system of the Saṃmitīya school.
This should be compared with the two sets of four characteristics found in the second fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The remaining text can be understood through careful reflection; it clarifies that there are causes and conditions for the two distinct characteristics arising from the *Abhidharmasamudaya-śāstra*.
Regarding "name-body" (*nāmakāya*)—up to "provisionally established as a name-body"—the commentary states:
Within the eighth section, there are three interpretations of the three dharmas; thus, the *Vyākhyā* (Explanatory Treatise) itself constitutes two parts, the first of which is as follows.

After explaining the three dharmas, there follows the explanation of their alternative names (*paryāya*). This section also has two parts: first, the individual explanation of the three; second, the collective interpretation of the three. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, the root text of the treatise; second, the commentary by the Master. This is the root text of the treatise. Regarding the term "augment" (*adhika*):
it is the name that is the "speech" (*vāk*); speech is sound, for it defines and distinguishes dharmas. Since the essence of a dharma has no name, the name is said to be an "augmentation."

"Augmentation" (*ādhika*) means "superimposition" (*samāropa*). Furthermore, "augmentation" refers to the fact that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), names (*nāman*), and so forth, which express phenomena, are superior to vocal sounds (*ghoṣa*);

for while vocal sounds can be joined with names and so forth, names and so forth do not [depend] on vocal sounds in that same way. Moreover, one who wishes to speak must necessarily rely upon names and so forth to produce speech, because speech is augmented by names and so forth;
thus, it is briefly said that [names etc. are the "augmentation of speech. Furthermore, "speech" (*vāk*) refers to vocal sound (*śabda*).

The intrinsic nature of phenomena is therein bent and curved; names and so forth are provisionally established upon it. Because they increase [the understanding] through speech, they are called "increasing speech" (*adhivacana*).
"Increasing" means adding. Although the meaning is likewise so, the essence is not such that the phenomenon cannot be expressed without speech;
therefore, because it does not possess both meanings, it is not termed "increasing speech."
Furthermore, regarding the "distinctions of intrinsic nature" (svabhāva-viśeṣa), it encompasses everything in its totality.
The commentary states: This subsequent explanation by the Master of the Commentary is as follows.

That which "manifests this notion" (*saṃjñā*)—where "notion" is a name—is explained as the cause of the name. Because it illuminates and manifests this name "eye" in a uniform manner, it is unchanging (*avikāra*).

This school [of thought] maintains that "transformation" (*pravṛtti*) signifies change and "alteration" (*anyathātva*) signifies difference. They hold that words merely abide as they were previously and do not undergo further transformation, alteration, or displacement.
