The term "transmigration" (*saṃsāra*) and those that follow are all explained based on the sequence of cause and effect;

thus, a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) is said to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Transmigration, however, can only be predicated of a continuum (*saṃtati*) and cannot apply to a single moment.

Regarding those who do not understand the term "uninterrupted," because its meaning is obscure, it is omitted here; however, this does not mean it is not part of the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*).
In this context, the word "continuity" (*saṃtati*) indicates that it is not a single moment, while the word "uninterrupted" (*anucchinna*) indicates that there is no gap.

Among the two interpretations presented in the *Vibhāṣā*, the first—that it refers exclusively to the establishment of the person (*pudgala*) based upon the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)—is similar in its broadness and narrowness to what was previously indicated.

Therefore, fearing that its substance would be subsumed under the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), it is only by being established within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) that its nature becomes manifest;

for it is not comprised of the sense-base of form alone. Second, [others] say that this is established upon the cause and effect of the five aggregates, as it is manifested within the sense-base of form.

However, the Master [Vasubandhu] rejects this interpretation, maintaining that it applies to all five aggregates because it is designated according to its basis, just as non-material qualities (*arūpadharma-guṇa*) follow their respective supports.

The form-body (*rūpakāya*) may also be said to pervade the ten directions; this [case of the ten dharmas] should likewise be so, for they can be described as existing throughout the ten directions according to their basis.
This is broader than the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), because within each direction there are three: first, the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*); second, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*);

and third, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). If it were not so, what would be explained here? For in the text concerning the subsequent ten dharmas, the sequence follows the momentum of their flow.
At that time, the four dharmas are distinguished solely on the basis of their sequential cause-and-effect relationship.
As for the remaining six dharmas—distinctness (*anyathātva*), association (*samprayoga*), sequence (*anukrama*), and combination (*sāmagrī*)—they pertain to all three time periods.

Within the category of distinctness, although wholesome and unwholesome actions each summon their own respective fruits as their distinctness, how could it be that co-arising dharmas also act as causes to produce feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth?
Because they are not fixed as distinct [entities], the *Traikālyaparīkṣā* (Treatise on the Three Times) cites one corner [of the case] to illustrate the correspondence [of cause and effect].
Although within this context it cites giving as resulting in wealth and so forth—thereby citing one corner—it also cites the fact that even in the present there are corresponding causes and effects;

thus, the text in the "Section on Directions" provisionally clarifies that it speaks only of the present. In reality, however, it applies to all three times, because in every age and every direction, [the principle] exists. If...
Just as spatial direction exists based on matter, yet it is said that within matter there is no distinct spatial direction with which it is associated;

so too, while there is the experience [of feeling] within sensation, it is said that within sensation there is no distinct experience with which it is associated. Regarding this meaning, one should carefully deliberate upon the point of conjunction (*saṃnipāta*).
Within the discussion of conjunction, one should provisionally argue for the present alone, because even when depending on cessation or depending on future objects, there is likewise conjunction.
This applies to all three periods of time; because the wording is general, it does not exclude them either.

Regarding the conditions such as "the faculties being unimpaired" and "the objects being present," take for instance the five consciousnesses: they necessarily require the four faculties to be complete.

When any one object appears, they do not depend on all [faculties] to arise through their own attention (*manasikāra*), nor do they depend on anything else. Other consciousnesses should be understood accordingly based on what is appropriate. Question: Do the five consciousnesses rely on four faculties?

If one [of the conditions] is missing, visual consciousness cannot arise; it must necessarily depend on both color (varṇa) and shape (saṃsthāna). If one is missing, [consciousness] cannot be produced. Answer:

It is because the basis (*āśraya*) provides the dominant influence (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and exerts power. If [the basis] is missing, [consciousness] does not arise. The object (*viṣaya*) serves as the remote objective condition (*parokṣālambana*).

Regarding the difficulty that attention (*manasikāra*) arises immediately upon encountering [the object], this should also be understood accordingly. One should consult and verify this against the *Yogācārabhūmi-viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* and the third section of the *Maulī Bhūmi*.

Within the establishment of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), there is first a question and subsequently an answer. Within the answer, there is first a brief exposition followed by a detailed one. Within the detailed exposition, there is first an explanation of the mind, which has two parts:

(1) the explanation of its alternative names, and (2) the proof of its existence. In the explanation of the alternative names, the root treatise first provides the explanation of the mind by citing its various names;

subsequently, the commentary explains the meaning of the preceding [term] by citing the alternative name "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*). Regarding the habitual tendencies, they are the objects of that which is explained.
"Infusion" (*vāsanā*) is a general term; it refers to the four names such as "all seeds" (*sarvabīja*), etc., because they are able to accumulate various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

This constitutes the meaning of the preceding [verse on] the mind. Among the many names for the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the verse says: "Non-perishing, the original abode, storehouse, seed, stainless, holder, object-condition, manifestation, transformation, mind, support, distinct consciousness, root, and birth—among these many names, only 'storehouse' (*ālaya') [is used here].

(Note: The text provided appears to be a commentary on a verse summarizing the various synonyms for the *ālayavijñāna*. The final sentence identifies "storehouse" (*ālaya*) as the specific term being emphasized in this context.)
One name, "ālaya," refers to that which undergoes transformation and maturation, and whose objects of discernment are exhausted within the aggregates of existence (*bhava-aṅga-vijñāna*).

Five names apply exclusively to the *vipāka-vijñāna*. The remaining eleven names apply to the *ādāna-vijñāna*, meaning it holds the seeds of the fundamental abode without perishing, and is the basis for the manifestation of the stainless mind.
These include the "fundamental consciousness" (*mūla-vijñāna*) and so forth; herein lies the *an-āśraya-vijñāna*.

This refers to that which can repeatedly cause [the continuum] to arise and persist— namely, *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)— and that which can grasp and take up the continuity of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*),
maintaining the sense faculties (*indriya*) and so forth so that they do not perish— namely, *vijñapti-mātra*. Because these two meanings—

the ability to maintain the seeds of all phenomena (*dharmas*) and the ability to appropriate the physical bases of the sense organs (*rūpīndriya-adhiṣṭhāna*)— are explained together as one, it is collectively termed [the ālayavijñāna].
The *Upādāna* (Grasping) treatise distinguishes the latter two [categories] based on the sense of being able to produce cognitive experience (*vijñapti*) and the sense of not producing it;

this [text], concerning the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), collectively names them the "five causes of grasping. Within the refutation of the grasped (*upātta*), there are two parts: first, one cause that generally refutes the non-existence of the six entities;
second, four [causes] that specifically refute the non-existence of the three natures and the six consciousnesses. Within these latter four causes, there are four further divisions.
The first [of the ten proofs] refutes the nature of good and evil; the latter three refute the maturation, the indeterminate, and grasping.
Regarding the "only-consciousness" (vijñaptimātra) proofs, the third proof at the end of the tenth [chapter] and the fourth proof are excellent.

Within this context, there may be the inclusion of various forms of conduct, such as those of yoga, the ordinary, majestic, artistic, and transformational; these are abbreviated here. Among the eight proofs, the first proof provides a general refutation.
Regarding the various schools, the second and third [sections] exclude the Mahāsāṃghika and others, as they assert that the six consciousnesses arise simultaneously.

The fourth [section] refutes the Sautrāntika and the Mahāsāṃghika; even if one were to grant the Sautrāntika position regarding perfuming from those [consciousnesses], it would still not be possible for the Mahāsāṃghika and others to maintain that the seeds of perfuming are received by the six consciousnesses arising together. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states in the section on "Proof": "Furthermore, those..."

Since consciousness would not be able to flow continuously for a long duration if it were interrupted for a long time, we know that within this [stream], the continuity of mind is interrupted for a long period, yet it continues to flow without ceasing for a long duration. This continuity is due to its admixture with the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
Furthermore, by citing the four types of karmic activity as evidence, one establishes each moment through the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) by means of inference (*anumāna*).

These four functions must exist for the consciousness at the moment of death to be established as *vijñapti-mātra*. In the third chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the six types of transformational consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*) are refuted as being such [consciousnesses].
However, both the *Yogācārabhūmi* and this treatise state only that "it is not the case that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) sometimes does not function.

This is based on the argument that, in states where consciousness definitely exists, it is present; whereas in the moments preceding death, the five sensory consciousnesses have already ceased. Thus, regarding all instances of the end of life:

The mind of the three natures may temporarily lack moisture, but the mind that produces birth must certainly exist; this is because ordinary beings possess the moisture of both present and seed-states.
"Intention" (manas) refers to the cessation of consciousness acting as the mental faculty (manas).
The commentary states: The second section, the explanation of the meaning, has two parts. Within this main text of the treatise, there are two sections:
first, the explanation of the seventh consciousness (the *manas*), and second, the explanation of the six consciousnesses, which likewise take the *manas* as their support.
Regarding the first part, according to the subsequent text, there are four sections, which analyze the *vijñapti-mātratā* through four gates; this is the fortieth gate.

In this section, there are four headings; however, there are only five [topics]: the lack of objective aspect (*ākāra*), the basis (*āśraya*), and the remaining three—concomitance (*sahabhū*), inclusion (*saṃgraha*), and bondage to the realms (*dhātu-bandhana*).
Regarding the four headings, first is the object (*ālambana*), which is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). As for the fourth, there are explanations from four masters;

these should be verified as they are set forth there. Here, it is explained according to the stage of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*) prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), where its nature is defined as conceptual deliberation (*vitarka-vicāra*).

As for that, "deliberation" (*manana*) means to measure; because it measures, it is a cognitive aspect (*ākāra*). Since this [consciousness] takes deliberation as its cognitive aspect, other [factors] are not mentioned.
This is as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Commentary on Consciousness-Only), where there are two parts:

first, the explanation of the seventh consciousness, and second, the explanation of the cessation of the manas. In the first part, there are again two sections: first, explaining the previously clarified points through four meanings, and second, providing a detailed analysis.

At the time of its prior arising, there were two [aspects] within it; for what reason is it that it will certainly not arise later? Because it is definitively non-existent, it is omitted and not discussed.
Regarding the noble path, various masters hold differing views as to whether the noble wisdom of any given vehicle is partial or complete.
Among the eight consciousnesses within the cause, there are three categories: first, those that are both defiled and pure and are coarse.

This means that among the first six consciousnesses, two are subtle whether defiled or pure; the eighth is subtle in both defilement and purity; and the seventh is coarse in defilement and subtle in purity.

As for why the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and the noble path (*ārya-mārga*) may, as the case may be, either cease or not cease [the preceding consciousness], it is because they differ from the meditative state in their opposition to it.

Regarding the "mind that has ceased immediately prior" (*anantara-niruddham manaḥ*), as explained in ancient commentaries, this was understood within the context of the six consciousnesses based on their uncommon support (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*), but the basis [for the seventh] had not yet been explained.
Chapter Two: Establishing the Elements (*dhātu*). Within this section, there are two parts: first, a brief establishment;

second, a detailed analysis through questions and answers concerning those factors not subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*). Question: For what reason are form (*rūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) combined [into single aggregates], while mental factors (*caitta*) are separated [into their own aggregate]?
Why are mental factors excluded from the aggregate of form? And why are form and mental factors excluded from the aggregate of consciousness? The *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
Based on those beings to be converted, the World-Honored One spoke with intentional meaning regarding the ten [categories] such as "possessing form" and so forth:

because those born by transformation are deluded, they are deluded in three ways—first, being deluded that form alone is the self; second, not understanding the teaching of the twelve bases, they are deluded that both form and mind are the self;
and third, not understanding the teaching of the elements, they are deluded that mental factors alone are the self, and thus fail to comprehend [the true nature of things].

Regarding the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is said: "Because of the three [factors]—delusion, faculties, and inclination—there are two [sections] in the beginning: first, a brief explanation of the establishment;

second, a detailed analysis through questions and answers. Within this second section of questions and answers, the question regarding why the *dhātus* (elements) are not subsumed under the *skandhas* (aggregates) arises because the *skandhas* were previously explained as being the eighteen *dhātus*.
Fearing that there might be no distinction between *dhātus* and *skandhas*, this question is posed therein.

There are two parts: first, the question, followed by the answer. Within the answer, there are again two sections: first, a brief enumeration of the names to answer the preceding inquiry regarding the fundamental treatise alone;

second, a detailed explanation following that enumeration to answer the inquiry common to both masters. Within this latter section, there are two parts: first, the master of the commentary’s analysis and resolution of difficulties;
second, the individual explanations. Within these explanations, there are four parts: first, the explanation of *tathatā* (suchness); second, the explanation of... [text fragment].
Regarding the three types of space (*ākāśa*), there are three [types of] non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and four [types of] analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);

for the remaining three, there are three each, as there is a general question-and-answer section below. In the "Explanation of Objections," it says: "Since the nature of emptiness is divided into three according to its states, why are the others not likewise divided into three?

This refers to the fact that while the nature of space transforms, the three natures of non-analytical cessation—such as the cessation of dharmas and so forth—are also [treated similarly]. This is also...

Otherwise, the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) and *tathatā* (suchness), depending on their stages, are threefold; this has already been explained elsewhere as being based on the distinct meanings of suchness.
If it were the case that the mind transforms into suchness, it would not be what is here discussed. Therefore, like space and so forth, there would likewise be no three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

If one were to rely on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), then suchness could be described as having the principle of the three natures accordingly; however, for the others [space, etc.], it should not be so, and thus it is untenable.

In the explanation of *tathatā* (suchness), there are two parts: first, the general explanation of the excellence of *tathatā*, and second, the specific illustration of its non-excellence and neutrality.

In the first part, there are two sections: first, a brief listing of alternative names, and second, a detailed explanation according to those names. Regarding the "actual reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*) within the term "actual reality":

"actual" (*bhūta*) means non-erroneous. There are two interpretations: first, that it is the limit of suchness (*tathatā-koṭi*); second, that it refers to the wisdom that accords with suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*). If one follows the latter interpretation, it is not different from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Because of these distinctions, the former interpretation is superior.
Regarding "space" (ākāśa), [it extends] up to "because it performs its function.

The commentary states: There are two kinds of space; this is the first, which is the root treatise, while the latter is the explanatory commentary. The capacity to perform its function is to be understood accordingly.
This should be explained as follows: In the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it is also permissible for the third [unmanifest karma] to not obstruct the functioning of the mind;
thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* itself reconciles this contradiction. Within this explanation, there are two parts: first, a brief summary, and second, a detailed exposition.

Regarding the nature of the formless (*ārūpya*), "up to this" is the brief summary of "space" (*ākāśa*), while the remainder is the detailed exposition. Within the detailed exposition, there are three sections: first, a broad explanation of the aforementioned mental objects (*ālambana*). Second... [text continues].

The preceding [passage] on "only contradicting form" (*rūpa-viruddha-mātra*) is expanded; the preceding statement regarding "the absence of nature and characteristics" (*niḥsvabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) is expanded according to its meaning rather than following the sequential order.

In the explanation of "only contradicting form," the phrase "to distinguish from the common True Suchness (*tathatā*) shared by feeling and so forth" means that the four aggregates beginning with feeling are also called "commonly contradictory True Suchness.
Therefore, the principle of "contradicting form" and so forth intends to show that the aggregate of form is not merely...
To contradict emptiness is also to contradict *tathatā* (suchness), as [the characteristics of] *tathatā* and so forth universally contradict the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Because [characteristics] such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth contradict only *tathatā* and the like, they are distinct from emptiness. Regarding "impermanence and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes emptiness, selflessness, and the like.

Although these were already explained in the lower part of the original commentary regarding "rabbit horns and so forth," the subsequent text below explains the external objection: "Why are rabbit horns not mentioned?"

The horn also contradicts the five aggregates; however, it merely mentions *tathatā* (suchness) and so forth. Now, the answer is that there is no contradiction because its substance (*svabhāva*) does not exist.
Furthermore, regarding the subsequent explanation of the "hidden objection" concerning rabbit horns and the like: why is this [horn] not mentioned alongside the statement "contradicting matter"?

The answer is that both contradict the five aggregates, yet they differ in terms of existence and non-existence. Now, the explanation is that this is not the case; this is an explanation of the hidden objection, not a failure to mention it.

The horns of a rabbit and so forth are equal to space and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) because they do not contradict the fact that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are ultimately non-existent.
Thus, this first interpretation cannot be said to be unconditioned, for it does not contradict the nature of the five aggregates being non-existent.
The subsequent re-explanation asks: For what reason are the horns of a rabbit not described as the unconditioned space? The answer is: It is not merely because they contradict form (*rūpa*).

Furthermore, it contradicts the five aggregates, not merely matter alone; thus, the statement regarding the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) indicates that [the object] is not sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth.

This is because sensation and the others contradict matter alone, yet they do not lack intrinsic nature and characteristics. Here, "nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the essence (*tattva*), and "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to function (*vṛtti*).

Among these three meanings, the two points—that the mental object lacks intrinsic nature and that both are real—are the actual meaning. The claim that it "contradicts matter alone" is stated based on coarse characteristics and is not the ultimate truth.

Regarding the "Gate of Principle" (*nyāyamukha*), the section on "Discernment through Cessation" (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) explains the latter three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*). This is divided into two parts: first, a detailed individual explanation;

second, the Master’s analytical summary (*vicāra*). Within this summary, there are two sections: first, distinguishing the dharmas that ought to be abandoned; second, revealing the basis upon which the unconditioned is established.

The passage beginning with "It should be known that because afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned... refers to the fact that what is relied upon here—the feeling (*vedanā*)—is taken as both the faculty (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*).
The feelings associated with all phenomena are collectively termed "feelings that serve as the basis for afflictions.

Alternatively, they may be termed "feelings of abandonment" when one either eliminates the bondage of association or the bondage of the object, or when one severs the quality of rigidity and harshness. This does not require that the essence of the feeling be non-existent;

rather, it refers to the seeds and active manifestations of phenomena belonging to the three natures, which are all included as appropriate. Furthermore, regarding the "feeling that serves as the basis," some explain this as referring exclusively to the feeling that arises simultaneously [with the affliction].
Because this [disjunction] is obtained through the severance of the bonds associated with it, it is not a solitary severance like that of feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth;
for the latter is an unconditioned attainment (*asaṃskṛta-prāpti*) of disjunction at an improper time.

This passage refers to one part [of the matter], whereas the *Vibhāṣā* and *Abhidharmasamuccaya* refer to the solitary severance as one part, stating that it is a "temporary disjunction. According to the former interpretation, this passage is taken to exhaustively encompass both [types].
Because all [these] are exhausted, it is said here that the second yoga of *dausthulya* (gross heaviness) refers to afflictions, which are called both *dausthulya* and *anuśaya* (latent tendencies).

Matured (*vipāka*) dharmas are called *dausthulya* but not *anuśaya*. Wholesome factors (*kuśala-pakṣa*) cannot be so named, because their substratum (*āśraya*) is either capable or incapable [of such states].
Therefore, the present treatise states that the feeling (*vedanā*) which serves as the substratum is not called *dausthulya*.

If one takes only the simultaneous support (*āśraya*) and the feeling (*vedanā*) associated with it as distinct afflictions, they are not mentioned briefly because they are "coarse and heavy" (*dauṣṭhulya*);

yet in reality, they are indeed coarse and heavy. If, however, one takes both the faculties (*indriya*) and the objects (*viṣaya*) along with their associated feelings collectively under the name "support-feeling," then because "feeling" is a broader category, "coarse and heavy" is not mentioned;
for "coarse and heavy" includes states that are not of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*). Therefore, the essence of this hindrance to concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) encompasses both categories.

Because of the obstacle: if both obstacles are present, one definitely attains the fruit of dissociation; if they are not both present, there is only the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), because it does not harm the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
By this principle, [it extends] up to and including the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
The commentary states: Within the section on the "Gate of Establishing," there are two major divisions. First, the root treatise establishes [the categories];

Regarding the statement that "consciousnesses each clarify three supports based on their quantity" and that "eye-consciousness performs a single function regarding the eye-object":

this means that the two eyes perform the same function toward the object because they operate together; furthermore, they jointly produce a single consciousness because they serve as conditions for that single function toward the object.

In this context, only the aspect of physical beauty is taken into account when establishing the name "organ. Since the ear and nose organs each possess two [physical parts], they have already been included [within the category of being dual].

It is clearly evident; how could it not be clear? The tongue and body should likewise be so. These three locations differ slightly from one another, yet they assist each other to form an elegant symmetry.

Each produces two kinds [of results]. If there were two tongues and two bodies, they would not be said to be a single entity, because the power of the tongue assists the body and they are somewhat close to one another.
It is like two lamps emitting a single light, or the two great elements (mahābhūta) producing a single derived matter (upādāya-rūpa); yet, one still perceives many reflections.
Because their spheres of activity differ, there is a distinction in the objects of the third text. A question is raised based on what precedes it:

first, regarding the "near" (āsanna); second, regarding the "obstructed" (āvṛta). In the response, it is explained that because they possess resistance (sapratigha), they are obstructed and thus not clearly manifest;
because they are obstructed by others, they cannot strike one another simultaneously. Because they possess resistance, subtle gaps and minute fissures arise.
It is not clearly perceived when it enters the ear from a great distance through many intervening forms; however, when it reaches the vicinity of the ear, it becomes clear.
Even if there are gaps and subtle sounds are faintly manifest, they enter the ear in an even more minute form, and thus are not clearly perceived.

One should accordingly assign these points to the various texts within the seven types of discernment (*vibhāga*). Why are the five consciousnesses not called "possessing signs" (*sanimitta*)? They are called "spontaneous" (*svarasa*). Why? Because...

The five determinate consciousnesses arise in accordance with their respective objects, whereas other consciousnesses do not; thus, there is a commonality. Regarding the two types of mental aspects (*ākāra*), the consciousness is named after its predominant factor and is said to belong to the eye.

As for the seeds of consciousness, they follow the sense organs and do not follow the objects. Those who maintain that the object-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) exists as a distinct seed apart from the seed of the object consider this to be a superior proof for the theory of "arising from the same seed" (*samānajātīya-utpatti*).
Those who maintain the theory of "arising from the same seed" hold that the seeing-aspect (*darśanabhāga*) and the object-aspect do not arise from different seeds.

It is said that this explanation of form (*rūpa*) and so forth is based on the power of direct perception; since form arises in accordance with consciousness, how can it be said that it arises in association (*samprayukta*)?
Furthermore, the "substantial form" (*dravya-rūpa*) mentioned in the treatise is not a "form subject to grasping" (*upādāna-rūpa*), and thus there is no contradiction.

Within the presentation of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), these [categories] are merely presented in brief and in detail, respectively, due to the three factors of delusion (*moha*), faculties (*indriya*), and inclinations (*ruci*). Alternatively, there may be an element of the eye (*cakṣur-dhātu*) that is not the eye itself, namely the sense-base (*āyatana*).
At the stages of the *kalala*, *arbuda*, and *peśī*, there is first a mixture of impurities; next it is called the "blister" (*ghana*), and subsequently it solidifies.

That which is called "matured blood" is also termed "solidification. Because it gradually thickens and becomes more substantial, at five or seven days it is called *praśākhā*, which means "endowed with limbs.
Why, then, does this treatise state that it is not yet called "endowed with limbs" at three or seven days?

Although the sense-faculties (*indriya*) already exist at the time of conception, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) increases its function; however, because it has not yet reached a state of solidity and thickness, it cannot be described as being conjoined with the body-faculty.
Therefore, only the "three seven-day periods" are mentioned. Furthermore, the subsequent passage states that the "body-element" (*kāyadhātu*) is formed;

this refers specifically to the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), where there is no body, and not to other stages. Thus, we know that in the fourth seven-day period, the sense-faculties gradually arise, and in the fifth seven-day period, [the body is further developed].
When the first ten days are complete, it is designated as the "boundary" (*sīmā*); in reality, however, for the other four faculties, it requires seven days.
Within those seven days, the preceding four days are still termed the "boundary. This brief citation of the initial meaning subsumes the fourth point.

In the section on the analysis through questions and answers, there are two parts: first, an analysis by means of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding the six internal faculties and the elements;

second, an analysis based on the mutual conditioning of higher and lower [realms]. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the explanation of the five consciousnesses; second, the explanation of the mental faculty (*manas*).

Within the explanation of the five consciousnesses, there is first the presentation of the main argument and subsequently the commentary on that main argument. Within the main argument, the eye is named first, after which the others are treated by analogy. Within the commentary, there are two sections.

First, the fourfold dilemma regarding the eye is resolved; subsequently, the fourfold dilemma regarding the body is resolved by analogy. The meaning of this fourfold dilemma concerns the seventh and eighth consciousnesses.

It is not that the immediately preceding consciousness has ceased; rather, because the final moment of the mind exists in the present, the consciousness that enters the past becomes the "mind-base" (*manas*).
This is because it possesses the sense of being a substantial entity. Alternatively, when the final mind is in the present, it can function as the "mind-base."
When entering the past, its characteristics become manifest; it is not that the meaning of the sūtra only applies once one has entered the past.

Therefore, the immediately preceding cessation [of the mind] is taken as primary. Regarding the second phrase, because one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the seventh consciousness is not taken [as primary].

The two masters, Anahbuddhi and Dharmapāla, offer conflicting explanations of these two phrases in this treatise: Dharmapāla maintains that within the attainment of cessation there is a pure seventh consciousness, whereas [Anahbuddhi maintains that] it exists in the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi*).

Since the seventh [consciousness] is neither defiled nor non-defiled, it does not exist; thus, according to Sthiramati, the eighth mental consciousness exists in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Why is it not mentioned? Because the discussion concerns the basis of defilement.

Regarding the mutual objectification between the upper and lower realms, there are three parts: first, the explanation of the eyes and ears; second, the explanation of the nose, tongue, and body; and finally, the explanation of the mind.

Regarding the meaning of the beginning, there are two parts: first, the root treatise; second, the subsequent commentary which explains it. Herein, the eleven kinds of "manifestations" (*vijñapti*) consist only of contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*).

If they were uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), there would be only nine, excluding the coarse (*audārika*) and the inferior (*hīna*). [Question: What is the meaning of the five, six, four, and eight? [Question:

In what sense is the meaning of "accumulation" (*caya*) called an "aggregate" (*skandha*)? [Answer: It refers to the meaning of various entities being summoned together, like sprouts [growing from seeds].
The sense of functioning in combination; the sense of a single class or general summary; the sense of superimposition and denial—these constitute the meaning of "accumulation" (*caya*).

Herein, the first [category] consists of three, which are the names of the accumulations; the second consists of four, which are the entities of the accumulations, or the four general entities that possess various types of accumulations according to their various names.
Within the [eighteen] elements (*dhātu*), the remaining elements are the sixty-two elements; the remaining bases (*āyatana*) are subsumed therein.

Regarding the meaning of the "bases" (*āyatana*) as the differentiation of all phenomena, there are now five ways of explaining the bases of liberation (*vimokṣasthāna*), as found in [treatises such as] the *Niniju* (96), the *Shichi* (97), and other commentaries.
Among these, one explanation is like that in the commentary on the metaphors for the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Another explanation follows the previous citation and assignment.

A third explanation holds that the four [bases] collectively pervade the five aggregates, because the perversions of perception (*saṃjñā*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), and mind (*citta*) pervade the five aggregates; this is as explained in the eighth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Now...

The *Nyāyānusāra* explains these according to their meaning; it is not necessary to follow the sequential assignment of the mind as "selflessness," form as "purity," feeling as "minor flavor," perception as "lack of solidity," and formations as "unreality.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* opens this into two, stating: "Because they are neither solid nor real.
In the eighty-third [section], the five aggregates are explained through metaphors: consciousness is like a magical illusion (*māyā*), and there is certainly no agent, recipient, or self to be found.
Having attained these, there are nine types of liberation: five liberations of the bases, and four types of practice—first, practice leading to the immovable;

second, practice leading to the sphere of nothingness; third, practice leading to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; fourth, the bodhisattva in the present life; and fifth, the noble liberation.
For what reason are these five liberations of the bases established? It is because a noble disciple who has already seen the path of truth but has not yet abandoned desire [for the form realm].
There are two types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*): namely, the affliction of desire and the affliction of further existence. Regarding these two, one diligently cultivates the purification of the mind.
When exerting oneself in the application of practice (*prayoga*) to sever the affliction of desire, one gradually relies upon three modes of conduct:

It is said that there are eight or seven types of discrimination based on the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*. According to the treatises on the first six consciousnesses, the five sensory consciousnesses only take the present as their object and are termed "spontaneous" (*svarasa*).

Vipāka (maturation) is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), as stated in the *Ṣaṣṭhadvāra-vijñapti* and other treatises. Six categories are common to both natures (indeterminate and wholesome):

namely, the sets of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), and spatial direction (*deśa*). These are exclusively indeterminate. Furthermore, contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena that are wholesome are exclusively indeterminate, whereas uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena are exclusively wholesome.

The nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is common to both the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), and thus it is severed by the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Phenomena abandoned through the Path of Seeing are likewise common to both [the unwholesome and the obscured-indeterminate].

Because it is by nature [indeterminate], it exists only within the cause; the material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta), as explained below in the fourth and fifty-seventh [sections].
Since it is stated they are "exclusively indeterminate," one should know that they are neither results nor of other natures; that they exist as results can be understood [from other sources].

As for the remaining fifteen types, they pertain to all three natures (trividha-svabhāva), which is consistent with both principle and textual authority. Regarding whether the six sense organs (ṣaḍ-āyatana) are sentient or insentient, there is no explicit Mahāyāna text [on this point]; one should infer based on [the following].

Regarding the bases (*āśraya*) established by the Hīnayāna, one should reflect on the seventh [chapter]: how many are nurtured (*aupacayika*) and how many are outflowing (*naiṣyandika*). As for the analysis of the eight [categories] such as those abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*), there are three types:

first, those that are not abandoned at all, namely the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); second, those abandoned solely by vision, namely the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*); and third, those abandoned by both vision and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*), namely the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*). The citations for these two [the last two] are as previously mentioned.

Regarding the eighth chapter, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it states that there are two senses of "abandonment": first, that which is not abandoned; and second, that which is abandoned solely by vision, referring to the state of being an ordinary person. These two are cited as before. The third category consists of those abandoned by both vision and cultivation, namely the state of non-conception.

The *Treatise on the Consciousness-Only Nature of the Maturation of Non-conceptualization*, Volume Eight: If it is said that [the non-conceptual attainment] does not arise because it is abandoned, then the non-conceptual attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth would be abandoned only by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
If it is said that they are abandoned by severing the objects and fetters, then their nature as wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth would be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

[However,] the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (53) states that the non-conceptual heaven (*asaṃjñi-deva*) and so forth are abandoned by insight; thus, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (53) also permits that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) likewise extends to being abandoned by insight.

Therefore, it is also admitted that those which are not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). This is because the sixty-ninth [treatise] states that the wholesome and the indeterminate are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Thus, these are abandoned by means of the objects of cognition (*ālambana-bandha*). The remaining twenty types are common to both abandonment by insight and abandonment by cultivation, as well as being non-abandonable (*aprahātavya*).

Among the seventeen [factors] categorized as threefold, excluding the three beginning with "name" (*nāman*), if the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and others are common to the non-abandonable category, they are excluded from the threefold classification.

Why is it that among the fifty-seven faculties (indriya), twenty-two are taught as being: fourteen partially abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and partially abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*);
twelve partially abandoned by cultivation and partially not abandoned (*aprahātavya*)—namely, the first six and the other six;
and two that are not abandoned? [The answer is: First, even with respect to the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*), they are also concordant [with their respective natures].
Since the principle is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the three categories such as the "body of names" (*nāmakāya*) exist if the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are universally uninterrupted;

if they do not exist, they are abandoned only through seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*). This cannot be used as an objection, because the matter included in the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*) also possesses spatial extension. Regarding the five stages:

first, the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*); second, the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), which is said to be the tenth stage of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) within the path of faith (*śraddhā-pratipanna*).
Regarding the statement that the four paths of seeing and the four paths of cultivation begin from the second bhūmi onwards:

if this were so, why does the fourteenth chapter state that among the ten stages of the bodhisattva path, the path that serves as the antidote to the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is cultivated even in the first bhūmi? Furthermore, since the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) involves the path of cultivation, it follows by analogy that the same must apply to the first bhūmi.

Moreover, the ninth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that the first bhūmi encompasses both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation. Thus, [the path of cultivation exists in the first bhūmi]. Five.
The ultimate path, the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and its retribution exist in the initial stage. The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:
"Śāriputra sought the path to bodhi for eighty thousand kalpas; the reason he regressed was that he had not yet attained the dharma of liberation," and so forth, as explained at length.
Thus, one regresses prior to entering that state to receive retribution; once one has entered it, one does not regress, nor does one enter that absorption again thereafter.
It is said that from the sixth stage of the ten faiths, the "non-retrogressive mind" (*avivartika-citta*) onward, this position contradicts the [calculation of] eighty thousand *kalpas*.

One single mind constitutes ten thousand *kalpas*, for it is only at the eighth mind that one truly becomes non-retrogressive. Upon inquiry, it is found that within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), there are those who proceed directly and those whose minds turn back.

Those whose minds turn back pass through all five stages, whereas those who proceed directly do not belong to the first two; however, once they have entered the [Bodhisattva] grounds (*bhūmi*), they certainly do.
There are many such passages as those in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and others; as explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, they do not accord [with this].

Regarding the statement that they exist "in the preceding four stages," this follows the principle previously explained regarding the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*). It also applies to the five stages, the thirteen realms (*dhātu*), and the nine levels (*bhūmi*).

The state of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is neither a realm nor the level of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-bhūmi*). The state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and its retribution belong only to the fourth dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*). This refers to names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*).
Since *vyañjana* (phoneme) is a differentiation of vocal sound, it exists only in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

If one considers the term "name" (*nāman*), then names—such as those arising from the perfuming of verbal expressions (*abhilāpa-vāsanā*)—pervade all three realms and nine stages (*navabhūmi*). Only [the category of] "name" exists in the two aforementioned realms and the five lower stages;
the remaining thirteen [categories] pervade all three realms and nine stages. Furthermore, for each of the individual gates below, a separate treatise is established based on these five [points].

Regarding the gates of understanding: [the first] twenty-four possess two; the mindless states possess five; the fruit of non-perception possesses four; and the remainder possess only three. Regarding the gates:
however, only that which maintains a single stage is called a "stage" (*bhūmi*); from the second stage upward, they are not designated by the name "stage. Other dharmas are not named "stages.

*Manaskāra* (attention) is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) that induces [them], and thus it shares the name "stage"; otherwise, it would not receive that name. This applies equally to the other three.
Although the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the fruit of non-conception (*āsaṃjñika*) is induced by attention, it is not mentioned because it is remote and not proximate.
Within the section analyzing the eighteen categories, first the nature and essence of "acquisition" (*prāpti*) is explained. In the fifty-second [treatise], it says:

"That which is the cause for the gathering, sustaining, and intensification of arising conditions is called 'acquisition. Its functional efficacy is conventionally designated as 'attainment' (*samanvāgama*); how does this differ from 'possession' (*samanvāgama*)? This is now explained.

The essence of a dharma (*dharmatā*) is the cause; when its causal function has not yet arisen, it is termed "possession" (*samanvāgama*). When that causal function arises and is grasped, becoming intensified, it is called "attainment" (*prāpti*).
Therefore, it is said below that there are three types of possession, namely: the possession of the seeds of afflictions (*kleśa-bīja-samanvāgama*), and so forth.

The subsequent section clarifies that the entities of the various noble ones (*ārya*) are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti-mātra*), as is extensively refuted in the first chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (the *Triṃśikā*).

Furthermore, because there are two distinct categories—the attainment of the name "accomplishment" through the cultivation of various dharmas as the causal condition for the ultimate reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), and the attainment of the name "establishment" through the dharma itself—there is a distinction between these two types of attainment.

That master [Sthiramati] follows the Hīnayāna view in this regard; however, since external dharmas manifest without seeds, they cannot be said to have *vijñapti-mātratā* as their essence, and thus there would be no attainment of them.
This reasoning is incorrect, for all seeds are termed "accomplished," and it is precisely on this basis that [the position is established].

The three types of attainment (*prāpti*) that encompass all phenomena are not exhaustive in this regard. In the Hinayana, one establishes a single "attainment" (*prāpti*) upon three categories of phenomena:
first, conditioned phenomena; second, the two paths, namely analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); and third, the basis, namely non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

This is explained in detail in the *Prāpti-varga* of the *Samāpatti-skandha* of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. Regarding space (*ākāśa*), there is no attainment; rather, attainment belongs to that which is attained, for its nature is such that it is invariably concomitant with what it attains.

Because it increases or decreases [in accordance] with that, that which belongs to the path is of a nature connected to the path; since its acquisition (*prāpti*) likewise follows the three grades of the path, it belongs to the path.

That which belongs to the basis—where "basis" refers to the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*)—is acquired neither through analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā*) nor as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nor by means of the path;

therefore, its acquisition belongs only to the basis. Now, in the Mahāyāna, the acquisition of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) definitely belongs to the acquired phenomenon itself, whereas the acquisition of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*)...
Furthermore, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) definitely belongs to the Path;

that is to say, when the six types of practice suppress the afflictions, their seeds do not arise due to the absence of conditions, and the resulting unconditioned state is subsumed under non-analytical cessation. All treatises state that this is not merely because it harms the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*);
therefore, apart from this, the acquisition of other non-analytical cessations definitely belongs to its basis, and that basis is precisely the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

Now, judging by reason, in the Mahāyāna, because the seeds that arise subsequent to the conjunction of non-analytical conditions are not permanently extinguished, "attainment through non-analysis" (*apratisaṃkhyā-prāpti*) belongs only to the seeds of dharmas;
it differs from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), where the essence of the dharma is eternally without a basis to which it belongs. However, there are now three types of attainment through non-analysis:
first, those belonging to the seeds, such as dharmas arising subsequent to the conjunction of conditions; second, those belonging to the seeds of the basis (*āśraya*).
Because it is extinguished, the *Pañcāśatikā* states that within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the meditative absorption of the non-percipient realm (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) will never arise;

thus, three [factors] belong to that path. The six practices (*ṣaḍākāra*) subdue the afflictions and one then enters the noble path (*āryamārga*); because seeds do not arise again, they do not belong to the seeds.

Because they are not ultimate and do not arise due to the absence of conditions, they do not belong to the basis (*āśraya*). Since they are obtained through the power of the path, they belong only to [the path].

It is thus: here again, we shall make a distinction. In the Hīnayāna, the attainment (*prāpti*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) pertains to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and includes both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

In the Mahāyāna, it is the same as in the Hīnayāna. Regarding the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), its attainment in the Hīnayāna is exclusively of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*) and pertains to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated;

in the Mahāyāna, it is wholesome in nature like that [Hīnayāna], yet it is subsumed exclusively under the uncontaminated. All treatises state that "analytical cessation" refers to the permanent destruction of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

That which is acquired without deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-prāpta*) in the Hīnayāna is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and impure (*sāsrava*), as it belongs to the [category of] generic similarity (*nikāya-sabhāga*);
whereas in the Mahāyāna, it encompasses all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). This is because it is established based on both the seeds (*bīja*) and their substratum (*āśraya*).

Since the *Abhidharmapada* (the fourth section of the *Jñānaprasthāna*) states that seeds encompass all three types, it is said that they include both the impure and the pure; thus, this acquisition exists within the body of a Tathāgata.

Therefore, erroneous principles do not arise. Furthermore, the absence of conditions for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth are established merely based on the two categories of sentient and insentient things.

Among the fifty-two types of causes explained as being subsumed under the conditions for arising—namely, the causes of appropriation (*parigraha*) and dominance (*adhipati*)—these are termed "attainment" (*prāpti*).

Since all external seeds that exist within the internal body are causes of those [conditions], they are also called "attainment. This "attainment" applies to both the insentient and the *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only).
The treatises state that the wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) accomplishes the seven treasures, including those that are non-sentient; this refers to the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*).

Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Second Chapter) states that if "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is taken as true suchness (*tathatā*), then one must necessarily attain it, just as one attains cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If, however, "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is taken as that which is transformed by the mind alone and is comprised within sentient beings, it is clearly revealed [as the meaning here].

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states that this [non-analytical cessation] is subsumed under the untainted (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, its acquisition (*prāpti*) also extends to both the tainted and the untainted;

since the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of things (*vastu-śūnyatā*) do not contradict one another, there is no conflict. As for the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it may belong to the basis (the support), because apart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), it has no separate entity.

Alternatively, it belongs to the seeds, because all seeds arise only when conditions are present; thus, [this cessation] consists in the non-arising of seeds due to the deficiency of conditions. However, as for...
Since the fruit of Buddhahood is not produced by false principles, how could it depend on seeds? Therefore, it belongs to the category of the "basis" (*āśraya*). Regarding its size:

the Hīnayāna establishes two [types of attainment], while the Mahāyāna establishes only one; for once that dharma has been attained, one is able to become perfected by oneself. However, there is no textual evidence for this;

in various treatises, it is only said that attainment is provisionally established in relation to dharmas, and we do not see attainment being established as something further separate from the attainment itself. Furthermore, if...

Regarding the establishment of the "acquisition" (*prāpti*) for minor instances of urination, it is permitted that one may briefly assume such a status while posing the question: For example, when a major acquisition occurs, there is no separate "acquisition of acquisition" (*prāptiprāpti*).

When the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) takes a seed as its object, there is no separate seeing-part [of the acquisition] that sees it. If you say: "The seeing-part takes the aspect (*nimitta*) as its object and understands it as an aspect;

however, when it takes itself as its object, it does not understand it as an aspect," [we reply]: That seeing-part does not take the acquisition as its own object. This is because it is explained according to the principle of "establishment" (*siddhi*); therefore, there is no separate [acquisition].

If that were the case, then by analogy with the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the acquisitions (*prāpti*) should likewise lack minor characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*). If minor characteristics were absent, one should explain it thus:

the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) is not of limited measure (*parimāṇa*), yet the seeing-portion does not perceive itself; therefore, the acquisition, though lacking limited measure, is able to perceive itself.

Furthermore, according to the principle that the characteristics of "arising" (*jāti*) and so forth exist upon [the primary dharmas] such as anger (*krodha*) and resentment (*upanāha*), one must admit that a secondary characteristic is established upon a provisional (*prajñapti*) dharma, and furthermore, a major characteristic is established upon that [secondary characteristic].
Although these are provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*), what prevents them from being further established as provisional? Even so, there is no obstacle;

for if they can be established independently, why must one further establish four time periods (*adhvan*)? Regarding the statement that "dharmas are obtained simultaneously" because only the present exists:

now, according to the three types of accomplishment, within one realm there are seeds of the three realms. Since there are seeds in a single period of existence, how can it be said that dharmas are provisionally designated as belonging to the three times?

There is no contradiction in one *dhātu* becoming three *dhātus*, nor in there being three time periods for a single momentary dharma (*ekakṣaṇadharma*), which is merely designated as having three time periods.

What contradiction is there in one *dhātu* becoming three *dhātus* at a given time? The designation of "dharma" based on its prior and subsequent states allows for the establishment of the three time periods without impediment;

thus, the three types of "attainment" (*prāpti*) are simply the act of acquisition itself. This is consistent with what is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (or *Vyākhyāyukti*), and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. However, the Hīnayāna...

Regarding the attainment of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), there are three types of attainment: those that exist previously, those that arise simultaneously, and those that arise subsequently—such as the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) at the conclusion of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

Now, one should reflect accordingly upon whether these are fully possessed or partially possessed. As for the four or five questions and answers concerning what was previously attained and what was not:
for example, the Prātimokṣa vows are called "not previously attained" because they are newly produced in every moment; nevertheless, they are still seeds of the contaminated (*sāsrava*).

Furthermore, as in the case of [the acquisition of] characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is established that acquisition (*prāpti*) and that which is acquired (*prāpya*) are co-existent and possess a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Now, in the Mahāyāna, acquisition is established as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for that which is acquired, and there is no contradiction in this. If that is so, one might ask why names (*nāman*) and so forth are not treated similarly.
The explanation is: because names and so forth cannot depend upon the sound (*śabda*) that expresses them, they do not constitute a co-existent cause; this is because they lack such power.

Because it possesses power over phenomena, acquisition (*prāpti*) constitutes a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). It can acquire conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), being subsumed under whichever conditioned phenomena exist;

it can also acquire unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), being subsumed under whichever unconditioned phenomena exist. However, the nature of phenomena does not mutually enter into one another, and the acquisition of an unconditioned phenomenon does not follow its basis, as has already been explained previously.
In each moment, many small acquisitions are formed, occurring only for phenomena that have never before been acquired.
It can be understood by reflecting that while [the seeds] increase moment by moment, the others do not.

Regarding the name and essence of "non-conceptual absorption" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*): according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts, it is an *upapada-ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative compound), meaning "the absorption based on non-conception";

alternatively, it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), meaning "the absorption that is itself non-conception. Now, if the seed of the mind’s aversion is called "absorption," then the substance of the mind that arises [therefrom] should likewise be called [absorption].
Emerging from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*) is the real seed, whereas emerging from absorption and entering absorption (*samāpatti*) are provisional seeds.

Furthermore, regarding the nine grades, which grade is the supreme grade? As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there should be two [types of seeds], yet the number of their entities would differ in magnitude.

Now, it is explained that the eighteen mental factors definitely exist: namely, the eleven—universal (*sarvatraga*), object-specific (*viniyata*), and wholesome (*kuśala*)—along with the mind itself, or perhaps adding the object-specific factors.
"One, two, three, four" refers to the twenty-two factors of a noble one (*ārya-dharma*). These twenty-two factors are not necessarily required;

as stated in the Hīnayāna, their essence may be a single entity that collectively relies upon various types [of seeds]. Now, it is said that this is not so, because this meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is established based on various types [of seeds].
The previous explanation is superior. Third, regarding the physical basis and location: he merely cites the *Abhidharmakośa*, but here we present the Mahāyāna explanation.

Fifty-sixth: First in the desire realm and subsequently in the form realm. Refer to *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle 7. Regarding the four preparatory means (*prayoga*), the first chapter of the *Vyākhyāyukti* (*Xianyang shengjiao lun*) states:

"Having abandoned the desires of the lower stages and regarding perceptions as like a disease and so forth, up to the thought that even the Heaven of Non-conception is tranquil and subtle, one takes the perception of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-saṃjñā*) as the preliminary means. Fifth: That which was previously attained and that which has never been attained before, now...

As explained previously, these are also both previously acquired and not previously acquired. However, because they are newly produced as something never before obtained, they are called "not previously acquired.
Since they are seeds of outflows (*āsrava*), they are also "previously acquired," just like the *prātimokṣa* vows.

Furthermore, because things such as the three untainted states (*anāsrava*)—like the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)—have never arisen from the beginning, they are called "not previously acquired. This [is the distinction].

Regarding the middle [point]: if it is asked whether there is cultivation through practice (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*) or cultivation through attainment (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) for the first six [perfections], the answer is no, because there are no dharmas that manifest [in those stages].

(7) There should be skillful means (*upāya*), which is not attained by being free from desire (*vairāgya-lābha*), but is attained solely through skillful means, because it arises from preparatory application (*prayoga*).

(8) If one were to claim it is attained by being free from desire, then for a noble one (*ārya*) who has already attained it, there would be the fault of [the perfection] being already accomplished (*samanvāgata*). Regarding those who fall back (*parihāṇika*) and those who do not (*aparihāṇika*), see the fifty-third [verse] and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

The seventh [point] states that there are three grades of cultivation—such as those subject to regression or non-regression—and distinctions such as those resulting in rebirth in this life (*upapadyavedanīya*) or subsequent lives. It explains that these apply generally to both those who regress and those who do not.
Regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it says that one first gives rise to [the path] here [in the desire realm] and subsequently in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, its interpretation is the same as that of the Hīnayāna: that it results only in rebirth in the form realm. How can it be said to result only in rebirth?

Regarding the ten types of collective and individual retributions, it is said that because they are not karma, they do not produce a collective retribution. If this is so, how could volition (*cetanā*) as a seed not produce one?

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "When the mind is clear and manifest prior to meditative absorption, volition produces a collective [retribution]; when the mind is unconscious, volition is obscure and thus produces individual [retributions].
The subsequent term "notion of departure" (*niḥsaraṇa-saṃjñā*) refers to the departure from the experience of transformation (*pariṇāma-vedanā*), for it is certainly present.

Regarding the karma of the desire realm that ripens in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*), although there is no textual evidence for its existence in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there is such evidence in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, because it states that in the northern regions there certainly exist such karmas that ripen in a subsequent life; the meaning is as explained in the standard commentaries.

As for the "distinction in the state of the basis" (*āśraya-bhūmi-viśeṣa*), the text says the "basis" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because it serves as the basis for the practitioner; furthermore, it says the "basis" refers to the body composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-kāya*).
It is established as a basis because it differs from the state of having a mind as previously described;

however, since the teaching of *vijñapti-mātra* holds that the basis—the body—is distinct between the two states of having a mind and being without a mind, "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*) is provisionally established.

Because absorption is taken as the agent of cessation and the actual mind and so forth are taken as the objects of cessation, it is said that it is called "cessation" by virtue of its capacity to cease [the mind].

Regarding the "Cessation Attainment" (*nirodha-samāpatti*), its name and essence are to be understood according to the preceding [attainments]. For one who has attained the cessation of consciousness-only, this "attainment" (*samāpatti*) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the attainment of cessation," or it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "cessation itself as the attainment.
It may also be called "mindless" (*acittaka*) or "the cessation of feeling and perception" (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha*);

these names are all based on what is predominant. Only the name used here [for this specific attainment] is exhaustive according to the underlying principle. Regarding the two entities and their numerical magnitude, they are the same as those previously mentioned. This [attainment] necessarily possesses wisdom (*prajñā*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Because these are untainted (*anāsrava*), they must necessarily comprise nineteen [mental factors]: the five universal (*sarvatraga*) factors, the discernment (*prajñā*) from among the five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) factors, and concentration (*samādhi*);
the remainder are all as previously stated. There should be fifty-six [factors] based on the physical body (*āśraya*).

Furthermore, this treatise states below that [the eighth consciousness] first arises here [in the desire realm] and subsequently manifests again in the form realm (*rūpadhātu), relying upon a material basis (*rūpāśraya*). Therefore, the teaching of the eighth consciousness has not yet been established here; if it were already established...
It is established that [this concentration] manifests everywhere; however, one might ask:

since there are no bodhisattvas born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) because they have necessarily abandoned birth there, how can it be said that through faith in the teaching one is born there and enters this concentration? There are two kinds of faith:

first, faith followed by practice, which refers to bodhisattvas; second, faith without yet practicing, which refers to those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Although they believe in the Mahāyāna teachings...

Because they are unable to practice it, faith having already arisen toward that [state], they enter this meditative absorption. Furthermore, one understands through the teaching on the eighth consciousness that those in the higher realms are permitted to enter it;

yet, there are those who do not believe in the teaching of the eighth consciousness, such as the followers of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), who maintain that those in the Formless Realm cannot enter this absorption.
The *Udāyin-sūtra* provides clear evidence for this, stating that one transcends the gods who subsist on physical food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) and is born among the gods of mental creation (*manomaya*).

Therefore, as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there should be no fixed regression. Why, then, is it said later in the section on the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) that [the defilements] manifest again?

This means that since the seeds have already been severed and do not arise again, they are "severed"; once severed, they are no longer existent, and we do not admit the possibility of their being lost later through the consciousness that serves as the basis for outflows (*sāsrava*).
Regarding the four applications of cultivation (*catvāraḥ prayogāḥ*), it is said that during the first two kalpas, one is equal to the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka-pratyekabuddha*).
One must first master the meditative absorption of the eight stages (*aṣṭabhūmi-samādhi*) through both regressive and progressive cultivation;

only upon reaching the ninth stage can one enter from the third *kalpa* onward, and thereafter the Buddha enters them spontaneously. As stated in the *Mahā-śāstra*, fascicle 12, and as explained in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, fascicle 18, this should be reflected upon.
However, it is said that even Śrāvakas who cultivate superior faculties (*adhimātra-indriya*) are also able to leap over one [stage].
Having thoroughly examined various texts, it appears that the number of persons [attaining liberation] varies; in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), there are twelve types of persons. These are:

those bound by all fetters in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), which constitute nine types according to their abandonment of the nine grades [of afflictions]; Arhats; Pratyekabuddhas; and Tathāgatas—since the latter abandon the ninth grade, they are included as being on the path toward Arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*).

Now, in the Mahāyāna, one adds those who have not yet abandoned [the afflictions of] the fourth dhyāna, the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

In some accounts, these are combined to form sixteen; if one calculates by stage (*bhūmi*), there are nine grades in each stage, which further adds the four lower stages—each with nine grades—to the previous twelve, totaling forty-eight.

Although a person capable of entering [the Peak of Existence] may still be bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) regarding the fourth dhyāna, they are no longer so bound regarding the ninth grade of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), as they have already abandoned it. Thus, this treatise’s ninth fascicle states: [text follows].

Those who have not yet abandoned desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) but attain the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and so forth—these are said to exist as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).

It is further taught that even those who have not abandoned desire for the first dhyāna may likewise attain them; adding these twenty-seven other types of persons to the previous seventy-five, there are thus seventy-five in total.

Although there are those bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) in the first dhyāna, their meaning is identical to those bound by all fetters in the fourth dhyāna; therefore, those who have abandoned the third dhyāna are not added separately.

The nine grades consist of those bound by all fetters in the fourth dhyāna; if one adds the ten stages of Bodhisattvas who attain sudden enlightenment, there are ten additional persons, totaling eighty-five.
Within each stage, there are thirty [types]—namely, entering, abiding, and emerging—which, when combined with the previous hundred and five, total one hundred and thirty-five.

When these are multiplied by means of the faculties and vehicles, they become immeasurable. As for the Bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment, they have not yet entered the stages prior to the grounds.

Having already entered the stages of the forty minds and the four levels of decisive discernment (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*), when one further adds the forty-five persons, along with the previous one hundred and fifty, these are capable of entering.

Regarding that master’s three explanations concerning the bodhisattva who proceeds directly: first, it is said that one enters at the first stage (*bhūmi*), though there is no textual passage for this;

second, it is said that one enters from the third stage onward; and third, the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* states regarding the third stage: "The practitioner of dhyāna [attains] the four dhyānas and liberation."

Regarding "liberation," it is because of the four formless [attainments]. However, in the sixth stage of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Vimukticandra asks and Vajragarbha answers that one can enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) starting from the sixth stage;
this is because in the preceding stages, there is an intermingling of contemplations involving signs (*nimittabhāvanā*).

Thus, the statement that one cannot enter it in the sixth stage is made according to the predominant [characteristic] of that stage. Why, then, can the first two fruits [of the path] not enter it? One explanation is that they possess transformation (*pariṇāma*).

Because it is difficult to subdue due to its distinct nature of sensation, [the first] two are mentioned; because the two afflictions—unwholesome and neutral—of the desire realm are heavy, [the second] six are mentioned.

Regarding the cultivation of skillful means, while the Buddha is free from desire, for others, from the eighth stage onward, although Bodhisattvas lack an applied mind (*prayoga-citta*), there is no fault because they attain entry through skillful means.
This principle is certain; although the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts state that [this occurs] at the seventh stage, [it is actually attained earlier].

Entering cessation moment by moment is also attained through preparatory effort (*prayoga*). Furthermore, it is said that for those who attain the "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) of the contemplation of persons and phenomena and so forth, there are seven types—previously attained and previously unattained—as explained before.

One should know that the eighth [attainment] involves the suppression of the obstacles to meditative absorption (*samāpatty-āvaraṇa*) and the abandonment of the obstacles to meditative absorption (*nirodhāvaraṇa*).

If one does not abandon the obstacles to meditative absorption, why does this treatise state in its second [chapter]: "The cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*) is established upon the basis of the attainment of cessation"?

If the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is comprised within analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and if it is attained through abandonment (*prahāṇa-lābha*), why does this treatise further state that by suppressing the consciousness of the fourth dhyāna and above, one is able to attain this concentration?

Regarding this, there are two interpretations: The first interpretation says it is not abandoned; however, it is only when the fetters (*bandhana*) are severed that the unconditioned is established, as it is named from the perspective of ultimate attainment.
The second interpretation says it must be abandoned; this answer is correct, yet it speaks of attaining it through the suppression of afflictions (*kleśa-vyutthāna*).
