Just as the path of seeing consists of three moments of mind, so too, based on the distinctions in the principles of the Four Truths according to their respective objects, these are designated as the "knowledges of the Four Truths.

These very knowledges of the ultimate and conventional truths, when at the stage of fruition, are given the superior names "knowledge of exhaustion" and "knowledge of non-arising. Furthermore, they are divided into two based on whether their objects are existent or non-existent.
Among the sixty-nine [categories], these ten knowledges are established last as being common to the three vehicles, followed by the dependent and the unshared knowledges.

The analytical knowledge of the ten powers (*daśabala-jñāna*) is established as distinct from conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) because their objects differ; it is distinguished by means of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

All forms of ultimate knowledge (*tattva-jñāna*), when contrasted with conventional knowledge, are given the collective name "knowledge of the ultimate" (*paramārtha-jñāna*). Because the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) both reside in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), they are collectively termed "ultimate knowledge.
Regarding the distinctions among these various knowledges, including the practice of the knowledge of the ten powers which is solely for the benefit of others, there are sixty-nine types.

It is said that there are five categories of objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the functions of these five categories of objects of knowledge: first, that which is called an object of knowledge by way of conventional designation;
second, that which is called an object of knowledge by way of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); third, that which is known as the culmination of what is to be done;

fourth, that which is known as the pure and impure conduct of the minds of others; and fifth, that which is known in all its various aspects. Conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) can know the conventional.

One establishes the correct understanding of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-yukti*), such as what is wholesome and unwholesome, what is blameworthy and blameless, and so forth, up to the phenomena of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
One understands that a certain portion of these phenomena should be abandoned and another portion should be cultivated.

Furthermore, one understands that all categories of phenomena—whether they arise through speech, through wandering in the world, or as various activities arising according to causes and conditions—are capable of being known by the wisdom that realizes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) regarding the objects of knowledge.

Through the knowledge of the exhaustion of phenomena abandoned by seeing and meditation (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), he realizes that what was to be done has been accomplished;
his mind attains certainty and is free from doubt regarding his own abandonments, being devoid of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

Through the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), he knows the pure and impure conduct of others' minds as they truly are, and through the ten powers (*daśabala*), he understands all their intentions, elements, and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) exactly as they are.
The thirteenth wisdom is that which knows all varieties of objects of knowledge; is able to correctly instruct and admonish others; is able to sever all doubts of sentient beings;
is able to skillfully establish all sentient beings in the realms of form, the elements, and liberation;
possesses great power; and is able to perform acts of benefit and happiness for all sentient beings. This is the thirteenth wisdom.

The wisdom of the ultimate meaning within the middle [vehicle] consists of the six types of knowledge, such as the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). The Mahāyāna wisdom consists of the ten powers (*daśabala*). While these ten powers encompass both self-benefit and benefit for others, they are exclusively for the benefit of others. When combined with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), these two constitute the ultimate wisdom. The conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is opened up into the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; these—namely hearing, reflection, and cultivation—will be explained as they occur later. As for the distinctions in the contemplation of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the four noble truths: 1. **Knowledge of Phenomena**: Contemplates the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena. 2. **Subsequent Knowledge**: Contemplates the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena. 3. **Knowledge of Suffering**: Contemplates suffering as suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self. 4. **Knowledge of Origin**: Contemplates origin as cause, accumulation, production, and condition. 5. **Knowledge of Cessation**: Contemplates cessation as cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation. 6. **Knowledge of the Path**: Contemplates the path as path, correctness, achievement, and deliverance. Regarding the distinction in the contemplation of the knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge:

the knowledge of phenomena contemplates the specific characteristics of phenomena, while subsequent knowledge contemplates their general characteristics. Furthermore, the knowledge of phenomena contemplates the specific characteristics of the truths, while subsequent knowledge contemplates their general characteristics. Regarding the distinction in the contemplation of the four noble truths: the knowledge of suffering contemplates suffering as suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self; the knowledge of origin contemplates origin as cause, accumulation, production, and condition; the knowledge of cessation contemplates cessation as cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation; and the knowledge of the path contemplates the path as path, correctness, achievement, and deliverance. This is the distinction in the contemplation of the four noble truths.

It is not the case that the abandonment of afflictions occurs through a path of investigation that lacks distinction among the thirteen knowledges, such as those of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation;

nor is there any fault in explaining that within the actual path of abandonment, there are the knowledges of the dharmas, the subsequent knowledges, and the four noble truths, because those who practice the distinct and general investigations of the dharmas and subsequent knowledges do so according to four brief examples: namely, the distinct, the general, the combined, and the individual.

Regarding the observation of inferior and superior [realms] as the objects of knowledge (*jñāna-viṣaya*): the arising [of these observations] occurs both initially and subsequently. As stated in the *Abhidharma* (the *Abhidharmakośa*) regarding the thirteen knowledges:
"The lower knowledge" refers to the initial observation of the Truths; "the higher knowledge" refers to the subsequent observation.

Here, the observation of the specific and general objects, as well as the observation of the inferior objects of the Desire Realm and the superior objects of the Form and Formless Realms, constitutes the observation as the object of knowledge. Since the terms "lower" and "higher" apply universally in this context, it is thus.

The path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*) that manifests reality is called "Dharma" because it is the first arising; the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that realizes reality is called "Subsequent" (*anvaya*) because it arises after [the former] and is of the same class as the preceding.
Since the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Weishi chao) and other texts contain only these three terms and three examples, when we examine this text through reasoning, we find it is comprehensive.

Therefore, one should know that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) arise solely within the state of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), provided they are not further differentiated.

The knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising—namely, "I have attained the permanent extinction of all outflows" and "suffering shall not arise for me again in the future"—is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) and exclusively supramundane (*lokottara*).
If one makes such a discrimination, it is comprised only of the untainted, the mundane-supramundane, and conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*);
furthermore, it is not for one's own benefit alone, and it exists only in the fruit, not in the cause.

Now, it is shown that the stages (*avasthā*) encompass both mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*); since they include consciousness (*vijñāna*) as well, they are said to be thirteen. Furthermore, these various knowledges (*jñāna*) are distinguished based on consciousness:

those that take the ultimate truth (*tattva*) as their object are collectively termed "knowledge conforming to reality" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), while those that take the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) as their object are collectively termed "knowledge of measure" (*pramāṇa-jñāna*).

These two types, when situated in the stage of outflows (*sāsrava-avasthā*), are collectively termed "preparatory application" (*prayoga*) because they involve diligent effort and aspiration; this is because their objects of focus all possess signs (*nimitta*).
Therefore, within the untainted state (*anāsrava*), because the objects consist of both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), they are divided into two types of knowledge:

the fundamental (*mūla*) and the subsequent (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*). These take only the conventional as their object and are still termed "knowledge of phenomena," because they do not realize the ultimate truth. Thus, untainted knowledge is divided into three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) based on their objects and causes:

that which takes external teachings as its object is called "wisdom derived from hearing" (*śrutamayī*); that which takes the principle as its object is called "wisdom derived from reflection" (*cintāmayī*); and that which relies on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as its cause is called "wisdom derived from cultivation" (*bhāvanāmayī*).

Among the seven types of objects difficult to discern within those cognized by wisdom, there is that which is unknowable: the discernment of the vessel-world (*bhājana-vijñapti*) and the discernment of [objects] within it.

Furthermore, among these phenomena (*dharma*), there should also be that which is "appropriated" (*sopādāna*); and when taking the external to manifest the internal, or the extensive to manifest the minute, there should likewise be an eighth mode of activity (*ākāra*).

This unknowable discernment is now clarified as the mode of activity of both the object to be discerned and the subject that discerns; this is the second gate, which makes clear the seven difficulties.
Each consciousness refutes the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) respectively; reflect upon this according to reason. Regarding the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), sixty-nine [texts] state:

first, the supernormal power of realization through knowledge of the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*); second, the supernormal power of realization through knowledge of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*);

third, the supernormal power of realization through knowledge of the diversity of minds (*cetaḥparyāya-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*); fourth, the supernormal power of realization through knowledge of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*); fifth, the supernormal power of realization through knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*).

The realization of the knowledge of death (*maraṇajñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*) comprises six [types], while the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*) comprises one.

[This section consists of: 1. Explanation of the names; 2. Definition of the essence (*svabhāva*); 3. Differences in cultivation; 4. Functions; 5. Analysis by way of various categories. First, regarding the explanation of the names: that which is difficult to fathom through sublime wisdom is called "divine" (*ṛddhi*);

that which acts without obstruction is "penetration" (*abhijñā*). To transform from one into many according to one's capacity, and for the body to move with sovereign mastery, is what is termed [the power of] *ṛddhi*.
The supernormal power of the base (ṛddhi-viṣaya) is so called because it is experienced and manifested within this sphere by means of the knowledge of the supernormal power of the base.
If that knowledge possesses great majesty and is produced by cultivation, being the fruit of cultivation, it is called the "knowledge of the supernormal power of the base" (ṛddhi-vidyā).

Because this knowledge is able to experience and manifest within that sphere, it is termed the "knowledge of the supernormal power of the base. The seeds of this very knowledge are then sustained by the conditions for their arising.
Because it is experienced, its power increases and continues to evolve; this is termed the "realization through knowledge of supernormal powers" (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*).

All such instances are subsumed under a single name: the "supernormal power of realization through knowledge of supernormal powers. Here, "supernormal power" (*ṛddhi*) refers to the domain, and "knowledge of supernormal powers" (*ṛddhi-jñāna*) refers to the primary knowledge.

This is a *karmadhāraya* (descriptive) compound, meaning that "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*) is itself the "supernormal power. This refers to the fruit of cultivation, which is comprised within the faculty of the ear.
Pure form is called the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*); the knowledge associated with the consciousness that relies upon the ear is called the knowledge of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-jñāna*).

Its realization and so forth should be understood as previously explained; that it is designated collectively as "one" should also be understood according to the previous account. The realization of the knowledge of the divine ear and so forth is as previously stated:
the various minds of others, which function through distinctions such as being possessed by greed and so forth, are called "distinctions of mind" (*citta-prabheda*).

Alternatively, if one possesses great majestic power (*mahānubhāva*) and it is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*), being the fruit of such cultivation and taking that [past state] as its object, this wisdom is called "knowledge of the differentiation of minds" (*cetaḥparyāya-jñāna*).

The rest is as explained previously. Regarding the etymological explanation of the knowledge of the differentiation of minds, such as "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*) and so forth, it is as stated before.

If, with respect to the past, there is a clear recollection (*smṛti*) of the distinctions within one's own personal existence (*ātma-bhāva-viśeṣa*), it is called "recollection" (*pūrvenivāsānusmṛti*). If the wisdom possesses majestic power... [text ends].
That which is accomplished through cultivation is the fruit of cultivation; it depends upon mindfulness and is associated with mindfulness, and only in this way can it proceed.

Therefore, it is called the "knowledge of the recollection of past lives" (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*). "Past" (*pūrva*) refers to what has gone by; "dwelling" (*nivāsa*) means having long resided. "Dwelling" is thus "past-dwelling.

The recollection of that past dwelling is "recollection of past dwellings. The explanation of the name of this supernormal power (*abhijñā*) is as stated before. As for sentient beings and their various forms, whether beautiful or ugly, and so forth—

The various distinctions arising from the death of this or that particular group of sentient beings and their birth among this or that particular group of sentient beings are termed "birth and death" (*saṃsāra*).

When one takes as a basis the pure form (*rūpa*) comprised by the eye that has been cultivated through fruition, and possesses a cognition associated with consciousness that takes the objects of death and birth as its conditions, this is called "knowledge of birth and death.
This intent is that the knowledge of birth and death is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in conjunction with the eye.

If consciousness is named after its object, and if the "knowledge of the divine eye" is designated according to its basis and its gateway, both are analyzed as *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compounds.

If the complete and permanent severance of all fetters without remainder is termed the "exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*), then within this context, the mundane knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are called the "knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
By means of these distinct instructions and admonitions, one knows the three periods of time.
Because they are equal [to worldly phenomena], they are subsumed only within the mundane; the rest is as previously explained.

However, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge and vision of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-viṣaya-jñāna-darśana-abhijñā*), up to the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge and vision of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna-darśana-abhijñā*), are all described as having the nature of "vision" (*darśana-svabhāva*), because they involve analytical investigation and discernment.

Second, regarding the essential nature (*svabhāva*) [of these powers]: if the supernormal power of psychic travel belongs to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), according to the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇa-pāda* and other texts, it is said to be for the purpose of benefiting others.
The supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear are associated with both the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

When they arise from a lower stage, they are exclusively indeterminate; when they arise from one's own or a higher stage, they are associated with both the wholesome and the indeterminate. The [supernormal powers of] recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) and knowing the minds of others (*paracitta*) are wholesome, as their essence consists of impure wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that if these five supernormal powers belong to those in training (*śaikṣa*) within the Two Vehicles, they are wholesome.

Furthermore, while those with outflows exist in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and the state of being without outflows exists there as well, this [latter] is designated "without outflows" based on its separation from outflows.

As for the nature of the supernormal power of the base of psychic power (*ṛddhi*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), these are in reality not without outflows for the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyānika*). Regarding the supernormal knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), the supernormal knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*), the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Volume 69) states that the supernormal knowledge of others' minds for the Two Vehicles is in reality not without outflows; as for the supernormal knowledge of past lives and the supernormal knowledge of others' minds... [the outflows remain].

In the sixty-ninth [chapter], it is explained that the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) takes both those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*) as its objects.

Although it is worldly (*laukika*), it is also untainted (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, even when the outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*), it is untainted; yet, this particular type of supernormal power is narrow while wisdom (*jñāna*) is broad.

If it has conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) as its nature, it also encompasses the tainted (*sāsrava*). When the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) preach the Dharma, it is not yet truly untainted; however, because it is free from outflows, it is given the name "past" (*pūrva*).

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are also associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, if one has attained the untainted five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) within the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) of the Mahāyāna, they may be associated with the untainted.

If one has not attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), these are exclusively tainted (*sāsrava*). The supernormal power of the basis (*ṛddhi-vidhi*) is associated with the untainted only through the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and wisdom (*jñāna*).

The same applies to the supernormal powers of recollecting past lives (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti*) and knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*). Because they are directed toward becoming a bodhisattva and are distinguished as being "directly proceeding" (*ekayāna*), they reach [the state of being untainted].

The Buddha’s [powers] are comprised of both untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), as they are mundane in nature. Regarding their essential substance, they are derived from wisdom;
as stated in the third chapter of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, the conditioned merits are subsumed under the four wisdoms.

Specifically, the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)—such as the divine eye and divine ear—are for the most part subsumed within the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), while the power of supernatural movement (*ṛddhi-viṣaya-jñāna*) is for the most part subsumed within the wisdom of accomplishing what was to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

Regarding the supernormal power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-abhijñā*): if one speaks of it in terms of its continuity within the stream of consciousness, it is subsumed under four types of knowledge;

however, if one speaks of it in terms of taking the exhaustion of outflows—that is, *nirvāṇa*—as its object, it is for the most part subsumed within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).

This is because, as manifestations of the basis of consciousness, the three transformations appear within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and manifest supernormal powers; thus, it is said to be "for the most part" subsumed under the supernormal power of the knowledge of psychic travel (*ṛddhiviṣayajñāna*).

The yoga of the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) is categorized as mundane because it takes altruism as its primary focus; however, since this discussion concerns both self-benefit and benefit for others, it is for the most part subsumed under the two knowledges (*jñāna*).

Nevertheless, with the exception of the five mundane supernormal powers of the Śrāvaka vehicle—each consisting of one path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), plus the ninth stage of the path of uninterrupted transition of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as the path of liberation—there is currently no textual authority for such [paths] in the Mahāyāna.

The stage of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is not one where fulfillment is achieved instantaneously, because it cannot be accomplished all at once.

For example, although one cultivates the perception of lightness and levity (*laghu-samjñā*), the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the ten stages—such as lightness and levity—progressively increase in excellence; it is not the case that a single uninterrupted path or path of liberation is itself complete.
As stated in the *Forty-Seventh [Chapter]*: "In a single kṣaṇa, a muhūrta, or an instant, a bodhisattva of the first stage..."
They are able to realize one hundred bodhisattva samādhis; with the purified divine eye, they can see one hundred Tathāgatas in various Buddha-fields;
and by means of their supernormal powers, they can shake one hundred worlds and travel to them.
From this point onward, it should be known that these bodhisattvas, through the power of their vows, possess immeasurable majestic power and miraculous transformations. (The third cultivation.)

Regarding the fact that there are differences in the dharmas, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (in the thirty-third fascicle) states that it is excellent to cultivate the twelve perceptions (*saṃjñā*). This is discussed in reference to the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the two vehicles;
it does not apply to Bodhisattvas. The power of Bodhisattvas is threefold: first, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) acquired through cultivation.

Although they have not yet seen the actual application of the methods for cultivating these, according to the beginning of the thirty-eighth [fascicle], they first hear the general teachings on the dharma of supernormal powers, and subsequently, by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), [they realize them].
Because one attends to and contemplates the meaning of those dharmas, practicing and cultivating them repeatedly, there arise superior and inferior results of cultivation.
This intention also belongs to bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), who have not yet attained innate power; what hindrance is there to their also relying on this cultivation?

Once they have entered the stages, they merely enter samādhi to analyze and suppress the obstacles to meditative concentration (*samāpatti-āvaraṇa*), thereby attaining the fruits of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). This is also stated in that fascicle.

The detailed explanation of the three kinds of power: first, the power of the two dharmas, which refers to that obtained by practicing the six perfections, as clarified in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the merits of the six sense faculties;

second, the power of co-nascence, which refers to obtaining this retribution through the Dharma. Fourth, regarding the karma performed: the causes of this karma are as explained in [the section on] the sixty-ninth.
Fifth, regarding the analysis by various categories: first, concerning the establishment and exclusion of names—why are there only two?

Establishing the two types of celestial consciousness (*divyacakṣur-vijñāna*); the analogy for establishing or discarding eye-consciousness; the establishment or discarding of the three types of consciousness and their three functions according to the functions permitted;

the division according to the four stages (*bhūmi*) as established; the basis upon which they depend; the fivefold establishment by way of power—namely, the distinction between those acquired at birth and those produced through application;

the thirty-three scriptural citations; the fact that the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is exclusively termed "application" (*prayoga*); and the establishment of the one [type] called "supernormal power" (*ṛddhi*) because it attains the name "supernatural," while the others do not.

Because their activities and functions are preeminent, the divine eye and ear are designated by the term "divine" (*deva*), whereas the others are not; this distinguishes them from those belonging to the human realm.
Within the classification of consciousnesses, why are the seventh and eighth consciousnesses not stated to be supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)?

In reality, they are indeed so, but they are not mentioned because they pertain to the causes of the three vehicles and ordinary beings, or because they are for the benefit of others; thus, the [supernormal] eyes, ears, and the six consciousnesses are [the basis]. As for the nose...
Why are the tongue and body not considered supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)? Because their functions are not universal and they do not involve the mutual operation of the sense organs.

According to the facts, as stated in the "Chapter on Entering the Body" of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-sūtra* (Ten Stages Sutra), the supernormal power of the Tathāgata’s body is immeasurable; the power of the nose is incalculably greater; and the power of the tongue is infinitely vast.
These are spoken of as the six supernormal powers from the perspective of the three vehicles. Now, there is an interpretation which says: [text continues]
These six types of activity are called "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*) because they are vast and superior; they are said to pertain to the Bodhisattva stages and not to others.
Thus, the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra* states that the divine ear knows all sounds of the past and future, reaching back to the very limit of existence (*pūrvakoṭi*).

The *Draṣṭavyapraśna-sūtra* clarifies the five supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, while the *Pūrvenivāsajñāna-sūtra* clarifies their knowledge of past lives, and the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* clarifies their knowledge of the future.

Regarding the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) and the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriyaviśuddhi*) mentioned in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma-Preacher" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:

why are the other three faculties not designated as "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*)? Furthermore, why are they named after the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) or after ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), rather than being established based on their primary function?

As for their worldly functions—such as acting as objects of perception—why is it that the two vehicles are able to take the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as objects through the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, whereas others cannot?
The mind cannot [directly] know birth and death; it can take the five aggregates as its object, or the minds of others, or the present.

If it takes the aspect of form (*rūpa*) as its object, it is not called a supernormal power (*abhijñā*). Knowing the four aggregates and knowing that wisdom is what is termed "attaining the stage" (*bhūmi-pratilambha*).

Regarding the basis upon which this is established or excluded: it relies solely on the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*). As stated in the thirty-third [treatise], it relies on the fundamental dhyānas to produce the sixty [types of knowledge].

The ninth explanation is also the same as for other concentrations. Although Bodhisattvas and others can also produce transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*), these are not the function of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) because their scope is narrow. Regarding the establishment and exclusion based on power:

the six supernormal powers have distinct limits among the six classes of beings—ordinary worldlings, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas—which range from inferior to superior. Through the supernormal power of the basis (*ṛddhi-vidhi*), one cultivates [powers] from the inferior to the superior;

through the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), one hears from the near to the distant; through the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), one sees from the short to the long; and through the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*), one knows from limited boundaries to the infinite.
One should understand the distinctions between those who know their past lives for long or short durations, those whose outflows are exhausted, and the fruits of the three vehicles.

Regarding those born into the pure realms: among the gods who sport with forgetfulness (*manasvin*), the gods of wrathful intent (*saṃjñā-pradūṣin*), the gods who delight in emanations (*nirmāṇa-rati*), and the gods who control the emanations of others (*para-nirmita-vaśavartin*)—these two groups are born through wrong aspirations.
Furthermore, there are those who dwell manifestly amidst sensual desires: all humans and the inhabitants of the four lower heavens.
Although humans are also subject to transformation, they are excluded here; likewise, the two lower heavens are excluded because they still experience harm from others.

[The remaining three] transform their own sensual objects themselves, while the third transforms the sensual objects of others. These two are named after their respective characteristics: the first is "Sporting" (Nirmāṇarati) and the second is "Wrathful" (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
Although these qualities extend throughout the four higher heavens, they are designated by these specific names; therefore, this reference applies only to the two lower heavens. (Examination)
In the fifth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there is a slight distinction regarding two points.

According to the fourteenth [category] among the thirteen wholesome factors in the fourth fascicle of the main treatise, and as stated in the fifth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, these are simply the four types—namely, seeds, non-associated [factors], and so forth—which are all subsumed within "co-arising" (*samutthāna*). Consequently, these seeds can exist in accordance with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Because they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they are also called "concomitants" (*anuvartin*); herein, their functional applications are divided to establish the remaining eight types.

These thirteen types are divided into four groups: first, the four types of inclusion; second, the two types of distinct categories; third, the three types of mundane wholesomeness; and fourth, the three types of supramundane wholesomeness.
Regarding the wholesome nature of form, sound, and so forth, it is as previously enumerated. That is to say, in this very context, it refers to faith (*śraddhā*).
Regarding the phrase "in such places" (*ādi-sthāna*), it means that one receives the fruits of faith and so forth; "places" (*sthāna*) here refers to locations. The current explanation is as follows:
when faith arises at the time of determination, and even up until the time of gathering sentient beings, there is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*);

these are the places where faith and so forth arise. Just as within the practice of wholesome deeds one cultivates pure goodness, this is also the general dharma-practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*).

In general, this encompasses all three types of wisdom. Regarding the practice of the Dharma as it has been taught: "the Dharma of cessation" refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); "the Dharma that accords with [the Dharma]" refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) and so forth.

Alternatively, the phrase "the Dharma of the Path that accords with the Dharma of Cessation" means practicing solely by cultivating the Truth of the Path, as explained in the *Saṃgraha* and elsewhere regarding karma and so on;

this refers precisely to the four types of reverential conduct (*upasthāna*). "Present worship" refers to making offerings to the two Jewels [the Buddha and the Dharma]; however, the Sangha Jewel is omitted here for brevity. Or...

To initiate offerings is to offer to the Saṃgha. Regarding the inclusion within the wholesome, this refers exclusively to the observation of wholesome *yoga*. It is also said that one cultivates this;

herein, according to the *Karma-nirdeśa* chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are meritorious actions (*puṇya-kriyā*) of the nature of giving that are not the act itself, and acts that are not merit.
As stated in that treatise, those which lead to birth in heaven or to wealth and nobility are wholesome factors of merit (*puṇya-bhāgīya-kuśala*) that accord with the dharmas of purification.
These are the four types of remedies for the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*): (63) the remedy of suppression, the remedy of separation, and the remedy of the two obstacles.
These three preceding remedies each encompass the full range of meanings; however, according to their specific distinctions, the outflows (*āsrava*) and so forth should be understood as appropriate.

In the ninth [section] below, within the explanation of "quiescent wholesomeness" (*śāntakuśala*), up to the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*), this single category—the obstacle to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*)—is not mentioned.

The "moving" [state] is so called because the obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) have not yet been exhausted; alternatively, it may not necessarily be taken here as exclusively unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), for the cessation-concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*) alone constitutes its essence due to its extreme tranquility.
If the obstacles to concentration are severed, it is also subsumed under *nirvāṇa*. Some say there is one, namely *mahāparinirvāṇa*;
some say there are two, namely *sopadhiśeṣa* and *anupadhiśeṣa*, or the two states of rest; or the two, the great and the small, as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Some speak of three [nirvāṇas]; this treatise speaks of the attainment of their stages. Some speak of four, because in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the attainment and establishment are explained together.
Some speak of five: nirvāṇa, further means, and purified nirvāṇa; the latter (the three types of nirvāṇa) are as explained in the section on the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

Furthermore, there are two other explanations regarding the essence of nirvāṇa with remainder and without remainder, as well as non-abiding nirvāṇa, which are like those in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

The tenth consciousness, the purity through expedient means (*upāya-śuddhi*), is the true cause (*tathatā-hetu*); because it is explained from the perspective of the aspect of purity manifested through expedient means, it is said to have no separate substance.
As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), Chapter Ten, regarding the inclusion of the wholesome within the absence of a substantial body for purity;

and as in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, Chapter Ten, and by analogy with the unwholesome, one should state that there are distinct retributive fruits for the human and celestial realms and the three evil destinies, which are the fruits drawn forth [by karma], corresponding to their respective counterparts.
Thus, it is omitted for brevity.

Regarding the unwholesome [karma], according to the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, it is said that in the cultivation of the path, karma is produced through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and rebirth is moistened by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The fourth fascicle of that treatise asks:
"What are the causes for the increase of immovable karma? First, volition (*cetanā*) can accomplish the karma; second, vision (*darśana*) can obtain the fruit. Why is this so?

Therefore, because karma is not completed through the exhaustion of *vitarka* (applied thought), and because the fruition of results is not induced by the exhaustion of [afflictions] abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), "thought" (*vitarka*) refers specifically to the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Among the twelve unwholesome factors, four are categorized according to the preceding principle. Within the eight neutral (*avyākṛta*) factors, those consisting of the spheres of form (*rūpāyatana*) are exclusively taken as those produced by nourishment (*aupacayika*).
This excludes all other forms within the sphere of form that are not comprised within those born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
The spheres of sound and odor are well-classified as being comprised within the innate neutral (*upapatti-lābhika-avyākṛta*) because they consist of resultant form (*vipāka-rūpa*) and so forth;

thus, there are sixty-six [factors] that possess five kinds of neutral roots, since they are comprised within what is born of maturation (*vipākaja*). Now, there are three textual passages concerning what is born of maturation:

first, that which is called "true maturation" is termed "born of maturation"; second, that which is called "figurative maturation" is termed "born of maturation," as previously stated in the sixth chapter.
In the first fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, it is stated that among the six types of phenomena, sixty-six are further explained as being of the nature of "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).

Now, excluding the wholesome and defiled factors within the third category, as well as the neutral factors within the first, second, and third categories— namely, those factors other than the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma,
such as those produced by nourishment (*aupacayika*) or uniform outflow (*naiḥṣyandika*)— the phenomena of "born of maturation" are themselves neutral by nature (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*).

However, because the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* establishes four types of indeterminate minds (*avyākṛta-citta*) as distinct from their maturation (*vipāka*), it does not clarify that matter (*rūpa*) is of the nature of clinging to dharmas (*dharma-abhiniveśa*).
Thus, among the five types of indeterminate states, the first four pertain to all five aggregates (*skandha*), while the fifth pertains only to the aggregate of matter.

Nevertheless, in this present treatise, both the category of mental associates (*caitta-samprayukta*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth are collectively termed "indeterminate by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*). Furthermore, these eight...
The form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) because they are explained according to the gates of conformity and in terms of their causes.

That master [Dignāga] includes the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya-vipāka*), the eighth consciousness, the faculties, and matter (*rūpa*) within the category of innate indeterminate (*upapatti-lābhika-avyākṛta*).

He maintains that the retribution of non-conception is indeed retribution, whereas the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth are designated as "retribution" only in a general sense and are not themselves retribution; thus, he subsumes them under their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This is also incorrect, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Since it is taught that these are exclusively maturations (*vipāka*), the retribution of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya*) is also included within the category of "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*);

this is because it is subsumed under the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "intrinsic nature and so forth. Regarding whether the word "and so forth" appears in the treatises, it is present in the original *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

Furthermore, since the views of self-existence and extremes (*satkāyadṛṣṭi* and *antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) along with their associated factors in the desire realm have no other place to be included below, they are [included] by means of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Although the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth are results of maturation (*vipāka*), because they are provisional (*prajñapti*), they are not subsumed under their own nature (*svabhāva*) in the same way as the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

Now, regarding the inclusion by self-nature, all dharmas that are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) are subsumed; however, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (Asvabhāva’s commentary), chapter three, does not permit the establishment of five types of indeterminate states (verify).
That which is associated with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) refers to one who harbors a mind that is neither defiled nor pure; this is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

That it is "encompassed by the sets of names, phrases, and syllables" (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) clarifies the meaning of its modes of activity (*ākāra*), because it proceeds through the gateway of mental verbalization (*manojalpa*). Regarding the phrase "it clarifies those modes of activity":

this means that the modes of activity of the primary minds and mental factors—such as deportment (*iryāpatha*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*)—are revealed by means of names, phrases, and syllables.

The claim that the mental states (*citta*) of deportment (*īryāpatha*) and craftsmanship (*śilpa*) are manifested by the phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), words (*pada-kāya*), and names (*nāma-kāya*) is now shown to be incorrect.
This is because those [manifesting] mental states are associated with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Thus, it is these very mental states of deportment and so forth that are manifested;
since this mind is appropriated by the names and so on, it becomes indeterminate. Now, it is being shown that the mental states of this mind are manifested by means of the names and so forth.

"That which you say reveals the meaning of its mode of activity (*ākāra*) because it proceeds by way of mental verbalization" means that "mental" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), "verbalization" refers to sound, and "proceeding" refers to its manifestation.
This is because the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables manifest and proceed by way of the sounds of speech uttered by the mental consciousness associated with deportment and so forth.
Furthermore, another explanation holds that it is due to [the influence of] names, phrases, and syllables...
"Apprehension" (*parigraha*) refers to the transformation of the mind’s aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) into the aspect of the object (*nimitta-bhāga*), such as names and so forth.
However, because this aspect of seeing is distinguished by what is expressed by those names and so forth within the aspect of the object, it is said to be "apprehended by names and so forth.

This reveals its mode of activity (*ākāra*); that is, these names and so forth are the expressive designators (*vācaka*) of the mode of activity of that mind's aspect of seeing, since they are mental verbalization (*manojalpa*).

"Turning by way of the gate" (*dvāra-vartana*) means "by means of" or "through. These [factors] such as names (*nāman*) and so forth turn and arise only by depending on that *vijñapti*-portion of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as their gate;
it is only then that these *nimitta*-portions, such as names and so forth, are able to turn and arise. Now, the explanation clarifies their mode of activity (*ākāra*) as previously self-explained:

"turning by way of the gate of mental verbalization" (*manojalpa-dvāra-vartana*) means that names and so forth are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), possess a basis (*sāśraya*), and consist of sound; furthermore, names and so forth exist solely as mental [phenomena].
The statement that "names and so forth" refers to the mental discernment and determination of objects according to their names; thus they are called "names and so forth.

Because those names and so forth depend upon mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) and proceed by way of the mind as their gateway, the supporting mind and its concomitants constitute the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*); this is the intended meaning here.
Regarding the *airyāpathika* (postures) and *śailpasthānika* (crafts): the former depends on the path of movement, while the latter depends on a specific location or site.
It may be renamed "also. Furthermore, regarding deportment (*iryāpatha*), it is acquired by taking the matter (*rūpa*) of the nature of karma as its path;

regarding craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), it is acquired by taking the matter of the faculties (*indriya-rūpa*) as its path, or it arises by taking the matter of the faculties as its basis. Alternatively, it takes the mind as its path and its basis.
(From the *Lengqie jing* [Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra], in the section on the heterodox views and the Lesser Vehicle Nirvāṇa, explained by Bodhisattva Deva.)
In the *Vaiśeṣika-śāstra*, it is said that Maheśvara created sentient beings; this is termed "present offering" (pratyakṣa-pūjā) and is considered unwholesome.
In the forty-ninth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, when Sudhana seeks spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), there is a king named Paripūrṇa who harms sentient beings;
this is termed "manifesting unwholesome [actions]" as a retribution. In the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, the Buddha was at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Śrāvastī, where there were five hundred [monks].
When a person severs the path, they reject the Buddha’s transformation; those who ride upon the wild goose are all like this.
Subsequently, that which is produced by great compassion within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) occurs.

Even if a bodhisattva were actually associated with afflictions (*kleśa*), these afflictions—arising from the subsequently attained wisdom induced by great compassion—are like poisons suppressed by mantras or medicines; they do not constitute a fault. III.

Regarding the classification by realm (*dhātu-bandhana*), the phrase "desire realm" (*kāmadhātu*) refers to those who have not yet abandoned even a small portion of desire and so forth. This intent clarifies that one who has already abandoned a small portion of desire—such as one in the initial stage of the *anāgamya* concentration—should not be considered bound to the desire realm.

However, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "If one is born here [in the desire realm] and has either not yet obtained the antidote, or has obtained it but emerged from it, these three times constitute its manifestation.
The meaning is: first, when the antidote has not been obtained; second, when the antidote has been obtained; and third, when one has emerged from it.
Having emerged from the defiled dharmas of the desire realm, the manifestation of defiled-neutral dharmas occurs;

this is consistent with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on Yoga Practice), fascicle 66, and also with the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Manifestation of the Noble Teachings). However, there are slight differences between the two; upon comparison, the text of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* is superior.

The Sūtra states that "all sentient beings arise through the predominant influence of their collective karma" (*sādhāraṇa-karma-adhipatya-ja*) in order to demonstrate that even those born in the Form and Formless Realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*) are still accompanied by the seeds of karma that have not yet abandoned desire; thus, there are these three explanations.

As for which person's karma produces the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), it is as explained in the second volume of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: that devas from the Form Realm come to this Desire Realm and manifest transformations.

That ground abides within itself; if one possesses a contaminated body (*sāsrava-kāya*) produced by the seventh mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) while dwelling in a lower stage and gives rise to a mind of a higher stage, it arises together with the seven [mental factors] of the lower stage.
For this reason, it is called "contaminated" (*sāsrava*).

According to their mutual conformity, this is not contradictory to the fact that external receptacle worlds (*bhājana-loka*) and so forth are all rendered contaminated by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), just as the sixty-six [types of] desire are predominant in the self (*ātman*).

Because those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to the predominant phenomena (*adhipati-dharma*) of the desire realm as being the self (*ātman*), or because the self is not [identical to] the desire realm yet is bound to it by way of predominance;

and because there is also a small amount of fixed form (*rūpa*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is not mentioned. This is the fifty-third [point], which accords with the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.

Regarding what is called the emptiness of sentient beings: it is like the absence of form in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and so on, up to the three poisons of Arhats and Stream-Enterers (*srotāpanna*).
The *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra) states that when the Buddha preached the sutra, the gods of the Formless Realm rained down exquisite flowers;

the flowers were as large as chariot wheels and accumulated like Mount Sumeru. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that the olfactory faculty of Bodhisattvas perceives the fragrance of the palaces in the Formless Realm.
The *Saṃyuktāgama* states that when Śāriputra entered parinirvāṇa, tears fell from the formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*) like a fine spring rain;
and when Vāśpa-vatī entered nirvāṇa, the gods of the form and formless realms stood by the Buddha’s side.

Thus, those in the formless realm are said to lack "karmic-resultant form" (*vipākaja-rūpa*), while those in the form realm are said to possess "meditative-resultant form" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), including a portion of the [eight] liberations and the ten types of [form-attaining] concentrations.

Within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there is a differentiation according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), and the three vehicles (*triyāna*), as well as the distinctions between ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*).
Within the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), there are sixty-six [faculties], beginning from the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

However, among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), only those from the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) onward are taken; this is as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* regarding the single fundamental stage within the twenty-two faculties.

The two stages of application (*prayoga*) and the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*) constitute the three types of discrimination. The *Pañcakaṣāya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Five Defilements) states the same.

Regarding the "unlearned" (*aśaikṣa*), the *Ṣaṭṣaṣṭi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Sixty-six) states that all wholesome dharmas of the unlearned body are [included]; however, the *Dvāṣaṣṭi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Sixty-two) states that the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is neither-learner-nor-unlearned (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, among the categories of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and so forth, there is the "wholesome acquired at birth" (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*); how then can this be called "learning" (*śaikṣa*)?

The same applies to the other dissociated [factors] and their respective seeds. Among these, those that are acquired through training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth follow the meditative attainment of cessation;
as for the minor portion of innate wholesomeness (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) that follows training, it is also omitted and not mentioned.
Regarding the question "What are those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and so forth?", the meaning of abandonment by seeing and the rest is briefly analyzed through four sections:

first, the essential nature of what is abandoned; second, the definition of abandonment; third, the stages of abandonment; and fourth, a detailed analysis through questions and answers. As for the essential nature of what is abandoned:

it refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, including both material (*rūpa*) and non-material (*arūpa*) dharmas, as well as all karma and its results. Among the non-material [dharmas], there are seven categories: first, the mind (*citta*).
There are seven categories: (1) universal, (2) object-specific, (3) wholesome, (4) root afflictions, (5) secondary afflictions, and (6) indeterminate.

Regarding the various provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) that are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) or cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they are explained according to their actual nature among the non-material (*arūpa*) factors.

Among these, for the first three categories, whichever [affliction] they correspond to, it is said to be abandoned by that [same path], as well as those that are not to be abandoned. Within the root afflictions, there are three [types].

Regarding views and doubt, because they arise solely from discrimination and are abandoned only by insight (*darśana-heya*), there is one interpretation that among the extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) is abandoned only by insight;

this is because the fourth *Abhidharma* [treatise] and the eighty-eighth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi* state that only the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through both insight and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

There is another interpretation that it also extends to being abandoned through cultivation, as the eleventh and eighteenth chapters of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* state that both the view of eternalism and the view of nihilism extend to both [types of abandonment].

Because they are both conceptual (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*), the remaining five afflictions, such as greed, are abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). This is because they arise based on views, taking views as their object, or taking the objects of views as their object.

Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the ten beginning with shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) are abandoned through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, as they can pervade unwholesome and defiled minds.

Regarding the ten beginning with anger (*krodha*), there is one interpretation that they are abandoned only through the path of cultivation, as they arise only by taking objects as their focus and do not involve delusion regarding principles (*tattva*). There is another interpretation...
All [of these] are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation; the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise on the Treasury) states this in fifty-eight places.

Since it says that envy (*īrṣyā*) can be untainted (*anāsrava*), and since the third chapter of the *Abhidharma* also states that anger (*vyāpāda*) and envy arise from renunciation (*naiṣkramya*), it follows that for non-Buddhists and others, even when taking views as their object or based upon views, there can still be the arising of wrath, avarice, and so forth.

Sleep (*middha*), vitarka, and vicāra are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation. Regarding regret (*kaukṛtya*), one interpretation holds that it is abandoned only through cultivation, as it takes a concrete object (*vastu*) as its basis.

The meaning of "arising" (jāti) also applies to those factors abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-heya), because [the mind] also regrets wholesome states and so forth based on views and the like.

As for the remaining dharmas, they are abandoned only by the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) or are not to be abandoned (aheya). This is because the *Pañcavastuka* (57) states that the five faculties, such as faith (śraddhā), are abandoned by cultivation or are not to be abandoned;
and the *Ṣaṭtriṃśat-dharmaka* (66) states that wholesome and neutral states are abandoned by cultivation. Thus it is.
The sixth and seventh fascicles of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* state that there are those who hold the view that wholesome [dharmas] and so forth are also abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).

The fourth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa* states that all aggregates, elements, and bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*) of the miserable realms are abandoned by insight. Furthermore, the ninth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"If one speaks of the abandonment of bonds through conditions, then wholesome dharmas and so forth are abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), based on non-arising abandonment as in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth."

Regarding the statement that [wholesome dharmas] are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), this traditional explanation clarifies that the distinct retributions for the three evil destinies consist of wholesome dharmas.

These karmas and their fruits are abandoned by insight; that is, the various karmas and the fruits obtained that are issued from previously defiled dharmas—whether they be material form (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*)—and the fruits obtained from those issued by what is abandoned by insight, as well as the fruits obtained from what is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

All are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as explained in the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* and elsewhere. Briefly stated, there are two types of those that are not abandoned (*aheya*):

first, those that are not bound (*abandhana*), namely all untainted (*anāsrava*) conditioned and unconditioned phenomena; the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharma* states that only untainted phenomena are subsumed under the category of "not abandoned.
Second, those that have already been definitively abandoned are called "not abandoned," as stated in the sixty-sixth [chapter]: "within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)."

Wholesome and indeterminate dharmas are called "not to be abandoned" (this is the first general definition of the nature of what is to be abandoned). Second, regarding the meaning of "to be abandoned," there are briefly two categories: 1. Abandonment by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*):

This refers to all defiled dharmas, which are abandoned through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation. 2. Abandonment by separation from bondage (*visamyoga-prahāṇa*): This has two types: a. Abandonment by separation from bondage:

This refers to the abandonment of those afflictions that take [the dharma] as their object or are associated with it; this is explained in the *Ṣaṭṣaṣṭi-dharmaka-śāstra*. Wholesome [dharmas] are [abandoned in this way].
Regarding indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, they are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). There are two types of non-arising abandonment (*anutpāda-prahāṇa*):

first, the non-arising of the fruit due to the cessation of the cause, which refers to the fruits of the three evil destinies abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); second, the non-arising of the cause due to the decay of the fruit, which refers to the wholesome dharmas abandoned by the path of seeing.

The *Pañcāśatikā-śāstra* states that within the path of seeing, the attainment of the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the power of rebirth (*upapatti-vaśitā*) can be rendered ultimate.

Because it is of the nature of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), its cause is also severed; such categories are of this kind. Those which are not to be abandoned (*aheya*) are of two types, as explained previously in the section on their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
This is the second [section] clarifying the meaning of what is to be abandoned (*heya*), as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Regarding the abandonment of the fruits of the evil destinies (*apāya*), there are two views: first, that their substance (*svabhāva*) also ceases along with the vision-path (*darśana-mārga*) because they are obstacles; the treatise states: "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).

Regarding those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), this is explained based on the remaining indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mixed-object fetters (*miśrālambana-bandhana*). One interpretation states that it refers only to the abandonment of karma-existence (*karmabhava-avyākṛta*);

[if one asks] how this does not exclude the inability to produce maturation (*vipāka*), [the answer is that] it is explained according to this resultant indeterminate entity existing within the fetters of mixed objects during the process of birth.

Third, regarding the clarification of the stages of what is abandoned: there is an interpretation that for both what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and what is abandoned by cultivation, both cause and effect are abandoned together.
In a single moment, when the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*) arises, all [karmas, afflictions, and their fruits] are severed instantaneously.

According to the intention of this master, it is said that when the path of non-interruption of the single-moment path of vision (*ekacitta-darśanamārga*) arises, at that time all karmas, afflictions, and their fruits are severed simultaneously.

Furthermore, during the two moments of the path of non-interruption of the three-moment path of vision, both cause and fruit are severed together; and during the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), [the same occurs].

Only when the principle is realized do the afflictions and karma that possess objective reality cease through the arising of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), at which point their projected fruits have already been severed.

When the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises simultaneously with the path of uninterrupted transition, those fruits are finally severed—just as when the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) arises.

If, during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), the seeds of the two obstructions have not yet been severed, then the path of uninterrupted transition severs the coarse residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the two obstructions.
The *ānantarya-mārga* (path of uninterrupted realization) and the *vimukti-mārga* (path of liberation) arise together, at which point the *dauṣṭhulya* (coarse heaviness) is finally severed;

this constitutes the distinction between the path of uninterrupted realization and the path of liberation, as explained in the ninth and tenth chapters of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Fourth, the analysis through question and answer: Question: Are that which severs (*prahātṛ*) and that which is severed (*praheya*) simultaneous or non-simultaneous?

Answer: They are neither identical nor different, just as light and darkness [cannot coexist], and just as when one end of a scale rises, the other end descends, while the balance itself remains level.
Question: Does this inquiry into equality concern the severance of the present, or of the past and future? Answer: It is not the severance of the three time periods;
rather, it is spoken of in terms of the three time periods. This is because the future has not yet arisen, the past has already passed away, and the present does not abide.

Nevertheless, when those afflictions are severed—whether by means of light or darkness—the three time periods do not shift; thus, it is said that the three time periods are severed. These various points above are as follows:

Regarding the *Fifty-nine [Verses]* and the Treatise, it is asked: "Is there a case where one has severed those seeds but has not severed the *dausthulya* (gross heaviness)? One should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

There is the case where one has previously severed the seeds but has not severed the *dausthulya*, namely, those of the two vehicles who have severed the seeds of the afflictions but have not severed their *dausthulya*.
This cannot be called the "permanent severance of habitual tendencies," as stated in the *Fifty-nine [Verses]*. There is also the case where one has severed that *dausthulya*...
Regarding the heavy latencies (*dausthulya*) that are not severed: Bodhisattvas of the ten stages sever the heavy latencies of the innate afflictions (*kleśa*), yet they do not sever their seeds;

there are also cases where the heavy latencies are severed. This is like the severing of the seeds and heavy latencies of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) through the path of seeing and the path of culmination.
The seeds and heavy latencies of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of Bodhisattvas in the ten stages are severed simultaneously and all at once. This is what follows above.
The two phrases are as explained in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, fascicle 78, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle 9:
there are seeds that are not severed and yet are not *dausthulya*. This is because the mundane path merely suppresses active manifestations and cannot permanently sever the seeds and *dausthulya*.

Thus, this passage appears in various sūtras and śāstras. Is it possible that one might first sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) without severing the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)?

Regarding the obstructions, one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). The first proposition refers to those of the two vehicles (*śrāvakayāna* and *pratyekabuddhayāna*). The second proposition refers to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The third proposition refers to Bodhisattvas of both the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of completion (*niṣṭhāmārga*).

The fourth proposition refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Is it possible for one born in a lower stage to abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*) of a higher stage? One should formulate four propositions. The first proposition refers to being born in a lower stage [and abandoning them].

The second phrase refers to one born in a higher realm who attains the abandonment of the *manas*-associated innate afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower realms upon attaining the fruits of the noble ones (*āryaphala*).

The third phrase should be understood accordingly. The fourth phrase refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), who, regardless of whether they are born in a higher or lower realm, merely suppress the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the afflictions without severing their seeds;
this is as explained in the section on the two obstacles (*dvividhāvaraṇa*) in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Regarding the discussion of what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and so forth, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* identifies the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) as primary;
the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, in its commentary on the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), likewise takes the view of a self as the foremost.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in its fiftieth fascicle, states that for a Bodhisattva who transforms afflictions (*kleśa*) at the seventh stage, it is by the power of merit and the observance of precepts that coarse afflictions are suppressed, allowing them to practice the Path with stability; yet, they still possess only craving and views (*tṛṣṇā-dṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the subtle [afflictions] such as pride, they are now also abandoned along with the subtle afflictions. When this treatise states that the seven stages are free from "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), what kind of view is it?
It refers to the view based upon views (*dṛṣṭyālambanā dṛṣṭi*). "Based upon views" means [taking them] as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) and so forth;

"conditions for arising" means taking them as objects (*viṣaya*). The three types of dependent origination are: (1) origination by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); (2) origination by way of the pleasant and unpleasant [experiences of] enjoyment (*upabhoga*); and (3) origination by way of the four conditions (*pratyaya*). As for origination by way of the four conditions:
The continuous succession of moments, bound together in segments throughout all internal sentient phenomena without beginning, is called "continuity" (*saṃtati*).

Within a single moment, delusion constitutes ignorance (*avidyā*); volition constitutes formative action (*saṃskāra*); consciousness constitutes mind (*vijñāna*); and the remaining factors constitute name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

The six sense faculties constitute the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the enumeration of contact constitutes contact (*sparśa*); the enumeration of feeling constitutes feeling (*vedanā*); craving constitutes thirst (*tṛṣṇā*); and the remaining afflictions constitute grasping (*upādāna*).

That is to say: bodily and vocal actions characterized by shamelessness and so forth constitute "arising" (*jāti*); the functioning of various phenomena constitutes "differentiation" (*jarā*); and the state of impermanence constitutes "death" (*anityatā*).

Because internal and external, sentient and non-sentient, and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) phenomena are bound together through the continuous succession of the cessation of the former and the arising of the latter, it is called "continuous bondage" (*sambandha*).

Since this essence permeates both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and because the twelve links of dependent origination differ across the three periods of time, it is called "segmented" (*paricchinna*).

In the *Vyākhyāyukti*, all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who maintain that all phenomena possess real activity (*kāritra*) and a real capacity for production (*janana-śakti*) are subsumed under three categories.
First, the refutation of the Vaiśeṣikas’ assertion that phenomena possess real activity, namely the phrase "that which possesses activity.
Second, [the refutation of] those non-Buddhists who hold that the essence of Maheśvara is real, pervasive, and eternal.
The same applies to other [factors] that can give rise to all phenomena; it is not for the sake of refuting the Mahāsāṃghikas and others of the future that this was said.
The Mahāsāṃghikas, the Mahīśāsakas, and others establish that dependent origination is eternal.

The third phrase refutes the theory of production from a single cause, namely the non-Buddhist adherence to the Great Lord (Maheśvara). This possesses three meanings: first, it exists as a substantial reality.
The capacity to produce [effects] has two aspects; second, the causes are permanent; third, a single cause produces all things.

Furthermore, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* also contains these three characteristics, and the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* likewise contains the "projecting" (*ākṣepaka*) and the "projected" (*ākṣipta*).

This differs from the *Yogācārabhūmi-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, which—as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*—asserts that at the time of the cause there are the projecting and the projected, while at the time of the fruit there is the actualizing (*abhinirvartaka*).
That which is produced—craving, grasping, and becoming—is the cause and not the fruit, because they are proximate to the ability to produce birth, old age, and death;

thus, the cause is also called the fruit by virtue of its proximity to the fruit. The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "Craving, grasping, and becoming give rise to birth, old age, and death; this is seeing the phenomena of future lives.
Furthermore, another interpretation of "fruit" is in the sense of "ripening," meaning that those previous seeds of karma are now acted upon by craving and the like.
Because that which is moistened will ripen to obtain the fruit, all that is currently ripening is designated as "fruit.
The phrase "preceded by non-knowledge regarding the objects of the Truths" indicates that the unique ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) underlying each of the Four Truths is capable of projecting karma.

Although the aspects (*ākāra*) of ignorance are only two—namely, regarding maturation (*vipāka*) and the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha*)—it can be deluded regarding the general and specific characteristics of the Four Truths alike; thus, desire has not yet been permanently severed.

The power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the power of the cause; that is to say, regarding the four [objects]—desire, views, precepts and vows, and the doctrine of self—the craving that arises toward them produces four results within those very objects such as desire.
This refers to the power of the object (*viṣaya-bala*). "Delighting in [them]" and so forth refers to the power of attention (*manasikāra-bala*). This explains the limb of craving.

As for the statement "because there is existence (*bhava*) and grasping (*upādāna*) consciousness," it says "because there is existence" because the limb of birth and so forth constitute the second existence, the future existence (*punarbhava*).

Regarding the term "grasping" (*upādāna*): it refers to the consciousness that is associated with grasping when one speaks of the branches of existence (*bhava*) as being "with-grasping" (*sa-upādāna*).

This is because the aspect of grasping is able to moisten the branch of karma so that it possesses grasping, thereby producing the results of the branches of birth (*jāti*) and so forth in a future life. Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "Grasping is twofold regarding karma:
first, it takes up a future existence, causing sentient beings to produce consciousness that possesses grasping. This explains that the branch of grasping accords with craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
I shall now explain the branches of existence (*bhavāṅga*) in detail. First, regarding "existence" (*bhava*), this refers to the existence of that which exists [in the present].

Second, "existence" refers to the existence of the future fruit. Regarding "appropriation" (*upādāna*), it refers to the seeds of karmic formations; this treatise designates them as the branch of consciousness (*vijñānāṅga*).

This is because, by means of that appropriation, one takes up the karma of future existence, and thus at the moment of death, one is about to undergo maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth. Next, the branch of appropriation (*upādānāṅga*) is discussed.

What is the meaning of "associated consciousness" (*saṃprayukta-vijñāna*)? There are two types of existence (*bhava*): first, existence as the state of being (*astitva-bhava*), and second, existence as the link of becoming (*bhavāṅga-bhava*).

Because this [consciousness] is capable of grasping the future link of consciousness (*vijñānāṅga*), it is called "existence-grasping consciousness" (*bhavopādāna-vijñāna*). Since it gives rise to craving (*rāga*), it encompasses both craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*).
Therefore, it is said that it "accords with craving. Otherwise, one should have said it "accords with grasping. Why, then, is it said to "accord with..."?

This follows the [explanation of] craving (*tṛṣṇā*). As for the explicit reliance on the three characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*), it is because the names of these three characteristics manifest this subsequent member;

by means of "desire," the reliance on the three characteristics is revealed, since the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* reveals the three types of suffering (*duḥkha*). Thus, one is separated from old age, sickness, death, and so forth.

Regarding the statement that this is not [the case] in the case of the womb-born body (*jarāyuja*) and so on: in the case of apparitional birth (*upapāduka*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise all at once; therefore, it should be understood that [the sequence] may occur later.
Because birth from a womb (*jarāyu-ja*) is necessarily not like this, it is singled out for exclusion; the same applies to moisture-born (*saṃsveda-ja*) and egg-born (*aṇḍa-ja*) beings.

Regarding karma, the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* should be applied to each [link] one by one, even citing the *Mahāvibhāṣā* and the *Yogācārabhūmi* to explain and resolve difficulties within each individual member.
Within the context of ignorance (*avidyā*) as karma, such a doubt arises: "Did I exist in the past, or did I not?"
