Nineteenth, ignorance (*avidyā*), as stated in the ninth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, refers to the lack of knowledge regarding: the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), the posterior limit (*aparānta*), both the prior and posterior limits;

the internal and the external; internal and external karma and its maturation (*vipāka*); the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; the four noble truths; causes and the formations (*saṃskāra*) produced thereby;
and likewise the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-sparśāyatana*). Regarding the prior limit, there are four [aspects], namely: "Did I exist in the past? or "Was I not? and so forth.
Is it non-existent? What kind of essence or what kind of category could it possibly have? Now, having raised the categories of existence and non-existence, there are two others;

previously, the eighteen types of ignorance were discussed. Within the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, regarding the merit and immovable formations of ordinary worldlings who are heedful of internal phenomena, these do not have ignorance as their condition.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that ignorance universally gives rise to the three types of karma. There are three assemblies [of this teaching]. One.
Regarding the internal factors, those ordinary beings who are heedful attain the definitive resolution of liberation; they do not experience a collective retribution.

This is because [retribution] is not produced by the ignorance of the four paths of seeing, but is produced solely by the ignorance of the path of cultivation, and thus results only in individual retribution. Therefore, the four types of ignorance pertain only to the path of seeing.

Furthermore, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* explains that [ignorance] is subsumed and suppressed by faith which is obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), and thus it does not fail to produce [its effects].

The wholesome [karma] arises from the four [defilements], while the unwholesome arises based on actual reality; furthermore, that which is obscured arises and also brings about a collective retribution.

Third, it is said that in the state of the unwholesome, consciousness exists solely as non-common and associated with two kinds of non-existence; it is not that seeds are absent, for in most states, the branches arise as distinct entities.

This is why they are not mentioned; however, it is not that there is no arising from latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), for the name of "collective retribution" refers to both karma of form and name (*nāmarūpa*).

The grasping of the sentient being’s own body constitutes the karma for entering the mother’s womb; furthermore, regarding the statement that consciousness enters the womb, why is it said that both [consciousness and name-and-form] enter?

There are two interpretations: first, the link of consciousness refers to the actual entry into the womb, while the statement that "name-and-form" enters the womb is because consciousness was previously described as the seed of karma.
Another interpretation holds that the link of consciousness [refers to the state] during the first seven days.

Before it has acquired shape, dimension, or characteristics, it is not yet the self-substance (*ātman*) of a sentient being; however, after one week, because it possesses characteristics, it is called the "substance of a sentient being.
This does not contradict [the teaching] that consciousness enters the womb.

Furthermore, because consciousness depends on the currently functioning consciousness which can maintain the karmic latencies (*vāsanā*), it is the consciousness produced by past karma that is designated as the basis for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); this is due to karma.

Regarding the entry into the mother’s womb, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that it is explained in terms of the present; the five [aggregates] such as consciousness are explained in terms of what is to come.

In the discourse on birth, old age, and death, it speaks of "producing the consciousness associated with grasping" (*sopādāna-vijñāna*). This means that from the link of existence (*bhava*), the consciousness associated with grasping (*upādāna*) arises simultaneously with the link of grasping.

It clarifies the distinctions among the five destinies, such as hell, and ensures that future existence (*punarbhava*) is not interrupted. This explains how one takes up future existence through grasping.
Regarding the statement that "the habitual tendencies of karma from the members of existence obtain a determined fruit" and that "it can also take up consciousness":

because the member of grasping (*upādāna*) gives rise to the karma of existence (*bhava*), it causes the future member of consciousness (*vijñāna*) to manifest; therefore, it is called "grasping-consciousness.

Due to the power of this member of grasping to moisten the karma, the habitual tendencies of the member of formations (*saṃskāra*)—once moistened by grasping—are transformed into the member of existence. Thus, [it is said].

Regarding the terms "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) or "appropriation" (*upādāna*), they signify the meaning of "outflows" (*āsrava*). Since outflowing karma is itself consciousness, it gives rise to outflowing karma;
this is explained in the same manner as the three types of defilement (*saṃkleśa*) in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. As stated in the ninth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:

"Three are afflictions (*kleśa*), two are karma, and the remainder are suffering (*duḥkha*). Regarding the performance of karma, some say that the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts speak only of the three afflictions, while the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* speaks [of them] in the context of consciousness.
It is taught that there is one portion of karma and seven portions of suffering; now, based on these three texts, they differ because consciousness and karma both pertain to the two [realms].
Among the eleven sections of the *Tattvārtha-śāstra* by Āryadeva Bodhisattva for refuting the treatises of the non-Buddhists, this is the first.

Regarding the *Vedānta* masters and the doctrines of the six heretical teachers, the non-Buddhist Kāraka-vaibhāṣika maintains that Brahmā is able to produce all things and serves as the cause for all phenomena; they establish Brahmā as the creator.

The treatise explains this view by stating that because [they rely on] Maheśvara and other such conditions, they know that everything is established through an unequal cause (*asama-hetu*), and thus they all fall into error.
Among these, the second refutes the Nirgrantha view that liberation occurs naturally after eighty thousand kalpas without the need to cultivate causes;
the third refutes the view of naturalism and the false calculation of the *ātman*, which posits the *ātman* as the cause of all phenomena;
and the fourth refutes the Ajita view that all phenomena do not arise from causes but exist spontaneously without depending on conditions.

Fifth, it refutes the Vaiśeṣika masters who establish that there exists a distinct function (*kāritra*) external to the self, asserting that all phenomena possess real functions (this being the question:
what kind of category is this?). Sixth, it refutes the Sāṃkhya calculation that *prakṛti* is eternal and serves as the cause for the twenty-three principles (*tattva*).
Seventh, it refutes the Saṃmitīya school regarding the momentariness, duration, and length of cause and effect. Eighth, it refutes the Sthavira school.

The arising and ceasing [of cause and effect] may belong to the same moment; alternatively, the Sautrāntika school clarifies that the maturation cause and its effect do not belong to the same moment, yet still maintains that there is no sense of "coming and going.
This explains the difficulty regarding the absence of the cause at the time of the effect, and the absence of the effect at the time of the cause.

In the third fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, section nine, it is explained that because non-Buddhists and others claim the four great elements produce all things, it is said that all phenomena face the difficulty of the simultaneous arising of sprouts and their causes, which serves to manifest their functional capacity (*śakti*).

Because the arising of similar characteristics is determined, the tenth [section] explains the objection raised by the Hinayana and others regarding a single cause producing a single body as its fruit, etc.;
it now demonstrates that multiple causes produce a single body or a fruit of a single type, such as the fruits of the five *ānantarya* [sins], which are experienced as a single body;

and how a single cause produces multiple bodies or fruits of multiple types, such as the various bodies experienced through rebirth (*upapatti-vedanīya*), etc. From the beginning, they are designated by their names.
Regarding the karma that ripens in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karman*), one cause produces one fruit; regarding karma that produces many fruits, it does so across multiple lifetimes.

Based on these four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), the meaning of the text can be easily understood. Since the eleventh [section] has already explained this, how could indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karman*) be called a "ripening"?

if one is in the state of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), the seven [consciousnesses] take the eighth as their cause, but the eighth does not take the seven as its cause, because it is not an object of perfuming (*vāsana*).

If, however, one is in the causal state (*hetu-avasthā*), then all seven preceding consciousnesses take the eighth as their cause, while the eighth takes the seven as its simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*). Thus, it is only in the latter case that they function as simultaneous causes.

Taking the seventh consciousness as the cause—excluding the maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*) within the six consciousnesses because they are not perfumers—the first six take the seventh as their cause, while the seventh does not take the six as its cause, for it does not manifest in dependence upon them.

The five [sensory] consciousnesses take the sixth as their cause but do not take the fifth as their cause; thus, among each respective group of consciousnesses, the preceding five do not act as causes for one another.

Regarding the associated mind and mental factors acting as mutual causes for one another, there are two theories concerning their objective conditions (*ālambana*). One theory states: the eight consciousnesses take the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) as their object.
Each of the seven derivative consciousnesses established therein acts as a cause for the others;

it is not that seven are the cause of eight, nor that seven are the cause of six, nor that six are the cause of seven, nor that six are the cause of five, nor that five are the cause of six, nor that five are the cause of six. Thus, each of the five [derivative] images is not the cause of the other five.

The same applies to their mutual observation: within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the primary mind (*citta-rāja*) serves as the cause for the objective aspect of the mental factors (*caitta*), but the objective aspect of the mental factors does not serve as the cause for the objective aspect of the primary mind, because it does not rely upon it.

Although the objective aspects of the primary minds and mental factors of the other seven consciousnesses are likewise co-existent, they do not act as causes for one another; rather, they arise by relying on each other. Thus, there is an interpretation that...

Although the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) exists because of other [aspects], it is not a simultaneous cause (*sahabhūhetu*) for others; as for what constitutes a simultaneous cause, it refers to those that are mutually intimate supports.

Furthermore, since the various objective aspects are not seeds in relation to one another, and since they are neither intimately conjoined with nor simultaneous causes of the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*), and since their manifestation is likewise not non-distinct from the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) and so forth, [this applies] within the objective aspect.
The primary elements (mahābhūta) act as causes for derived matter (upādāyarūpa), and derived matter that coexists with the primary elements acts as a cause for them;

because they are said to be causes insofar as they are never deficient and are mutually inseparable, the primary elements serve as causes for other primary elements, and derived matter serves as a cause for other derived matter, as appropriate.
This differs from other schools, which do not allow for the ten types of concomitant factors (*anuvartaka*) to ever function as effects.

Because the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) is established, its seeds are like those of a different nature; the seeds of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) serve as causes for the seeds of names-and-words (*nāma-kāya*), yet names-and-words and karmic seeds are not the causes [of one another].

The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as causes for derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), but derived matter does not serve as a cause for the primary elements, because it does not depend on them for its arising.
The seed of the eye serves as a cause for the seed of visual consciousness, but the seed-consciousness is not the cause of the eye.

Those that rely on other characteristics as causes are all like this. If they rely [on one another] as causes, they are causes only within the same stage (*bhūmi*). If they are simultaneous, they may belong to different stages.

Herein, based on the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), they function as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), such as the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) and so forth. As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as described here.

Regarding the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) among these, only the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that act together toward a single object serve as the cause; this treatise relies upon this.
Regarding the discussion of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) in terms of the mutual relationship between manifest activities:

what is called the "associated cause" (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caittas*) which, in mutual dependence, experience objects and possess their own functional capacity, much like a caravan of merchants.

It is not apart from this functional capacity that the *ālaya-vijñāna* gives rise to seeds as its support; rather, it acts as the cause for the associated dharmas. This is a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). This [category] encompasses all causal conditions.

Regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) among non-causal conditions: as for the realms (*dhātu*), it belongs only to its own realm; as for matter (*rūpa*), it belongs only to the aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*); and as for the [other] four, they belong only to the four aggregates.

Regarding their moral quality, those that are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral belong only to their own nature. Furthermore, the obscured [neutral] view of self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) also act as causes for unwholesome afflictions because they increase through habituation.
However, unwholesome afflictions do not [act as causes] for the co-arising view of self and view of extremes, because [the latter] do not manifest with increased intensity.
Because causes, conditions, and so forth do not increase in excellence compared to non-causes, they are of a different nature; because they are dissimilar to non-causes, they are not [identical].

Regarding the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), there are two parts: first, the main treatise explains it through two meanings; second, the commentary asks about all minds and explains the meaning of "immediately succeeding" based on the principle of uninterrupted succession.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), regarding the present mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*):
Regarding the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), with the exception of the mind of nirvāṇa, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"If these consciousnesses arise immediately after those [preceding] consciousnesses in a determinate manner, then these are said to be the immediate conditions for those.

This is as explained in the fourth and eighth chapters of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and within the section on the four conditions in the sixty-ninth fascicle, it clarifies how various minds arise in succession.

The eighteen [mental states] of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) are likewise; however, they differ slightly from those of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), which may be formulated as twelve mental states.

Regarding the mutual arising of the three realms: immediately following a wholesome mind of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), ten minds arise—namely, the four [minds] of the Desire Realm, the wholesome and obscured-neutral minds of the Form Realm (the latter being the "birth-sustaining" mind), and two [minds] of the Formless Realm.

According to the *Ṣaṭtriṃśat-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (or similar source cited as "Sixty-nine"), if one has long practiced [the Formless], then after a wholesome mind of the Desire Realm, [the Formless arises].

Regarding the arising of wholesome minds of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa-citta*), and the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-citta*), sixty-three [minds] are taught.

If one considers the sequential order, the mind of one in training arises after a mind of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*); immediately following the mind of one in training, the mind of one beyond training arises.

However, for those who have long practiced with mastery, it may also arise after a mind of the desire realm (*kāma-dhātu*). This wholesome mind of the desire realm arises immediately after nine minds.
This refers to the four [minds] of one’s own realm, the wholesome minds of the form realm and the formless realm, and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

When a defiled mind of the form realm arises, and once that defiled mind has already arisen, one gives rise to a wholesome mind of the desire realm in order to guard against that defilement. This is explained according to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna); for the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), there is no textual authority.

Furthermore, immediately after an unwholesome mind, the four [minds] of one’s own realm arise; there are also cases where they arise after an interval, as well as those of the higher realms, from the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) onwards.
The superior mind arises immediately after eight minds; namely, the four [minds] of its own level, the two wholesome minds of the form realm, and the obscured-unspecified mind.
The Mahāyāna treatise states: "Furthermore, when ordinary beings fall back from the worldly dhyānas and formless attainments previously acquired, it is because a defiled mind becomes manifest;
thus they fall back. This defiled mind of a lower level arises from a wholesome mind of a higher level."
The defiled mind also arises immediately after [other minds]; it arises from two types of minds in the formless realm—wholesome and defiled—as explained for the form realm.

Regarding the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta), six minds arise immediately after it: namely, the four minds of its own level, the wholesome and obscured-unspecified minds of the form and formless realms.

This refers to the state at the moment of death; the dying consciousness is always unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta). When descending from a higher level to a lower one, the dying consciousness is obscured-unspecified.
Because it arises after the mind, the mind at the moment of death must necessarily belong to its own level (*svabhūmi*).

Therefore, this discussion is based on all minds of one's own level and does not concern distinct consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). If one were to base it on distinct consciousnesses, these six minds that arise would constitute the actual moment of death;

this is the view of the Master [Sthiramati] regarding the sixth consciousness. If one follows the Master [Asaṅga], who maintains that the eighth consciousness arises immediately [after death], then four [minds] arise in succession, or otherwise [it is different].
Seventh, in the discussion, one further adds the obscured mind (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*) and the unobscured-neutral mind (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*) of the form and formless realms.
When entering the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), if one enters the untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā*), then ten minds arise;

if it pertains solely to the seventh [consciousness], there are four untainted minds. One should understand each of these cases accordingly below. This [seventh consciousness] arises immediately after the ten minds.
Regarding one's own level, there are four [minds]; for each of the two higher realms, there are three—namely, the wholesome, the unobscured-neutral, and the defiled.

According to the Yogaśāstra, when one dies from a higher level and is reborn in a lower level, from a wholesome mind of the higher level (whether it be innate-wholesome or acquired-through-exertion), and from a defiled or neutral mind, there arises immediately only a defiled mind of the lower level;
therefore, from an unobscured-neutral mind, nine minds arise immediately, including those of its own level.

Regarding the three types of wholesome minds that arise in the four form realms (*rūpadhātu*), because the transformation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the desire realm gives rise to those wholesome minds, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"Furthermore, immediately following an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛtacitta*) of the desire realm, a wholesome mind of the form realm arises—just as the transformation-mind of the desire realm [arises] from the fruit of the form realm.
This refers to a mind that resembles a desire-realm mind but is actually a form-realm mind, as it manifests transformations within the desire realm.
It is not the case that a neutral (avyākṛta) mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) does not give rise to a wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

When one gives rise to a defiled mind of that [upper] realm, it is like how, following a non-obscured neutral mind of the desire realm, there subsequently arises a "mind that moistens birth" (*upapatti-saṃdhāna-citta*) belonging to that [upper] realm; thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"When one is born in a higher stage from the desire realm, a defiled mind of the higher stage arises immediately after a neutral mind of the desire realm, and a non-obscured neutral mind belonging to that [higher stage] arises."

Regarding the mind, it is based on the sixth consciousness as the primary [consciousness] at the moment of death and rebirth, because the initial mind of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is a resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
If one were to take the eighth consciousness as the mind of death and rebirth, this meaning would not hold;

for there is no successive arising of a defiled mind in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), nor of an unobscured-neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*), as is explained regarding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

According to the explanation of the actual desire realm mind, it arises only from eight minds and does not give rise to those wholesome [minds], because if the eighth [mind] were taken as the mind at death or rebirth, it would arise only from six minds and not from the non-obscured-neutral minds of the two upper realms;

therefore, this [desire realm mind] arises from nine minds: four from its own realm, three from the form realm, and as previously stated, the fruit of the form realm arises from the wholesome mind of the desire realm.
Regarding the transformation of the mind within the realms (*dhātu*), as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:

that which arises from a defiled mind of the two higher realms refers to the case where, following a defiled mind for the sake of rebirth (*upapatti-pratisaṃdhi*), the sixth consciousness of the desire realm arises at the moment of death.

That which arises from an unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind is as previously stated regarding the initial mind of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and so forth. If the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is considered the mind of death and so on, it should be excluded according to reason.
Immediately after a wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), eleven minds arise:

three of its own level, four of the desire realm—namely, those arising from the mind emerging from meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and so forth—and the wholesome, unwholesome, and obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the desire realm, which refer to the time of death and rebirth from one's own level into a lower realm, as well as the time of falling away and giving rise to afflictions of a lower level; and the unobscured-unneutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind, which refers to transformation.
Regarding the statement that the transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) belongs to the desire realm: this is not the case for the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind.

When one is born into the formless realm, it refers to the wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*) and the obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*). Furthermore, regarding the obscured-unspecified mind, it is spoken of in reference to the mind at the time of death.

Also, when one is born with a mind of training (*śaikṣa*) or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), this wholesome mind of the form realm arises from nine types of minds: three from its own level, two from the desire realm—namely, the wholesome and the transformative—and [the remaining four from other levels].
