According to the actual reality, as indicated below, this concerns the attainment and non-attainment of seeds. At the beginning, based on the essence and its activity, the subsequent path of antidotes is initiated;

subsequently, based on the essence itself, this is explained. Herein, first, regarding the afflictions of the worldly path, both those to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and...
Based on consciousness, one should reflect upon and determine whether the afflictions of principle and phenomena within the cultivation of the afflictions are established or not;
this applies generally to both mundane and supramundane states within the context of mastery. "Dhyāna" refers to the four meditative absorptions (*dhyānas*).

"Liberation" (*vimokṣa*) refers to the four formless liberations, or the eight liberations, or all untainted concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*), which are all termed "liberation samādhis. Furthermore—

The meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the three realms consist of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; the attainments (*samāpatti*) consist solely of the wisdom of cultivation belonging to the higher stages.

Regarding all such qualities as *samāhita* (equipoise) and so forth—whether mundane or supramundane, according to their respective natures, whether they possess a nature or lack a nature, whether they have a body or not, and whether they are based on the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) or the useful or useless among the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) wholesome states—they likewise depend upon the useful or the useless.

All these points should be explained in detail: regarding those who have severed the roots of goodness (*samucchinna-kuśalamūla*), since the masters of the theory of seeds (*bīja-vādin*) maintain that [defilements] of one stage can manifest from another stage, this applies generally to the seeds within a single realm (*dhātu*) or across the three realms.
As for whether their essence and function are established or not, the wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) are determined to arise only from their own respective stages;
however, this discussion concerns only their establishment within their own stage, while the principles for other stages and so forth are to be understood by analogy.

In the context of accomplishment (*siddhi*), since it has not yet been discussed whether one’s own stage (*svabhūmi*) is accomplished or not, we shall now explain it in relation to the seeds of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

For those who possess the nature of existence (*bhavāstitva*), it is said in general that while their essence (*svabhāva*) is accomplished, their function (*kāritra*) is not. If one is of a nature incapable of attaining *nirvāṇa* (*aparinirvāṇadharman*), the untainted (*anāsrava*) is entirely unaccomplished;

as for the tainted (*sāsrava*), if one is of a non-severing nature (*asaṃvaradharman*), both essence and function are accomplished, whereas if one is of a severing nature (*saṃvaradharman*), the essence is accomplished.
The non-actualization of the application of wholesome roots belonging to those who have severed their wholesome roots is also termed the "severance" of the innate wholesome roots;
furthermore, it is called "non-actualization" because one cannot produce them in the present while remaining in a common meditative absorption. Other points should be understood according to reason.

The severing of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) is analyzed by way of five sections: (1) explanation of the name; (2) determination of its essential nature (*svabhāva*); (3) the basis upon which it depends; (4) the categories and numbers, as in the old manuals;

and (5) whether that which is severed resides in all six consciousnesses, or whether only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of severing them, because the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter One, states this.

(1) Regarding the explanation of the name: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter One, states: "In this context, the seeds are also called 'roots of goodness' (*kuśalamūla*). There is no... [text continues]

Greed, hatred, and delusion are also termed "roots of virtue" (kuśalamūla) by way of conventional designation; however, the severance of the roots of virtue refers to the continuity of the manifest roots of virtue being contrary [to their own nature], not to the permanent uprooting of their seeds.

Thus, the three types of virtuous roots belonging to the Desire Realm—whether manifest or seed-form, and whether contaminated (sāsrava)—are all termed "roots of virtue," because they are not yet useless like the uncontaminated (anāsrava).
Furthermore, these are exclusively those acquired at birth (upapattilābhika), not those produced through application (prāyogika), as the latter do not exist prior [to the moment of birth].
Because they have already ceased to arise, they are not the fruit of the higher realms; it is said that the roots of goodness acquired at birth in the higher realms are severed.

Regarding the statement "severing [the roots] in the three realms," this means making it impossible for them to arise. It is because the power of the seeds of false views, which had previously not arisen, can now cause them to manifest and continue in succession.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Due to those with sharp faculties, they accomplish superior grades of evil intentions."
The practice of such conduct constitutes the power of the cause; following after those evil friends constitutes the power of the conditions;
because that entanglement of false views is extremely heavy, perfected, and brought to its ultimate limit, it is able to sever one's own nature;
because one attains fearlessness regarding the manifestation of all evils, shamelessness and lack of remorse serve as its companions; and because there is no compassion.
That which has non-compassion as its essential nature and power to induce the severing of the roots of goodness is called the "severance of the roots of goodness.
Regarding the second [point], the definition of its essence: it takes as its essence the manifest and seed-state false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Just as a seed that does not obtain the cause of defilement is termed "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*), so too this [state] is by nature an affliction; thus it is likewise termed "non-acquisition" or "non-possession" (*asamanvāgama*).

Because it is of the nature of the noble ones (*ārya*), its essence consists of the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of defilement; this is the consensus among the ancients and the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), who hold that it is solely non-possession as its essence.
This is because, at the stage where the roots of goodness have not yet arisen, it is merely a provisional designation and thus not considered the actual essence.

If that were so, the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*) would also have to consist of non-possession; furthermore, it is not the case that only the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of false views constitutes its essence, for [afflictions] do not exist as mere manifestations.

Because wholesome states that have arisen must be continued, it is not the case that [the roots of goodness] are merely seeds; otherwise, the previously arisen roots of goodness would have to be severed before their actual manifestation (*samudācāra*).

Now, we take the seeds of the predominant type as capable of producing actual manifestations, and the manifesting mind itself as that which, through immediate succession and liberation, is capable of destroying the roots of goodness.
Furthermore, one may say that the seeds of false views are called "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*) of the seeds of the roots of goodness; thus, non-attainment constitutes its essence.

Because it lacks the function of a name, it is not the acquisition (*prāpti*) of an entity; therefore, acquisition should be designated as "existent" because its function is present, whereas non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) has the absence of such function as its essence.

This [non-acquisition] takes a provisional phenomenon (*prajñaptidharma*) as its essence. This seed resides in the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); following its support, it is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Furthermore, because false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) universally denies the four truths by means of the aspect of total negation, it may either take all four truths as its object or take only suffering (*duḥkha*) as its object.

Regarding the two truths: it has its own realm as its object; it is without cause, like the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*); and it is without fruit, like the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
As for the false view that can sever [the roots of goodness], the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that it is the "predominant false view" because it reaches its ultimate limit.

Third, concerning its basis: it exists only in the desire realm, not in the two upper realms; only among human beings, not others; among the four continents, it is not in Uttarakuru; and it pertains to both males and females, not others.

Because they possess only the practice of bodily conduct and sharp faculties, because all others lack evil views, and because their renunciation is firm and their afflictions are likewise [extinguished].

The reconnection of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) is analyzed through five aspects: first, the essential nature; second, the etymological explanation; third, the temporal period; and fourth, the categories and numbers.

The first section on the Yoga of the Five Consciousnesses states: "Because of having naturally sharp faculties, and because of seeing close friends cultivate meritorious deeds, one approaches virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa*) and hears the True Dharma.
By the power of these two conditions, one gives rise to doubt and thereby realizes certainty; this is the power of the cause.
One continues to reconnect with the roots of goodness because of naturally sharp faculties upon encountering superior conditions, yet the mind gives rise to hesitation."
Because it exists as both manifest and latent, it is able to reconnect [the roots of goodness] by means of the seeds of wholesome dharmas acquired through desire-realm birth;

these take as their essence both the capacity for present activity and the present activity itself, rather than taking the manifest alone as their essence. If they did not take the manifest as their essence, wholesome states would not arise, and the continuity of goodness would not be maintained.

If they did not take the seeds as their essence, then even when subsequent wholesome conditions are active, it would have to be called "reconnecting the roots of goodness" [without the seeds being present]. Therefore, it takes both the manifest and the seeds as its essence.
Regarding the two explanations for the name [of "reconnection of the roots of goodness"] based on the substance that can be conventionally designated as having been attained as previously severed:
first, it is called "reconnection of the roots of goodness" because it causes the seeds of the roots of goodness—which have the function of arising—to manifest and continue;
thus, the continuation of the roots of goodness is the "reconnection of the roots of goodness," which means the reconnection of the present roots of goodness. Both explanations are valid.

Regarding the three time periods, both those who have committed an *ānantarya* (immediate) offense and those who have not may continue their existence in this present life, as was the case with King Ajātaśatru;
thus, they differ from the followers of the Hīnayāna, for whom one who has committed an *ānantarya* does not continue in this life.

However, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that when entering hell and when emerging from hell, the roots of goodness are restored: for light offenses, it occurs upon entry, while for heavy offenses, it occurs upon emergence.

At that time, because the power of conditions (*pratyaya*) and the power of causes (*hetu*) differ in their relative weight, it is further said that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) may or may not receive its retribution based on this discussion of weight.

If it receives [retribution], it is heavy and thus continues at the moment of death; if it does not receive it, it is light and thus continues at the moment of birth. This is because it arises in conjunction with the manifestation of retribution.

Alternatively, there are four categories: those who continue at death due to the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), and those who continue at birth due to the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
The nine grades [of afflictions] are difficult to reconnect once severed, yet easy to reconnect while they persist; furthermore, their arising necessarily occurs in sequence.

Regarding the initial reconnection of the five types of consciousness, it is only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). As stated in the first chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*: "The unique function of the mind is that its continuity arises from doubt.
Thus, the initial reconnection of the sixth consciousness occurs in this manner.

In the sixth fascicle of the main treatise, regarding the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, there are two major sections: first, it demonstrates that this section as a whole consists of four chapters; second, following the headings, it provides an extensive analysis.

Within the chapter on the "Determination of Truths" (*Satyaviniścaya*), the major section is divided into three parts; first, it provides a general heading stating that there are four determinations of truth.

Next, following the headings for the explanation, after the Truth of the Path has been explained in the tenth fascicle, there is a question-and-answer analysis regarding the distinction between the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) of the mundane and supramundane paths, or their division into two.
Since these questions and answers concerning the sixteen aspects pertain to the Truth of the Path, here, within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), there are two parts:
first, the presentation of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the Truth of Suffering, and second, the discernment of the four aspects of the Truth of Suffering.

The beginning and middle [of this section] have two parts: first, a brief presentation that reveals only the essential nature and characteristics; second, an extensive exposition that reveals the distinctions among the characteristics of the truths (*satya*) as taught in various sūtras.

Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, an explanation of the characteristics of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); second, an explanation of the characteristics of the untainted pure land (*anāsrava-śuddha-kṣetra*).

Alternatively, it may be divided into two: first, a general heading; second, a detailed explanation. Within the detailed explanation, there are two further divisions, the second of which concerns the world-receptacle (*bhājana-loka*).
One should understand each of the remaining specific divisions of defilement and purity.

Second, in explaining its four modes of activity, this is divided into two parts: first, an explanation of the four common characteristics; second, a response to the previous difficulty regarding impermanence mentioned below, which further pursues the initial inquiry.
Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the heading; second, the explanation. Within the explanation, each division is treated individually.

One should contemplate the gravity [of suffering]. Within the section "Resolving Difficulties," there are two parts: first, an extensive explanation of the preceding impermanence; second, a brief enumeration of its eight types.

Below, there is an extensive explanation of the preceding suffering. Within the extensive explanation of impermanence, there are two parts: first, resolving difficulties regarding the impermanence of the external vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*);

second, explaining coarse and subtle form. Within the preceding characteristics of suffering, there are two parts: first, a brief enumeration of its eight types; second, an extensive explanation of internal suffering. Within the extensive explanation of internal suffering, there are further divisions.
Second, first there is a general expansion on the suffering within [the realms], followed by an expansion on the suffering of birth and death.
The Pure Land is analyzed through five gates: 1. Determining its essence; 2. The difference in the essence of the three lands; 3. Explaining the name and how it is derived;
4. The causes that give rise to it; 5. The persons who give rise to it. Regarding these various gates, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the Brahma King Śikhin spoke to Śāriputra:
Do not say that this buddha-field is impure. When the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* describes the matter of the thousand-petaled lotuses;
the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* speaks of the benefits of post-retrogressive retribution arising in the abode of the wisdom of Maheśvara.
The first fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, the ground of the trichiliocosm became entirely soft and supple, without any mounds or hollows."

Ruins, earth, stones, sand, gravel, and so forth constitute the third cause. Among these, there are both *sāsrava* (with outflows) and *anāsrava* (without outflows), which follow their respective primary and secondary causes as transformations of the various consciousnesses.
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states, "Generosity is the pure land," and so on. According to the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*, filial piety and the support of one's parents serve as the cause;
according to the twenty-first chapter of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, such acts as sweeping and cleaning the grounds of the Buddha’s Dharma lead to rebirth within a pure land.

The *Contemplation Sūtra* states that at the moment of death, when one has no leisure to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, if one encounters a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and achieves ten recitations, one will immediately attain rebirth in the Buddha-ground.
Vasubandhu and others all state that this arises from superior supramundane roots of goodness;

all other [causes] are remote, whereas this is the proximate and direct cause. As for the various "gates," they refer to the meaning of the eighteen perfections and so forth, as set forth in Vasubandhu’s *Treatise on Rebirth*.
Regarding the non-arising of those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna-gotra*), the *Contemplation Sūtra* states that those of middle capacity have already attained arhatship;

that treatise [the *Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*] relies on the sūtra concerning those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) who do not arise [in the Pure Land], whereas this sūtra relies on the sūtra concerning those of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*) who attain rebirth there.

Regarding women and those with physical deficiencies not being born there, the *Contemplation Sūtra* mentions that five hundred women, including Vaidehī, were all reborn together; that [other] treatise says that while the cultivation of causes is common to both men and women, they are reborn in male bodies there.

This is also difficult to resolve: how can the *Drum-śvara-rāja-sūtra*’s statement that the Mother of Amitāyus is named "Supremely Wondrous Countenance" be reconciled with the *Amitāyur-dhyāna-sūtra*, which states that those who have committed the five grave offenses (pañcānantarya) are not reborn there?

Furthermore, regarding the claim that those who commit the grave offenses and sever their roots of goodness are not reborn, while those who commit the grave offenses but do not sever their roots of goodness are reborn, and that prior to reaching the happy realms, one is constantly submerged [in suffering].

Because those who commit the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) are considered the lowest, it is said that within the states of the happy realms (*sugati*), encountering conditions to commit such a transgression constitutes the highest;

as in the case of King Ajātaśatru and others, through repentance and so forth, their sins were extinguished and they were reborn there. The places where they are born are inconceivable and are realized only by a Buddha.
That is to say, even the *svasaṃbhogakāya* realm and the *parasaṃbhogakāya* realms manifested by the Buddha are not yet attained [by them].
Those who practice meditative concentration (dhyāyin) and the like do not know [the Buddha-lands], let alone those who merely engage in discursive thought;

this is because they are known by all Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, since a practitioner of meditative concentration only knows the sublime concentrations attained by those below them and does not know the lands of those above, even those Bodhisattvas who are called "attainers of concentration" do not know the fundamental nature of the Buddha-lands.
61. The Yoga of Suffering Arising from Causes has five parts: First, being followed by manifold sufferings: namely, the hells, which are exclusively suffering;
the animal realm and the realm of hungry ghosts; and those born from a womb or an egg, who at the very moment of birth are oppressed by this suffering.

This [suffering] is narrow here and wide there, and it is necessarily a state of oppression during the fetal stage. It is established based on the human path in order to engender world-weariness, for that [human condition] is pervasive.
To speak truthfully, because that second [suffering] is accompanied by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), the seeds of the afflictions of the three realms follow along with its arising;

therefore, it is said that the three encompass the eight, and it is not mentioned [separately]. Furthermore, because there is no suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) in the higher realms, the third is called the basis of suffering (*duḥkha-āśraya*);
this refers to the basis of the second and fourth [types of] afflictions, as well as the fifth, which does not accord with one's desires.

In this context, that [aging] is not mentioned because it is proximate [to birth], because it is not suffering-as-suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), and because it is already subsumed within this very basis for other forms of suffering;

thus, all other phenomena are fully encompassed by reasoning. One should correctly apply this principle to the five types of decline in aging, which are all subsumed under "transformation" (*vipariṇāma*).
These five are: the excellence of complexion, physical strength, the sense faculties, enjoyments, and lifespan. (5, 5, 5, 3, 8) [The categories] are mutually subsumed.

There are two successive expositions. In the first gate, it is the same as here; in the latter gate, the first seven types of suffering are *duḥkha-duḥkhatā* (suffering as suffering), while the seven births that give rise to afflictions are *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā* (suffering due to change).
According to the actual fact of the inclusion within the three characteristics, the first four—birth-suffering and so forth—are accompanied by heavy burdens (*dausthulya*), and so on.

It is not that these do not exist in the higher realms; however, because they are characterized by many forms of oppression, they are taught as *duḥkha-duḥkhatā*. As for the two types of *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*, they exist only in the lower realms.

There are those who establish the first seven [types of suffering] based on the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and those who establish the final one based on all three realms; this is also without error.

Regarding the establishment of the gate of *tathatā* (suchness): it means that by taking the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) as the gate, one provisionally establishes the contemplation of *tathatā* during the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).

Subsequently, through the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one realizes and knows that the suffering of conditioned existence is its objective sphere (*ālambana*). Alternatively, it refers to the specific establishment of *tathatā* by means of the distinctions within subsequently attained wisdom.

By means of reasoning, one attains the door of realization that this is known as the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); thus it is called the ultimate (*paramārtha*), because through the door of reasoning, one knows it to be oppressive.

Among the twelve types of impermanence, they are divided into three groups: the first seven apply to both the internal and external; the next three apply only to the internal; and the final two apply only to [the internal].
The first seven [days] of the external [contemplation] are divided into two parts: first, one day contemplates what is non-existent; next, six days contemplate what exists.
Within the contemplation of what exists, there are three parts: first, two days contemplate subtle impermanence; next, one day contemplates coarse external impermanence;

and finally, three days contemplate worldly impermanence—present, future, and past, respectively. Next, the three [days] contemplate the internal; of these, the first contemplates the general nature of the self.

Next, one contemplates the transformation of the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) [existence], followed by the contemplation of the subtle movements of the mind. Among the two external [transformations], the coarse characteristics can be known: the transformation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) refers to disease;
the transformation of time refers to old age; and the transformation of lifespan refers to death at this present location.

One should consult the second and fourth sections of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* regarding the formation and destruction of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). Within that, there are three parts: first, the formation and destruction [of the world]; second, the clarification of the limit of the calamities (*saṃvartanī-kūṭa*); and third...

The fire of the minor intermediate kalpa destroys [the world] from below; subsequently, water and wind arise together from above, forming [the world] from the top down until it reaches the four heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Only after this is the earth and the heavens of the Desire Realm formed. When the kalpa is finally completed, the three minor calamities emerge; they emerge specifically during the period of decrease at the end of the kalpa.

Regarding the twenty kalpas of increase and decrease mentioned in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, this [minor kalpa] consists of eighteen because it proceeds toward decrease and then toward increase. Thus, it is not [twenty].
The contradiction is resolved by this enumeration of kalpas. Regarding the life spans of the gods in the form and formless realms, these are calculated based on their respective portions of lifespan;
for instance, the first dhyāna is equivalent to the desire realm, and its destruction is reckoned at sixty kalpas, which constitutes the lifespan of a Brahmā.

Thus, death occurs when merit is exhausted, when craving for meditative concentration wanes in the higher realms, when the power of merit is depleted, or when the lifespan itself ends—just as explained in the first and second [sections] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Regarding death through the exhaustion of lifespan, merit, and karma, as stated in the first chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there are three types of death; the first two are the same as here, while the third differs from this.
That [text] bases death upon nine kinds of conditions, such as immoderate eating and so forth.

However, that treatise defines death through the total exhaustion of the maturation (*vipāka*) of the three realms as "death through the exhaustion of lifespan," whereas death through the specific exhaustion of the power of merit is called "death through the exhaustion of merit. It is not merely a case of the exhaustion of distinct maturations.
The exhaustion of all virtuous merit is exactly like that deficiency of yoga; it is based solely on this that the death resulting from the exhaustion of merit is explained.

The same applies to the exhaustion of karma. Regarding the exhaustion of the body’s collective retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka-karma*), the non-collective is not mentioned because it is not collective.

Nor is the indeterminate mentioned because it is indeterminate. However, although both the first two [types of karma] are indeed karma, they are [distinguished] by the power of present life-span and merit.

Second, regarding the acquisition of distinct names through increase, there are two points: first, the determination of the timing for total retribution; and second, the fact that this karma exists when there is birth from karma, but does not exist when there is no such birth.

Within the section on the characteristics of suffering, there are two parts: first, the analytical distinction pointing to what precedes and follows; and second, the explanation of the intent of the sutra. Within the intent of the sutra, there are again two parts. First...
Following the citation of the sutra, the commentary provides three successive expositions. First, it explains by means of the three types of impermanence.

Second, it explains that while the category of suffering arises and the category of pleasure also ceases, the category of equanimity (*upekṣā*) likewise does not transcend these two dharmas; because eight forms of suffering are present therein, the Buddha stated that "all that is impermanent is suffering.
This, however, is not the case [in this context], as it differs from the initial interpretation. In the present explanation, there are the two characteristics of arising and ceasing.
Among the accompanying [factors], there are eight aspects of suffering that are described as impermanent;
because they were previously explained as suffering due to the three types of impermanence, and now as suffering due to the two types of impermanence—arising and cessation—there are eight sufferings.

In this third section, those among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) for which the eight characteristics of suffering can be discerned are termed "suffering due to impermanence" (*anitya-duḥkha*), thereby distinguishing them from uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) conditioned phenomena.
In the first major section, there are two parts: first, the explanation; second, the citation of scriptural evidence based on this meaning to establish the preceding [points].

What is the distinction between the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of selflessness (*anātma-lakṣaṇa*)? The characteristic of emptiness involves the removal of formations (*saṃskāra*), which is a remote expedient (*dūra-upāya*); the practitioner of selflessness retains formations, which is a proximate expedient (*āsanna-upāya*).

This is because one contemplates the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) as being without the characteristic of self. Thus, the three vehicles (*triyāna*) give rise to distinct phenomena according to their respective capacities.
This serves as the gateway for entering true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*).

Within the extensive treatment of impermanence (*anityatā*), there are two parts: first, establishing the characteristics of impermanence; second, establishing the coarse and subtle [distinctions] through the analytical wisdom that deconstructs primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Thus it is said that there are eight types of impermanence. Of these, the first six apply the analysis of matter by analogy to the mind, while the latter two apply subsequent [analyses] by analogy.

Among the first six [categories], the first five consist of dispersed forms (*vikīrṇa-rūpa*), which correspond to the subsequent one [category] of fixed forms (*niyata-rūpa*). Within the dispersed forms, the first four consist of internal forms (*ādhyātmika-rūpa*), which correspond to the subsequent one [category] of external forms (*bāhya-rūpa*).
Regarding the impermanent essence (*anitya-svabhāva*), there are two parts: first, the explanation of the great elements and their derivatives (*mahābhūta-upādāya-rūpa*);

second, the analysis of the atom (*paramāṇu*). Within the first part, there is first the question and then the answer. Within the answer, there is first a general response and then a specific response. Within the specific response, there are two sections; first...
Following the correct understanding, within the subsequent section on the extent of suffering, the first part relies on the latter to clarify the stages of suffering.

It clarifies that death has three [or eight] types, such as the non-quiescent states; the primary existence (*pūrvakālabhava*) is explained first, followed by the death-existence (*maraṇabhava*), then the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), and finally the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*).

Alternatively, regarding the eight kinds of suffering: the first five pertain to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while the latter three rely on noble ones (*ārya*); or alternatively, the first seven rely on the substantial [existence].
The latter one is not real; among the first three, the first two pertain to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the latter two pertain to the two higher realms.

This is because the desire realm possesses the suffering of tranquility (*śānta-duḥkha*), and it is capable of definitively pacifying that suffering. Alternatively, the stage of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) is itself termed "tranquility" because it differs from other ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
However, this is stated only with respect to the desire realm; regarding the two higher realms, this specific kind of liberation is not mentioned.
Since this tranquility-inclusion (*śānti-saṃgraha*) is of the same category as the preceding one, it is not mentioned;

or, because in the two higher realms there is definitely no capacity for this life to produce the fruit of the meaning of "tranquility from suffering. Regarding the suffering of death, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the period leading up to death and the actual moment of death;

second, the explanation of the signs of death, namely the gradual cooling of the body from the top or bottom. Within the context of dying with an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), the stage of a sharp mind is clarified during these two periods.

This refers to the state when the mind is characterized by the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the state of craving that moistens rebirth (*upapatti-saṃyojana-tṛṣṇā*), or the stage of lack of clarity—that is, the precise moment of death.

Alternatively, it may be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) because, due to the absence of two conditions, one’s own preparatory effort (*prayoga*) lacks the capacity for deliberation regarding previously performed wholesome or unwholesome acts;

or because there is no external force to induce wholesome or unwholesome states. Or, it may be indeterminate because the preparatory effort itself lacks functional efficacy. Regarding this latter point, there are two interpretations.
First, it is said that because the power of one’s own mind is weak, one cannot reflect upon or measure the wholesome and unwholesome deeds previously committed;

even if there were instruction from another, one would be unable to give rise to wholesome or unwholesome states, but would instead die with a mind born of craftsmanship, deportment, or maturation, which is neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Second, it is said that when one previously gave rise to a mind of the three natures based on two conditions, this was precisely the state of attachment to the self (*ātma-sneha*). Upon seeing [the signs of death], [one dies].
Having realized [the truths], because the power of the antidote is strong, although the first two fruits may arise, they will be weakened; thus they are subtle and do not conflict [with the path].
As for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), their power is weak and their greed is intense, so that when wholesome functions arise, each is weakened by what it craves and is consequently subdued.

Regarding the arising of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the *Vyākhyā* states: "It should be known that this refers to the stage of the mind associated with self-love (*ātmasneha*), as previously explained."
A general discussion of the mental states regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): here, the mind at the moment of actual death and the mind of self-love are omitted for brevity.

There are ten sections for the analysis of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). First, the manifestation of signs: this includes the yoga of being about to die and the two distinct signs after death.

Within this, there is a general discussion. Second, the location of manifestation: it occurs in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) at the stage of actually undergoing birth, during the state of entering the womb.

Since the state of birth necessarily involves an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), one who passes away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is born in a lower realm, rather than being born in the formless realm itself.
Alternatively, at the very moment of taking birth, one dies in the desire or form realms and is reborn in the two lower realms;

the place where the intermediate existence is currently arising is precisely the place where the present body died. When one dies in the formless realm and is born in a realm possessing form, that is the death in the formless realm.

Regarding the place of death: although there is no distinct location for the place of death, it is precisely at the place where one previously died and was born in the desire or form realms that one experiences the maturation (*vipāka*) of the formless state.
Thus, even though kalpas of formation and destruction may pass, the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) manifests in that very place.

Therefore, when it says "in the stage after the end of life," according to the intent of this passage, the former interpretation is correct; it is intended to clarify the presence or absence [of the intermediate state] within the three realms.
Because there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is therefore called "nirvāṇa. Some say that the intermediate state exists, while others clarify that it does not exist.

In the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), for those who pass away quickly—such as when a person transforms into a tiger and so forth—the intermediate state does not exist. Because there is no [intermediate state], one falls directly into hell.

Since there is no intermediate state arising at the periphery of hell, one does not take a human body into hell to undergo suffering; rather, one dies near that [hell] or is transformed [into a hell-being].
That fruition is not [subject to] karma because it has already matured as a fruition; it is like a person [escaping] from a tiger or similar creature.

Among the third category of names, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that it is also called a "destiny" (*gati*) and a "birth" (*upapatti*), and is thus termed "and so forth" (*ādi*). Fourth, regarding the limit of lifespan: due to its force, it lasts at most seven days;
this applies equally to both the Desire Realm and the Form Realm. Some explain that for those who subsist on fragrance, even in the Form Realm, it is seven days.
How is it that this [intermediate state being] does not exceed seven days? Because its duration is fixed, it does not wait for conditions such as those provided by its father or ancestors;

therefore, it is called a "seeker of fragrance" (*gandharva*). This exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is not so, as there is no fragrance to seek, though it is still termed an "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*) and the like.

Thus, the meaning may be understood accordingly. Refer to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Sui-yüan wang-sheng ching) regarding matters such as the hundred-day limit and so forth. Fifth: The Formation of the Intermediate Existence.

One should examine and differentiate the various cases where karma follows prior habituation, such as when ten types of karma are performed simultaneously. How can there be killing, stealing, and so forth?
Consult the *Garbha-avakrānti-sūtra* (Sutra on Entry into the Womb), which explains that Bodhisattvas teach beings within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Consult the sixth [chapter], "Beholding Beings of One's Own Kind," and the first [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, "Discriminating the Good and Evil Realms. Seventh, the form of the intermediate state resembles that of one’s future destination.
Regarding the places of birth, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that the gods face upward, while those in the three [upper] directions and the hells face downward.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says that humans and devas face sideways, while those in the three evil realms face downward. Regarding the eighth [chapter], the destination is unobstructed and its vision is far-reaching, exceeding the scope of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

It is not like being born in the Western [Pure Land], which exceeds the measure of supernatural powers; one should contemplate and examine this until the conclusion of the ninth [chapter] on death and rebirth.
The tenth chapter, "The Yoga of Birth," explains its characteristics in detail; the "Yoga of Rebirth and Sustenance of Delusion" also explains its characteristics;
and the "Yoga of Birth within Existence," the characteristics of taking birth, as well as the fourth fascicle’s description of the stages of gestation in the womb, are all as described therein.

The four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) are analyzed through various categories, such as which realms and destinies they comprise, the presence of determinate karmic causes and conditions, and the stages of realization;
these are explained in the second fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and their nomenclature may be verified in the *Bunshaku-shō*.

Regarding the essence of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*): the Buddha, observing dependent origination, saw that old age and death have two causes for birth—the coarse birth and the subtle birth—both of which are termed the Truth of Origination.

Thus, all contaminated suffering (*sāsrava-duḥkha*) is termed the Truth of Origination. If one relies on the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) perspective, all twelve links are the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), and suffering is also the Truth of Origination.

If one relies on this present text, the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and the external dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) are termed "suffering," while karma and afflictions are termed "origination."

The term "affliction" (*kleśa*) refers to the first gate of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), which analyzes its essential nature; the second gate concerns its general and specific natures; and the third gate concerns their individual natures.

Regarding the Truth of Origination, there are two parts: first, the question, and second, the answer. Within the answer, there are three sections: first, a brief summary answer; second, a detailed analytical answer beginning with the words "As for afflictions...";

and third, an explanation of the four aspects (*ākāra*). Within the first of these, there are again two parts: first, explaining that two factors constitute origination; and second, resolving contradictions.
In the lower fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Six Universal Pervasive Conditions of Craving*, it also explains the universal pervasives (*sarvatraga*). Next, it analyzes the four types of craving;

as in the fifty-fifth [fascicle], this accords with what follows regarding the universal pervasives of the three times. Why is the past not mentioned, speaking only of four types? This is stated according to their predominant activity (*adhika-pravṛtti*).

In reality, regarding the past, there are also both craving for the object (*ālambana-tṛṣṇā*) and craving for the entity (*vastu-tṛṣṇā*). Alternatively, the past may be included because its active manifestation (*samudācāra*) is the same.

Having entered [the realm], because one attains the gate of the objective sphere of the body, only four [types of seeking] are mentioned; the three seek sensual desire, specifically sexual desire, because the name [of the eye] and the objective sphere of the subtle desires are preeminent.
Because there is seeking within the two realms, the internal body itself is preeminent, thus it receives the general name.

Seeking an improper holy life (*mithyā-brahmacarya*) refers to seeking liberation while not being liberated from birth and death; seeking the true Dharma refers to correctly seeking liberation from birth and death, and therefore it is not included [among the former].

The three types of seeking: the third is the seeking of transcendence (*abhiniṣkramaṇa*). Because one seeks liberation from all three realms, this seeking of transcendence may be either wholesome (*kuśala*) or defiled (*kliṣṭa*).

Seeking that is not transcendence is exclusively wholesome; false seeking is pervasive across both the wholesome and the defiled. As for the six characteristics among these [characteristics], the ancients said:
"Doubt, view, pride, delusion, greed, and hatred are, in order, the six characteristics. This is because they are also the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the fundamental [afflictions].

The fifty-ninth [fascicle] states that there are two characteristics of afflictions (*kleśa*): first, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) subsumed within greed, hatred, and so forth—namely, these six;

second, the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which refers to their lack of tranquility at the time of arising. Third is the characteristic of differentiation, referring to [terms such as] fetters (*saṃyojana*) and bonds (*bandhana*).

The eighth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* also mentions the common characteristic, but this current interpretation is not correct; it is actually an explanation provided in the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary).

Regarding the sixth category, "universal characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of consciousness-only, a certain master explains: these [six], such as distraction (*vikṣepa*) and so forth, are the universal characteristics of the afflictions (*kleśa*), not their specific characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*).

This was already explained previously in the first fascicle. Alternatively, it may be that the names of these six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are borrowed to manifest the various universal characteristics;
or else, because the eight great secondary afflictions pervade all defiled mental kings (*citta-rāja*), they are combined with the six primary afflictions to form the state of non-quiescence.
The inversion of tranquility (*śamatha*) should each be combined with the two characteristics of "having a self" and "knowing. Heedlessness (*pramāda*) is laziness (*kausīdya*);

the two characteristics of heedlessness are shamelessness (*anapatrāpya*) and lack of faith (*āśraddhya*). Just as one who lacks shame is inverted, all such inversions are delusions regarding principles and phenomena according to their respective applications.
As for "shamelessness," this refers to that which is common to the three realms; it is not merely the absence of *hrī* (modesty) and *apatrāpya* (dread of blame), but rather a defiled state of mind.
All disturbances arise because of being slight and lacking shame.

Regarding the three types of *yoga* of the arising of afflictions mentioned in the eighth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are six [factors]; among them, the first, second, and sixth correspond to the three factors within this [text].
The third [factor of that text], "intimacy," the fourth, "false teachings," and the fifth, "instruction and habituation," are not mentioned here.
This teaching is definitive regarding internal conditions, while that [other] teaching concerns both internal and external;

therefore, they are not contradictory. Within the objects of the spheres (*viṣaya*), there are four parts: first, a general clarification of the conditions of afflictions (*kleśa*) and their bases; second, the clarification of the mutual conditioning between lower and higher realms; third, the clarification of the uncontaminated conditions (*anāsrava-ālambana*);
and fourth, the clarification of conditions involving both existent and non-existent bases. Among these, within the mutual conditioning of various afflictions, one observes...

The ten [afflictions] mutually serve as objects for one another and can also act as causes; they generally take the five doors as their objects. On the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they take their own kind as objects, but do not take the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) as an object.
If it were otherwise, there would be no distinction between the paths of seeing and cultivation. This passage summarizes the point;

the fifty-eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also states that the ten afflictions mutually serve as objects for one another. Furthermore, "thing" (*vastu*) refers to the objective sphere (*viṣaya*); "principle" (*dharma*) refers to the conventional thing (*saṃvṛti-vastu*).

"Phenomena" (*vastu*) refers to the substantial entity (*ātman*), the basis and the object of the afflictions. Regarding the "object of observation" (*ālambana-vastu*) within the sixth chapter on *vijñapti-mātra*, the intention here is to exclude greed, hatred, pride, and the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
This is because [these] do not take higher realms as their objects; it is explained according to the predominant coarse characteristics rather than the ultimate limit of reasoning.

Furthermore, since the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) arises subsequent to the view of self, it is not mentioned here. Among these, only the associated ignorance (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*) is said to serve as the condition.
Regarding "other stages" (*anya-bhūmi*): this is also stated based on the majority of cases, as there is also ignorance regarding higher stages;
thus, the afflictions of a higher stage do not take a lower stage as their object. This is explained according to the majority, or because they follow along [with the mind].

Regarding the fact that they take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as an object, as in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, here it is stated generally that the objects conceived by discrimination (*vikalpa*) are not separate from discrimination itself, because they depend on objects that lack substantial essence or function; therefore, all is merely mind (*citta-mātra*).
Regarding the fifty-nine [categories] within the "Objectless" (*anālambana*) section, they are the same as those in the fifth fascicle [of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*].

The fifty-eight [categories] explain that those which take [erroneous] views as their object are called "objectless" (*avastuka*), while the remainder are called "with objects" (*savastuka*). The *Nyāyānusāra* cites a sutra to explain "objectless" and "with objects," stating:

"That which is abandoned through the Path of Seeing is called 'objectless'; that which is abandoned through the Path of Cultivation is called 'with objects'. [The text] provides one explanation for the term *satkāyadṛṣṭi*.

The other nine types [of afflictions] arise with "non-existent objects" (*avastuka*) as their condition; taking this as the basis, they are explained from that fundamental perspective and thus termed "cultivation of the path with non-existent objects.

This is not the case for [the view of] a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because *satkāyadṛṣṭi* is exclusively an exaggeration (*samāropa*) while false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are exclusively a deprecation (*apavāda*);
since neither of these apprehends a real entity, they are called "non-existent objects. Greed and the others [arise] from this basis and are therefore named accordingly.

The afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are not like this; therefore, they are called "with objective basis" (*savastuka*). There are three explanations for this: the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) are delusions regarding principle and lack coarse, manifest objects, so they are called "without objective basis" (*avastuka*);
the afflictions abandoned through cultivation arise by taking objective things as their basis and have coarse, manifest objects as their spheres, so they are called "with objective basis.

Now, the Mahāyāna is not like this, as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-guhya-mukha* (Essentials of Consciousness-Only). This present volume follows the definitive [explanation] therein.
Because each [subsequent category] is increasingly superior, the view of self and the view of extremes (*satkāya-antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) are taught.
In the section on associated factors, the texts regarding greed (*rāga*) not being associated with hatred (*dveṣa*) are all the same;

as for its association with the other five types of pride (*māna*) and so forth—fifty-five in total—one should consult the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Wei-shi). Regarding hatred not being associated with pride, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* base this on the aggregate of pleasure (*sukha-skandha*).

Because pride does not give rise to hatred, the *Abhidharmakośa*—relying on the totality of the two [afflictions] and a small portion of the three views within the aggregate of suffering—states that it is dissociated from them.

In reality, however, it is associated with a small portion of the three views. When the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that it is contradictory and associated with others, it refers to delusion (*moha*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
As explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, among the [six] types of pride, it is stated only that it is not associated with hatred or doubt.
The rest should all be understood by analogy.

Regarding the distinctions, since the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter eight, mentions faculties (*indriya*) and great elements (*mahābhūta*) which are not found in this treatise, it uses the term "and so forth" (*ādi*).

Here, there are only twenty-five [factors] that can conjoin with suffering, and for this reason they are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*); in reality, however, all afflictions (*kleśa*) are capable of doing so.

The nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) that are exclusively afflictive are increased [in this context]; therefore, among these nine fetters, the two types—envy (*īrṣyā*) and stinginess (*mātsarya*)—cause those who have gone forth to be poor in wisdom and those who live at home to be poor in wealth.
Consequently, among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), these two are established as independent fetters. The remaining seven types are primary afflictions (*mūlakleśa*);

they are categorized separately because the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*) serves as their seed and the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśasaṃyojana*) serves as the means for their mental engagement and cultivation. Thus, they are opened up [as distinct categories].

The remaining [factors] each stand alone and together constitute two types of fetters (*saṃyojana*): those arising in householders—namely, attachment, aversion, pride, parsimony, ignorance, views, and grasping—and those arising in renunciants—namely, doubt and envy.
Attachment, aversion, and pride are all "fetters with a cause" (*sahetuka-saṃyojana*). Parsimony is the cause for poverty regarding wealth in future existence.
Attachment and aversion arise toward both sentient and non-sentient objects; pride arises only toward sentient beings; and ignorance, views, and grasping constitute the three [remaining fetters].

Associating with the wicked plants the seeds for the three [hindrances] of listening, reflecting, and practicing; one doubts the sublime Dharma and lacks resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), and one is impoverished in wisdom.

Therefore, they are established as afflictions of sentient beings that neither decrease nor increase. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "These two are exclusively unwholesome and arise spontaneously (*svatantra*);

therefore, they are established as fetters (*saṃyojana*). Furthermore, because these two frequently act as the cause for poverty and universally manifest as secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), they are [established as] vexations (*paryavasthāna*)."

Because the two categories [of defilements] are intermingled, as stated in the twenty-first [chapter] of the *Abhidharmakośa*, regarding the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), it merely says "lack of knowledge in the three realms.

Consequently, it states that one does not understand or comprehend suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*). In reality, however, this also implies a lack of comprehension regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

When emphasizing the profound delusion concerning one's own and others' realms, the rest is omitted for brevity. This is because it is said that [ignorance] is a composite cause of suffering; thus, it is discussed within the context of the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
"‘I shall be liberated’ and so forth is the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi); ‘I shall abide eternally’ and so forth is the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi);

‘there is certainly no liberation within the Buddha-dharma’ and so forth is wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi). Within the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), to reject the Eightfold Path and instead cling to the view of self and so forth is grasping at views;
and preceded by that [grasping], to regard either vows or ascetic observances as the path to purification is also grasping at views."

Regarding the three fetters (*bandhana*) arising from the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), in reality all of them are called "fetters," which refers to the consciousness associated with them.
However, here [the text] speaks of them based on their increase in accordance with the three [types of feeling]. This is not a case of increasing or decreasing [the number];

the commentators explain that because greed, hatred, and delusion constantly underlie (*anuśerate*) pleasant feelings and so forth, these underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are described as "increasing" defilements and are said to exist in the future. They are all deluded regarding the one [feeling].
Thus, lack of mastery over wholesome application is called bondage. Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 8 and fascicle 89, establish the same [distinctions] as the two metaphors below:

the first metaphor concerns not following one's desires regarding the wholesome; the second metaphor concerns the three feelings (*vedanā*) increasing in accordance with the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) within birth and death.
According to the actual seeds, all [of these] exist; if they increase according to their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they likewise follow accordingly.
Because they increase all dharmas and manifest as the fundamental [afflictions] that increase along with them, there are briefly seven types of increase (*anuśaya*).
*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, Fascicle Seven;
*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, Fascicle Eight (Treatise Text, Fascicles 7 and 8).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of the Great Ci’en Monastery.

Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), there are two types: first, those that are general; second, those that are specific. Regarding the specific ones, three reasons are established hereafter for their designation as such.
They are called "secondary afflictions" because they afflict the mind. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Because they pervertedly defile the mind, they are called [afflictions]."

Regarding the three phrases beginning with "the secondary afflictions cause one not to be free from passion," greed, hatred, and delusion are respectively explained as the three unwholesome roots in the eighth and ninth [chapters].
Because they are extremely heavy, the greed, hatred, and delusion of the form and formless realms do not increase there as secondary afflictions;

or rather, because their seeds exist there, they are not established as such in that context. It is by means of these three that all beings are caused not to be free from passion and so forth, even in the higher realms.

Because greed and the other [afflictions] cause one to depart from detachment, the eighth [chapter] states that those which frequently manifest as active states are called *paryavasthāna* (entanglements);

however, these [other afflictions] do not reach the degree of this [greed]. Furthermore, it adds that they "entangle" the mind. The eighty-ninth [chapter] states that all afflictions which manifest as active states are entirely termed *paryavasthāna*.
Nevertheless, there are eight types that frequently manifest at four specific times: namely, when practicing the training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā*), and [when lacking] shame (*ahrī*).

The frequent occurrence of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is an obstacle when practicing the training in concentration; the frequent occurrence of lethargy and drowsiness (*styāna-middha*) is an obstacle when practicing the training in wisdom because it hinders the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*);

the frequent occurrence of restlessness and misconduct (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) is an obstacle [to the training in morality]; and envy and avarice (*īrṣyā-mātsarya*) are obstacles to the mutual enjoyment of wealth and the Dharma by fellow practitioners.
These two—envy and avarice—are obstacles common to both wealth and the Dharma. Regarding the eighth among the floods (*ogha*), it is said that it is "deep and difficult to cross."

Because they drift along with the current, they are called "floods" (*ogha*). In this context, they possess only the sense of drifting, drowning, and surging in accordance with the flow of birth and death, and of conforming to the defilements (*saṃkleśa*) of birth and death;
they lack the sense of being deep and difficult to cross. Because of this drifting and surging, they are deep and difficult to cross.

As stated in [the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*] 89: "Desire, greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth—these afflictions bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kleśa*) are what the practitioner [encounters] in the desire realm."
The superior-grade afflictions (*kleśa*) that bind [beings] have not yet been abandoned or fully understood; these are known as the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*).

Furthermore, the three types—views (*dṛṣṭi*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)—also take predominance (*adhipati*) as their essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the flood. Specifically, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those who have not yet attained freedom from desire—excluding the various non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*)—are called the flood of desire.

Those who have already attained freedom from desire are called the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*). As for the various non-Buddhist outsiders, according to the majority of treatises, they should be classified accordingly.
It should be understood that there are two other types of floods (*ogha*): all various wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are briefly subsumed under one name, the flood of views;
and the causes and conditions of those wrong views are briefly subsumed under one name, the flood of ignorance (*avidya*).

Herein, the intended meaning is that, with the exception of those outside the [Buddhist] fold, all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm—including superior grades of greed, hatred, and so forth—arising in those who have not yet abandoned desire, are called the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*).

Excluding the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), all superior-grade afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire, form, and formless realms that are free from passion are called the "flood of existence" (*bhava-ogha*).
Its essence consists of the superior-grade views and ignorance (*avidyā*) regarding the paths outside the three realms;

it does not include the middle or inferior grades, as their meaning would not correspond [to the definition], for they are not floods. Furthermore, the various forms of the view of self and extremes (*ātma-antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) possessed by those who are not non-Buddhists...
Delusion is also called the "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*) because it is not an "unrighteous holy life" (*abrahmacarya*);

thus, the greed, hatred, and so forth possessed by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are also subsumed under the "outflow of views" (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*), as this is discussed from the perspective of the majority, with views being primary.

Furthermore, since they are explained as "floods" (*ogha*), the superior [grade] is taken first, while the medium and inferior grades are likewise included; otherwise, the inclusion of phenomena would be incomplete, as many external paths arise beyond these categories.

If one asks whether the views of others, as well as ignorance associated with those views, are also subsumed under that [view of self-existence] because they are also seekers of a false holy life (*mithyā-brahmacarya*) and are discussed through many gates, the answer is no.

Among the three outflows (*āsrava*), the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) should be called "arising from non-Buddhists" (*bāhyaka*) only because it differs from the two types of seeking among non-Buddhists regarding the upper and lower realms; thus, within the latter two [outflows], there is the relationship between the basis and that which depends upon it.
Because they are divided, they are not both; since both desire *nirvāṇa*, they grasp [the path]. The eighty-ninth passage explains this very well:

"The two arise from the presence of delusion. This refers to ignorance as the root, and the pursuit of liberation through three views and the application of perversions as the two types of grasping (*upādāna*).
The eighth [topic] within the *Yuga* (Hitching-Post) states that the meaning of *yuga* is the "expedient means of wrong conduct" (*mithyā-pratipatti-upāya*).

Just as a chariot’s hitching-post is the expedient means for pulling the chariot, here it is said that being an obstacle to dissociation (*visamyoga*) and being contrary to purity is like a hitching-post; the hitching-post restrains the ox so that it cannot escape.

This serves as a metaphor for obstacles preventing the conditions for dissociation. Now, the eighth [section] does not take the obstacle itself as the metaphor for dissociation, but rather uses the chariot as a metaphor for wrong conduct.

The yokes (yoga) guide [the mind] and are not inconsistent with this; they are explained according to two meanings. The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Treatise on the Compendium of Ascertainment), fascicle 89, states:
"If those afflictions are of equal proportions—neither increased nor decreased—they are precisely the 'all afflictions' mentioned above, which are designated as yokes.
Inferior-grade [afflictions] are not subsumed under either [of these categories]; they are neither floods (ogha) nor yokes."
The eighth section of the *Jñānaprasthāna* states: "To be able to grasp one's own continuum so that it is not severed is 'clinging' (*upādāna*).

Within this, there are two meanings: first, grasping at the root of contention; second, grasping at future existence (*punarbhava*). The latter alone is intended here. The eighty-ninth [section] states:

"The four types of clinging are established based on the categories of householders and non-Buddhist renunciants—namely, that which is clung to, that which clings, and that for the sake of which one clings."
All these are grasping (*upādāna*). That which is sought to be seen—namely, rules and observances (*śīla-vrata*) and the doctrine of self (*ātma-vāda*)—is the "grasped" (*upādāya*).
These four kinds of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are the "grasping. Initial grasping arises for the sake of obtaining various desires and for the sake of enjoyment.
Furthermore, second [grasping] arises through the power of craving for gain and honor, either to refute the arguments established by others or to escape the challenges posed by others.

Taking the branch of *śamatha* as its basis and foundation, for the purpose of proceeding toward the worldly detachment from desire up to the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it gives rise to the third grasping;

and for the purpose of following along with the conventional discourse regarding the person (*pudgala*) who is conceptually imputed as the agent of actions and the experiencer of their results, as well as for the purpose of following along with the conventional discourse regarding cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
The signs of a person who has turned away from cessation give rise to the grasping at a self-identity;

for this reason, the Blessed One, as the Great Teacher who is the authoritative master for the full knowledge and permanent abandonment of all forms of grasping, declared that those who vow to practice this Dharma, even if they die while still possessing afflictions, will not establish any further grasping therein.
Such individuals, having no lingering attachment to sensual desires, go forth into homelessness.

Therefore, because there is no grasping toward views, precepts, or the doctrine of self (*ātmavāda*), and so forth as explained at length, those who follow the poorly taught Dharma possess two distinctions and so on, being sustained by false discrimination and views; thus, guarding of body and guarding of speech are called "precepts" (*śīla*).
Following this undertaking, the physical appearance, clothing, food and drink, and modes of conduct are called "vows" (*vrata*); they are termed "precepts" (*śīla*) and "prohibitions" (*saṃvara*).

Because it is prohibited, because it is a settled view, and because the treatises state that there is a self, this is called the adherence to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*). Because it asserts the existence of a real entity, it is called a "truth" (*satya*);

because it asserts that [the self] can be established, it is called a "settled view" (*sthiti*). Furthermore, in the second explanation: with craving for sensual pleasures as the condition, the first type of clinging (*upādāna*) is established;

with craving for gain, honor, and so forth as the condition, the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*) is established; and with craving for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as the condition, [the clinging to rules and observances is established].

The clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is established with craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) and craving for non-existence (*vibhavarāga*) as its conditions; the clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*) is established [with craving for existence as its condition].
This treatise provides another explanation, stating generally: "It is further explained.

Regarding the eighth [type] among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), it says: "Because it is difficult to liberate from, it is called a fetter"; this [treatise] states: "Because it can obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*)."

Because their nature is that of the mind-body (*manomaya-kāya*), they are called "bound" (*baddha*); this is difficult to understand in terms of their essential nature, while the other is difficult to understand in terms of what is realized.
These two types are similar; the eighty-nine [categories] are established solely based on non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Among these, the first two are the "heedless" (*pramatta*) non-Buddhists, the third is the "heedful" (*apramatta*) non-Buddhist, and the last one is the "both" non-Buddhist. Alternatively, within this context, the first two rely on the category of householders (*gṛhapati*), while the latter two are external.
In the "Chapter on Leaving Home" (*Dàochūjiāpǐn*), this is not discussed; that treatise still states, "as previously explained," which should be verified.

For instance, the eighth [chapter] of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* speaks of "concealing the true meaning" (*fù zhēnshíyì*), while here it says "that which causes wholesome factors (*kuśalapakṣa*) to fail to manifest.

All of these rely upon the "superior dharma" (*viśeṣadharma*). This is based on the general gate (*sāmānyadvāra*); it is not necessarily the case that this refers to ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*).
However, this explanation that wholesome states do not turn back refers only to conditioned wholesome dharmas, not to the ultimate meaning.
In reality, when the proximate mind accords with the distant, subtle principle, even if it undergoes transformation, it still accords with the subtle principle.

Among the eighty-nine [faults], the first is to contradict the holy teachings and be swept away by desire; the second is to contradict the dharma that is lovely and desirable, becoming incapable of accepting admonition.

The third [hindrance] obstructs meditative concentration (*samādhi*) such that there is no basis for attaining tranquility (*śamatha*); the fourth obstructs the category of insight (*vipaśyanā*) such that it does not arise;

and only the fifth is due to being contrary to the Dharma, the treatises, unerring discernment, the thorough investigation of all phenomena, and the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the Great Teacher’s holy teachings and *nirvāṇa*.

Why, in the treatise, is doubt (*vicikitsā*) an obstacle to equanimity (*upekṣā*), while among the previously mentioned envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) are taught as obstacles to equanimity?

This obstructs the simultaneous meaning of both [practices], preventing the initial abandonment from arising; it causes the habitual tendencies of those [other] discursive entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) to arise repeatedly, thereby encircling this [initial] discourse.

This constitutes an obstruction to that [subsequent] discourse later on. Furthermore, the cessation (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) herein are as previously described regarding cessation, exertion, and equanimity.

This is precisely what is called "equanimity" (*upekṣā*) in the context of the initial cultivation of the stages of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as well as the state of "abiding in equality" when they have been long cultivated and perfected. Thus, there are five meanings in the eighty-ninth [verse].

It is taught that these are obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), which differs from what was stated previously. In the eleventh fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the characteristics of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are explained in detail;

here, they are analyzed by way of five gates: (1) defining their essence, (2) explaining their names, (3) establishing their inclusion or exclusion, (4) why they are specifically identified as predominant obstructions in three stages—or, alternatively, as predominant obstructions in the five stages according to the eighty-ninth fascicle—and (5) why other fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) are not included.
Ignorance (avidyā) acts as a general obstruction rather than a specific one; pride (māna) involves mental exaltation and is conducive to the arising of wholesome factors;
the five views (dṛṣṭi) are defiled wisdom, and since their nature is not that of an obstruction to wisdom itself, they are not said to obstruct it.

In summary, regarding these five stages when first practicing virtue, other obstructions—considered inferior in character compared to these five—are not mentioned here because these five are superior. Thus they are established [as the primary obstacles].

In these three major treatises, there is naturally a fourth section clarifying the common characteristics [of the hindrances], and a fifth section clarifying these five fruits—how they are like food and non-food—which corresponds to the eleventh [chapter].
Because torpor and drowsiness are proximate and accordant in producing various afflictions, they are established together as a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*);
because restlessness and remorse operate within the same object, they are established together as a hindrance. Each point is consistent with that great [treatise].

This [hindrance] exists only in the Desire Realm; it is now discussed as pertaining to both the states of meditative concentration (*samāhita*) and non-concentration (*asamāhita*). In the eleventh chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is generally stated to be an obstacle to all forms of meditative concentration.

Within the section on "stumps" (*sthāṇu*), there are two parts: first, the presentation of its essential nature (*svabhāva*); second, the explanation of its name. Here, it is explained as being difficult to sever, as stated in the eighth [chapter].
It destroys the field of the harvest of virtue; it is characterized by a mind that expects only its own [desires], being unpliant—this refers to greed (*lobha*);

it lacks functional capacity—this refers to hatred (*dveṣa*); it is difficult to liberate—this refers to delusion (*moha*). Alternatively, due to these three, the mind is not compliant, turns away from correct principle, lacks adaptability, and is full of obstructions and rigidity, making liberation difficult;
this is called the "obstruction difficult to sever. As stated in [Treatise] 89: "The mind is neither pliant nor supple; the mind is extremely..."
Because ignorance causes harm to one's own welfare, when combined with the eighth [category] here, the two explanations are identical to those in the eighty-ninth [chapter].

Regarding the eighth among the defilements (*mala*), where that text says "defiled by its very nature" (*svabhāva-saṃkliṣṭa*), this text says "stained and impure," which is the same as in the eighty-ninth.

The same. In the eighth [section] of the *Dāha* (Burning) chapter, it says: "Because one constantly harms and is constantly able to cause harm, one consequently experiences the suffering of birth and old age;

thus, one is constantly harmed. This is identical to the present [text]. Furthermore, in [the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*] 89, it says: "Because this is frequently practiced, it constantly flows forth and burns with affliction."

The extreme deterioration of body and mind is termed "affliction" (paridāha); however, this does not refer to present harm, but rather to harm that will occur in the future, whether it pertains to the eighth [consciousness] or applies universally.

Regarding the statement that "the arrow strikes at the various existences (*bhava*), wealth (*dhana*), the Three Jewels (*triratna*), and the Four Truths (*catur-āryasatya*) by means of the gates of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), thereby piercing and wounding":
this means that one generates craving for existence and wealth, and gives rise to doubt regarding the Truths and the Jewels. These two serve as the gates;

through the three poisons (*tri-viṣa*), they pierce and wound practitioners who turn their backs on the Truths, the Jewels, and the state of the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*). As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 8, states: "Because of the characteristic of non-quiescence."
