They are called "arrows" because they follow after [the object] from afar; the meaning here is that they are like arrows in their lack of tranquility, following without interruption or beginning, constantly causing injury.

As stated in [Treatise] 89: "Because greed, hatred, and delusion cause one to abandon shame and dread of blame, giving rise to shamelessness and fearlessness of blame, which are entirely uninterrupted and irrepressible, they are able to shoot and wound."
Regarding "possessor" (*svāmī*), it should be named according to its fruit as "one who possesses wealth, fear, distraction, and so forth," which is called "possession" (*svāmya*).

Because possession arises from greed and other [afflictions], it is named after its fruit. The *Aṣṭagrantha* (or *Jñānaprasthāna*) states: "The eighth [member] is that which can grasp the basis of things, namely wealth;
this is the thing that serves as the basis, for this [member] can grasp that. The *Aṣṭādaśadharmaka* (or *Mahāvibhāṣā*) states: "If greed and the other two [afflictions], as well as shame..."
Because shame is interspersed due to its continuity rather than occurring in a single moment, and because it can be suppressed, it is termed "possessed" (*sāsrava*);
this refers to the meaning of being extremely base and defiled, as it is spoken with reference to those who possess superior roots of goodness.

Evil conduct is named after its fruit; the same applies to the paths. Herein, the explanation of the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*) further comprises twenty-four [factors], which, when analyzed individually, amount to twenty-five.
Within the "Great Gate" [of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*], it is stated that they are equivalent: unwholesome dharmas are designated by the name "roots.
The meaning of "root" is explained according to two senses, as found in the sixth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Regarding the three outflows (*āsrava*), one [of them] establishes its essential nature as explained in the sixty-fourth [chapter]. The three outflows are entirely distinct; one should understand their establishment of essential nature through the eighty-ninth [chapter]:
all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), are called the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*);
all afflictions of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*), excluding ignorance, are called the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*). If sentient beings, whether...

Whether they have not yet abandoned desire or have already abandoned it— excluding all heterodox practitioners whose minds are shrouded by the evil views born of perverse discrimination and ignorance—
they rely on these evil views to seek after a portion of those desires while abandoning another portion,
up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; thus, they possess the totality of ignorance regarding that triple world.
They are subsumed under a single name, the "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyā-āsrava*). Regarding the division of its basis into two and the explanation of the name as the eighth [topic]:

it is said that "causing the mind to flow" is called an outflow (*āsrava*); here, too, it is the same. Because afflictions and so forth cause the mind to flow and disperse in a continuous stream without interruption, they are called outflows.
As for the name "reproach," the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (89) states that one takes only the afflictions (*kleśa*) and does not include [the secondary afflictions].
Regarding the establishment of categories based on their prominence: because the term "outflow" (*āsrava*) applies to all defiled phenomena as its substance, three [categories] are excluded.

All afflictions are termed the "gate of cause" (*hetu-mukha*); this single gate alone pervades all defiled states. This demonstrates that the eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) also arise throughout all defiled minds.

Since they do not rely solely on the fundamental [afflictions], they should be subsumed under the single gate of the fundamental [afflictions]. The others are established separately from what is distinguished [by them], while the rest are combined.
Regarding the single faculty that serves as the basis for various differentiated categories of the realm (*dhātu*), there is no difference [in its nature], and thus it is designated as one.
Since the basis from which [the faculties] arise should also be twofold, and since the arising faculty should also be one in accordance with that basis, [it is nonetheless one].

However, because the arising faculties are of many kinds—such as the four types including those associated with the desire-realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those bound by the fetters of desire—and because the objects of desire are manifold, they are collectively subsumed under these four categories.

The seven outflows (*āsrava*) are correctly subsumed as follows: the outflows of views (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*) and the outflows of cultivation (*bhāvanā-āsrava*) correspond respectively to the faculties of feeling (*vedanā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*). As for the roots (*indriya*), the first two are established according to their respective applications.

Regarding the remaining five outflows, they are established as "outflows" when associated with them, and as "non-outflows" (*anāsrava*) when dissociated from them. In the analysis of the questions and answers concerning these: why are the floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*) and so forth established separately from the outflows, whereas this [classification of the outflows] is not done in that way?

It is because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) speak of them in terms of the opening and closing of the basis (*āśraya*) and that which depends upon it (*āśrita*); here, they are taught as a single totality.
If one analyzes them by opening and closing [the categories] and discusses them individually according to their respective meanings, they do not contradict one another.
The eighth [category] in the *Kauśalya* states: "That which causes enjoyment to never reach satiety is called 'lack' (*parigraha*).
Therefore, that treatise relies on the sense of being "insatiable" (*atṛpta*), and "insatiability" is precisely what is meant by being afflicted by poverty and suffering.

Because one is obsessed with and attached to the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), giving rise to craving and defilement, the body and mind are scorched and tormented; this is the eighth [affliction].
Because it causes what is desired to always remain deficient, it is called "scorching. That which causes those realms to burn is precisely what is meant here by "deprivation" (*vaikalya*).

Since that heat and that scorching are one and the same, the subsequent passage refers to the fuel of accumulated roots of goodness being burned as "fire"; this is the heat-affliction (*paridāha*) arising from that.
The result is called "contention" (*raṇa*) and "affliction" (*paridāha*); likewise, from the result, evil karma constitutes the "dense forest" (*gahana*).

The eighth [category] is called the "dense forest" because it is a gathering of various great trees that are one's own bodies; being the root of the dense forest, it causes sentient beings to dwell in saṃsāra.
The primary cause is the three poisons, and because this great tree-dense forest is difficult to escape, one remains in saṃsāra.
The causes are the three poisons; the fruits of the three poisons are birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); birth-and-death is the dense forest (*gahana*); the dense forest arises from the great trees;
and the great trees are the three poisons, because the three poisons give rise to the dense forest of birth-and-death.

Regarding "obstructions" (*parāmarśa*), the eighth [chapter] states that because they cause sentient beings to delight in and become attached to various subtle objects of desire (*viṣaya*), and because they can obstruct the realization of supramundane dharmas, they are called obstructions.
The first [of these] refers to these two [types], and the latter refers to these three; these five obstructions are precisely the fifth set of obstructions.
Furthermore, the instruction on these five obstructions is as presented in the twenty-seventh [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which contains four types of teaching.
"Instruction" refers to the unerring sequential teaching and the teaching of realization and admonition, as explained in detail in the first fascicle regarding the three wheels and so forth.

Among the types of misconduct, "delusion regarding objects" refers to delusion regarding phenomena; these two [types of delusion] pertain to both internal and external, as well as general and specific objects. Therefore, from...
Externally, this name is established because herein we do not speak of sentient beings as being objects of a collective synthesis (*saṃkalana*).

Although greed and hatred also arise with respect to sentient beings, they do so by way of the door of the objective field (*viṣaya*). Thus, confusion regarding the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) pertains to both principles (*nyāya*) and facts (*vastu*). As for confusion regarding views, it is because [sentient beings] are seen as following [those views].
As for confusion regarding the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), it is based on what is predominant; yet in reality, it is also not an antidote, as it applies to the past, future, and so forth.

The characteristics of these [afflictions] are not clearly understood here because they are explained based on the manifestation of increased greed that does not coexist with the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) or the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*);
or it is said that because their associated modes of activity are shallow and superficial, they merely delude regarding the objective sphere and are not among those [afflictions] to be known.

Regarding the arising of the notion of a precipice toward cessation and the path, this is because one gives rise to the thought that they are difficult to cultivate and realize, thereby conversely producing afflictions; the rest may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the five among the *āvaraṇa* (obstructions) and the first five *āvaraṇa*-bases, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter eight, explains the term "affliction" (*kleśa*) as follows:

they cause sentient beings to delight in and become attached to various wonderful sensory objects (*viṣaya*), and because they obstruct the realization of supramundane dharmas, they are called *āvaraṇa*.
The former refers to these five *āvaraṇa*s, while the latter refers to the basis from which these arise; that is, because one cannot cultivate various wholesome dharmas due to these two meanings.

First, being bound; second, being unable to emerge from [the cycle]; third, having no realization—this refers to being attached to and delighting in sublime objects, never following the instructions of the Great Teacher.
What was previously termed "false grasping" refers to the characteristics of improper conduct and the characteristics of consciousness defiled by such signs;
this is called "false practice."

The seventh section on the gates of the elements (*dhātu*) has three parts: first, it clarifies the full or partial presence of the elements and stages (*bhūmi*); second, it clarifies the five feelings (*vedanā*) within the elements and stages;

and third, it clarifies the association (*samprayoga*) of the elements and stages with consciousness. Within this, the associations are the same as those in the fifty-eighth [verse], but they differ from those in the fifty-ninth [verse] and the fifty-ninth [verse] of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The fifty-ninth [verse] states: "First, one distinguishes the afflictions associated with the various faculties (*indriya*), but this is done only in terms of..."
Coarse characteristics are established through reasoning so that beginners may understand them without confusion;

now, subtle and coarse reasoning are employed to establish [the distinctions] so that long-practitioners may comprehend the various modes of practice and understanding regarding their own and others' bodies.

In clarifying the five types of feeling associated with the realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*), there are two parts: first, the specific associations are clarified; second, a question-and-answer session concerning all [feelings] associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Regarding the principle of correspondence (*yukti*), there are seven [points] at the beginning, excluding only the fourth. As for the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth, they are analogous to pride (*māna*).

Regarding all other texts, there are two locations: first, the root treatise; second, the commentary (*bhāṣya*). Third, within the section on pride, there is first the root treatise and then the commentary.

Within the commentary, it first distinguishes that objects in the desire realm do not possess the characteristic of pleasure; subsequently, through a question-and-answer format, it distinguishes the first and second dhyānas.

What is meant by "associated with pleasure" (*sukha-samprayukta*)? It refers to the mental state of joy (*cittābhipramoda*), because it proceeds with delight (*prīti-carita*) and because it is free from the actual occurrence of sorrow and suffering (*daurmanasya-duḥkha*).

Regarding "the heart leaps with delight," this refers to the movement and leaping [of the mind]. This is distinct from the pleasure of the third dhyāna, because that pleasure is tranquil. As for "the mind is at ease" (*citta-prasāda*), this means being serene; it excludes the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), as equanimity is not serenity.
"The mind is harmonious" (*citta-samprasādana*) indicates the essential nature of joy (*prīti*); it signifies the general state of the feeling of well-being (*prasrabdhi-vedanā*).

Regarding the phrase "superior" (*uttama*) mentioned above: since that which has been described as superior is a pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) and not an unpleasant one, it is subsumed under the category of feeling (*vedanā*) among the mental factors (*caitta*).

It is not merely a single word such as "mental joy" (*cittaprīti*) and so forth; rather, it refers to the mind itself. Now, in order to distinguish it from the mental factors, it is said to be "subsumed under feeling.

Alternatively, "the mind being harmonious and at ease" (*cittasya praśrabdhi-prasāda*) constitutes a single phrase. These four phrases refer to the feelings of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and these four [qualities] are capable of [accomplishing this].
That which is subsumed under mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not spoken of as being identical to all mental factors (*caitta*).

Among these mental factors, that which possesses joy and so forth is subsumed under feeling (*vedanā*). This characteristic—namely, that feeling co-arising with the sixth mental consciousness can cause the mind to experience joy and so forth—is attained by one who has undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), because they have eliminated the obstacle of the heavy dullness (*dausthulya*) of lethargy (*styāna*) and lack of functional capacity (*akarmanyatā*).

The fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*) and so forth are called the "basis of capability" (*karmanyatāśraya*). One who has attained the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) is as described in the second fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, which cites a sūtra:

"As the sūtra says, because one is free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, possessing applied and sustained thought, and born of seclusion, joy and bliss, one dwells having fully attained the first dhyāna," and so on, according to the sequential sūtras, up to the detailed explanation regarding the realization of bliss and so forth.
Because the ālayavijñāna subsumes the basis of the body, and because that manovijñāna possesses a feeling of joy (*saumanasya*), it attains a state of serenity and well-being;
this is what is subsumed under "feeling" (*vedanā*). This well-being is a feeling, and it is subsumed under the category of "number" (*saṃkhyā*).

The intended meaning of this sūtra is as follows: the subsequent [passage] explains the two preceding sūtras by clarifying that both result in exultation. The preceding text explained the former "joy" (*prīti*).

Furthermore, regarding those who have abandoned the lower [levels] yet harbor doubts concerning the characteristics (*ākāra*) of the bliss of the higher *dhyānas*, they are "induced" (*ākṣipta*) and "sustained" (*dhṛta*).

Because they previously entered that state, they now induce this afflicted mind to arise; thus it is called "induced. That which is induced is precisely that which is sustained, for it is sustained by its association with the meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
"Host" (*gaṇa*) has the meaning of "category"; that is, the five classes of afflictions are called the "host of defilements" (*kleśagaṇa*).

Regarding the statement that "the delusions concerning the four truths are not of a single type, but each has ten [or two], and there are differences between the two gates," it cites two interpretations from the Tripiṭaka Master.

The first says: "There are ten gates based on what is deluded (*ālambana*), and eight based on the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*). This is consistent with the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. The second says:

"There are ten gates based on the gates of the true principles (*tattva*) that are deluded; and based on the gates of the abandonment of the intended meaning (*artha*) and the discourse on the expression (*vyañjana*), there are three [sets] of eight."

Because the two [types of] conduct are exclusively suffering, if one becomes deluded regarding this and gives rise to wrong conduct, it is precisely this that is abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).

This is because that which takes [the object] as its cognitive support (*ālambana*) is abandoned by means of what is deluded; for there is no fixed rule among the four permutations—such as depending on the many to abandon the few, or depending on the few to abandon the many—as seen in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-ṭīkā* (The Essential Commentary on the Sixth Chapter).
Alternatively, that which is taken as the cognitive object (*ālambana*) may be considered what is deluded, or...

If one asserts that [defilements] are deluded with respect to either the basis (*āśraya*) or the object (*ālambana*), then since afflictions associated with the Truths of Suffering and Origin would universally take all five sense-gates as their objects, they would necessarily be abandoned through all five paths of abandonment.

Furthermore, if one considers those afflictions that arise intermittently with respect to the four Truths—whether based on the basis or the object—to be "increasing" (*anuśerate*) because they are to be abandoned, then what does it mean for them not to understand the principle of any given Truth?

By "increasing" based on the basis, one means increasing from the perspective of the basis; by "increasing" based on the object, one means increasing from the perspective of the object. How can one fail to understand the principle of a Truth in such cases?
Because delusion increases with respect to certain truths, the question is asked: "If one takes this as an object, does one thereby give rise to wrong conduct regarding this?

This question asks whether, in the desire realm, taking this as an object constitutes delusion regarding this, such that both the object and the delusion increase together. The answer is: "Not necessarily.
This is because, among the various truths, it depends on what is appropriate; furthermore, cessation and the path are distinct from the fruit of suffering.
Within the assembly, there are two [sections]: first, a general overview, followed by a detailed analysis. Within the detailed analysis, there are two parts:

first, the explanation of the afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and second, the explanation of the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Within each of these—those of seeing and cultivation—there are again two parts: first, a detailed explanation, followed by a summary. Within the initial [detailed explanation], there are three sections, as they pertain to the distinctions of the three realms.

Regarding the Four Noble Truths within the Desire Realm, first is the root treatise, followed by the questions and answers of the commentator (*vyākhyā-kāra*) concerning the *ḍhakkā* (the drum/clarification).

Regarding the initial explanation of the cultivation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are two parts: first, the main treatise separately enumerates their names and numbers; second, the commentator explains their characteristics.
Within the explanation of the characteristics, there are three sections: first, a question-and-answer on the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*); second, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*);

and third, the explanation of the four [afflictions] beginning with greed (*rāga*), excluding those that arise based on views. Within the section on the view of self, there are two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Within the answer, there are...
The second part consists of the initial response of the treatise followed by the citation of a sutra. Within the sutra, there are three sections: first, the Dharma; second, the metaphor;

and third, the application of the Dharma to the metaphor. In the section on the Dharma, the Buddha tells the "slave-child" (*dāsa-putra*); according to this, there should be the word "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) in the passage stating that "in the five aggregates of clinging, there is the conceit of self (*asmimāna*) and so forth," yet it is omitted here.

Alternatively, the metaphor may have two purposes: to prove that the one who has seen the Path is being addressed as the "slave-child," and not the entire multitude. Otherwise, for what reason would [the text] below—[at the point where it says] "not so"—[be stated]?
Regarding pride and the others, the Buddha did not speak of them as "view of self" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); rather, "desire" refers to greed (*lobha*).

As for "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*), because the view of self is subtle and arises simultaneously [with other afflictions], it is called an "latent tendency. Alternatively, the seeds of pride and greed are called latent tendencies.

Furthermore, there is the excellence of the permanent abandonment of the origin (*samudaya*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha*), the cessation (*nirodha*) of suffering, and the path (*mārga*) that leads to its exhaustion and expulsion. Moreover, "abandonment" refers to the manifest entanglements (*paryavasthāna*); "knowledge" refers to knowing suffering; and "abandonment" refers to severing the conditions for the entanglements that lead to future results of suffering.

When the seeds of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have not yet been eternally extinguished, when they have not yet been eternally vomited out, or when the causes have not been severed and the fruits have not been fully known—such that they have not been eliminated by the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) nor vomited out by the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)—the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that takes [these] collectively as its object is what is referred to.

This is explained in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stage of the Buddha), fascicle 6, and in the lower volume of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on Dependent Origination), fascicle 59, and so forth; these texts discuss only the three aspects (*ākāra*) of impermanence, suffering, and non-self as being the inducers [of the path], and do not mention emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

"Practice" (*caryā*) is itself "non-practice" (*acaryā*), as it excludes and indicates what is different. Regarding the three unsurpassed [knowledges], consult the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, lower fascicle, from the section on severing the three times, as in [Treatise] 59.
The main text concerning karma has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Within the answer, there are three sections: first, a brief indication; second, the five types of karma.

Next, regarding the section on "volitional action" (*cetanā-karma*): first, there is the brief explanation of what was initially indicated; second, the extensive explanation found in the eighth fascicle.

Regarding the initial point, as the World-Honored One has said that the maturation of the karma of sentient beings is inconceivable, this section explains, based on the sūtras, both conceivable and inconceivable karma.

Within the initial brief explanation, there are two parts: first, clarifying the two types of karma; second, indicating the five types of karma. Under the heading "What is volitional action? follows the extensive explanation, which contains [further subdivisions].

Second, first the intention-action (*cetanā-karman*) and the action subsequent to intention (*cetayitvā-karman*) are indicated; subsequently, under the heading "these three actions of body, speech, and mind," these two types of action are explained in detail by way of the five actions.

Here, "action" (*karman*) refers only to the designation for a single mode of operation; it is not a correct explanation of the accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome karma subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), as such will not be further analyzed later.
In the extensive explanation of the two types of karma, the main text is divided into three sections. First, the extensive explanation of the preceding *cetanā*-karma (volitional action).

Since the fundamental paths of action (*karmapatha*)—whether wholesome or unwholesome—are narrow in scope, they are explained first, as stated in the Sūtra: "There are three kinds of karma: meritorious karma, non-meritorious karma, and immovable karma.
Below, the *cetanā*-karma is extensively explained as encompassing the preparatory, fundamental, and subsequent stages; all of these together are designated as such.

Regarding the gravity of the paths of action of volitional karma (*cetanā-karma*), because [the latter] is performed only after having first intended [it], it is narrower; this [present discussion], however, is a general designation, and thus it says "after having intended.

Furthermore, there are three types of distinctions in karma: namely, the karma of restraint (*saṃvara-karma*), the non-restraint (*asaṃvara-karma*), and the neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint (*naivasaṃvara-nāsaṃvara-karma*).

Among these, the former two types of karma have already been explained extensively. Here, first, within the karma of having intended, there are five parts: (1) the actual explanation of the fundamental paths of action (*maula-karmapatha*); (2) by means of the five... [text fragment ends].

The *Śāstra* explains five types of karma: first, the classification of the paths of action; second, the three types of intentional karma; third, the four types of determinate karma; and fourth, the karma that receives its fruit.
The root text mentions only "intentional" (*cetanā*) karma, but it extensively analyzes "preparatory" (*prayoga*) karma because it is complete.

The *Śāstra* states: "Is there not also a small portion of 'actualization' (*maula*) and 'attainment' (*prāpti*) included within this? No, for these are not separate from what has already been subsumed under the preparatory stage."

Because [the meaning] is exhausted, the root treatise does not explain it; since there is only a slight meaning, the actual analysis of the unwholesome courses of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*) is briefly presented here. Among them, killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct are exclusively *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compounds, because they consist of the mental application of the intention to kill and so forth. False speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter are both *tatpuruṣa* and *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds, because they involve the mental application of false speech and so forth. The latter three [of the wholesome courses of action] are exclusively *karmadhāraya* compounds. As for wholesome karma: The path of right speech is the abandonment of false speech. The path of right action is the abandonment of taking what is not given. The path of right livelihood is the abandonment of wrong livelihood. The path of right effort is the abandonment of killing. The path of right mindfulness is the abandonment of divisive speech. The path of right concentration is the abandonment of harsh speech. The path of right view is the abandonment of frivolous chatter. In this way, the ten courses of action are established. Furthermore, regarding the ten courses of action: the first three unwholesome ones are exclusively *tatpuruṣa*; the next four are both *tatpuruṣa* and *karmadhāraya*; and the latter three are exclusively *karmadhāraya*. As for the wholesome ones: the first three are exclusively *tatpuruṣa*; the middle four are both *tatpuruṣa* and *karmadhāraya*; and the last three are exclusively *karmadhāraya*. This concludes the explanation of the courses of action. Regarding the nature of these courses of action, they are all of the nature of volition (*cetanā*). However, when one performs an action through body or speech, the primary factor is volition, while the bodily or vocal action is secondary. Therefore, although the courses of action are nominally designated as "bodily" or "vocal," they are in fact all of the nature of volition. Thus, it is said that the courses of action are all of the nature of volition. As for their basis, the first seven courses of action have the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their basis, while the latter three have the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as their basis. This concludes the explanation of the courses of action. Regarding the distinction between the courses of action and the preparatory and subsequent stages: the preparatory stage is the initial application of the mind toward the object; the course of action is the actual completion of the act; and the subsequent stage is the state following the completion of the act. For example, when one intends to kill a sentient being, the initial thought is the preparatory stage; the actual striking with a weapon is the course of action; and the subsequent state of satisfaction after the death has occurred is the subsequent stage. This applies similarly to the other courses of action. Regarding the distinction between the courses of action and the preparatory and subsequent stages, the preparatory stage is the initial application of the mind toward the object; the course of action is the actual completion of the act; and the subsequent stage is the state following the completion of the act. This concludes the explanation of the preparatory and subsequent stages. Regarding the distinction between the courses of action and the preparatory and subsequent stages: the preparatory stage is the initial application of the mind toward the object; the course of action is the actual completion of the act; and the subsequent stage is the state following the completion of the act. This concludes the explanation of the courses of action. Regarding the distinction between the courses of action and the preparatory and subsequent stages: the preparatory stage is the initial application of the mind toward the object; the course of action is the actual completion of the act; and the subsequent stage is the state following the completion of the act. This concludes the explanation of the courses of action. Regarding the distinction between the courses of action and the preparatory and subsequent stages: the preparatory stage is the initial application of the mind toward the object; the course of action is the actual completion of the act; and the subsequent stage is the state following the completion of the act. This concludes the explanation of the courses of action. Regarding the path, the first seven [types of karma] are only *tatpuruṣa* (dependent designations), while the latter two have no such name; their essence is precisely the "seeing of seeing," and because this essence is itself correct, it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).

As for the nature of the paths of action, the first three—such as those established in the first chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and in the fifty-third [chapter], etc.—all take the volition that initiates body and speech as their manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) moral discipline (*śīla*). This very initiation is the preeminent [factor].
Regarding the latter three [mental paths of action], they are designated by their names;

furthermore, the three volitions that give rise to greed, hatred, and wrong view constitute the essence of unwholesome paths of action, while the three—non-greed, non-hatred, and right view—constitute the wholesome nature.

Taking extremely grave wholesome or unwholesome dharmas as the essential nature of the paths of action, this provides an explanation of the preliminary application (*prayoga*), the fundamental (*maula*), and the subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) stages, which constitutes the sixtieth [section] within the general title.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that volition (*cetanā*) is karma, whereas the [first] seven [paths of action] of body and speech are both karma and paths of action; greed, hatred, and wrong view are paths of action but not karma. According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the third [category]—volition—is that which is traversed by the first two types of volition and is so called "path" because it leads to the production of the ripening fruits of suffering and pleasure. Why, then, is it said here that volition is not [the path]? This is explained as follows: [The *Abhidharmakośa*] says: "Volition is the mental karma that impels the body and speech. Since volition is the agent that initiates the physical and vocal actions, it is designated as "karma. However, because it does not itself manifest as a physical or vocal form, it is not designated as a "path of action. Furthermore, since the seven paths of action of body and speech are the actual manifestations of that volition, they are designated as "paths. Volition is the precursor to these seven; therefore, it is designated as "karma," while the seven are designated as both "karma" and "paths. As for greed, hatred, and wrong view, they are the motivating factors for the commission of those seven paths of action;

thus, they are designated as "paths of action" but not as "karma. This is the meaning. Regarding the statement in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* that volition is the "path": this refers to the fact that volition serves as the basis upon which the preceding two [types of volition] operate, thereby leading to the production of the ripening fruits of suffering and pleasure; hence it is termed a "path. Why, then, is it stated here that volition is not [the path]? This is explained as follows: [it is not the path in the sense defined in the *Abhidharmakośa*]. This is what is being said.
The first two [types of volition] are those; they speak of the third volition, therefore there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, regarding the volitions associated with manifest greed and so forth, if one considers them horizontally across the present without reference to the past or future, they are merely karma and not paths of action (*karmapatha*). Here, however, we consider them vertically; thus, karma is also a path.

As for the third [realm], it is bound to the three realms. Regarding the ten unwholesome paths of action, the *Ṣaṣṭitantra* states that they are bound only to the desire realm and are capable only of [producing results therein].
The maturation (*vipāka*) of the desire realm is experienced there, and not elsewhere; this does not preclude the existence of wholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*) in the higher realms.

Among the devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and others, there are wholesome ten courses of action, such as those undertaken through the reception of the precepts. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are only the final three.

Even hell-beings of the desire realm can possess the full set of unwholesome courses of action, including impure envy and malice, without exception. If one says that there are discriminating afflictions (*vikalpaka-kleśa*) in hell...

The commission of karma does not preclude the presence of wrong views; however, in the present case, such [wrong] principles are absent. Therefore, although other people may fall into the three lower hells, there is no occurrence of killing or similar acts [there].
According to the *Daśacakra-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, even sentient beings in hell listen to the Dharma;
what prevents them from receiving the precepts? For a Bodhisattva transforms sentient beings therein. Thus, the ten paths of wholesome action apply universally to all places. (Chapter Six)
Regarding the ten [paths of action]: killing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and malice—these six types arise in relation to sentient beings;
frivolous speech arises in relation to various objects; taking what is not given and covetousness arise in relation to material possessions;

and the path of wrong view arises in relation to the various formations of conditioned phenomena. Now, it is correctly stated that six arise in relation to sentient beings, one arises in relation to non-sentient things.

Regarding the third [type of] volitional action arising from the distinction between sentient and insentient objects, there are two aspects: the intention based on perception (*saṃjñā*) and the intention regarding the undertaking of action (*kartavya-saṃjñā*).
Yoga is divided into two: the second is perception (*saṃjñā*), and the third is desire (*chanda*). Without this preliminary application (*prayoga*), that perception would be as follows:

it would not be the perception of "that" regarding what is not "that," nor would it be the perception of "not-that" regarding "that"; rather, it would be the perception of "that" regarding "that," and the perception of "not-that" regarding "not-that."
Regarding that, the perception of it as not being that belongs only to the third [category], which is the characteristic of the path of action (*karmapatha*).

The third is the desire (*chanda*) produced by inversion; herein, one generates the intention (*āśaya*) to act. That very third desire is produced by a longing based on either inverted or non-inverted perceptions.
The preliminary effort (*prayoga*) herein refers to the initiation of the three types of action (*trividha-karman*), whether performed by oneself or incited by another.

Since the preparatory means (*prayoga*) for killing and so forth are themselves the objects of desire, and because that [preparatory stage] and the mind of desire are conjoined in a single locus, there is no separate preparatory action (*prayoga*).

This is clarified by the fact that both perception (*saṃjñā*) and desire (*chanda*) can take a single object as their focal point; thus, the clarification that the objects of the three types of karma are one and the same does not contradict the distinction between desire and pleasure (*ruci*).
Nevertheless, the ninth *maula-bhūmi* states: "First, the arising of desire and pleasure; second, the arising of defilement (*kleśa*)."

The defiled mind arises three times; there are four matters for the preparation (*upāya*) and fifty-nine for the completion (*niṣṭhā*). It speaks of the defiled mind, the three roots, and so forth, extensively explaining the number of factors until completion.

Alternatively, at a later time, regarding the portion where the karma created has not yet reached completion—such as when one receives the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*), it is only then that the matter becomes a full course of action (*karmapatha*). [This] does not answer the point that clarifies the fault of non-completion.

The eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*) result in the cessation of unwholesome intentions once the limit is reached; thus, like the undertaking of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), receiving the precepts beyond one's capacity results in non-restraint.
However, the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*) and so forth do not constitute [non-restraint], because there is no intention to act [unwholesomely] with finality.

Since even that which was previously produced does not increase, how much less could new [unwholesome states] arise? This explains the characteristics [of the precepts]: although later on the wholesome mind may fail, they do not become [non-restraint] because of the prior commitment to complete abstinence.
Because it is completed, taking what is not given reaches its culmination; this is defined as "taking for oneself.

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, this refers to moving an object from its original location, or refusing to repay a debt or return a deposit, and so forth, as described in that [text], chapter fifty-nine. "Improper" (*aprāpti*) refers to what is not a constituent part (*aṅga*).

Regarding one's own wife or concubine, with the exception of the birth canal, all other parts are improper. There are five types of improper times (*akāla*), namely: during menstruation, when she has recently given birth, when she is nursing, when her breasts are full, and when she is pregnant.
When a child is fasting or ill, there are four improper places, namely: the presence of a superior, an assembly, a shrine, or before a multitude;
improper locations, namely: uneven ground up to and including monasteries and the like; excessive quantities;

and the five types of irrational conduct—taking what is improper, acting contrary to reason, failing to observe worldly etiquette, and acting as a matchmaker for oneself or others regarding all males, eunuchs, or those who are manifest or hidden. All such acts are forbidden.
Regarding the paths of action from sexual intercourse down to [malicious] speech, each is like the fifty-nine great marks; they are explained in detail here and will not be further elaborated upon.
Regarding deception (*mṛṣāvāda*), it constitutes a path of action only when another person understands [the lie], because the intention (*āśaya*) must be fulfilled.

In contrast, for harsh speech (*pāruṣya*) and the others, it is established merely by their utterance, without waiting for another to understand; even if the other does not understand, it is still ultimate (*niṣṭhā*) because the original mind has been carried out, and thus it is so named.
This is because, having made [the other] aware [of one's intent], one utters coarse and malicious words, reviling them in their private parts, so that one’s own desire is not immediately fulfilled;
the same applies to *vyāpāda* (malice). The treatises state that these two courses of action (*karmapatha*) arise only in relation to sentient beings (*sattvādhiṣṭhāna*). As the Sūtra says:
"What is intentional action (*saṃcetanīya-karman*)? Regarding this, it is said that there are five types of intentional action, while the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter nine, speaks of two kinds.

First, increase; second, non-increase. Regarding non-increase, there are eleven types: (1) that which is done in a dream; (2) that which is done through ignorance; (3) that which is done without intentional reflection;
(4) that which is not intense or frequent; (5) that which is done by one who is deranged; (6) that which is done by one who has lost mindfulness; (7) that which is done without a desire to do so;

(8) that which is neutral by nature (*avyākṛta*); (9) that which is impaired by regret; (10) that which is impaired by its antidote; and (11) actions other than these. These remaining [actions] are called [non-increasing].
Among those ten, the four types—namely, dreaming, lack of knowledge, madness, and loss of mindfulness—are subsumed within this third category of "lack of comprehension.
Furthermore, the single type of "absence of desire" encompasses the first two categories, because it includes both formal instruction and formal request;
for when there is no such [desire], it constitutes a request for action, or rather, the absence of intentional thought itself is that very request.
This [action] is an instruction from another; that is not a desire for it, whereas this is an exhortation.
Only in that treatise are those actions described as non-beneficial, infrequent, impaired by regret, and impaired by their antidotes—none of which are mentioned here.

This treatise speaks of actions that are beneficial and frequent, and are not impaired; therefore, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those [actions] is neutral (*avyākṛta*), whereas these are wholesome or unwholesome (*kuśala-akuśala*) actions.

In this context, the sixty-first fascicle does not mention it; rather, it states that there are four categories. First, regarding "that which is performed but does not increase," there are five types:
(1) an infant who lacks consciousness, (2) dreaming, (3) acting without intention, (4) acting without personal desire, and (5) performing an act of repentance as an antidote.
Among the ten bases, those that are disadvantageous are excluded and not counted; furthermore, the four types—insanity, loss of mindfulness, and those of neutral nature—are also excluded.

Because those explanations clarify benefit or number and are not the karma of insanity and so forth, the ninth and tenth [chapters] of the *Mūlabhūmi* are fully subsumed within the fifth remedy (*pratipakṣa*).

As for the "unconscious infant" and "dream," these are subsumed under the third of the five [categories] in this treatise, namely "that which is not cognized," which includes the first two gates of "inattention" and "lack of desire. Regarding the remedy for remorse (*kaukṛtya*), it is included herein.
Because it does not speak of the remedial action for what has been confessed and not yet atoned for, [the first] sixty fascicles, within the four phrases, have the second phrase;

the third and fourth phrases can all be understood. In the first seven bases of action (*karmapada*), all four phrases exist, because there are instances where the mental factor of volition (*cetanā*) increases even without being performed.
Greed, hatred, and false view lack this single partial phrase, as there is no case where they do not perform [the action].
Because they increase through deliberation and act by increasing it, the sixtieth [verse] states that there are four types of karma: first, determination by maturation (*vipāka-niyata*);

second, determination by state (*avasthā-niyata*); third, both; and fourth, neither. Here, these three determinations correspond as follows: the second [determination by state] is the first of those [four];
this third [determination by both] is the third of those, or perhaps also the second of those. This [text], however, merely discusses those...

Regarding the results, they are definitely not [of the same timing] as these three types of karma; since this treatise discusses determinate karma, there is no fourth category of "indeterminate-in-all-respects.
The fifth major section clarifies the ripening (*vipāka*) [results], which consists of five parts: first, the results of unwholesome paths of action; second, the results of wholesome paths of action;

third, the clarification of projecting and completing results; fourth, the clarification of single versus multiple results of karma; and fifth, the sequence in which the results of karma are experienced, beginning with the unwholesome.

Regarding the first of the karmic fruits, the root treatise and the subsequent commentary distinguish the three types of karma—lower, middling, and superior—and assign them respectively to the experience of the fruits of the evil destinies.
While these general and specific fruits pertain to humans and devas as well, there are also specific unwholesome fruits therein;
for this reason, because false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) here is foul and filthy, it is explained in conjunction with harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). If it were not so, how could one obtain such foulness?
If there is defilement and deception, it constitutes the path of divisive speech; if there is also harshness, it constitutes the path of frivolous speech. Thus, these two karmas become one karma.
According to the *Ṣaṣṭitantra-śāstra*, they both "lead away" and "kill," and because their predominant conditions appear as one, two [karmas] arise sequentially.

However, this path of vocal action must necessarily occur simultaneously, whereas those [other paths], such as moving to another location or the severing of life, differ; therefore, they constitute two [distinct paths]. Nevertheless, in secret...
He alone kills [the victim] without moving [the body] from its original place; thus, both karmas are established simultaneously.
This differs from the *Yogācārabhūmi*, wherein one should cross-reference the three fruits [of karma] with the ninth and sixtieth fascicles of that work.

For the most part, the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) is metaphorically designated as such within the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), because internal dharmas do not serve as outflowing fruits for external dharmas, as is the case with killing.

One should further reflect upon all [karmas] such as those resulting in short lifespans. Furthermore, there is one type of karma by which a single body is obtained through a single action; this is categorized as sixtyfold according to the yoga within that single body.
It is designated as "to-be-experienced-in-this-life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and so forth, based on whether it is experienced in the present, the next birth, or subsequent births.

Regarding this, the second phrase is as stated in the Sūtra: "There are three types of karma, namely: meritorious (*puṇya*), non-meritorious (*apuṇya*), and immovable (*āniñjya*) karma," and so on. Below...

The second section, the explanation of the karma of volition (*cetanā-karma*), consists of five major parts: first, the presentation of the explanation of the three types of karma—meritorious and so forth;

second, the explanation of the distinctions in how karma is initiated by ignorance (*avidyā*) as taught in the sūtras; third, the explanation that the three roots serve as the preliminary (*prayoga*) and the consummation (*niṣṭhā*) for unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-karmapatha*);
fourth, the explanation of the sūtra concerning common and uncommon karma; and fifth, the explanation of how various individuals act in such and such ways.

Karma results in such and such maturation (*vipāka*). Regarding the sūtra’s opening and middle sections, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the three types of karma; second, their explanation.
Within the explanation, there are two further parts: first, the master of the treatise provides a brief explanation; second, the commentator explains through questions and answers.

In explaining the name "immovable karma" (*āniñjya-karman*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Chapter 8) and the *Yogācārabhūmi* (Chapter 9) state: "Wholesome karma that brings about [rebirth] in the form realm is called meritorious karma."

Regarding "karma conducive to rebirth in the realms" (*gati-vipāka*) and "karma conducive to experience in the five realms" (*pañca-gati-vedanīya*): non-meritorious karma refers to that which brings about the maturation (*vipāka*) of the miserable realms and is conducive to experience in the five realms;
unwholesome karma refers to that which brings about the maturation of the five realms and is conducive to experience in the five realms. Regarding "immovable karma" (*āniñjya-karman*):

it refers to wholesome karma that brings about the maturation of the form and formless realms and is conducive to experience in the form and formless realms. Why is it said that wholesome karma is "conducive to the five realms"? There are two interpretations, as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.

Furthermore, regarding the determination of realms and stages (*bhūmi*) within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (specifically the ninth *yoga-sthāna*), this excludes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), and the realm of Maheśvara; all other stages are fixed herein.

As for those who transmigrate within these [stages], they must necessarily reach the upper limit through wrong views that deny *nirvāṇa*. Deeply supported by inferior karma, their superior outflows-free (*anāsrava*) qualities are manifold.

Because the spontaneously functioning karma (*anābhoga-karman*) cultivated through perfuming cannot be diverted, it is not the same as the case in the Desire Realm, where karma generally moves according to whichever category of action it relies upon.
Even while at the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), one who upholds the sūtras can cause such karma to be transformed; how much more so when one has attained the Noble Path?

Furthermore, while one may be situated in a realm that is subject to transformation, one dwells in a stage that is not subject to transformation. How could the karma of the Desire Realm then be diverted by the stage of the [higher] realms? This interpretation is untenable.

Alternatively, because the karma of the lower three dhyānas is for the most part unchangeable, and because it is subsumed under those specific dhyāna stages, its cause is established as "unshakable" (*āniñjya*);

furthermore, since the wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*) follow this same characteristic, they are also termed "unshakable," and this applies to the time of meditative concentration as well.
The second major section, the explanation of the two delusions that initiate karma, has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Within the answer, there are two parts:
first, the root treatise; second, the commentary by the Master. Within the root treatise’s answer, there are two parts: first, the heading; second, a brief explanation.
Herein, the question is identical to the ten questions in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which state: "How do meritorious and immovable formations arise through the power of correct discernment?"
As for the cause from which [these delusions] arise, that passage answers by taking ignorance (*avidyā*) as the condition; however, its response is not as comprehensive as this present text.

Nevertheless, both of these delusions should be termed "maturation" (*vipāka*), and both should be termed "the true meaning," because both fail to understand maturation and both fail to realize the true meaning of the truths.

Yet, while "maturation" refers to the coarse fruit, the former is named according to its deep delusion regarding characteristics and its predominance, whereas the latter is named according to its profundity.

They are truly "fools" because they are deluded regarding the meaning of the fruits [of karma] and lack a shallow understanding of the principles of the truths; thus, they are designated as such from the outset.

Furthermore, it is said that those who, based on the suffering of humans and devas, have attained the principles of the truths are "aware," whereas those who do not know these principles are "deluded";
therefore, they are called "true fools. Regarding the suffering of the three evil realms, worldly beings perceive this very delusion as primary; hence, it is termed "maturation" (*vipāka*).

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* names conventional suffering (*saṃvṛti-duḥkha*) and ultimate suffering (*paramārtha-duḥkha*), or the suffering of the three realms (*traidhātuka-duḥkha*), collectively as "maturation" (*vipāka*).
This is because it does not fully comprehend all forms of suffering; it produces non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya*) and understands only the suffering of the fruits of the three evil destinies.

Thus, it is called the "ultimate meaning" (*tattvārtha*). Furthermore, because it understands only the three types of suffering (*tri-duḥkha*) within the limited scope of humans and devas, it is designated from its origin as "coarse."

These two types of evil views are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Regarding the fact that the eighth consciousness (*vijñāna*) is *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), there is indeed authentic textual evidence in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

If one does not know the principles of the truths (*satya*) as they truly are, yet dwells in right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), one may perform meritorious deeds (*puṇya-karma*) or engage in tainted cultivation (*sāsrava-bhāvanā*) that induces immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*);
however, if one does not dwell in right mindfulness, one gives rise to non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-karma*). Therefore, it is known that all [such views] are abandoned through the path of seeing.
In the latter part of this treatise, it is also seen that [ignorance] regarding the truths does not produce karma, clarifying that it is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Why, then, is it said here that ignorance regarding maturation (*vipāka-moha*) is abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)? This [ignorance regarding maturation] merely deludes one regarding the principle (*tattva*); however, there are coarse and subtle [degrees].

The coarse produces non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya*), while the subtle produces the other two [types of karma]. Because these are invariably defiled in nature, it is not meant that karma itself is exclusively defiled; thus, the coarse [ignorance] regarding maturation is [abandoned by] wholesome resolve (*adhimukti*).
When there is the aspect of right view regarding the maturation of evil or all maturations, one dwells in right mindfulness and does not perform non-meritorious deeds;
yet now, when ignorance is conjoined with non-merit, this mindfulness necessarily cannot admit the aspect of right view that understands the coarse results such as maturation.
Although one has not yet seen the traces of the Truths within the delusion regarding the true nature of reality, [this remains the case].

When a wholesome mind arises, it is bound by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); subsequently, when these manifest, one fails to perceive the subtle sufferings of the three realms among humans and devas, and thus gives rise to two types of karma.
According to the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, for non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), both types of karma take the four types of ignorance as their conditions;
internally, they take the three types of ignorance associated with negligence as their conditions, while those who are not negligent do not take ignorance as a condition.

There are also latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) [that do not project rebirth], which are praised as being distinct from the three [types of karma] in order to manifest the profound penetration of the Truths;

for it is only upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) that their seeds are severed. Otherwise, when would the sovereign power of the ten kings—the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*)—be produced?
It must be through karma supported by desire that one becomes a king; thus, those "immovable" (*āniñjya*) actions result only in specific maturations and cannot produce a general [rebirth].

Since this is the collective retribution, it is said that it is not induced by ignorance; because one performed the karma of the Ten Kings in the past during times of non-negligence, one now receives these as provisions—what fault is there in being born here? It is like being born among the Mahāśvara devas.

First, they are named after their future fruits; second, the remaining coarse latencies (*dausthulya*) do not constitute unwholesome states because they have already been abandoned;

third, they do not obstruct the fruit. Regarding these remaining karmas that still persist despite having attained the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), there are three interpretations:

first, it refers to entering *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which is spoken of in terms of the "future fruit"—that is, from the perspective of the ultimate fruit—since for those who are non-returners (*anāgāmin*), [the obstacles] have already been severed. Second... [text continues].

Because the remaining unwholesome karma has been exhausted and its residual *dausthulya* (dysfunction) no longer exists, the three [types of suffering] are called the "transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) in the state of "without remainder.

As previously assigned to the first three [stages], this meaning is difficult to fathom and should be reflected upon. Herein, that which causes [karma] to be experienced in the present is due to the power of those possessing the merit of upholding the sūtras;
it is not by means of the untainted antidote (*anāsrava-pratipakṣa*). Regarding the sixty [verses]: "One attains the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*)."
Since all [karmic traces] have been severed and exhausted at that time, this interpretation accords with the meaning of the "unlearned" (aśaikṣa) state as being without further rebirth.

If it accords with the meaning of "rebirth" (upapatti), then these are karmas of distinct retribution (*vipāka*)—namely, karma that results in birth in the evil destinies, karma whose timing is fixed but whose manifestation is uncertain. Furthermore, other [types of karma] cannot be diverted.

Moreover, if present karma were to be diverted so as not to be experienced, it would be either indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karman*) or fixed karma (*niyata-karman*) for which the basis has already been transformed; this has already been explained.

Because one is liberated [from the former], one does not undergo [the retribution] based on the body that was not yet liberated; this establishes the determinate karma (*niyata-karman*) for those such as Ajātaśatru who repent and hear the Mahāyāna.

Based on the remaining support (*avaśeṣa-āśraya*), through the power of hearing the teachings and the Mahāyāna, they transform their basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); because they do not undergo even light [retribution], it is said that they only rely on what does not increase. Regarding the determination of receiving [retribution] for a short time, if one relies on the previous judgment, one undergoes nothing at all;

however, by the power of repenting and hearing the Mahāyāna, the basis has already been transformed, and thus one does not undergo even the light [retribution]. Therefore, it is said that one only relies on what does not increase.
Because long-term karma undergoes transformation, it does not necessarily result in maturation (*vipāka*).

In this context, "powerful" refers to that which is taken by the force of the treatise’s own textual momentum as the object of opposition—namely, unwholesome intentional karma (*saṃcetanīya-akuśala-karma*)—because it is determinately experienced. In the sub-commentary (*vyākhyā*), the antidote is taken as powerful;
thus, the lower [text] establishes the higher by taking the path of the antidote in relation to the person (*pudgala*) who possesses that [karma].

The karma of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is called "strong" because it takes what is to be countered as its object; as the subsequent passage states, "because of transformation and cessation.
"Transformation" means that karma of the hells becomes manifest in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), while "cessation" means that karma of the present life is not experienced [in this life].

This is correlated with the preceding [categories] in ascending order. Fourth, regarding "karma of strong power with determinate maturation (*niyata-vipāka*) which cannot be severed by the Noble Path," there are two meanings.

First, following the preceding [discussion] and according to what follows, this karma is called "of one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*); while this karma remains in the body, one necessarily cannot enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*), because the Noble Path cannot sever it.
Second, this follows from the preceding point that for one beyond training there is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*); this very text serves as proof.

If, in terms of total retribution, determinate evil karma obstructs the noble state such that one does not enter it; yet if, in terms of individual retribution, determinate retribution does not obstruct entry into the noble state, then one enters it.
The path is not severed when the noble ones experience the maturation (*vipāka*) within their own bodies. Among these ten types of powerful karma, the first two are powerful as antidotes;
the next three are powerful as objects to be countered; the next two are powerful by combining both aspects; the next one is powerful solely as an object to be countered;

the next one is powerful by combining both aspects; and the final one is powerful solely as an antidote. Alternatively, the first seven are the karma of those possessing a [specific] nature, and the next one is...

Regarding those without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the latter two [categories] of karma are combined with two [other] karmas; the first two [of these three] are the remedies (*pratipakṣa*), while the next three are the objects to be remedied (*vipakṣa*).
The final two are combined into one, making ten karmas in total. Among these, the first nine are distinct and separate, while the tenth karma contains nine [sub-elements].
From the beginning to the end, one should reflect according to reason upon their progressive cultivation within the superior [stages].

and second, the opening of the way to understanding. Within the negation of understanding, there are two parts: first, the main treatise; and second, the commentary on the treatise. The commentary on the treatise has three parts:
first, explaining that one should not practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*); second, explaining the limit of the exhaustion of suffering; and third, the conclusion.
