Regarding the explanation of the *Sūtra on White Karma* and other texts, as the Blessed One has said: "In this way, all sentient beings are governed by their own karma; they are separated from one another by the power of karma."

In the section on "disputes" (*raṇa*), there are two parts: first the heading and then the explanation. Within the explanation, there are three sections, as they concern the distinctions among the three types of action (*trividha-karman*).

In the first of these, there are again two parts: first the enumeration of the three, followed by the explanation of the three. Within the explanation, the text is divided into three sections, corresponding to the distinctions among the three types of action.
Within the *Prātimokṣa*, there are three parts: first, the seven classes of practitioners are distinguished; second, they are explained individually;

and third, regarding the "near-abiding" (*upavāsa*), it refers to both male and female near-abiders collectively as one category of "lay follower" (*upāsaka*). This is indicated by a single name because it does not take women as a separate [category].

One who serves for a long duration is called a "lay follower," while one who temporarily relies [on the precepts] is called "near-abiding. As for those with non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), they are like the wicked.
Śīla (virtue) and non-śīla are named "evil" because śīla has the meaning of "cooling";

since that which harms the cooling of others is not a proper ritual, it is called non-restraint (asaṃvara). It is not merely a matter of improper ritual; rather, when one investigates through wrong views, its essence is also evil.
That which is cooling is named śīla, while unwholesome dharmas are non-śīla.

In the detailed explanation, there are three parts: first, the establishment of the three categories based on their respective causes; second, the questions and answers regarding the breadth and narrowness of those who receive the *upāsaka* precepts;
third, the distinction between the monastic and the lay. Within the first part, there are three sub-sections because of the differences among the three categories.

Why is there a distinction established within the monastic community but not for the laity? Because the dharma of the monastics involves the severance [of worldly ties], whereas such is not the case for the laity. Therefore, the distinction arises from this.

The distinction between householders and those who have gone forth is explained differently. While for those who have gone forth there are the remaining trainings (*śaikṣa*), householders likewise possess the one-day fast (*upavāsa*);

this constitutes the difference. Furthermore, among those who have gone forth, the *bhikṣu* is established as two [categories], and the *bhikṣuṇī* is established as three, as explained in the fifty-third [chapter].

Regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the fifty-third [chapter] asks: "For what reason did the Blessed One establish the *bhikṣu*, the lay follower (*upāsaka*), and the one who observes the one-day fast (*upavāsastha*)?"
Answer: The three types of discipline are established based on three causes; that is to say, there are three categories of beings to be converted:

some are capable of practicing both the abstention from misconduct and the abstention from sensual desires; some are capable of practicing the abstention from misconduct but not the abstention from sensual desires;
and some are incapable of practicing either the abstention from misconduct or the abstention from sensual desires. Based on the first category, the bhikṣu precepts are established.
The three [actions] of the body and one of speech are called "misconduct" (*duścarita*); sexual misconduct is called "desire-conduct" (*kāmacaryā*).

Its nature is that of a fundamental transgression (*mūlāpatti*), and its ripened greed is the basis for desire. Regarding the second type of person to be converted, the lay follower (*upāsaka*) is established.

Among these, the three of the body and one of speech are called "misconduct," while actual sexual intercourse is called "desire-conduct," because sexual misconduct is the fundamental transgression; thus it is designated as "misconduct."

Furthermore, it is because they are free [from the household]. Why? Because although they do not dwell in the confinement of a home and remain amidst the dust of worldly desires, they are nevertheless able to continuously and perfectly observe all the training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
Based on those to be converted who rely on the third [type of discipline], the one-day fast (*upavāsa*) is established. Why?

Because by means of this, they are unable to practice the conduct of total renunciation; rather, they should only be encouraged and supported through these two causes, lest they [fall away] on their own.

This refers to being oppressed by the heavy burden; that is, one cultivates the first three branches to abandon unwholesome conduct, and the subsequent four branches to cultivate the abandonment of sensual desire—that is, the abandonment of non-celibacy.
Thus, both types are cultivated through the latter four branches, namely, abstaining from drinking alcohol and so forth.

These latter four are not for the purpose of prohibiting natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), but rather, because they arise from the locus of craving and desire, they are termed "cultivation of the abandonment of sensual desire. There are those who understand this in relation to the five objects of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).

Because they arise from the basis of adornment, they are called "desire-conduct" (*kāmacaryā*). If one follows this interpretation, how can it be said that abstaining from unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*) constitutes "abstaining from desire-conduct"?
My current explanation does not rely on the nature of the offense itself to define "abstaining from evil conduct" (*duścaritavirati*), for the nature of evil conduct is inherently evil.

Rather, the latter four [precepts] are designated as "abstaining from desire-conduct" because they prohibit sensual desire; those who practice both [abstinence from unchastity and abstinence from desire] do so by abandoning sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*).
Because sexual misconduct is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), even temporary, correct sexual intercourse is not permitted for those practicing the cultivation of abandoning evil conduct;

therefore, the restraint of one's greedy desire is called "conduct of renunciation. This differs from that of the ordained, who must necessarily abandon all such acts. If they violate [the precepts], whether correctly or erroneously, it is all termed "evil conduct.

For householders, the possession [of a consort] is permitted; however, only the erroneous [form] is termed a natural transgression, whereas the correct [form] is termed greedy desire and is not [a natural transgression].
Regarding the paths of action, the present [text] excludes covetousness and names this only "practice of detachment from desire.
Question: Why are the restraints divided into three categories, yet only one "non-restraint" (asaṃvara) is established in total?
It is difficult to achieve restraint through gradual instruction, whereas it is easy to accomplish misconduct; thus, one does not rely on gradual training when practicing even a single portion.

One who trains in even one part [of the precepts] is called a lay follower (*upāsaka*); one who does not train is called one who dwells in the middle. It is the same for all violations of the precepts and the loss of the precepts.
A lay follower may possess only one part [of the precepts], and the same applies to the one-day fast (*upavāsa*), because they are of the same category.

Regarding the monastic precepts, they are only fully established when the four root [precepts] are complete; herein, as usual, there are two meanings: that of losing the precepts through a grave violation and that of not losing them.
As for the remaining three [vows], even if one does not maintain the verbal [precepts], they still constitute the four fundamental root offenses of a bhikṣu and so forth;

this is because a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or one observing the one-day vows (*upavāsa*) who commits no grave offense abandons the vessel [of the vow] through such transgression. Alternatively, it is said that a lay follower may possess only a partial [observance], whereas the one-day vows do not;

for since the resolve [to observe them] is extremely immediate, there is no room for their practice [to lapse]. Second, regarding the sequence of their arising, one asks: for what reason are these restraints established?

Question: Is one who maintains only a single portion [of the precepts] called "one with restraint" (saṃvara) or "one with non-restraint" (asaṃvara)? Answer: Non-restraint requires receiving [the vows] completely with a fierce evil intention;
however, for restraint, even a small portion suffices if the intention is fierce, because it excels that [non-restraint] by virtue of its superiority over wholesome dharmas.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the fact that even one who performs only a single portion with fierce intent possesses non-restraint, just as one portion of restraint constitutes [restraint]. Thus, there is no difficulty.
However, while the higher grade of volition brings about both restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), the middling and lower grades bring about the intermediate state (*madhyama*).

Within each of these, there are further three grades. As for the Bhikṣu precepts, why must they necessarily consist of seven factors? Because they possess four branches: first, undertaking and training in the points of training (*śikṣāpada*);
second, being well able to guard the Prātimokṣa restraint; third, the perfection of both ritual conduct (*īryāpatha*) and behavior (*caryā*); and fourth, [the perfection of] livelihood (*ājīva*).

The fourth view is that one feels great dread toward even the most subtle transgressions; this constitutes the six bases of the Śrāvaka, by which the seven [limbs] are complete—otherwise they are not.
The Upāsaka possesses three limbs: first, the limb of abstaining from the most excellent form of harming others, namely the three types of physical [misconduct];

second, the limb of exceeding the received [vows] through intensive practice, namely the abstention from false speech, for one who speaks falsely is unable to practice intensively; and third, [the limb of abstaining from intoxicants].

"Not transgressing what has been undertaken" means abstaining from drinking various intoxicants; for by drinking various intoxicants, one transgresses what has been undertaken. Thus, the *upavāsa* (fast-day observance) consists of five factors:
first, abstaining from harming others, which means abstaining from killing and taking what is not given;

second, abstaining from harming both oneself and others, which means abstaining from unchaste conduct, as one abstains from the wives and concubines of both oneself and others; third, not transgressing what has been undertaken.

The factors of intensive practice refer to abstaining from false speech, abstaining from eating at improper times, and abstaining from high beds, perfumes, and ointments for the body—these three constitute not transgressing that which has been undertaken.
These three are constantly practiced; if one remains far removed from them, one repeatedly recalls to oneself:
"I am now established in the definitive fast (upoṣadha), and at all times I firmly maintain right mindfulness."
The fifth limb, the non-decline of right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), consists of abstaining from intoxicants.

Although one may abide in the limb of right mindfulness, thinking, "I now abide in the definitive observance of the fast," if one becomes intoxicated by various liquors, one will become deranged and lose self-mastery.
Therefore, among the bhikṣus, only two groups are established, while three are established for the bhikṣuṇīs, as explained in the fifty-third [section] regarding the eight [precepts].

Regarding the questions and answers concerning the opening, closing, increasing, and decreasing of the ten precepts, it is also as stated there: those who are *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs) are not comparable to those who lack sexual organs (*anupastha*) within the two assemblies, for they are incapable of performing the service.
One interpretation holds that this is also comparable to the *śāstra*, which briefly states [the following].

Second, it says they are not comparable because they lack the two faults of being male or female; thus, they are capable of serving, just like the various gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), all of whom likewise lack sexual organs.

Because the prohibition against receiving [those other precepts] does not cause one to lose the nature of that [Bodhisattva vow], this conversely demonstrates that the formless [vow] does not cause the loss of the Great Precepts.
Within the Bodhisattva Precepts, a bhikṣu certainly does not lose his distinct reception of these five precepts;

according to this analysis, how could a śrāmaṇera fail to be a lay follower (upāsaka) among such groups? Regarding these, there are three interpretations: first, because of the transgression of both male and female [precepts].

Furthermore, they may not go forth and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) for three reasons: first, because their afflictions (*kleśa*) are so numerous; second, because these afflictions are extremely obscuring;
and third, because such virtuous persons are difficult to find. Due to these three points, they are not permitted to go forth and receive full ordination.
While they cannot be called lay followers (*upāsaka*), they should not associate closely with the monastic community, nor should the monastic community associate with them or touch them.
Furthermore, it is not appropriate for a *śrāmaṇera* to be as intimate with [laypeople] as a *upāsaka* is; nevertheless, the merit protected by their vows is no different.
Regarding the *bhikṣu* precepts, they should not be received if six conditions exist, such as an intention to cause harm; if these six are absent, they may be received.
A *upāsaka* is established through two conditions, while a *upavāsastha* is established through only one condition, just as there is no difference in their manifest expression (*vijñapti*).
In the exposition of the conditions for attaining and relinquishing [gender], it is said: *śaṇḍha* (translated as "one without virility," meaning one who lacks it for life);
*paṇḍaka* (translated as "one who desires others," so called because taking pleasure in others constitutes a transgression for oneself);

among these five, the first two attain [the state] and the second three are exclusively *paṇḍakas* and not *śaṇḍhas*, because they lack male virility throughout their entire lives; as for the last one, if he is not afflicted by another...

If one is deficient in the male organ due to a lack of virility, it is called a *śaṇḍha*; if another is deficient in the male organ toward oneself because of having sexual desire, it is called a *paṇḍaka*.
These differ from the first type of person [the *ṣaṇḍha*]. That person (*paṇḍaka*) lacks the function of the organ throughout their entire life;

whereas the fifth type [the *ubhaya-vyañjana*] previously possessed that function—though lacking its physical form—the nature and power of the organ still remain, as they can still give rise to that function. For this reason...
Because they lack the desire for others to commit transgressions against them, they are not called *paṇḍaka*;
this differs from the previous four types, for whom such desire arises only when others have committed a transgression against them.

Thus, while the former three are described by the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* as being characterized by the absence of initial desire and the presence of subsequent desire due to others' transgressions against them, this present teaching posits five types, excluding those who are so by nature (*prakṛti-paṇḍaka*).

Regarding the phrase "to perform the sprinkling," it means that others have committed an offense against oneself by performing an impure sprinkling; thus, [the commentary] states fifty-three [instances].
The *Chaojie* (Excerpts) says this is not so, because jealousy is explained separately and does not mention sprinkling; therefore, this treatise combines jealousy [with it], adding the sprinkling.

As for the meditative restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*), its abandonment through counteraction occurs only in the first [stage], the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), specifically during the nine paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), which are distant [from the defilements].

The seven fundamental [dhyānas] and the intermediate [dhyāna] are partially applicable; the first *anāgamya* and the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are called "antidotes by sustaining" (*dhṛti-pratipakṣa*), while the others are called "distant" (*dūra*).

If one enters the nine grades of cultivation in reverse order, it is as explained in the section on the four paths regarding the "antidote by abandonment" (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), the "antidote by sustaining," and the "distant antidote.
The untainted discipline (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) and so forth are as explained in the fifty-third [fascicle]. Furthermore...
In the commentary on this chapter, regarding the non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), there are fifteen types of yoga within it;

the ninth [chapter] speaks of twelve, as three of these are absent here—namely, those of the fisherman, the ox-killer, and the deer-hunter—and one type is not found there, namely that of the jailer. The ancient commentators say this...
The harming of oxen is subsumed within the category of sheep; this harming of fish is subsumed within the category of birds; the hunting of deer is included within the category of rabbits.
That which is described as "severing the prison" is subsumed within "guarding the prison. Thus, they are not the same. In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are sixteen types:
sheep, pigs, oxen, and chickens—these four constitute the "fat ones bought"; killing them after purchase constitutes another four, thus totaling eight. [The text] does not mention [the others].
These three—deer, rabbits, and birds—and the remaining seven types [of animals] are all included here;

as for the hunter who captures these three, since this text states that those who delight in harming others and so forth are included among all who harm life in water or on land, one may kill them at will and sell their flesh to sustain oneself.
Furthermore, because killing horses and donkeys to maintain one's livelihood constitutes non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), it is known that [these beings] are captured.
The deer has merely raised a small portion; it is not necessarily exhaustive. One cannot reconcile [this with] the butcher of sheep.
For the sake of sustaining life, he slaughters, raises, buys, and sells; this already encompasses nirvana.

Whether buying lean or selling fat, or having already bought and slaughtered, now further adding the term "thief"—to say such things as these, for the sake of sustaining life, giving rise to superior volitions (*adhimukti*) and so forth, and performing such deeds—all are termed [unwholesome].
Regarding non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), the treatise states that it applies accordingly to those who either practice killing or do not practice killing.

For example, one might bind an elephant and purchase it for money, or take goods from a king and return them to oneself to sustain one's life; the same applies to reciting mantras to enliven a dragon.

Alternatively, one might take such things for amusement and pleasure, sustaining oneself directly through play without intending to sustain one's life—this latter case does not belong to the category of killing mentioned above, nor is it considered taking what is not given (*adattādāna*).

There are only two types of taking what is not given: the category of sexual desire, which involves prostituting one’s own female form, and the category of force, which involves slander and instigation.
Here, only the act of sowing discord is mentioned, and not flattery or deception, because these are the fundamental means for seeking wealth by alienating those who are close.

As for those who compose ornate writings or engage in frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*) to scheme for wealth, since they constantly rely on this as their livelihood, it constitutes a transgression even if it does not yet constitute a full course of action (*karmapatha*); nevertheless, it is not non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). Thus it is said.

Regarding those who possess non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), even when they undertake a particularly grave course of action (*karmapatha*), does their non-restraint not last for the duration of their life?

Since there are cases where it is only partial, there are also instances where it does not last for the duration of one’s life; however, in cases such as the monastic vows (*bhikṣu-śīla*) where the resolve is grave, it necessarily lasts for the duration of one’s life.
For others, it is not so. Or, although the duration may be brief, because the action performed is grave, it constitutes non-restraint that lasts as long as one lives.
Non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is not [incurred] because it is produced by a mind of retribution (*vipāka-citta*), as it does not involve a formal vow; this point should be reflected upon.

Regarding birth in that family or birth in other places, as explained in the fifty-third [fascicle] and in the first fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vivaraṇa*, concerning the experience of the three types of sensation (*vedanā*) in the realms of existence:

some say that when one casts off the retribution of life and dies in the sixth heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is the casting off of retribution by a mind of a lower stage; however, they do not permit [the casting off of retribution] in the [higher] stages.
Regarding the sixth, the mind of retribution (*vipāka-citta*) that abandons life and ceases immediately, it is as stated in the first fascicle of the *Abhidharma* (the *Abhidharmakośa*).

Among the three types of karma across the three times, there are three [sections]: first, the enumeration of the names; second, the explanation of their reasons; and third, the resolution of objections regarding these karmas, starting from the stage of initial ripening.
Within the karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya-karman*), there are two parts: first, the main treatise enumerates four or three [types].
Following the subsequent commentary by the Śāstrin, the reason for the name is explained through a fourfold analysis in the original sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*): first, the determination of the essence.

In the Mahāyāna, volition (*cetanā*) is taken as the essence of the three types of karma; one should clearly distinguish the differences among these volitions, or apply the principle accordingly to whether they consist of five aggregates (*skandha*) or four aggregates.

Second, the explanation of the names, consisting of general and specific names. The general name can be understood as follows: it refers to the taking up (*upādāna*) of the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma across the three time periods, distinguished by their co-arising.

The general designation is also called "maturation" (*vipāka*). As for its specific names: "karma to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*) refers to the *dharma*, which means the principle;
it is the karma that accords with the principle of being experienced in the present life. "Experiencer" (*vedaka*) refers to the maturation. Regarding this karma:

it is the agent that accords with the experience, and it is that which is accorded to—the experience itself. It is the "accordance" of what is to be experienced in the present life; it is the karma that accords with such experience. This is an *upapada* compound (a dependent determinative). Because it is common to both [the present] and those born subsequently, it is termed generally...
Regarding "distinct maturation" (*vipāka*), the term "dharma" (*dharma*) is added to distinguish it from those [other types of karma] by specifying that it refers only to a distinct fruit.

Alternatively, taking the first example as a model, what harm is there in admitting that all [types of karma] exist therein? Karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*) should be understood accordingly.

Third, regarding the production of both general and specific retribution: since wholesome and unwholesome [karma] produce general and specific results across the five destinies, this explains both the essence of these general and specific [retributions] and their production.
Contemplate the distinctions regarding the greater or lesser degree of excellence among the twelve bases (*āyatana*); yet there are differences between them, such as those of ghosts and animals.
One should also consider how the five sense faculties and so forth are produced by wholesome karma, while the five sense faculties of humans and devas may also be summoned by unwholesome karma.

Fourth, regarding the differences in meaning across various categories: first, clarifying the determination of whether the cause and fruit of worldly attainment belong to the same or different lifetimes.

If various schools differ regarding this, they distinguish between the ripening of karma that is non-dual in terms of time—where there is a cause at the time of the fruit and there is a fruit at the time of the cause—and apply these arguments to the various schools.

Thirdly, regarding the distinction of realms: the bodily sensations of the three realms are the maturation of causes belonging to one's own realm or another realm; this is also applied to the various schools.

Regarding the four categories of karma—those that yield results, those that do not, and those that are determinate or indeterminate—it should be understood here from what these terms "determinate" and "indeterminate" derive their names.

There are two explanations: first, they are named in relation to all [beings], because even an Arhat still experiences the results of unwholesome karma until, having undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), he enters the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*);
second, they are named in relation to whether one has attained or has not yet attained the fruit, based on the transformation of the basis.

Based on what has been stated previously, although it may be certain that even King Ajātaśatru’s karma for attaining the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) through the power of the antidote is not yet determined, it is nonetheless certain that his karma for the transformation of the basis will occur if there are no superior conditions to obstruct it. Therefore, as the *Ṣaṣṭitantra* states:

"The karma leading to the evil destinies of those such as the stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) is entirely exhausted," and so forth. In this context, one should understand the lightness and heaviness of the fifth type of karma according to the beginning of the sixty-fascicle version [of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*].
One should understand that the lightness and heaviness of karma, as well as its performance and non-increase, are also as described in the *Ṣaṣṭi-prakaraṇa*.

Regarding the karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*) therein, such as the first dhyāna of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) and so forth—the *Ṣaṣṭi-prakaraṇa* states:

"Loving-kindness arises because one dwells in a superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the supreme benefit and happiness of all sentient beings; therefore, it obtains its fruit in the present. Why is this not mentioned [here]?"
Regarding the interpretation found in old manuscripts concerning the one who possesses compassion (*karuṇā*), my current explanation is that it is not so.

While the one who possesses loving-kindness (*maitrī*) does not deeply engage in causing harm and therefore certainly does not kill, the one who possesses compassion, although they do not kill, nevertheless abandons harming and does not bestow happiness; thus, loving-kindness is superior, and this is not the case for others.
This is also true for the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) and so forth. The *Ṣaṣṭitantra* states: "The absence of conflict arises from protecting all sentient beings."

Because it arises from the mind abiding [in equipoise], it is superior to the vows, knowledges, and so forth; because it arises from the noble dwelling that resembles the bliss of the first cessation—the most quiescent nirvana—it surpasses all meditative concentrations involving a mind.
This is called the stage of the cause. As for the stage of the fruit, even if one does not enter meditative absorption, one still experiences the present retribution:
at the initial attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), one acquires the restraint of non-action regarding all unwholesome deeds.
Therefore, those who have excelled [others] are subsequent to those still in training (*śaikṣa*), for they are not the first.
The fifth, characterized by the ultimate purity of the mental continuum, refers to the community of great bhikṣus headed by Arhats and Buddhas;
this includes the first, the fourth, and the second [categories], with the Buddha as the preeminent leader. The Pratyekabuddhas are also included therein.
Regarding those types of yoga, the ninth chapter contains two causal conditions that yield results in the present life: first, intention (*āśaya*), and second, by way of the actual deed (*vastu*).
There are eight kinds of intention: namely, four that are wholesome and four that are unwholesome. These are: (1) regarding oneself versus not regarding oneself;
(2) abandoning affliction versus compassion; (3) malice versus pure faith; and (4) abandoning kindness versus recognizing kindness. All of these...
The attainment of results experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) through the cultivation of the higher mind (*adhicitta*) occurs by way of two factors:

the intensity of one's desire (*chanda*) and the strength of one's resolve (*adhimokṣa*); it is not due to the nature of the object or other such conditions. These eight types of desire and resolve constitute this third category.

Furthermore, because other intense mental dispositions and applications (*prayoga*) can range across both the wholesome and the unwholesome, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that results may also be produced in the present life by virtue of the "matter" (*vastu*) itself.

Regarding "Dharma-affairs," there are the five immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) and their counterparts (*sabhāga*). The five immediate transgressions consist of such acts as currently manifesting leprosy, being killed, and so forth.
The counterparts include: [killing] one's mother who is defiled; striking an *aśaikṣa* nun; killing a final-stage Bodhisattva; slaughtering sheep at temples, crossroads, or markets;
extreme severity toward close relatives; speaking with deceit to the poor and others; causing harm and affliction; robbing and plundering; and destroying the gates of the Sangha.
Regarding those acts such as the construction of spirit shrines which are designated as "unwholesome manifest karma" yet are actually wholesome deeds:

when one’s parents lack right faith, violate the precepts, are stingy, or possess evil wisdom, to cause them to turn toward right faith and so forth constitutes karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).

This [karma] is capable of yielding a superior manifest fruit for others, such that their country or home becomes like a Buddha-land or a royal city, and so on at length. This matter differs from [the case of] desire and resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
Regarding the two dharmas, because their objective gravity is paramount, the five immediate (*ānantarya*) volitions (*cetanā*) receive their distinct fruits first while they are still present;
or, the volition of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of a lower level is not the fundamental action (*maula-karman*), and thus it is not an immediate retribution.

Furthermore, how could it be realized that a single volition receives its distinct fruits in multiple worlds first, and subsequently receives the collective fruit? Moreover, regarding the body that benefits, why would one receive the collective and distinct fruits later?

Since these are emanations, there is no fault in first distinguishing them individually and then treating them collectively. [The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] states that there are three causes for the arising of karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*):
first, by way of vastness, such as the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*);

second, by way of the vastness of intention, which refers to giving pure material wealth with profound, earnest, and pure faith toward such fields of merit; third, by way of purity of continuity, which refers to if—
In previous lives, when others gave clothing and other such items, one did not create obstacles nor did one conceive defiled thoughts;
because there were no obstructions, that continuity was unimpeded. One should know that this is called "purity of continuity.

When these three are all fully possessed, one should know that [the result] will certainly be experienced in the present life, certainly in the next life, or in subsequent lives. This is associated with this [karma].

The same applies to the arising of unwholesome karma through contradiction. This is the title of this treatise from its beginning, and it also serves to clarify that karma extends to [rebirths] such as the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
Within the category of *upapadyavedanīya* (karma to be experienced in the next life), it says:

"Furthermore, there is other wholesome and unwholesome karma that, for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), all results in retribution in the immediately following birth. Thus it is said. Now, regarding the five conditions for killing and so forth:

1. The predominance of mental karma (*manas-karman*); 2. the increase of the three poisons (*tri-viṣa*); 3. the frequent contemplation of the two means; 4. the lack of antidotes and the failure to apply them to the mind;
5. the superiority of false attachments; and 6. the nature of the object—namely, that thoughts of harming those with large bodies produce many births [of retribution].
These are explained in detail in that treatise.

Regarding the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*), they are established through three gates: first, their essential nature; second, that they consist of volitional action (*cetanā-karma*); and third, [the specific actions involved].

Regarding the four [deeds] excluding the shedding of a Buddha’s blood, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 8 and fascicle 60, these involve killing and false speech. However, in the case of the [other] four—namely, killing one's father, mother, or an Arhat, and causing schism in the Saṃgha—the act itself constitutes the full path of action (*karmapatha*).
As for the shedding of a Buddha’s blood, this is merely the preliminary application (*prayoga*) of killing and not the fundamental path of action itself. This is because...
The preparatory acts (*prayoga*) of the various karmas are each considered "weighty by nature" (*prakṛti-guru*) in relation to their respective results.

Even if one who has not killed a Buddha should take his life, because that act is based on malice (*vyāpāda*), it is not this [preparatory act] that serves as the root for killing any other life; therefore, it is not a course of action (*karmapatha*).

If that is so, why is it that the other cases of killing living beings are compared to this? Why is it not the same? Because the two types of immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) are of the same class.

As previously cited from the *Yogācārabhūmi*, committing the offense of "correctly defiling one's mother" (*mātṛ-dūṣaṇa*) is of the same category as killing one's mother; violating a nun (*bhikṣuṇī-dūṣaṇa*) is of the same category as killing a nun;

and striking a final-stage Bodhisattva and so forth is of the same category as killing an Arhat. Furthermore, within the detailed classification of "grave offenses" (*guruka*), acts such as killing an elder are of the same category as killing one's father.
The other two [categories] may be understood accordingly. Third, the analysis through question and answer establishes that these [offenses] exist only among human beings.

The men and women of the three continents see [the results of] unwholesome conduct and nothing else; this is explained in the *Vibhāṣā* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* as found in the commentaries (*śāstra*).
Third, the ninth and fiftieth [chapters] clarify the experience of retribution (*vipāka*), which is the same as here at the beginning of the treatise regarding the text on the three times.

However, the sixtieth fascicle explains that a single karma can also obtain fruits to be experienced in the present life and future lives, which is the same as this; below, the treatise’s text is explained regarding the slander [of the Dharma].

Because the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other texts state that one enters the hells of the ten directions, this accords with the passage in the sixty-fascicle version which says that those who commit the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) receive their retribution all at once.
This is explained as receiving the retribution for all [crimes] instantaneously within a single kalpa. Furthermore, the third fascicle of the *Sūtra on Right Mindfulness* states:

"The retribution for one heinous crime is one kalpa; the retribution for committing the five heinous crimes is five kalpas. This is the same as the present [text]. Among the four types of karma, such as black and so forth, this refers to one instance.

The "black-black" [karma] refers to all purely unwholesome karma within the ten unwholesome courses of action, including the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) and subsequent stages (*pṛṣṭha*) of the karmic restraint.
The "white-white" [karma] refers to the wholesome karma of the three realms. The "black-white" [karma] refers to the mixed karma of the desire realm;
that is, when both the underlying intention (*āśaya*) and the means (*upāya*) are considered together, it is generally termed black-white. Apart from these, there are other intentions and means...

Thus, both the karma of the desire realm and the karma of the form and formless realms are "wholesome-white" (*śukla-śukla*). This is as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, Chapter Nine. Regarding "black-black" karma, it is the same principle.
As for "wholesome-white" karma, this refers to immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*). "Mixed" karma refers to meritorious karma (*puṇya-karma*), because it has unwholesome karma as its adversary;
it is established based on the meritorious karma existing at a time when non-meritorious karma has not yet been abandoned. For this reason...
Since there is opposition between them, they receive the names "black-and-white" (*kṛṣṇa-śukla*); these are the karmas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that lead to the abandonment of desire.
They are of a mixed nature and are thus also called "black-and-white. As for why the two treatises differ:

the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 66, states that "white karma with white maturation" refers to the acquisition of an unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) ripened fruit that is exclusively desirable, which is comprised within the seeds of experience.
Because it is experienced, one should know that it is exclusively desirable and exclusively agreeable; the same applies to its opposition, namely black-black karma.

Since this karma, along with its fruit, is entirely both desirable and undesirable, it is said that because it is pursued by the two kinds of seeds—black and white—the resulting ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) should also be known to be of two kinds of ripening.

"Rebirth-feeling" (*upapatti-vedanīya*) refers to two types of distinct karma and their two types of resultant maturation (*vipāka*). "Feeling-arising" (*abhinirvṛtti-vedanīya*) likewise refers to two types of distinct karma and their two types of resultant maturation.
Although this is stated in general terms, it is [also] his own specific statement regarding these mixed karmas.

Furthermore, black-and-white karma is established based on the distinction of the classes of beings; that is, in a case where both black and white exist together, the karma belongs to that very place.
The general establishment of "black" and "white" here intends to say that although there is both intention (*āśaya*) and application (*prayoga*), they are collectively termed "white.
However, because they are established based on the category of rebirth (*upapatti-gati*), they are now termed "mixed. This is because unwholesome [karma] can mix with the wholesome;
thus, even karma that is purely wholesome regarding its rebirth may receive the name "mixed," and it cannot be called "black-black" karma.
Because they are similar in their category of birth (*jāti*), they are also called "mixed" (*miśra*); it is not that the white [karma] can mix with the evil, but rather because the white is weak.

This is established according to the ninth section on the basis of categories of birth in the aforementioned *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, where immovable karma is designated as "white-white" (*śukla-śukla*) and that of the desire realm is designated as "mixed.
Furthermore, its second section states: "Moreover, it is established by way of the distinction of entities (*vastu-viśeṣa*). That is to say, there is one who, in accordance with any one..."

When a mind intent on benefiting a particular object arises and is present at one time, and at another time a mind intent on not benefiting that same object arises regarding that very same object—or when one seizes another's property and yet gives it away as a gift—this is established by way of the differentiation of the object (*vastu-viśeṣa*).
This intention demonstrates that there is both mixed and unmixed karma with respect to the object; according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, this is based on the mixture of objects.

The *Abhidharma* refers to "mixed" meritorious karma (*puṇyakarman*) based on a single instance; however, there is also that which is "unmixed. Therefore, even in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there exists "white-and-white" [karma].
Furthermore, the third section states: "Moreover, by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), such black-and-white karma is established.
That is to say, suppose there is someone who, having performed a beneficial act toward one person, subsequently performs another [beneficial] act toward yet another person."
Regarding actions that are unbeneficial: suppose there is someone who gives rise to a volition associated with hatred toward one who commits violent evil;
although they do not delight in that evil, it should be known that because this volition is associated with hatred, it falls within the black category (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
Yet, because they do not delight in that evil, it falls within the white category (*śuklapakṣa*). Therefore, this karma is called "black-and-white" (*kṛṣṇa-śukla*), and thus it is established.
In this context, because the means (*upāya*) are black, it gives rise to an intention (*āśaya*) that is white; thus, one does not delight in that unwholesome yoga.
Based on this, only the "white-white" is mentioned. This is called "immovable meritorious karma.

As for the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* (or *Vibhāṣā*), it states that when both the intention and the means are white, it applies to all three realms and all three types of action, which are all termed "white-white. This is further clarified in the latter two successive sections.

Regarding this distinction, the two masters differ in their views. The Yogācāra school, relying on the first of the two successive expositions, maintains that all karma of the desire realm is termed "mixed.
The Abhidharma (Dharmapada), relying on the latter two successive expositions, holds that there are distinctions within it;
thus, because there is also "white-and-white" karma in the desire realm, the two positions are not contradictory.
The fourth is non-black-and-white karma. The ancients said it "abides in twelve [moments of] thought-moments" (*cetanā*).

"Black-and-black" refers to the four truths and the first eight uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) in the desire realm; the thoughts associated with these only sever black [karma].

Although they also slightly sever [the karma] that takes [the higher realms] as its object, because it is not yet completely exhausted, they do not receive the name "severance. It is by means of the thoughts associated with the fundamental dhyānas of the four formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*) that one is able to sever [it].
Regarding the "white-and-white" [karma], it is discussed in terms of its point of exhaustion:

because the volition (*cetanā*) of the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) in the desire realm is able to sever both the black and white categories, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states that there are twelve types of volition capable of severing karma with black retribution, four capable of severing white [karma], and one capable of abandoning both.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter sixteen, states: "The four dharmas-knowledges (*dharmajñāna-kṣānti*), the abandonment of desire, and the first eight paths of uninterrupted transition [sever these]."

The twelve types of untainted volition (*anāsrava-cetanā*) exhaustively eliminate purely black karma; the ninth uninterrupted-path volition (*ānantarya-mārga-cetanā*) of the fourth dhyāna eliminates mixed and purely black karma;

and four [volitions] exhaustively eliminate purely white karma. Now, according to the Mahāyāna, nine volitions eliminate only the black, while eight volitions can eliminate the white, and one [volition] eliminates two or three [types of karma] as appropriate.
Thus, in the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), there is one grade of the desire realm’s cultivation.

The eight uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) prior to the Path [of Seeing] are called the nine thoughts that abandon the black; the uninterrupted paths that abandon the four form and four formless realms are called the eight thoughts that abandon the white.

If one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the "white-white" refers exclusively to the immovable [attainments], because the ninth uninterrupted path of the desire realm abandons only the black and the mixed, as there is no white in the desire realm. However, according to this treatise [the *Abhidharmakośa*]:

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is also the "white-white" [action]; because the volition (*cetanā*) of the ninth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the desire realm can sever three types [of action], it is said that one [type] is severed, two, or three, according to what is applicable. Since this applies to both the two and three realms as appropriate, such a statement is made.

When combined with the eighteen volitions of the uninterrupted paths, these are taken from this treatise as referring exclusively to the preparatory (*prayoga*) and uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) stages.

Because these various karmas are the antidotes for abandonment, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states: "That is to say, supramundane, untainted (*anāsrava*) karma is the antidote for the abandonment of the three previous types of karma;
since only the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) serves as the antidote for abandonment, there are only eighteen volitions (*cetanā*).

Alternatively, this may refer generally to the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*); however, according to this treatise, it takes the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) into account.

Seventeen moments of volition (*cetanā*) are counted because there is no uninterrupted preparatory application (*anantarya-prayoga*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); together with the previous thirty-five moments of volition, the ancients said there were thirty-nine.

This is because they added the preparatory application of the path of seeing to the four [moments] of the path of seeing itself; however, this is not the definitive position, as it does not accord with the meaning.

If one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, adding the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and further including the preparatory application for the desire realm within the path of seeing, eighteen more [moments] are added.
The nine stages of the form realm and the four stages of the formless realm involve further superior progress and so forth, which should be added accordingly as appropriate.

At present, the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is not included here because the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) is also capable of severing active manifestations (*samudācāra*). Since the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) severs the seeds, there is no such function for the path of liberation;
this is explained based on the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) observing the severance of the nine grades of cultivation. This is because of those belonging to the two vehicles.
The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that swiftly enters contemplation and abandons multiple categories [of afflictions] is also considered relative to its own preceding mind;

it is not considered relative to subsequent categories because it serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*). Since minds arise individually as the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation, the path of liberation is neither the liberation from the preceding category nor the preparatory application for the subsequent one, because a single preparatory application has already been initiated in total. Thus, it cannot be a preparatory application.

Therefore, the treatise does not state that this [view] can exhaust all karma; it only takes the preparatory (*prayoga*) and uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) paths as being capable of severing them, because those [paths], such as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), are also by nature able to sever [karma].

Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that all untainted (*anāsrava*) karma is abandoned prior to the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)—which lasts for only one or three moments—or prior to the vajra-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) during the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

In summary, because it severs the fetters of the objects of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*), a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) of the Bodhisattva on the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) exclusively severs the "black" [defilements].

Alternatively, three or ten thought-moments may sever them; this is explained in terms of the stages (*bhūmi*). If one attains the two fruits by means of instantaneous transcendence (*skandhaka-samāpatti*), nine thought-moments exclusively sever the black defilements of the Path of Seeing, while eight thought-moments sever those of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
One thought-moment, however, universally severs all three types of defilements across both the Path of Seeing and the Path of Cultivation.

Regarding the explanation of the names based on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*: if one attains the second or third fruit by means of leaping (*pluta*), the treatise itself explains that the first two [categories] are established by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and whether their fruits are desirable or undesirable.
These are repeated here because they both reside in the cause. "Pure-white" (*śukla-śukla*) refers to the maturation (*vipāka*) of pure-white karma;
this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. As for "black-and-white" (*kṛṣṇa-śukla*), it is both black and white; "black-and-white" is simply "black-and-white."
Regarding the distinction between black and white maturation and the karma that matures: because evil is powerful, it may be termed "black-and-white";

however, it cannot be called "white-and-black" because the wholesome is weak. That which is neither black nor white refers exclusively to this treatise’s explanation—that karma which is neither black nor white is precisely karma without maturation (*avipāka*).
That these karmas which are neither black nor white and so forth can exhaust all karma means that herein [it is shown] that...
Because it is untainted (*anāsrava*) and not of the nature of affliction (*kleśa*), it is called "non-black. Because its karma is pure, it is termed "white.

In the ninth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, "neither black nor white" is used to distinguish it from both of the preceding two types of karma. This treatise, however, excludes the afflictions while including the white and pure;

thus, they are combined and termed "yoga. It merely excludes [karma] that serves as a cause. However, if one were to say only "neither black nor white," then white and pure karma would also have to be termed "neither."

To distinguish black karma from white karma, it is stated that the latter has no maturation; this is said for fear that the contaminated wholesome karma present in the bodies and so forth of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) might be mistakenly conflated with it.
Furthermore, it is added that [this white karma] is capable of exhausting all karma.

Third, regarding maturation based on persons: it should be understood that this is explained generally across ordinary beings and noble ones, those who have abandoned desire and those who have not, and those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the three vehicles and the Great Vehicle, in terms of whether the manifest or the seeds are matured.

These karmas may be categorized as two—because one is [the result of] view and one is [the result of] cultivation—or as four—because one is [the result of] view and three are [the results of] cultivation—or as eleven—because eight are [the results of] view and three are [the results of] cultivation.

Thus, there may be eighteen [paths], because the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) sees one [truth] while the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) cultivates seventeen, or thirty-five, by adding the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
Or there may be fifty-three, by adding the eighteen paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Or there may be seventy-one, by adding the eighteen [paths of liberation];

these are stated according to the sequential attainment of the fruits (*phala-prāpti*). If, however, one attains the fruit by leaping over stages (*vyutkrāntaka*), there are further superior advancements (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
Because the path is not fixed, one should reflect upon its meaning according to the principle that here both black and white [karma] are explained in accordance with their specific sense.

The "crooked, defiled, and turbid karma" as explained in the ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* is excellent. Regarding the statement here that it is "subsumed under the view of negation (*apavāda-dṛṣṭi*) and increases malice toward the established principles of purification":

the former refers to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), while the latter refers to the grasping at views and precepts (*dṛṣṭi-śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*). The three types of pure karma and so forth are likewise [to be understood in this way].
As in the ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, passages that appear to contradict this [text] are all to be reconciled according to that [work].

Furthermore, regarding the various pure karmas such as giving, there are two sections in the sixth major division of the lower part; first, it presents the heading for the upcoming exposition on the karma of giving, saying, "How is the karma of giving?
and so forth, and second, it specifically elucidates [the details]. The ninth *Yogācāra* [fascicle] also clarifies the three types of pure karma, which are not [discussed] here.

Since it is explained that [the perfection of giving] exists within the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya), there are two parts: first, the explanation of the act of giving (*dānakarman*), and second, the explanation of the act of morality (*śīlakarman*).

Within the first [act of giving], there are three: first, the act of giving; second, the fulfillment of giving (*dānaparipūri*); and third, the fulfillment of the object of giving (*deyavastuparipūri*).

"Act" (*karman*) has the meaning of functional activity (*kāritra*), which is explained by four characteristics. Regarding the second [point], the fulfillment of giving, there are two successive expositions. In the first of these, there are three reasons for the explanation.
Regarding the latter middle section, because there are six [points], the commentary explains by correlating the Sūtra with the Śāstra according to their sequence.

In the subsequent explanation of the commentary’s resolution, the first two do not follow the sequence in resolving the difficult passages of the original Śāstra, while the latter four resolve the difficult passages of the Sūtra, explaining them point-by-point in accordance with the sequence.

Regarding the third section on the objects of giving, because there are five [points], the commentary explains them within that context; therein, the original Śāstra and its commentary should be understood according to their respective meanings.
One should know that what has been discussed above is not the Bodhisattva-bhūmi; rather, it is identical to a small portion of the Śrāvaka-bhūmi.
Therefore, within the eighty-third [chapter], the precepts are also explained as being twofold.

First, the five passages from the Sūtra are interpreted, which corresponds to the twenty-second [chapter] of the extensive and excellent Śrāvaka-bhūmi that should be adopted for exposition. Following this, one relies upon the śīla (ethical discipline).

The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) provides a detailed explanation of the meaning of "precepts" (*śīla*) within the Sūtra. Regarding the first of these, the six phrases that mark the beginning of what is not to be practiced, the five families, the proclamation, the *kaṭhina* robe, and so on, should be verified against the *Yogācārabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*.
Concerning those who are well-versed in undertaking the various training rules (*śikṣāpada*), the *Yogācāra-bhūmi* states:
"After having received the precepts, one [should act] before fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*) in accordance with all the trainings."
Because one has already undertaken the training in all [precepts], one should protect the body and other bases through equal guarding;

this is what the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi* (in twenty-two fascicles) and others explain. Within this, there are two parts: first the heading, and second the explanation. Regarding the explanation of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and freedom from regret, as stated in the seventh chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*:
"Because ethical discipline is perfected, there is no regret; because there is no regret, joy arises; because joy arises, the mind..."

Because of a joyful mind, there is physical pliancy; because of physical pliancy, one experiences happiness; because of experiencing happiness, the mind becomes concentrated; because the mind is concentrated, one contemplates reality as it truly is;

because of contemplating reality as it truly is, revulsion arises; because revulsion arises, desire is abandoned; because desire is abandoned, there is liberation; and because of liberation, one thinks:
"I have now realized liberation; my births are exhausted. In this context, one merely attains concentration and ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because the impure samādhi does not manifest, regarding the maturation within ethical discipline (*śīla*), [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] states in the twenty-second [chapter]:
"Of all the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) that I have undertaken to study, I do not fail in physical action, nor do I fail in verbal action; they are without deficiency and without breach.
This concentration merely maintains the precepts without failing in body or speech; this treatise states that one is able to receive and able to protect them purely.
Because of *śīla* (ethical discipline), there is first the undertaking and subsequently the protection. The *Vinayavibhaṅga*, fascicle 53, states:

"If one performs the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and the fourth *karmavācanā*, as well as the abbreviated acceptance, according to the coarse rules of training (*śikṣāpada*), this is called the 'initial bhikṣu' who possesses the bhikṣu-precepts; thus, the formal announcement and so forth are that which can undertake [the precepts].
The abbreviated acceptance of the coarse aspects—the four *pārājika* offenses and so on—is that which can protect [them]. Fascicle 50 [states the same].

Third, it is said that "receiving" is the subsequent cause. Regarding "one who is well able to guard the prātimokṣa-vinaya," the *Twenty-two [Questions]* states, "well guarding the bhikṣu-vinaya, etc.
Therefore, herein it is called "being well able to guard and maintain the śīla of renunciation.
Based on this, "liberation" refers to nirvāṇa or untainted (anāsrava) resolve. In the fifty-third [section], it says: "Self..."

Thereafter, regarding all the precepts for bhikṣus that accord with the Vinaya and Prātimokṣa, and the numerous rules of training (śikṣāpada) derived therefrom—guarding against and practicing all of them is called "maintaining the Prātimokṣa restraint.
This is what is meant by the "perfection of the conduct and rules" as the branch of training in accordance with the Dharma; this constitutes the twenty-second [point].

Whether in the course of deportment (*airyāpathika*), in the performance of tasks (*kṛtya-kriyā*), or in the application to the cultivation of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-pakṣa-prayoga*), one accomplishes the rules of conduct (*ācāra*) that conform to the world and do not transgress the world, and conform to the Vinaya and do not transgress the Vinaya.
Regarding the phrase "conforming" and those that follow, they all apply to the three preceding categories. That treatise explains this extensively; this treatise states: "All modes of deportment..."

Regarding the fulfillment of the activities and applications to be performed: [the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*] states at twenty-two that one should avoid five types of families, which is the same as this treatise;
it states at fifty-three that these two are branches for protecting the minds of others, seeing great dread even in subtle faults;
and it states at twenty-two that one should contemplate even a minor fault in this manner.
"May I not, due to the causes and conditions of transgressing these [precepts], lose the capacity to attain what has not yet been attained, and so forth;

may I not, because of this, fall into the evil destinies, and so forth. Thus, this treatise states: "Just as with natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), one who is well-perfected in all the training rules (*śikṣāpada*)—as stated in the twenty-second [chapter]—[refers to] the *prātimokṣa* vows previously received and the full ordination (*upasampadā*) received through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations)."

At that time, one hears from the preceptor (śikṣācārya) a small portion of the essential nature of the training rules (śikṣāpada), and further hears from the instructor (ācārya) the remainder of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra as it is briefly proclaimed in its entirety—namely, all the more than two hundred and fifty training rules—which one vows to study, and so forth, as explained at length.
These two [factors] protect the branches of the training as it was received: namely, by virtue of a profound perception of fear and by virtue of intelligence.
The first branch concerns the formal reception of full ordination; the second branch concerns the subsequent reception of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) according to the Dharma;
the third branch concerns protecting the minds of others; and the fourth branch concerns protecting the training rules as they were received, as mentioned previously.
One should always practice and train in all twenty-two [factors]. Of these three [sections], the first branch reveals the characteristic of ethical discipline (*śīla*) being free from impairment;
the next branch reveals the characteristic of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of ethical discipline; the subsequent four reveal the characteristics of the qualities of its intrinsic nature.

The following two branches reveal the characteristics of the qualities of one's own intrinsic nature as observed through others, according to what has been received; by observing others in this way, [one realizes] thus.
The perfection of conduct according to the rules inspires faith in those who lack it and increases the faith of those who already possess it; these latter two factors are as previously described.

Regarding the characteristics of one's own self-nature qualities: having attained the characteristics of the superior qualities of others through contemplation, one subsequently gives rise to one's own virtues;
the latter four factors constitute the total characteristics of one's own self-nature qualities, which are summarized into three.
Furthermore, there are three types: first, the morality of undertaking; second, the morality of renunciation; and third, the morality of cultivation.

Following the sequence of the three trainings, the training in morality is primary because it is the cause for renunciation. Subsequently, the four modes of cultivating morality—which are in fact a single type of morality—are explained as being sixfold.

The seventh major section, the explanation of karma, has two parts: first, a general enumeration of the six types of karma; second, a detailed explanation of each. Within the detailed explanation, there are three divisions:

first, the three types of karma that pertain exclusively to saṃsāra; second, the type of karma pertaining to liberation; and third, the two types of karma common to both ordinary beings and noble ones.

As the Blessed One said: "The maturation of the karma of sentient beings is inconceivable. This concludes the third major sub-section within the discussion of karma, which clarifies that which is conceivable.
Regarding the discussion of inconceivable karma and so forth, there are two parts: first, the explanation of worldly [karma], and second, the explanation of supramundane [karma].

Within the worldly section, there are three parts: first, the explanation of the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) of karma; second, the explanation of the external dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*); and third, the explanation of worldly matters such as the *maṇi* jewel.
Within the first part—the explanation of the ripening fruit of karma—there are two sections; the first is the commentary on the sūtra’s statement that the ripening of karma is inconceivable.

Regarding the inconceivable states following deliberation, there are two parts: first, citing the sūtra, and second, providing the formal explanation. Within the supramundane section, there are three parts:
first, clarifying the eighteen transformations of the two vehicles and others; second, clarifying the ten masteries of the bodhisattvas and others;
and third, clarifying the deeds performed by the Buddhas and so forth.
The ten masteries (*vaśitā*) are distinguished by way of five gates. First, regarding their essential nature:

since they take the six perfections as their cause, according to Vasubandhu’s *Nirākāra-śāstra* (Chapter Nine), they all have post-meditative wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as their nature. His explanation of the mastery of knowledge (*jñāna-vaśitā*) states:

"It is because various kinds of vocal expressions manifest before one accordingly. Thus, we know that it is exclusively post-meditative wisdom. If one follows the explanation in Vasubandhu’s *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* (Chapter Nine):

The "Mastery of Wisdom" (jñāna-vaśitā) refers to the thorough understanding and penetration of all cognitive objects (*ālambana*); this is called mastery of wisdom because these cognitive objects are themselves identical with True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, this treatise states: "By the power of mastery over wisdom, one attains perfection and ultimate consummation regarding the meanings of all phenomena.

Since it speaks of reaching ultimate consummation regarding meaning, according to both treatises, this can be understood as referring to correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*), while the other nine matters refer to discerning wisdom (*prajñā*). This is the first point.

Because the two types of wisdom—those pertaining to phenomena (*dharma*) and meaning (*artha*)—are without intrinsic nature and teach the Dharma according to the inclinations [of beings], one takes only the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) as the mastery of wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*).
Since the Lord of Heaven (Mañjuśrī) relies on the essential realization that objects are dispelled and only then become empty, he takes these two types of wisdom as the mastery of wisdom.
This treatise, based on the establishment of the four analytical knowledges, subsequently explains the Dharma; this also applies to both types of wisdom, for such is the principle.

Regarding their differences: this [attainment] is common to both the physical body and the mind; its essential nature is distinct from that of the life-faculty, wealth, and karma. Regarding its arising, it is said to be common to six categories.

As for its nature, according to the later masters, it takes wisdom as its essence. Regarding the mind, according to Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, it is said that at the time of death there is no defilement, and thus it takes the mind alone as its essence because it is not defiled.
In this treatise, however, it is held that it takes meditative concentration (*samādhi*) alone as its essence. Among these three...

Because one possesses mastery over entering and emerging from *samādhi*, it is "without intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*). It takes both the mind (*citta*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as its essence.
As that treatise states: "That which is undefiled within birth and death is precisely the mind.

Furthermore, because one can, according to one's inclination, correctly provide others with the necessary requisites and operate the mind with mastery therein, this mind is itself concentration (*samādhi*). Alternatively, the intention of the term "without intrinsic nature" is also...

Taking only the mind as the essence, this treatise takes the union of concentration (*samādhi*) and resolve (*adhimokṣa*) as its substance. Regarding resolve: according to one interpretation, it takes the name itself as its substance;

according to another, it takes both desire (*chanda*) and resolve as its substance. Regarding wisdom (*jñāna*): for those who possess mastery over wisdom, it takes supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as its substance. As for the two explanations of the names:

the five—life-force, wealth, karma, birth, and phenomena—are all called "name" (*nāman*) by way of the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound; the remaining five are [called "name"] by way of the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. If one takes wisdom as the substance, [the analysis is as follows].

Only the [powers] of wisdom (*jñāna*) and knowledge (*vidyā*) are *karmadhāraya* compounds; the remaining eight are *tatpuruṣa* compounds. Regarding the analysis of their characteristics, this treatise explains that the four—wisdom, resolve (*adhimukti*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and dharmas—are not different from those in other treatises. As for "mastery over the mind" (*cittavaśitā*), this treatise bases it on the ability of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to sustain the mind, naming it after its support (*āśraya*). As for "mastery over wealth" (*pariṣkāravaśitā*), Vasubandhu and Asvabhāva cite the gathering [of resources] as its basis. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the essence of the mind is unstained," it refers to the mastery over the mind itself. As for "mastery over aspiration" (*praṇidhānavaśitā*), it refers to the drawing forth [of results]. As for "mastery over dharma" (*dharmavaśitā*), it refers to the non-obstruction of the teaching of all phenomena. As for "mastery over action" (*karmavaśitā*), it refers to the non-obstruction of the maturation of karma. As for "mastery over birth" (*upapattivaśitā*), it refers to the non-obstruction of taking birth according to one's will. As for "mastery over vows" (*praṇidhānavaśitā*), it refers to the non-obstruction of fulfilling all vows. As for "mastery over miraculous power" (*ṛddhivaśitā*), it refers to the non-obstruction of manifesting various transformations. As for "mastery over wisdom" (*jñānavaśitā*), it refers to the non-obstruction of the unimpeded knowledge of all phenomena. As for "mastery over the twelve links of dependent origination" (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpādavaśitā*), it refers to the non-obstruction of the unimpeded knowledge of the twelve links of dependent origination.
