As for "mastery over the nineteen types of emptiness" (*ekonaviṃśatiśūnyatāva
Regarding the mastery over the requisites for life and various implements, Vasubandhu states that it refers to mastery over ten kinds of requisites, such as food.
Mastery over karma means attaining great sovereignty over all actions, performing only wholesome deeds and not unwholesome or neutral ones, as well as encouraging others to do so.
Vasubandhu further states that there are two kinds of birth from karma: namely, this [mastery] encompasses the capacity to bring about that [birth].
Because of the cause and the fruit produced from it, one proceeds with mastery over bodily and vocal actions, since the karma intended to arise manifests according to one's wish.
Regarding "mastery over birth," this refers to being born in various realms of existence according to one's wish. Although karma is a single category, there are two distinct types.
In Vasubandhu’s commentary (*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*), it is stated that a Bodhisattva performs further karma; this intention does not refer to [karma as] maturation (*vipāka*).
Because [the Buddha] acts solely through outflow-free (*anāsrava*) karma, he is not constrained by the karma or afflictions (*kleśa*) of birth and death;

indeed, this is precisely why the Buddha performs only outflow-free wholesome karma. Regarding the Buddha’s activity, it is taught that his production of material wealth (*āmiṣa-utpatti*) is no different from [the production of] non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*).
It is said that both Maheśvara and Niḥsvabhāva claim that [this occurs] due to past diligence (*vīrya*), in accordance with whatever [conditions] arise.
Because it brings about the ultimate goal, at this present time all that is wished for is attained. This treatise is thus led by great vows;

whereas those two treatises are said to have their intentions fulfilled based on vows, this treatise is said to have its vows fulfilled based on vows. Because the vows are fulfilled, it is said that everything fulfills the intention.
That which fulfills the intention does so because the vows are fulfilled. Furthermore, while those two [treatises] rely upon the vows of the Buddha, this one speaks of the bodhisattva’s own vows.

Because they are the *sattva* (the being), they are not mutually contradictory; rather, they are the mastery of wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*). The three treatises differ as has already been analyzed in the section on defining their essential nature (*svabhāva*). Fourth, the causes are clarified:

the first three are the causes of giving—namely, the Dharma, fearlessness, and material gifts—which are assigned in order to the first two [perfections]; the next two are the causes of ethical discipline (*śīla*);

and among the last two, which are the causes of wisdom (*prajñā*), the three are subsumed according to their names, as stated in the ninth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. Fifth, the distinctions are explained through questions and answers.

Question: Why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state that the Buddha possesses the ten masteries (*vaśitā*), while here it is said that Bodhisattvas attain them with reference to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)?

Furthermore, this [text] says they are attained partially; if one considers them as partial attainment, they are attained at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). If one considers their respective increases, there are also distinctions according to each stage.
Although they are attained at the first stage, they are not yet called "masteries" because the meaning is only partially attained; these are the four characteristics of karma.
What does mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*) comprise, and for what reason is it said that this is attained in the eighth stage?
It is because these two alone are mentioned, as they arise from their own gateway rather than from the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Why are only ten masteries taught? The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states:

"Because they counteract the ten fears: life [counters] the fear of death; mind [counters] the fear of afflictions (*kleśa*); wealth [counters] the fear of poverty; and birth [counters] the fear of evil [rebirth]."

The fear of the path is countered by the aspiration for the attainment of what is sought; the fear regarding the lack of attainment is countered by resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), which treats the fear of slandering the Dharma (the meaning of this point is somewhat difficult to verify).

Supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) counter the fear of bondage during the time of seeking; wisdom (*jñāna*) counters the fear of being in a crowd; and the Dharma counters the fear of doubt. Furthermore, because of five characteristics, the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) possess three masteries (*vaśitā*):

namely, mastery over the vessel [the field], mastery over the assembly, and mastery over perfect enlightenment and perfect knowledge. Moreover, the five immeasurables (*pañcāpramāṇa*) are subsumed within these same characteristics.

This is also as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. Regarding the question of how many among the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is asked:
upon which stage do the ten masteries (*vaśitā*) depend, how are they cultivated, and how many constitute the stage of retribution for self-benefit and benefit for others?

Furthermore, regarding each of these, one should understand that within the mastery of knowledge (*jñāna-vaśitā*), there are the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*): namely, those of phenomena (*dharma*), meaning (*artha*), linguistic expression (*nirukti*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Why are four aspects taught for the Truth of Origination? Because they serve as the antidotes to the four kinds of craving;
that is to say, the first two [aspects] specifically counteract [the first two cravings], while the latter two generally counteract all four.

Within the Truth of Cessation, there are six divisions: first, the definition of its essence; second, the clarification of its profundity; third, the distinction between the provisional and the real; fourth, cause and effect; fifth, superiority and inferiority.

In the sixth section, the *Mūla-saṃgraha-vyākhyāna*, and in the *Yogācārabhūmi*’s *Savitarkā-savicārā-bhūmi* (the stage of wisdom derived from reflection), it is explained that the cessation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) without remainder is equivalent to the three bases (*tri-āśraya*).

Regarding the seventeen explanations of specific names within the profound [section], one must examine whether there is the fault of grasping at difference—such as in sections sixty-eight and others—or the fault of grasping at non-difference.

Furthermore, one must analyze the faults of the individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the faults of mutual contradiction in the logical permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), and the fault of impairment resulting from neither [of the two].

The reduction of the excesses in the Chinese version has two parts: first, the presentation of the essential nature; second, the explanation beginning with "In this way," which is divided into three sections.

First, a general demonstration that it is not any of the four propositions; second, the explanation beginning with "Why is this so?"; and third, the citation of evidence beginning with "As the World-Honored One said.

In the second explanation, there are two parts: first, the interpretation by the Master; second, the interpretation of the root treatise. Within the section on distinctions, there are two parts: first, the citation of the sūtra; second, [the explanation].

The detailed explanation is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the heading; second, the explanation of the specific terms. Within the explanation of the specific terms, there are three sections:

first, the differentiation of names based on the seven supports and what is to be abandoned; second, the twenty-one names that explain their own respective meanings; third, the five pairs of names differentiated in relation to the Truth of Suffering.
Below this, there is an extensive explanation of the specific names (83), followed by an explanation of the four modes of practice (55).

Because the four types of craving within the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) are extinguished, it is the same as here in the section on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This third [aspect] is exclusively blissful and pure; the fourth is exclusively permanent.
The first two are the state of disjunction (*visamyoga*), which is precisely the meaning [of cessation], because this cessation also manifests the extinction of suffering and its origination.

That [text] relies solely on the extinction of suffering without remainder, whereas the *Yogācārabhūmi* poses a question and answer regarding permanence and impermanence therein. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Question: Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)..."

Is cessation the Truth of Cessation? Or, if it is the Truth of Cessation, is it the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)? Answer: That which is the Truth of Cessation is also the cessation of all conditioned phenomena.

However, there is the cessation of conditioned phenomena that is not the Truth of Cessation; this refers to the cessation of conditioned phenomena due to impermanence or through non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: If this Truth of Cessation did not previously exist but exists later, how can it be permanent?
If it is permanent, why do not all sentient beings attain parinirvāṇa at all times? Answer:

The characteristic of non-transmigration and the characteristic of non-manifestation are the characteristics of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). How could this Truth, which previously did not exist, come to exist later?

Furthermore, the characteristic of non-arising and the characteristic of non-ceasing are the characteristic of permanence; the Truth of Cessation is likewise so. Therefore, it is called permanent. If one realizes it...
Those who have attained the eternal cessation of all coarse heaviness (dauṣṭhulya) enter parinirvāṇa;
those who have not yet realized it do not enter parinirvāṇa. Because the truth of cessation exists, there are sentient beings who realize it;
therefore, parinirvāṇa is manifested by realization, not manifested by birth.

In the clarification of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), there are three parts: first, the question; second, the answer; and third, the explanation. Within the four-line answer, there are two sections: first, the brief manifestation of its characteristics and function;

second, the manifestation of its essence according to the stages. Regarding the practitioner who knows suffering, abandons the origin, realizes cessation, and cultivates the path, the *Pañcāśatikā* states:
"Because that Truth of Suffering is the basis for the four perversions (*viparyāsa*), it is for the purpose of eliminating those perversions."

Therefore, having fully understood suffering (*duḥkha*), and now having fully understood its origin (*samudaya*)—since that truth of origin is subsumed within the truth of suffering—even though suffering has been fully understood, it remains pursued by the truth of origin;
thus, it is necessary to further explain the permanent abandonment of the truth of origin.

Because the seeds of its causes have been eliminated and suffering will never again exist, it is said that one "touches and realizes" (*sparśa-sākṣātkriyā*); this means direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by virtue of the truth of cessation (*nirodha*).
Because one sees [the truth] manifest before oneself, fear does not arise; rather, there is joyful acceptance.

Therefore, it is next stated that one should strive to realize the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). If one diligently cultivates the Path, one will be able to accomplish the three aforementioned meanings.

Therefore, it is subsequently stated that one should cultivate the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). This explains the cause for entering the path and contemplating the truths, as well as the means by which those sufferings are accumulated and extinguished.
Since cessation is realized solely by means of the path, this now demonstrates that the Truth of the Path possesses this function.
It clarifies that there are five types of paths within the Truth of the Path; first, the five names are listed, and subsequently, they are explained individually.

Among these, what is here called the "Path of Provisions" (sambhāra-mārga) refers to the ethical discipline (*śīla*), the guarding of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*), and so forth, belonging to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). [This is stated] in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, Chapter Twenty.
Regarding the first stage of the Śrāvaka, it is taught that there are those who do not possess the nature of a Bodhisattva; they encounter two kinds of conditions: superior and inferior.
The superior condition refers to the voice of another based on the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and internal correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).

The inferior condition refers to either personal perfection, the desire for wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*), right renunciation (*samyak-niṣkramaṇa*), the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), or the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*).

Regarding moderation in food, constant diligent practice of the yoga of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, dwelling in clear comprehension, delighting in seclusion, purifying the hindrances, and the full perfection of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) based upon these—within this [context], there are five factors:
(1) obtaining a human body (either male or female); (2) being born in a noble land (such as the Central Land); (3) possessing all faculties...

Being free from defects (neither tall nor short, nor mute, etc.), one possesses pure faith in the four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*; the "bases of mastery" refers to the True Dharma, for by giving rise to faith therein, one can eliminate all defilements of affliction).

Fifth, being free from all karmic obstructions (this means remaining far removed from the five deeds of immediate retribution [*pañcānantarya*] and so forth; if any one of these is committed or increased, one will not be able to enter the state of a noble one [*ārya*] in this present life).

These five aforementioned types are called "perfection of oneself and perfection of others. There are also five phrases [for the latter]: first, the appearance of the Buddhas in the world; second, ... [and so on].

1. The teaching of the True Dharma (referring to the teaching of the Four Noble Truths); 2. The long endurance of the threefold teaching of the Dharma (during the Buddha’s lifetime and thereafter, before the True Dharma has vanished);

3. The persistence of the four conditions for the Dharma (the realized ones instructing others according to their capacities); 4. Compassion from others (donors giving rise to a mind of generosity and so forth toward the practitioner); 5. These five preceding points are termed the "perfection of others.

Together with the "perfection of both self and others," they constitute the ten factors beginning with the desire for wholesome dharmas, ethical discipline, and the restraint of the faculties, which serve as the conditions for [the arising of] wholesome dharmas.
First, regarding the desire for wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*): having heard the true Dharma, one attains pure faith and gives rise to a mind of weary detachment from wife and children;

one physically departs for the homeless life and diligently cultivates right practice until it is brought to perfection—this constitutes the arising of such desire. Second, regarding the formal renunciation:

through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion and three proclamations), one receives the *śrāmaṇera* precepts and so forth. Third, regarding the restraint of the precepts: having gone forth, one maintains firm and rigorous protection [of those precepts].
From the prātimokṣa restraint up to the restraint of the six bases and four faculties, one guards right mindfulness through this śīla;
one cultivates constant and diligent mindfulness, using mindfulness to guard the mind so that it dwells in a state of equanimity.

Having seen forms with the eye, one does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics, lest the mind run wild and leak out evil and unwholesome states. Likewise, one knows moderation in the five kinds of food and does not act for [the sake of]... [pleasure].

Free from dissipation, pride, and negligence, and adorned with a dignified appearance, he consumes his food with right reflection for the sake of maintaining the body, supporting it, and removing hunger and thirst;
he upholds the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and, by abandoning past sensations so that new ones do not arise, sustains his strength and dwells in blameless ease and security.
During the first and last watches of the night, he constantly and diligently practices the yoga of wakefulness.
During the daytime, he practices two modes of conduct—walking meditation and sitting meditation—to purify his mind of obstructive states; he does the same during the first watch of the night.
Having passed this period, he goes outside his dwelling, washes his feet, and lies down on his right side with one foot upon the other.
Maintaining the perception of light, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, he dwells with the thought of rising in mind. He does the same during the last watch of the night.

Second, purifying the mind through the two types of deportment; seventh, dwelling with right mindfulness in eight instances—whether going or staying, looking or gazing, bending or stretching, carrying the robes and bowl, eating, drinking, chewing, tasting, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, waking, speaking, remaining silent, or dispelling fatigue and sleep—one dwells with right mindfulness in all these;
eighth, delighting in seclusion and remaining detached from all craving for bedding and requisites, dwelling in solitude.
In forest retreats, at the foot of trees, in empty dwellings, mountain valleys, and so forth, even up to the edges of the plains—regarding these nine types of pure bedding and seats;
having purified the mind of the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the mind becomes free from all hindrances and dwells in firm, wholesome, and supreme *samādhi*.
Regarding the ten bases of *samādhi*: having abandoned the hindrances, the mind is free from secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and evil, unwholesome states.
Having entered the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and characterized by joy and bliss, accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and having fully attained and dwelt therein,
up to the fourth dhyāna, having fully attained and dwelt therein— this gradual cultivation that becomes increasingly superior is called the cultivation of inferior conditions.
From this point onward, in order to bring about the knowledge, abandonment, realization, and cultivation regarding the Noble Truths, one possesses the respective capacity for the voice of another.

The arising of capability, the application of attention (*manasikāra*), and so forth, leading to the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) up until parinirvāṇa, is called the "excellent condition" (*pratyaya*).
In this context, it does not mention the initial desire for wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*) and right renunciation (*samyak-niṣkramaṇa*);

rather, it mentions only the third [stage], the restraint of morality (*śīla-saṃvara*), up to the seventh, dwelling in full awareness (*saṃprajānan-vihāra*). These consist of only five phrases. Although these—desire for wholesome dharmas and renunciation—are indeed present, [they are not explicitly stated].
Furthermore, because the path of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*) is not yet a superior stage, the treatise omits it;

as for the three qualities such as delighting in seclusion (*viveka-rati*), they are the preliminary preparations (*pūrvaprayoga*) prior to the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*), which is why they are not mentioned [there], or perhaps they are also subsumed within the path of accumulation, and thus are explained in full here.
Immediately following this, the treatise states: "There are further remaining [qualities] such as the cultivation of various virtues," which subsumes the latter three.

Nor is there any contradiction in this, for this *śīla* (ethical discipline) subsumes that [discipline] of the renunciants; thus, the *jñapticaturtha-karman* and so forth are also considered renunciation.
Herein, the paths of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*) and preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) are termed the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). As it is said in [the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*], verse 64:

"These paths of accumulation and preparation are indeed the Truth of the Path," though the Blessed One has in some places taught that only the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) constitutes the Truth of the Path.

Based on its preeminence, it is also the same as this; within these two paths, the untainted [factors] are omitted because they lack the support of the vision of the truths (*darśana*) and the hearing of the熏 (*vāsanā*).
Since that which is not supported by the former is not [the path], one takes the tainted (*sāsrava*) as its essence.

The third [section], the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), has two parts: first, the question, and second, the answer. The answer has three parts:

first, clarifying the essential nature and characteristics of the path of seeing; second, clarifying the wheel of the noble path (*āryamārgacakra*); and third, explaining the meaning of the scriptural passages concerning the locus of the path of seeing. Within the first of these, there are again two parts:

first, clarifying the essence of the path of seeing, and second, clarifying the distinctions among the true characteristics of the path of seeing. Regarding the former, if explained in summary: first, the essence is set forth; subsequently, the objects of focus (*ālambana*) are presented.

From "The object-condition and so forth" below, the distinctions between the true and conventional aspects are explained. Within the section on the distinctions between the true and conventional aspects, there are two parts:
first, taking the single mind as the primary reality, the aspect of the equality of the object-condition and the subject-condition is identified as the characteristic of the true single mind;

second, from "Furthermore, by means of... below, the three minds and sixteen minds are explained as conventional. If the three minds were taken as the primary reality, the three minds would be explained first.

These [three minds] collectively constitute the definition of the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) following the sixteen moments of wisdom; this concludes the general presentation of their essential nature within the true [path].

Since they all take the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) as their characteristic, and because their distinctions are subsequently revealed, they are described as three minds. Furthermore, regarding the first [mind], as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is "the culmination of the single-mind event";
however, speaking according to the actual reality, there are three minds, as explained in the seventeenth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.

The *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* chapter on "Attaining Clear Realization" (*abhisamaya*) explains the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). However, below the section on the three moments of mind, there are two further passages:

one states that prior to the three moments of mind, the preceding is the "True" (*tattva*) and the subsequent is the "Manifestation of Signs" (*nimitta-prakāśa*). Within the "True," the Bodhisattva has three moments of true mind, while for the Bodhisattva’s sixteen moments of mind, if one relies on the two vehicles (*yāna*), these two categories are considered "True.
This is because they merely sever the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*) across two categories; thus, they are explained as the sixteen moments of mind.

Within the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), there are two [sections]: first, the explanation of the Path of Vision; subsequently, the summary that it is not [merely] conventional. Within the explanation of the Path of Vision, there are three [parts]:

first, the enumeration of the sixteen knowledges (*jñāna*); second, the specific citation and explanation; third, a general and concise selection by means of the Dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*) and Dharma-knowledge (*dharmanirvedha*) within this stage.
Within the specific citation and explanation, there are two [parts]: first, the elucidation of the four knowledges regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

Regarding the statement in the section on the subsequent patience of the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) that "all subsequent noble dharmas (*ārya-dharma*) are of this same category," how does this knowledge function within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*)? It cannot be said that it takes subsequent noble dharmas as its object.

This category is like subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); because it is of the same type as the preceding cause, it is called "subsequently attained. This, however, takes only knowledge as its object.

Regarding the division of the objects into initial and subsequent [moments] as "category-patience" (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and "category-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna*), why is it necessary to establish these characteristics?

Alternatively, one may simply understand that they take similar categories as their objects; here, we clarify that knowledge takes as its object the category of the knowledge of suchness (*tathatājñāna*).

Therefore, in this brief summary, the text is divided into three parts: first, explaining the distinction between dharma-knowledge and category-knowledge; second, explaining the name "signless contemplation" (*animittadhyāna*); and finally, the manifestation [of the result].

The sixteen moments of mind are collectively termed the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). These sixteen moments of mind encompass the aspects of the contemplation of the truths (*satya-darśana-ākāra*) exhaustively;
they are subsumed solely under subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), as they are not described as wisdom that takes other objects as its domain.

Second, regarding the explanation of the name, the "signless contemplation" (*animitta-bhāvanā*) is divided into three parts: first, the discussion of the primary meaning of the name "signless contemplation"; second, the commentary’s citation of scriptures to establish this proof.

Subsequently, the six kinds of signlessness (animitta) are specifically explained. Within this stage, all signs (nimitta) are absent; that is, there are no different objects of perception, no ten signs of the contaminated (sāsrava), and no signs of male or female.

Here, the absence of aspiration (apraṇihita) regarding the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) and so forth is called "signless" because it lacks the specific characteristics of conceptual differentiation, not because all things are entirely non-existent. This explains the sixteen moments of mind (cittakṣaṇa).
In the main text of this treatise, it is stated that there are four minds and so forth; this is because the commentator has combined them into four.

Furthermore, when examining the textual flow from the perspective of a single mental moment, they are all subsumed as one. According to the concluding summary below, each Truth (satya) is called "one mind," because [the mind] takes one Truth as its object and reaches its culmination.
Thus, in the preceding section, the three minds are established as true by means of the sixteen moments of the three [Truths].

The mind is conventionally pervasive across the three minds; regarding the four aspects of the Path Truth within the Wheel of Dharma of the Path, why is it necessary to establish the initial [viewing] and the subsequent seeing?
It is because the true stage is contemplated again in anticipation of what will be explained later, and this remains the case even up to the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Within the section on the four wheels, there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the exposition; and third, the conclusion. This meaning is explained by means of the śrāvakas and others: first, the training in the preparatory application (prayoga);
second, the realization (adhigama); and third, the perfection (niṣpatti). Subsequently, these are further designated as "wheels."
The commentary on the sūtra, "Distant from the Dust," is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the three phrases of the sūtra; second, the explanation of the nine phrases of the sūtra.

Regarding the first part, there is an initial general explanation followed by a detailed explanation. Furthermore, concerning the phrase "in these two stages of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*)," it refers to either the thorough knowledge of suffering and the abandonment of the origin [of suffering], or—following the reverse order—the abandonment via the path of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the knowledge via the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Alternatively, it may refer to nothingness.
Because the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) knows that what was to be abandoned has already been abandoned by means of the intervening paths (*antara-mārga*).
Next, the fourth [section] clarifies that within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), there are two parts: first the question and then the answer. The answer has two parts:

first the summary (*uddāna*) and then the explanation (*nirdeśa*). Within the summary, there are two: first, the nine meanings revealed by the name as the general characteristics of the path of cultivation; second, the distinctions among the three types [of practitioners].

The middle section specifically elucidates the unique, distinct, and superior five categories of the ten stages of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Regarding these five classes, which constitute the first of the preceding virtues, there are further two parts:
first, the specific analysis of the nine meanings into three types of distinctions; second, the explanation by the commentator.

As for why this is so, the subsequent explanation analyzes the second [category] according to what was previously indicated, clarifying the names rather than the two distinct types themselves. Thus, the initial cultivation is explained.

Regarding the names, there are two parts: first, the detailed explanation of the nine meanings; second, the ancillary discussion of the meaning of cultivating the preceding dharmas. Within the first nine meanings, there are three divisions:

first, the distinction between the mundane and supramundane; second, the distinction between the two grades; third, the distinction between the paths of the four classes and the mundane and supramundane.

Regarding the second [division], they are distinguished according to their respective names. Within the mundane path, there are two parts: first, the eight mundane meditative attainments (*dhyāna*); second, [the subsequent].

Based on these eight, they are distinguished by four aspects. Although these eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) generally pertain to both the supramundane and the post-supramundane, within the category of the eight knowledges (*jñāna*), they actually pertain to the mundane.
However, regarding the mundane, the school clarifies that these are *sāsrava* (contaminated) absorptions;

because the essence of the eight absorptions is broad and their capacity to suppress active defilements (*samudācāra*) is predominant, they are designated as "mundane. This is correctly proven by the fact that [the eight knowledges] pertain exclusively to the category of the eight knowledges.

Although they are designated by the term "untainted cause" (*anāsrava-hetu*) and are not mutually exclusive, prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it is not that the categories [of the path] are not fully present;

rather, their aspects (*ākāra*) are complete and extensive. However, it is specifically within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) that these are mostly already attained, and because there are distinct superior qualities therein, the eight [categories] are not described as being [exclusively] of the path of no-more-learning.
Furthermore, because they are cultivated during the stage of the path of cultivation itself, it is called the "path of cultivation."

However, regarding the cultivation of hearing, reflection, and meditation above the desire realm, the afflictions are subdued by relying on the meditative stages (*dhyāna-bhūmi*) alone, as these are not [directly] opposed [to them] in the desire realm;

therefore, the four characteristics of hearing and reflection in the desire realm are not mentioned. Among these four, the first two pertain to what can be cultivated across the eight stages, while the latter two pertain to the superior basis across the eight stages. (Note: The text discusses the distinction between the cultivation of *śruta*, *cintā*, and *bhāvanā* in the desire realm versus the form realm.

It clarifies that while the desire realm lacks the meditative concentration required for the direct subduing of afflictions, the higher realms rely on the power of *samādhi*. Furthermore, it distinguishes the application of these practices across the eight stages—namely, the four dhyānas and the four *ārūpya-samāpattis*—noting the specific roles of each.)

Section Eight: Clarifying the Defilements of Understanding. Within this section, there are three parts: first, the enumeration; second, the detailed explanation; and third, the conclusion regarding defilement.

Herein, "this" refers to the four graspings (*upādāna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the sixty-two views (*dṛṣṭigata*). Doubt (*vicikitsā*) arises from these: according to this treatise, it is the cause of those [views], while according to that [other] treatise, it is their result.

Furthermore, doubt arises from delusion (*moha*). Moreover, among these four types, the views and doubt are exclusively conceptual (*vikalpita*), whereas craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and pride (*māna*) are both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual.

Why is it said that the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) has obstacles? Because the obstacles to the path of cultivation are explained generally for all [stages], they are here described as "roots" (*mūla*).
This is because, due to these four kinds of fixed afflictions, there is no entering or exiting from the state of retrogression;
they serve as the roots for the arising of scattered afflictions. The sixth category of delusion is not the seventh. As the ancients have said:
The seventh [type of concentration] does not arise without an object;

because it arises with an object, as stated in the twelfth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, this object-possessing concentration—comprising both the antidotes and their opposites—is pure and extends through all eight fundamental dhyānas and the preliminary (anāgamya) stages. These superior concentrations are named after their objects of craving and likewise extend through the eight fundamentals and the eight preliminaries.
Regarding these, there are two theories: one says they exist, while the other says they do not. Thirdly...
In establishing the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there are two parts: first, a general enumeration of four types, and second, a detailed explanation according to their specific distinctions.

Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the root text’s enumeration, and second, the masters’ explanations. Regarding the establishment of the eight meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*)—both in terms of their commonality and their specific branches—there are two sections:

first, clarifying the establishment of the branches, and second, clarifying why the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) do not establish branches. Within the first of these, there are two sections: first, explaining the four dhyānas.

Regarding the number of factors (*aṅga*) possessed [in each dhyāna], there are two parts following the explanation: first, a general question and answer concerning the increase and decrease of factors;

second, a detailed explanation of the reasons for the number of factors, which consists of four sections: defining their essence, explaining their names, establishing their inclusion or exclusion, and the specific establishment of the stages (*bhūmi*).

Within the establishment of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), there are three parts: first, the presentation of the seven entries and eight stages; second, the detailed explanation of the seven; and finally...

Regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the coarse and the calm at the beginning: as for the "subsequent yoga" (*paścād-yoga*) in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*, there are four yogas in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*, and the fourth yoga is called "subsequent.
This refers to the thirty-third fascicle. Among those four successive stages, the first and third are the same as here;
the second is characterized by the arising of joy and bliss (*prīti-sukha*) through detachment, which varies in its degree of intensity; and the fourth consists of the four [dhyānas].
Regarding the cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*) and the four remedies (*pratipakṣa*), these explain the sixty-six [categories].

There are four remedies that subsume the twenty-eighth [category], and four yogic characteristics (*yoga-lakṣaṇa*) that subsume the eleventh. There are forty types of mental attention that subsume the seven mental attentions.

This is the analysis according to eight gates. First, concerning the essential nature (*svabhāva*): ancient masters held that wisdom (*prajñā*) is its essence because it is that which can sever the path of afflictions; however, our current interpretation takes mental attention as its essence.

Since this treatise states that the attention (*manasikāra*) co-arising with the first path of abandonment is called "attention of withdrawal" (*prāvivekyamanasikāra*), we know it is not wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, it can be categorized as a mental factor of concentration (*samādhi*). This is because the *Abhidharmapada* (First Treatise on Abhidharma) states: "One who has attained concentration of mind is said to have attained 'attention-concentration' (*manasikārasamādhi*).
Thus, it is designated by its excellence; the name is derived from it, just as in the case of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth. Or, according to this treatise...

It is said that because of the mental application (*manasikāra*) of the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), one knows the category of mental application belonging to the stage of concentration. Regarding the two explanations of the names and characteristics:

"clearly performing the aspect" means that clarity is mental application; "resolute determination and distancing" refers to the simultaneous mental application of distancing, wherein distancing is the essence of the path.
Regarding "joy" (*prīti*), "gathering and gathering-joy" means that gathering is mental application; "observation" refers to the simultaneous mental application of observation.

Regarding "examination" (*vicaya*), it refers either to the mental application (*manasikāra*) of observation, which does not reach the level of the previously explained "culmination of application" (*prayoga-niṣṭha*), or to the mental application that is the fruit of the culmination of application, or the mental application that is the fruit itself.
Since this fruit is wisdom (*prajñā*), it constitutes the path; therefore, the previous explanation is superior.

Regarding the three bases (*āśraya*): based on these, one first enters the stage of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*), which has six stages, and the fundamental stages (*mūla-bhūmi*), which have seven. First...

Secondly, regarding the uninterrupted preparatory stage (*anantarya-bhūmi*), there are seven [types of attention], and the seventh is not mentioned because it is the fundamental [stage]. This principle should likewise apply;
otherwise, since the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) does not enter the fundamental stage, by what attention would it be subsumed?

This clarifies that it is subsumed under impure (*sāsrava*) attention, as explained in the sixty-sixth [section] based on the four paths. In the eleventh [section], forty types of attention are clarified.

Since the explanations regarding the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) also apply to the untainted (*anāsrava*), one knows that among these seven [stages], the single stage of "comprehending the characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedana*) is exclusively tainted, while the remaining six are both tainted and untainted.
This is because they take resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) as their preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for the untainted path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Alternatively, "comprehending the characteristics" may also be untainted, just as the three [stages] beginning with "comprehending coarseness" (*audārikādilakṣaṇapratisaṃvedana*) and the four [stages] beginning with "comprehending the characteristics of the truths" (*satyalakṣaṇapratisaṃvedana*)—such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*)—are likewise.
The two types of patience (kṣānti) are designated as such because they constitute the definitive discernment (nirvedha) of the stage of superior resolve (adhimukti).

Since this has already been cultivated, what prevents it from also possessing these characteristics? Now, to correctly explain the fourfold inclusion of the four yogic characteristics within the preceding [stages]:
there are twenty-eight [characteristics], five in each of the four paths, six in the four types of remedies, and forty types of mental attention (manasikāra). These are sevenfold.

Explanation of Objections: Why is it that in the first stage of the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*), two preparatory stages (*prayoga*) are mentioned because they are difficult, whereas in the second stage of abandonment, the preparatory stage is not mentioned because it is easy?
Furthermore, although it shares the same name, the third stage of abandonment is also difficult because observation serves as its preparatory stage;
thus, it is said that its initial arising is most difficult and requires both preparatory stages.

Regarding the other [stages], it is summarized as one, or sometimes not explained at all. As for why the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is mentioned for the third path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*), while it is not mentioned for the other two:

it is because of the subsequent mental application (*manasikāra*). Just as in the first chapter, the path of liberation is subsumed under "joyful acceptance" (*ruci*), and because joyful acceptance has already been established, the second path of liberation is likewise so;
since both are subsumed under joyful acceptance, they are not separately explained as being free from conceptual differentiation (*nirvikalpa*). Alternatively...
That is, the second [liberation] is named after its preparatory stage (*prayoga*), which consists of the observation subsumed under the second [contemplation].

Although the subsequent liberation path (*vimukti-mārga*) has not yet performed such observation, there is no contradiction in naming it after the prolonged [preparatory] stage rather than the brief one. Question:

Regarding the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*), why are only three "uninterrupted paths" (*ānantarya-mārga*) mentioned? Answer: Because the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) possesses only three grades of the path.

If that were so, there would be no such person as an "ekavīcika" (one-interval practitioner), because it is by relying on the Noble Path that one attains the state of being separated by only one interval.

Furthermore, through the mundane path, one must abandon nine grades: when one has abandoned the superior-superior grade through the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratyavekṣā*), and has abandoned the superior-middle grade through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), and has distanced oneself from the superior-inferior and middle-superior grades until they are exhausted, at that time one is designated as "distant" (*dūre*).
This does not mean that the preceding grades were not abandoned; rather, the second and third grades are to be understood accordingly.

One should reflect on its characteristics: if one attains concentration through the six modes of practice, one will necessarily suppress the afflictions; however, if one attains concentration by contemplating the truths prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), one does not necessarily suppress the afflictions.
Since there are nine grades within the three uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), they are not explicitly stated as being of nine grades because they are of the same category.
Among these, the first two grades cannot sever the afflictions; here, the cultivation consists solely of the contaminated (*sāsrava*), which is the same as the original.
In the fourth volume of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is further explained that through renewed perfuming (*vāsanā*) in the tenth stage, one is born above Akaniṣṭha;

this twelfth [section] has already been discussed previously as consisting of three categories of cultivation. The twelfth section explains how the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) are produced through the mixed cultivation of the four dhyānas, both with and without outflows (*sāsrava* and *anāsrava*), as well as the principles regarding those who fall from them and are reborn therein.

Within the section on the supramundane, there are two major divisions: first, explaining the nature of the supramundane; second, explaining its basis. Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, a general explanation, and second, a specific explanation.
Regarding the general explanation, it refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Within the specific explanation, there are two parts:

first, explaining that wisdom and its associated mental factors depend upon the eight stages (*bhūmi*); second, explaining that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) does not depend on them. This latter point is not explicitly stated here.
The intermediate dhyāna is subsumed under the first dhyāna; since it does not exist in the higher stages, there is no need for further distinction.

It exists only in the initial "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya) state because it possesses the untainted (anāsrava). Fearing that this might be confused with the "not-yet-arrived" states of the higher stages, the question is asked: Why is the intermediate dhyāna absent in the higher stages while present in the lower?

Because when first attaining those [higher] concentrations, one encounters great difficulty; because the Brahma Kings and others have distinct roles as subjects and lords; and because the eight knowledges (jñāna) take them as objects.
Regarding the distinctions as explained in [the section on] the sixty-ninth [topic], why is it that only the initial stage of the "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*) possesses the untainted (*anāsrava*)?

As stated in the sixty-ninth [topic], the name "non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*) refers to the mundane and does not include the path for severing afflictions; therefore, this [section] speaks of the sharp and clear path for severing afflictions as being supramundane (*lokottara*).
Based on this, one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): there are those that are supramundane but not mundane, namely, the clarity of the lower eight stages.

Regarding the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) that is beneficial, there are three possibilities: some are exclusively mundane (*laukika*) and not supramundane (*lokottara*), some are all contaminated paths (*sāsrava-mārga*) that are both, and others are not.

This refers to the uncontaminated path (*anāsrava-mārga*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); otherwise, the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) would not be supramundane. Furthermore, there are four permutations:

the first permutation consists of the non-conceptual fundamental wisdom (*nirvikalpa-mūla-jñāna*) of the ten stages; the second permutation consists exclusively of conventional, contaminated wisdom (*saṃvṛti-sāsrava-jñāna*). Both [of these] coexist.

The phrase refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*); since this also includes the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it is said to be "the third stage.

Third, the clarification that within the cessation attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) there are two parts: first, the identification of the essence of the cessation attainment as supramundane (*lokottara*); second, the determination of its basis in the stages (*bhūmi*).

Within the determination of the basis in the stages, there are two sections: first, clarifying the stages from which it arises; second, clarifying the stages from which it does not arise through a series of questions and answers. Within the first section on the stages from which it arises, there are two further divisions. First:

The section on the subsequent arising of the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) following the initial arising of the stage of clear realization is divided into two parts. First, a general explanation; second, an explanation through questions and answers concerning the subsequent arising in the desire and form realms. Regarding the former:

it is said that in the form realm, one may repeatedly give rise to [attainments] where latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) have been suppressed and the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) has been attained.

As stated in the *Ṣaṣṭi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Sixty): "The noble ones, through their subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), become free from desire up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). This refers to the sixty [types of practitioners].
The textual phrasing suggests that even one who is like a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) may attain the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);

why, then, is it not stated that they attain the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)? This treatise speaks only of attaining the six [liberations] by abandoning the afflictions of the three lower concentrations.

Although it does not explicitly say that one attains the attainment of cessation, through the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one can suppress the afflictions of the levels below Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and thus also attain the attainment of cessation. (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi, Chapter 7)

The second fascicle states that all [positions] have scriptural evidence. Regarding the first explanation, it refers to the *Abhidharma*; furthermore, according to that person’s actual state, even one who has not yet abandoned the first dhyāna may attain it.

According to the latter explanation, the sixty-ninth [verse] of the *Samyuktabhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* concerns those who have attained the third fruit, and it is not necessarily limited to those of the first fruit.

The sixty-ninth [verse] does not say that a non-returner who has not yet abandoned the first dhyāna attains the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); this is the correct view according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.

The *Treatise on the Compendium of the Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*) by Vasubandhu states that the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), the non-retrogressive bodhisattva, and those of the three vehicles who have attained no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) possess this [insight] exclusively because it is fixed for them;
therefore, one knows that the first two fruits [of stream-enterer and once-returner] cannot be discussed in this regard.

Furthermore, according to this treatise and the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, chapter fifty-eight, there is a "single-moment path of seeing" (*ekacitta-darśanamārga*), while the seventeenth chapter of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*) speaks of a "three-moment path of seeing."

Regarding the fifty-eight [minds] and the further nine minds of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), this treatise later mentions sixteen minds of the path of seeing, four minds of the path of seeing, and so forth.

Why are there such differences? There are two explanations from the West: first, some say that the true path of seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*), being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), consists of only a single mind, as stated in the *Fifty-Eight*; the three minds and so on are all merely provisional.

Regarding the explanation of the相见道 (sākṣātkāra-mārga), why is it called "contemplating the non-established truths" (apratiṣṭhita-satya)? Why is it said to arise from the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgra-dharma)?

What is the purpose of stating that three moments [of mind] each sever the heavy hindrances (dauṣṭhulya)? Furthermore, regarding the sixteen moments of mind and so forth, why is it stated that they arise from the supreme mundane dharma?
And what is the underlying reason for this? The commentary states: Because the timing and the nature of the realization differ, the explanations vary. Within the true contemplation (bhūta-darśana)...
The single mind consists of two stages: first, one practices the preparatory application (*prayoga*) by learning the observation of persons and subsequently learning the observation of phenomena;

these two observations together lead into the true observation (*tattva-darśana*). Following this, within the true observation itself, there are two moments of mind that constitute the prior stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
These involve practicing the preparatory application through the dual observation, wherein the person and phenomena are each distinct and their coarse and subtle aspects differ.

First one trains in abandoning the coarse, and only afterward does one train in the subtle. Regarding the third pair, because the meaning of the analytical discernment of *tathatā* (suchness) differs, there are three minds;

thus, the three minds of the Bodhisattva’s path of vision (*darśanamārga*) are not identical. The characteristics of the true contemplation (*bhūtadarśana*) are difficult to know, whereas the characteristics of the contemplation of signs (*nimittadarśana*) are easy to explain.

In terms of the meaning, the true contemplation is said to consist of only three minds; however, because it is spoken of as "abandoning the heavy obscurations" (*dausthulya*) through conventional terminology, it is said to proceed from the first [moment].

The dharma-arising conditions are non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) and also consist of sixteen moments of mind. First, regarding the characteristics of a Bodhisattva’s contemplation: it is also as previously explained.

Within the true nature (*tathatā*), there are distinctions in meaning and function; both the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) take the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) as their object.

Because they reflect back upon their own substance, they are called the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*). Therefore, in the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), the Dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) and Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) constitute the first two paths of the learner (*śaikṣa*).
Regarding the self-witnessing portions (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of the subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the learner (*śaikṣa*):

although these take the preceding mind as their object, since subsequent knowledge arises from patience, it can be considered analogous to the self-witnessing portion of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). By extension, one should understand that the self-witnessing portion of the mind in the learner’s path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is likewise similar.

Furthermore, when persons of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) engage in the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) of the sixteen moments of mind, even when entering the true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*), they contemplate only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Regarding the subsequent observation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) following the mind, those who practice the preparatory application (*prayoga*) to study true observation (*bhūta-darśana*) have already been explained as before.
Since true observation is difficult to describe, one speaks only of the mind that observes characteristics, provisionally designating it as "true";

therefore, it is said that immediately after the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), sixteen moments of mind arise, or that the sixteen moments of mind consist of the observation of characteristics belonging only to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and not to the work of a bodhisattva.

Regarding the statement that there are nine minds, there are three interpretations among them, one of which asserts that there are eight minds based on the distinction between the categories of the four patiences (*kṣānti*) and the four knowledges (*jñāna*);

since patience and knowledge are discussed together, they are said to constitute four types, and the same applies to patience and knowledge. Furthermore, because it is explained based on a single *śamatha*, there are nine minds.

Moreover, as for the statement that there are four in the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), since the term "category" (*pakṣa*) is used, it clarifies that this is not necessarily fixed; herein...

The intention here is to take four *dharmakṣāntis* (receptivities to the dharma); the same applies to the *anvayakṣāntis* (subsequent receptivities), as they are combined when counting the *kṣāntis*. Thus, there are eight kinds based on the categories of *dharmajñāna* and *anvayajñāna*.

Furthermore, because there are eight moments of mind associated with the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), and because it is taught based on a single moment of mind—specifically, by speaking of only one moment of mind—there are nine in total.

Moreover, it is taught that the eight moments of mind, consisting of the *dharmakṣāntis*, *dharmajñānas*, *anvayakṣāntis*, and *anvayajñānas*, together abandon the afflictions of the lower realms; therefore, they are spoken of collectively.

Regarding the four categories of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), there are likewise eight moments of mind because they sever the afflictions of the higher realms; therefore, these are combined and explained as four.
Subsequently, by re-examining the sixteen mental objects previously [contemplated] to bring them to completion, it is based on a single *śamatha* that only one moment of mind is spoken of.

These are collectively termed the "nine minds. As for those four minds, this is a classification made according to the Truths (*satya*); they do not constitute four within the actual process of contemplation. This will be clarified in the relevant passage.
It can be known that both schools agree on this interpretation.

Regarding the second explanation, which asserts that the three moments of mind constitute the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it takes the fifty-fifth passage—beginning with "taking as its object the non-established [truths]" (*anabhisaṃskṛta*)—as proof;

it holds that the subsequent sixteen moments of mind constitute the conventional path of seeing (*prajñapti-darśanamārga*), and that all three moments of mind are said to abandon the coarse [defilements].
Regarding the "heavy" (*dausthulya*), there are many types; there is no impediment to explaining them here, and they can be understood through reflection.

As for the statement "fifty-eight [moments] constitute one mind," the commentary explains: The abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*) during the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is not like that in the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), where [afflictions] are divided into nine grades.

Because the task of abandoning the afflictions to be severed by seeing is accomplished by binding them into a single grade, it is collectively termed "one mind"; this is likewise free from any difficulty or contradiction regarding the remaining characteristics.

The contradiction is as previously explained. As all treatises state, the third [moment] is conventional knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*); however, regarding the term "dharma-knowledge" (*dharma-jñāna*), the meanings of these two types—dharma and anvaya—are manifold. First, that which severs objects belonging to the two upper realms is called *anvaya-vidha* (subsequent severance), while that which severs objects belonging to the lower realm is called *dharma-vidha* (dharma severance). This is as it is said: "Dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) severs the afflictions of the lower realm, while anvaya-patience severs the afflictions of the upper realm. Second, that which takes principle as its object is called dharma; that which takes phenomena as its object is called anvaya. Furthermore, that which takes the truths (*satya*) as its object is called dharma; that which takes the aggregates (*skandha*) as its object is called anvaya. Third, that which takes the Four Noble Truths as its object is called dharma; that which takes dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as its object is called anvaya. Fourth, that which takes the four aspects (*ākāra*) of each truth as its object is called dharma; that which takes the four aspects of dependent origination as its object is called anvaya. Fifth, that which takes the sixteen aspects as its object is called dharma; that which takes the twelve links of dependent origination as its object is called anvaya. Sixth, that which takes the three realms as its object is called dharma; that which takes the five aggregates as its object is called anvaya. Seventh, that which takes the three times as its object is called dharma; that which takes the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena as its object is called anvaya.
