"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the sixteen moments of mind; based on their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), three distinct methods of contemplation are taught.

"Dharma-contemplation" (*dharma-anupaśyanā*) refers to the specific [contemplation], while "general dharma-contemplation" (*dharma-sāmānyānupaśyanā*) refers to that which is the opposite of this. Based on these three stages, one contemplates all phenomena.

Regarding the statement "one mind" or "three minds," since these constitute the paths of insight (*darśana-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they are the reverse of the former; alternatively, it may refer to a single distinct moment of mind.

Regarding the liberation through conditions (*pratyaya-vimukti*), one also attains those three minds; their designations are all the reverse of the preceding ones, and the logic for "liberation" (*vimukti*) may be inferred accordingly.
Regarding the third mind alone, there are two interpretations: first, that a distinct mind arises as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*);

second, that it is the very moment of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) within the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*). Both interpretations are consistent with reason. Furthermore, some say that the patience regarding the dharma of suffering effects the abandonment [of afflictions].
Regarding the meaning of the arising of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) within true contemplation, it may be explained as the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
As previously stated, for one who perceives with a single mind, the contemplation of the mind in the path of vision is resolved into a single category.

Within this, is it a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) or a succession of many moments? There are two explanations: first, that it is a single moment; second, that it consists of many moments. This is because...
Because the matter has been fully resolved, how can one ask about the three types of mind?

Furthermore, regarding the statement in [the *Abhidharmakośa*] 69 that "Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) in the path of seeing abandons the afflictions of the desire realm, while subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) in the path of seeing abandons the afflictions of the form and formless realms," the interpretation of this is as in the previous treatise:

there is no separate Dharma-knowledge that abandons the afflictions of the upper realms; rather, it is a general statement that Dharma-knowledge serves as the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*). Dharma-knowledge...
The three points should be understood as before; one should reflect upon this by applying that same explanation. One should understand the subsequent passage of that treatise as follows: Question:
When all types of *anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge) are present, are they all capable of discerning the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*)? Answer:
If one has previously correctly grasped the characteristics (*nimitta*) of the phenomena belonging to the higher realms, then one is able to discern them; if not, then one is not.
The various Dharma masters are generally able to discern this because the text states that one who has previously practiced *anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge) can discern the higher realms;
it is therefore clear that [the abandonment of the higher realms] relies on *anvaya-jñāna*.

If it were not so, one would be unable to discern [this], yet the text immediately says that for a person practicing the initial stages, the afflictions of the higher realms are abandoned by means of *dharma-jñāna* (dharma-knowledge). This principle is incorrect, as there is no such [teaching] in any of the treatises.

Regarding the text stating that "Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) abandons the afflictions of the upper realms," the current discussion concerns analytical discernment (*vibhaṅga*). This refers specifically to the observation of the distinctions among objects through wisdom.

Because one has previously cultivated those dharmas, one can observe them through subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). However, for a person who has not previously practiced this, they cannot achieve clear discernment;

it is merely that subsequent knowledge is excluded from being able to discern them. Thus, it is said that [this] must necessarily be Dharma-knowledge. Although a person who has not previously practiced may subsequently take the upper realms as their object, in reality, it is Dharma-knowledge that abandons them.

Regarding the statement in this treatise that "the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the delusions of the three realms can only take the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) as its object," and the further remark that "subsequent knowledge abandons [the afflictions] of the higher realms," these are merely explanatory passages (*anuvṛtti-grantha*) and do not represent the ultimate principle.

As for the stages upon which the entry into the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) relies, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Abhidharma), fascicle 69, it relies on those very same bodily bases;
furthermore, it relies exclusively upon the initial stage of "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*) and the four dhyānas.
It is not the case for others, such as those in the *anāgamya* or the formless realms (*ārūpya*), as explained below; there are further passages to the same effect.

Although there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is not said to enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because it is a state of contemplative observation (*vihāra*) of the untainted and because the abode of Brahmā (*Brahmāloka*) is largely distracted.

Its basis consists of five stages (*bhūmi*); all of these are the bases for the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*). That which relies on the *anāgamya* stage pertains only to the first two fruits. If one attains the first dhyāna, it relies on seven [stages].

One must apply attention (*manasikāra*) to the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), for it is only through the abandonment of the nine afflictions of the desire realm that its ultimate attainment is secured;

this is likewise true for those non-returners who practice "leaping" (*pluta*) and so forth. Whether the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are abandoned all at once in a single contemplation (*ekadṛṣṭi*) or abandoned individually—this principle will be explained in the twelfth fascicle.
Regarding the statement within the *dharmajñāna* that "liberation is attained and realized," Master Zhuan says: "This is an explanation by way of provisional characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

It refers to the realization of unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*), as previously explained regarding the single mind and three minds of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). These two explanations may be understood as before.

Here, it is spoken by way of provisional characteristics because delusions are severed by means of *dharmanirvedhabhāgīya-ksānti*; therefore, liberation is taken as being realized through wisdom (*jñāna*). This is not the ultimate principle; its category is similar [to what was stated above].
Regarding this statement within the context of patience (*kṣānti*), various treatises speak of the abandonment of higher-level afflictions; this should be reconciled as explained previously.
Furthermore, the *Śāstra* states that there are six types of abiding in the signless (*animitta*), which may be understood from the text itself. As the *Mahāśāstra*, fascicle 58, says:

"Those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) as the sixth type of signless practice; they are not those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), or those who have realized the body (*kāyasākṣin*)."

Regarding the names "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukta*) and "doubly liberated" (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), five [types] obtain these names. As Master Bei said: "This is explained from the bottom up as the sixth;

it is not that the upper [categories] descend from below. This, however, is what Master Jùn stated. Regarding the passage where the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn) speaks of "those who follow by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) and "those who follow by dharma" (*dharmānusārin*) entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), this treatise explains it directly by way of the dharmas themselves.

*Note: The final sentence appears to be a fragmentary commentary on the distinction between the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which discusses the practitioner (*pudgala*) as the primary subject, and this treatise, which discusses the dharmas themselves.*
Because this refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is no contradiction. It has not been heard that these six types differ from those six dharmas;

rather, they are distinct because those refer to persons (*pudgala*) while these refer to dharmas. Those [six] are: simultaneous liberation (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), wisdom-liberation (*prajñāvimukta*), bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin*), one liberated by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and the sixth, the one who practices according to faith or dharma (*śraddhānusārin* / *dharmānusārin*).

This is a general explanation of the six types which lack specific characteristics; those [six] are defined according to the six modes of practice (*ṣaḍ-ākāra-caryā*), which constitute the ultimate state.
The path is twofold: the path of cultivation and the path of seeing; the latter consists of sixteen moments of mind.

Regarding those who are practitioners by faith or practitioners by Dharma, according to what follows in the thirteenth [chapter], they possess the equipment for the stage of the highest degree of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Why is this not contradictory? The answer is: those practitioners by faith and practitioners by Dharma...
Because those who enter the path of seeing do not take up the stage of "following through faith," this is different [from the previous case]. It is asked:

In the thirteenth section below, it is stated that those who follow the Dharma through faith reside in the stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and do not enter the distinctions of the fruits;

why then does the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stages of Yoga Practice), fascicle 58, say that entering the path of seeing differs from what was previously explained, such that there are three types of persons in the path of cultivation and one type of person in the path of seeing combined?

Regarding the entry into the path of seeing through following faith or the Dharma, as stated in the *Vibhāṣā*, the four types are explained together because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) and so forth are identical.
In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, it is said that Śrāvakas preach the Dharma with subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Regarding the two views of Master Zhun:

first, that they preach the Dharma with an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*); if this were the case, then their bodily and vocal actions would also have to be untainted, just as a Bodhisattva [acts] with an untainted mind.
Furthermore, it is explained that this type of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is called "subsequently attained wisdom" because it is outflowing (*sāsrava*).

If that were so, why is it not said of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*)? We now adopt the latter explanation: because the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are inferior, their untainted wisdom cannot preach the Dharma.

Moreover, their physical and vocal actions are outflowing and are not like those of a Bodhisattva, whose physical and vocal karma are also untainted by virtue of being spoken through untainted wisdom.

Therefore, the treatise states that "citing the sūtra on being far removed from dust and free from defilement," etc.; "far removed from dust" refers to the *dharmakṣāntis* (patience regarding the dharma) of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while "free from defilement" refers to the *dharmajñānas* (knowledge of the dharma).

In the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 83, it says that patience and knowledge extend through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). That treatise further states: "This refers to the view of pride (*māna*) and the pride of self (*asmimāna*).

By extension of this meaning, there are [aspects] within the path of cultivation that are not explicitly clarified; thus, when the treatise speaks of the path of cultivation, it refers to that specific passage within the same work.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that this is not so, I have examined and read it again but have not yet seen such a text; this is spoken with reference to the "superior" [meaning].
In the *Dharmadṛṣṭi-mahāśāstra*, fascicle 83, there are two successive expositions. The first exposition states: "To see the Dharma means to attain the two types of patience (*kṣānti*);

to obtain the Dharma means to attain the two types of knowledge (*jñāna*); to penetrate the Dharma means the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) is the 'firm' [stage]; and the noble liberation (*vimukti*) is the 'sage'."
Furthermore, following the path, these [explanations] are likewise cited and interpreted here;

yet, when cross-referenced with the Master’s separate records (bi-ji), none of this text appears in fascicles 53, 63, or 93, nor is such an explanation found in the commentaries (shu). Regarding the four roots of the indeterminate (avyākṛta-mūla), it is asked:
"All four of these afflictions arise within the manas; the Treatise states that they occur within the gates of all defiled meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi)."
The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) here intends to indicate that these four afflictions serve as the gateway for the defilement of dhyāna.
Regarding the phrase "the gateway," it means that these afflictions are the cause by which the two types of views—the great and the small—arise concerning the prior limit (*pūrvānta*).

These are subsumed under the sixty-two views, such as the views regarding the prior limit and the views resulting from discrimination regarding the prior limit, as explained in the section on the sixty-two views. As for pride (*māna*), it refers to [the conceit] toward lower realms.
The arising of pride (*māna*)—taking one’s own level as superior and so forth—is to be understood as previously explained.
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) refers to the affliction of doubt; as the preceding text stated, because doubt increases through ignorance (*avidyā*), it arises from ignorance.
Regarding the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), they are explained in detail there; however, this treatise states that they arise solely from the seventh category of delusion.

Regarding the phrase "the delusions of the sixth [consciousness] within the two higher realms": this refers to the fact that in the Desire Realm, unwholesome states are predominant and there is no antidotal path;

thus, the delusions of the sixth consciousness within the sixth [dhyāna] should arise spontaneously. However, in the two higher realms, there are antidotal paths, so the delusions of the sixth consciousness within the sixth [dhyāna] should not be able to arise.
Because of this objection, it is stated that those delusions of the higher realms "should not be able to arise," based on the reason provided.
Because of the seventh affliction, the sixth [consciousness] is defiled; because of the sixth, afflictions arise. Regarding the phrase "seeking liberation" in the text that resolves doubts:

this is merely explained by taking those seeking liberation as an example. Even ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet seen the Truths, if they are born in that realm, will give rise to these afflictions.
If even those seeking liberation give rise to such doubt, how much more so for other ordinary beings? As long as one has not yet seen the Truths, it is thus...

The doubt of ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) within the internal stage of the seeker (śaikṣa) is the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*). For those seekers who have been born into those realms, it is provisionally described as "clinging to phenomena" (*dharmagrāha*) and "doubt," as explained in the context of the higher-tier fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, because ignorance (*avidyā*) increases alongside doubt, even though the seeker has abandoned doubt, it is still designated by the name "doubt";

this ignorance is also explained according to the [explanation of] the higher-tier fetters. Moreover, this discussion is formulated with respect to ordinary worldlings and does not apply to those [who have attained the fruit].
How is it known that there is no hindrance to training? As the subsequent passage states: "Regarding what is realized at the superior stage, it concerns liberation or non-liberation," and so forth;

thus we know that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are not those in training (*śaikṣa*). Furthermore, the preceding passage, in its commentary on the Sūtra, states: "If one realizes the true reality (*tattva*), it is not through the guidance of another, but arises spontaneously as a certainty.
Moreover, the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (19) states that at the initial stage of the threshold (*anāgamya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is present.
The *Mahā-śāstra*, Chapter Twelve, Section on the Meaning of the "Pure and White," states that "pure and white" refers to the pure dhyānas (*viśuddha-dhyāna*).

According to this treatise, these are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*). However, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, Volume Two, explains that "pure and white" refers to both the pure dhyānas and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

This is because the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* treats the paths belonging to all eight stages collectively as the "Dharma-pervading" [path], encompassing both the contaminated and the uncontaminated; whereas this present treatise speaks only of [the former].

Regarding the fact that "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) is not stated as "without outflows" (*anāsrava*): at the very beginning of this treatise, nine gates were first opened, the first of which was the gate of the mundane (*laukika*).

Within that, the gate of the pure and white (*śukla-avadāta*) was separately set forth; therefore, it refers exclusively to that which is with outflows. Since the *Xianyang* [Śāstra] treats this as the gate of both the mundane and the supramundane (*lokottara*), it encompasses both the tainted and the untainted;
thus, in principle, there is no contradiction.

In the exposition of the factors (*aṅga-vyavasthāna*), the meaning of the dhyāna-factors is clarified as eighteen when names are combined; this is discussed in terms of both the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the real (*dravya*).
As stated in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (XIX), there are instances of expansion, contraction, and establishment or rejection. In essence, there are only seven universal factors (*sarvatraga*):

sensation (*vedanā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) among the specific-objective factors (*viṣayapratiniyatālambana*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) among the wholesome factors (*kuśala*). To these are added the two indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), vitarka and vicāra; thus, by separating these, they become eighteen. If one considers them only...

In reality, when including both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), their substance consists of only six factors. This is because *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) are provisional constructs and do not exist as distinct entities within the uncontaminated state;

they correspond to "right thought" (*samyaksamkalpa*) among the Eightfold Noble Path. Thus, the masters of the Dharma maintain that their substance is solely wisdom (*prajñā*), for *vitarka* is exclusively contaminated.

Furthermore, it is stated that the factors of *vitarka* and *vicāra* are coarse and exist only during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-yoga*), as explained in the subsequent sections of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

In meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there is no applied thought (*vitarka*) or sustained thought (*vicāra*, though subtle forms of these exist). One should understand that while there is no coarse *vitarka* and *vicāra* that trigger speech, there is subtle *vitarka* and *vicāra*.

It is known that in absorption, *vitarka* and *vicāra* function as constituent factors (*aṅga*). In the untainted (*anāsrava*) state, although the factors are not eighteen and so forth, they are still termed "factors of the four dhyānas" and "factors of one-pointedness of mind.
The meaning [of *aṅga*] is that of benefit (*anuśaṃsa*) and conformity (*anuloma*). Regarding the establishment and rejection [of these factors], the following questions and answers are given:

Form (*rūpa*) is not conducive to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and therefore it is not called a "limb" (*aṅga*). Consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) are not taken [as limbs] because they are both the objects of what is to be remedied (*pratipakṣya*) and the remedies themselves (*pratipakṣa*), as they are equally grasping;
thus, they lack the specific quality of being a remedy that provides benefit. The same applies to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), as it lacks the benefit of being a remedy.

Furthermore, within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), other factors such as suffering (*duḥkha*) and mental distress (*daurmanasya*) do not possess the sense of being beneficial, and moreover, they do not exist in those stages [of meditative absorption].

Regarding the establishment and exclusion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): these twenty-four [mental factors] are dissociated (*viprayukta*). They are not included because they do not accord with the meaning of "benefit" (*anuśaṃsa*) or "conformity" (*anuloma*).
Among the five universal factors (*sarvatraga*), four are excluded because their number corresponds to the four [objects] of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), such as the object and its purification.

The specific objects (*viśeṣālambana*)—desire (*chanda*) and resolve (*adhimokṣa*)—are likewise excluded. Within the wholesome factors (*kuśala*), only equanimity (*upekṣā*) is included, while the lower states of concentration and inferiority are specifically excluded.

Because it is powerful, it alone is selected; the others are not so. Since the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are not antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), they are not included among the indeterminate states.

Furthermore, regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) are not included because they are not antidotes that accord with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). As for the increase or decrease of four or five factors, this is based on the practice of "leaping over" (*vyutkrāntaka*);

because the two obstacles are numerous in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the unwholesome states of the desire realm are excluded. Because the joy (*prīti*) is full in the second dhyāna, agitation (*auddhatya*) increases there.

Furthermore, within the Eightfold Noble Path, *vitarka* (applied thought) takes wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence; thus, it functions as a factor for the abandonment of afflictions through wisdom. This will be explained in detail below.
Regarding *vitarka* and *vicāra* (sustained thought), they take wisdom as their essence. Moreover, concerning their establishment or exclusion in relation to the dhyānas:

*vitarka* and *vicāra* exist only in the first dhyāna, while *prīti* (joy) and *sukha* (bliss) extend to the second and third dhyānas but do not reach those above. This is because these are factors bound to specific stages (*bhūmi*) that do not extend to the higher realms.
It is unnecessary to resolve this difficulty. Why is it that *vitarka* and *vicāra* are said to be abandoned in the second dhyāna, whereas *adhyātmasaṃprasāda* (inner clarity) and so forth are not?

This is because inner clarity also pertains to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state, and furthermore, it is not an obstacle [to the first dhyāna]. Therefore, its abandonment is not mentioned. How then is "inner clarity" designated as the name for the second dhyāna and not other meditative concentrations?
Regarding the first point, the name is as stated in the second fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*: "It is included [in the second dhyāna] in order to counteract *vitarka* and *vicāra*."
Through mindfulness and clear comprehension, one purifies the mind within oneself and dwells in equanimity, free from the turbidity of applied and sustained thought;

therefore, it is called "internal serenity" (*adhyātmasamprasāda*). As stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Exposition), fascicle 63: "Internal serenity has mindfulness, clear comprehension, and equanimity as its intrinsic nature.
This is identical to the text in the nineteenth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*. Regarding the second meaning, other concentrations do not establish "internal [serenity]."

Within the internal door, one abandons the three factors of dullness (*laya*), agitation (*auddhatya*), and equanimity; because this brings the mental states (*citta-dharma*) to a state of equality and purity, it is called "internal serenity" (*adhyātmasamprasāda*). The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Xianyang lun), fascicle 2, states: "Because the internal substance is universally pure, the name 'purity' is established. As the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, fascicle 19, asks: "In what sense do mindfulness, clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) exist in all stages? Why is 'internal serenity' not established in the first dhyāna and those above? It answers: [The answer follows:

Because in the first dhyāna, there is still the factor of vitarka (applied thought); since vitarka is a form of mental distraction, it obstructs internal serenity. Furthermore, in the second dhyāna, although vitarka is absent, there is still vicāra (sustained thought), which likewise obstructs internal serenity. From the third dhyāna upward, because both vitarka and vicāra are absent, the mind is naturally serene and tranquil, and thus the name "internal serenity" is not separately established.

However, in the first dhyāna, although vitarka is present, because the mind is focused on a single object and free from the hindrances of sensual desire and ill-will, it is also said to possess a degree of internal serenity. It is simply that because vitarka is a coarse factor, it prevents the mind from being as profoundly settled as it is in the higher stages. Therefore, while the first dhyāna possesses the quality of serenity, it does not receive the specific designation "internal serenity. As for the second dhyāna and above, because they lack vitarka and vicāra, they are characterized by a natural, profound tranquility; hence, the specific term "internal serenity" is not applied to them. Thus, the distinction lies in the presence or absence of these two factors of vitarka and vicāra.
In the first dhyāna, because it is induced by way of vitarka and vicāra, although they exist, they are not mentioned;

in the second meditative absorption (dhyāna), because it is characterized by the activity of the essence of exultation (*prīti*) and is enveloped by a portion of the mental factors that are afflictions, it is designated by the name "inner serenity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*); in the third dhyāna, those mental factors which are a portion of the afflictions...

Because all [of these] are free from [their respective defects], their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are revealed: although the first dhyāna is free from the craving for sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), it is not yet free from the craving for joy (*prītirāga*);
although the second dhyāna is free from the craving for applied and sustained thought (*vitarkavicāra*), it is not yet free from the craving for joy;

and within the fourth dhyāna, this very equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣāsmṛti*) are extremely pure and clearly manifest. Therefore, one should understand the distinctions among the various dhyānas according to what is appropriate for each.

This is identical to the text in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn), fascicle 63. Regarding the third dhyāna, since it is already free from desire, applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and the craving for joy (*prīti-rāga*), why is it not called "pure" (*viśuddha*)?

The answer is: because there is pleasure (*sukha*) within its own stage [the third dhyāna]. Although the fourth dhyāna stage possesses neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*), it is described as pure because it is not an obstacle.
If it is not an obstacle, why is it not said to possess "correct awareness" (*saṃprajanya*)? Therefore, we know that [the absence of] neither-pain-nor-pleasure [is what constitutes purity].

Although these hindrances exist, they are weak and inferior; because there is no hindrance of lack of vigor (an-uttaptatva) in the third [dhyāna], the sensation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure exists only in the fourth dhyāna and not in the lower stages.
This is because in the lower stages, joy and pleasure function as beneficial factors (anuśaṃsa-aṅga), and thus it is not established [there].
Why is correct knowledge (saṃprajanya) not established in the fourth dhyāna? There is no textual passage in this Mahāyāna that does not establish it; however, the *Vibhāṣā* does [not establish it].

Furthermore, to explain one point: because the essence of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*) is characterized by a contradiction between darkness and light, it is not established [as a separate faculty].

If that is so, why is equanimity (*upekṣā*) established? It is because it counteracts the pleasure of the lower stages; it is precisely the cognition (*saṃprajanya*) that is diametrically opposed to that pleasure, not the two factors of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and equanimity.
These two dharmas are also as described in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 56, regarding the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Regarding the passage that states these two are contrary to correct knowledge (*samyak-prajñā*): why are these two termed "purity" (*pariśuddhi*) in the fourth dhyāna? It is because of the absence of pleasure (*sukha*).
Unlike the third dhyāna, it does not take faith (*śraddhā*) and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) as its factors (*aṅga*), because there is pleasure belonging to the mental ground (*manobhūmika-sukha*).

Since there is no pliancy [in the fourth dhyāna], and since the three factors constitute the essence of internal purity (*adhyātma-saṃprasāda*), faith is not employed as a factor. This is determined by the principle of inclusion and exclusion regarding the mental states (*citta*).

Regarding the fact that the untainted (*anāsrava*) factors pervading [the stages] are immeasurable, why are they established as only seven? According to the following text, this is due to three conditions;

other numbers are not employed because perfection is achieved through these three branches, without depending on further dharmas, and because other dharmas also accord with these meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
For these three reasons, they are not established [in greater number], as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Abhidharma), fascicle six.
Thirteen: Regarding the nineteenth [section], there are immeasurable further instances; however, for now, we shall take this passage from the treatise to avoid the prolixity of extensive citations.

Why are the first three [dhyānas] established with four factors (*aṅga*) and five factors respectively? Furthermore, regarding the first dhyāna, it is because it is the basis for abiding. That is to say, vitarka and vicāra. As stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 63: "Question:
For what reason are the four dhyānas established with four and five factors respectively? First, as for the first dhyāna, it is because it is the support for dwelling. Namely, vitarka and vicāra.
Because they abide in benefit, they are called "abiding in joy and bliss"; because they are the intrinsic nature [of the state], they are called the factor of "one-pointedness of mind.

These various dhyānas should be understood according to their respective meanings. Furthermore, there is no need to cite extensively from the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, as it accords with this treatise.

Regarding the formless realms (*ārūpya*) and so forth, the first dhyāna is not established; there are five factors to be abandoned, as stated in the nineteenth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*: first, greed (*rāga*).

The two [types of] harmful thoughts (*vyāpāda-vitarka*), the three [types of] suffering, the four [types of] grief, the five [types of] transgressing precepts, and the six [types of] distraction—as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on Great Wisdom), fascicle 63:

first, sensual desire (*kāma-rāga*); second, sensual harmfulness (*kāma-vyāpāda*); third, the three types of discursive thought (*vitarka*); fourth, grief and suffering; the remaining two are the same as these.

Why is there this contradiction? For instance, according to the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, although sensual desire (*kāma-rāga*) and sensual discursive thought (*kāma-vitarka*) both belong to the category of greed (*rāga*), [they are distinguished].

However, although desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*) gives rise to many afflictions regarding the objects of the five desires, it is predominant among them; thus, "desire-thought" (*kāma-vitarka*) refers to the superior desire for objects not yet encountered.
Because this is merely a mental desire, it is divided into two: manifesting as both "mental desire" (*manorāga*) and "desire-attachment" (*kāmarāga*).

Since these two factors—mental desire and desire-attachment—are present simultaneously, they are both designated by the single name "desire-thought" (*kāma-vitarka*). This is known because desire-attachment exists concurrently with them.

Furthermore, according to another interpretation, only desire-thought (*kāma-vitarka*) is mentioned and not desire-attachment (*kāma-rāga*), because the latter is omitted due to brevity; thus it is not discussed [separately] in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

While both sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*) are included within the category of suffering, although these hindrances are severed in the second dhyāna, they are subtle and therefore treated together.

The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* explains them separately because their respective modes of consciousness arise differently, and because suffering is a manifest activity (*samudācāra*). There are five hindrances in the second dhyāna: first, attachment to the first dhyāna; second, discursive thought (*vitarka*).

[Regarding] the three types of suffering, the four types of restlessness, and the five types of inferiority in concentration, it is asked: Why is there suffering as an obstacle in the first dhyāna, yet it is said to exist again in the second dhyāna?

As stated in [the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*], fascicle 63: "Question: For what reason is it known that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) has not yet been abandoned within the first dhyāna?
Answer: Because the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of that category has not yet been removed. If, in a certain state, the faculty of suffering has already been abandoned, then..."
When abiding in the second dhyāna, there should be no distinction [from the first];

therefore, one should know that although those [defilements] of the first dhyāna have been severed, their seeds and so forth have not been thoroughly severed, as they remain as *dauṣṭhulya* (coarse heaviness). In the third dhyāna, there are four obstacles: first, craving for the second dhyāna; second, joy (*prīti*);
third, exultation (*praharṣa*), which refers to the mental attention directed toward joy; and fourth, inferiority of concentration (*samādhi*). These are the hindrances to the fourth dhyāna.

There are five [factors]: (1) inhalation and exhalation; (2) craving for the third dhyāna; (3) pleasure; (4) the mental application (*manasikāra*) regarding pleasure, which consists in the arousal of awareness and the manifestation [of that pleasure];

and (5) the inferiority of concentration. Regarding the lack of contradiction with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise 63) and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Treatise 19), it is as recorded in the notes on Treatise 63.
As for the exclusion of the factors belonging to the Path (*mārga-pakṣya*), these shall be reconciled when reaching the section on the Path, where the mind is one-pointed.

Regarding the nature [of these], according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Chapter 36: that which is associated with the nine concentrations (*dhyāna*) is called "concentration" (*samādhi*), and that which is associated with the four wisdoms (*prajñā*) is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*).

Among these, that which is associated with concentration is termed "concentration. Within the nine concentrations, which one is it? It should be the ninth concentration, because its functional application (*prayoga*) is perfected.
In the establishment of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), seven mental attentions (*manasikāra*) are clarified as explained at length in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, volume thirty.

According to that commentary, there is a broad and significant interpretation: the "mental attention that discerns characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manasikāra*) seems to pertain to all three realms, while the other six mental attentions belong only to the higher realms.
In the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, these seven mental attentions exist in the two upper realms, but not in the lower realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that because those [two] are taught in relation to the fundamental [dhyānas], they pertain only to the upper two; this treatise, however, speaks generally, as it takes the initial hearing and reflection (*śruta-maya* and *cintā-maya*) as its preparatory means (*upāya*).

Since the first act of attention (*manasikāra*) within the first dhyāna is interspersed with hearing and reflection, its essential nature is exclusively wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī prajñā*).

Thus, while the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* speaks of only the upper two based on what is predominant, this treatise argues for the reality of the matter, asserting that the "characteristic-perceiving" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedin*) [attention] is indeed [present there].

Although there is this explanation that [the mark of discernment] is based on hearing and reflection as its means, it still does not fully resolve the point; for according to the *Triṃśikā*, it states:
"This mark of discernment occurs during the interval between hearing and reflection; after this has been removed, one employs only the mark of cultivation."

In the explanation of *adhimokṣa* (resolute conviction), the preceding text is concluded and the subsequent section is introduced: because one has already previously initiated resolute conviction in accordance with what was contemplated, it is known that the preceding stage is also the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).
How could it exist in the desire realm? If there were only the two higher realms, then there would be thirty-three [mental applications]; furthermore, the text below states:

"Moreover, the mental application of discerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) gives rise to a mind of aspiration for the sake of abandonment or attainment; the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika manaskāra*) is precisely [that which follows]."

Because one initiates the preparatory application (*prayoga*), one knows that the "characteristic of knowing" (*jñānalakṣaṇa*) pertains to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Since the remaining six [aspects] and those above belong to the higher realms, once the higher meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) has been attained, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower realms cannot arise.
If the characteristic of knowing already belongs to the higher mind, then the afflictions of the lower realms should not arise at all.

Why, then, is it said that one first generates a rarefied aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) before the afflictions are extinguished, and only then does one employ the six aspects? It is because the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) serves as the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), whereby the higher afflictions are suppressed.

Regarding the statement that the immediate path (*ānantarya-mārga*) should suppress the seeds [of defilement], the text following the explanation of the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) states:

"As for the concentrations mentioned above, it is not necessarily the case that they have already been attained. Why? Because even after one has completed the cultivation of the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*), one only attains them later.

Nevertheless, the treatise states: "The sixty-two [types of meditation] are subsumed under the 'neighboring' (*sāmantaka*) [stages]. Having finished discussing the six types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), it says: "These seven [mental attentions] begin with the first dhyāna... and so forth.

Regarding the inclusion [of mental applications] within the four types—namely, those that accord with the higher states such as "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and so forth—the application that accords with the superior is subsumed under the same category.

Furthermore, regarding the first of the four types beginning with "forcible effort" (*balavāhana*), if the "application of discerning characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) belongs to the stage of non-concentration (*asamāhita-bhūmi*), why is it not stated that this discernment of characteristics is subsumed under the "forcible application" (*balavāhana-manaskāra*) and the "interrupted application" (*sachidravāhana-manaskāra*)? Moreover, there are the three yogas.

When one abandons the superior grade of the mind, one first abandons the afflictions of that same grade within the practitioner’s body, causing the nature of rigidity and coarseness to cease and not arise again, thereby making the body pliant and compliant.
Furthermore, one subdues the heavy impediments (*dauṣṭhulya*) upon the seeds so that manifest afflictions do not arise;
this is what is meant by "abandoning the heavy impediments. Otherwise, this passage refers exclusively to the untainted (*anāsrava*). Second, furthermore:
The commentary explains that through the cultivation of the attention of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*), one becomes free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

As stated in the *Mahāśāstra* (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra), Fascicle 33: "By delighting in the abandonment and cultivation [of the path], the afflictions of the desire realm no longer manifest while one is walking or staying. Thereupon, one thinks:
'Regarding these afflictions, am I aware of them or not? When one attends to and contemplates a single object of truth (*satya-viṣaya*), one cannot be obstructed by them."
One is able to feel revulsion toward those [defilements] and forms this thought: "I am not yet fully liberated; for the sake of increasing my abandonment, I shall apply this attention.
If one relies on such a passage, it would imply that being without afflictions is called "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*).

Now, having already been cautioned thus, one further investigates so as not to give rise to the deep-seated conceit of thinking one is already liberated. Furthermore, the twenty-eighth [chapter] asks: "What is..."?
Being free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) means that regarding what has been attained and realized, one is without overweening pride;
being free from inverted grasping, one forms the notion of attainment with respect to what is truly attained, and likewise for true realization. This is being free from overweening pride.
Because one is far removed from this pride, one is far removed from the thirty-three [types of pride]. Thirdly, the explanation of "being free from overweening pride" is to resolve its apprehension.

Regarding the remaining text, it may be noted that while the seventh mental application (*manasikāra*) is explained in the ninth fascicle as being common to both the mundane and the untainted (*anāsrava*), I have not yet seen a textual passage stating that the mental application of observation (*paryeṣaṇā-manasikāra*) extends through the paths of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*) and uninterruptedness (*ānantarya-mārga*). This can be understood by reflecting upon the text.

If "mental application" is defined by way of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*), then all of these are indeed the wisdom of cultivation; however, if "mental application" is defined by way of the mental application associated with the wisdom of cultivation, then [the classification differs].
These seven have mental attention (*manasikāra*) as their substance. Just as when the joy born of seclusion (*viveka-prītisukha*) arises, it brings gratification to the body;

so too, at times when the application of effort (*prayoga*) has become subtle and its culmination is reached, that very joy and bliss increase and become more excellent until, upon reaching the ultimate fruit, they pervade the entire body and give rise to that joy and bliss.

Regarding how these are subsumed within the four types of attention (*manasikāra*) without any gaps: the two, namely "attention that discerns characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) and "attention of resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣika*), are collectively termed "conformable attention" (*anulomika-manasikāra*).

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 11, states: "The twenty-fifth attention, if it is [the stage of] 'separation' (*viveka*) or 'culmination' (*niṣṭhā*), is named 'counteractive attention' (*pratipakṣika-manasikāra*).
Furthermore, the twenty-sixth, "attention of delight in cultivation" (*ratisaṃgrāhaka*), is named both "counteractive" and... [text fragment].

The "attention that accords with purification" (*anuloma-manasikāra*) corresponds to the twenty-seventh [chapter]; if one observes the "attention of investigation" (*paryeṣaṇā-manasikāra*), it is named the "attention that accords with investigation" (*anuprekṣā-manasikāra*) and corresponds to the thirty-ninth.
Regarding these four types of attention, as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Great Commentary), fascicle 28:

"Attention that accords with [the path] (*anuloma-manasikāra*) refers to when one generates a profound sense of revulsion toward the object of focus and initiates correct application (*prayoga*), yet has not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*). If one consults the thirtieth [chapter], [it is as follows].
The third [stage] consists solely of the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) and is called the "correct initiation of application" (*samyak-prayoga-ārambha*).

Since the first two attentions are subsumed under the "conducive attention" (*anuloma-manasikāra*), and the "attention that discerns characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manasikāra*) also initiates correct application, does this not constitute a contradiction? [Response: This would indeed be so if taken literally; however, according to the actual fact, the attention that discerns characteristics is also a correct application.
This is as stated in the twenty-eighth fascicle. Furthermore, while the "conducive attention" is the preliminary application (*prayoga*), the present [text], the thirty-third fascicle, states:

This is stated with reference to the immediate path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and its proximate superior stage; thus, it speaks only of "resolute confidence" (*adhimokṣa*) and does not discuss "comprehending characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*).

In reality, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, because "comprehending characteristics" is interrupted by hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*), whereas resolute confidence is exclusively cultivation (*bhāvanā*), [the text] refers to the superior [stage] and mentions only resolute confidence, rather than taking "comprehending characteristics" as the attention that acts as the antidote (*pratipakṣa-manasikāra*), which is capable of severing afflictions and conduces to purification.
*Manasikāra* (attention) refers to the mental application that, by drawing down the mind and grasping pure and sublime signs, exhorts it to joy and proceeds with observation.
*Anulomika-manasikāra* (conformable attention) refers to the mental application that conforms to observation regarding whether afflictions have been abandoned or not yet abandoned.

This is explained in detail in the eleventh fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, within the section on the forty types of attention; there, the latter part explains how the seven [types of attention] are subsumed within the forty, such that they are contained therein.
Regarding the seven [categories], since the seven now subsume the forty, they subsume only the four types and do not discuss the remainder;

as for their mutual inclusion, it is as explained in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*. Among the sixty-two [views], there is the mutual inclusion of the four paths; comparing this with that, one finds the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the sixty-six [factors] are mutually contained within the four paths, and separately, they correspond to the four types of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).

Regarding "inclusion," as stated in the *Triṃśikā* (Trimsika), it is subsumed under four types of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*). First, the inclusion of the sign and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) are the antidote of revulsion and destruction (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*), which is the application for distancing oneself from [defilements].
Second, the third is the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*). Regarding the remaining three, although there is no explicit text, their meaning may be understood by inference.

As for the single type of "delighting in cultivation" (*ruci-saṃgraha*), because it abandons the afflictions, it is also included within the antidote of abandonment; this refers to the attention of analytical observation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*). Alternatively, [it may be understood otherwise].
This is the "retentive counteragent" (*dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa*), because it is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for the preceding chapters;

it is also the "counteragent of distancing" (*dūribhāva-pratipakṣa*), because it is the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*); and the mental attention to the ultimate fruit (*niṣṭhā-phala-manasikāra*) is both the retentive counteragent and the path of liberation.

If one considers the preceding uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) as the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*), then the subsequent mind, in relation to its own category, constitutes the uninterrupted path.
Thus, the [stages] beginning with "withdrawal" (prahāṇa) and "delight" (ratisaṃgrāhaka) all possess the sense of being antidotes that suppress and destroy [the afflictions].

Excluding the first path of immediate succession (ānantaryamārga), all subsequent paths serve as the path of liberation (vimuktimārga) for the preceding one; furthermore, among the remaining four stages, each successive stage possesses the sense of being an antidote relative to the one before it.

Moreover, from the second path of immediate succession associated with the mental application of "delight" onwards, when viewed in relation to the first path of immediate succession, they are all termed the path of superior progress (viśeṣamārga).
All possess the sense of being "counteractive to the distant portion" (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*). Examining the text on the four types of cultivation below:

if this mental attention (*manasikāra*) is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is called "subduing counteraction" (*vighāta-pratipakṣa*); if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is "counteraction of dissociation" (*visamyoga-pratipakṣa*).

Regarding the two initial [types] of outflow-free mental attention, they belong to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and are thus termed "subduing counteraction" when with outflows; the remaining outflow-free ones are termed "counteraction of dissociation."

If those of the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*) and a portion of bodhisattvas desire to sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and [the seeds of] outflows (*sāsrava*), these seven are the antidotes to the afflictive hindrances.
If a portion of bodhisattvas [desire to sever] attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), it is therefore called the antidote to the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
These are subsumed under four types of mental attention (*manasikāra*): first, the mental attention of forceful application (*balavāhana-manasikāra*), which refers to the initial stage of practice.

This causes the mind to abide and abide evenly; that which has not yet attained the cultivation of *manasikāra* (mental attention) still belongs to the stage of non-concentration (*aniyata-bhūmi*) and is not subsumed under the seven types of *manasikāra*.

Regarding the two types of *manasikāra* that operate with intervals: once the cultivation has been attained, one gradually advances, and this is then subsumed under the *lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manasikāra* (the mental attention that discerns characteristics).
Since it is interspersed with hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*), according to this text, the *lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manasikāra* is also [considered] cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The three types of attention that operate with effort (*sābhoga-pravṛtti*) are those from the "attention that discerns characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manasikāra*) up to the "attention at the culmination of application" (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*).

The effortless operation (*anābhoga-pravṛtti*) refers to the "attention at the fruit of the culmination of application" (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala-manasikāra*), as explained in [sections] twenty-eight, twenty-nine, and thirty.
As stated in twenty-eight, regarding their inclusion within the three yogas: first is the yoga of the beginner (*ādikarmika-yoga*), which is further divided into two types; first, regarding...

Regarding the application of attention (*manasikāra*) for one who first practices yoga—that is, a beginner who dwells with the mind on a single object but has not yet attained application of attention or realized a concentrated mind—it is known that the "characteristic of discernment" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Regarding the purification of afflictions:

once the beginner has already attained the application of attention through practice, they desire to purify their mind from all afflictions; thus, the "characteristic of discernment" subsumes both [the initial stage and the subsequent stage]. This constitutes the stage of having practiced the conduct.

Yoga refers to the three types of mental engagement (*manasikāra*) among the five types of mental engagement—from those that exclude signs (*nimittāpagata*) up to those at the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭha*)—in which one has already become well-practiced.
Yoga refers to abiding in the mental engagement that is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala-manasikāra*);
by this, one transcends the mental engagements cultivated through the methods of application and dwells in the fruit of cultivation. This is subsumed within the six clear realizations (*abhisamaya*).

This will be explained further below in the section on the ten types of clear observation (*abhisamaya*). Furthermore, their inclusion within the forty types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) is explained in detail in the eleventh fascicle of the *Mahāśāstra*.

Regarding the coarse characteristics (*audārikatva*) of the lower stages as explained in the treatise, there are two successive expositions in the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Mahāśāstra*; the first concerns the coarse characteristics.

Furthermore, there are two types of coarse characteristics (*audārikatā*): first, "coarseness as substance" (*dravya-audārikatā*), which means that although all stages (*bhūmi*) possess the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), those of the lower realms are most base and evil, and thus deeply loathsome;
second, "coarseness as number" (*saṃkhyā-audārikatā*), meaning that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) in the lower realms consists of many varieties and so forth.
A third point is identical to this text; the thirtieth and thirty-third [fascicles] state that there are six coarse characteristics.
This refers to meaning (*artha*), entity (*vastu*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), category (*pakṣa*), time (*kāla*), and principle (*yukti*), as explained at length in that [text].

"Meaning" refers to the sense conveyed within words. "Entity" refers to the two types of entities: internal and external. "Characteristic" refers to specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). "Category" refers to categories such as white and black.

"Time" refers to the names for the past, future, and present. "Principle" refers to the four kinds of reasoning. This is a general discussion of all coarse characteristics, as explained extensively [therein].
In the tenth fascicle, there is another passage that is identical to this text; its application of the extremely loathsome dharmas is explained at length in that treatise.
As explained extensively in the second fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā*, it would be redundant to cite it here in full, continuing until the section on birth in the formless realm (*ārūpya*).

The realms lack palaces and the like because there is no craving for form (*rūpa-rāga*). Regarding the phrase "and so forth" in the context of transcending the world, it refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), wherein one realizes and penetrates through the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) until one illuminates and understands things as they truly are.

The meaning of the passage here is that, from the *anāgamya* stage up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), there exist untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledges and patiences (*kṣānti*) belonging to eight stages, including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). All these eight stages...
There are also cases where one can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (63) and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (19):

"One enters the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of the Noble Truths by relying solely upon the various dhyānas and the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna; it is not possible in the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This is because *vipaśyanā* is deficient within the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); thus, one born in the formless realm cannot enter clear observation, for it is difficult there."
Because they give rise to revulsion, as explained in the *Mahā-śāstra*.

Regarding the six types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), three depend on five [factors]. The Westerners explain that these three are: the clear realization of wisdom (*jñānābhisamaya*), the clear realization at the limit of the truths (*satyāntikābhisamaya*), and the clear realization of ethical discipline (*śīlābhisamaya*).

Their faith (*śraddhā*) pertains to both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*); their volition (*cetanā*) is exclusively tainted; and their culmination (*niṣṭhā*) is exclusively untainted.
Regarding the reason for taking only the first three sets of five bases (*pañca-vastūni*): these refer to the initial *anāgamya* stage up through the fourth *dhyāna*.

The intermediate *dhyānas* and the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are not included because one enters the stage of clear observation (*abhisamaya*) based solely on these five. By entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) within these five stages, one attains the first three types of clear observation at the very beginning of the path of seeing. As for why the intermediate *dhyānas* are not taken: [The text continues: Because [the intermediate dhyānas] lack the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), they cannot serve as the basis for the path of seeing.

Furthermore, since the path of seeing is characterized by intense application (*pragraha*), it requires a state of mental pliancy and stability that the intermediate dhyānas do not provide. Thus, only the five stages from *anāgamya* to the fourth *dhyāna* are suitable for the entry into the path of seeing.

Because the abode of the Brahmā King is characterized by much distraction, although there are untainted states within the intermediate [dhyāna] that do not abandon the afflictions—just as the perception of earth is merely for the purpose of contemplation—and because the entry into the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) is not said to depend upon those stages, only the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna can serve as the basis for entry, and not the other preparatory stages;
for all other preparatory stages are exclusively tainted (*sāsrava*). Thus, it is the initial preparatory stage.
The distinction between the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) is established because the noble disciple initially lacks fixed meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Thus, while abandoning the afflictions of the lower realms by relying on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage, from the first *dhyāna* upward—where there is fixed concentration—one abandons the afflictions by relying solely on the fundamental stages and not on the *anāgamya*.

This is explained in detail in that treatise. Furthermore, regarding the abandonment of afflictions through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it relies generally upon all eight stages, beginning from the initial *anāgamya*.

Up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), that treatise explains at length: "When noble beings (*ārya*) are born in those two higher realms, they are all able to give rise to and cultivate knowledge (*jñāna*).

Regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there exists untainted [knowledge] capable of entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth;

this [attainment] is merely a state of contemplative wandering (*vihāra*) and does not involve the severance of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*), as is extensively analyzed among the various masters in the section on the severance of afflictions. Most [masters] consider it to be [the intermediate stage].

It is not the case that those who practice *antara-abhisamaya* (intermediate realization) also enter the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). This is because no such textual authority has been seen and no such principle has been investigated;

rather, it adopts the meaning of the Hīnayāna. As the treatise says: "Or, regarding the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), [the meditative attainment] is able to manifest before one's eyes, having already arisen previously and subsequently manifesting again.

This is as explained extensively in the fourth of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) within the commentary on the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) in the third fascicle. How is it that a noble disciple (*ārya-śrāvaka*) has already attained [it]?

"Having already abandoned desire for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) through the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), is one reborn in the form realm again? The intent of this question is as follows:

does it ask whether one who has already abandoned desire for the form realm attains the formless attainments, or whether one who has already attained the formless attainments is subsequently reborn in the form realm?

Because these are combined into a single inquiry, this passage appears. The first question refers to those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), because they have not yet attained the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*). The second...

Question: Regarding the person who has attained the third fruit (*trtīya-phala*), it is explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* that they abandon the afflictions from the third dhyāna downward by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) and suppress the afflictions from the fourth dhyāna upward, thereby attaining the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Even after passing away and being reborn in the fourth dhyāna, they subsequently attain the absorption of cessation by relying on the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*). Now, a question is raised concerning the afflictions from the fourth dhyāna upward: [how can they be suppressed?]

Since one has already suppressed [the afflictions] by means of the superior, untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) and dwells in contemplation thereby, how is it that the untainted state of that stage arises?

Why is it that when one is later born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), like an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the six classes of [afflictions] and so forth arise, yet those of that stage do not arise?
To answer this objection: "The noble ones (*ārya*) are born in other stages because they moisten birth through seeds; ordinary persons [are born] through active manifestations (*samudācāra*)."
Because it moistens and gives rise to [existence], it cannot be analogized to what was stated previously in the third fascicle, and so forth; as noted in the commentary on the second fascicle:
"This is the samādhi of tranquil liberation (śānta-vimokṣa-samādhi); it is not necessarily the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).

Now, according to the explanation of the attainment of cessation in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*: "If noble ones who have already attained the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) wish to dwell in temporary tranquility..."
Because one seeks further advancement from the mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and finds nothing to be attained, the mind ceases and does not arise;
thus, one knows it to be the tranquility of liberation (*śānta-vimokṣa*). Regarding the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the *Śāstra* states:

"By abiding in the maturation (*vipāka*) of the tranquility of liberation" means that it is called "tranquil" because it is the maturation of the four aggregates produced by the craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (XVIII) states: "The name of the formless absorptions is..."

Regarding the fact that the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) does not manifest within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) in such inquiries as those concerning "quiescence" (*śānta*), this refers to the basis for its arising (*utpādāśraya*) and not to the basis for its establishment (*siddhyāśraya*).
As stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, and other treatises:

if the ālayavijñāna has not yet been established as the basis, the attainment of cessation will not be initiated in the formless realm; however, once it is established as the basis, one enters that attainment even in that realm.

Regarding this cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*), it has been stated previously that it pertains to the limited characteristics (*parīttanimitta*) rather than the ultimate, final principle, as explained extensively in the seventh fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Among the three paths—mild (*mṛdu*) and so forth—this refers to the abandonment of the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) and not those of vision (*darśana-heya-kleśa*), because the afflictions of vision arise from delusion regarding the [ultimate] principle (*tattva*). Cultivation...
Since delusions arise from the objects of perception, it is as explained in the treatise that inferior wisdom (*hīna-jñāna*) abandons superior delusions; this is easily understood.

But how should the principle be stated regarding inferior wisdom abandoning inferior delusions? As stated in the thirteenth [chapter], in establishing the two fruits, the delusions of the three realms are subsumed into nine grades:
beginning with the first grade of the Desire Realm and ending with the first grade of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Thus, these are combined into a single grade. Is this not so?
Does not inferior wisdom abandon inferior afflictions? Answer: Wisdom has degrees of intensity while faculties have degrees of superiority and inferiority.
When wisdom is weak and the faculties are inferior, it is as stated in this passage. When wisdom is intense and the faculties are superior, it is as in the thirteenth fascicle.

Even when the path is intense and the faculties are superior, if one considers the path in relation to the initial afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it still constitutes inferior wisdom abandoning superior afflictions. In truth, there is no contradiction in this principle within the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

The *Mahāśāstra* (Great Treatise) on the severance of afflictions through the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-bhāvanā*), volume 58, states that the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and that it effects the severance or suppression of afflictions and the attainment of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), as can be understood from the usual explanations.

As stated in the *Mahāśāstra*, volume 69, there are many further sequences that do not contradict this text. Furthermore, the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) transforms the basis of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) and attains a state free from such coarseness.

Regarding the "heavy" [defilements], there are two interpretations of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). The first states that at this stage, one has not yet abandoned that state of unfitness (*akarmanyatā*), which is currently manifest;
thus, what is called "abandoning" here refers to abandoning the designation [of being heavy], just as one has not yet given rise to the thought of killing an enemy.

The second states that this [state] is called "abandoned" because the seeds of the obstacles have already been extinguished. As the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "In some cases, one acts without interval (*ānantarya*) in order to sever the remainder."

Regarding the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) for this category: what was called the "path of excellence" (*viśeṣa-mārga*) in the preceding category is here termed the "path of preparation" with respect to the afflictions to be abandoned in the subsequent category.

This treatise states: "In order to abandon the remaining afflictions of this category, all paths of preparation, uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are, in comparison to this [preceding category], the path of excellence.

This treatise, according to the actual facts, discusses the relative distance; thus, the latter three paths are all the path of excellence for the preceding one. As stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*: [the path of preparation is so called because it prepares for the abandonment of afflictions].

This refers to an explanation given in terms of a single path that is proximate [to the fruit], as well as the statement regarding the arising of a distinct preparatory application (*prayoga*) after this contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to direct the mind;
it does not mean that nine grades of the path arise within a single contemplation. Furthermore, regarding the second "further explanation" (*punaḥ krama*) herein, there are three interpretations.

The first two both state: "Alternatively, through diligent application (*abhiyoga-prayoga*)," while the sixty-ninth [variant] states: "Alternatively, through the uninterrupted [path] (*ānantarya-mārga*)," and the middle [variant] states: "The word 'alternatively' (*vā*) means 'or abiding' (*sthiti*)."
Regarding the statement "either through diligence and skillful means" or "abiding in negligence," this treatise cites the explanation from within the commentary:
"Alternatively, because one abides in the observation of the dharmas previously contemplated and realized, it says 'either through diligence and skillful means.

Furthermore, that treatise offers another explanation, stating: "Or there are those who do not practice skillful means without interruption, but [merely] give rise to [realization] based on their previous category."

The notion of contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi-saṃjñā*), which does not seek further progress, is identical to this passage. Furthermore, regarding the discourse on negligence (*pramāda*) in that treatise, another interpretation explains it as follows:
"Alternatively, even after [defilements] have been abandoned, one may further examine them with the wisdom of observation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).

This is also consistent with the present text. Nevertheless, there remains a contradiction between that treatise’s statement that they have been "abandoned" and this treatise’s statement that they are "realized."

Taking up the previous [explanation] again, it further explains "superiority": if one establishes the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) as being named such because it gradually increases in excellence, then since it is said that even abiding in negligence is a path of superior progress, what would be the use of this treatise?

Or, regarding the phrase "diligent application," if one continues to inquire into it in detail, one should consult the tenth and sixty-ninth [sections] of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, where four paths are established as chapter headings.

Regarding the four types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), "cultivation through acquisition" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) refers to the Small Vehicle’s cultivation through acquisition, which pertains to the future; however, here, in the Mahāyāna, cultivation through acquisition refers to the present.

Since the seeds have not yet produced the superior states of mind, one cultivates these seeds so that they give rise to actual manifestations (*samudācāra*); this is called cultivation through acquisition.

As for the phenomena that are already manifest, cultivating them so that they increase is called cultivation through practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*). This is as explained in the second section of the commentary.

In the initial stages, when the arising of the manifest path causes it to increase, this is termed "cultivation through practice" (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*); when one's own seeds are established and successively increased, this is termed "cultivation through acquisition" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).
This does not necessarily refer only to the seeds at the time when the manifest [path] has not yet arisen.

Among the four types of remedies (*pratipakṣa*), this refers to the remedy of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*). The Master [Vasubandhu] claims that this includes both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) wisdoms such as those arising from hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī* prajñā);
however, this interpretation is incorrect. Here, the meaning is distinct: wisdoms arising from hearing and reflection are exclusively contaminated.

How then could they be said to include both contaminated and uncontaminated wisdoms? As for the remedy of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), it refers to the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) and the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) that precede the seven [stages].

Regarding the mental orientations (*manasikāra*), the first two are the antidotes to revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*) and both belong to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*). The [subsequent] three mental orientations—separation (*viveka*) and so forth—are the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Since it is now stated that these are the "antidotes of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), they must pertain to the paths of preparation and the uninterrupted paths;

however, the mental orientation of revulsion belongs to the path of preparation and not the uninterrupted path, so does this not constitute a contradiction? The commentary explains: "The first two mental orientations are the path of preparation."

This [stage] is the antidote to weariness (*udvega-pratipakṣa*), which here subsumes the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) and the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) as the antidote to abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*).
This is because, having taken up the attention of seclusion (*viveka-manasikāra*), the uninterrupted path preceding the subsequent uninterrupted path constitutes the preparatory path;
thus, these two together are the antidote to abandonment. Although both of the former two are preparatory paths, they are not mentioned here because they consist of weariness.
Because it serves as the antidote for the non-abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Second, the second section provides an explanation of the eleven types of paths within the five categories, which is divided into two parts: first, an explanation of the five categories and the eleven paths;

second, an explanation of the meaning of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). The first part contains two sections: first, a brief enumeration and explanation; second, a detailed individual exposition. This is the first section.

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the enumeration, and second, the explanation. Within the enumeration, there are again two parts: first, the listing, and second, the conclusion and attribution.

Regarding the tenth chapter of the treatise, the correlation with the factors of dhyāna will be reconciled below, based on the fifth fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* concerning the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).

The Dharma is briefly categorized as thirty-seven and extensively as immeasurable; within each of these individual gates, the names, their establishment and exclusion, and the "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are explained separately.

Because they serve as the causes for the four wisdoms of the Buddha-fruit, they constitute the "path. Since all thirty-seven of these exist within the causal stage and assist in the realization of the path to fruition, they are called the "auxiliary dharmas of the path.
Regarding the general derivation of their essential nature, according to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, they are established by means of equality.

Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) constitutes the essence of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*); all other factors of enlightenment ultimately culminate in meditative cultivation and are entirely equal.
According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle three, if one considers the ultimate meaning, each category of wisdom fully encompasses all meritorious qualities and dharmas;
