however, from the perspective of coarse characteristics, the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (wonderful investigative wisdom) subsumes the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Because all phenomena are equal and because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is samādhi, the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) subsumes the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Although these have diligence as their essential nature, because they are embraced by the Tathāgata’s Wisdom of Equality, they are devoid of the characteristics of high or low.
The five faculties (*indriya*) and the five powers (*bala*) are subsumed within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and the Wisdom of Equality.

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are subsumed within the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). If their individual essential natures (*svabhāva*) are set forth, the various Dharma masters all take ten dharmas as their nature:
faith, diligence, mindfulness, wisdom, joy, pliancy, intention, equanimity, morality, and samādhi.

While the Lesser Vehicle takes right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) as a factor of enlightenment, in the Mahāyāna this dharma is considered contaminated (*sāsrava*) and thus cannot constitute one of the eightfold noble path.

Regarding the claim that this *vitarka* (applied thought) takes *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from reflection) as its essence, while *prajñā* constitutes the factor of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and *samyaksaṃkalpa* (right intention) takes *cetanā* (volition) as its essence—this reasoning is incorrect, for no such textual authority has been seen.
As the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 29, states: "Right intention is subsumed under the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*).
Furthermore, the text below states that it is included within *vipaśyanā* (insight), and the commentary on the twenty-second [chapter] of the fifty-seventh [fascicle] explains this accordingly.

Regarding the faculties (*indriya*), it is asked: Are the five faculties subsumed within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), or are the thirty-seven subsumed within the five?
The answer is: the thirty-seven subsume the five, but the five do not subsume the thirty-seven. What is not subsumed?

Namely, verbal action (*vākkarman*), livelihood (*ājīva*), joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), equanimity (*upekṣā*)—these are either six or four [depending on the classification]—and these are not subsumed therein. If one asks what "right reflection" (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is: *Note: This passage appears to be a commentary on the Abhidharmic categorization of the factors of enlightenment and their relationship to the five spiritual faculties.*

Regarding the enumeration of *vitarka* (initial application) among those not included [in the faculties], one should state that seven factors are not included because *vitarka* is absent among the twenty-two faculties.
Since right *vitarka* (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence, it is subsumed under the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) among the faculties.

Why is it that when speech is initiated, both *vitarka* and wisdom are involved, yet only wisdom is taken [as the faculty] and not *vitarka*? It is because [wisdom alone] initiates the fivefold aggregate-body (*pañca-skandha-kāya*). Thus, [only wisdom is designated].

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is not identical to volition (*cetanā*), as stated in the *Mahāśāstra*. Now, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) of the Mahāyāna take nine factors as their essence:

faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, joy, tranquility, equanimity, and the path-factors of ethical discipline (*śīla*). Alternatively, there are eleven, by expanding ethical discipline into three.

Although "correct mental application" (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) appears in the text [as a distinct factor], it has wisdom as its essence; how does it differ from "correct view" (*samyak-dṛṣṭi*)? Correct view is a [distinct] limb [of the path].
Regarding the distinction between the branches, the commentary states: within the observation of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), one discriminates that which has not yet issued as speech;

this is right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), by means of which one speaks for the sake of teaching the Dharma to others. Speech is initiated based on this [thought], because in untainted observation (*anāsrava-darśana*) there is no speech produced by vitarka and vicāra, and because the Buddha is devoid of vitarka and vicāra.

Furthermore, in the seventh chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is stated that [right thought] has vitarka as its essence; thus, among the thirty-seven [factors], it is included in the hundred [dharmas].
The categories of dharmas can be understood through their mutual inclusion; when wisdom (*prajñā*) is expanded, it constitutes nine factors:

namely, the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), the factor of investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and deliberation (*vitarka*). As for the other factors, they are expanded into eight.

Regarding these four applications of mindfulness, this treatise, as well as the *Mahāśāstra*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, and the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, frequently state that mindfulness itself constitutes the application of mindfulness. In this treatise, the application of mindfulness is [defined] by...

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Taishō 1594), fascicle 28, and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Taishō 1602), fascicle 2, state that the two dharmas of wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) constitute the essence [of the foundations of mindfulness].

Furthermore, they hold that the three types of wisdom—those arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-maya*, *cintā-maya*, and *bhāvanā-maya*)—constitute the essence of the foundations of mindfulness. Among these, the wisdoms of hearing and reflection are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), whereas the wisdom of cultivation pertains to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Moreover, the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka* (Taishō 1579), fascicle 28, states that the foundations of mindfulness consist of prior observation; if one follows this by taking the three types of wisdom as their essence, then the word "mindfulness" [in the term "foundations of mindfulness"] refers to the wisdom of reflection.
Abiding has wisdom as its essential nature and a single moment of thought as its substance, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Taishō 1509), fascicle 29.

These are all the faculty of mindfulness and the power of mindfulness among the faculties and powers; they are the simultaneous predominant factors of the four foundations of mindfulness. This explanation of their substance is not the ultimate truth.
As for vigor, it opens into eight: the four right endeavors, the faculty of vigor, the power of vigor, right effort, and vigor.

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and so forth are expanded into eight; the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment, and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*)—when combined with the three aforementioned groups of dharmas—are expanded into twenty-five.

Mindfulness (*smṛti*) and recollection (*anusmṛti*) do not remain as a single category, but are expanded into the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the factors of the path.
Faith (*śraddhā*) is expanded into two: the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the power of faith (*śraddhābala*). When combined with the preceding [categories], there are thirty-one.

Dharma-joy, tranquility, and equanimity—these three do not open up the portion of the path-concomitant precepts. Right speech, right action, and right livelihood are established as the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
One abides with mindfulness fixed upon these four objects; because one possesses both wisdom and a concentrated mind, they are called foundations of mindfulness.

These consist of the pervasive objects, the objects for purifying conduct, and the objects for skillfulness regarding the pure precepts, as explained in detail in the eleventh fascicle of the *Smṛtyupasthāna-śāstra*. Why are more [foundations] not added?
As for "diminution," it is because of the removal of the four kinds of inverted perceptions. Why is "initial clarity" mentioned first?
It is because one first desires to remove these inversions by means of focused mindfulness; therefore, "initial clarity" is stated first.

In this passage and within the sequence of the fifty-three aggregates (*skandha*), the mind (*citta*) is taken as the self-essence (*ātman-svabhāva*), while phenomena (*dharma*) are considered the basis for defilement and purification.

This is precisely what is meant in the subsequent section on the cultivation of the fruit (*phala-bhāvanā*), where, among the removal of the four inversions (*viparyāsa*), the mind is identified as the inversion of permanence (*nitya-viparyāsa*).

The contradiction between these two passages—found in Chapter 28 of the *Mahāśāstra* (the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*)—is likewise resolved by the following text, which states that the purpose is to eliminate attachment (*abhiniveśa*) to the mind, consciousness (*vijñāna*), and mentation (*manas*).

Because the fool is deluded regarding the self and its objects, the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) is established; that is, with respect to the mind, one constantly regards it as "mine" and as the basis of the self.

To eliminate this grasped notion of a self, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is established; that is, because the self can defile or purify through delusion, one eliminates the very substance of the self.

If one examines the preceding and following contexts of that treatise, one observes that phenomena are taken to be non-self; thus, it is only the grasping for a "mind-self" that is eliminated, not [the mere observation of] phenomena.

Apart from the elimination of the self and its essence, there are further contradictions; as reconciled at the end of the second fascicle, according to the *Mahāśāstra* (Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 57:
"Among the twenty-two faculties, in how many faculties is the foundation of mindfulness of the body established? It is established in seven faculties, namely, the seven material faculties.
In how many faculties is the foundation of mindfulness of sensation established? It is established in five faculties, namely, the five sensations. In one..."

The application of mindfulness of mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) is established based on the faculty of mind (*manendriya*); the application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is established based on the nine faculties, namely the last eight and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Regarding what constitutes their essential nature, and so forth, it is as extensively explained in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka*, the eighteen great treatises, the twenty-eighth [chapter] of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, the second and nineteenth [chapters] of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, and the three types of each of the four applications of mindfulness in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Twenty-fourth, furthermore, to explain and examine that passage: according to the *Mahā-śāstra*, fascicle 28, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) through the three types of wisdom—namely, hearing (*śruta*), reflection (*cintā*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).

It is only the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) that is both contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). In various treatises, up to the section on the five powers (*pañcabala*), nowhere is there seen a text stating that these are uncontaminated.
Only in this [text], within the explanation of the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness regarding internal and external feelings (*vedanā*), is it so stated.
Furthermore, regarding the sensation that arises conditioned by another’s body: this sensation, when considered in relation to other sentient beings, is also included within the "internal.

In this context, the treatise combines [the categories] and establishes them according to their nature, such as the body; it separately establishes the sense-bases for one's own body and its supporting sense-faculties and objects, and likewise separately establishes the internal bases for another’s body.
All these are termed "internal" and "external. Now, in this section, they are combined as explained at length in the *Mahāśāstra*.
This explanation is as found in the *Mahā-śāstra* (Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 28, where it appears six times; one should verify this by cross-referencing.

Furthermore, within the section on cultivation (*bhāvanā*), none of these afflictions (*kleśa*) are enumerated individually under this name; rather, each individual affliction may be assigned [this designation] separately, which can be understood through careful reflection.

Regarding the "whipping of the mind," as explained in the *Mahā-śāstra* and other texts within the context of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), this specific phrasing does not appear there; only the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) are mentioned.

In the [preceding] sections on abandonment, there is the mind of exertion (*pragraha-citta*) which treats laxity (*laya*), and the mind of maintenance (*dhāraṇā-citta*) which treats agitation (*auddhatya*).

Here, however, the mind of exertion treats both laxity and agitation simultaneously. In those [other] texts, the mind of exertion and the mind of maintenance are distinguished so that each treats its respective fault;

in this treatise, they are combined into a single "mind of exertion-maintenance" (*pragraha-dhāraṇā-citta*), and thus it treats both simultaneously. Question: Does this same text also appear in the four subsequent sections on abandonment? Answer: Yes.
Regarding the contradiction [of the sequence]: why is Right Effort (*samyakprahāṇa*) explained next? Because when a Bodhisattva wishes to cultivate wisdom, they must diligently practice it;

therefore, Right Effort must be explained immediately following [the preceding topics]. As stated in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, it is called "Right Effort" and also "Right Exertion" (*samyagvyāyāma*).

Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 29, it is also called the "Path of Right Exertion," while fascicle 20 of the same treatise refers to it as "Right Victory."
The ninth [section], the explanation of the four right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), has four types: 1. **Abandonment through restraint** (*saṃvara-prahāṇa*):

This refers to generating desire, exertion, and so forth, in order to abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen; one should cultivate restraint so that they are brought to cessation. 2. **Abandonment by abandonment** (*prahāṇa-prahāṇa*):

This refers to generating desire and so forth, as previously described, in order that unwholesome states not yet arisen do not arise, and so that they do not manifest; it is for the sake of their abandonment.

1. Abandonment through abandonment (*prahāṇa-prahāṇa*): [the abandonment of] the three [types of unwholesome states]. 2. Abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*): for the sake of causing unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise, one exerts the mind and sustains the mind;

by repeatedly cultivating and practicing those wholesome dharmas not previously attained so that they manifest, one is able to abandon what is to be abandoned, and thus it is called abandonment through cultivation.
3. Abandonment through protection (*anurakṣaṇā-prahāṇa*): for the sake of maintaining already arisen wholesome dharmas, one exerts the mind and sustains the mind.
Because it guards wholesome dharmas so that they are not forgotten or lost, it is called "guarding and severing.

Regarding the practitioner’s cultivation, each of the five phrases is explained in reliance upon the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). This is as found in both the *Mahāśāstra* (the *Abhidharmamahāyānasaṃgraha*) and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, where both texts contain this passage.

As the eighty-third fascicle of the *Mahāśāstra* states: "Desire" refers to that in which one delights in acting and delights in attaining; "vigor" refers to the initiation of application (*prayoga*).
Regarding the mind being "courageous" and the statement "exerting effort": once it is courageous, one correctly and diligently practices those preparatory applications (*prayoga*).

Among the evil states that have arisen, there are these five phrases: the first three manifest the inferior counteractive measures consisting of the wisdoms of hearing and reflection within the non-concentrated stages (*asamāhita-bhūmi*);

the subsequent [two] manifest the counteractive measure of cultivation (*bhāvanā-pratipakṣa*), which is the wisdom of meditation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*). As for the characteristics of dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*), they are as explained above.

The arising of unwholesome dharmas is also as previously explained. Regarding the non-arising of wholesome dharmas, the first three phrases refer to the wholesome dharmas of hearing and reflection belonging to the indeterminate stage (*aniyata-bhūmi*), while the latter [phrase] refers to the wholesome dharmas of exertion, maintenance, concentration, and cultivation. Regarding the arising of wholesome dharmas, it is also as previously explained.

Each of these five phrases applies universally to both the basis (*āśraya*) and that which depends upon it (*āśrita*). This principle should also be applied to the four categories; since the text here applies to all four, [the same logic holds].
One should correctly apply the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) to rouse the mind, sustain the mind, remedy laxity (*laya*), and remedy agitation (*auddhatya*),

reflecting in accordance with the principle. Regarding the auxiliaries of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), namely desire (*chanda*), effort (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*), the *Mahā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Vehicle), fascicle 29,

states that the five phrases beginning with "arousing desire" from the second chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavāca-śāstra* (or *Xianyang lun*) show that each of these factors of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) universally pervades the four bases of psychic power when they are active amidst the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).

That which enables one to distance oneself [from unwholesome states] without yet having permanently destroyed the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) is called the concentration obtained through the predominant power of desire (*chanda-adhipati-bala*).

Regarding the objects of the three time periods that are conducive to the arising of unwholesome dharmas, among the three grades of envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) associated with these objects, that which has not yet arisen is prevented from arising, and that which has already arisen is severed, without yet having permanently destroyed the underlying tendencies;
this is called the predominant power of exertion (*vīrya-adhipati-bala*).

The concentration attained by cultivating superior equanimity (*adhipaśama*) while contemplating the faults of the afflictions and the remedies for unwholesome states is called the "concentration attained through the predominance of mind" (*cittādhipateya-samādhi*).

The concentration induced by the power of superior insight (*vipaśyanādhipateya*), which involves further reflecting upon the wholesome states thus attained, is [the concentration] "attained through the predominance of insight.
According to this text, if these are assigned respectively to the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), they are combined into one.

Each of the four right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) possesses the five factors beginning with desire (*chanda*). Now, this treatise takes up the desire, diligence (*vīrya*), and so forth of the right abandonments and sequentially assigns them according to these five phrases;
how could this not be contradictory? As the *Mahāśāstra* states: "By the predominant power of these four samādhis," and so on, up to:
"in order to permanently destroy the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and to attain the remedial wholesome dharmas, [the practitioner] generates [them] anew."

Because of [the need for] generating desire, exertion, and so forth, there is no contradiction with the eight *prahāṇasaṃskāras* (abandoning-efforts), as also stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 29.

They are also called the eight *abhibhvāyatanas* (bases of mastery). In this regard, since there is no further contradiction with other treatises, why is it that while *saṃprajanya* (clear comprehension) exists here, it is not treated as an antidote, whereas *cetanā* (volition) and *upekṣā* (equanimity) are taken as having the meaning of antidotes?
The answer is as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 29, concerning the object: [The text continues: "As for the object..."
The volition that takes past and future non-manifest objects as its domain can serve as an antidote; however, regarding present manifest phenomena, equanimity (*upekṣā*) serves as the antidote.
By means of these two causes, one is able to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Furthermore, in that same treatise, while explaining equanimity among the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*), it states that there is an unpolluted mind of equanimity taking the three periods of time as its object, which also extends to non-manifest objects. In fact, this equanimity extends to taking all three periods as its object.
The contemplation of the world is likewise; the textual structure within that explanation of contemplation is also thus.

However, because that treatise previously explained "exertion" (*pragraha*) by treating the manifest and the non-manifest as one, whereas here we are separately addressing this specific meaning—which is not according to the ultimate reality—there is no contradiction.

If one considers the abandonment of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) through contemplation as one factor, and the cultivation of the remaining six [perfections] as complete for the sake of meditative concentration as the second causal condition:

The cultivation of the eight formative forces (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) is as explained below. To provide an explanation: these four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) arise during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) before the actual abandonment of afflictions.

As stated in the *Mahāśāstra*, among the characteristics of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and so forth, volition (*cetanā*) is able to initiate the three types of karma, while equanimity (*upekṣā*) is able to abandon unwholesome dharmas.
Correct knowledge (*saṃprajanya*) belongs to the category of insight (*vipaśyanā*) and is wisdom (*prajñā*); however, it is actually wisdom that serves as the true antidote here.

If one initiates unwholesome actions of body and speech, this is called the arising of afflictions such as lethargy (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*); because one can then counteract those unwholesome actions of body and speech by initiating wholesome ones through right reflection (*samyak-manasikāra*), this reflection serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
While it is said that wisdom (*prajñā*) is the antidote in the sense of knowing the cause of faults, it is not stated to be the actual substance of the antidote;

this is explained from the perspective of its predominance (*adhipati*), and thus the meaning is not contradictory. Now, since this reflection is said to coexist with both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), [how is it distinguished?]

It is clearly known that bodily and vocal karma constitutes the *dhyāna-saṃvara* (concentration-precept), but because the untainted (*anāsrava*) state has not yet been attained, it is not the *mārga-saṃvara* (path-precept).
These eight superior practices are cultivated for the sake of the yoga that severs the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

This yoga for harming the latent tendencies consists of the four yogas, as explained in the twenty-eight [treatises]: namely, desire, diligence, faith, and skillful means; these are assigned sequentially to the first three [stages].

The remaining five are all skillful means, as explained extensively elsewhere. Furthermore, one cultivates the eight formative forces of abandonment (*aṣṭau prahāṇasaṃskārāḥ*) for the sake of perfecting meditative concentration;

this is because they are said to induce the characteristics of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and so forth. Since the two treatises [the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] are largely identical in their treatment of these, and since the wisdom of the eight formative forces of abandonment subsumes the four yogas—given that the four yogas all involve the abandonment of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)—it is known that there are eight types.

Wisdom can sever the seeds through eight kinds of wisdom, and wisdom can attain meditative concentration; specifically, it is said that thought severs the seeds. However, this refers exclusively to one particular sense.
Herein, these are subsumed as four [factors], which differ from the four yogas; the details are as found in that commentary (*chao*), and they should not be conflated.

Furthermore, there are two types of cultivation through desire, diligence, mind, and investigation (*chanda-vīrya-citta-mīmāṃsā-bhāvanā*). Regarding these, many eminent masters have explained what is to be grasped:

here, based on the text, there are two kinds of cultivation—the former is the cultivation of that which is to be abandoned (*pratipakṣya*), and the latter is the cultivation of the essence of virtue (*kuśala-bhāvanā-svabhāva*).

For example, just as the diligent abandonment of the two evils is called "right effort" (*samyag-vyāyāma*), it is the same here: the cultivation that abandons unwholesome dharmas is also termed "cultivation. Just so...

Regarding the two phenomena of *saṃkṣepa* (concentration) and *vikṣepa* (distraction), each has its own causes and conditions; these should be distinguished together with their respective causes and conditions.
However, here, in accordance with the original phrasing, the word "together" (*ca*) is placed first.

As for "causes and conditions," this refers to the characteristics of reflecting on faults and reflecting on [the object], as well as the essential natures associated with these reflections—namely, restlessness (*auddhatya*) and sleep (*middha*). Within this context, concentration and distraction are as explained in the text.
This can be understood; however, for a detailed analysis, it is as explained extensively in the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

While that treatise speaks of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), this text speaks of obstacles to śamatha and vipaśyanā. If these are combined and referred to as "flowing" or "distracted," they constitute obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) due to their causal conditions, which differs from the explanation in that treatise.

Furthermore, regarding what the treatise calls "relying on the characteristics of observation," this is as extensively distinguished in the twenty-fourth fascicle and pertains to the subsequent scriptural passage.

When there is precisely the perception of before and after, as stated in the *Mahā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Vehicle), fascicle 28: "At the time of cultivating wisdom (*prajñā*), one cultivates the aspect of insight (*vipaśyanā*) with the perception of before and after;
that is, while standing one observes while sitting, or while sitting one observes while lying down, or while walking behind one observes what has been walked before.

This refers to the wisdom-insight (*prajñā-vipaśyanā*) abiding in the three periods of time and exhorting [the practitioner] toward sitting; this means that by means of the present mind, one contemplates what is yet to come.

Regarding the phrase "the coming of all conditioned phenomena": when they are in the present state of consciousness (*manas*), having already arisen, they are called "dwelling. Future dharmas have not yet arisen but are about to arise; therefore, they are called "sitting.
To observe those who are lying down while sitting can be said to mean observing past formations with the present consciousness.
Because the present consciousness is about to cease, it is called "sitting"; because the past has already passed away, it is called "lying down" within the present.
The world is also said to be "dwelling" (*sthita*) and "reclining" (*śayita*). This is discussed with reference to what has already arisen: in relation to the future, it is called "dwelling";
having dwelt, one then sits, which in relation to past phenomena is called "sitting.

Alternatively, when observing what preceded while walking behind, this refers to the present mind observing the immediately preceding mental engagement (*manasikāra*), that is, the mental engagement that has already arisen immediately following the one that just ceased.
The attention (*manasikāra*) that takes as its object that which has already ceased is called the "preliminary" (*pūrvagama*);

if immediately following this, a newly arising attention that takes as its object that which was previously ceased arises, it is called the "subsequent" (*paścādgama*). This relies on the observation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) through wisdom (*prajñā*). As the treatise states:
"It means relying on the perception of impurity (*aśubhasaṃjñā*) to observe matters such as hair and body hair. This belongs to the subsequent section of the sutra and should be applied accordingly.

Regarding the perception [of impurity], the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 28, states: "When practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one cultivates the perceptions of the upper and lower parts belonging to the category of tranquility (*śamatha*).
This means observing this body exactly as it resides and according to its nature—from the crown of the head above to the soles of the feet below—it is filled with various kinds of impurities;
that is to say, all the various things within this body, such as hair, body hair, nails, and teeth."

As explained extensively above, it should be understood that herein, for the sake of cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā, one cultivates the perception of superior radiance belonging to those two categories;
this is precisely what is meant here. As a basis for those two, one practices in accordance with them, fearing that the mind might sink into depression.
To uplift and stimulate the mind, one takes as an object the radiance of the various devas in the higher realms. By relying on this, one practices without inferiority therein.

That which is subsumed under the category of *vipaśyanā* (insight) eliminates the aforementioned causal conditions as well as the non-dispersal of that aggregate; it accords with the cultivation of the category of *śamatha* (calm abiding).

That which is subsumed under the category of *śamatha* eliminates the aforementioned dispersion of that aggregate as well as its causal conditions. The basis for these two is precisely the essence of their elimination.

This meaning applies generally to the cultivation of both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Their characteristics are mutually inclusive, and the bases for both rely upon this to establish the cultivation of distant insight (*dūravipaśyanā*).
The three kinds of light are as explained in the eleventh cited scripture;

therein, "my desire" is a general statement, and so on, through the phrases "and the perceptions of above and below," which are sequentially correlated, up to "not distracted, practicing in accordance with development.
This single phrase concludes the preceding points, while "far removed" and what follows correlate to those two bases in the eleventh [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
It is also said that the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) are for the most part similar to this.

Regarding the categories of meaning of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and the five powers (*pañcabala*), as stated in the text: in order to eliminate the five obstructions, there are exactly five antidotes—namely, because there are five obstructions such as lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) and so forth.
Their power subdues all afflictions (*kleśa*), though it does not constitute permanent severance; thus, one is not overcome by any of the celestial Māras.
The extent of what is overturned is as described in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*. As stated in the *Mahāśāstra* (Treatise on Great Matters), fascicle 29: "Faith is the foremost;

the others, such as diligence and so forth, are also called 'powers' (*bala*). The sūtras speak of the faculty of faith and the power of faith as being identical to the "purification through faith" (*avetyaprasāda*) within the [four] purifications.

The Blessed One spoke of them based on the principle of cause and effect, rather than because they are identical in essence to those [purifications]. This is because, once the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) have been attained, one's faith and the other [faculties]...

Because it is firm and capable of generating noble wisdom, the fifth [faculty] is called a faculty (*indriya*). Because it cannot be turned back by celestial Māras and the like, and because karma and afflictions cannot subdue it, it is called a power (*bala*).

The faculty of diligence (*vīrya-indriya*) and its corresponding power are the diligence within the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), which serves as the application for realizing the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛti-indriya*) and its corresponding power are the mindfulness within the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), which is able to sever all inversions (*viparyāsa*) without exception and brings about meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The faculties and powers (*indriya-bala*) are the four dhyānas, which serve as the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for realizing the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).

This is because those who have attained the first two fruits have not yet attained the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*), whereas only upon attaining the third fruit can one give rise to the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and attain meditative concentration. Based on this principle, the same applies to the fourth fruit.

Furthermore, [the faculty of wisdom] is mentioned briefly because it pertains only to those who possess the harmony [of the faculties], and not to those who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Thus, it is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).

Because power (*bala*) consists in the realization of the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) through the wisdom that takes the truths as its object, the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are explained according to their sequence as follows:

based on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and the extensive treatise [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*], they are summarized most concisely as being subsumed under three categories of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). These are:
the factors of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), vigor (*vīrya*), and joy (*prīti*); vigor, which acts as the spur; and wisdom (*prajñā*), which leads to renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).

Reaching [the goal] brings joy and movement, which are not in accordance with the characteristics of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). These three factors are subsumed under the category of tranquility (*śamatha*): namely, the factors of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Pliancy exists only within the concentrated mind; joy (*prīti*) is the state of mental delight; and equanimity is the state of impartiality that supports concentration.

Thus, the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*) is subsumed under two categories, as mindfulness serves as the basis for the preceding six factors. Regarding the remaining eight factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*), the *Śāstra* states: "The mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is exclusively non-... [text fragment].

Regarding the statement that [joy] is either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), this is explained in reference to the stages beyond the ground (*bhūmi*). That treatise explains it as applying to the stages prior to the ground as well.
As for the apparent contradiction between the two statements—that in the "branch of exertion" (*vīrya-niryyāṇāṅga*) it is a branch of purification (*viśuddhy-aṅga*)—there are two explanations:

first, because it supports wisdom (*prajñā*), it is merely termed "arousing" (*samuttejana*); second, because it leads to swift deliverance (*niryyāṇa*), it is also capable of abandoning afflictions (*kleśa*). This is the doctrine of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Regarding the benefit, as stated in the *Bodhisattva Sūtra*: "One gives rise to a mind of joy toward the Dharma, does not sink into despondency, and generates pure gladness (*prāmodya*);
body and mind are at ease. Reflecting on this meaning within the five cultivations and the attainment of the five fruits, one attains the bliss of the Dharma-garden (*dharmārāma-sukha*).

This refers to the remaining factors, which are all omitted here in this treatise and in the sūtras; thus, the two dharmas of joy (*prīti*) and tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) are absent from the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).

Wisdom alone realizes this; herein, based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one attains the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Since the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) induce the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are explained separately according to their specific meanings, yet there is no contradiction in principle.
Regarding the "abandoning of phenomena," herein greed and craving are forever eliminated; the distinction from what follows will be understood below.

As for the statement that "only greed and craving are forever eliminated," it is because greed is predominant within the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); this is as reconciled with the discussion on sensation (*vedanā*) in the sixth fascicle.

Among these, the remaining four [faculties] possess both cause and fruit and are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Only the single faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is exclusively wholesome or unwholesome; it is not indeterminate, nor is it a karmic fruit, because it is a mental dharma.
Furthermore, because it is a formless dharma, it is not subsumed under the training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā*), but is comprised solely by the two trainings [of concentration and wisdom].

As will be explained below in the commentary, all of these are according to my own interpretation. Why is there no "right intention" (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) among the faculties? Because there is no higher life-force (*jīvita*) [to support it]. Why is there no "right speech" (*samyag-vāc*)? [Because it is a vocal action, not a faculty.]

Are right speech, right action, and right livelihood exclusively factors of the path? As stated in [the *Abhidharmakośa*] 29: "The sudden arising of wisdom is called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), while long-term cultivation is called the Path of Meditation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
For this reason, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are only established as such within the Path of Meditation, not in the Path of Seeing.
Right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essential nature; it is capable of initiating speech, and although the Path of Seeing... [is characterized by that wisdom].

Since the meaning of speech is severed when Huike achieves realization, it is also solely cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and not the establishment of views (*dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, what is the reason for not establishing faith (*śraddhā*) as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?
For now, let us explain: although faith generally penetrates the untainted (*anāsrava*), at the time of the factors of enlightenment it is called "unshakeable faith" (*avekṣika-śraddhā*).

This is because the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) is beyond language, whereas faith in the Three Jewels gives rise to language; therefore, [faith] does not [function as a factor of enlightenment] within the Path of Vision.

If that were the case, why would the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) lack the "path of seeing" (*darśanamārga*)? It is because [the former] excels in seven respects. Therefore, faith, desire, and so forth are not established [as the path of seeing]. These seven respects are:

(1) the basis (*āśraya*), (2) the self-nature (*svabhāva*), (3) renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*), (4) benefit (*anuśaṃsa*), and (5–7) the three aspects of non-defilement (*asaṃkleśa*). Because these seven respects pertain to non-defiled bases, non-defiled natures, and non-defiled states, others are not mentioned;

as explained in detail in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Great Commentary), fascicle 29. Furthermore, it is established that faith consists of the "purities" (*avetyaprasāda*). Thus, [faith, etc.,] are not established [as the path of seeing].
Regarding the cultivation of the factor of enlightenment of great inquiry (*mahā-vitarka-sambodhy-aṅga*), as it is clearly explained in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:

"The basis of tranquility refers to the desire realm, because it is the basis for tranquility therein. The basis of detachment refers to the two upper realms, because they are the basis for detachment from desire.
The basis of cessation refers to the three factors already attained, because they lead toward the remainderless cessation. The basis of relinquishment refers to the three factors yet to come."

The continuity [of the argument] is not contradictory to this treatise, as it provides a distinct interpretation of the meaning. Regarding the "three dharmas," these are the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas).
As for where the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅgas) reside within the Mahāyāna, the text states: as found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Taishō 1509), fascicle 29, up to the passage:

"At that time, one obtains the seven factors of enlightenment; therefore, having first become a learner (śaikṣa) who has seen the path of the noble truths, one has forever severed and extinguished [the view of a self]."

Since all afflictions abandoned by the path of seeing have been eliminated, leaving only those to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, one knows that the correct view of the path of seeing consists of both non-conceptual and subsequently attained wisdom.
As stated in the *Mahāśāstra*: "The analytical branches [of the path] are taken as the essence of correct view.
By the predominant power of this correct view, there arise renunciation, non-ill will, and non-harming.
Discerning reflection is called right intention; that is, untainted volition constitutes the essence of right intention.
When such a state of reflection is characterized by the absence of ill-will and so forth, it is termed right intention. If one reflects and utters speech accordingly, it is termed right speech.

Taking the right view of the path of seeing and the other factors as the basis, these constitute the ten dharmas of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) and the fivefold body of dharma (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*).
What is the difference between this "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) and the "body of knowledge and vision of liberation"? This [latter] correct view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) pervades all;

it takes only a single object as its condition, whereas this [former] correct view pervades both principles (*nyāya*) and phenomena (*vastu*). Why must they both be called "correct view," such that their essence is one and the same? This interpretation has not yet been seen in the treatises (*śāstra*);
one should further examine whether they are different or the same and provide an explanation.

Among the ten dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) alone takes the principle (*tattva*) as its object, the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*) likewise takes the principle as its object;

thus, it is identical to the eye of wisdom. As for the body of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana-kāya*) taking the dharma of liberation (*vimukti*) within the body of liberation as its object, there are broad differences and similarities, all of which are explained below.

Question: What is the difference between right speech, right action, and right livelihood? Answer: Bodily and vocal actions prompted by non-hatred and non-delusion constitute right speech and right action.

Furthermore, bodily and vocal actions prompted by the wholesome root of non-attachment and a portion of non-delusion constitute right livelihood. There are five types of wrong livelihood which are the objects to be abandoned:
first, feigning extraordinary qualities for the sake of gain; second, [feigning such qualities] for the sake of gain... [text truncated].
1. To proclaim one's own virtues for the sake of gain and honor; 2. To practice divination of good and bad fortune and preach the Dharma to others for the sake of gain and honor; 3.
To speak in a loud voice and manifest an air of authority to inspire awe and respect in others for the sake of gain and honor; 4.

To claim to have received offerings in order to stir the hearts of people for the sake of gain and honor—this livelihood sustained by improper conditions is called "wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*); it is the opposite of right speech and action, and is termed "hated by the Noble Ones" (*ārya-dveṣya*).

The *Śīlaparivarta-śāstra* states: "The precepts realized and cherished, delighted in, and admired by the noble ones over a long period are called the 'precepts beloved by the noble ones' (*āryakānta-śīla*).

As for diligence, it is as previously explained. Herein, right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) serves as the factor of antidote; within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), it is subsumed under the factor of support.

Although it is a factor of support within the factors of enlightenment, it is also an antidote to the afflictions; specifically, the non-forgetfulness of what is wholesome is the antidote to forgetfulness.

The reason they differ is that "mindfulness" (smṛti) refers here to the sense of non-contradiction with what precedes it and as a basis for support, while "recollection" (anusmṛti) emphasizes the sense of excellence regarding subsequent antidotes;

thus, because each is based on a different meaning, their explanations differ. Regarding how these are subsumed within the three trainings, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Taishō 1509), fascicle 29, states:

"Right view, right thought, and right effort are wisdom; right mindfulness and right concentration are concentration; and right speech, right action, and right livelihood are morality. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 4... [text continues].
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the first three constitute the gateway to concentration (*samādhi*), while the last one constitutes the gateway to wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, this treatise maintains that all four foundations of mindfulness have wisdom as their essential nature. Moreover, in the *Mahāśāstra* (Treatise), fascicle 78, it is stated that diligence (*vīrya*) is subsumed within the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).

Furthermore, among the categories of merit (*puṇya*) and wisdom, diligence and concentration belong to the training in wisdom; and among the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*), the first four constitute the gateway to concentration, while the last one is [the gateway to wisdom].

In the *Huimen dalun* (Great Treatise on the Gate of Wisdom), fascicle 29, regarding the discussion of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and the Eightfold Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), the difference in their inclusion within mindfulness (*smṛti*) is as follows:

according to the actual reality, among the seven factors of enlightenment, "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is said to pervade both bases; whereas in the path factors (*mārgāṅga*), mindfulness is categorized under the factor of dharma (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) because it accords with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), thus belonging to the gate of concentration (*samādhimukha*).

According to actual reality, this does not contradict the examination of the seventh factor of enlightenment. Furthermore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (*Zhidu lun*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) include form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), mind (*citta*), and phenomena (*dharma*).

Regarding the question of why the gate of concentration (*samādhi-mukha*) takes joy (*prīti*) as its basis while the gate of wisdom (*prajñā-mukha*) is categorized differently under feeling (*vedanā*):

this *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) treats joy as a state of mental agitation and surging, and thus classifies it under the gate of wisdom. The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, however, discusses it from many perspectives and includes it within the category of concentration (*samādhi*), as it does not differentiate joy [from other factors] nor does it speak according to their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
If one were to speak according to their essential nature, all applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) take wisdom as their essential nature.

Regarding the categorization of the gates, the sequence of their characteristics differs from the preceding three; the former three constitute *samādhi* (concentration), while the latter one constitutes *prajñā* (wisdom).
As stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 78, diligence (*vīrya*) pertains to all three trainings, and because it serves as a general incentive, it is as explained in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.

Furthermore, within the categories of merit (*puṇya*) and wisdom (*jñāna*), diligence acts as the incentive for the three trainings, and the mind is entirely a factor of wisdom. As mentioned above, that which is able to generate wisdom through concentration is termed [wisdom].

Wisdom realizes actual merit, as discussed in the twelfth fascicle on the six *pāramitās*. Furthermore, regarding the inclusion of the first four among the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) as gates of concentration (*samādhi*):

why is diligence (*vīrya*) also considered a gate of concentration? This treatise treats it as a gate of wisdom (*prajñā*). Just as in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, diligence permeates all three trainings;
what hindrance is there to the first four faculties and powers being gates of concentration? As for mindfulness of the Dharma (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), it is applied accordingly.

The characteristics of conformity (*ānulomika*) are as previously discussed in the assembly. If that is so, why does the *Mahā-śāstra* state that diligence (*vīrya*) is the gateway to wisdom (*prajñā*)?

This is because it emphasizes the function of increasing the power of swift and sharp conformity through exertion and arousal. However, from the perspective of actual reality, this training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*) pervades all three [trainings]. When one reaches the stage of the *pāramitās*, the other assemblies should be interpreted accordingly to resolve any contradictions or difficulties.
One should further reflect upon this. As for the inclusion of the remaining characteristics, they are the same as those in the *Mahā-śāstra*; why is this so? [This requires further investigation.]

The investigation of speech, action, and livelihood are not established as factors of training (*śaikṣāṅga*), as can be understood from the previous discussion on the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

Why are joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) not included among the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*)? Because at the beginning of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one first attains the bliss of the Dharma; tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) arises immediately, and all afflictions are severed.

Joy, tranquility, and equanimity increase sequentially within the path of seeing as factors of enlightenment. Therefore, they exist [as such]; however, regarding the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the meaning of the factors of the Dharma increases over time.

Having attained the bliss of the Dharma and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), the various afflictions are gradually eliminated; thus, while their meanings may be hidden or manifest, they are not [inherently] factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).

Therefore, the three dharmas [of right view, right effort, and right mindfulness] do not exist [as distinct path-factors]. If that is so, one might object: "In the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), Right View, Right Effort, and Right Mindfulness should not exist. The answer is:

If one considers them from the perspective of their initial attainment, they are "view" (*darśana*) rather than "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). However, because the Path of Cultivation is distinguished by the seeking of the fruit through training, it is clearly manifest as the Path of Cultivation; therefore, these [factors] do exist therein.

Do the four dharmas, such as "seeing" (*darśana*), not constitute the path of seeing? Since the initial attainment of true wisdom is termed "discernment of dharmas" (*dharmapravicaya*), and although the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) also takes principle as its object, it is called "right view" (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) because the aspect of "dharma-meaning" is predominant;

thus, their sequence is established. As for the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) position that the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) belong to the path of cultivation while those of the path of seeing are excluded, this is as stated in the *Vibhāṣā*.
Now that this meaning has been newly established here, why labor further to construct [an alternative] interpretation?

Beyond these eight, no further categories are established extensively; rather, based on six conditions, they are analyzed and taught to inspire faith, purify hindrances, sever those hindrances, and attain the merit of purification.
Because of these six conditions, no further "increasing" meanings are established. Although wholesome dharmas exist that do not increase, they are not so designated;
the Path of Seeing is termed the "limbs of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*) simply because it first realizes *tathatā*, whereas the Path of Cultivation has already achieved this realization.
The noble factors (ārya-saṃkhyā) are obtained by means of eight, through which one attains that nirvāṇa; they are designated simply as the "limbs of the noble path" (*āryamārgāṅga*).

As stated in the lower fascicle of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, there is a sequence of the Eightfold Noble Path along with its rationale; upon examination, these consist of both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).

Regarding the four right practices (*samyak-pratipatti*), as stated in the second chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*: "Attaining abiding in happiness in the present life is called 'happiness' (*sukha*," which refers to the four fundamental dhyānas because wisdom (*prajñā*) and calmness (*śamatha*) are balanced;
being unbalanced in calmness and insight (*vipaśyanā*) is termed 'suffering' (*duḥkha*"). This is identical to the meaning of this [present] text.

Within this context, there may be references to the "transformation of faculties" (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), the "transformation of stages" (*bhūmi-parāvṛtti*), and the "transformation of persons" (*pudgala-parāvṛtti*), all of which pertain to the meaning of the Hīnayāna and are not our own school's tenet. Here, "transformation of faculties" refers specifically to the sharp or dull capacities.
One attains the distinctions of dhyāna through the faculties (*indriya*), stages (*bhūmi*), and degrees (*mārga*). "Degree" refers to the difference between the initial and final fruits;

for example, a *anāgāmin* entering the fourth dhyāna and an *arhat* entering the third do not know one another’s states. A *anāgāmin* does not know [the state of an *arhat*] by way of degree, nor does an *arhat* know it by way of stage.
Alternatively, a dull-facultied (*mṛdv-indriya*) *anāgāmin* may enter the fourth dhyāna, while a sharp-facultied (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*) *anāgāmin* [may enter a different stage].

Regarding the statement that one does not know what is below by means of the faculties (*indriya*) when entering the first dhyāna, nor by means of the stages (*bhūmi*), it is as explained extensively in the *Kṣudrakavastu* (Minor Treatise).

As for "slowness and speed" and "penetration such as the supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*): "slowness and speed" refers to dull and sharp faculties; "penetration" refers to spiritual practice (*pratipad*).

As stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Great Commentary), fascicle 63: "Among those who have attained the path of swift penetration (*kṣiprābhijñā-pratipad*) and have already seen the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*), there are furthermore ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet attained the path."

One who has already attained the immeasurable states based on sentient beings and is free from desire, and who has realized the supernormal power of knowledge regarding birth and death—this is called the purification of knowledge and vision.

Furthermore, regarding both the path of pleasant progress with slow superknowledge and the path of pleasant progress with quick superknowledge, for one who has already attained the practice and seen the truths, why speak of the "path of suffering progress with slow superknowledge"?
What is the intended meaning? It is simply that the "path" (mārga) refers to the causal basis; it is termed a "path" because it serves as the cause for its support.
Because it is not that which is to be remedied, it is called a "trace" (*pada*); other treatises are all the same in this regard, and there is no contradiction.

Regarding the nine types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the contradictions found in the twenty-sixth fascicle are reconciled as follows in the eleventh fascicle; the reconciliation here is explained in detail in the thirtieth fascicle.

The treatise states: "Regarding the taming [of the mind] amidst the causes of distraction, such as the phenomena of form (*rūpa*) and so forth," as explained in the *Mahāśāstra* (Treatise on the Great Vehicle), Chapter 30.

"Form and so forth" includes, by way of the term "and so forth," the attachment to the flavors of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), the three unwholesome roots (*trīṇy akuśalamūlāni*), the characteristics of male and female, and the pacification of evil discursive thoughts (*vitarka*), namely desire (*kāma*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).
Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), this refers to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) and so forth. "Equanimous maintenance" refers to cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Through repeated practice and cultivation, one attains a path that proceeds spontaneously without the effort of application; it proceeds spontaneously without the exertion of mental effort and is free from distraction.
The remaining explanations of the text are the same as this. However, it differs from the *Triṃśikā*, which uses the six powers to distinguish nine kinds of mind:
first, the power of hearing; second, the power of reflection; third, the power of mindfulness; fourth, the power of correct knowledge; fifth... [text fragment ends].
Through the power of application (*vīrya*), one practices six stages by means of the two powers of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*). These distinguish either two or three mental states:
namely, "internal abiding" (*adhyātma-sthāpana*)—which is making [the mind] abide—and "continuous abiding" (*saṃsthāpana*).

Although there is "stabilized abiding" (*avasthāpana*), it is not necessarily included here, because "stabilized abiding" is already accounted for within the power of mindfulness (*smṛti*) in the subsequent text. For this reason, some maintain that there are two [stages], while others maintain that there are three.
Because one abides in and remains close to the first three powers, there is no obstacle to the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*).
This establishes two: because of abiding (*sthiti*) and remaining close (*upasthiti*), one does not grasp [the object]; this distinct explanation of abiding divides abiding into two parts:

one part applies to the first two [powers], and one part applies to the latter one. The power of correct knowledge (*samyak-jñāna-bala*) establishes two; the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*) establishes two: namely, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and tranquility (*śamatha*).
Within the state of extreme tranquility and one-pointed concentration, the power of cultivation brings about singleness, which is then equally maintained;
the subsequent details may be understood according to the text.

Furthermore, there are four types of mental engagement (*manasikāra*) that subsume the nine stages of mind: (1) the mental engagement of forceful application (*balavāhana-manasikāra*), which occurs during internal placement (*sthāpanā*) and close placement (*saṃsthāpanā*).
Among these nine modes of mental engagement (*manasikāra*), how many are preliminary (*prayoga*) and how many are fundamental (*maula*)?

Within the seven types of mental engagement, there are two that operate with interruptions during the stages of *sthiti* (abiding), *upasthiti* (close abiding), *damana* (taming), *vyupaśamana* (pacification), and *ekotībhāva* (one-pointedness); three that operate without interruptions during the stage of *samādhi* (concentration);

and four that operate effortlessly (*anābhoga*) during the stage of *samatā-samādhi* (equanimous concentration). Among these nine, how many are preliminary and how many are fundamental? [The answer is: Seven are preliminary mental engagements.

How are these explained in relation to the categories of *sāsrava* (with outflows) and *anāsrava* (without outflows)? As explained extensively in the text, there are four kinds of *vipaśyanā*. To explain them generally:

*yāvadbhāvikatā* (the nature of all that exists) was previously translated as "knowledge according to measure" (*yathāmātra-jñāna*); *yathāvadbhāvikatā* (the nature of things as they truly are) is "knowledge according to reality" (*yathārtha-jñāna*).
"Universal investigation" refers to *sāsrava* wisdom that discriminates among phenomena; "thorough examination" refers to the preceding stage [of investigation].

"Distinctly and extensively investigating" refers to the four types of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*). "Observing" refers to knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), or because it is preceded by prior contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*).
The term "subsequently" indicates that it is uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).

"Thoroughly and carefully" means that either the preceding [wisdom] is also uncontaminated, or having generally realized all phenomena, one subsequently becomes uncontaminated and further investigates them in detail. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 30: "That is to say, regarding..."

Skillfulness regarding the objects of pure conduct, skillfulness regarding the objects of focus, and skillfulness regarding the objects for purifying afflictions—when one correctly contemplates and discerns the nature of all that exists, this is called "discernment" (*pravicaya*).
If, according to this meaning, the latter three of the seven phrases in the treatise were to have a separate substantial entity, it would not be so;
the latter three are simply the first phrase. That is to say, it refers to the most intense contemplation directed toward those very same objects of focus.
Discerning the nature of things as they are is called "ultimate discernment.

As explained in the treatise, regarding that same object of focus, one employs wisdom-concomitant conceptual attention to grasp its characteristics, conducting a thorough investigation and seeking it out with precise scrutiny;
this thorough examination is likewise consistent and not contradictory. As stated at length in the *Mahāśāstra*, fascicle 83: [the full explanation follows].
As stated in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, from fascicle eleven to fascicle twenty-six, and again in fascicle thirty-seven, paragraph eighty-three, it is recorded there:

"Regarding the one who discriminates all phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*): first, 'discrimination of phenomena' (*dharmapravicaya*) is explained; next, 'thorough discrimination' (*pravicaya*) is explained.

Because one has already attained the untainted (*anāsrava*) true attention (*manasikāra*), all untainted attentions associated with the objects of the Noble Truths are called 'discrimination of phenomena.'"
Regarding "discernment" (*pravicaya*): it refers to the comprehensive grasping of all categories of suffering phenomena as the Noble Truth of Suffering.
That is to say, untainted wisdom discerns the category of suffering as the Noble Truth of Suffering; this is called the discernment of all phenomena. Regarding "the most extreme discernment":

first, the general statement of this phrase is explained, followed by a further explanation of the "most extreme" aspect of discerning phenomena. To explain the general statement: each is analyzed individually.

Because it takes up all forms of suffering, such as birth, aging, and so forth, it is called "extreme discernment. One who discerns phenomena through extreme analysis relies upon this basis to discern the teachings of the *sūtras* and other scriptures;
that is, by relying on the suffering of birth and so forth, one discerns the teachings of the *sūtras* and other texts. Furthermore, "discernment" refers to definitive understanding (*pariccheda*).
"Understanding" (*parijñā*) refers to the application of attention and the utterance of speech regarding the objects of knowledge; thus, it is the most ultimate discernment.

"Discernment" (*vicaya*) refers to thorough determination (*pariccheda*). "Understanding" (*avabodha*) means having already understood; once speech has been uttered, one employs skillful means to seek and thoroughly discern the dharmas.
"Thorough determination" (*pariccheda*) refers to near-understanding (*upavicaya*). "Near-understanding" means having sought and reached certainty.

That which precedes it is the path of seeking, meaning that after understanding has occurred, it is explained by the first two phrases of the commentary. That which follows is the path of certainty, meaning the latter one.

Regarding the passage beginning with "thoroughly investigating the pervasiveness of phrases" (*padaparyeṣaṇā*), the preceding three knowledges (*jñāna*) pertain to both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*). They await the subsequent [knowledges] for their full realization;

the first two are untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that is provisionally described as increasing according to its objects, while the former is so called because it takes phenomena as its object, and the latter is correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) because it pertains to the nature of things as they are (*yathābhūtatā*).
The latter two are tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*). The first four are the thorough investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*), and the latter is as previously explained.
Regarding the two preceding [types of] true knowledge (*bhūta-jñāna*), although they are with-outflow (*sāsrava*), there is also the sense of grasping the outflow-free (*anāsrava*);

as for the two subsequent [types], although they are outflow-free, there is also the sense of grasping that which is prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*), whether taken collectively as "prior to the stages" or collectively as "outflow-free. There is no contradiction in this principle; examine and read it carefully, as it is the same as in the thirtieth fascicle.
Thus, vipaśyanā proceeds by way of three doors and six objects of focus. Regarding these three doors:

first, when one briefly reflects upon instructions, admonitions, and so forth, without yet having analyzed, measured, inferred, or investigated them, this is called wisdom that functions solely according to signs (*nimittānusāriṇī prajñā*).
Second, when one analyzes, infers, and investigates those very things, this is called the second [type], wisdom that follows investigation (*paryeṣaṇānusāriṇī*).
Once the wisdom of investigation has performed its analysis as established, one further examines it with scrutiny; this is called the third stage, the wisdom of investigative examination.

These are the three doors. If one seeks them in detail, the latter two doors correspond respectively to the two types of wisdom. Regarding their characteristics, if one follows the first characteristic, as stated in the twenty-sixth [section]:
"The first two phrases have textual evidence that they are *sāsrava* (with outflows) and so forth, and are treated as non-existent."

Regarding the observation of the outflows (*āsrava*), the first phrase refers to that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*). The first two phrases—namely, the eighty-third and the tenth fascicle—refer to that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Neither of these is included within this initial gate. This initial gate concerns the "with-outflows" aspect of the first two phrases;

as for the statement regarding "without-outflows," if one speaks of existence, it cannot be said that there are six matters. The first refers to the meaning (*artha*); that is, the existence of the meaning is itself the existence of the words.
As stated in the *Trayastriṃśa* [Sūtra], "The various desires have many faults and afflictions," and so forth; there are two kinds of things, namely internal and external.
Regarding these, there is no explanation as found in the *Trayastriṃśa* or in the subsequent passages.

That [text] explains the coarse characteristics of internal and external things by referring to internal and external craving (*rāga*); this [text], however, does not know [how to distinguish] the internal and external of all things.
"Identical in the three characteristics" refers to three kinds, namely: specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Next, "identical in the four categories" below the text refers to the white category (*śuklapakṣa*) and the black category (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).

Next, "identical as in the thirty-third [section]" means that all such desires follow the black category, up to the five periods of contention and so forth. "The times" refers to past, future, and present phenomena. Next, "identical as in the following text."
The *Triṃśatikā* states: "Regarding the three times, the six objects of desire, and the principles—namely the four kinds of reasoning.
The subsequent passage is the same as that in the *Triṃśatikā*, which says: "All desires are, from beginningless time, coarse and impure by nature, inconceivable, and so forth;

these measures are called 'principles' (*yukti*). Why is it that there are similarities and differences? The *Triṃśatikā* bases its explanation on the coarse characteristics within the six modes of inquiry.
The reason the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) are frequently applied specifically to the various desires is that this [treatise] discusses them universally; thus, there are differences.

Furthermore, the explanation of the coarse characteristics (*audārikalakṣaṇa*) in the subsequent text is identical to this passage, yet it contradicts other passages. These three gates and the six characteristics encompass all wisdom (*prajñā*).
Thus, these six characteristics and four types of wisdom are established according to the three types of awakening (*trividhabodhi*), as stated in the treatise. (One sentence.)

Regarding the six aspects within the investigation of meaning (*arthaparyeṣaṇā*), because one contemplates the meaning, there is the investigation of words (*niruktiparyeṣaṇā*). Because one investigates things (*vastu*) and their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the investigation of the limits of things (*vastuparyantatāparyeṣaṇā*) arises.
Among the six aspects, one is the entirety, namely "the thing" (*vastu*); one is a partial portion, namely "the specific characteristic.

This is because "the nature of all that exists" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which is the self-essence of all phenomena, whereas the "common characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is *tathatā* (suchness), and thus it is not [included in] the nature of all that exists.

When there is the investigation of the nature of things (*dharmatā-paryeṣaṇā*) regarding the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), because of the principle of time and logic, one gives rise to realization as it truly is (*yathābhūta-avabodha*). That which is called "contemplating the entity" (*vastu-vipaśyanā*)—namely, the nature and common characteristics as they are—is the principle that explains the individual and common characteristics among the preceding six characteristics. Below this, the six characteristics of impurity (*aśubha*) will also be clarified; these three sets of six characteristics are similar, yet the three types of realization (*avabodha*) differ. Question: Do the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) pertain to all four types of wisdom (*prajñā*)? If it is the case that the "nature of exhaustiveness" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) pertains only to the first two types of wisdom, then the latter two types of wisdom would not possess the six characteristics.

If one discusses the six characteristics in terms of their common application, there is a great obstacle to the purity of the knowledge of the six characteristics. This is because the treatise states:

"Among the three faculties (*indriya*), the first faculty apprehends fifteen moments of mind. The Dharma Master says: "What is the intention [behind] stating that the path of insight (*darśanamārga*) apprehends sixteen moments of mind?"

Do the faculty of knowing that one has known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) take fifteen moments of mind? No; because they have never before attained the simultaneous apprehension of the principles of the Truths (*satya*), the practice has not yet been perfected.
It is only at the sixteenth moment that the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) becomes complete, and thus it is called the faculty of knowing that one has known.

Although the previous three Truths are known repeatedly from the sixteenth moment onward, because the Truths have not yet been fully encompassed in their entirety, this is not yet termed "repeated" [knowing].

Because of concealment (*nivṛti*), fifteen moments of mind constitute the faculty of "initial knowledge" (*ājñendriya*). From the sixteenth moment of mind onward, it is called the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Regarding the stages of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is designated as both previously attained and not yet attained; however, in the stage of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is exclusively not yet attained, for all sixteen moments of the path of seeing are previously unattained.
It is called the faculty of "already known" because one knows [the truths] repeatedly. The sixteenth moment of mind is the faculty of patience (*kṣānti*).

Because the practice is perfected by being covered by the characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*), if one says that the fifteen moments of mind constitute the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and from the sixteenth moment onward it is called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), this is the doctrine of the Hīnayāna.
As stated in [the *Abhidharma-kośa*] 57: "When attaining the first fruit, the initial faculty (*indriya*) is both extinguished and abandoned.
That treatise previously stated: "The faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) up until the third fruit exists by way of enumeration," which refers to...
This [treatise] transcends the theory of human agency (*pauruṣeya-vāda*), for it is based on the sequence of persons; thus, when one attains the fruit, one abandons the initial faculty (*indriya*).

It should be understood by analogy that the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is likewise abandoned upon attaining the fruit of arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*). Regarding the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), its essence consists solely of the contaminated (*sāsrava*); it is not the essence of a primary faculty (*mūlendriya*). As the treatise states:

"Because it arises within a particular state, it is designated as the 'essence'—just as the wholesome factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) cultivated in the lower realms are said to have the body as their object."

The three feelings associated with the mental consciousness—faith and the others—are obtainable as the substance of these four roots of goodness. These four roots of goodness are all states of meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is exclusively non-concentrated (*vyagra*) and belongs only to the lower realms; it is not one of those roots of goodness.

When one enters contemplation and subsequently emerges from meditative absorption, whichever root of goodness one follows upon emerging, that faculty of sorrow arises taking *nirvāṇa* as its object, giving rise to grief and lamentation; thus, it is taken as the substance of the first root.

Question: The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) exists in the desire realm and thus constitutes the substance of the initial root; likewise, thought (*vitarka*) and observation (*vicāra*) exist in the desire realm and also constitute the substance of the initial roots such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
Answer: The faculty of sorrow, while residing in the stage of "Heat," does not constitute the actual substance of "Heat" and so forth;

it is merely the substance insofar as it arises at that specific stage, rather than being defined by its substantial reality. As for thought and observation, they exist only within the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of the lower realms.
The coarse and subtle characteristics of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) differ, such that they cannot arise within a single stage;

furthermore, if one considers *vitarka* (initial thought) to be the essence of the "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) and other stages, this is not tenable because *vitarka*, as a mental factor (*caitasika*), is not itself a faculty (*indriya*).

However, according to the text in fascicle thirteen, it is possible for *vitarka* and *vicāra* (sustained thought) to arise during the stages of warmth and so forth, and thus they may serve as its essence. This shall be explained in detail in fascicle twelve; for now, let us say "one of them."
