Furthermore, there are three further aspects: first, the intrinsic nature of the skillful means (*upāya-svabhāva*); second, the intrinsic nature of the vows (*praṇidhāna-svabhāva*); and third, the intrinsic nature of the power (*bala-svabhāva*). Among these, skillful means refers to giving that is never exhausted. Vows refer to the giving that is never interrupted. Power refers to the giving that is never overcome. These three constitute the intrinsic nature of giving. Furthermore, there are three further aspects: first, the intrinsic nature of the stage of faith and understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*); second, the intrinsic nature of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); and third, the intrinsic nature of the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*). Among these, the stage of faith and understanding refers to the giving of ordinary beings. The ten stages refer to the giving of Bodhisattvas. The stage of Buddhahood refers to the giving of the Tathāgatas. These three constitute the intrinsic nature of giving. Furthermore, there are three further aspects: first, the intrinsic nature of the past; second, the intrinsic nature of the future; and third, the intrinsic nature of the present. Among these, the past refers to giving already performed. The future refers to giving yet to be performed. The present refers to giving currently being performed. These three constitute the intrinsic nature of giving. Furthermore, there are three further aspects: first, the intrinsic nature of the internal; second, the intrinsic nature of the external; and third, the intrinsic nature of the internal-external. Among these, the internal refers to the giving of one's own body. The external refers to the giving of material wealth. The internal

It is said: "Wisdom (*jñāna*) is the seed from which insight (*prajñā*) arises; based on the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), giving (*dāna*) assists in the accomplishment of the *dharmakāya*, and is therefore also called the 'basis of self-nature.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, *prajñā* refers to wisdom regarding principles (*tattva-jñāna*);

*vipaśyanā* refers to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); it broadly distinguishes itself from calm abiding (*śamatha*). *Prajñā* refers to wisdom within the causal state (*hetu-bhūta-jñāna*); *tat-saṃprayukta-prajñā* refers to wisdom within the resultant state (*phala-bhūta-jñāna*)."

Regarding the explanation of the term "free from faults" within the context of "distancing oneself," the phrase "because one distances oneself from faults such as unequal pursuit" refers to what will later be explained under the "supremacy of skillful means.
This means that it is a fault to seek out evil causes, such as Maheśvara and other such [deities].

Furthermore, regarding the statement that within the transcendence of faults such as morality (*śīla*), one "removes the superimposition (*samāropa*) of a self," there are two interpretations. The first meaning is:

by means of upholding morality, one is able to remove the superimposition of a self-centered mind; it does not refer to the observance of the precepts of dogs and other such [animal] practices. The second meaning is:

the phrase "transcendence of faults such as morality" refers specifically to removing the superimposition, because morality follows after generosity (*dāna*); hence, the term "morality" is stated next.

Regarding the passage below this, since it specifically singles out the explanation that the grasping at superimposition (*samāropa*) is a fault of wisdom (*prajñā*), it says "according to what is appropriate.
As the *Mahā-śāstra* states, wisdom removes both superimposition and denial (*apavāda*); thus, one knows this is a fault of wisdom.
The seventh fascicle of the *Saṃgrahaṇī* also speaks in this way, and these [passages] do not contradict one another.

Regarding the unique interpretation of the term *śīla* (precepts), there are two aspects of "coolness": first, because *nirvāṇa* is called coolness, the treatise states that it is the basis upon which *nirvāṇa* relies;
second, because the precepts themselves are coolness, the treatise states that they are free from all the heat and ashes of anger.
This corresponds to the meaning of "coolness" as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 83.
The eleventh fascicle, Chapter on Dharmas (Dharmavarga).
The sequence of the chapter divisions is as in the first fascicle. This chapter has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer.

Within the answer, there are two sections: first, clarifying the dharmas common to the three vehicles; second, clarifying the specific dharmas of the bodhisattvas. Furthermore, for what causes and conditions [is this so]? Twelve.
Within the division of the Noble Teachings, the section on the Vaipulya is called the Bodhisattva-pāramitā Piṭaka. Regarding the first part of this [text], there are three sections:
first, distinguishing the teaching that expresses (the *vyañjana*) based on the truth of the principles expressed (*artha*) discussed previously;

second, [addressing] "For whom is this Tripiṭaka the sphere of activity? and below, clarifying the methods of practice—the object and the subject—based on what was previously established; third, [addressing] "How? and so forth.
Regarding skill in the phenomena (*dharma-kuśala*) among all phenomena, what is meant by skill in meaning (*artha-kuśala*) and skill in the composition of words and meanings?

There are two parts to the beginning: first, an explanation of the twelvefold division of the teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), and second, an explanation of the meaning of how they are subsumed within the three baskets (*tri-piṭaka*).

Within the first part, there is first a general enumeration and subsequently a detailed explanation. Regarding the *sūtra*, there are two sections: first, the analysis, and second, the questions and answers concerning how it is subsumed within the three baskets and so forth.

The middle section is divided into three parts: first, the mutual inclusion of the three collections (*piṭaka*); second, the establishment of the causes for the three collections; and third, the measure of the *dharmaskandha*.

Thus, as for the question of who takes these three collections as their sphere of activity, the second section follows what has been previously established to reveal the [agents] capable [of such practice].

Within the section on the phenomena that serve as objects of focus (*ālambana*), there are two parts: first, an explanation of the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*); second, a discernment of the four types of reasoning, which follows [the explanation of] the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*).
Within the first part, there are three sections: first, a discernment of the nature of the two non-dharmas that act as subjects (*ālambaka*);

second, a discernment of the characteristics of the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the subject that takes dharma as its object, including its having an object of focus and so forth; third, a specific elucidation of the distinctions among the objects of focus that are dharmas. This is the second [section].

Regarding the analysis of phenomena (*dharma*) within the context of the characteristics of objects of cognition and mental formations, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the analysis; second, the demonstration of its establishment.

The demonstration of the establishment has two sections: first, citing four meanings from the sūtras; second, explaining them individually. Regarding the distinctions among the objects of cognition (*ālambana*) of phenomena, there are two parts:

first, the question; second, the answer. The answer has two parts: first, the presentation; second, the explanation. This constitutes the detailed explanation of the distinct practices of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), as elucidated in the preceding fascicle.

The first part concerns the essence of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* through the object of meditation that is "pervasive throughout" (*sarvatraga*). The latter three clarify the actual practice of cultivation.

This cultivation is divided into three stages—initial, intermediate, and final—which correspond respectively to the initial, intermediate, and final phases of training, as one enters the stage of application (*prayoga*) only after these.

Within the subsequent stage of application, there are four principles; these four principles are the means for the stage of application, consisting of the four investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*) and the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*).

Regarding the four types of *yathābhūta-jñāna* (knowledge of reality as it is) at the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*), following the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), there are two principles by which one can enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) through the five yogas of both the preparatory (*pūrvaprayoga*) and fundamental (*maula*) stages. First, the heading; second, the detailed explanation.

The explanation has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Within the answer, there are two parts: first, the heading; second, the detailed explanation. Regarding the investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) of true knowledge, there are three sections each. First, the heading; next...

In the analysis of the subsequent conclusion, there are two parts to the five yogas: first, the question, and second, the answer. The answer has three sections: first, the heading; second, the analysis;

and third, the correlation of cause and effect. Within the analysis, there are five [points]. Regarding the initial four, the ancient interpretation holds that the four wholesome roots correspond respectively [to the four stages]; however, the present interpretation is not so.

This is because the first two are the wholesome roots of the preparatory means for entering [the path], while the mirror-like stage is in *uṣmagata* (heat) and *mūrdhan* (summit), and the clarity is in *kṣānti* (patience) and *laukikāgradharma* (supreme mundane dharma). Or alternatively:
The mirror is in the first three [stages]; the illumination of the first dharma is within the question-and-answer section. The initial question asks:
"How does one train so as to realize non-apprehension within the path of seeing? This is not a question regarding the seal of the first dharma or the two types of non-apprehension.

In the subsequent answer, there are two parts: first, it clarifies the provisions for completing the first eon; second, it clarifies hearing the Dharma, upholding it, and applying correct mental attention (yoniśo-manasikāra) in both directions.

Having generated the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), one subsequently induces the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*); thus, it is known that the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) follow the preparatory means (*prayoga*).

The response to the text consists of two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the scriptural proof. Within the explanation, there is first the explanation of the initial stage—the cultivation during the first eon—and subsequently the explanation of the four [stages] beginning with the faculties and powers.
Within this, there is first the explanation and subsequently the citation of the sutra.
In the third major section, "Skillfulness in the Meaning of the Text," there are two parts: first, the explanation of skillfulness; second, the explanation of establishing the stages.

Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the commentator explains how the five questions arise from the verses; second, the response cites the sūtra to establish that the five [questions] constitute four dharmas;

third, a specific elucidation of them. Regarding the establishment of the stages, there is first the question and then the answer. Within the answer, there are three parts: first, the treatise master...

Regarding the self-explanation of dwelling and non-dwelling: following the scriptural passage beginning with "Venerable One, you should know," the text cites scripture to explain dwelling and non-dwelling.

Because this follows the flow of the text, dwelling is explained first and non-dwelling is explained afterward. Subsequently, the passage beginning with "Therefore, the Blessed One, because of the dharma of dwelling, for the bhikṣu...
cites scripture to establish the meaning of the aforementioned "dharma of dwelling. This has three parts; first, it cites scripture as proof that [the dharma] exists.
The section on "Possessing the Attainment" concludes the preceding discussion on the non-abandonment of yoga;
this fourth major section, which explains the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, is further divided into six parts: first, a detailed exposition of its names and essence;

second, an explanation of contradictions regarding the Vaipulya; third, an interpretation of the intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) of the Vaipulya; and fourth, a definitive clarification of the Vaipulya.

The fifth [section] clarifies the *Vaipulya-phala* (the fruit of the Vaipulya), and the sixth clarifies the *Vaipulya-puṇya-utpāda* (the arising of merit from the Vaipulya). Within the first [of these], there are two parts:

first, the clarification of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), and second, the clarification of the name "Vaipulya. Within the clarification of the essential nature, there are two parts: first, the brief [explanation], and second, the extensive [explanation].

Within the brief [explanation], first is the question-and-answer regarding the *Pāramitā-piṭaka*, and second is the question-and-answer regarding the place of exposition. Within the first question, it asks: "By what causes and conditions [are the ten...]"?
Within the two divisions of the teaching, the division of Vaipulya is called the Bodhisattva-pāramitā-piṭaka and the practice of pāramitā.
"Piṭaka" refers to the teaching; because it is based on the Vaipulya portion, it is termed the teaching of the pāramitās.

In reality, not all other divisions are excluded from this piṭaka, as the Vaipulya is complete within them; therefore, it is specifically mentioned here. This is explained extensively in the *Vyākhyā*.

Regarding the second [section], there is first the question and subsequently the answer; herein, there are two gates: first, the elucidation of the five aspects (*pañca-lakṣaṇa*), and later, the elucidation of the four aspects (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only), there are seven [aspects] according to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and six kinds of aspects according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. These are subsumed within the *bodhicitta* (awakening mind). Among these, there are five;

the fifth consists of the three types of karma as the essential nature (*svabhāva*), which is not a mere characteristic (*nimitta*). This is the combined exposition of both the essence and the characteristics, as categorized under *vijñapti-mātratā* in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
These [treatises] merely explain the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and do not take the essence (*svabhāva*) as their subject, because the essence has its own separate section. Question:

Regarding the three types of excellence—first, excellence of skillful means (*upāya*), second, excellence of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and third, excellence of purity (*viśuddhi*)—since these three are subsumed within the *praṇidhāna* (vows), why are they combined here by extracting the essence separately?
Answer: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Wei-shi lun) does not explicitly mention "lineage" (*gotra*); it speaks only of six [types], namely those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
The absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) should be understood as the perfection of wisdom (*pāramitā*).

Furthermore, regarding the four characteristics explained later—namely, non-definitive dedication and so forth—the first two among these four characteristics are the causes with respect to the characteristic of the fruit, while the latter two are the essence and function of the fruit itself. In this context, based on the perfection of the fruit, one also partially attains them within the stage of the cause;
this should be reflected upon accordingly.
In the explanation of the general name, as found in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun), there are two successive sections; likewise, in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other texts, there are two parts:

first, the explanation of common terminology, and second, the explanation of non-common terminology. Within the section on the common, there are five successive sections. The *Akṣayamati-paripṛcchā-sūtra* is none other than the final six assemblies of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Regarding the phrase "distant from the self and the superimposition [of existence]," this refers to the various observances of the precepts which lead to my liberation.
Because I am one who increases [virtue], it should be understood that wrong patience, wrong diligence, and so forth are all to be known by this same principle.

Among the twelve sections, "not seeking worldly pleasure" distinguishes one from ordinary beings; furthermore, "supreme transcendence" distinguishes one from the Two Vehicles because of its great fruit.

Now, to explain: correctly seeking worldly pleasure is the foremost among great uninterrupted [actions] (*ānantarya*). The Middle [Treatise] says: "Benefiting oneself and others without interruption or deficiency. Herein, it is "benefit."
Because there is no separation or interval, one causes others to produce the fruit of giving; or, because self and other are non-dual, one practices "uninterrupted" and "constant.

This is because it is vast, supreme, and eternal. Regarding "without difficulty," because past acts such as sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) regarding giving do not act as obstacles, there are no hindrances.
Regarding "arousing the superior," this refers exclusively to the highest grade of patience (*kṣānti*).

This is because the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) consists of a single moment and cannot be divided; furthermore, as it lacks any manifest form, whereas at the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*), specifically the lower stage, there is a long duration and a manifest form.
Therefore, the treatise states that it is "free from the two marks of grasping. Thirdly, regarding the meaning of *pāramitā*:

since "supreme" (*parama*) refers to the supreme activity (*karman*), it means "the activity that has reached the other shore" (*pāra-gata*). Furthermore, since "supreme" (*parama*) refers to the meaning of "reaching" (*prāpti*), it means "that which has reached the other shore."
Fourth, reaching the other shore of the fruit; furthermore, reaching the other shore of the knowable—this should be subsumed under the fifth [topic], the teaching that reaches the other shore.
Although one practices with the ability to abandon transgressions, because the teaching is primary, it is described among the "unshared" [qualities].

Wisdom arising from others refers to the wisdom derived from the vocal sounds of others; this is *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom born of hearing). Proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) is *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom born of reflection); meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom born of cultivation), which is internal.

It is not mentioned separately because it is subsumed under realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*). Furthermore, the latter is explained as being subsumed under appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), while the former is explained as the three types of wisdom of the faith-follower (*śraddhānusārin*), and the latter as the three types of wisdom of the dharma-follower (*dharmānusārin*).

That which should be included within the seventh "Inclusion Gate" (saṃgraha-mukha) of the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages consists of an initial heading followed by an explanation.

Within the explanation, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the number; second, the specific manifestation [of the categories]. Regarding the fourth, the inclusion by ultimate meaning (paramārtha-saṃgraha), there are two parts:

first, inclusion by means of the wisdom of suchness (tathatā-jñāna); second, the analogy for the remaining inclusions. Within the first part, there are three: first, the heading; second, the manifestation; third, the conclusion. As for the analogy for the remaining, it refers to the inclusion by initial practice (prathama-caryā-saṃgraha).

Regarding the inclusion [of the perfections] by means of generosity (*dāna*), as explained in the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are various ways such as the inclusion of the six perfections within generosity, or their inclusion within merit (*puṇya*) or wisdom (*jñāna*).

All of these are known to be included within wisdom. Among the four [categories], the first three are included in wisdom; the remaining five are included in the latter one (wisdom). This is because the latter one includes its own essence, whereas the others do not include their own essence.
In the tenth section, the "Gate of Determination," there are two parts: first, the heading, and second, the explanation. Within the explanation of the means (*upāya*), the first part is as follows:

Regarding the distinctions within the remaining perfections after giving—namely, the initial and middle stages, the general and specific, and the intermediate differences—there are two parts. First, the headings for the fourfold distinctions;

second, the detailed explanation of the essence of giving, its pervasiveness and limitation, and its classification by lineage and planting. Within this demonstration, first is the heading and then the explanation. In the explanation, there are two parts:

first, the presentation of the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) through the mutual comparison of the various perfections, based on the distinction between the initial and final cultivation; second...

Regarding the two sets of four propositions based on purity and mixture: first the heading, then the explanation. Within the explanation, there is first the application [of the principle] and then the analogy.

In the second major section, "The Vaipulya [Sūtras] Contradicting [the Teachings]," there are two parts: first, the failure to understand and the resulting fear; second, the arising of understanding and the inability to transcend.

Within the latter, there is first the question and then the answer. Within the answer, there is first the logical response and then the citation of evidence. Within the logical response, there are three parts.

First, the two meanings are stated; next, the two are explained individually; finally, they are concluded with citations of proof. Within this section, first there is the general [explanation], followed by the specific.
In the specific explanation, first there is the inquiry regarding the twenty-eight views, next there is the individual interpretation, and finally there is the explanation of the reasons.

In the third major section on the underlying intent (*samdhāya*), there are two parts: first, the explanation of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); second, the explanation of [the scriptural passages on] non-arising, non-ceasing, and so forth.

Regarding the first of these, there is first the question and then the answer. Within the answer, there are three sections: first, an explanation based solely upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); second, an explanation based upon the three natures (*trisvabhāva*);

and third, a summary that establishes the conclusion. Regarding the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the presentation of the four gates; second, the explanation of their meaning. Based upon...

Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the first section presents the headings and the latter provides the explanation of "non-arising," "non-ceasing," and so forth; this consists of an initial question followed by a fivefold answer. The fourth major section, which resolves these points, has two parts:

first, the explanation of the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*), and second, the explanation of the esoteric meaning (*saṃdhi*). Within the first part, there is an initial heading followed by the explanation;

within that explanation, there is first an inquiry and a listing [of categories], followed by their individual exposition. Within the explanation of the esoteric meaning, there are likewise two parts: first, the heading, and second, the explanation.
In the explanation of the middle [section], first there is the interrogation and enumeration, followed by the detailed exposition.
The fifth major section, which clarifies the five fruits, is divided into two parts: first, the enumeration of the five fruits; second, the clarification of the five cultivations.

Within the first part, there is first the question and then the answer. The answer consists of three sections: first, a general statement of the answer; second, a detailed enumeration of the answer; and third, an extensive explanation of the answer.
The explanation of the answer has two parts: first, the presentation of the praise based on three types; second, the individual explanation of the skillful means (*upāya*).

Regarding the statement that "fearless giving (*abhaya-dāna*) exists in all places," this is based on one type of giving as it applies generally across the six perfections; in reality, the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*) is also equal [to them].
There are four intentions: first, to remove the obstacle of fear; second, to remove the obstacle of indolence; third, to remove the obstacle of contempt... [text truncated]
The fact that one must practice under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas before hearing this sutra and so forth constitutes the fourth removal of the five obstacles, as can be understood from the text.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* does not go as far as this. However, hearing that the Buddha Prabhūtaratna appeared here spontaneously, along with the distinctions of the four separate secrets and other such points, is largely consistent in its remaining meaning.
As for "well-abiding in inversion," one knows that those are the four inversions.

Reversing this, to overturn [the correct view] constitutes "inversion" (*viparyāsa*); each is based on a distinct meaning and thus they do not contradict one another. Regarding the sevenfold distinctions:
first, as for the "spiritual lineage" (*gotra*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Śāriputra practiced the bodhisattva path for sixty *kalpas*.

According to the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra*, by practicing the ten practices such as faith for one, two, or even up to ten *kalpas*, one attains entry into the ten stages (*bhūmi*) over the course of *kalpas*.
There is no difference in the duration of time, whether long or short, as stated in the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*.
Śāriputra practiced the bodhisattva path for eighty thousand kalpas and yet regressed because he had not yet attained the dharma of the stage of liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*).

Nevertheless, even so, he surpassed those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of sharp faculties who have not yet reached the seventh stage, the Stage of Right Mind (*samyak-citta-vihāra*), among the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Therefore, within this context, one should examine the practice of benefiting oneself and others.

Regarding which stage corresponds to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, for now we shall explain it according to the seven stages (*bhūmi*). Thus, "lineage" (*gotra*) refers to the Stage of Lineage (*gotrabhūmi*).

"Generating the mind" (*cittotpāda*) and "generosity through resolute conviction" (*adhimukti-caryā*) are subsumed under the Stage of Practice through Resolute Conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*). "Generosity that involves grasping" (*parigraha-dāna*) is the first [stage] of the Stage of Pure Superior Intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*), because at this point one begins to gather both oneself and others.

"Generosity without grasping" (*aparigraha-dāna*) pertains to the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh stages; these constitute the Stage of Correct Practice (*pratipatti-bhūmi*). All of these are included therein.

Although the stages (*bhūmi*) are already free from grasping (*anupādāna*), this state possesses both self-benefit and benefit for others. On the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), these two benefits are newly established;

on the sixth stage, they are superior because of the non-grasping of the three spheres (*tri-maṇḍala-pariśuddhi*). It is called the "contemplation of the true meaning" (*tattvārtha-darśana*) because it realizes and encompasses [the truth], and thus there is no grasping.

This refers to the giving of the eighth and ninth stages, which constitute the Stage of Definitive Practice (*niyata-caryā-bhūmi*), as well as the preceding seven stages. Although one is able to manifest material resources (*sambhāra*) through transformation, [it is still superior].
Although one gives material wealth and the like, one has not yet attained mastery; thus, one still practices gathering and accumulating before giving.
In this stage, it is not so, and is therefore called "without gathering. Giving according to circumstances refers to the tenth stage, which is a portion of the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*).

Because this seventh [stage] is the Tathāgata, he gives in accordance with the capacities and needs of beings, like clouds raining down the Dharma and so forth; hence it is called "maturation" (*vipāka*).

Among the fruits, there is great wealth: first, a favorable rebirth; second, freedom from enmity; third, indestructibility; fourth, the non-disruption of the gateway to virtuous deeds, which results in abundant joy and happiness;
fifth, being honored among sentient beings as a fruit of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); and the fruit of the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*), which is free from impairment;

and the fruit of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which does not engage in discrimination between self and others. These constitute the great fruits, which are subsumed within the fruit of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Regarding "sentient beings" (*sattva*), according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the great fruit is the fruit of patience (*kṣānti*). Now, the correct interpretation states that "veneration by sentient beings" is the fruit of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding "absence of harm within one's own body" and the "vast fruit," consult the sixth external base (*bāhyāyatana*) in the third chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Regarding the cultivation of the six types of intention based on the underlying disposition (*āśaya*), as detailed in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are three modes of mental attention (*manasikāra*).

The designations established differ according to their respective intentions. That treatise, concerning the offering made to the Tathāgata, refers to every single moment from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood:
at each and every moment, one relinquishes all body and life;

at each and every moment, amidst blazing fires, one constantly lacks all requisites while practicing the six *pāramitās* with all modes of conduct, never feeling weary or satisfied. This is stated in reference to each individual [moment].
Because it occurs in a single moment, it relinquishes all objects; its initial designation is "vast," yet in reality, it is also characterized by insatiability.

Thus, through uninterrupted cultivation, it is also called "long-term intention. This "insatiability" is merely another name for that same essence when considered from a different perspective regarding its scope.
In this treatise, it refers to the lack of satiety even when giving to all sentient beings universally; this is simply a difference in meaning based upon the preceding entity.

The name "insatiable intention" (*an-alaṃpratyaya*) is a synonym for "long duration. Because one practices over a long period until reaching enlightenment, such that not even a single moment involves regression or interruption, it is called "vast" (*vipula*).
In the *Treatise on Non-Differentiation*, the fourth [name] is "gratitude" (*upakāra*);
in that treatise, it is called "bearing a debt of gratitude," which is a synonym for this. When giving to sentient beings, one does not hope for a return of gratitude in the future.

The term "uncontaminated" (*akliṣṭa*) in this treatise refers to the intention [of not seeking reward], whereas the intention that all sentient beings, through returning the gift, may obtain superior fruits is called "great resolve" (*mahāśaya*) in that treatise.

In this treatise, not hoping for gratitude from sentient beings is called "uncontaminated," while in that treatise, referring to sentient beings themselves obtaining superior fruits is called "great resolve.
The sixth [point] is termed "pure goodness" (*viśuddha-kuśala*) in that [treatise], while it is termed "excellent goodness" (*praśasta-kuśala*) in this one; thus they differ.

These six types of mental engagement (*manasikāra*) are so named because they approximate the six perfections (*pāramitā*); since each individual mental engagement is permeated by the mental engagements [of the perfections], they too approximate the six perfections.
Other minor categories differ significantly, and as the text would become overly verbose, I have not cited them here.

The six mental engagements are subsumed within three types of mental engagement: first, cherishing (*adhimukti*); second, sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); and third, aspiration (*praṇidhāna*). These are based upon reliance.

Regarding the cultivation of skillful means (*upāya*), the Dharma Master says: "The basis (*āśraya*) refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); skillful means refers to that which precedes the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*).

Because one trains in the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) prior to the stages and [attains] non-conceptual [wisdom] upon the stages, it is called 'skillful means. Furthermore, the basis and skillful means are themselves non-conceptual wisdom;
taking this as the skillful means, the three spheres attain purification. Moreover, because of the correct cause (correct wisdom) and the correct fruit..."
Wisdom serves as the means because it is able to bring the fruit to fulfillment by purifying the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*).
Next, the basis for mastery is explained; regarding the "three spheres," the Dharma Master says there are two interpretations:
first, the purity of body, speech, and mind is called the three spheres; second, the giver, the recipient, and the object given are called the three spheres. 10.

The eighth is "sustenance" (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which refers to the phrase "possessing power" at the beginning of the sūtra; it is the application of diligence (*prayoga-vīrya*) that sustains the full realization of the roots of virtue.
Because one is able to realize awakening through this application, at the time of full realization, there is no occasion where this [diligence] is not present.

Thus, when practicing the diligence of non-cowardice, even if the mind experiences those sufferings, there is no retreat or discouragement. Being unmoved by the afflictions of others is called "non-retreat."

The transformation of unremitting diligence in practice is called "lack of complacency. As it says in the Sūtra: "Possessing courage, firmness, and ferocity, one does not abandon the yoke of the wholesome.

The meaning here is that, just as conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-prajñā*) is termed "entry into the great stages" (*mahābhūmi-praveśa*) because it serves as their support, so too this [diligence] acts as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
There are further passages where the sequence differs; consult the seventh fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* for details. (18) Support.

Regarding how many precepts the Buddha possesses: it is said that he possesses all three types of precepts. Within the category of the *prātimokṣa* (individual liberation) precepts, there are both those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*).

Because the Buddha’s body possesses the specific prevention of wrongdoing (*pratikṣepa-virati*) and the distant counteractive remedy (*dūre-bhāga-pratipakṣa*), he possesses them. If he possessed only those with outflows, he would lack the specific prevention of wrongdoing and thus would not be complete.

According to the meaning, when he is complete [in these], he possesses the other two types of precepts as well: the absence of enmity and harm, and the state of being at peace and free from suffering.

Regarding the functions of the meanings of "receiving" (*pratigraha*), there is no contradiction whether they exist or do not exist. The patience of reality (*dharmatā-kṣānti*) likewise possesses the functions of diligence (*vīrya*) and concentration (*samādhi*);

thus, it is also possible for the treatise to be complete according to the arising of its characteristics, as in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. In that [treatise], there is only the third, diligence, and lacks the first two.

Among the types of wisdom (*prajñā*), the wisdom that takes conventional reality as its object is so called because it is an applied knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*); such [wisdom] does not exist in the Buddha-body. If it were absent...

Regarding the contaminated preparatory stages (*sāsrava-prayoga*) from the eighth stage upward, there are also those that, according to their meaning, are no different from the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Even if such cases exist, they do not pose an obstacle;

rather, it is based on the absence [of such distinctions] at that time that this is considered optimal. As for these eighteen modes of sustenance (*dhṛti*), they may be accepted as applicable when discussed in general terms.

However, regarding the preceding contaminated stages, how many modes of sustenance are fully present? The explanation states: If one considers them in accordance with the objects (*viṣaya*) and the mental aspects (*ākāra*) produced therein, they can also be fully present as eighteen.

If we consider them by way of their essential nature (*tattva*), there is both completeness and incompleteness. For instance, within the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), the "patience that scrutinizes phenomena" (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*) gives rise to wisdom by taking the truths as its object.

As explained in the ninth fascicle regarding the patience that scrutinizes phenomena: if it is still on the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), it is called "knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*); once one has entered the grounds, it is then termed "patience.

The stage prior to the grounds is as previously explained in the eighth fascicle concerning the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*), "summit" (*mūrdhan*), and so forth.

As for the name "patience that accords with the truths" (*anulomikī kṣānti*), this is also designated according to its meaning as being similar to what precedes the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*). It is not yet the patience that arises regarding the truths. If it were already the patience that has arisen, how would it differ from the patience on the actual stages?

Therefore, one knows that it certainly does not exist [as such]. Furthermore, among the types of wisdom, that which takes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as its object is exclusively non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

If, prior to the stages, one takes principle (*li*) as an object, this is merely the "dharma-as-object" (*dharmālambana*); while it is spoken of as "meaning" (*artha*) in a conventional sense, in terms of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), it is not [non-conceptual wisdom]. Moreover, it is also...
Regarding the distinction between conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-prajñā*) [and other types], the treatise states: "By means of this, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Therefore, it is known that even prior to the stages, its substance does not exist [as a distinct entity]. If categorized by the sixteen aspects, it may be either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).

These two preceding types are not yet clearly defined in principle. If categorized by the complete set of objects, there are eighteen; however, regarding the point of their arising, according to the treatise, there are further cases where they are incomplete.
Read this carefully and seek its meaning.

Among the three types within each of the six pāramitās, as explained in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra (Taishō 1509), fascicle 78, the first is the precept of abandoning unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma-virati-śīla*), which corresponds here to the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint) consisting of the sevenfold non-informative (*avijñapti*) precepts.
The second is the precept of generating wholesome states (*kuśala-dharma-samutthāna-śīla*), which corresponds here to...

The precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), when considered in relation to virtue from the perspective of the aforementioned restraints (*saṃvara*), is called the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas.

Third is the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*); the meaning of the text here is that this is also the transformative sense of the preceding precepts, capable of producing them.

As explained in the *Śīlaparivarta* (Chapter on Ethics) of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, regarding the restraint of ethics (*saṃvara-śīla*), it says: "This very [restraint] is able to encompass and establish the latter two types of ethical discipline (*śīla*)."

Based on this protection, one is able to cultivate offerings to the Buddhas and so forth; this refers to the second precept. Furthermore, it is able to benefit sentient beings, which refers to the third precept.
Discussing it in this way, the first [precept] arises first, while the latter two do not necessarily take the preceding restraint as their essence.
Moreover, regarding diligence, one type is said to be that which is unbeneficial, while the second type refers to that which transforms into rebirth.

If one considers this essence as a single category yet divides it into many stages, the preceding precepts should likewise be understood as "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) because they arise successively.

If, according to the previous explanation, the subsequent [precepts] arise through transformation from the preceding ones, why is it that for those that ascend further, "transformation" is not mentioned?

This is because, when analyzed in this way, it is not necessarily the same preceding essence; since the term "transformation" here refers to arising based on a different state, it does not imply identity of essence.
I also consider that what is heard in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* is likewise a sequential progression. A definitive great treatise states:
"Non-conceptual wisdom is tranquil, supremely tranquil, faultless, the antidote to the manifold sufferings of afflictions, and a joyful dwelling in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

This treatise speaks directly of "joyful dwelling in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*). According to this treatise, regarding whether it is with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), one attains [the state described] in the great treatise exclusively.

Regarding the statement "untainted" (*anāsrava*): from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, this is discussed in terms of the superior [attainments], because of the use of such expressions as "existence" and "non-existence" in relation to conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

It is also said that the third [stage] "induces" (*āvahati*) this treatise; for the mindless meditative absorption (*acittaka-samādhi*) is able to induce benefit for sentient beings. Alternatively, they are called "induced" because they arise in successive order.

Regarding existence and non-existence, these should be further considered in accordance with what was previously reconciled. As for the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the six perfections (*pāramitā*), it is wealth (*dharma*).

The giving of material things (*āmiṣadāna*) has the four or five sense objects as its essence; the giving of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*) has non-attachment (*alobha*) as its nature. According to the subsequent text, the ethical discipline (*śīla*) consists of the five perfections (*pāramitā*):

among these, the discipline of benefiting sentient beings is included within ethical discipline; the patience of enduring enmity and harm is included within patience; the diligence of benefiting sentient beings is included within diligence;
the meditative concentration of benefiting sentient beings is included within meditative concentration; and the wisdom directed toward sentient beings is included within wisdom.
The term *kuśala* (wholesome) is explained according to its meaning or etymology, or even as that which is associated with wisdom (*prajñā-saṃprayukta*).

One should know that "wisdom" is as explained below in the commentary on the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*). In the subsequent section concerning the nature of the six *pāramitās*, the *śīla* of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) encompasses all six types;
specifically, within this *śīla*, the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* includes that which enables the attainment of the powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth.

All Buddha-dharmas are called "precepts" (*śīla*). Within patience (*kṣānti*), they consist of the patient acceptance of the investigation of dharmas (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*); within diligence (*vīrya*), they consist of either the preparatory application (*prayoga*) or the donning of armor (*saṃnāha*);

within concentration (*samādhi*), they consist of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that are induced; within wisdom (*prajñā*), they consist of either the wisdom that takes conventional reality as its object or the wisdom that takes ultimate reality as its object;

or, in the case of giving (*dāna*), they take non-attachment (*alobha*) as their nature. As stated in the eleventh fascicle, they may have the three types of action (*trikarma*) as their essence, or they may have wisdom as their nature.
Alternatively, it may have the category of desire (*chanda*) as its essence; or, regarding fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), while one part of giving possesses it, the other five do not.
Dharma-giving possesses all six, whereas the others possess only fearlessness. Alternatively, according to the meaning, among the six there is the sense of fearlessness;
that which corresponds to the sense of dharma-giving has this as its essence, while that which does not correspond follows the essence of its own respective *pāramitā*. Question: Great!
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Śāriputra cultivated the bodhisattva path for sixty *kalpas* (as recorded in the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*).
According to the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, those who regress after eighty thousand *kalpas* have not yet attained the stage of liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-dharma*).

According to the *Ratnakaranda-sūtra*, if one cultivates the ten practices, such as faith, for one *kalpa*, two *kalpas*, or even up to ten *kalpas*, one attains entry into the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). The Dharma Master says this is "comprehending the wholesome" (*kuśala-saṃgraha*).

The *dharma-śīla* (Dharma-precept) is defined by the subsequent passage as having the nature of the bodhicitta, the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, and the three types of action (*karma-yoga*).

The ten *pāramitās* are identical to this. The *sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of acting for the benefit of sentient beings) has the same essence as the preceding two precepts, because it employs these precepts to establish sentient beings in the happy realms and the three vehicles (*yāna*).
According to the subsequent passage, its specific essence is the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*).

The four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth have as their essence purely altruistic conduct; their further nature is explained at length in other chapters. Regarding the lineage (*gotra*) and its cultivation (*vāsanā*), they are explained extensively in other locations.

The treatise states that "majestic power" (*anubhāva*) refers only to the eighth and ninth stages and does not include the tenth, because the tenth stage is the stage of fulfillment (*niṣpanna-bhūmi*).
Regarding the tenth stage, among the five fruits of merit, the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) is explained as follows:
as explained in the *Mahā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Vehicle), fascicle 78, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* also contains six types which are identical to those mentioned in this text.

The treatise states: First, the attainment of great wealth; as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun), fascicle seven, says, "that which is subsumed under prosperity and nobility" refers to the excellence of giving (*dāna*).
Second, rebirth in the happy realms (*sugati*); as the *Saṃgraha* says, "that which is subsumed under noble birth" refers to the excellence of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Third, being without enmity or ruin and possessing abundant joy and happiness; as the *Saṃgraha* says, "that which is subsumed under having great allies and great kin" refers to patience (*kṣānti*).
"Victory" refers to the patience of practice, because all return for support and because there is no enmity or harm;
the meaning of this passage is that those endowed with *prajñā* have all sentient beings as their followers, as their expectations differ. Fourth, being the lord of sentient beings:
here, the term "venerable among sentient beings" is used; the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "The application of great undertakings is accomplished."

“Comprehension” refers to the vast and extensive undertaking that is the excellence of diligence; it means that within such [undertakings], one exerts effort, which is called "application" (*prayoga*), and because all tasks are accomplished, it is called "attainment" (*niṣpatti*).
Fifth, “the body being free from harm” is the excellence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). As the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states:

“It is comprised of being free from afflictions and harms, and having a nature of attenuated defilements (*rajas-mala*); this is what is comprised by meditative concentration, for it is through concentration that [such results] are brought about.”

The power of the Dharma (*dharmaprabhāva*) arises from this very meditative concentration; because the various afflictions are suppressed and do not arise, the nature of their defilements becomes thin.

Regarding the "great lineage of the six realms of existence" (*ṣaḍbhavānām mahākulam*), it refers to the broad and great clans within this [state]. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "That which consists in thoroughly knowing all crafts, treatises, and fields of knowledge is the excellence of wisdom (*prajñāviśeṣa*);
that is based on self-benefit, while this is based on the benefit of others. Upon examining the *Samuccaya*, this is so.

The *vyañjana* (phrasing) is not a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*), but rather a dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), because skillful knowledge of the crafts, treatises, and fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Since the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains [the fruits] in terms of the ripened fruit, it is stated that the "vast majority" (*bāhulika*) are included within the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the general explanation of the benefits (*anuśaṃsa*) therein. Moreover, skillful knowledge of the crafts and so forth is a dominant benefit (*adhipatyanuśaṃsa*) of wisdom; for this reason, it is considered a minor [benefit] compared to others.
Because it is supported by those who possess wisdom and learning, it possesses vast and great branches and leaves; this is also a fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).

Examining this closely, one determines that [qualities] such as freedom from affliction and harm are not necessarily fruits of maturation. This applies generally and specifically to the distinctions of retribution and maturation.

To be thoroughly familiar with these details means to inquire into their specific differences. "Exhortation" refers to verbal action (*vāk-karman*); "rejoicing" refers to bodily action (*kāya-karman*); and "delight" is...
Regarding mental action (*manas-karman*), there are textual explanations stating that one may simply exhort others to train and then rejoice with sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*);

I have forgotten where this was discussed and it should be sought in the *Prajñā-śāstra*. It says: "The perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) comprises the six [perfections]: material goods, fearlessness, and the Dharma;
herein, the first, second, and third are called the 'abiding in practice' (*pratipatti-sthiti*). Wuxing states: "Within the nature of giving, the six perfections are presently present."

Because the *Prajñāpāramitā* is subsumed under the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), the giving of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), and the giving of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*, *dharmadāna*), the treatise states: "Giving" refers to the giving of material wealth;

"fearlessness" refers to the remaining five [perfections], because they do not constitute the substance of material wealth. Thus, it says that "giving" is the giving of material wealth, while the remaining five are taken as the substance of fearlessness.

It says that "fearlessness" refers to the remaining five because they are distinct from the giving of material wealth. Therefore, it does not say that there are six kinds of fearlessness, for fearlessness itself is material wealth.
Since all forms of giving are termed "Dharma-giving," it is said that Dharma-giving encompasses all six [perfections].
Regarding their function of sustaining the eighteen [dhātus], one may take them either collectively or individually, as reconciled above.

Since the force of this passage does not exclude the other five [perfections] among the three types, and since the remaining six are entirely Dharma-giving and are never excluded, they would otherwise be conflated; however, this is not the case, for there must be distinctions.
As previously understood from having examined the *Ekavyavahāra-mukha*, because all [practices] are practiced as giving, it appears as if they are taken collectively.

Regarding the fifth chapter of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-viniścaya*, which extensively explains "pure" and "mixed," the treatise itself states that when one practices only for oneself without looking toward others, it is "pure";

when it is directed toward others, it is "mixed. Furthermore, if one relies solely on the practice of giving, it is called "pure," whereas if it is contrasted with the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*), it is called "mixed" giving.

Regarding the attainment of the three phrases and the remaining four or five phrases, because subsequent factors do not depend on preceding ones while preceding ones depend on those that follow, there are three-phrase and four-phrase formulations, totaling seventy-eight.

As for the mutual inclusion of the three trainings (*śikṣā*), the first three constitute the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*), the one regarding concentration (*samādhi*) constitutes the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitutes the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
This differs from the case where diligence (*vīrya*) is common to all three trainings, as explained in the tenth fascicle within the section on the eight branches of the path (*aṣṭāṅga-mārga*).
Regarding the explanation of what is subsumed under merit (*puṇya*) and wisdom (*jñāna*): the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) is merit, while wisdom (*prajñā*) is wisdom;
diligence (*vīrya*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) pertain to both merit and wisdom. In some instances, the first five [perfections] are merit and the last one is wisdom;

in others, the first three are merit and the latter three are wisdom; and in yet other instances, the first three along with meditative concentration are merit and wisdom, while the last one is wisdom.

Vigor pertains to both [merit and wisdom]. In some instances, the first three [perfections] and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are designated as merit, while wisdom (*prajñā*) is designated as knowledge.
Alternatively, when concentration suppresses afflictions, it is described as knowledge in accordance with wisdom; when its essential nature is emphasized, it is called merit.

Furthermore, some define merit in terms of benefiting others, while the latter one is defined as knowledge in accordance with the preceding three in terms of self-benefit. Or, there are those who [define them] by means of vigor...

The three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) pervade both merit (*puṇya*) and wisdom (*jñāna*). Alternatively, it may be that because they are previously discussed in terms of their pervasive characteristics, the "pervasive" exertion (*vyāyāma*) that manifests as diligence (*vīrya*) is also merit.

Or, according to the actual fact, the pervasive exertion of the three trainings pervades both merit and wisdom. Or, by way of emphasizing the increase of wisdom through exertion, it is called "wisdom"; this should be understood according to its correspondence.

As for why, in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, there are only four perfections (*pāramitā*) [in certain contexts], one should consult the commentary to reconcile this. Why is it that in other cases there are only four?

Because the first six have the [first] three as their auxiliaries, the first three take skillful means (*upāya*) as their auxiliaries; because the first three comprise three [categories], they take skillful means as their auxiliaries.
Aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) is the companion of diligence (*vīrya*), for it cannot induce meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), or supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, regarding those who practice in the lower realms, they make aspirations for the sake of future lives, and so forth.
With afflictions attenuated, may one have diligence as a companion; with the superior resolve for the higher realms turning into inferior intention, may that resolve turn into superiority;

with the mind abiding within, may there be the capacity for endurance as a companion to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); through hearing and reflection, may cultivation arise, and through cultivation, may wisdom be generated;
by means of this wisdom, may supramundane insight arise; and with this wisdom as a companion, may there be the cultivation of that which is still associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Regarding the arising of wisdom, the production of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), and the statement that "if it is like the Buddha-body" and so forth:

because subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) arises after correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), each *pāramitā* possesses seven purifications, as explained at length in that treatise. There are many further successive explanations of different categories (*naya*), which one should seek out;
the matter of those lacking the spiritual lineage (*agotra*) is extensive and is treated in a separate chapter, so it shall not be cited here in detail.
Regarding the distinction between difference and non-difference among the twenty-eight views of emptiness, there are two interpretations.

The first holds that difference refers to the contrast between conditioned causes and *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (nirvāṇa), as explained extensively in the preceding treatise. The second holds that "difference" refers to the distinct natures of maturation-causes and their effects, while "non-difference" refers to the identical nature of dominant causes and their effects;
this latter interpretation is superior. This interpretation pertains to the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
Therefore, it is not understood that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) also possesses the distinction of cause and effect, nor the distinction of being different or non-different.

Furthermore, when phenomena are of the same category they are called "non-different," and when they are of different categories they are called "different. To deny the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature) is to engage in the error of deprecation (*apavāda*).

This deprecation of its name—that is, its designation (*prajñapti*)—is what is meant by "name" and "term" (*śabda*). As stated extensively in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is often referred to as "sound" (*śabda*), or sometimes described as "designation" (*prajñapti*).

This very point is explained in detail as it is determined in the *Mahā-śāstra* (*Abhidharma-mahāyāna-saṃgraha-bhāṣya*). If one holds to such [views], they are persons who diminish the Dharma and exaggerate [non-existent] qualities regarding phenomena and persons.
Since the substance of the objects of their discourse is non-existent and exists only as a name, yet they revile that which is merely nominal, they are called "diminishers" (*apavādika*).
The various treatises differ, but all are to be understood in this way; the *Saṃgraha* is consistent with this. These twenty-eight constitute a single [category].

Do these arise in a single person, or do they arise in many people before they constitute twenty-eight? It is not contradictory for them to be fully present in a single person, nor is it impossible for them to arise in many.
Furthermore, how are the sixty-two views subsumed within the twenty-eight? This shall be explained in detail in the section on the sixty-two views.
Moreover, these arise only among those who are internally foolish and ignorant; they do not arise solely among non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). This shall be discussed separately.
This is subsumed within the sixty-two views and various other views.

The treatise asks: regarding the statement that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), if one follows the explanation of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), there is a nature of spontaneous arising upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
However, the dependent nature does not exclude the nature of arising in dependence upon conditions; it merely [denies] intrinsic nature.

This refutes the nature of spontaneous arising; furthermore, it specifically refutes the existence of the past and the present through the following two points. Here, the first point refutes the existence of the future:

it is claimed that the nature of future phenomena definitely exists because they will certainly arise in a future time. However, since their nature does not definitively exist prior to the conditions for their arising, they lack the nature of spontaneous existence.
If they only exist when the conditions for arising are met, one cannot deny their dependence on conditions. How, then, can you speak of a "future"?

If phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and if this future nature were to exist spontaneously, it would be identical to the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and could not be said to arise through conditions.
If it has already arisen through conditions, how can one say it is "future"? A detailed refutation of the future is further explained as cited from the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
The treatise states: "Regarding the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) in the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), etc.

This refers to the section on the establishment of the lack of intrinsic nature in the sixteenth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, the "Chapter on Establishing the Lack of Intrinsic Nature," where the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are first explained, followed by the three lackings of intrinsic nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*).

One should know that the lack of intrinsic nature is not separate from the natures themselves; as for the manner in which the ancient masters established the essence (*svabhāva*) of these three natures, there are various perspectives based on both principle and fact.

The gates of defilement and purity, the gates of objects and consciousness, the gates of phenomena and principle, and so forth—all such [categories] are merely false conceptualizations because they do not accord with reality.

According to the Western tradition, there are only two pairs of gates: first, the gate of the permanent and the impermanent; second, the gate of the outflowing (sāsrava) and the non-outflowing (anāsrava).

If one takes that which is permanent to be the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) and that which is impermanent to be the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), this is as stated in the "Chapter on the Absence of Nature" (*Niḥsvabhāva-pariccheda*) of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
That which is called the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) refers to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena produced in dependence upon various causes and conditions;

this very text proves that what is impermanent is the dependent nature. That which is called the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) refers to the intrinsic nature of the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena;
this very text proves that what is permanent is the perfected nature. Thus, all the merits of the Buddha-fruit are based upon [the perfected nature].
If the other-dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is the dependent-arising; as the fifth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states in verse:

"That which is spoken of as the four purities is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). These four purities are: first, natural purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), which refers to suchness (*tathatā*);
second, purity through the removal of stains (*vaimalya-viśuddhi*), which refers to that very same [suchness] being free from all obstructive stains; third, the attainment of this path...
"Purity" refers to all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and the perfections (*pāramitā*);

"the purity of the object of their arising" refers to the sublime and correct teachings of the Mahāyāna. Thus, one should know that all the merits of the fruit of Buddhahood are perfectly accomplished and real (*pariniṣpanna*).

This passage serves as proof that that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), while that which is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) is the perfectly accomplished nature.

Only the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), space (*ākāśa*), the immovable (*āniñjya*), and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*) possess profound meanings that are difficult to understand.

These all lack intrinsic nature and are merely transformations of the mind. For instance, regarding the three—cessation through deliberation, the immovable, and the cessation of perception and feeling—they are simply the non-arising [of phenomena] due to the abandonment of afflictions;
this very non-arising, established as a conventional designation upon suchness (*tathatā*) in accordance with reality, is what is termed "cessation through deliberation" and so forth. If...

When discussing the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), it takes *tathatā* (suchness) as its essence; when discussed in its two aspects, both take the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as their essence.
If one considers them as phenomena produced from the transformation of the mind that are non-arising, they are subsumed under those two respective essences.

Regarding space and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), as explained extensively in the second fascicle, these two lack substantiality and are merely provisionally established within the realm of insentient emptiness.

The non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—which is provisionally established based on the deficiency of conditions for all phenomena within space—is, in terms of its essential substance, non-existent;

it exists only as a transformation from the mind and is thus of the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*). If categorized by way of the gate of permanence and impermanence, it is of the nature of dependence.

If categorized by way of the gate of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), although this is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is not permeated by the taints; thus it is untainted, which is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*).
If one considers that all phenomena take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their essence, they are subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, regarding the two types of emptiness—the unity of existence and non-existence: first, the emptiness of principle is the perfected nature; second, the emptiness of phenomena is that which is elucidated here.

Next, to clarify the three natures of non-nature, as stated in the verses of the "Chapter on Non-Nature": "The three natures of non-nature should be known as not being separate from the three self-natures;
because of the non-nature of characteristics, the non-arising of nature, and the ultimate non-nature of nature, they do not exist apart from the preceding three natures.

That is to say, the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) exists only as a name but lacks a substantial characteristic; this is the "non-nature of characteristics and names," which does not mean that the *parikalpita-svabhāva* itself is eliminated.

There is another "naturelessness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), which refers to the fact that within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) there is production by causes and conditions; because one clings to it as being produced spontaneously, it is called the "naturelessness of production.
Furthermore, this naturelessness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) does not exist apart from the dependent nature;

rather, its very essence is naturelessness. Moreover, because the naturelessness of all phenomena constitutes their self-nature, the naturelessness of the ultimate is precisely the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, regarding the essential nature of these three types of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is as follows: the *parikalpita* (imagined) and *paratantra* (dependent) natures lack the characteristics of the two types of objects of apprehension (*grāhya*);
thus, they are called "non-nature. The *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) nature is itself non-existent, or rather, it is the absence of the imagined nature within all phenomena;

this is called "ultimate non-nature" (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*). These are designated as "non-existence" simply because they lack that which is grasped through false attachment, or they exist [as such absences].

Even if one generates attachment to names regarding the *parikalpita* (imagined nature), or generates attachment to the reality of dependent origination regarding the *paratantra* (dependent nature), these are all non-existent;

however, because they are for the purpose of eliminating external attachments, we speak here only of the attachment to the lack of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) in terms of arising and so forth—such as the snake [arising] from a rope—as explained in the first fascicle of the *Vyākhyā*.
For a detailed analysis, refer to the seventy-third section of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.

The sixteenth section of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, chapter four, provides an extensive explanation which the reader should consult; its relationship with the five characteristics is detailed in a separate chapter.

As explained in the second fascicle regarding the meaning of the five dharmas, the commentary on the treatise states that among "all phenomena are without arising or ceasing," etc., it is as stated in the fifth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*:
"From beginning with 'permanence' up to 'intrinsic nature nirvāṇa'..."

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the two are non-existent and are as [both] permanent and impermanent," the essence of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), which is suchness (*tathatā*), is permanent;
however, from the perspective of the aspect of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), its essence is impermanent.

Because this nature is both permanent and non-existent, it is called "impermanence" in the sense of being a permanence that is non-existent; it is not called impermanence because of arising and ceasing. This meaning refers to what is upon the *paratantra*.

Suchness is as it is, eternally without actual arising or ceasing; yet, according to the nature of phenomena as they are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*), it is neither eternal nor impermanent.
Based on the fact that it is the substratum for both [aspects], it is said to be neither eternal nor impermanent. Furthermore, regarding suffering and pleasure:
their non-dual perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is pleasure, while their conceptually constructed portion is suffering. That which is non-dual is the dependent nature (*paratantra*).
Thus, this explains the categories such as "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) as being subsumed under the categories of that treatise.
The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Treatise on the Explanation of Intent), chapter five, states: "Observing others from afar with the desire to provide for them is called 'intent' (*abhiprāya*);

this refers to teaching those who have first resolved their minds toward awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*). Observing others closely with the desire to lead them to realization is called 'explanation' (*nirdeśa*)."

"Secret" refers to the initial generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*) for the purpose of entering the path; it is called "secret" in this sense, and for this reason there is a distinction.

Regarding the "initial intention," it refers to the remedy for the obstacle of disparaging the Buddha. This means that others might think, "The Buddha only recently became a saint; my teacher has long since attained the path.
Therefore, [the Buddha] says, "I was once that very Buddha," and so forth, as explained in that treatise. This is what is meant by the words "that very Buddha."

The second intention (*abhiprāya*) refers to the mutual similarity of intentional conditions; it is intended to counteract the obstacle of indolence by instructing one to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and so forth.
This is an "intention regarding another time" (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*), meaning that one may be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss through the mere power of aspiration.

This does not obstruct the fact that practice and aspiration must support one another, for it is through their mutual support that one reaches the first stage (*bhūmi*). It is like [the case where] by means of a single coin...

To counteract the obstacle of disparaging the Dharma, this treatise explains that [the Mahāyāna] possesses only the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) and so forth, based on the underlying intent regarding three thousand distinct meanings.
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Only those who have served as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges can understand the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
This serves as proof that there is a profound difference between the Mahāyāna of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahāyāna*) and the Mahāyāna of the teaching (*deśanā-mahāyāna*).
This means that just as sentient beings disparage the Dharma, so too do they disparage the Mahāyāna Dharma because they do not perceive it as being profoundly deep;

therefore, it is said that only by encountering and serving many Buddhas can one understand its meaning. Within the meaning of the words, there is a profound distinction regarding internal realization (*pratyātma-adhigama*).
The fourth intentionality is taught in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* solely for the purpose of eliminating small virtues, the arising of complacency, pride, misconduct, and the nature of non-intentionality.
There are those who have removed the obstacle of being content with minor virtues and have no others remaining; because this refers to a specific case, they praise the Buddha-fields and so forth.
Because they crave worldly wealth and pleasure, they praise the Pure Lands for their abundance of riches and delights.

Because they rely on their own physical strength and intellectual wealth, they praise the Buddha. Because they have previously committed sins and fear not being reborn in heaven, they remove the obstacle of remorse (*kaukṛtya*).

Regarding the citation of the indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) śrāvakas, this is explained at length in separate commentaries and records, as well as in the sixteenth chapter of the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* and other texts, which extensively discuss the four types of śrāvakas.

As for the four types of secret names, they were explained previously; the first was taught for those who fear the severance of obstacles, stating that the mind is eternal, [referring] to those who lack the spiritual disposition (*agotra*).
Because of obscurations, it is taught that within the Śrāvaka vehicle itself, there are two [types of] attachment to form and so forth;

three [teachings on] the lack of intrinsic nature and so forth are taught to remove the obscuration of deluded clinging; four [teachings] are taught to remove the eight obscurations; and the teaching of intentional language (*saṃdhābhāṣya*) is taught to remove the obscuration regarding manifest speech.
These may or may not rely upon the formal treatises (*śāstra*), but as for the inclusion of the four intentions (*abhiprāya*), they exist only in the [intentions] themselves.

Third, because of the eight obstacles; since the third [section] consists of the eight obstacles and the Dharma of the Buddha follows in sequence, the teaching of the Dharma after the Buddha is based on the four intentions (*abhiprāya*).
This is the third [section], which does not follow the sequential order of the Abhidharma, as the latter seeks [truth] through essential nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The remaining [sections] are to be assigned to the four intentions according to their respective order.

Regarding the statement that five fruits are taught within the characteristics of the skillful bodhisattva due to five causes, this refers to the cause of meaning (*arthahetu*)—the cause of causal conditions—and not the cause-and-effect cause.
As for these five fruits, they follow the sequence of the text; there is no dispute among the treatises regarding this.

As for the claim that the five fruits are attained through five types of cultivation, the great meaning is as stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*: first, the cultivation of accumulation (*saṃbhāra-bhāvanā*).

This refers to: (1) the concise cultivation that gathers all things into a single mass, wherein the Dharma is able to produce the cessation of delusions so they do not arise again, dissolving the heavy obstructions (*dauṣṭhulya*) and resulting in the uninterrupted excellence of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*);
