and (2) signless cultivation (*animitta-bhāvanā*), which, within the true *dharmadhātu* devoid of all signs, practices by eliminating the distinctions of phenomena; thus, this cultivation can produce the transcendence of manifoldness.

1. The cultivation of the joy of the Dharma-garden (*dharmārāma-sukha-bhāvanā*): because it operates spontaneously, free from effort, having transcended the application of effort, this cultivation can bring about the fruit of realizing the immeasurable light of the Great Dharma, which illuminates all conduct.
2. The intense cultivation (*pracaṇḍa-bhāvanā*), which is to say, the superior cultivation:

this cultivation can bring about the fruit of the manifestation of signlessness (*animitta*) that accords with the factors conducive to purification (*viśuddhi-pakṣya*), and it can lead to Buddhahood.

Because it is the fruit, there are five types of cultivation characterized by lack of complacency: one does not become complacent with what is inferior, one greatly aspires to what is superior, and subsequently, this [cultivation] is able to produce the fruit of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
This is because it is the cause capable of producing the Dharma-body that constitutes the fruit of perfection.

Furthermore, if one discusses this cultivation according to reality, every stage (*bhūmi*) possesses the minds of entering, abiding, and emerging; yet, when discussed according to their specific distinctions, these first two [stages] are as follows:
Because one cultivates the mind that enters the stages (*bhūmi*) by performing tainted actions (*sāsrava-karma*) as when not yet having entered the stages,

one is unable to gather the general and concise cultivation, nor is one yet able to produce the superior tranquility (*praśrabdhi*). Furthermore, because one cannot sever the heaviness of the basis (*āśraya-dausthulya*),

and because various signs (*nimitta*) remain while True Suchness (*tathatā*) has not been realized— such that one is unable to be signless within the garden of the Dharma of True Suchness— therefore, there is [the distinction of] entering the stages.
These two minds—both of which are minds observed through right knowledge—are the third stage when abiding in the ground (*bhūmi*).

Although, while not yet abiding in the ground, one observes with right knowledge and illuminates [the object] with wisdom, because this involves effortful application (*sābhisamskāra*) and is unable to induce the factors conducive to purification (*pariśuddhi-bhāgīya*), it cannot increase in excellence;
therefore, these two modes of activity pertain to the mind that abides in the ground. All of these...

The subsequently attained [wisdom] takes as its object all things and so forth, arising within the minds that have reached the fulfillment of the stages (*bhūmi*). It constitutes the fifth type of cultivation.

When the stage is not yet fulfilled, it serves only as a preliminary cultivation for the true *dharmadhātu*. Because the stage has not yet been perfected and purified, it is only upon reaching the mind of the fulfilled stage that one truly realizes purity.

This is accomplished by the two types of wisdom acting in tandem. In each stage, there are the minds of entry, abiding, and emergence; these should be understood by analogy with what has been considered above.

Furthermore, because one cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) and the perfections (*pāramitā*) from the first through the sixth grounds, these are all termed "collective cultivation.
Only on the seventh ground is it termed "signless" (*animitta*), for the preceding grounds are all characterized by signs (*nimitta*) and thus cannot be called "cultivation with and without signs.
Although this seventh ground possesses the signless, it still involves functional activity toward the eighth ground.
The *Bhūmi* states that there is "effortless cultivation" (*anābhoga-bhāvanā*) because, within this stage, one has not yet attained the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).
The ninth stage is called "blazing cultivation" (*jvalana-bhāvanā*) because one attains blazing eloquence through cultivation.

Regarding the tenth stage, it is named "cultivation without complacency" (*asantuṣṭi-bhāvanā*), because like the rain falling from the Dharma-clouds, one is never satiated; this meaning is discussed in terms of increasing excellence and is not established otherwise.
Regarding the true meaning, if it is indeed the true meaning, it should be understood that it exists in each stage (*bhūmi*) as previously described.

In the thirteenth chapter of the treatise, the "Chapter on Attainment" (*Prāpti-varga*), types of conduct such as those dominated by greed (*rāga-carita*) are explained extensively as in the *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 26). Here, we take only that which is diligent but not sharp (*apratibala*).
The "combined category" (*ubhayathā*) is subsumed within the "equal-share with slight defilement" (*samabhāga-tanumala*) for the remaining two categories.

Furthermore, regarding their characteristics, that treatise states: "If, in relation to those objects, greed and so forth manifest, and if superior objects give rise to superior greed and so forth, this is the first two categories;
these are commensurate with the objects and are likewise subsumed under the 'equal-share' [category]. Moreover, it explains that these two categories alone...
In the preceding section, only the first two lines of this passage are taken up.

Regarding "thin defilements," as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 26: "To give rise to a slight and inferior attachment toward an object of superior grade constitutes 'thin defilement';

toward objects of middle or inferior grades, attachment does not arise at all. Furthermore, according to this text, how could one give rise to desire of an inferior grade toward an object of middle grade? How could that be?

This does not refer to those of slight defilements; here, the discussion is based on a single category, and it should be understood that this is a statement regarding the method of practice rather than a literal definition.

As for the term "one who practices in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipanna*), it has been explained extensively above. First, the teaching is called "Dharma," and practicing it is called "practicing in accordance with the Dharma.

That is to say, one who acts in accordance with the teachings is called "one who practices in accordance with the Dharma. Furthermore, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is called "Dharma," and the Path (*mārga*) is called "practicing in accordance with the Dharma."

Because one practices in accordance with the extinction of [defilements], it is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*). Furthermore, such right knowledge regarding the Dharma is called "accordance with the Dharma," and so forth, as explained in the preceding commentary.

In the *Śāstra*’s explanation of the Pratyekabuddha, it says: "Or, previously not having yet arisen [the stages] conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), or even previously having already attained the fruit," and so on.

It is said that those who have not yet arisen in the stages leading to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and have not yet attained the fruits—these two types of those who turn their minds toward enlightenment (*cittavivartana*)—become rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas]. As for the remainder, they become those who emerge from the assembly.
Among these, what is the difference between one who has already attained the stages leading to penetration and one who has not yet attained the fruits? Master Jùn says:

"In the Mahāyāna, it is said that among those who turn their minds before attaining the stages leading to penetration, only this [first] type becomes a rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha]; the other three cases do not."

Regarding the formation of the [logical] sequence, since it is stated that one has not yet attained the fruit, the preceding clause is established as its counter-correlative; therefore, this interpretation is incorrect.

As explained below: furthermore, for those who turn their minds from the Śrāvaka path toward the Pratyekabuddha path, they may turn their minds from the stages of *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, or *kṣānti* without reaching the stage of *laukikāgradharma*.
This is because the three preceding stages consist of many moments (*kṣaṇa*), whereas the stage of *laukikāgradharma* consists of only a single moment.
Therefore, it cannot be transformed at that time. This is as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda* (Vibhāṣā-śāstra) and as the verse in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says:

"Transforming the three [roots], the rest... The commentary explains: "Transforming the three roots of goodness of a Śrāvaka results in the attainment of the vehicle of a Pratyekabuddha or a Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Furthermore, even the *anāgāmi-phala-pratipannaka* (the stage of the supreme worldly dharma) does not turn back from the mind for even a single moment; thus, this is the doctrine of the Hīnayāna. Now, in the Mahāyāna, it is not so.
However, the meaning [of this] is as follows: the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) also consist of many moments. How is this known?
This very treatise states that the Supreme Mundane Dharmas arise in this very life; therefore, they are not a single moment.

If, according to this principle, one may turn the mind [toward the Mahāyāna] during all four stages, then since one cannot emerge from contemplation during the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas—remaining only within that contemplation—how could one turn the mind at that time?
The mind, too, cannot be apprehended. However, regarding the first three stages, persons of indeterminate nature each possess the seeds of the three vehicles (*yāna*).

If they turn their minds [toward enlightenment], the seeds of a *pratyekabuddha* produce the fruit of a *pratyekabuddha*, because even those such as *arhats* who have turned their minds can likewise become *pratyekabuddhas*.
If one has already been a *śrāvaka* for sixty kalpas cultivating the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and then turns the mind to enter [the Mahāyāna]...

Regarding the Pratyekabuddha who attains enlightenment alone: if one who has emerged from the assembly reaches the stage of the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and so forth, and further refines them for forty *kalpas*, they become a "rhinoceros-like" (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*) Pratyekabuddha.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that those who have already attained the stage of "definitive penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and emerge from the assembly refer to those who enter *nirvāṇa* without refining their faculties; this passage, however, refers to those who have not yet produced the "definitive penetration" stage.

Regarding those who have not yet attained the fruit but turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] to become *khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa* (rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddhas), there is an interpretation which states:

"If one has not yet given rise to the stage of *nirvedhabhāgīya* and turns the mind, all such individuals become *khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*; this applies equally to both the Great and Small Vehicles. This interpretation is definitive. A doubt arises:
if one has already spent sixty *kalpas* practicing before turning the mind, and after turning the mind practices for another forty *kalpas*, is this possible?

Even if one has already practiced the turning of the mind (*cittavivartana*) for sixty *kalpas*, yet does not further refine the faculties (*indriya-pariśodhana*) for forty *kalpas*, or if one was not previously a person of sixty *kalpas* but merely a person of three births (*tri-janman*), such that after turning the mind they do not practice again—even if they have not yet produced the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)—because they have not practiced extensively, what kind of person is this? The answer is: this person is exclusively...
Those of sharp faculties who have previously not practiced, whether they have already turned their minds toward enlightenment or have not yet turned them, have practiced for sixty *kalpas*;
those who have turned their minds must necessarily pass through the stage of a Pratyekabuddha, practicing for either one hundred *kalpas* or forty *kalpas*.

Because the text states that they will certainly become a "rhinoceros-like" (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*) [Pratyekabuddha] without distinction, this is explained according to the sixty-fourth passage of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, which clarifies the stage of having already entered the *viniścaya-bhāga*.
There are two types of those who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]: first, those who have already practiced for sixty kalpas, whether they have turned their minds or not;
and second, those who, having turned their minds, further refine their faculties (indriya) for forty or one hundred kalpas—such individuals are certain to become rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddhas.

Thus, the treatise states that even those who have not yet attained the fruit may become rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, there are those who have turned their minds after sixty kalpas, and those who have not yet reached sixty.

If one has already turned the mind [toward awakening] after the kalpa has passed, and subsequently practices for no more than forty to a hundred kalpas, this person becomes one who emerges from the assembly (*saṃgha-uttīrṇa*).
Therefore, the treatise says: "One who has already produced the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) becomes one of the Solitary Victors (*pratyekabuddha*. Furthermore, the treatise says:

"There are those who have already produced the aids to penetration and become those who emerge from the assembly, yet have not attained the fruit; these become those with the horn of a rhinoceros (*khadga-viṣāṇakalpa*). There is such a case.

The two textual traditions differ because the others—the three fruits and those directed toward them—do not turn their minds [to the Great Vehicle] to become rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddhas, as they have already attained their respective fruits.
Regarding at what stage each of the three vehicles turns its mind [toward the Great Vehicle], the *Da yi* states:

"If persons of the two vehicles turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle, from the initial generation of the bodhicitta until they attain the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles, they all obtain it."

The differences in the results have been explained as before. Regarding those who regress from the Mahāyāna Pratyekabuddha path and so forth, this will be explained below in the section on regression.

Furthermore, concerning the stage at which one turns the mind [toward enlightenment] and the stage at which one attains the fruit of that turned mind, the explanation states: for those in the Mahāyāna, it is until the stage of initial practice (*ādikarmika*).

As for those who turn their minds to attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha, because their mode of practice regarding the objects of perception is similar to that of the Śrāvakas, [they attain the fruit] at that same stage.
Because they resemble [the śrāvaka path], at whichever stage one turns the mind from the *mokṣabhāgīya* (aids to liberation), one proceeds sequentially to this stage of a pratyekabuddha;
furthermore, one may return to the initial stage of a pratyekabuddha’s practice because their faculties and dispositions differ, making it impossible to skip stages.

If one has already attained the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (aids to penetration) or has gone beyond the fruits [of the śrāvaka path], one likewise proceeds sequentially to this stage of a pratyekabuddha. Now, regarding the taking up of the pratyekabuddha [path]...
When awakening to the fruit, one must first attain the fruit of anāgāmin before subsequently attaining the fruit of a pratyekabuddha;

this is because the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) is not something to be loathed by a mind that is still subject to outflows (sāsrava), as explained in detail previously.

Regarding those of Mahāyāna root-nature who are said to purify Buddha-fields and receive the great prediction, this refers to abiding in the eighth stage and attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that one attains the patience of non-arising at the first stage; the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* identifies two types of patience of non-arising:

the first is the same as the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* (at the first stage), while the second is the same as the present text (at the eighth stage). This distinction is based on the difference between the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the segmentary body (*prādeśikakāya*).
Because they differ, the eighth stage is taught for the sake of realizing the principle, while the first stage is taught because one dwells in the non-abiding state.

Furthermore, the eighth stage is taught because of the continuity of the untainted (*anāsrava*) and so forth, while the first stage is taught because one attains the untainted. Regarding the cultivation of pure Buddha-fields, there are many types of receiving predictions (*vyākaraṇa*):

some receive them prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), which is merely a general prediction that they will eventually become Buddhas, without yet receiving [the specific prediction] regarding cities and realms.
The *Mahāvyutpatti* (or *Daibetsuki*) records that there are distinctions such as those for disciples of a land, father and son, and so forth;

or, from receiving a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) at the eighth stage up to being named as a foremost disciple (*agra-śrāvaka*), these are termed "Great Predictions" (*mahā-vyākaraṇa*). Upon cross-referencing the eighth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, there are six types of predictions.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (or *Ziliang lun*) lists five, which are the same as those in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*. The fifth [type] alone lacks a time limit; since this is identical to the preceding four, it is the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* also states that among the five classes of persons who have not yet perfected their faculties, within the three types of factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the three types of factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
with the exception of the single moment of the proximate factor conducive to penetration and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*),

all possess three stages. For example, once one has attained "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), it is certain that at the time of its arising, or immediately upon its arising, one will either enter the Path or [proceed further].

There are cases where *kṣānti* (receptivity) has not yet been definitively produced; thus, one does not immediately enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in this very life. Although a certain stage may be posterior [in the sequence], one enters the path quickly;

although a stage may be prior, one enters the path later. For this reason, one must not take the literal text at face value to claim that "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth constitute the initial stage, and that "Receptivity" (*kṣānti*) constitutes the final stage.
Within each stage, there are those who possess three levels of capacity—those who are incomplete and so forth.

Therefore, regarding the first dharma, the *Śāstra* states that because it arises as this very [dharma], it is called "many moments"; yet even though there are many moments, they remain a single contemplative continuum (*ekāvalambana-saṃtati*).

Furthermore, according to the correct interpretation, once this very World-First Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) has arisen, one is certain to enter the vision of the truths (*darśana-mārga*), and does not do so apart from the arising of this single [moment].
Thus, it is only a single moment, according to the passage concerning falling away (*parihāṇi*).
Regarding the statement that those in the stages of the aids to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) and the aids to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*) are subject to retrogression—

except for the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) within the aids to penetration— it is because the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth consist of four distinct levels, which subsume the first three [stages] each into three grades and the last one into a single grade. For this reason,
all others except for the "Highest Patience" (*adhimātrā kṣāntiḥ*) and the superior grade of the aids to liberation are excluded, as they are already determined by what precedes them.

Therefore, it is not the case that one who possesses the lower or middle grades necessarily undergoes regression. Regarding the statement that although one may regress from the middle or lower grades, one only regresses from the manifest activity (*samudācāra*) and does not regress from the seeds (*bīja*):
this is explained in terms of the non-attainment of the manifest activity, not in terms of the loss of the seeds.

It is like the sevenfold precepts (*saptāṅga-śīla*), where one is said to "abandon" them by not generating them anew, yet their original seeds are not lost. In this context, although one may regress from the lower grade, it still does not...
Because newly created unwholesome karma leads to falling into the evil realms, the Buddha spoke of "regression" (*parihāṇi*) in this context.
Those who regress within the stages of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) are not fixed in their destiny; however, if they are fixed, they will certainly attain the stage toward which they are directed.

Since there is no regression from a higher stage once attained, for this reason, there is both regression and non-regression regarding the stages of *uṣmagata* and so forth, as previously explained regarding those who have not yet fulfilled the requirements.
The three types of persons know only the Pratyekabuddha; by this principle, [the others] may be understood accordingly. Furthermore, there is an interpretation as stated in the Commentary:

because one who has attained *kṣānti* (patience) does not regress and will certainly not enter the evil destinies, what is here called "superior intention" (*adhyāśaya*) does not necessarily imply that all those at the stage of the "lesser portion of liberation" (*mṛdu-mokṣabhāgīya*) are subject to regression.
As for those in the Mahāyāna who do regress, according to the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, Śāriputra had already [attained it] eight times.
The *Bodhisattva-mūla-karma-avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that after practicing for ten thousand kalpas, one may fall back from the seventh mind of the Ten Abodes;

the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states a fall occurs after forty kalpas, while others state sixty kalpas. In reality, all these refer to falling from the seventh mind, though the stated numbers of kalpas differ, resulting in variations.
Upon inquiry, it is found that if pure karma is discussed, sixty kalpas are mentioned; if mixed karma is discussed, eight [kalpas] are mentioned.

Within the ten thousand [stages] of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), the "desire for wholesome dharmas" (*kuśaladharmacchanda*) is itself the essence of the factors conducive to liberation;

it is called "desire for wholesome dharmas" because one cherishes [the goal of] enlightenment and so forth. Regarding the three types of persons who have not yet attained [the stages], one should infer the meaning accordingly.

For the first two [stages], they have not yet attained them; for the third and fourth, they rely on the lower two [stages] in sequence. According to the text of the inquiry, the general meaning is as follows: the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vyupaśama-citta-bhāvanā*).

The preparatory stage (*prayoga*) consisting of the lower-grade discernment (*viniścaya*) of the mind through general and specific mindfulness is subsumed under the "stage of discernment" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Now, while the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), such as *uṣmagata* (heat) and so forth, are taught as the stage of discernment, one should examine whether the five stages of settling the mind (*pañca-vastuka-citta-sthiti*) and others are not also part of the "stage leading to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

According to the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, there are six stages of discernment; the first three correspond to one's own vehicle (*yāna*) and consist of the three [levels] beginning with the "not-yet-fully-equipped" (*aparipūrṇa*).
In their respective order, the fourth [category] refers to those within this stage who possess either a determinate or indeterminate lineage (*gotra*);
when they turn toward supreme enlightenment or toward the state of a *pratyekabuddha* and transition to another birth, this is called "transitioning to something else" (*anyathā-vivarta*).

Regarding this, the Dharma Master says: "One uses the three wholesome roots of a Śrāvaka—Heat (*uṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*)—to seek the state of a *pratyekabuddha*, as previously described."

It should be understood that when Śrāvakas at the stages of *ūṣman* (heat) or *mūrdhan* (summit) turn their minds toward seeking Bodhi, they attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) through Śrāvaka-forbearance (*kṣānti*); therefore, they do not seek Bodhi.

Although the Dharma Master [Sthiramati] distinguishes between those who turn their minds [toward Bodhi] and Pratyekabuddhas as being distinct from the Mahāyāna, he has still not grasped the intention of the Dharma Master [Vasubandhu].

One may infer accordingly that when Pratyekabuddhas turn their minds toward seeking Bodhi, this is the case here; thus, the term "turning the mind" (*cittavivartana*) used in the treatise refers to this.

Regarding the first three phrases, all refer to those who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]. If these first three phrases all refer to those who have turned their minds, then how can it be said that they have already fulfilled the three requirements such as the equipment (*sambhāra*) and are certain not to regress?
As for the previous statement that they have already fulfilled the equipment and are certain not to regress—how could that previous statement allow for regression?

This discussion of turning the mind does not concern those who have already fulfilled [the requirements] regressing; rather, it means that all three types of persons within these three phrases are capable of turning their minds. If...
Regarding "turning the mind toward the Great [Vehicle]" and so forth: as for the Pratyekabuddhas, they are explained in the same way as those who regress previously;
however, their *laukikāgradharma* (supreme mundane dharma) can only regress and cannot turn the mind, because it lasts for only one contemplation and one moment.

The third phrase is also called "one birth," and the fifth phrase is also called "one birth. What is the difference between them? The Dharma Master says: the third refers to those of inferior and middling faculties who turn [the mind] downward.

Regarding the attainment of the superior faculties (*indriya*) and the penetration of clear realization (*abhisamaya*, *kṣānti*): the fifth [category] is stated from the perspective of one who undergoes a transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), while it is stated from the perspective of one who does not undergo such a transformation.

How is it that "transformation" and "non-transformation" are spoken of here? Is there a case where, having already proceeded from the lower or middle [faculties] toward the superior within the stage of penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*), one is said to be "not transforming"?
If the original [faculty] was already superior and one does not transform it, then since the fundamental faculty is already superior, it should be understood as such.

Regarding the transition from the stage of indeterminate birth to this fifth stage of "one birth": if one proceeds from the stage of indeterminate birth to the stage of one birth, how can it be said that there is no retrogression?

For this reason, another consideration is made. The third phrase refers to the period from the initial generation of the mind until the mind has not yet been turned back, spoken of in relation to one's own vehicle.
Since the fifth [phrase] concerns the turning of the mind, it follows the perspective of that specific turning of the mind.

Because the path is further explained, there are distinctions. Since it is stated that the first three phrases refer to the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), this does not necessarily mean they refer to those who have not yet attained full ordination (*asaṃvṛta*) and so forth.
Those who have not yet attained full ordination and the like merely undergo a change of birth (*janma-parāvṛtti*), not a transformation of the faculties.

For this reason, they follow the previous interpretation; since the sixth phrase applies to both the determinate (*niyata*) and the indeterminate (*aniyata*), it is judged that the first three phrases apply to both the determinate and the indeterminate.

The fourth and fifth phrases refer to those of the nature of a person who follows their own vehicle according to their aspirations; the sixth and first phrases apply exclusively to those who have already turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna].
Furthermore, the sixth phrase alone also applies to both types.

Regarding those who follow by faith or by dharma, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states: "That is to say, having already completed the provisions, their nature is that of dull or sharp faculties," and so forth. This refers to the Great [Vehicle].

The fifty-eighth [section] on contradictions is as before in the ninth fascicle. Regarding the twenty-sixth point, "only two," although there are many explanations of the text, none equal this interpretation.

The Dharma Master said: "Since it is stated that 'the provisions are already complete,' this refers to a person who has attained the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) within a single lifetime and will certainly enter the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Since it is not certain that this will take a long time, he simply says that the provisions are already complete."

Why exclude those who attain liberation in one lifetime or on a single seat? Furthermore, why restrict [the category] solely to those who possess the roots of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and have already completed the provisions (*saṃbhāra*), such that they will certainly enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in one lifetime or on a single seat?

This would imply that those at the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) are all merely followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or followers by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), because they too possess [the potential for] birth in one lifetime and so forth.
According to the Mahāyāna doctrine, however, it is held that only those possessing the roots of merit conducive to penetration are [included].

Regarding those who attain [the fruit] through a single faculty (*indriya*), because they are proximate to the excellence of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), they belong to a single session (*ekāsana*) as they are directed toward it;

thus, they are not included herein. The distinction between those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by Dharma (*dharmānusārin*)—whether they rely on a teacher or do not rely on a teacher—is as explained in the twenty-sixth [chapter].

Furthermore, to explain in detail: Question: Why are these two persons not included in the classification of the distinctions among the fruits (*phala*)? Answer: Because they have not yet reached the fruit. Question: [Why is this? [End of excerpt]

[The opponent] says: "If that is so, then those who are in the three preceding stages of application (*prayoga*) have not yet reached the fruit; they too should not be included within the distinctions of the fruits. [The respondent] replies:
"It is said that although those in the three preceding stages of application have not yet reached the fruit, they are already close to the Noble Path and have already attained the fruit.

Therefore, this is not a pressing objection. Furthermore, [the opponent] asks: "Regarding the practitioners by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the practitioners by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), since these are stages of the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), why are they not included among the fruits?"

Regarding the statement that the "candidate for the stage of penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) should not be included within the category of "fruit": this is because those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) attain the fruit after one more birth, rather than realizing the fruit in a single moment of contemplation (*ekakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, although the initial candidate takes up the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and attains the fruit in a single contemplation, it is not subsumed under the specific categories of the fruits;

there is no contradiction here, and it is even more difficult to conceive. As for the "resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) and the "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), they are as follows:
Regarding those of dull and sharp faculties who have previously attained the fruits, they follow the four fruits;

as stated in the twenty-sixth [section], "Those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin), those liberated through conviction (śraddhādhimukta) due to the instruction of others, and those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) through personally contemplating the teachings—these are called 'those who have attained vision' (dṛṣṭiprāpta) because they have realized the fruits of śramaṇaship.
Thus, it is known that the four fruits are taken up.

Regarding the statement that one must realize the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) through bodily realization (*kāyasākṣin*) to be called a "bodily witness," if one does not fully attain the eight liberations—attaining only one or two, or even up to six or seven—one is not called a bodily witness. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Taishō 1509), fascicle 26:
"There are two successive expositions; as in the following exposition, it says: 'A person who is a bodily witness personally realizes and fully possesses the eight liberations.'"

One who abides in the [attainment of] cessation but has not yet attained the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), and so forth—up until having listed the names of the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) and being able to enter and emerge from them with mastery in both direct and reverse order—is called one who has "bodily realized" (*kāyasākṣin*). Thus, it is known that one who does not fully possess these attainments is not named a bodily realizer.

According to the preceding ninth treatise, among the four propositions, one attains the extinction of outflows only when the afflictions below the third dhyāna have been severed and the afflictions above have been suppressed.
It is established that only such a non-returner (anāgāmin) is designated as "one who has realized through the body" (kāyasākṣin).

If one has abandoned the afflictions of the third and fourth dhyānas up to the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), yet does not attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti); or if one has abandoned the afflictions of the first and second dhyānas but is unable to suppress the afflictions and attain the meditative absorption of cessation—one is not called "one who has realized through the body.
Question: Is this person considered to be another type of non-returner, such as one who proceeds with exertion (sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin), and so forth? Answer: No.

If one does not practice or practices with ease, attaining the higher stream (*ūrdhvasrotas*) and being born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) to attain parinirvāṇa;

or if, having suppressed the afflictions and attained concentration, one falls away from that meditative absorption (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one will likewise be born in the Fourth Dhyāna. This is explained in detail as in the previous fourfold analysis.

Furthermore, such a person is also born in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). As for those in the Desire Realm who do not practice the "with-effort" (*sābhisaṃskāra*) type, since those in the Form Realm who flow toward the Formless Realm necessarily attain the meditative absorption of cessation, [the former] also [attains it].

If a person of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*) turns their mind [toward liberation] while still in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), why is it that they do not attain parinirvāṇa after being born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), but must instead be born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
The answer is: because they have already attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) within the desire realm.

If one were to reach the form realm and only then seek to cultivate the absorption of cessation, this would apply only to those who are not subject to retrogression (*aparihāṇadharman*), and solely for the sake of the blissful concentration of the formless realm.
Incorporating this meaning, it is truly as extensively explained before.

Those who possess both wisdom-liberation (*prajñā-vimukti*) and liberation through both [wisdom and concentration] (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukti*) and fully realize the eight liberations are called "liberated by both.

Those who attain only one or two liberations, or those who do not attain them at all, are not "liberated by both," but are "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukta*). How is this known? It must be fully realized.
The eight directions are called both "complete" and "incomplete. Those who realize [the fruit] through wisdom alone are termed "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukta*).

Regarding these two types of persons, because the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* contains the term "complete realization," and because it states that among those liberated by wisdom there is only the ultimate abandonment of the hindrance of wisdom (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), we know that although they may attain one, two, or even up to seven liberations (*vimokṣa*) and abandon the hindrance of meditative absorption (*samāpatty-āvaraṇa*), they do not abandon it ultimately; therefore, they are not "complete" persons, just as in the case of the Great [Vehicle].
This is the twenty-sixth section, the second successive explanation.

Within the stage of the candidate for stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*), taking the preceding [stage], it is said that one enters the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) through the sixth session of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), because this is not a prior stage.
Thus, it speaks of "fifteen moments of mind. This follows the characteristics of the sequential discourse; hereafter, the same principle shall apply accordingly.

Furthermore, regarding those who know the meaning—namely, the practitioners following through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the practitioners following the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*)—those who have attained one seat (a stage) as well as those of both determinate and indeterminate natures, if they have already turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], their single seat is not the initial orientation;
rather, the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, are all the initial orientation because they each possess one seat.
Thus, if one is at the stage of Heat or Summit (*mūrdhan*), it is the subsequent attainment of one seat by the practitioner following through faith or the practitioner following the Dharma.

The two stages of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit), such as patience (*kṣānti*), are not yet the initial stage of entering the path (*pratipannaka*). Excluding these, what remains is subsumed under the initial stage of entering the path. Furthermore, there are two types of this initial stage of entering the path:

first, the "leap-over" (*vyutkrāntaka*), and second, the "gradual" (*anupūrva*). The gradual type is easily understood. As for the leap-over type, it refers to one who first suppresses five grades of afflictions and subsequently enters the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*);

even if they have not yet reached the path of weakening (*tanumārgeṇa*), they are still considered to be in the initial stage of entering the path. Regarding the gradual suppression and abandonment of the five grades:
This is the second candidate; others should be understood by analogy with this, as it is easy to explain.

Regarding the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the *Śāstra* states that those who have not yet abandoned desire enter into the determination of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and attain the fruit of stream-entry.

Even those who have slightly abandoned desire are still termed "those who have not yet abandoned desire," because while they were in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they had suppressed the desires of the desire realm through the worldly path (*laukika-mārga*).
Regarding the five grades of afflictions and so forth that enter the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), according to this text, they are spoken of only in general terms without distinction;

furthermore, by one principle, it is said that during the six stages of practice (*ṣaḍ-abhyāsa-kāla*), one merely suppresses the manifest [afflictions] of the five grades, whereas upon entering the Path of Seeing, one then cuts off their seeds.

This very passage from the treatise is taken as proof. Question: The afflictions of seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms obstruct the first fruit (*prathamaphala*); when entering the Path of Seeing, can these be severed?

Regarding the statement that the seeds of the five grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation do not obstruct the first fruit, why is it said that upon entering the path of seeing, these seeds are abandoned? The explanation is as follows:

First, one has already suppressed the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of these five grades by means of the worldly path (*laukikamārga*). Consequently, although their power as seeds is weak and they do not constitute an obstruction to the fruit, they are nonetheless severed upon entering the path of seeing.

Furthermore, this abandonment is known from the tradition of our shared Dharma Master, who cites the nineteenth chapter of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*), which states: [text follows].

First, by means of the mundane path, one subdues the afflictions from the sphere of nothingness downward and enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), whereby one severs only the nine grades of the desire realm;
the [afflictions] of the first dhyāna and above are not severed, because they do not obstruct the third fruit.

Based on this principle, one may infer that for the first fruit as well, the five grades of the cultivated seeds (*bhāvanā-heya*) of those [higher realms] are not severed, because they do not obstruct the first fruit. As in the case of the second...

Regarding the three fruits, I have searched for this passage repeatedly without finding it. A question is raised: "If superior afflictions are abandoned by inferior wisdom, and inferior afflictions are abandoned by superior wisdom, then since the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are subtle, how can they be abandoned by the inferior wisdom of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and how can the inferior afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) be abandoned [by that same inferior wisdom]? The Dharma Master explains this in three ways;

the first explanation is as follows: they are abandoned simultaneously with the afflictions of the path of seeing, but because there is a single uninterrupted liberation (*anantarya-vimukti*) within that single moment of seeing, [the distinctions are established].

Next, regarding the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) taking up the fourth fruit: because one uses inferior wisdom (*hīna-jñāna*) to abandon the ninth affliction of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), and does not abandon lower afflictions, there is no fault.

This is because of sharp wisdom (*tīkṣṇa-jñāna*). Thus, there are two explanations, as in the case of the sixteen moments of mind. Only at the stage of the Dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) are the eight afflictions of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) abandoned, because they are subtle.

It takes thirty-six moments of mind to complete the abandonment of the afflictions of seeing; without emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one gives rise to the wisdom of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-jñāna*) to abandon the five [remaining categories].

Regarding the afflictions of the stages and so forth that are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), although each individual affliction requires its own uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*), here, following the five categories of afflictions abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are treated as a single uninterrupted path.
Although three explanations are given, the intention is to take the first one:

just as one who has previously suppressed the afflictions attains the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), so too should it be understood according to reason that one who has previously suppressed the afflictions may attain the second or third fruits through "leaping over" (*vyutkrāntaka*). One who has previously suppressed the afflictions attains the first fruit.

If a person who has attained the fruit [of the path] has severed only three or four grades [of afflictions] and enters the Path of Seeing, they are a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) after passing through births.

If one has severed five grades [of afflictions] and so forth, and there remains only four grades of afflictions to be cultivated, how can these [remaining] afflictions moisten birth in the Desire Realm?

Furthermore, what kind of person is this who passes through births? The commentary explains: Since this person has already severed five grades [of afflictions], the sixth grade of affliction is extremely weak; how could it possibly moisten birth?

Regarding the non-sequential attainment of the first fruit (*srotāpattiphala*): when one abandons the five categories [of afflictions], one necessarily abandons the sixth as well. This is because the mind has increased [in strength] and these delusions are weak in their force.

Therefore, for one who has attained the first fruit by suppressing the delusions, although they have previously abandoned the five categories, the power and function of that prior knowledge are strong, while the force of this category of delusion is weak;
thus, it is absolutely necessary to abandon the sixth category of delusion before one can undergo rebirth and so forth. There is no exception to this.

If one who abides in the abandonment of the fifth grade of afflictions were to undergo further rebirth, then it would follow that they would take birth moistened by seven or eight grades of afflictions;
thus, those in the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and the Single-Interval (*ekavīcika*) would still harbor doubt and remain undetermined.

To address this objection, there is no logical inconsistency in first suppressing the afflictions through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) and then entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) without abandoning them during the interval. If that is so, then how [is it]?

Regarding the statement that "those noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire produce existence through the moisture of active [defilements]," since such a person has already suppressed the active [defilements] and possesses only seeds from the sixth category onward,
if one were to claim that existence is produced by the moisture of the seeds of the first five categories,
it would contradict the treatise which states that [this applies to] noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire. If, however, one uses the active [defilements] and seeds of the sixth category...

If the seeds that moisten rebirth prior to the fifth stage already possess the power to moisten rebirth without interruption, how can one become a *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) without employing those five preceding seeds?
Furthermore, the argument states that one does indeed employ those five preceding seeds to moisten [rebirth].

If this is so, how does one explain the scriptural passage concerning noble ones (*ārya*) who have not yet abandoned desire? The text explains: "Regarding the phrase 'noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire,' etc."

According to the sequence of the treatise, there is no contradiction in using the words of one who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) but has not yet suppressed the afflictions (*kleśa*). How could this preclude a noble one (*ārya*) who has suppressed the afflictions but has not yet abandoned desire?

This is because they moisten the seeds; as the treatise states: "Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) moisten the seeds through their active manifestations (*samudācāra*)," and "In the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), when one is later reborn in the lower realms, even though there is no mind, [the continuity] is not interrupted, but exists solely by means of the moistening of the seeds. Although noble ones of the Desire Realm possess active manifestations, [the principle remains the same].
Question: Why is it not discarded that there is a separate [function] consisting solely in the moistening of the seeds?

Furthermore, consider a person who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) but has not yet employed the untainted path of cultivation (*anāsrava-bhāvanāmārga*), and who, through the mere practice of rejoicing in the higher and loathing the lower, attains the first *dhyāna* or above.

When such a person dies, how is their birth moistened? Since the seeds for rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have not been severed, one cannot immediately be born in a higher realm simply because they have attained the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

Furthermore, because one does not regress [from the higher realms], the lower realm must again be moistened by means of active manifestation (*samudācāra*). Since there is no active manifestation [of the defilements to be abandoned], it would follow that there is no possibility of birth in the lower realm.
To this, it is said: Just as previously explained regarding the cultivation of dhyāna, one should interpret it accordingly:

at the time of death, one must necessarily employ the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) to abandon the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) in order to be born in the upper realm; otherwise, one would necessarily fall away from the higher meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and it is certainly impossible for one to not have employed [the untainted path].

Regarding those who die in the desire realm using only the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*) while possessing the uncontaminated path (*anāsrava-mārga*): this refers to non-retrogressive persons (*aparihāṇadharman*).

For retrogressive persons (*parihāṇadharman*), there is no obstacle to their undergoing birth and death in the desire realm. If one is retrogressive only in the third and fourth dhyānas but not in the first and second, even if they die [there], such a person does not exist;
they must necessarily use the uncontaminated path. Otherwise, they would retrogress from both simultaneously. If they do retrogress...

Up to the point where one merely suppresses one, two, or even up to seven or eight grades of the desire realm—as previously described without severing the seeds—one attains the first fruit (srotāpanna) and is designated as a "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
Regarding those who are "doubly detached from desire," there are nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm;

since the lower three grades have not yet been severed, and compared to the six [remaining] grades, they are "doubly detached. Furthermore, compared to the previous three [severed] grades, these [remaining] six are also "double."
This can be understood.

Regarding the statement "self and what belongs to self" (*ātma-ātmīya*) among the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) abandoned in the first fruit (*phala*), this refers to the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of self and what belongs to self within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), up to twenty phrases or sixty-five phrases;
it should be understood that the view of self within the manas on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is as previously described.

The commentary explains the three fetters as follows: this treatise provides two successive expositions. First, regarding the "lesser" [fetters], because one perceives the Four Truths through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), "view of self" (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) subsumes all views of self from the level of suffering (*duḥkha*) downward, as it is the root of all such views of self.

"Adherence to precepts and rituals" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) subsumes all adherence to precepts and rituals from the level of the path (*mārga*) downward, because one takes the inferior precepts and rituals of the path-level as the true path.
"Doubt" (*vicikitsā*) subsumes those from the levels of the Four Truths downward, as well as those pertaining to origination (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
Because they cause all [beings] to doubt the causes of the mundane world and the fruits of the supramundane, and because they increase [defilement], the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are taught.

Furthermore, they are taught according to their corresponding causes: namely, *satkāyadṛṣṭi* and *antagrāhadṛṣṭi* arise together; *śīlavrataparāmarśa* arises with *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*; and these arise following *vicikitsā* and *mithyādṛṣṭi*.
Thus, the three are taught as a combined cause, from which the three realms of existence (*bhava*) arise. The remaining four are dull.

Because these [three] arise based on these three [fetters], only the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are said to be eternally severed. This applies only to those who progress through the stages in successive order;

it does not apply to those who have previously suppressed the afflictions, as explained extensively above. Furthermore, regarding the *kulaṅkula* (one who goes from family to family) who undergoes rebirth versus the one who does not undergo rebirth, these two types of candidates (*pratipannaka*) are distinct in essence.
Moreover, this candidate who has not yet undergone rebirth is a candidate; if they are moistened [by craving], they are a candidate.

Those who advance all attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*. Regarding the moisture of rebirth (*upapatti-saṃyojana*) and its lack thereof, they are called *sakṛdāgāmin* because they have abandoned six categories of afflictions (*kleśa*).
The stage of the *anāgāmin-pratipannaka* (candidate for the fruit of non-returning) should be understood by analogy with the *sakṛdāgāmin-pratipannaka*.

Within the fruit of *anāgāmin*, the manner of transcendent entry (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*) is as previously explained; the failure to suppress or abandon the afflictions of the higher realms is likewise as described before.

It was previously stated that although the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—which are causes for the three lower realms—are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because suffering and its origin are abandoned at this stage, it is said that humans and devas [fall] due to craving and aversion as their causes; thus, they do not transcend the lower realms.

Although these are also abandoned during the path of seeing, because they are exhausted from the ultimate point within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is said that the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*) encompass all afflictions of the path of seeing.

It is said that greed and hatred exhaustively encompass all afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because the abandonment of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) in two stages constitutes one stage of *anāgāmin*, and because for those who transcend [the lower realms], both views and cultivation are abandoned simultaneously.
Alternatively, it may be said that for those who follow the sequential path, one should not speak of abandoning the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
For this reason, it is as previously stated regarding the superiority [of the simultaneous path]; see the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (顯揚聖教論), chapter nineteen.

Regarding the statement that [the Anāgāmin] has not yet seen the texts concerning the subduing of afflictions and so forth: this third fruit (the Anāgāmin) does not undergo rebirth in the lower realms.

There are those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain it upon being born (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and those who attain it with effort (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*). Because they have not been reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) again, and because they previously moistened their births through past karma, these noble ones (*ārya*)—having grown weary of the suffering of birth—do not take birth in the higher realms;

this will be explained extensively below. Furthermore, they do not sever the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭamanas*) or the defilements within the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) regarding the notion of self.

This is to be understood as explained in other chapters and in the fourth section of the first fascicle of the *Śāstra*. Furthermore, those who progress toward the [fourth] fruit also abandon afflictions sequentially;

they are not those who enter the path of seeing while merely suppressing the afflictions, as previously stated. Those who attain the "Upstreamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) and so forth do not take rebirth in the stages they have abandoned.
This refers to those who, while possessing the third fruit, proceed toward the next, such as those proceeding toward the second or third fruits; these cases should be interpreted accordingly.

Those who enter the vision of the truths while remaining subject to the latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) do not sever the seeds [of those afflictions] and thus cannot be persons who "proceed toward" [the fruit] while "carrying" the fruit; there are only those who proceed toward it in successive order.
This is because those who sever the afflictions through the leap-over method (*vyutkrāntaka*) become persons who proceed toward the fruit while carrying it.

Regarding the fifth category of fetters (pañca-ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana) within the fourth fruit [of Arhatship]: if one were to say that when suffering and its origin are abandoned in two locations, all fetters are thereby said to be exhausted, this would not be the case.

Rather, it is only the two types of craving belonging to the upper realms (*ūrdhva-dhātu-tṛṣṇā*) that are designated as the "two parts," while ignorance (*avidyā*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) and pride (*māna*) constitute the five.
This specific number is taken because these factors are predominant. As the treatise states: "As for 'doubt' (*vicikitsā'), it is by means of doubt that ignorance is explained; regarding doubt..."

At that time, because ignorance (*avidyā*) increases, there may arise either attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) or doubt; this doubt—such as mistaking a tree stump for a person—is the essence of ignorance itself, not the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*).

As explained previously in the ninth fascicle regarding the four indeterminate roots (*avyākṛtamūla*), these [attainments] and the three preceding fruits and their paths are all common to those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
This fourth fruit is free from the six subsequent types of non-learners (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, regarding those who possess both wisdom and liberation, they have no external substance; a detailed explanation is found elsewhere.
As for their severing of afflictions and rebirth in the higher realms, this is explained at length in the second fascicle on the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

In the treatise on the maximum of seven returns, there is no separate text regarding the Mahāyāna, as is extensively detailed in the *Vibhāṣā*. First, regarding the objection concerning the name "seven births":
Why is it called "seven births"? It is because the maximum number of births does not exceed seven. Second, regarding the objection concerning the excessive number:

Why is this statement made? The commentary states: Because if one combines the births in the realms of humans and devas with both the existence of birth (*upapatti-bhava*) and the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), there would be twenty-eight [existences].

Regarding the statement that from "original existence" (*pūrvakālabhava*) onwards, all do not exceed seven births—just as in the Wheel of Dharma with three turns and twelve aspects (*dvādaśāṅga*), where one Truth has twelve aspects, totaling forty-eight aspects;

yet because each Truth does not exceed twelve, it is simply called the "Wheel of Twelve Aspects"—this case is likewise. [The text notes: "Three should reach eight," which is an obstacle. Question: For what reason is it only...?

Question: Does the seventh [existence] not reach the eighth? Answer: Regarding increase or decrease, there is doubt in both cases; yet one does not become deluded regarding the Dharma because of such doubt.
By the power of karma, one undergoes only seven existences, and by the power of the Noble Path, one does not reach an eighth. It is like a seven-step snake:
because it possesses the poisonous power for seven steps through its four great powers, it does not reach the eighth. If it were to reach the eighth, then it would be...

Regarding the external ordinary person (pṛthagjana) within the Buddha-dharma, they must undergo eight births and so forth due to their karma; now, having attained non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), they have only seven births remaining.
Just as among worldly people, these seven successive lives constitute a family lineage, if one exceeds seven births, they are no longer part of the Buddha’s family.
Through the stage of superior patience (adhimātra-kṣānti), with the exception of those seven births, one attains non-analytical cessation regarding all other future births. If not...
Since each of these individual karmas leads to the experience of immeasurable births, this [statement of "seven births"] is based on a definitive nature for human beings.

Alternatively, it may be explained that some do not complete seven, such as two births in heaven, one birth as a human, and two births in heaven, or one birth as a human and one birth in heaven; thus, it is taught as a maximum limit.
Therefore, there are seven births. If one were to count the births in which one attains the Path, there would be twenty-nine births, and they could no longer be called "seven births."

If one were to calculate by combining the seven births, there would be twenty-eight existences; this would contradict the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, which states that a *srotāpanna* undergoes twenty-eight existences.

If this interpretation is followed, it would mean that one does not necessarily attain the Path while born among humans; rather, one might attain the Path in the heavens and attain *nirvāṇa* in the heavens.
Conversely, if one attains the Path among humans, this refers to the five or seven births [remaining]. If the Noble Path arises [in such cases], it should [be understood accordingly].
There are those who enter *nirvāṇa* who are hindered from attaining the noble path (*āryamārga*) during their seven births; because of the power of their karma, they do not enter *nirvāṇa*.
This noble path does not eradicate afflictions (*kleśa*), but because it is merely a state of contemplative observation, they do not enter *nirvāṇa*.

Sixth, if a Buddha exists in the world, one who has completed the seven births and become an Arhat should appear in the form of a renunciant; if no Buddha exists in the world, there would be no such renunciants.

They are mutually exclusive because an Arhat necessarily possesses the marks of one who has gone forth; if there is no Buddha in the world, one must necessarily go forth within another teaching before attaining the fruit.
According to one interpretation, it is possible to attain the fruit while remaining at home;

however, having attained the fruit, one does not remain at home but goes forth within another teaching and receives the dharma-robes. There were five hundred Pratyekabuddhas who were originally Śrāvakas, and they went forth there.

A householder may also attain [the fruit]; if not, it is as previously stated. As in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, if a Buddha does not appear in the world, one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship while remaining a householder will certainly not continue to live as a householder;

by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), they must necessarily adopt the deportment (*īryāpatha*) of a bhikṣu. Furthermore, some say that they may adopt the deportment of a forest-dwelling practitioner (*āraṇyaka*).
Regarding the seven or nine grades of karma that together moisten rebirth (*upapatti-saṃdhi*) to establish the various fruits, what from the past provides this moisture?
The Master Sheng stated that there were two ancient interpretations. According to the Master Jing and the Master Xiu, they argue based on fourteen births:
the three upper grades of karma collectively moisten four births, the three middle grades collectively moisten two births, and the three lower grades collectively moisten one birth;
the highest-of-the-high grade alone is capable of moistening fourteen births, while the middle [grades] moisten four.
The superior-middle and superior-superior [defilements] together moisten four types of birth, while the middle-superior [defilement] alone moistens two types of birth.
Although they are said to "moisten together," all possess the sense of moistening four types of birth; therefore, it is said that "the categories [of defilements] collectively moisten four.

Thus, when the superior-middle and superior-superior [defilements] are severed, the superior-inferior and inferior-superior [defilements] alone have the power to sustain two births. Because their own strength is weak, the superior-superior [defilement] alone must rely on the assistance of the middle-middle, middle-inferior, and inferior-middle [defilements].

The moisture [of the defilements] nourishes two births as described above for the three grades; it nourishes one birth alone for the upper-middle grade, and both the lower-middle and lower-lower grades together nourish one.
The meaning is as follows: if one abandons three or four grades, it is clear that two or three births remain;

if one abandons the middle-upper grade, two births remain. Therefore, we know that when the three upper grades are abandoned, there are three births remaining. Thus, we know [the nature of] the three upper grades.
When the moisture that nourishes the four types of birth (*catur-yoni*) is severed, the four types of birth no longer exist; rather, only three types of birth remain.

Since when the moisture of the middle and superior grades is severed, the remaining two grades of moisture still exist, we know that these [two] are capable of nourishing two births. This should be understood by analogy for those non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who delight in wisdom (*prajñā-rata*) and others.

Objection: If the superior-middle and superior-superior grades together nourish the four types of birth, why is it that when the superior-middle grade is severed, the superior-superior grade still nourishes two births?
If birth alone is capable of moistening [the seeds], why do you say it is "shared"? As explained previously, when the weak path follows the strong, the weak is moistened alone;

when the strong follows the weak, they are moistened together. Furthermore, since the three grades—superior-superior, superior-middle, and superior-inferior—are equal in their moistening of birth, how can they be called "three grades"?
Master Xiu says: "Master Fa says that Master Nian explains the 'seven births' as being moistened by the superior-superior grade."

The two [types of] arising—superior, middling, and inferior—each moisten one birth collectively; although the superior and middling are severed at times, the inferior and superior still moisten one birth.
Within the three grades of a single life, there is originally no fixed position, for all dharmas exist only as superior or inferior.

Thus, the three middling grades may be partially assigned to the superior or partially assigned to the inferior; because the middling-superior grade belongs to the superior category, it likewise moistens one middling birth.

The middle and lower [karmas] together moisten one lifetime; because they belong to the lower category, they are coarse. The upper [karma] is the same as the three upper grades mentioned above, while the subtle ones are the same as the three lower grades.
Since the three lower grades together moisten one great lifetime, the same applies to their impairment (*upaghāta*).

If the middle grade has no separate status and belongs to both the upper and lower categories, then why is it that the two grades—upper-middle and upper-upper—which do have separate statuses, are treated in this way?

It appears that [the number] for one life is eight; if there were only seven, then a Once-returner who is not yet fixed in their destiny (*aniyata-gotra*) would be unable to turn back toward the Great Vehicle.

To address this, it is said that those who "return seven times" are of two types: first, those of a fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*), as previously described; second, those of an unfixed nature (*aniyata-gotra*).

This is because when they attain the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), they have not yet turned their minds [toward the Great Vehicle]; thus, they are persons who will undergo seven births, and even though they may later turn back, they remain counted among those based on those seven births.
Regarding the statement that those who have already turned their minds after seven births are also "seven births" when speaking from the perspective of the cause:

if those of indeterminate lineage turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna—such as described in the second fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*—they may no longer undergo further births and instead receive the retribution of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). How is this so?

It is because they obtain the untainted limit-concentration (*anāsrava-sīmā-vimokṣa*) of the fourth dhyāna stage, which moistens the birth of the transformation body; or it refers to the nine grades [of afflictions].

Although one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) prior to the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), because the Mahāyāna’s non-analytical cessation allows for further rebirth, one must undergo many more births—receiving both *paricchinna* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) retributions—before finally attaining the fruit of Buddhahood. This is explained in detail in the second fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
Furthermore, these seven births are necessarily "moistened" (productive of future results), unlike the case of a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) who may experience births that are not so moistened.
This refers to one who does not produce further rebirths; it is not the case that this applies to all.

Within the various families (*kula*), there is no textual passage regarding the Mahāyāna that definitively establishes the characteristics of a "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) practitioner based on the abandonment of one, two, three, or four grades [of defilements]. If five are abandoned, there must be six;

if six are abandoned, one is a "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*). Therefore, the treatise states: "At most, they undergo two more existences, because they have not yet [fully] exhausted the grades of afflictions. Thus, birth occurs [only to that extent].

If those who have seven births at most (saptakṛtparama) possess all nine grades [of afflictions] together, or undergo only one or two more births, how could this be due to the moistening power of the grades of affliction?

Furthermore, since there is still one birth remaining even when the seventh or eighth grade has been abandoned, it follows that a Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) does not necessarily abandon five grades, but must abandon six.

This principle is like the case of those who enter the state of a noble one (ārya) by abandoning five [grades] through the fruit of transcendence (abhisamayaphala). The answer is: "An 'interval' (ekavīcika) refers exclusively to those who have emerged from the desire realm."

Because [the afflictions] belong to different realms, there is no severance of the five grades of patience (*kṣānti*), and one does not reach the sixth grade; however, since it is now explained that such [severance] exists, there is likewise no contradiction.
Only the severance of two or three grades constitutes "moistening birth" (*janma-sneha*), as previously stated.

There is no contradiction in not mentioning the severance of five grades or the first two grades regarding moistening birth (this should be placed in the third [section]). The commentary states: If the severance of one or two grades constitutes moistening birth, then [I] say:
This person does not exist because the treatise does not establish them as a distinct category of noble one (*ārya*).

For instance, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dazhidu lun) designates those who have severed one or two grades [of afflictions] and are "moistening their birth" (*rūnsēng*) as "intermediate *srotāpanna*s. However, the Mahāyāna does not establish such a category because this person does not exist [therein].

How could it be that this person does not exist simply because they are not explicitly established according to the text? It is like the case of the *anāgāmin* in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which is difficult to describe.
It is said: "The formless [attainments] are precisely those in which there is bliss. Regarding the "one who flows upward" (*ūrdhva-srotas*) among these, why is this cited as an example?

Furthermore, it is difficult to establish; one cannot take a single case as representative of many people. However, if one has abandoned five grades [of defilements], one must necessarily increase the abandonment of the sixth.

Because the sixth dharma is weak and inferior, it cannot act as an obstacle. The mind intent on proceeding toward the fruit is sharp, unlike the other three or four grades, and thus it cannot serve as an example. Is this not so?

Because they are directed toward the fruit [of the path], because those afflictions (*kleśa*) create obstacles, and because the substance of the afflictions is powerful—[these are the three reasons]. Third, what is the "Family-to-Family" (*kulaṃkula*)? (This should be placed in the second section).

There are two types of Family-to-Family, as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Exposition), fascicle 26: "There are two kinds: first, those among devas; second, those among humans.
As cited below, regarding the one among humans: a Family-to-Family person is one who is born among humans in either one world-system or two world-systems.
They are born in three continents, or in one, two, or three families within a single continent; it is likewise in the case of two heavens.
Or they are born in one, two, or three heavens, or in one, two, or three families within a single heaven.

One attains the state of a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) noble one when the conditions for three factors are complete; if even one is lacking, it cannot be so called. Thus, it is a combination [of these factors].
The mind says: "If one severs three or four types [of afflictions], there are five [reasons]: (1) severing the fetters and accomplishing their antidotes;

(2) by means of the faculties, namely the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), while the remaining two arise in three births; (3) by means of karma, since it differs from that which moistens birth, one severs two grades;
(5) regarding birth, one is born after severing three grades and two grades, as explained extensively before. It is said that the noble ones (*ārya*) do not create karma for these reasons."
One does not create karma that results in collective retribution, but rather karma that results in individual retribution.

As it is said, when the Blessed One spoke of the time Maitreya would attain Buddhahood, there were among the assembly those who were still in training (śaikṣa) and had not yet abandoned desire; upon hearing this teaching, they all made a vow together, saying:

"May we first hear and see such a sublime and wondrous event as this, and only then enter parinirvāṇa. How is this to be reconciled? The answer is: this refers to a brief moment [of existence] within that state.
If one lacks nothing and is not oppressed by suffering, yet has a wish;

or if one is oppressed by suffering and has no further desire for any state of birth—should such a person be able to feed upon the air like a bird, they would wish to attain parinirvāṇa this very day.
If one speaks thus, it means that a noble one (ārya) does not take on a body within the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).

Regarding those who create karma, they say that such a person—whether a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner or one who will undergo two or three more births—is, while still an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), one who has severed three or four fetters (saṃyojana).
This may be severed while an ordinary person, meaning through previous worldly [attainments], or it may be severed while a noble one (ārya), meaning by virtue of attaining the untainted (anāsrava).
Furthermore, there are those who say that a noble one creates [the karma for] receiving a body in the desire realm.

Regarding the karma created by a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) *srotāpanna*, they will necessarily undergo two or three births due to the collective karma they have created—whether that karma was created while they were an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or while they were a noble one (*ārya*).
They have severed three or four types of fetters (*saṃyojana*), whether those were severed while they were an ordinary person or while they were a noble one.

Now, in the Mahāyāna, this is suppressed—not permanently severed—by means of the six practices while one is still an ordinary person, because it is suppressed by a mind that does not intend permanent abandonment.
