The same applies to the stage of patience (*kṣānti*). Even if this principle were to exist, it would not hinder [the argument] that the creation of karma occurs only when one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and not when one is a noble one (*ārya*).
Regarding the first two and the third fruit: if one passes through successive births into the higher realms, one does not loathe birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), which constitutes an obstacle.

The meaning of the term "one-interval seed" (*ekavīcika-bīja*) is as follows: having attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) in this life, one will reach the ultimate end in this very life; this is what is meant by "one-interval."

Upon the exhaustion of the outflows (āsravakṣaya), one may undergo seven more births as a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner, or attain the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), or become a "one-interval" (ekavicika) practitioner, or attain parinirvāṇa in the present life.

Such noble ones (ārya) are not reborn in the form or formless realms, because they have developed a distaste for their place of birth through the established nature of their bodies resulting from the Noble Path.

When a noble one passes away, there are necessarily three things that do not occur: first, falling back; second, refining the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra); and third, being born in the form or formless realms.

The seventh section explains the resolution of objections: namely, that there should be one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life, meaning one who attains the fruit in this very body and attains parinirvāṇa in this very body.

However, such a person is not established as a separate category here; in reality, they exist. According to our current interpretation, such a person does not exceed the four fruits and is subsumed within the aforementioned four fruits and their corresponding paths (*pratipannaka*).
This is why they are not established separately. If it were not for this principle, they would be established separately from the others. Such a person exists upon the attainment of the fruit.

Those who undergo births but not seven times, those who do not undergo births during the stage of the candidate (*pratipannaka*), those who are not "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) and do not undergo further births to attain the fruit, and those who are not of indefinite nature (*aniyata*)—these are combined and established as such.
Furthermore, those who undergo births during the subsequent fruits or the subsequent stages of candidacy and attain *nirvāṇa* therein are termed "indeterminate.
This refers to individuals in the first fruit who, while abiding in that fruit, undergo births even though they do not complete the full seven.
Although they have not yet undergone rebirth, those destined for seven births are already subsumed within the category of "seven-births" (saptakṛtvah-parama).

This is just as one who dwells in the desire realm or the Brahma heavens and is a "higher-streamer" (ūrdhva-srotas) is still called a higher-streamer because they are destined to flow upward, even if they have not yet flowed upward.

Similarly, although a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner has not yet undergone rebirth due to the presence of specific causes and conditions that determine their direction toward rebirth within a family, they are nonetheless called "family-to-family," as they are not included among the three preceding categories.

Regarding those who, after being reborn in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), have already passed away and attained the third fruit and so forth: now, by inferring from the meaning, all such cases may be termed "indeterminate" (*aniyata*).

Although this is not explicitly stated in the text, it must logically exist; for when one investigates by means of this principle, both [the *antarāparinirvāyin* and the *upapadyaparinirvāyin*] are fully present.

Nevertheless, in the current establishment of the twenty-seven noble persons (*āryapudgala*), these two types of individuals are not established, as in the case of the person of indeterminate parinirvāṇa. This is what is meant.

Regarding the second stage, those who have abandoned one or two categories [of afflictions], as well as those who previously abandoned five categories and enter the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) after having been reborn, do not exist at all in this present Mahāyāna system, as explained previously.
If they do exist, why are they not established? Because there are only three types of *kulaṃkula* (family-to-family) practitioners;
this is determined by the definition of a *kulaṃkula*, which involves being born in three of the four continents, as detailed previously.
Commentary:

Regarding the person with one interval (*ekavīcika*), as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on Great Wisdom), Volume 26, there are two types: first, those who have abandoned seven grades [of defilements]; second, those who have abandoned eight grades.

As the *Mahāprāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "That is to say, they are those who have already permanently [abandoned the defilements] while practicing toward the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and heading toward the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*)."

Having abandoned the upper and middle grades of the desire realm, with only the lower grade remaining, one will undergo rebirth as a deva in the desire realm only once more before attaining parinirvāṇa in that very place.
Question: If seven grades have been abandoned and two seeds remain, why is this called the state of "One-Interval" (ekavīcika)?
Answer: It is not named "One-Interval" because of the presence of a single seed; rather, it is named so because there is only a single existence (eka-bhava) intervening [before nirvāṇa].

Regarding the *ekavīcika* (one-intervener), some say that one is called an *ekavīcika* solely by having severed seven grades of fetters, and not by severing the eighth, because when the eighth grade is severed, one is necessarily able to become free from the ninth grade;
for example, when the fifth grade is severed, one must increase the severance of the sixth, as there can be no obstacle or hindrance to becoming free from the fetters of desire.
Furthermore, others say that [one becomes an *ekavīcika*] by severing five grades and increasing the severance [of the sixth].

Regarding the six categories [of defilements], because they cannot create obstacles or hindrances, they do not constitute the severance of the eight categories; thus, one is called a "Single-Seed" (ekabījika) practitioner. Question:

Since the nature of the ninth category of fetters is likewise weak and unable to create obstacles, why is it that there is the severance of the eight categories but no increase in the severance of the ninth category, such that one is named a "Single-Seed"?
Answer: When one has severed the five categories, one has not yet abandoned the fetters of the desire realm entirely.

Therefore, while it is still possible for rebirth to occur, it cannot be obstructed; this is because the eighth category of afflictions has not yet been severed, whereas the ninth is severed through the exhaustion of the fetters of desire (*kāma-yoga*), which enables obstruction since one no longer undergoes rebirth in the lower realms.

There are three occasions when afflictions and karma can act as extreme obstacles: first, at the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) when turning toward "Patience" (*kṣānti*), wherein karma leading definitely to the evil destinies (*apāya*) can act as an obstacle.

If an obstacle arises when patience (*kṣānti*) is produced, in what place will this karma result in birth? When the two types of noble ones (*ārya*) transcend the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the determinate karma of the desire realm can act as an obstacle.
If one has transcended desire, in whose body will this karma receive its retribution?
Thirdly, when the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is attained, determinate karma that ought to be experienced in a future existence can act as an obstacle. If one attains Arhatship...
Regarding this karma, for whom is the retribution received? For this reason, there are those who sever the eight fetters and become "one-interval" (ekavicika) practitioners;

it is absolutely impossible for them to be "house-to-house" (kulaṃkula) practitioners who sever only the fifth [fetter]. This is because they are clearly explained as being recipients of either one birth or two births.

Thus, the treatise states: "A child among humans" refers to one birth in the human realm; "a child among devas" refers to one birth in the heavenly realm. This is based on the fact that both [births] may be attained in these two respective places.
Regarding the attainment of nirvāṇa by those in the fruit-stage or the path of approach, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 26, states: "It is said that one attains nirvāṇa among the gods.

This refers to attaining the fruit while in the human realm; it does not mean that one enters nirvāṇa while remaining in the heavenly realms, nor does it speak of attaining the fruit within the heavens themselves.
If we discuss the Mahāyāna, how could it be that one attains nirvāṇa only in the heavens while attaining the fruit in the human realm? Surely this is not the case.

Regarding those who attain the fruit among the devas: there is one type who enters *nirvāṇa* while still among humans. This is due to a "single-seed karma" (*eka-bīja-karman*) created during the time they were a worldling (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding its creation for a noble one (*ārya*), some say it is created only at the time of being a worldling and not at the time of being a noble one;

this occurs when severing the seven or eight fetters (*saṃyojana*). Alternatively, it may have been severed previously during the time of being a worldling, or it may be severed during the time of being a noble one; some even say it is severed by a noble one.
At the time of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one also creates a single type of karma that must be experienced in one lifetime (*ekajātipratibaddha-karma*).

This may be severed while one is still an ordinary person, or it may be severed when one becomes a noble one (*ārya*), as previously explained. Now, according to the Mahāyāna, this applies only to ordinary persons and not to noble ones, because they have developed a profound weariness with birth;
this is explained in detail elsewhere. Furthermore, among the four types of noble ones, those who take rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) will certainly not be reborn in the higher realms.

Regarding the realm: because this single-interval person (*ekavīcika*) moistens rebirth within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are not born in the higher realms. As for the aforementioned "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*):
if one attains the fruit through the sequential abandonment of fetters, one does not undergo further birth.

However, at the stage of having abandoned six fetters, if one is subsequently able to increase the abandonment of desire-fetters and be born in the higher realms, while remaining at that stage of having abandoned six fetters, one is also called a "once-returner. This applies whether one proceeds sequentially or by leaping over.

One who has transcended six fetters and must necessarily undergo one more birth is a *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner). If there remains one karma in the desire realm that necessitates one more birth, one may indeed be called a *sakṛdāgāmin*.

However, if one abides in the stage of abandonment and subsequently increases the abandonment of the desire-realm fetters such that they no longer undergo birth in the desire realm but instead take birth in the higher realms, how can such a person be called a *sakṛdāgāmin*, given that they will undergo many births in the higher realms? The answer is: How could it be [by that definition]?

Later, when one is able to further increase the abandonment of the fetters of the desire realm and is born into the higher realms, does one who abides in the six stages of abandonment not possess the fruit of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*)?

Just as a person who has attained the fruit of a Non-returner— excluding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life— is called a "Non-returner" because, having been born into the higher realms, they will never again be reborn below,
why is it that one who abides in the six stages of abandonment and later increases the abandonment of the lower fetters while being born into the higher realms is not so named?

Regarding the meaning of "Once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*): it is said that one who abides in the six stages of abandonment, having undergone rebirth in the lower realm but not being born again in it, is specifically termed a "Once-returner.

Although they are able to further increase their abandonment of defilements later on, because they abide in these stages while still subject to rebirth in the higher realms, they are designated by the name "Once-returner.
This is even more difficult to understand; reflect upon it deeply.

Question: Why is it that those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) do not experience the present fetters (*paryavasthāna*), nor do they receive the mind that moistens the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), and thus do not receive the fruit of future birth?

They enter the womb with full awareness (*saṃprajānan*); this is what is meant by "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state. Regarding the term "birth-fetter" (*upapatti-saṃyojana*) mentioned below, it refers to the fact that while there is currently no [fetter] for the fruit of future birth, it means that through the process of being born again, the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) exhausts this [fetter].
This constitutes the remote exhaustion of the defilements of a noble one (*ārya*). As for "with full awareness," it is also the case for the Pratyekabuddha.

Since these afflictions have already been severed for those noble ones born in the higher realms, there is at times a "moistening of birth" (*upapatti-sneha*) by means of their active manifestation (*samudācāra*).

Although these afflictions have been severed, that which gives rise to the fetters (*saṃyojana*) continues; as will be explained in the following text, the continuity of existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises solely through the power of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Thus, when a noble one born in the higher realms dies, the seeds [of the afflictions] moisten the intermediate state during the death-existence (*maraṇabhava*).
Master Zhun states: "If these seeds have not yet been severed, one who is a person of the third fruit (anāgāmin) and will not undergo rebirth in the desire realm is born in the form realm;
this intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) therein is bound to the form realm. This should be verified against the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

Question: Why is it that when one dies in a certain level of the upper realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*) and is reborn in another level of the upper realms, there is no intermediate parinirvāṇa (*antarāparinirvāṇa*), whereas when one dies in the lower realm (*adharadhātu*) and is reborn in the upper realms, there is intermediate parinirvāṇa? Answer:

It is because one who necessarily abandons the body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and dwells in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is able to attain nirvāṇa due to the extreme sharpness of their revulsion toward the suffering of the three realms, as well as their revulsion toward being born in the long-lived states of the upper realms.
One who is born in the form realm after having relinquished a body of the form realm has no suffering to loathe, because they have not yet relinquished a body of the lower realms;

therefore, there is no mention of "intermediate parinirvāṇa" (antarā-parinirvāyin) for them. As for those who have suffering to loathe, it is because this intermediate state (antarā-bhava) belongs to the form realm and, having already begun to feel loathing, is thus called "loathsome.
It is not that there is suffering to loathe at the very moment one attains parinirvāṇa; even when relinquishing a body of the form realm, although...

Disgust for suffering is not as profound in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as it is when one develops a deep sense of revulsion by abandoning the body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which is subject to suffering;

thus, one attains *antarāparinirvāṇa*. If this were the case, then the two fruits—the Sakṛdāgāmin and the Anāgāmin—should also possess *antarāparinirvāṇa*. However, because the third fruit (the Arhat) has long cultivated the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), the Noble Path is fully accomplished and the categories of afflictions (*kleśapakṣa*) are extremely subtle and weak;
consequently, there is only the abandonment of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) afflictions, and for this reason, [only the Arhat] possesses it.

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*)—who are neither of the first nor second fruits of the path—although they have long cultivated the Noble Path and thus possess suffering that can be loathed, they lack the inferior afflictions that are easily removed;

nevertheless, they do attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* provides four successive explanations for this: because the Path has not yet been fully perfected; because volition does not manifest;
because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are not of an inferior grade; and because it is difficult to escape from the Desire Realm. This is according to the *Vibhāṣā*.
The Master explains it thus: furthermore, there are many things that ought to be accomplished—first, the extinction of afflictions of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature;
second, the attainment of the second and third fruits of śrāmaṇya; and third, the transcendence of the three realms (*tridhātu*).

If one were in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), these matters could not be accomplished. Since indeterminate afflictions are easily severed, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state are established [as such].

Regarding the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) of those in the form realm who attain the third fruit: one should establish that they attain *antarā-parinirvāṇa*. This is because they possess aversion toward non-virtue and the like, nor do they abandon the body of desire at the very beginning;

thus, the fault remains as previously stated. Furthermore, if it were argued that one cannot attain *antarā-parinirvāṇa* because there is no non-virtue to be averse to, then it would follow that the Vajra-like Mind [of the Arhat] could not attain it either, since there is likewise no non-virtue to be averse to therein.
To this, it is said: "The power of the Noble Path arises within that birth-body."
It is not that the strength of the [prior] body coming first prevents the arising of the Noble Path within that intermediate existence; it is simply that this is not the case here.
Because it is not the first abandonment of the body of the desire realm, it differs from the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), for which the body of the intermediate existence is strong.
Question: Birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) possesses powerful force and is able to give rise to the Path;

however, the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the lower realms can give rise to the Noble Path, whereas birth-existence cannot give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*). Because the intermediate existence can give rise to it, [you] argue that this is not so.

But how could it be that simply because birth-existence gives rise to the Path—though distinct from the intermediate existence—it follows that birth-existence in the lower realms must likewise give rise to the Noble Path by virtue of the intermediate existence being able to do so?

[Question: Is it not the case that one attains the suppression of afflictions through the six practices within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)? [Answer: Although there is no textual authority for this, even by way of interpretation, it cannot be attained.
[Question: For what reason can it not be attained? [Answer: Because the mind in the intermediate state is weak; therefore, it cannot be attained. [Question:

Since the noble path (*āryamārga*) arises within the intermediate state, why does it not function as the six practices? [Response: Because although the untainted (*anāsrava*) has previously arisen in the present life, [it is not so here].
Therefore, the Noble Path arises within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

A question is asked: "If one has already subdued the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and gives rise to the First Dhyāna, and this intermediate state of the First Dhyāna arises while one is within that intermediate state, why does the meaning of the sixfold practice (*ṣaḍvidha-abhyāsa*) not arise?
The various Dharma Masters say: "It is simply because the mind is inferior, which hinders and obstructs its realization."

Regarding the meaning of "inexhaustible": because one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) must first cast off the body of the desire realm, there is a distinct category of *antarāparinirvāyin*.

This is because one does not attain the six types of practice through the initial casting off [of the body]; therefore, among all intermediate states (*antarābhava*), there are none that perform these six practices.
Because few among those arising in the intermediate state give rise to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), they are not distinguished individually.

The fetters produced by birth are, according to the Hīnayāna, ultimately non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) that will never arise again; however, in the Mahāyāna, this is not necessarily fixed.

If the nature of one's production of fetters is determinate, then they will never arise again; if the nature of one's production of fetters is indeterminate, then after their production, they will certainly arise again.

Question: At what time does the person who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) turn their mind [toward rebirth] so that the fetters arise and they are born again? Answer: It is as explained in the *Yìzhōng* (義中): for the antarāparinirvāyin, the afflictions of the path should likewise be so.
At the moment of casting off life, one whose Mahāyāna faculties have matured turns the mind and makes a vow;

thus the fetters arise and they are born again, undergoing the retribution of birth and death throughout three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Furthermore, it is said that as soon as they reach the intermediate state (antarābhava), they are about to enter parinirvāṇa.

When favorable conditions manifest before them and their Mahāyāna faculties have matured, those who have turned their minds toward the Great Vehicle may take rebirth; thus, even those who had previously formed the bonds of existence can be born again.
Question: For what reason is it possible for the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to encounter manifest favorable conditions? Answer:

Regarding the great significance of this, as the sūtras state that the Buddha remained in the intermediate state for twenty years teaching and transforming sentient beings, based on this precedent, [the possibility of such encounters] is established within the intermediate state.

In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as well, one may attain the turning of the mind (*citta-parāvṛtti*). If it were interpreted according to the former view—that the intermediate state is identical [to the state of being born]—then there would be no turning of the mind;

for although the Buddha, while in the intermediate state, teaches and transforms sentient beings, there could not be one who turns their mind while in that intermediate state, because the fetters of birth (*jāti-saṃyojana*) have attained ultimate non-analytical cessation (*atyanta-apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If, however, the latter interpretation is adopted, let one examine it at length; since there is no distinct scriptural authority (*yukti*), it is difficult to standardize [the position].

Regarding those who turn their minds [toward liberation] and receive either a *paricchinna* (segmented) or *pariṇāmin* (transformative) body, this is explained as in the section on the *pariṇāmin* body;

consult the second fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*. Furthermore, as for the general explanation within the section on the "Upstreamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*), if one were to allow that the fetters of birth arise again, then even a noble one (*ārya*) born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) would also have to give rise to lower rebirths;
however, this is not the case, because they lack the capacity for transformation (*nirmāṇa*), and since there is no transformation, [such a thing does not occur].

The notion that "the arising of form" is not the meaning of the Mahāyāna; furthermore, regarding the statement that "arising fetters" and "originating fetters" refer only to the time when birth is moistened by craving and grasping, this is explained as follows:
it may also be the case that the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) arises through the attraction of a single karma.

While the functional power of this karma may attract the intermediate existence, there is no [karma] that attracts the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) alone; rather, it is by means of the existence at birth...

Among these, there are two distinct explanations: one states that the "bond of birth" (*jāti-saṃyojana*) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), while the "bond of arising" (*samudaya-saṃyojana*) refers to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

Therefore, the lower treatise explains that when the afflictions are already severed, it refers to the bond of birth; when the latent dispositions are not yet severed, it refers to the bond of arising. Alternatively, one may interpret this according to the meaning of "moistening through craving" as explained previously.
Or, since the moistening by karma is likewise consistent, there is no contradiction; one may follow whichever interpretation one prefers.
Regarding these three types of persons, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Taishō Vol. 25, No. 1509), Fascicle 26, there are three similes:

like a small spark of fire that vanishes as soon as it is raised; this illustrates the first type of person. Like a glowing iron ball or a heated spearhead from which sparks fly when struck by a hammer, yet they are extinguished before they fall;
this illustrates the second type. Like those same heated iron objects from which sparks fly and fall before they reach the ground... [the third type].
Upon reaching the ground, they immediately pass away; this is the third analogy. This same principle also exists within the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya* (Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra).
As the treatise states regarding the *Saptasatpuruṣagati-sūtra*: "The seven types of noble persons (*satpuruṣa*) are as follows:

namely, the five types of persons in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), consisting of three types of *antarāparinirvāyin* (those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state) and the four types such as those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisamskāraparinirvāyin*); these combined are called the seven kinds."

Regarding the two fetters (*saṃyojana*) among those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), they are as extensively explained before; however, their parinirvāṇa is with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and not without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*). This is the doctrine of the Hīnayāna.
Now, in the Mahāyāna, if one considers it from the perspective of the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect), it may be the same:

only when the body is extinguished and wisdom is exhausted does one attain parinirvāṇa without remainder. If speaking according to ultimate reality, at the moment of the Vajra-mind (*vajracitta*), one has already attained nirvana without remainder; all future [defilements]...
If it were so that karma does not induce results and seeds do not arise, then the characteristics [of this state] would be as previously explained;
such a person would merely give rise to the eight aspects of suffering and its origin and then enter parinirvāṇa.

If the characteristics were as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*—that this extinction has a remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and that "having a remainder" refers to being endowed with both types of nirvāṇa—that is not correct, because at the time of relinquishing life, there is no mastery. The meaning is that this follows...
The *Xiāngshuō* (Commentary on Characteristics) and the doctrines of the Hīnayāna—even those such as the *Zaxin* (Abhidharmahṛdaya)—are all likewise contrary to this text.

As this treatise does not mention the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), whereas the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 27, states that after one has been born into that realm, if one were to be born only in the form realm according to this text, there would be no "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth" (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*) in the formless realm;
thus, what the *Mahāvibhāṣā* refers to as "that realm" is in fact the form realm.

If one reflects upon the realms according to their underlying principles: suppose there is a person whose body resides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who, without having previously severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the fourth dhyāna and below, passes away and is reborn in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*);
having been reborn in the sphere of infinite space, they then enter *nirvāṇa*. Who is this? The answer is:

this is the "one who delights in meditative concentration" (*abhinirvṛtti-dhyāna-ūrdhvasrotas*). Question: Since they do not undergo rebirth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth, should they not be included [among those who pass away in the intermediate state]?

If those of the Hīnayāna who are non-returners (anāgāmin) in the formless realm are classified under the "Upstreamer who delights in concentration" (samādhi-rata ūrdhva-srotas), then consider one who, having severed the fetters of the second dhyāna and below, is reborn in the third dhyāna and so forth, and there attains parinirvāṇa:

would this not be included among those "Upstreamers who delight in wisdom" (prajñā-rata ūrdhva-srotas)? Why, then, is it established that both types of "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" (upapadya-parinirvāyin) do not pass through the stage of the second dhyāna? Answer: If this principle is applied [to your case], [it would follow that they are indeed included]. However, since the Upstreamers who delight in concentration proceed upward from the first dhyāna to the fourth, and those who delight in wisdom proceed upward from the second dhyāna to the fourth, the distinction between the two categories is maintained based on their respective points of departure.

Thus, even if one were to argue that the former is included in the latter category, the formal classification remains distinct because the Upstreamer who delights in concentration does not bypass the second dhyāna stage when ascending. Therefore, the two types of "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" are established as not passing through the second dhyāna stage. Hence, the answer is: if this meaning is joined with the argument, [the classification holds].

Because there is "attainment of birth" (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*), the *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*) speaks generally of those who are born into that realm; however, this treatise [the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*] refers exclusively to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Whichever principle one adopts, it should be understood that the discussion of those of definite or indefinite nature regarding the turning of the mind and the reception of fragmented existence (*prādeśika-bhava*) is the same as for the three types of persons mentioned below, which will be explained collectively in the section on the "Upstreamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
Regarding the parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) in the Mahāyāna, there are two types: the one without application (*anabhisamskāra*) and the one with application (*sābhisamskāra*).

The former is superior because it attains parinirvāṇa without performing preparatory effort (*prayoga*); the latter is inferior because parinirvāṇa is attained only through the performance of effortful practice.

These correspond to the aforementioned "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth" (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) in the form realm; having just been born, they attain parinirvāṇa immediately. Once born there, they attain parinirvāṇa without initiating any preparatory effort.

The term "attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion" (*anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin*) refers to one who, having been born in that place, attains parinirvāṇa by initiating effort; this is called "attaining parinirvāṇa with exertion" (*sābhisamskāra-parinirvāyin*).
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* follows the majority view rather than the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, as its interpretation agrees with this treatise.

According to the Sarvāstivādins, "with exertion" is considered superior because it takes the three truths as its object, whereas "without exertion" takes only two truths as its object and thus involves outflowing (*sāsrava*) activity. Attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion is likewise [defined in this way].

The two [types of parinirvāṇa] take the unconditioned as their object, specifically cessation (*nirodha*), while the four [types] take the untainted (*anāsrava*) [truths] of cessation and the path (*mārga*) as their objects.

One attains *nirvāṇa* through the difficult conditions of the tainted (*sāsrava*), whereas one attains *parinirvāṇa* through the easy conditions of the untainted; thus, the "with-effort" (*sa-abhisamskāra*) is superior and the "without-effort" (*an-abhisamskāra*) is inferior.

However, this is not the case in the Mahāyāna, as the principle has been explained previously. It is difficult for these two types of persons to exist within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), just as it was definitively stated regarding those who attain *parinirvāṇa* upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*).
The determination of their nature is as follows: those in the Great Vehicle who attain parinirvāṇa through practice take the principles of the Four Noble Truths as their object;

since there is no scriptural passage prohibiting this, at the time they sever the afflictions, they attain parinirvāṇa with remainder and without remainder by taking the principles of the Four Noble Truths as their object, just like those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*).

Regarding the "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas), there are two types: first, those who delight in meditative concentration (samādhi), and second, those who delight in wisdom (prajñā). Is there a distinction between those born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and those in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)? This can be understood from the treatise.
Both of these types of persons include those who leap entirely (sakalābhisamkrama), those who leap halfway (ardhapluta), and those who vanish in every stage (sarvasthānacyuta).

For instance, among those who delight in wisdom, there are three kinds of persons; one is the "entirely leaping" type, which refers to one who, at the end of their life in the First Dhyāna, is reborn in the Akaniṣṭha heaven of the Form Realm.
"Ultimately skipping two and a half" refers to being born in the first, second, or third *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) and only then being born in the *Akaniṣṭha* (Ultimate Form) heaven.
"Dying in all places" refers to taking birth in each and every stage of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) before finally being born in the *Akaniṣṭha* heaven.
This treatise mentions only "within each stage" because it is based solely on the method of dying in all places; this is the cultivation [of the seeds].

The essential point of dhyāna is that one cultivates the initial dhyāna through perfuming within the desire realm; only after having given birth to the initial dhyāna does one begin to cultivate and perfume the higher dhyānas.

Because the lower realms are first perfumed and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) serves as the basis for subsequent perfuming, one must pass through the four dhyānas and below before the form realm is fully established.

Regarding those who perfume the dhyānas or leap over them (*vyutkrāntaka*), once they have given birth to the initial dhyāna, they subsequently transcend the desires of the lower three dhyānas to attain the fourth dhyāna.

Only when the cultivation is fully perfected—such as in the case of one who completely transcends [the lower realms] after passing away from the first dhyāna—is he born in the fourth dhyāna because he has cultivated the karma for the fourth dhyāna;
this is called "complete transcendence" (*skandhaka-samāpatti*). If the cultivation is not perfected or if there is regression, he is born in the second or third dhyānas;

subsequently, through further cultivation, it is called "partial transcendence" (*ardhapluta*). Or, if at the time of prior cultivation he only attained the cultivation of the second dhyāna and passed away from there...
They are born in those places in this manner, gradually being born in all locations; this is called "passing away from all locations.
Such persons merely avoid the Brahma-heavens. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that these are places of deviant views, and for this reason the Noble Ones are not born there.

This is consistent with the *Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, which says they undergo one birth. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, this refers exclusively to the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) when speaking of "leaping over" (*pluta*).

This can be understood by applying the same logic; there is no need for extensive citation. Some who attempt to equate the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* with the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explain the *Hṛdaya*:
"Why is it said that one is born in the first dhyāna? Because from the third dhyāna downward, both ordinary beings and noble ones can cultivate the dhyānas.

Fearing that they might not know of this cultivation (*vāsanā*), it is stated that even at the lowest level, one is 'born in the first dhyāna'. Regarding this treatise, it is explained: "As for the term 'ground' (*bhūmi*..."

Regarding the "stages" (*bhūmi*), some claim they refer to the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*); however, this interpretation is problematic because it contradicts the specific tenets of our own school. Nevertheless, as long as the general principle remains consistent with the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya*, there is no logical fault.
For those who delight in wisdom (*prajñā*), this is so; for those who delight in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it should be understood accordingly.

According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, those who delight in concentration consider only the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) in this context. Thus, such a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) attains the fruit of non-returning after having undergone rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

This refers to those categorized as "undetermined" who, having attained the fruit within an ordinary body of the desire realm, attain parinirvāṇa without undergoing further rebirth; this is the meaning of "attaining parinirvāṇa in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*), as explained previously.

Although one has not yet discarded the body of the desire realm when attaining the fruit in an ordinary body, if one resolutely practices for the state of "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyin*), that person belongs to the category of *antarāparinirvāyin*.

The same principle applies to the three types of persons who attain parinirvāṇa after being born (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*). If one resolutely practices for the state of "one who flows upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*), they then belong to that category.

How is it known that this is included within the "Upstreamer" (Urdhvasrotas)? In the first of the four propositions in the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, it says: "One who is to advance, not one who does not advance.

This refers to one who dwells in the body of the Desire Realm or the Brahma Heaven; because such a person, while dwelling in the Desire Realm, has not yet flowed upward, they are subsumed under the category of the Upstreamer.

By this principle, it should be understood that the same applies to others. Regarding the first two fruits (*phala*), one should know accordingly that this person of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*)—in terms of... [text ends] ...is [so designated].

The distinctions regarding faculties (*indriya*), stages (*bhūmi*), lineages (*gotra*), dispositions (*dhātu*), and detachment (*vairāgya*) are immeasurable; as stated in a verse from the *Miśraka-hṛdaya-śāstra*:

"Faculties, stages, lineages, and dispositions—these are extensively established. Among these, those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*) have dull faculties and natures compared to the previously mentioned non-returners (*anāgāmin*);
because they cannot attain parinirvāṇa early on, even if they possess sharp faculties among those who go upstream and do not regress, they do not necessarily cultivate the dhyānas."

Because those with dull faculties might fear falling back, they cultivate *vāsanā-dhyāna* (perfuming meditation). For example, consider a person who has attained the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) while still in a lower realm;

having severed the desires of the lower realm but not yet abandoned the desires of the upper realms, they suppress their afflictions and attain the fourth *dhyāna*, thereby initiating the karma of *vāsanā-dhyāna*.

When such a person dies, where will they be reborn? Such objections and difficulties are explained in the second fascicle, in the section explaining the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
In the section on the "Five Grades of Perfuming Meditation" (*pañca-vidha-vāsanā-dhyāna*), it asks: what is the meaning of "progression"?

It means that the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) perfumes the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) so as to cause it to increase and become superior, just as one adorns a *caitya* with flowers; here, *caitya* refers to a *jina-stūpa*.

According to the twelfth volume of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, regarding which heaven this perfuming occurs, based on the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, within the concentration of the "decisive factor" (*nirvedhabhāgīya-samādhi*), the outflow-free mind arises in immediate succession, producing stages such as "superior progression" (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*).

Furthermore, because it is the most excellent among the four dhyānas, if it is perfumed by afflictions, it refers to the path of retrogression; if it is perfumed [by the path], it refers to the path of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Regarding pure dhyāna, there are two types of perfuming: the dhyāna that serves as the basis and the fourth dhyāna which serves as the basis, while the lower three dhyānas serve as the perfumers.
These lower three dhyānas perfume that fourth dhyāna because it is the most excellent; thus, although the lower three dhyānas exist...
Because perfuming (*vāsanā*) is not superior, one must attain the fourth dhyāna before the [beings of] the three lower dhyānas can be perfumed to produce karma for the Śuddhāvāsa heavens;
otherwise, it would not be the case that the third dhyāna is perfumed based on the fourth. If that were so, it would simply constitute the perfuming of karma for the lower dhyānas.

If, however, the most excellent [perfuming] relies upon the fourth dhyāna to perfume the three lower dhyānas, only then is it called "superior perfuming. Although the sequence of the method of perfuming is as previously stated...
When attaining the three lower dhyānas up to the time of perfuming, one must first perfume the fourth dhyāna before being able to perfume the lower ones;
this is because one first perfumes the outflow-free (anāsrava) states of that level with the outflow-free states of that same level, and subsequently the lower levels do likewise.
Since it is the most excellent among all dhyānas, one perfumes the fourth dhyāna first when wishing to be born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; this is how one performs this perfuming. If...
For one who follows the gradual path (*ānupūrvika*), there is first the cultivation of the lower stages, followed by the cultivation of the four stages.

Regarding the cultivation of the dhyāna methods through the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the immediate path (*ānantarya-mārga*), and so forth—whether they be contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—all involve the paths of preparation, the immediate, and the liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

These all take the Four Noble Truths as their object and perform the sixteen aspects of contemplation (*ṣoḍaśākāra*). Initially, for many moments, both the contaminated and uncontaminated [states] are present; subsequently, for two moments, only the contaminated [state] remains.

Regarding the number of categories for the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) states, up until the moment of accomplishment: there is one moment of non-outflow and one moment of outflow.

As for the relative quantity of these categories, the method of perfuming the dhyāna results in five categories of fruits and nine categories of afflictions (*kleśa*). How do the karmas of these nine categories produce their fruits?
The three lower categories of karma each have the nature to induce the production of the fruit of a single heaven; as for the three upper categories of karma... [the text continues].

Because their essential nature is increasingly intense, each produces its own distinct fruit; when combined with the five aforementioned types of karma, and further joined with the untainted (anāsrava), there are fifteen minds in total.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states, "There are forty-five minds"; the logic for combining the latter with the former can be understood through reflection.

Question: For instance, within the seven births and nine afflictions (*kleśa*), there are the upper-upper, upper-middle, and upper-lower grades. Why is it that the three middle grades now coincide with the three lower grades of affliction?

Answer: Regarding the meaning of the five fruits (*phala*) of the seven births and nine afflictions: because they produce many births and many afflictions, the five fruits are cultivated through meditation (*dhyāna*).

Since the afflictions are numerous, they produce small births; how could the categories of affliction be identical to the nine? This is the first difficulty raised by the questioner. Question: [Regarding] the five fruits and the seven births...

Question: Although the fruits are not equal, how is it that the nine afflictions (*kleśa*) produce unequal results? Answer: Because the seven births are superior and the three types of karma are sharp, they produce many fruits.
Regarding the five fruits among these karmas, how is it that they are similar to the lower [births] yet produce different results? Answer:

While the fruits of the seven births are produced by karma of equal ripening (*vipāka*), the fruits of the five heavens are produced by karma of unequal ripening; thus, from the lower to the upper, the fruits gradually increase.

Because it is superior, those seven births do not gradually increase in excellence. The deluded followers of the Lesser Vehicle grasp at this as if it were a breeze against a cicada’s wing, suddenly claiming it is like a vast expanse of earth;
they bristle with indignation like a fierce bird and question the realized masters of the Mahāyāna, saying:

"As previously stated, the subtle and profound principles of the Great and Small Vehicles are harmoniously integrated, yet they are difficult for the ordinary and the ignorant to fathom. Even so, since the white colt has already galloped eastward..."
As the years have passed since these teachings were first propagated, many have engaged in speculative interpretation, resulting in various deviations and stagnations.

This is because, although I have applied myself to profound reflection, my understanding remains merely tentative and uncertain regarding the nature of those with indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) whose faculties have matured and who turn their minds [toward liberation], as well as the difficult-to-penetrate subtleties of the distinction between *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence) and *parinirmita-vipariṇāma* (transformed existence). I beg you to set forth what has not yet been heard so as to dispel my ignorance.

For instance, it is known that for those who undergo at most seven more rebirths (*saptakṛtvah-parama*), there is no further birth beyond the seventh; yet, when such individuals turn their minds toward enlightenment, [the process is far more complex].

How can it be that one who has received a great [result] has not yet attained the transformation-body (*pariṇāmi-kāya*) retribution at the limit of the outflows (*anāsrava*), which contradicts the principle of the *prādeśika* (segmented) body being exhausted after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and seven births?
Furthermore, how can one receive the retributions of *kulaṅkula*, *ekavīcika*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, and *anāgāmin*?

If the principle were as you say, the meaning would be equivalent to the obstacles mentioned previously. Moreover, regarding those who attain *antarā-parinirvāṇa* (nirvana in the intermediate state), their fetters of birth have already been exhausted; what is the meaning of the statement that "only these fetters of arising remain"?

If those who have turned their minds toward the wondrous enlightenment already dwell among humans and devas, then in *parinirvāṇa* they would lack the faculties for maturation; furthermore, there would be no "upward-streaming" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) in the formless realms, as they would lack a body and the marks of arising.
If such beings in the Mahāyāna have matured faculties, why would they turn their minds [toward the Lesser Vehicle] in the absence of a Buddha? For now, I shall briefly set forth these points;

the remaining doubts will be resolved through the determination of meaning. In the past at Vaiśālī, I maintained silence to clarify the reason for my attainment of realization, yet I did not detail it then.

The disposition of a benevolent person is as settled as your words; do not look beyond what is before you, Mahākāla. A sword can strike down a thousand men, yet whether the matter is right or wrong, why need one concern oneself with its magnitude?
Having roughly perceived what lies before you, your doubts should be resolved. Now, I say that it is indeed so; I hope you will reflect further and examine the principle of this thoroughly.
Thereupon, the Great Vehicle’s compassion universally extends, pitying those who are deaf and blind, and he consoled them with composure.

I say this: do not, because you have once observed the glow of fireflies, now be startled by the light of the sun; it is truly like mistaking a mere trickle within a stream for the waves of the vast ocean.
I have heard that a crossbow of a thousand *jin* does not release its trigger for a field mouse, and a bell of ten thousand *shi* will not vibrate with sound for a blade of grass.
Since I have followed the staff of a deluded spirit to uphold the Buddha-sun, I am indeed... [the text here appears to be truncated].

Out of compassion for your ignorance, I shall explain this to you; listen attentively, listen attentively, and do not harbor other thoughts. Regarding the dharma of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), there are two aspects:
first, that it will never arise again; second, that it may arise once more.

Although those born beyond the seven births all attain non-analytical cessation, through the power of their vows and the influence of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state, they further manifest bodies as a result of their cultivation of *bodhi* throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas.
If one intends for this physical body to experience birth and death for a long duration until the attainment of Bodhi, what fault is there in that?

Since the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) can arise again, what fault is there if one who has attained parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) changes their mind and undergoes further rebirth?
Therefore, it is said in the Sūtras that the Tathāgata remained in the intermediate state for as long as twenty years while teaching and transforming various beings.

The author uses this principle as proof and further explains that those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*)—just like those who attain it upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), those who attain it with effort (*sābhisamskāraparinirvāyin*), and those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*)—are all of a fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*).
This is because they do not undergo transformation (*nirmāṇa*); since their faculties have not yet matured, the Buddha does not transform himself to guide them.

If such beings existed whose faculties had matured, the Buddha would surely have said that he should go to transform them; since the Buddha has never gone to transform them, it is clear that such persons do not exist. If they did not exist... [text ends]

Regarding certainty, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) abide in the fundamental existence (mūlabhava); as for those who previously resided in the lower realms and have already turned their minds [toward liberation], by what principle or teaching would there be any contradiction in their place of birth?

The objection states: "Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) among the formless realm beings (*ārūpyadhātu*), this principle may be accepted. However, as for those subject to seven more births (*saptakṛtvabhava-parama*), if they have already completed seven births, it can be explained in this way.
But if they have not yet completed seven births—having already undergone only one or two births—and then turn their minds [toward liberation], how is this to be reconciled?

The response says: "Regarding the turning of the mind toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), there are both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). The case of those beyond training will be explained later; for now, let us explain those in training. It is said: 'Or, according to... "

The power of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that induce rebirth, having induced that birth, suppresses the various afflictions in one's final existence and gives rise to the power of meditative vows (*samādhi-praṇidhāna-bala*) to support the causes for future bodies, according to the principle previously explained, until the attainment of Buddhahood.

Alternatively, once the mind has been turned [toward enlightenment], one immediately suppresses the afflictions and gives rise to the power of meditative vows to support the causes for the present body, according to the principle previously explained, until the attainment of Buddhahood. An objection is raised: [How can this be?]

Why is it said that after the birth has been experienced, one turns the mind [toward awakening], speaking of nourishing the causes for future bodies, and that by turning the mind and subduing the afflictions, one speaks of nourishing the causes for the present body?

The meaning is this: since all afflictions have already been subdued, they cannot further produce results; therefore, "after the birth has been experienced" refers to nourishing the causes for future bodies.
Once the turning of the mind and the subduing of delusions are completed, one speaks of nourishing the causes for the present body. Both of these two types [of causes] are permanently subdued.
Therefore, it is asked: "Is this a *paricchinna-vedanīya* (segmented) retribution or a *pariṇāma-vipāka* (transformational) retribution? It is answered:

"All functions that are assisted by untainted meditative concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*) and vows (*praṇidhāna*) are inconceivable and are subsumed under the transformational body (*nirmāṇakāya*). If, however, it is a matured body (*vipākakāya*) produced by the power of afflictions (*kleśa*), it is a segmented body."

Regarding this summary based on reality, it is difficult to maintain that *śrāvakas* are not transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). To this, the objection is raised: "To which realm (*dhātu*) is this body of transformation bound?

The answer is: "It follows one's desire; when the mind is turned toward the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it belongs to that very realm. The question is asked: "By whom can this body of transformation be seen? The answer is:
"Since even devas cannot see it, how much less so humans? It can only be observed by the noble ones (*ārya*). The question is asked: "What is its experience..."
Regarding the question of whether this transformation involves abandoning the coarse, fragmented existence (prādeśika-maraṇa), the answer is: it does not abandon it;
rather, it transforms this very body into something pure, subtle, and difficult to discern, which constitutes the death-rebirth of transformation (pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa).

Question: If he did not relinquish [his body], for what reason did Śāriputra turn his mind [toward the Mahāyāna] and, at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, transform his body into fire and ashes?
Answer: It was because he wished to encourage sentient beings to resolve upon Bodhicitta, and so that they would know Śāriputra had entered Parinirvāṇa.
For this purpose, he manifested a separate transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) which transformed the fire to incinerate his original, substantial body, thereby causing it to become purified.
The measure [of his wisdom] is vast and its capacity follows whatever is desired, being unfixed yet omnipresent; it is encountered among the Buddhas and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Then the one known as Zhongxuan, who was not actually foolish, assumed a solemn expression and said with a sense of shame: "I am no fool. Previously, I saw this resolve my doubts, yet they were not fully settled;
I request you to clarify them once more. If all these śrāvakas have emerged from birth and death, for what reason do they not take up final nirvāṇa?"

Is the Dharma taught for the purpose of leading one toward Great Bodhi? Regarding the meaning of undergoing the suffering and affliction of birth and death throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* during the stage of transformation and change:
it is said that by extinguishing the physical body and ceasing cognition, one achieves Buddhahood through the limited view of self-benefit;

yet, because one also saves sentient beings through the benefit of others, providing universal relief, one is exhorted to turn the mind [toward Mahāyāna]. Within this state of transformation and change, there is neither suffering nor fault.
Question: Since the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) exists, how can it be said that there is no fault? Answer:

Although one undergoes this suffering, it enables the attainment of the merits of the three bodies (*trikāya*), which bring about infinite great joy and great bliss; therefore, there is no fault. Objection: All great bliss does not exceed *nirvāṇa*.
Since they have already realized it, what more is lacking that they would further seek *bodhi*? Answer: Although *nirvāṇa*—though... [text fragment]... [is indeed the goal].
There is the bliss of quiescent extinction (*śānti*), which is without the pleasure of sensation; the bliss of the threefold awakening (*trividha-bodhi*), which severs the pleasure of sensation;

and so forth, including immeasurable virtues. The Buddha possesses five kinds of bliss: first, the bliss of *nirvāṇa*, which takes the category of sensation as its single bliss, namely the enjoyment of the pure land and the bliss of the Dharma;
second, the bliss of the threefold awakening, which takes as its single bliss the joy of the union of the illuminating wisdom with the principle (*tattva*). This severs the pleasure of sensation.

Question: Since the bliss of the extinction-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) involves the cessation of sensation and perception, why employ the conditioned bliss of the suffering of formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) when one has already attained the unconditioned bliss of *nirvāṇa*?
Answer: The unconditioned, untainted states such as the three types of enlightenment (*trividhā bodhi*) are untainted;
therefore, like *nirvāṇa*, they are not subsumed under the suffering of formations. Furthermore, if one attains Buddhahood, one is able to transform immeasurable beings.
Because those of a transformative nature (nirmāṇa-sattva) are born from within saṃsāra, a question is asked:

"Since uncontaminated conditioned phenomena (anāsrava-saṃskṛta) are, by virtue of being uncontaminated, identical to that nirvāṇa and are not the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkha), why is it that because uncontaminated conditioned phenomena possess arising and ceasing—and because they possess arising and ceasing—they are certainly the suffering of conditioned existence, just like the truths of suffering and its origin?
Why, then, is the example of the uncontaminated used to claim they are not the suffering of conditioned existence, unlike nirvāṇa? Furthermore...
Question: Since those who have attained Buddhahood possess the power to transform sentient beings, why is it necessary for them to further undergo transformation? Answer:

Although conditioned *anāsrava* (untainted) phenomena involve arising and ceasing, they conform to the Principle (*tattva*) and oppose birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Therefore, they are not the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). This is because the two truths of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-satya* and *samudaya-satya*) accord with the suffering of birth-and-death and oppose the True Principle;
thus, they constitute the suffering of conditioned existence. I [maintain] that the essence of that birth-and-death is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Just as with *nirvāṇa*, how could one equate [the Buddha] with suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) based merely on arising and ceasing?

Furthermore, because from beginningless time there exists a natural principle (*dharmatā*) whereby those who can be transformed and those who transform them are either related or unrelated, those who are related are exhorted to achieve Buddhahood to transform them, whereas those who are unrelated do not turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], and thus they are not taught or transformed;
this refers to those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) who have already attained birth [in their respective stages].
Feeling both sorrow and joy, he sighed deeply and said: "For a long time I have drifted in the ocean of ignorance, unaware of the source of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Although I have heard the teachings, how can they compare to this? It is like a banquet of a hundred delicacies where one suddenly swallows a single sublime flavor.

One might say that hearing of the Ultimate Way first is already marvelous; yet who would have thought it would unfold so profoundly, circling back to reveal ever more subtle wonders? Though I have refined my essence..."
Since antiquity, it has been difficult to hear of such a principle; indeed, it is said that former sages have not beheld it and past philosophers have not heard of it.

The eminent scholar raised his hand to stroke [the other’s] head and comforted him, saying: "Are the men of this world so stubborn and foolish as to be beyond ridicule? To see the good and follow it is truly extraordinary.
To recognize the pivotal moment and master the principle is what has been admired throughout both ancient and modern times; yet you perceive the principle and do not follow it."
"You have brought this calamity upon yourself. Since you have already entered the ocean of the Buddha's teachings, you ought to recognize the mountain of the uncut jade;

to seek out the extraordinary by probing the depths, one values the pearl while simultaneously benefiting others. Have you not heard that those of the Lesser Vehicle, such as the 'evil spiritual friends,' should quickly turn their minds and make great, expansive vows?
Upon awakening, the enlightened one knelt long and prostrated at his feet before withdrawing, saying: 'Is this not due to the fortunate resonance of past karmic conditions?'"
When the Venerable Akṣayamati received this great empowerment, he said, "I have not heard [of such a thing]; it would be most fortunate, most fortunate indeed.

Regarding the meaning of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*) and others, the intended sense lies in the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). If one turns the mind toward awakening (*cittavivarta*), there may be cases like those who turn the mind after seven births;

having already suppressed the afflictions (*kleśa*), they manifest the causes for their present body and thus attain parinirvāṇa in the present life. However, if one does not suppress the afflictions as previously explained, there would be an obstacle. If that were so—
As in the case of one who has already turned their mind after seven births, they nourish a future body; because of this future body, they receive the fruit for that [future] body.
If the fruit were received by this present body, how could karma of a future body cause the fruit to be experienced in the present body?

If it were to experience the fruit of a future body, one would have to abandon this body to take up the retribution of the future life. To prevent such an objection, the explanation says: "Having abandoned this body, one receives the next."

There is no impediment to the body itself becoming untainted (*anāsrava*). This text also includes those of indefinite lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) and the three types of those who go upstream (*ūrdhva-srotas*) among the higher births;

these should be understood accordingly. Regarding the above, according to the second fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, as stated in the fifty-seventh fascicle of the *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*) concerning the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*):

"If one who is a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) refines their faculties, they also attain the refinement of the faculties. Furthermore, it says: "One also attains [the fruit of] once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*)."

Because it is difficult to obtain the antidote for one who has come [to this life] but has not yet realized the state of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and because the meaning of what is to be attained is extremely vast;

furthermore, if one first uses worldly paths to suppress [defilements] up to the fourth dhyāna and enters clear observation (*abhisamaya*) to attain the state of a Non-returner, it is difficult to progress when subsequently cultivating the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
Thus, one does not realize the state of an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*) for the reasons previously stated. However, once the faculties have been transformed, one realizes everything. If...
From the perspective of the meaning of "stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*), why must one not fall back?

Regarding the explanation of the six types of Arhats from the "one liable to fall back" (*parihāṇadharman*) downwards: among these six, the first five were formerly practitioners who followed by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), while the last was a practitioner who followed the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
If, within these six types, one has attained all dharmas and can no longer progress further, they enter parinirvāṇa immediately.

The statement in this passage—"not refining the faculties" up to "necessarily regressing"—refers to those who are fixed [in their nature]. This is based on the certainty that among these six types, each possesses its own distinct lineage (*gotra*).

If one were to regress from the initial *parihāṇadharman* (one liable to fall away) and transform into an *akopyadharman* (one immovable), this would not mean that the six types are fixed as distinct natures from the outset;
for it is possible for one of the first five types to transform into the *dharmānusārin* (follower by dharma) through the stage of *śraddhānusārin* (follower by faith). Thus, the first five...

Since they do not attain dwelling in happiness in the present life, these are persons liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*). Those who subsequently possess the adornment of concentration regarding the final existence are those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).

Regarding their transformation and so forth, it is as previously stated. According to the two explanations in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, among these six types of persons, one explanation holds that the first four belong only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because they are necessarily subject to falling back and cannot refine their faculties (*indriya*) to abide in the state of "dharma-abiding" or "immovability."

These keen-facultied [beings] who possess the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) exist throughout the three realms; however, those who regress do so by relying on the conditions for regression. Since the higher realms lack such conditions for regression, there are two views regarding this:
why must one who regresses necessarily regress immediately? This is because it is discussed in terms of spiritual lineage (gotra).

Regarding that regression, it is said to be due to lineage; thus, those with the six supernormal powers exist in all three realms. Furthermore, among these six supernormal powers, those of the fixed or unfixed nature who are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) certainly do not [possess them].

Regarding those of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*), because they lack virtuous friends and have not yet generated the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), they do not possess the necessary verbal expression.

However, if those of indeterminate nature belonging to the two lower realms rely upon the supreme untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) at the limit of the fourth dhyāna, they repeatedly employ the power of their vows and meditative stability to nourish the causes that previously induced their present existence.
This causes the continuity of the resulting effects to manifest over a long period, gradually increasing in excellence until the attainment of Buddhahood.

Although it is said that this retribution is fully exhausted through the influence of contaminated causes, because it is supported by uncontaminated meditative concentration and vows, it is called the "inconceivable transformation-death" (*nirmāṇa-cyuti*).
Since these uncontaminated meditative concentration and vows are inconceivable, as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:

"With ignorance as the condition and uncontaminated karma as the cause," this refers to the fact that it is supported by the superior power of the uncontaminated; therefore, it is described as being without [contamination].
Because the outflows (*āsrava*) serve as causes and possess great power, if ignorance (*avidyā*) were absent, the outflows would be unable to provide support.

Thus, it is only by relying on the power of the outflows that they can support karma; and while karma is the direct cause of ignorance, it actually depends on the support of others. Therefore, it is described as a "condition" (*pratyaya*).

A detailed explanation is as stated in another chapter: "Ignorance" refers to the attachment to the existence of a real Buddha held by those in the Small Vehicle who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The questioner, who was able to seek [the truth] and capable of being delivered, asked: "This ignorance (*avidyā*) is the non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) that functions in the present;
for what reason does it serve as a condition to cause karma to continue? The answer is: Because ignorance acts as an auxiliary condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) for karma.

When it is supported by the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), it is able to increase the life-span formations (*jīvitasaṃskāra*). This ignorance is like an auxiliary condition, similar to that of the Arhat in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), [the Buddha] knew that he was about to enter *nirvāṇa* and relinquished his robe and bowl to the community of monks (*saṃgha*).

Because this was an action involving outflows (*sāsrava-karma*), he subsequently used the ultimate concentration free from outflows (*anāsrava-prāntakoṭika-samādhi*) to support these roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*), causing this present body to remain for a long time.
This meaning is somewhat similar. Furthermore, "ignorance" (*avidyā*) refers to the karmic actions of this previous body; as stated in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, Chapter 16.
It is said that *parivṛttāśaya* śrāvakas attain the fruit of Buddhahood by relying on the *nirmāṇakāya*, not the *sambhogakāya*.

Regarding the three points of inquiry, the *Nirdeśapatala* states that the *nirmāṇakāya* is so named because it is supported by untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), rather than being a literal transformation body.

Although its physical form remains, it is like a magical emanation; this is explained in detail in other chapters. Other meanings are as above, and for further detail, see the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle [number].
The three fascicles explain this.
Regarding the passage on the four types of śrāvakas turning their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] and so forth, it is as recorded in the separate notes.

In the discussion of the "nature of regression" (*parihāṇadharman*), it is said that those who "seek to harm themselves" refer to cases such as the bhikṣu Kokālika harming himself; however, the "regression" mentioned here is not like the retrogression found in the Hīnayāna.

Regarding the attainment of the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*), as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Abhidharma), Volume 26: herein, only the retrogression from the concentration of the out-flowing (*sāsrava-samādhi*) is termed "retrogression" (*parihāṇi*); it is not the loss of the fruit itself that is termed "retrogression.

This is explained in detail below in the section on "Attaining the Fruit and Abandoning the Path" (*phala-prāpti-mārga-tyāga*), where one may understand it through the mind that protects the Dharma (*dharma-rakṣā-citta*).
Regarding those who train their faculties while abiding in the immovable state, this is because they have already attained sharp faculties;
thus, the intention here is that such a person cannot further train their faculties, as once the faculties have been trained, they are already established as sharp.

Since the sixth person—the one in the immovable state—is already of sharp faculties, it is not said that they can train their faculties; rather, this serves to preclude the possibility of them training their faculties further once they have already become so.

Regarding the clarification of the "cultivation of faculties" (*indriya-saṃcāra*): "cultivation" refers to refining the lower [faculties] to achieve the higher. Another interpretation states that the intent here is to clarify that those with dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*) must first refine them to become those with superior faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*).

Since there are those with dull faculties who are unable to refine their faculties to achieve the higher, sharp level, this "immovable dharma" (*akopyadharman*) is not said to be capable of refining its faculties;
for it is already a sharp faculty, and thus [the text] does not mention it. This should be read in full because it is not explicitly stated.

Regarding the statement that there are two types of "attainment of security" (*kṣema-lābha*), it means that this [attainment] does not refer to one who can refine their faculties (*indriya-saṃvaraṇa*) nor to one who possesses sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).

Therefore, although this "immovable one" (*akopyadharman*) is of dull faculties, they are unable to refine their faculties. The term "one of immovable nature" (*akopyadharman*) refers precisely to this state of abiding in immovability;

because the expression is abbreviated, it is called "one of immovable nature. This is not the same as the sixth type of person, the "one of immovable nature" (*akopyadharman-pudgala*). According to this treatise, only the former is mentioned.

Regarding the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 57, among the twenty-two faculties: "All those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—namely, the five types:

the one subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), the one who reflects (*cetana-dharman*), the one who guards (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), the one who abides (*sthitākampya*), and the one capable of penetration (*prativedhanādharman*)—are able to refine their faculties.

This is not the case for Pratyekabuddhas, nor for Bodhisattvas, because they possess naturally sharp faculties. However, since those of the 'unshakable' (*akopyadharman*) type in this present treatise also possess sharp faculties, they do not refine their faculties."
This treatise summarizes the major divisions; therefore, it does not specify which of these is "immovable. Why is this?

Because this treatise speaks of only one type of *aśaikṣa* who sharpens their faculties—namely, the "one capable of penetration" (*prativedhanā-dharman*) among the five types mentioned in the Great Treatise.

Furthermore, the meaning is that in this treatise, only the "capable of penetration" type proceeds through successive stages to achieve the method for sharpening the faculties, whereas the other four—those who are "fixed," "subject to falling back," "reflective," and so forth—do not further sharpen their faculties.
Regarding the faculties (*indriya*), that treatise establishes them based on actual fact, knowing that the first five types of persons are all able to refine their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).

The sixth type has already been explained. Furthermore, as for the statement here that neither Pratyekabuddhas nor Bodhisattvas are able to refine their faculties, this is consistent with what is discussed later in the fourteenth fascicle of this treatise itself, where it is stated that Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas are similar in this regard.

The *Mahā-śāstra* (Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 26, states: "These six types of persons are combined into two categories: first, those liberated by time (*samaya-vimukta*), which includes those who may regress from dhyāna, as explained extensively therein;
second, those of immovable nature (*akopya-dharman*), which refers to the sixth type of person.

According to this principle, although among the first five types there are those who are dull-witted yet do not regress, it is not the case that all of them are 'liberated by time,' for the meaning of being 'dull' implies liberation by time."
