The first five [types] may be so described; that is to say, "by the perfection of three" refers to the subtle discrimination [of one who has attained the fruit]; "by the perfection of one faculty" refers to the person of immovable dharma;

"by the perfection of two concentrations" should be understood as previously explained; and thirdly, "all those beyond training by the perfection of the fruit," as explained at length in the *Mahāśāstra*, fascicle 57.
The *Śāstra* states: "Wandering and scattering are described as the mental application (*manasikāra*) that encompasses [the mind]; the meaning is explained according to the text.

Regarding the two types of skillful means (*upāya*) in the *Saṃprayukta-hṛdaya*—namely, the constant and the sudden—the two types of regressive reflection (*pratyāgamana-cintā*) both lack these two skillful means.

The *parihāṇadharman* (one liable to fall away) is similar, but the *cetanādharman* (one capable of volition) differs in that it possesses the capacity for volitional aspiration (*cetanā-praṇidhāna*). Both [types] together hold a blade to take their own lives; those who protect the Dharma possess the constant [skillful means]."
Having thus remained unmoving, the person possesses the sudden (*tun*) means; since there is no further liberation to be attained, it is not known whether they possess the constant (*chang*) means.

Because the former person possessed [the sudden means] and this [latter person] likewise possesses [it], we infer by analogy that the one capable of transcending (*kandaren*) also possesses both the constant and the sudden means.

This differs from the previously mentioned Dharmapāla’s distinction regarding the refinement and non-refinement of the faculties (*indriya*). The sixth type, the single lineage (*ekagotra*), is those of sharp faculties who possess both means.
This is explained in detail in the sixty-fourth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states that there are thirteen types of *pudgalas* who possess this [quality] but lack that.

Regarding these Bodhisattvas: those who have attained the meditative absoritions (*dhyāna*) associated with the abandonment of birth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) do not take birth in the formless realm once they have entered the stage of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Specifically, among the Bodhisattvas of the desire and form realms, those who have attained the meditative absoritions associated with the cessation of birth in the formless realm do not take birth in the formless realm after having entered the path of truth.
Because they lack the practice of benefiting others, [ordinary beings] abandon birth in the formless realm; however,
because this bodhisattva is endowed with superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he abandons the formless realm and, being endowed with the bliss of superior dhyāna,
dwells in these dhyānas and is born in the desire or form realms, thereby remaining free from birth in the formless realm.

Regarding the term "supreme majesty" (*parama-tejas*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts all state that "supreme" refers to Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward who possess the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
According to this interpretation, Bodhisattvas during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa do not take birth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as there is no unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*) there.
From the first stage onward, Bodhisattvas equally realize the ultimate truth and are born in the pure lands of the Buddhas, where they abide in supreme majesty.

Because virtue, by means of possessing the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*), transcends the first *kalpa*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 78, states that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, each stage possesses majestic power (*anubhāva*).

This explains the meaning within the section on the "Eight Purities" (*aṣṭaviśuddhi*). According to the present principle, a Bodhisattva in the first *kalpa* who cultivates the practices for enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*) is likewise able to benefit others;
such a person must constantly listen to the Dharma while abiding in stages such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), which are bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Nor are they born in the formless realms (*ārūpya*). This treatise explains that they attain mastery [over meditative concentrations];

just as a bodhisattva who has cultivated and attained the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) during the first eon may still be born in the formless realms because they have not yet attained mastery, whereas from the first bhūmi onward, they have attained mastery and thus are said not to be born there.

According to the intended meaning, one should know that they are also not born there because they lack the benefit of others; this is stated with reference to the superior status [of those on the bhūmis].

Therefore, they are not born there; rather, they abide in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). This refers to the Bodhisattva’s skillful mastery of rebirth, whereby they are born in the desire or form realms according to their vow.
Because they are not bound by karma or afflictions (*kleśa*), it is like poison that has been neutralized by a mantra and can no longer cause harm.
In this sense, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, they are called those of supreme majesty and power, which is certainly not the case for those below.
Because they benefit sentient beings in various places throughout the two lower realms in their successive stages of existence (*pariccheda*).
How can it be said that from the eighth stage onward one abandons the "insect body" (*kīṭakāya*) and attains the "transformation body" (*nirmāṇakāya*)?

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, from the first stage onward, why should it not likewise be the same transformation body? This is because, though not bound by karma, they have attained a superior mind.

To summarize this meaning, it is said that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, because Bodhisattvas have attained mastery, they may either undergo transformation-rebirth (*pariṇāmikī-jāti*) or undergo ordinary birth-and-death (*prākarṣika-jāti*).
If, while listening to the Dharma in a pure land or performing deeds for the benefit of others, they must cause devas and humans to see them, how could they not manifest an ordinary body?
It is said that this occurs at the eighth stage, because with a transformation-body, they would not be seen by devas and humans.

Based on the state of one who has departed, which is characterized by effortlessness (*anābhoga*) and the continuity of the untainted (*anāsrava*), and according to the literal discourse on reality, a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) attains the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) upon its relinquishment and immediately attains the appropriated body of segmented existence (*prādeśika-kāya*).

This is like the case of those who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] described in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, whose present bodies serve as the provisions for future bodies; once such persons who have turned their minds attain the first stage, they obtain it in this manner.

Because they have attained mastery over birth in successive segments and because they take birth according to their vows, there is no contradiction in the fact that those who have not yet reached the stage of direct progression (*anupūrvika*) or turned their minds (*parāvṛtta-citta*), and who have not yet attained the fourth dhyāna, may still possess the meditative concentration acquired through cultivation even while not having severed [defilements]. Furthermore, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of this Bodhisattva is bound to the place of rebirth;
it is not like the body of the transformation-rebirth (*nirmāṇakāya*), which exists as a separate, distinct segment of the body born in that realm of form.

Regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) within the realms: if it is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it follows from the perception of bodily characteristics; if it is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is as described in the sixth fascicle concerning the birth of Bodhisattvas.

It is not through the moisture of unwholesome craving that they take birth, but solely by the power of their vows (*praṇidhāna*). Thus, they may take birth in any location within the lower two realms, including the three evil destinies (*durgati*).

This is because these births are the fruit of wholesome karma, and they intentionally take birth there through the power of their wholesome karmic vows, just as with [the birth of] hungry ghosts and animals.
Because their fruit is also an unwholesome retribution, these Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world when no Buddha is present;
once they have appeared, they immediately come forth as soon as a Buddha appears in the world. They come to be taught by the Tathāgata; this refers to those of indeterminate lineage.
As for those of determinate lineage, whether they see a Buddha or do not see one, they both attain parinirvāṇa, as explained extensively above.
The inconceivable Tathāgata encompasses all bodhisattva practices and all tathāgata practices; this teaching of the eight phases is not transmitted falsely in various treatises.

As for the interrogation, it is recorded separately: because the Tathāgata is purely untainted, has transcended the three realms, and is inconceivable, he is not the same as the bodhisattvas and others.
Regarding the two types of sudden extinction (*sadyonirvāṇa*), the preceding section has provided a detailed explanation of the seven kinds of persons (*pudgala*).

Hereafter, the second part reveals their two fruits; this contains two sections: first, the presentation and enumeration, and second, the detailed explanation. The detailed explanation is divided into two parts. Within the second [section on] sudden extinction, there are three divisions:

first, revealing the characteristics of sudden practice; second, citing scriptural evidence; and third, explaining the characteristics of indeterminate practice. Regarding the first [of these], the root treatise states:

Later, the Master [Paramārtha] relies solely on the stage of *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) and so forth, as cited in the initial question and subsequent answer within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-yan-lüeyao* (Essential Summary of the Compendium of Consciousness-Only).
This section has two parts: first, citing the *Sūtra on the Modes of Activity*; second, citing the *Sūtra on the Two Fruits Moistening the Modes of Activity*.

Within the former, there is first the citation and then the explanation. Regarding the terms "one part," "one mass," "one accumulation," and "one collection": these refer to the addition of the four aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

Having sequentially assigned the practices as described above, one correctly gives rise to the four practices. Based on such contemplation, the following explains this treatise. Third, regarding the explanation of the indeterminate [lineage]:
this encompasses both those of determinate lineage and those of indeterminate lineage. Those of determinate lineage attain arhatship at the moment of death;

those who do not so attain it are of indeterminate lineage, which transforms into that of a pratyekabuddha. It is absolutely impossible for one of determinate lineage to undergo rebirth before making progress.

This refers only to those of indeterminate lineage who attain arhatship and further refine their faculties to achieve *vaimuktya* (emancipation from the multitude); this meaning should be reflected upon.

What is the difference between an arhat attaining *vaimuktya* and others? If one of indeterminate lineage does not necessarily attain arhatship but instead transforms to attain *vaimuktya*, there is no distinct characteristic [between them].
Alternatively, these two fruits are taken here as referring only to those of indeterminate lineage with sharp faculties.
Therefore, it is said that they do not transform [into a different stage] through discernment. Why is it unnecessary for them to undergo further births to correctly become Arhats?
Because they have already cultivated superior training across lifetimes and refined their faculties (*indriya*), they attain Parinirvāṇa swiftly upon being born in the Desire Realm.

Furthermore, because their mind of revulsion toward existence is so powerful, they do not seek anything else; such persons of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*) will certainly be reborn in the higher realms.
Because the realms do not exist, because the faculties are sharp, and because one does not again give rise to afflictions through investigation but rather practices cultivation.

In the second major section, the explanation of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), the main text is divided into three parts: first, explaining clear realization; second, explaining the dharmas practiced during clear realization;

and third, a miscellaneous explanation of various meanings regarding the stages of clear realization. Within the first of these, there are two sections; the first explains the ten types of clear realization. First, [it explains] the ten...
The second section, "Observation," clarifies the distinctions; this is divided into two parts: first, the enumeration of headings, and second, the detailed explanation.

Regarding the former, the "clear observation" (*abhisamaya*) of the higher stages refers to faith in *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and so forth, which includes both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated faith.

Among the eleven types of clear observation, the sequence and terminology differ from those in the sixth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. Here, the retinues (*parivāra*) are augmented, whereas that [text] lacks them; here they are few, while there they are excluded.

The sixth and seventh [perfections] are collectively termed the "distinctions of purification" (*viśuddhi-viśeṣa*). Because they are explained in the same context as the cultivation and purification of the Buddha-field, this [treatment] is brief.
Since the causes of purity are not yet sufficient within the causal stage, it is only in the resultant stage that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions are completely severed;

thus, there is a distinction in the result. That clarity and purity has two aspects: the purity of what is to be remedied (*pratipakṣya-viśuddhi*) and the purity of what is cultivated (*bhāvanā-viśuddhi*). Because these two entities are distinct, their retinues are not discussed here.
Since this refers to the specific excellence of birth— namely, being born into the family of the Tathāgata—
the distinction of birth mentioned here and the distinction of taking birth mentioned there do not contradict one another in meaning.
Chapter Thirteen: Attainment. First Question, Subsequent Answer. The answer is first brief and then extensive.
Although the *pudgala* (person) is not substantially existent, there are three sections below for the extensive explanation: first, the extensive explanation of the *pudgala* who can realize;

second, "Briefly, there are ten kinds of establishment of clear realization (*abhisamaya*)," which extensively explains what is realized through clear realization; third, Chapter Fourteen, "Explanation of All Aspects of the Sublime."

Furthermore, regarding the stage of various clear realizations (*abhisamaya*), when one realizes each subsequent superior grade of the path, there is a brief distinction between the two—the means of realization and that which is realized.
Within the extensive establishment of the means of realization, there are two parts: first, the basis for its establishment; second, the actual establishment.

Regarding the basis for its establishment, there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the enumeration; third, the explanation. Within the establishment itself, there is first the question and then the answer.
In the response there are three parts: first, the enumeration of seven categories; second, the detailed explanation following that enumeration, which has two sub-sections:

first, the enumeration, and second, the conclusion; third, the specific citation and explanation of each, which has two sub-sections: first, the specific citation and explanation of the seven categories, and second, the explanation of the distinction between gradual and sudden transcendence regarding the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), including the differentiation of those with "diseased" conduct.
Previously seven were indicated, but now they are reduced to four: first, greed; second, by analogy; third, the three divisions; and fourth, the slight.

Regarding the distinctions of the departure from defilements (*rajas-niḥsaraṇa-viśeṣa*), there are three [aspects] within the "support" (*ādhāra*). Of these, the preceding section indicated three, which are now divided into two: first, the liberation and the discernment (*viniścaya*) each have three;
second, from "In this way" (*evam*) onwards, there is a brief distinction of the first [part], which is further divided into two. Within the brief distinction of the middle part, there are two:
first, a combined brief distinction of the two stages; second, a separate explanation of the two stages. Within the combined explanation, there are four: first, the explanation of the two stages.

First, the characteristics of each of the three [categories] are explained in succession; next, the characteristics of the distinction between the two stages are explained; following that, the positions of the three grades of analytical discernment (*viveka*) are resolved;
and finally, the characteristics of retrogression and non-retrogression regarding the two stages are explained.

Within the twenty-seven distinctions of the noble fruits (*āryaphala*), they are divided into six: the first two are based on the distinction of preparatory application (*prayoga*); the next one is based on...

Regarding the distinctions of meditative concentration (*samādhi-viśeṣa*): first, there are eight based on the attainment of the eight concentrations; next, two based on the distinction of obstacles, as they differ in their severance of the obstacles to concentration;
next, eight based on the distinction of the path; next, eight based on the distinction of birth;

and finally, six based on the distinction of falling away versus non-falling away. This is stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 26. Although that [text] initially explains twenty-seven, it itself explains the latter six from below.

Within the [nine] stages (*bhūmi*), the distinction between those who practice according to faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who practice according to the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) is not mentioned as a difference in their preparatory application (*prayoga*).

This is because it is explained that these two individuals, upon reaching the fruit, are designated as "those resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) and so forth; thus, they may also be called a distinction in their preparatory application.

Furthermore, when that treatise explains the distinction between those subject to regression and those not subject to regression as being "liberated by time" (*samayavimukta*) and "not liberated by time" (*asamayavimukta*), what fault would there be in expanding this into six categories? However...
Regarding the six types of non-learners (*aśaikṣa*), each of these six persons is counted as one; this designation of "abiding" is made because they do not further refine their faculties (*indriya*).

In the *Pañcavastuka*, five types of persons are said to refine their faculties; even those who are immovable (*akopyadharman*) refine them, yet this refinement pertains to their own nature and not to another nature.

This is just like the sixth type, the immovable one, who does not refine [the faculties] with respect to his own fruit, but does refine them with respect to the Pratyekabuddha and Bodhisattva fruits. The Bodhisattva is also like this, for he does not refine them with respect to his own [fruit].
The fruit is precisely the refinement [of the faculties] as explained at the end of the fourteenth [chapter].

Regarding the "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) and "seven-times-at-most" (*saptakṛtvah-parama*) stages, there are two interpretations among the masters of old: first, that those with one remaining birth are the "family-to-family" practitioners;

second, that those with seven remaining births are the "seven-times-at-most" practitioners. Furthermore, regarding the superior-superior, superior-middle, and superior-inferior [faculties], there are respectively one, two, and three [births]; the superior-middle and superior-inferior involve the reduction of one [birth], while the middle-superior involves the reduction of two [births].

Furthermore, [the intermediate grades]—namely the intermediate-intermediate, the intermediate-middle, and the intermediate-inferior—collectively [constitute] "benefit," while the inferior-inferior grade collectively constitutes "harm" for one birth. Now, it may be that this is not the case for the Mahāyāna;
since all afflictions within the entire realm produce and moisten rebirth, they mutually support one another.

However, as the Path gradually ascends, the afflictions are gradually severed until exhausted, and rebirth naturally diminishes. This is not because there is a fixed determination of harm or benefit for each specific grade, but rather because when one [grade] is severed, [rebirth] follows accordingly.
Regarding the two types of *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) and the five types of *kulaṃkula*, there is no contradiction in principle.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* merely states that the distinctions between gods and humans as *kulaṃkula* differ from the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) explanation, which establishes them based on three conditions: first, by karma; second, by the path; and third, by the severing of fetters.
Since one achieves the antidotes for three or four categories [of afflictions], and because the remaining two births or three births correspond to these three conditions, there is no discrepancy.

Regarding the contemplation of the Tathāgata: since neither the Dharma-body nor the Reward-body can be discussed in terms of realms, their modes of activity are explained within the Transformation-body, such as the eight manifestations in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, as described in the commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

In the second major section, "The Extensive Manifestation of What is Realized through Clear Observation" (*abhisamaya*), there are three parts: first, a general explanation of clear observation; second, an explanation of the distinctions within clear observation;
and third, an explanation of how all virtues are subsumed under clear observation. Within the first part, there are two further sections: first, the enumeration of the ten [topics];

and second, the detailed explanation of the distinctions in clear observation. Regarding the latter, the sequence of the names differs slightly from that found in the sixth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

Unlike the virtues subsumed under the third realization (*abhisamaya*), there are three parts here: first, the question and answer; second, the detailed explanation of each preceding point by means of five gates;
and third, the clarification of the functions of these virtues. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the question, and second, the answer. Within the answer, there are two sections:
first, the response regarding their subsumption, and second, the enumeration of their names.
Within the explanation by way of five gates, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the five gates to reveal their characteristics; second, the detailed explanation of each.

Regarding the two types of immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), there is first a listing and then an explanation. The explanation of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) consists of two parts:

first, the individual explanations; second, the explanation of their sequence. Regarding the first liberation, there are three parts: first, the heading that points to it; second, the individual explanation; third, a brief distinction.
The *Śāstra* explains that there are five [form] liberations and four formless liberations because they possess the characteristics of liberation;

the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter twelve, elucidates all the liberations, spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*)—one should consult it extensively as therein described.
The following single page should have been at the beginning of this chapter; because the title and volume number were missing, it has been placed here after the preceding section.
Regarding the attainment of the fruit through prior cultivation, there is that which is achieved and that which is realized; thus it is called "Attainment.

While the preceding "Chapter on Accomplishment" encompassed both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), as well as previously cultivated and uncultivated, already entered and not yet entered, and all phenomena of the three natures, the present treatise clarifies only the uncontaminated.
Regarding the "Never Having Set Out Toward the Good," the Chapter on Dharmas has two parts:

first the question and then the answer. Within the answer, there are two sections: first, the indication of the persons and the dharmas; second, the extensive analysis. Within the first of these, there are two parts:
first, the main text of the treatise; second, the master’s commentary. In the master’s commentary, there are two divisions; first, the explanation... [text continues].

Second, the reason why the former is the "means of realization" (*sādhana*) and so forth, while the latter is the "person" (*pudgala*), is an explanation intended to resolve potential objections. [The objection is:

Since a phenomenon (*dharma*) is so called because it maintains its own essence, it can be something realized; however, if there is no permanent, unitary self (*ātman*), who is it that acts as the realizer?
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* explains that the phenomena to be studied are such that one who studies and is able to cultivate them in this way is called a bodhisattva prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
The dharmas to be studied, such as those in the *Dharmapada*, and these dharmas of clear realization (*abhisamaya*)—it is the person who studies in this manner who is able to practice them.
Regarding "the immeasurable dharmas of distinctions such as form," the dharmas signified (*lakṣya*) are immeasurable.

Regarding "the immeasurable conceptualizations of the characteristics of distinctions," the conceptualizations of names (*nāma-saṃjñā*) that signify [those dharmas] are immeasurable. An ancient commentator explained: "First, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is immeasurable."

Later, since the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the sense-base (*āyatana*) are immeasurable, this [explanation] does not conform to the text; how then can it be called "perception" (*saṃjñā*)?

Furthermore, there is an interpretation that the preceding [term] refers to the object-condition (*ālambana*), while perception is that which is capable of apprehending it, because its characteristic of delimitation (*pariccheda-lakṣaṇa*) is predominant.

Although such an interpretation exists, it is not as good as establishing a single number for the name and the entity, namely, the "person" (*pudgala*). Alternatively, the immeasurable distinctions of form and so forth are themselves the perception within immeasurable form.
Because they exist solely as mental conceptions and understandings, they are not at all substantially real.

The twenty-seven noble persons (ārya-pudgala) comprise six general categories; these are established as two based on differences in cause, faculty, and lineage, namely those who attain through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those who attain through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta);

one is established based on the difference of the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), namely the bodily witness (kāyasākṣin); and eight are established based on the differences of path and fruit.

The four candidates and four fruits are established as eight based on differences in birth: namely, the one who returns at most seven times (*saptakṛtparama*), the one who goes from family to family (*kulaṃkula*), the one with one interval (*ekavīcika*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), and the one who goes upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*). Six are established based on the distinction between those subject to regression and those not: namely, the regressive type (*parihāṇadharman*) and so forth.

These are further divided into five because each category includes its own sub-types. Two are established based on obstructions: namely, those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) and those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). Finally, there are those liberated from afflictions (*kleśavimukta*).
Because the two—the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the meditative hindrance (*samāpattyāvaraṇa*)—are distinct in their abandonment, there is a difference in their fruits.

Regarding the manifestation of skillful means within the differentiation of these fruits, such as the attainment of perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) and so forth, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Chapter 9) explains this among the eight phases (*aṣṭākāra*).
Although this [system] includes the dwelling in the celestial palace (*vimāna*), that [other system] lacks the examination and questioning.

As stated in the Sūtra, in the second major section below concerning the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) and so forth, it clarifies that all phenomena subsumed within clear realization (*abhisamaya*) are of two kinds.
First is the question, followed by the answer. Within the answer, there is first the summary of what is subsumed, followed by a detailed investigation to reveal the distinctions.

This detailed investigation is divided into two parts: first the inquiry, then the explanation. Within the explanation, there are three sections: first, the individual names; second, the commentary on the arising of each; and third, [the specific analysis]. Each of these is further subdivided.
Regarding the three sections following the explanation of the five gates: first, the detailed explanation of the five gates; second, the explanation of their elicitation (*āvedha*);

and third, the specific explanation of the functions of these twenty merits. Within the detailed explanation of the five gates, there are seventeen sections: one section explains the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*);

one section explains the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*); and one section explains [the marks and signs]. Regarding yoga... [text continues]
In the twelfth fascicle, it is said that all things are categorized into three types of sentient beings: first, those who possess neither suffering nor pleasure; second, those who possess suffering;

and third, those who possess pleasure. Because these [three] arise sequentially from the three [realms], because they give rise to the abandonment of desire, hatred, and so forth, because their objects of focus are vast, because the contemplation of benefit and happiness is supreme, and because their fruit is immeasurable—due to these three meanings, they are called "immeasurable" (apramāṇa).

The perfection of abiding in the measure (*pramāṇa*) is called "perfection" because it is pure and white; it is called "perfection of cultivation" because the meditative practice one has cultivated is fully complete.

Because one focuses day and night and focuses at all times, it is called "concentration" (*yoga*). Therefore, the following passage states: "The perfection of the aspect of beneficial and blissful conduct is called 'perfection of abiding'."
The thirty-fourth treatise takes the three dharmas of non-desire, non-hatred, and non-attachment as its essence, because they respectively take the three types of sentient beings as their objects.
The *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Mahāyāna), fascicle four, maintains that it consists only of non-attachment and non-hatred, because it excludes the two states of opposition and harm;

furthermore, it takes the three types of sentient beings as its objects respectively. Moreover, upon careful examination of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) [states]: [text follows].

This means that the first three have non-hatred (*adveṣa*) as their essence, while the last one has non-attachment (*alobha*) as its essence; they are distinguished by the varying degrees of depth in the three stages of bestowing happiness, removing suffering, and rejoicing in benefit.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "These are the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*). At the stage of Buddhahood, they are untainted (*anāsrava*);

at the stages of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), they are only tainted (*sāsrava*) prior to the [first] seven grounds. From the eighth ground upward, these are untainted. This concludes the section below.

14. Regarding the arising [of compassion], it is subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) obtained subsequently (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*), while its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is subsumed under non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, these four objects are: the object of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*), which takes as its object the provisional designation of the name "sentient being"; the object of phenomena (*dharmālambana*), which takes as its object the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);

and the objectless object (*anālambana*), which is ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) and nirvana. 15. Regarding the object of sentient beings, it refers to sentient beings in impoverished households; regarding the object of phenomena, it refers to... [the five aggregates].
Regarding the forty-fourth discourse on the stage of the Tathāgata and Bodhisattva, which gives rise to all requisites for life and is characterized by objectless conditions (*anālambana-pratyaya*):

first, because it shares with non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) the mark of self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*); second, because it shares with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) the mark of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*); and finally, because it does not share [these marks] with the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*).

According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, this refers to the Bodhisattva practicing the Mahāyāna object-condition (*dharmālambana*) during the stage of correct practice (*samyakpratipatti*) that arises from the initial generation of the mind (*prathamacittotpāda*), which takes sentient beings as its object (*sattvālambana*).
Taking the teachings as their object, these two [compassion and sympathetic joy] are largely with outflows (*sāsrava*);

because Bodhisattvas cultivate the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) which has no objective referent (*anālambana*), compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are likewise so. This is because it is stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and the thirty-fourth chapter of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* explains three aspects that universally encompass the four great excellences;
furthermore, the characteristics of what is to be remedied differ from those in the ancient *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and thus they are contradictory.

Regarding this, the *Śāstra* states that the benefit and happiness [taught] therein are the same as those in the forty-four *Upadeśa* treatises; it says they are the same in twelve ways and identical in all respects.

As for the objects of focus (*ālambana*) among these forty-four, they consist of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the individual phenomena (*dharma*), and the provisional person (*pudgala*). These are distinct phenomena.
There are those that do not have an object, namely the True Principle (*tattva*) and the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), which are not encountered in the same way as the eleven [other categories].

In all instances, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* does not state that fire is added to the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Within the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā*), the original treatise mentions only the three grades of patience (*kṣānti*).
This is because the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā-bhāga*) is divided [from the preceding], and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) lasts for only a single moment;

therefore, the thirty minds are not described as "patience," nor as the "stage of patience" within the aids to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*), nor as the suppression [of afflictions] among the five patiences prior to that.

Because it is subsumed under patience (*kṣānti*), and by extension, the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) below are categorized into three grades: "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) is the lower grade, "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) is the middle grade, and the "First Dharma" (*āgradharma*) is the upper grade.
This stage alone is superior; as for those who claim it is brief, this refers to their specific explanation.

According to the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and other treatises, it belongs only to the first stage (*bhūmi*), because one first attains the untainted (*anāsrava*) state there. The second stage is called the "Stage of Having Characteristics" (*sanimitta-bhūmi*).
In this context, it is stated that [the path] common to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) refers to those who, upon first attaining it, obtain only the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the two fruits, why is it that among the second and third fruits, one does not attain the fourth fruit by abandoning even the highest-grade afflictions up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), whereas the abandonment of afflictions through their antidotes is restricted to the first fruit? This distinction is clarified at times such as the final moment of life.

Regarding the "Noble Ones" (*ārya*): when one attains the first fruit up to the fourth fruit, one has not yet known how the *pratyekabuddha* abandons afflictions—whether it is by way of stages (*bhūmi*) or by way of categories (*prakāra*), as in the case of the nine stages and nine categories of an *arhat*. One should reflect upon this point of difficulty herein.

Regarding the first of the ten types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), some say its essence consists solely of the three types of mundane wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*), while the second, the "Section on Ascertainment" (*viniścaya-bhāga*), constitutes its essence.

My own interpretation is that there are two [types], and among the six [wisdoms], the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) constitutes the first. Here, the first two take the wisdom of reflection as their essence.

This [wisdom] has a beginning and an end: the former arises by taking the teachings (*dharma*) as its object, and the latter arises by taking the meaning (*artha*) as its object. It is named "Dharma" based on its objective referent.
The essence of the meaning is contemplation (*cintā-vipaśyanā*). Based on this contemplation, the discernment of the truths (*satya-pravicaya-kṣānti*) constitutes three types.

One interpretation holds that the first is the preliminary application (*prayoga*), while the latter three are the four roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) which follow the three wisdoms (*prajñā*). Among the eighteen categories of inclusion, these roots of goodness are termed "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*);

they take the subsequent [stages] as the true subsequent [realization], which differs from this [present case]. This [text] relies on the distinction between seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) for the true subsequent [realization], whereas the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other works rely on the distinction between the fundamental and the subsequent.

Wisdom (*jñāna*) is likewise not contradictory [to this], for they both rely on a single meaning; one should reflect upon and examine this. Alternatively, "dharma" refers to the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmābhisamaya*);

although it also takes principle (*tattva*) as its object, because "dharma" is predominant, one contemplates all phenomena based on dharma. "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) arising from the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*), as it takes meaning as its object.
Works such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* do not mention this [as a distinct category] because its function is narrow, and it directly gives rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, it is said that all merits are as explained in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (XIX.39), which establishes their meaning by setting aside [the discussion of] increase and decrease.

Regarding the essence of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) as being comprised of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), one should consider which of these six types of clear realization includes its own specific understanding, such as the faculty of joy (*prītīndriya*) and so forth.

This is the inquiry concerning the clear realization of this chapter. Furthermore, the explanation of the realms (*dhātu*) and so forth is given according to the basis (*āśraya*), as in the *Mahā-śāstra*.

In the seventy-third [fascicle], the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (Exposition of the Teachings), in seventeen fascicles, it is stated that within this [text], the true [subsequent realization] and the subsequent [realization] each take correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) and subsequently attained cognition (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as their essence.

This contradicts the *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośa*). Upon examining its "True Manifest Realization" (*bhūta-abhisamaya*), it states that one attains the cultivation of conventional cognition (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

In the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), the three truths [of suffering, origin, and cessation] are taken as the path-truth (*mārga-satya*), while the subsequent cognition (*anvaya-jñāna*) pertains to the path; however, in the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*), the four truths take the path-truth as the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*). Thus, there is a discrepancy.

For what reason is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) not cultivated at the conclusion of the untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) of the path of cultivation? Regarding the four immeasurables: loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is non-ill will;
compassion (*karuṇā*) is non-harming; sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is non-envy; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the absence of both greed and ill will.

As stated in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (the twentieth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācāśāstra*) and the fourth *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, there are three types of loving-kindness: that which has sentient beings as its object (*sattvālambana*), that which has phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana*), and that which is objectless (*anālambana*).

Regarding "sentient-object compassion" (*sattvālambanā karuṇā*): it arises by taking sentient beings as its object. Regarding "dharma-object compassion" (*dharmālambanā karuṇā*): it takes the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) as pure and arises by eliminating grasping.

Regarding "objectless compassion" (*anālambanā karuṇā*): this refers to the Buddha’s [compassion] which takes their *nirvāṇa* as its object. Because non-attachment is the essence of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and because it is explained from the perspective of the requisites within dharma-object [compassion], its objective sphere (*viṣaya*) is exclusively the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Its basis (*āśraya*) consists of the six stages; regarding the color realm (*rūpadhātu*), it concerns both near and distant enemies, etc. (as verified in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 7).

The thirteen [topics] such as the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) are subsumed within the five dharmas of the Great Treatises; their worldly knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*) takes wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence.

The same applies to the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*). Regarding the first three liberations, they are by nature the root of non-attachment (*alobha-kuśalamūla*);

the latter four are by nature the four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*); in the Mahāyāna, they are by nature the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) has exclusively the meditative absorption of cessation as its essence. All [of these] are...

Regarding the passage in the *Mahā-śāstra* (Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya), fascicle 73, which states that [this wisdom] is both mundane and supramundane, the Dharma Master’s commentary on the *Mahā-śāstra* explains that there are two views regarding its status as mundane or supramundane.
Furthermore, it is also mundane. If this were so, would not subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) be omitted?
This is logical, because within the context of "correct wisdom" (*samyag-jñāna*), the meaning of subsequently attained wisdom is subsumed; as stated in the *Mahā-śāstra*, fascicle 72.
The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* explains the twenty-two [bases] as follows: those that are untainted (*anāsrava*) but not ultimate are the deliverances (*vimokṣa*);

those that are ultimate but not untainted are the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*); those that are both are the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). Because they are untainted but not the fruit, they are not ultimate;
within the fruit, there is an essence that is not untainted, yet it is ultimate. That which is not untainted but is the fruit has an essence that is untainted and is both.

The statement that this is the same as the Sarvāstivāda school—wherein the initial phrase "based on liberation for the sake of cultivation, with liberation as the priority" and so forth—is explained according to the initial contemplation.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun) states that taking the "universal bases" (*kṛtsnāyatana*) as the cause refers to the explanation of those who have achieved realization;

that is, within this very context, liberation is the ultimate fruit. This is consistent with the sixty-second [chapter] of the *Mahā-śāstra*, which likewise takes liberation as the fruit, just as in that [text].

When summarizing and synthesizing [the teachings], it is understood that at the time of arising, one relies on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to sever hindrances. Regarding the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and so forth, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) maintains that they are accomplished based on all four dhyānas.
The Sarvāstivādins maintain that they exist only in the first two dhyānas. Now, the Master says: "Look at the following text; the Noble Ones mostly abide in these two.
This is the same as the Sarvāstivādins in maintaining they exist only in the first two dhyānas. I do not yet know what the ultimate difference is.
A questioner asks: Since this [attainment] is close to the Desire Realm, it takes the three dhyānas of the lower realms as its object;
because there is pleasure therein, it is called "conducive to liberation" (*anuloma-vimokṣa*). It does not speak of the third liberation, for only the fourth dhyāna is fully perfected.

As for the Sphere of Infinite Space and the others, they take the nine grades of liberation as their essence when one becomes free from the desires of the lower stages. According to the extensive treatises of the Hīnayāna, these are cultivated in the present.
Because there are three future [moments] for each of the six [liberations], it is known that only the ninth liberation-path (*vimukti-mārga*) constitutes the "emptiness" and other liberations.

Regarding the Master who expounds emptiness, since he states that one present [moment] and three future [moments] are cultivated within the same stage, it is known that all nine grades of liberation constitute the extensive treatise.
One should not take the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) as being included here, because it is a process of progression and does not accord with the liberation [itself].

Those who have emerged from the stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) also attain this pure concentration (śuddha-samādhi), which accords with the untainted (anāsrava); it is not like that of external ordinary beings or non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika).

Therefore, although they attain pure concentration, it does not accord with the untainted. Regarding "liberation" (vimukti)—which refers to the tranquility of liberation—the Dharma Master provides two interpretations: first, attaining the untainted;
second, because the higher tainted concentrations are superior to the lower, it is said to "surpass" (atikrānta) the realms of form and formlessness. It is "superior" (viśeṣa).
Regarding the latter four among the spheres of mastery (*kṛtsnāyatana*), why is it that external formlessness is not mentioned, while only internal formlessness is taught?
It is because they flow forth from the third liberation (*vimokṣa*). Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* includes the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) but does not include the "Great Fire" [sphere].
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other treatises include it because it is characterized by the absence of anything [to be perceived].

Because they exist in few places, lack universal objects, and do not include the three objects of sound, smell, and taste— since these are absent in the higher realms and thus not universal— they are not included;

this is as explained in the *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise), fascicle 69, regarding the inclusion of various knowledges within the three knowledges, the inclusion of the ten knowledges within the three gates of liberation, and so forth,
wherein all such merits are contained within the "Great Essential" (*madhyama-vaipulya*).

In the fourteenth fascicle of the *Śāstra-mūla*, it is stated that the previously mentioned immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), absence of contention (*araṇā*), knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),

and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are shared with the followers of the two vehicles (*dviyānika*). However, from the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*) downward, these are accomplished by the Buddha alone.

Regarding the nineteenth [of the] qualities, the fifth, "Non-contention" (*araṇā*), and "Knowledge resulting from aspiration" (*praṇidhijñāna*), their explanations are found respectively in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Chapter 4), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* (69), and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (27), along with their respective commentaries;
the "Unimpeded knowledge" (*pratisaṃvid*) is explained in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* (17), the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (4 and 45), and so forth;
and the "Ten Stages" (*daśabhūmi*) is most thoroughly explained in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, which may be cross-referenced with Chapter 9.
The *Ṣaḍdhātuvibhaṅgasūtra*, the *Mahāvyutpatti* (as cited in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Fifth Yoga-sthāna),
the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* (Fourth and Twentieth fascicles), the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* (Tenth fascicle), the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* (Fifth fascicle),
the "Dharmabhāṇaka-puṇya" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and the *Satyaka-irṣika-paripṛcchā*.
The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Exposition of the Characteristics of the Sūtras), Chapter 4, Yoga Section 49; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Chapter 57;
various locations in the *Pañcaśatikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; the *Sūtra-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the Sūtras); the *Vyākhyāyukti*, Chapter 4, Yoga Section 49;
the seventy-fourth [section] on the four purities; the *Daśabala-bodhisattva-piṭaka-sūtra*, Chapter 4; the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, Chapter 5; and the *Vyākhyāyukti*.
The fourth [section], twenty; the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, third, ninth, thirty-ninth, fifty-seventh, and sixty-ninth;
the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, fourth; the *Catuḥpratisaraṇa-sūtra*, fifth; the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, fourth; the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, forty-ninth, fifty-seventh, and sixty-ninth;

and the commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which cites the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* regarding the Bodhisattva’s four fearlessnesses, mindfulness foundations (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and non-protection (*arakṣa*). *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, fourth.

The forty-nine [qualities] of the non-forgetfulness of the Dharma, the permanent severance of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and the sublime wisdom in all its aspects are proclaimed in the *Śāsanodbhāvana-śāstra* (4.49), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (5.7), and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-upanibandhana* (6.9).

The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* (5) proclaims the forty-nine [qualities], the forty-nine [qualities], the sixty-nine [qualities], and the seventy-nine [qualities], as well as the ninety-one [qualities]. The *Aveṇika-dharma-sūtra* (6) [proclaims] the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
The *Xianyang lun* (47.9), the *Wushi lun* (57), and the *Liushijiu lun* (69) and others state that there are three ways of explaining the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*):

first, the enumeration; second, the individual explanation; and third, the analytical discussion. The analytical discussion has two parts: first, the explanation of the two benefits; second, the explanation of the four characteristics.

Regarding the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the citation; and third, the conclusion. Its essence consists of mindfulness, correct knowledge, and equanimity; among these, it is specifically mindfulness.

Regarding "non-protection" (*arakṣa*), there are also three [aspects]: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion. Non-protection refers to the non-forgetfulness of the three types of action (*trikarma*). Furthermore, it is the mindfulness that severs habitual tendencies;

it is the true ability to sever [afflictions], which is the function arising from right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Its essence consists of the three types of action, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), and non-delusion (*amoha*).

As stated in the fifty-seventh [section on] the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), there are four parts: first, the heading and the establishment [of the categories]; second, the explanation of the names; third, the distinctions; and fourth, the summary.

Following the explanation [of the previous section], the preceding heading of the initial text has three parts: first, the heading; second, the inquiry; and third, the clarification of the rejection and establishment [of the positions].
Regarding "the supreme wisdom of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*), fifty [verses] explain its capacity to know the three objects: the meaningful, the meaningless, and their combination.

As for "how is it brought forth," the third section provides a general explanation of its activities, which has two parts: first, the basis; and second, the activity itself. Within the first part (the basis), there is first the question and then the answer.
The answer is twofold: first, the analysis of the basis; second, from "Furthermore, such qualities" onwards, the analysis of the nature of the activity.
Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, clarifying the attainment of the person who is the basis; second, the conclusion.

Within this, from "This demonstrates" onwards, there are three parts: first, clarifying the common dharmas of the internal and external; second, clarifying the common dharmas of the Great and Small Vehicles; third, clarifying the induction.

Regarding the subsequent section on the causes, there are three parts: first, the heading indicating the three things to be revealed; second, the question concerning the means of elicitation (*ākṣepa-upāya*);
and third, the explanation of their characteristics. Within the explanation of their characteristics, there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the reference; and third, the analogy.

Within the analogy, there are three parts: first, the heading "Among these..."; second, the explanation "This is called a power (*bala*)"; and finally, the combined analysis of the ability to realize and that which is realized to explain the meaning of the term "power."
The third major section has five parts: first, obtaining the fruit and abandoning the aspiration; second, the distinction between the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles;
third, explaining the undeclared matters, as the questions raised above ought to be answered;
fourth, why the first three fruits are not the fourth fruit; and fifth, explaining the five kinds of skillful means that should be cultivated. The first of these [five] has two parts.

The initial argument—that one attains the fruit and abandons the path (*mārga*) because the path is of a different category from the non-path, whereas the path does not abandon the path because it is of its own category—thereby implying that a Bodhisattva attains a higher stage without abandoning the lower because it is not a "fruit"—is also incorrect.
The root treatise merely states that one attains the superior and abandons the inferior;

the commentator points out that this refers to cases such as attaining the fruit and abandoning the path, but it does not mean that all Bodhisattvas who attain a superior stage do not abandon the lower.

Since the preceding inferior stages are also not of one's own kind, the second [point] separately cites them. Furthermore, at the time of attaining the fruit, one realizes the abandonment of the accumulations (*saṃgraha-prahāṇa*);

as it is said regarding the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*) and the five upper fetters (*pañca ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), this refers to the ultimate locus of accumulation.

Regarding the five types of skillfulness (*pañca kauśalya*), the first lists the five, and subsequently explains them individually. Skillfulness in means (*upāya-kauśalya*) should be understood according to the twelve kinds of skillfulness in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Commentary: The tenth [section], the analysis of distraction (*vikṣepa-vikalpa*), has two parts: first, a general overview, and second, a detailed classification. Regarding the names arising within the inner way (*adhyātma-yāna*), there are those induced by correct reasoning (*yoniśo-nīta*).

Within the detailed classification, there are three parts: first, the enumeration of the ten types of analysis; second, the citation of sūtras to correlate [the categories]; and finally, the explanation of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*).

Within this, there are two parts: first, the presentation and enumeration; second, the detailed explanation. In the explanation of the third [topic], non-conceptualization free from discursive proliferation (*aprapañca*), there are two parts:

first, a general interpretation; second, the departure from five characteristics. Regarding the departure from the five characteristics, there are two parts: first, the presentation and explanation of the departure from the five characteristics;

second, the explanation of the characteristic of non-conceptualization free from discursive proliferation. The first section has three parts: first, the presentation and enumeration; second, the detailed explanation; third, the conclusion.

Regarding the four points within the subsequent explanation of the absence of conceptual proliferation and non-discrimination—namely, the first question, the second answer, the third objection, and the fourth resolution—the fifteenth chapter, "The Discussion on Benefiting Others," has two parts:
first, a brief question-and-answer session; second, an extensive detailed explanation. Within the determination of the meaning, there are two parts:

first, the heading; second, the explanation. In the explanation, there is first a listing and then a differentiation. As for the establishment of the cause, it refers to that which is obtainable through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That which is subsumed under the "correctly stated as unobtainable" refers to that which, within the context of a thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth,

does not contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)— this is called "obtainable"— and does not contradict inference (*anumāna*) and the like— this is called "unobtainable. The five kinds of functions of correct statement are as explained previously in the seventh fascicle.

The second [section], the explanation of the *Viniścaya*, has two parts: first, a general explanation of the *Viniścaya*; second, a specific explanation. The specific explanation has two parts: first, an explanation by means of six meanings;
second, an explanation by means of fourteen gates. Within these fourteen gates are: the origins and sources of various sūtras; the principles and reasons;
the meanings of the phrases and what they signify; the causes; the sequence and order; and the intended purports.
"Returning" means releasing difficulties and removing hindrances.
Regarding the *Sūtra on the Total Collection of the Twelve Leisures*, it clarifies that by obtaining the twelve leisures, one enters the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*).

The *Sūtra on the Total Collection of All Practices* translates this as entering the noble ranks through the absence of leisure; thus, I know, I see, and I declare the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), which is the foremost cessation.

The phrase "I am one who knows" refers to having attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); the phrase "I am one who sees" refers to having attained the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*).

By means of the parable of the axe handle, the third [view] is refuted: just as when a person grasps an axe handle, it gradually wears away by itself, so too the practice of cultivated wisdom, once undertaken, naturally eliminates its own timidity.
By means of the parable of the raft, the fourth [view] is refuted: just as a boat or raft must have provisions for its journey, so too [must there be the path].

If provisions are lacking, there is nothing with which to provide relief; therefore, one must travel by means of the boat of wisdom. Because the provisions must be supplied, if they are lacking, one will not reach the further shore.

Regarding the establishment of the distinctions, there are two parts: first, the heading, and second, the explanation. The explanation has two sections: first, based on the five aggregates, and second, based on...

Regarding what has been accomplished, there are two parts at the beginning: first, the section on form, and second, the section on the four aggregates. Regarding the methodological approach (*naya*), there are two parts: first, the heading, and second, the explanation.
Within the middle [section], there is first a listing and then a detailed analysis. "Thoroughly knowing as it truly is through these three turnings" refers to the three previously mentioned aspects:

gratification (*āsvāda*), disadvantage (*ādīnava*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*); or alternatively, it refers to the characteristics of thorough knowledge (*parijñā-lakṣaṇa*) explained in the subsequent section.

The three distinctions are: (1) the single flavor, (2) renunciation, and (3) thorough knowledge (*parijñā*). Since thorough knowledge is the third turning, it constitutes the relationship between the dependent and the basis.

"Characteristics" refers to the manifestation of the characteristics of reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth as the nature of the successive bases—that is, the preceding characteristic of reality serves as the basis for what follows.
Thorough knowledge is the basis for permanent abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and permanent abandonment is the basis for cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Realization relies on the basis of realization as its support for cultivation; that is, it relies on the sequence of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
That which possesses power is termed "powerful," and that which lacks power is termed "powerless."

The gate of inducing [insight] has three parts: first, the heading; second, the manifestation; and third, the conclusion. Within the manifestation, there are two sections: first, citing four phrases from the sūtra;

second, individually presenting those cited four phrases. Within the first section, there are three parts: first, the general heading; second, the manifestation of the four phrases; and third, the explanation of the four reasons.

Within the explanation of the four reasons, there are three further sequences: first, the removal of the four obstacles; second, the manifestation of the abandonment and the remedies; and [third, the application].

Following the section on "Departing from the Inferior," the accumulation of merit and wisdom (*puṇyajñāna-saṃbhāra*) is explained. Within this, the latter three [verses] are interpreted in two successive parts:

first, causing entry through the gates of the three vehicles; second, the distinction of conditions. This means that while the first [verse] concerns generating a mind of loving-kindness toward sentient beings without obstruction, the subsequent two concern the Bodhisattva assembly—namely, the practice of realization (*adhigama-pratipatti*) which encompasses benefiting others, and the practice of teaching (*deśanā-pratipatti*) which extensively opens the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*), giving rise to each [of these benefits] individually.
In all four [cases], there is first a thesis and subsequently an explanation; within the explanation, there is first a general statement and subsequently a specific analysis.

Regarding the specific analysis, that which serves as the basis comes first, and the specific distinctions come last; these are to be assigned in sequence. Within a single line, if one considers the eye, does it also apply to the ear-base?

There are four permutations, and this is likewise for the mind-base. This is not so; for how could there be four permutations between the body and the eye? How could there be consciousness in the eye?
It is not the case that the body is present here; it is logically sound to judge that it does not exist.

As for the principle of "as it should be explained," the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* on the fourth [chapter], etc., has three successive sections: first, question and answer; second, establishment and refutation; third, the categories of dharmas (*dharma-paryāya*).

Regarding the first of these, there is the initial heading followed by the explanation. Among the six points concerning the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), four are explained while the fifth is not.

3. The three accomplishments are as explained previously in the second [section] on "Attainment" (*prāpti*). 4. The four defilements (*saṃkleśa*) are as explained previously in the section on the Truths of Suffering and Origination (*duḥkha-samudaya-satya*).

Regarding consciousness and so forth: there are six types of consciousness; two types of sensation (*vedanā*); twenty faculties (*indriya*), as explained at the end of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 26);
seven types of attention (*manasikāra*); ten types of knowledge (*jñāna*), as explained previously in the third [section]; and nine types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).

The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Third Chapter) explains that there are nine types of knowledge regarding the abandonment of what is to be abandoned (*prahātavya*) and the full comprehension (*parijñā*). These nine consist of seven [types of] abandonment and two [types of] purification.

Regarding the nine purifications, as stated in the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*, if one follows the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, the two vehicles possess only eight purifications, excluding the ninth, because they rely solely on the causes;
thus, it speaks of seven purifications. The eighth [purification] pertains exclusively to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and therefore it is included within all [nine].

Regarding the dharmas, there are eight aspects as previously described. Regarding the penetration (*prativedha*) of the mental objects (*cittagocara*), there are five types: 1. Penetration of the characteristics (*nimitta*) of letters, which is the manifestation [of meaning];
this is the opening of the third [category]. 2. Penetration of the characteristics of the single letter and the two letters; this is the opening of the second [category]. 3.

Penetration of the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*), which is the opening of the first [category]. 4. Slow [penetration]. 5. Rapid [penetration]. Because these arise subsequent to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) based on the dharmas, they are called "penetration" (*prativedha*); they constitute the perfect realization (*pariniṣpatti*).
There are four fruits, etc., which follow specific meanings as explained elsewhere.

Because they are the twenty marks and secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) that bring about manifestation, the *Śāstra-vidhi* (Treatise on Methodology) consults the fifteenth volume of the Great Treatise (*Mahāśāstra*), where there are great differences, such as those in the *Hetuvidyā-ṭīkā* (Commentary on Logic), which clarifies the statement for the purpose of distinguishing it from "unobtainable causes" (*anupalabdhi-hetu*) such as those with obstructions;
thus, objects not present before one [are excluded]. This is found in the fifteenth [volume].

The three obstructions cover and obscure [the mind] as previously described; according to the *Tai Chao*, there are eight [types], though other treatises do not elaborate on them. Regarding "collected by those who possess much learning" (*bahuśruta*):

it is named after the person, the teaching, and the principle upon which it relies. Thus, since kings in the Western Regions (India) frequently provide offerings to those who possess much learning, this is used as a metaphor.
As for "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "collected by etcetera," it refers to the person, the teaching, and the principle. Therefore, [it is so called].
*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Ten (End).
This fifth commentary, from this point downward, contains passages that are disordered and some portions not written by the author of the *Ṭīkā*.
Recently, the novice monk Jitsujin of Kōkai-ji Temple in Nanto sent me a copy; this is the version from the second year of the Enshō era.
The copies transcribed and collated over the years were not entirely without slight discrepancies; I have now adjusted them as appropriate and engraved them upon the printing blocks.
May readers further examine and correct them.
